title: מבנה הסוגיות – Ketubot
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a virgin marries on Wednesday (the fourth day) and a widow on Thursday (the fifth day), because courts sit in towns on Mondays and Thursdays, so if the husband has a claim about virginity he can go to court early the next morning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a virgin marries on Wednesday and a widow on Thursday, because courts sit on Mondays and Thursdays, enabling a husband to bring a virginity claim the next morning.

items.text: First explanation of the Mishnah's reason
items.text_en: First explanation of the Mishnah's reason
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a tradition from Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the virgin marries on Wednesday because of the rule that when the wedding time arrives and they are not married, she eats from his food and eats terumah. If the time arrived on Sunday, he would have to provide sustenance immediately, but since he cannot marry her until Wednesday, the rule forces him to marry within the week. Rav Yosef questions this rationale because both the rule about sustenance and the rule about wedding day are explicit, so one cannot be explained by the other.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a tradition that the virgin marries on Wednesday because of the rule that when the wedding time arrives and they are not married, she eats from his food and eats תרומה (priestly portion).
Rav Yosef explains that if the time arrived on Sunday, he would have to provide sustenance immediately, but since he cannot marry until Wednesday, the rule forces him to marry within the week.
Rav Yosef objects that one cannot explain an explicit rule (the wedding day) by another explicit rule (the sustenance rule), since both are equally explicit.

items.text: Revised explanation and the reason of 'Shakdu'
items.text_en: Revised explanation and the reason of 'Shakdu'
items.desc_en: Shmuel is quoted with the correct version: the virgin marries on Wednesday so that if he had a claim of non-virginity he could go to court immediately. The Gemara asks why not marry on Sunday, and answers that the Sages decreed (שקדו) that he should be busy with the wedding feast for three days (Sunday, Monday, Tuesday) and marry on Wednesday, to delay the marriage and allow for a proper celebration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a revised version of Shmuel's statement: the virgin marries on Wednesday so that if the husband has a claim of non-virginity, he can go to court immediately the next day (Thursday).
The Gemara asks: why not marry on Sunday, so that if there is a claim of non-virginity, he could go to court on Monday (the next court day)?

The Gemara answers that the Sages decreed (שקדו) that the groom should be busy with the wedding feast for three days (Sunday, Monday, Tuesday) and marry on Wednesday, to delay the marriage and allow for a proper celebration.

items.text: Consequence of 'Shakdu' for the sustenance rule
items.text_en: Consequence of 'Shakdu' for the sustenance rule
items.desc_en: Now that the Mishnah's reason is 'Shakdu', the earlier rule about sustenance applies only when the wedding could have happened: if the set time arrived on Sunday, since he cannot marry due to 'Shakdu', he does not provide sustenance. Similarly, if he or she is sick or she becomes a niddah, he does not provide sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the reason 'Shakdu' that if the set time arrived on Sunday, the groom does not provide sustenance because he cannot marry due to the Sages' ordinance.
The Gemara extends the same logic to cases where the groom or bride is ill or she becomes a niddah, ruling that he does not provide sustenance.

items.text: Inquiry about illness: he is sick
items.text_en: Inquiry about illness: he is sick
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether if the husband falls ill, he must provide sustenance. Is the reason for exemption in 'Shakdu' because he is forced (anús) by the Sages' decree, so here too he is forced? Or is the exemption only for the Sages' decree, but not for natural illness?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if the husband fell ill, what is the ruling regarding his obligation to provide sustenance?
The Gemara suggests that perhaps the reason for exemption in the earlier case (Shakdu) is that he was forced (anús), and here too he is forced, so he should be exempt.
The Gemara offers an alternative: perhaps the exemption applies only when forced by the Sages' decree, but not when forced by natural illness, so he would be obligated to provide sustenance.

items.text: Inquiry about illness: she is sick
items.text_en: Inquiry about illness: she is sick
items.desc_en: Assuming the husband does provide when he is sick, the Gemara asks about when the wife is sick. Can he say 'I am ready', or can she say 'his field has been flooded' (i.e., he is responsible for damages)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a conditional inquiry: assuming that when the husband is sick he must provide sustenance, what is the law when the wife is sick — can the husband claim he is ready to marry, or can the wife argue that his field has been flooded (i.e., he bears responsibility)?

items.text: Inquiry about niddah and the beginning of the next case
items.text_en: Inquiry about niddah and the beginning of the next case
items.desc_en: Assuming she can say 'his field is flooded', the Gemara asks about when she becomes a niddah. If it is at her expected time, the question is not needed; the discussion continues.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the case where she becomes a niddah at her expected time, concluding that the question is unnecessary.

items.text: Gemara's question about אונס when not during her fixed period
items.text_en: Gemara's question about אונס when not during her fixed period
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman can claim 'his field was flooded' (i.e., an unavoidable circumstance) when she requests sustenance not during her fixed time, or whether it is considered like her fixed time because some women change their cycles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a woman who requests sustenance not during her fixed period can claim 'his field was flooded' (unavoidable circumstance), or whether it is considered like her fixed period because some women change their cycles.

items.text: Rav Achai's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Achai's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Achai cites a Mishnah that says women who reached the time for marriage but were not married eat from his property and eat terumah. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah says 'were not married' (not 'did not marry'), implying an unavoidable circumstance, and deduces that in such a case they still eat.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achai cites a Mishnah stating that women who reached marriage age but were not married eat from his property and eat תרומה (priestly portion).
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'were not married' (לֹא נִישְּׂאוּ) rather than 'did not marry' (לֹא נָשְׂאוּ), implying an unavoidable circumstance.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that any unavoidable circumstance does not allow her to eat, and the Mishnah refers to women who are delaying themselves. The Mishnah used the passive 'were not married' to match the active phrasing of the first clause.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that in all cases of אונס (unavoidable circumstance) she does not eat, and the baraita refers to women who themselves delayed; the mishna's wording is adjusted for stylistic consistency.

Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah should have used the active 'לֹא נָשְׂאוּ' (they did not marry), but it used the passive 'לֹא נִישְּׂאוּ' (they were not married) to match the active phrasing of the first clause.

items.text: Rava's ruling on גיטין
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on גיטין
items.desc_en: Rava states that regarding divorce (גיטין), the law is not the same; he holds that there is no concept of אונס in divorce.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that regarding bills of divorce (גיטין), the principle of אונס (unavoidable circumstance) does not apply.

items.text: Gemara's search for Rava's source
items.text_en: Gemara's search for Rava's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to find the source for Rava's position, considering various Mishnayot and a story about Samuel, but each potential proof is refuted. Ultimately, the Gemara concludes that Rava stated his own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rava derive his ruling that there is no coercion (אונס) in divorce?

The Gemara proposes that Rava's source is a Mishnah: if a husband says 'this is your get if I do not return within twelve months' and he dies within that time, it is not a get, implying that if he merely fell ill, it is a get.
The Gemara objects: perhaps even illness does not render the get valid, and the Mishnah only teaches that there is no get after death.
The Gemara objects further: the principle 'no get after death' is already taught in the first clause of the Mishnah, so the second clause must be teaching something else.

The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's second clause comes to exclude the opinion of 'our Rabbis' (the court of Shiro Mishcha), who follow Rabbi Yosi that the date of the document proves its validity.
The Gemara proposes a different source: from the latter clause of the Mishnah, where the husband says 'from now, if I do not return' and dies — it is a get, and the same applies to illness.
The Gemara objects: perhaps only death is specified because the husband does not want his wife to fall before a yavam (levir), but illness is not equivalent.

The Gemara proposes a story as source: a man said 'if I do not return within thirty days, let this be a get'; he came at the end of thirty days but the ferry broke; Samuel ruled he is not considered to have arrived.
The Gemara objects: a common coercion (אונס) is different, because since he should have made conditions and did not, he caused his own loss.
The Gemara concludes that Rava stated his own reasoning: because of modest women and because of immodest women.

items.text: Rava's own reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's own reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rava gave his own reasoning: because of modest women and because of brazen women. If one says the divorce is not valid due to אונס, modest women would be reluctant to remarry, and brazen women would falsely claim אונס.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rava stated his own reasoning: the principle 'no אונס in גיטין' is due to modest women (צנועות) and licentious women (פרוצות).

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about rabbinic annulment of kiddushin
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about rabbinic annulment of kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the rabbis can permit a married woman to remarry based on concerns for modest and promiscuous women, if the get is invalid by Torah law. It answers that since betrothal is contingent on rabbinic consent, the rabbis can retroactively annul the kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the rabbis can permit a married woman to remarry based on concerns for modest and promiscuous women, if the get is invalid by Torah law.
The Gemara answers that since betrothal is contingent on rabbinic consent, the rabbis can retroactively annul the kiddushin.

items.text: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.text_en: Ravina's question about betrothal through intercourse
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was through intercourse, how can the rabbis annul it? The answer is that the rabbis render his intercourse an act of licentiousness.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if the betrothal was through intercourse (ביאה), how can the rabbis annul it?
Rav Ashi answers that the rabbis render his intercourse an act of licentiousness (בעילת זנות), thus annulling the betrothal.

items.text: Rava's statement about coercion in gittin
items.text_en: Rava's statement about coercion in gittin
items.desc_en: Some say Rava stated that the same principle applies to gittin, indicating that Rava holds that coercion is a valid consideration in divorce.

sub.text: Some say (איכא דאמרי) in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Some say (איכא דאמרי) in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Some say that Rava stated the same principle applies to gittin, indicating that Rava holds that coercion (אונס) is a valid consideration in divorce.

items.text: Objection from a mishnah about conditional gittin
items.text_en: Objection from a mishnah about conditional gittin
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah: if a husband says 'This is your get if I do not return within twelve months' and he dies within that time, it is not a get. This implies that if he became ill, it is a get, contradicting Rava. The Gemara deflects by saying that illness also does not make it a get, and the mishnah teaches that there is no get after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah: if a husband says 'This is your get if I do not return within twelve months' and he dies within that time, it is not a get, implying that if he became ill, it is a get, contradicting Rava.
The Gemara deflects by saying that illness also does not make it a get, and the mishnah teaches that there is no get after death.
The Gemara objects that the point about no get after death was already taught in the first clause, and the answer suggests it is needed to exclude the opinion of our Rabbis.

items.text: Second objection from a different mishnah
items.text_en: Second objection from a different mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another mishnah where the husband says 'From now, if I do not return within twelve months' and he dies, it is a get. The Gemara suggests this implies the same for illness, but rejects it, saying death is specific because he does not want her to fall before a yavam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah where a husband says 'From now, if I do not return within twelve months' and he dies within that time — the get is valid, implying the same would apply to illness.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that death is specifically different because the husband does not want his wife to fall before a yavam (levirate brother-in-law).

items.text: Third objection from Shmuel's ruling about a river
items.text_en: Third objection from Shmuel's ruling about a river
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where a man said 'If I do not come within thirty days, let this be a get,' and he came at the end but was blocked by a river. Shmuel ruled that this is not considered coming. The Gemara distinguishes: a common coercion like a river is different, as he should have made provisions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where a man stipulated a conditional get and arrived at the end of thirty days but was blocked by a river, and Shmuel ruled that this is not considered 'coming'.
The Gemara distinguishes that a common coercion like a river is different, as the man should have made provisions and thus caused his own loss.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak's distinction about court days
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak's distinction about court days
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak explains that the mishnah's rule applies only after Ezra's ordinance when courts sit only on Mondays and Thursdays, but before that, when courts sat daily, a woman could remarry any day. The Gemara questions the relevance of 'before Ezra' and clarifies that if there are courts sitting daily nowadays, the same applies. It then notes the requirement of 'shakdu' (diligence) is still needed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak distinguishes that the mishnah's rule applies only after Ezra's ordinance when courts sit only on Mondays and Thursdays, but before that, when courts sat daily, a woman could remarry any day.
The Gemara questions the relevance of 'before Ezra,' asking why the past matters.
The Gemara clarifies that Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak meant that if courts sit daily nowadays, as before Ezra's ordinance, the woman may remarry any day.
The Gemara objects that even with daily courts, the requirement of 'shakdu' (diligence) is still needed, as it is burdensome for the husband.

items.text: Explanation of 'Shakdu' and the reason for Wednesday weddings
items.text_en: Explanation of 'Shakdu' and the reason for Wednesday weddings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the term 'Shakdu' by citing a baraita: the Sages decreed that a virgin marries on Wednesday so that if the husband has a claim of non-virginity, he can go to court early. They also instituted that one should prepare for the wedding feast for three days, starting from Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'Shakdu' means.

A baraita is cited explaining that a virgin marries on Wednesday so the husband can bring a claim of non-virginity to court early, and that the Sages decreed preparation for the wedding feast for three days starting from Shabbat.

items.text: The custom after the danger and the prohibition of Tuesday
items.text_en: The custom after the danger and the prohibition of Tuesday
items.desc_en: After a certain danger, people began marrying on Tuesday, and the Sages did not protest. However, one should not marry on Monday, unless due to coercion. Additionally, the groom is separated from the bride on Shabbat eve because he makes a wound.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that after a certain danger, people began marrying on Tuesday, the Sages did not protest, but one should not marry on Monday unless forced, and the groom is separated from the bride on Shabbat eve because he makes a wound.

items.text: Gemara's question about the nature of the danger
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the nature of the danger
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is this danger? If it means that people said a virgin who marries on Wednesday should be killed, then why did people only adopt the custom partially? They should have completely uprooted the practice!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the danger is, and rejects the possibility that it means a virgin marrying on Wednesday would be killed, because then the custom should have been completely abolished.

items.text: Rabbah's explanation: the danger of being violated by a governor
items.text_en: Rabbah's explanation: the danger of being violated by a governor
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the danger was that people said a virgin who marries on Wednesday should first be violated by a governor. This is not mere coercion but a danger, because modest women would give up their lives rather than submit, leading to danger.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the danger is not that the virgin would be killed, but that she would be violated by a governor first, and modest women would give up their lives rather than submit, leading to actual danger.

items.text: Why not teach that coercion is permitted, and why not uproot the decree
items.text_en: Why not teach that coercion is permitted, and why not uproot the decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not teach that coercion is permitted? Because there are also promiscuous women and priestesses. And why not uproot the decree entirely? Because the persecution might subside, and we do not uproot a rabbinic decree in the face of a temporary persecution. If so, why not marry on Tuesday? Because one does not risk his life for a doubt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not teach the women that coercion is permitted, so they would not risk their lives?
The Gemara answers: because there are promiscuous women who would exploit the permission, and also priestesses who are forbidden to engage in relations with a non-priest even under coercion.
The Gemara asks: why not uproot the entire decree of marrying on Wednesday, since the danger is the only reason for the practice?
The Gemara answers: because the persecution (שמדא) is temporary and may subside, and we do not uproot a rabbinic decree in the face of a temporary persecution.
The Gemara objects: if so, why not marry on Tuesday (the third day) as well, since the danger is only a doubt?
The Gemara resolves: one does not risk his life for a doubt, so the danger on Tuesday is not a concern.

items.text: Question about the distinction between danger and coercion
items.text_en: Question about the distinction between danger and coercion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's terminology: why is the case of the governor called 'danger' while the case of Tuesday is called 'coercion'? And why is one a custom and the other merely permitted?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's terminology: why is the case of the governor called 'danger' while the case of Tuesday is called 'coercion'? And why is one a custom and the other merely permitted?

items.text: Rava's explanation: the coercion of a general arriving in town
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: the coercion of a general arriving in town
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the coercion refers to a general arriving in town. If he passes through, one could delay the wedding, but if he settles, one cannot. However, why not marry on Tuesday? Because the general's supplies arrive on Tuesday.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the coercion refers to a general arriving in town; if he settles, one cannot delay the wedding, but the general's supplies arrive on Tuesday, preventing a Tuesday wedding.

items.text: Alternative explanation: coercion due to a death in the family
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: coercion due to a death in the family
items.desc_en: Alternatively, the coercion is as taught in a baraita: if the groom's bread is baked, his meat slaughtered, and his wine mixed, and then the groom's father or the bride's mother dies, they bring the deceased to a room and the couple to the wedding canopy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the coercion (אונס) mentioned in the baraita refers to a case where the groom's bread is baked, his meat slaughtered, and his wine mixed, and then the groom's father or the bride's mother dies, in which case they bring the deceased to a room and the couple to the wedding canopy.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Order of events when father dies on wedding day
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Order of events when father dies on wedding day
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if the groom's father or the bride's mother dies, the groom performs the mitzvah intercourse and then separates. He observes seven days of feasting followed by seven days of mourning, and during all those days he sleeps among the men and she among the women. Additionally, the bride is not prevented from wearing her adornments for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the halachic order when a parent dies on the wedding day: the groom performs the mitzvah intercourse, separates, observes seven days of feasting then seven days of mourning, sleeps apart, and the bride may wear adornments for thirty days.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: Only the parents of the couple
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: Only the parents of the couple
items.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that the mishnah's ruling applies only when the deceased is the groom's father or the bride's mother, as there is no one else to trouble themselves for them. If the situation is reversed (e.g., the groom's mother or bride's father dies), the ruling does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that the mishnah's ruling applies only when the deceased is the groom's father or the bride's mother, because there is no one else to trouble themselves for the couple; if the situation is reversed, it does not apply.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction and Rava's and Rav Pappa's qualifications
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction and Rava's and Rav Pappa's qualifications
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the mishnah's ruling applies only if water was placed on the meat (i.e., the wedding feast was prepared). Rava adds that in a city, even if water was placed on the meat, the meat is still sold (so the feast is not considered fully prepared). Rav Pappa counters that in a village, even if water was not placed, the meat is not sold. Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case is like the town of Machseya, which has both city and village characteristics.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the mishnah's ruling applies only if water was placed on the meat (i.e., the wedding feast was prepared); otherwise the meat is sold.
Rava adds that in a city, even if water was placed on the meat, the meat is still sold (so the feast is not considered fully prepared).
Rav Pappa counters that in a village, even if water was not placed, the meat is not sold (so the feast is considered prepared).
The Gemara asks: How can Rav Chisda's original distinction be found in practice, given Rava's and Rav Pappa's qualifications?
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case is like the town of Machseya, which has both city and village characteristics.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Chisda: if the groom's bread is baked, his meat slaughtered, and his wine mixed, and water was placed on the meat, and then the groom's father or bride's mother dies, the procedure is as the mishnah states. The baraita also adds that if the wife becomes a niddah, the same separation applies, and the couple may not engage in intercourse on Friday night or Saturday night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that supports Rav Chisda's position, describing the procedure when the groom's bread, meat, and wine are ready and the groom's father or bride's mother dies.
The baraita adds additional cases: if the wife becomes a נִדָּה (menstruant), the same separation rules apply; the couple may not engage in intercourse before Shabbat or after Shabbat.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle on private mourning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle on private mourning
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's ruling that the couple sleeps separately supports Rabbi Yochanan, who said that although public mourning is not observed during the festival, private mourning practices are observed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's ruling that the couple sleeps separately supports Rabbi Yochanan's position.
Rabbi Yochanan states that although public mourning is not observed during the festival, private mourning practices are observed.

items.text: Rav Yosef's distinction and the Gemara's objection
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's distinction and the Gemara's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rava in the name of Rava states that the separation applies only if the groom has not yet performed the mitzvah intercourse, but if he has, his wife may sleep with him. The Gemara objects from the baraita, which deals with a case where intercourse has occurred (since it mentions the mitzvah intercourse) yet still rules that they sleep separately. Rav Yosef explains that his statement refers to the case where the wife became a niddah. The Gemara then points out that the baraita says 'and similarly' (וְכֵן), indicating that the same rule applies to both cases, implying that even after intercourse, separation is required.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Rava in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Rava in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rava in Rava's name distinguishes that the separation (sleeping separately) is only before the groom has performed the mitzvah intercourse, but after he has performed it, his wife may sleep with him.
The Gemara objects by noting that the baraita (which Rav Yosef was addressing) deals with a case where intercourse has occurred, yet it still rules that they sleep separately.
Rav Yosef clarifies that his statement refers to the case where the wife became a niddah (menstruating woman) after the wedding, not to the initial case of mitzvah intercourse.

The Gemara objects further that the baraita uses the word 'וְכֵן' (and similarly), indicating that the same rule applies to both cases, implying that even after mitzvah intercourse, separation is required.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'and similarly' refers to a case where a wife becomes a niddah without intercourse, and the husband sleeps among men while she sleeps among women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'and similarly' refers to a case where a wife becomes a niddah without intercourse, and the husband sleeps among men while she sleeps among women.

items.text: Challenge from the leniency of niddah compared to mourning
items.text_en: Challenge from the leniency of niddah compared to mourning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether mourning is stricter than niddah, citing Rav Huna's statement that a niddah performs all household tasks except three, while a mourner's spouse is prohibited from cosmetics but still performs those tasks. This suggests mourning is stricter, contradicting the Mishnah's comparison.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah implies that mourning is stricter than niddah.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's statement that a niddah performs all household tasks except three, and contrasts it with a baraita about mourning where the spouse is prohibited from cosmetics but still performs those tasks, suggesting mourning is stricter.

items.text: Resolution: Distinction between his mourning and her mourning
items.text_en: Resolution: Distinction between his mourning and her mourning
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the mourner's own mourning (which is stricter) and the mourning of his spouse (which is more lenient). The Mishnah's case involves the spouse's mourning, not the mourner's own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the mourner's own mourning (stricter) and the spouse's mourning (more lenient), noting that the Mishnah's case refers to the spouse's mourning.

items.text: Challenge and further resolution regarding the distinction
items.text_en: Challenge and further resolution regarding the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the distinction between his and her mourning with a baraita that treats both equally. It then reinterprets the Mishnah: the phrase 'and similarly' applies only to cosmetics, not to sleeping arrangements, and 'with him' means in the house, not in the bed, citing Rav's instruction to his son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the distinction between his mourning and her mourning by citing a baraita that treats both equally.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: the phrase 'and similarly' applies only to cosmetics, not to sleeping arrangements.
The Gemara objects that the baraita says 'with him', implying in the bed, but resolves that it means in the house.

sub.text: Rav's instruction to his son Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rav's instruction to his son Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav instructs his son Chiyya to observe mourning in her presence but not in her absence, supporting the interpretation that 'with him' means in the house.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: Leniency of wedding mourning
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution: Leniency of wedding mourning
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi distinguishes between regular mourning (strict) and wedding mourning (lenient), explaining that the leniency of wedding mourning might lead to disrespect, hence the stricter separation. The leniency is that the groom engages in the mitzva act and then separates, and observes seven days of feasting before seven days of mourning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi opens by distinguishing wedding mourning from regular mourning, arguing that the leniency of wedding mourning could lead to disrespect, hence the stricter separation.

The Gemara asks what leniency Rav Ashi refers to, considering that the groom's act of performing the mitzva act and then separating is not a leniency but due to the fact that mourning has not yet begun according to Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Gemara clarifies that the leniency is the ruling that the groom observes seven days of feasting before seven days of mourning, which could lead to disrespect if not strictly separated.

items.text: Question about the prohibition of intercourse on Saturday night
items.text_en: Question about the prohibition of intercourse on Saturday night
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the groom may not engage in intercourse on Saturday night, given that the prohibition on Friday is due to the wound, but Saturday night has no such concern. Rabbi Zeira begins to answer.

items.text: Gemara's question about calculating accounts on Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara's question about calculating accounts on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the Mishnah's reason that one may not marry on Shabbat eve due to 'accounts', citing multiple sources that permit calculating accounts of mitzvot on Shabbat. Rabbi Zeira then offers a different reason: a decree lest one slaughter a bird (which is prohibited on Shabbat). Abaye objects by comparing to Yom Kippur, and the Gemara resolves the objection.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the reason one may not marry on Shabbat eve is due to calculations (for the wedding feast).
Abaye challenges the Mishnah's reason, asking whether calculations for a mitzvah are prohibited on Shabbat, and cites multiple sources that permit such activities on Shabbat.

Additional sources are cited permitting going to theaters and circuses for public matters, and making matches for children on Shabbat, further supporting that calculations for a mitzvah are permitted.
Rabbi Zeira offers a different reason: a decree lest one slaughter a young fowl on Shabbat due to preoccupation with wedding preparations.
Abaye objects by comparing to Yom Kippur that falls on Monday, arguing that if the decree were valid, it should also be postponed, which is not the case.

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: on Yom Kippur eve one prepares for oneself and is not preoccupied, whereas for a wedding one prepares for others and is preoccupied; alternatively, there is an interval of time on Yom Kippur eve, but not for a wedding at the conclusion of Shabbat.

items.text: Conclusion: the decree applies to Shabbat eve as well
items.text_en: Conclusion: the decree applies to Shabbat eve as well
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the decree lest one slaughter a bird applies also to Shabbat eve, so the Mishnah's concern is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the decree lest one slaughter a bird applies also to Shabbat eve, so the Mishnah's concern is valid.

items.text: Inquiry about the virgin's wedding day and consummation
items.text_en: Inquiry about the virgin's wedding day and consummation
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does a virgin marry on Wednesday and consummate on Wednesday, or on Wednesday and consummate on Thursday due to concern for cooling of the mind? Bar Kappara's teaching is brought as evidence that she marries on Wednesday and consummates on Thursday, because of the blessing for fish, implying no concern for cooling of the mind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does a virgin marry on Wednesday and consummate on Wednesday, without concern for cooling of the mind, or on Wednesday and consummate on Thursday, due to concern for cooling of the mind?
Bar Kappara's teaching is brought as evidence: a virgin marries on Wednesday and consummates on Thursday, because of the blessing for fish, implying no concern for cooling of the mind.

items.text: Discussion of the widow's wedding day and the difference between reasons
items.text_en: Discussion of the widow's wedding day and the difference between reasons
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a widow does not also consummate on Thursday for the blessing of fish, and answers that the blessing for man is preferable. Alternatively, the reason is 'shakdu' (the Sages' concern that the husband should rejoice with her for three days). The Gemara then asks what practical difference exists between the reasons of 'blessing' and 'shakdu', and answers: a man who is idle, or a festival that falls on Shabbat eve.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the reason for the virgin's consummation on Thursday is the blessing of fish, then a widow should also consummate on Thursday for the same blessing.
The Gemara answers: The blessing for man is preferable for him, so he delays to Friday.

Alternatively, the reason is 'shakdu' (the Sages' assiduousness): a baraita teaches that a widow marries on Thursday and consummates on Friday so the groom rejoices with her for three days—Thursday, Shabbat eve, and Shabbat—lest he leave early for work.
The Gemara asks: What practical difference is there between the reasons of 'blessing' and 'shakdu'?

The Gemara answers: The difference is in the case of an idle man (who has no job to leave early) or a festival that falls on Shabbat eve (when work is prohibited anyway), where the 'shakdu' reason does not apply but the 'blessing' reason still does.

items.text: Homily: the deeds of the righteous are greater than creation
items.text_en: Homily: the deeds of the righteous are greater than creation
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that the deeds of the righteous are greater than the creation of heaven and earth, citing verses. A Babylonian named Rabbi Chiya objects with a verse that seems to attribute creation to God's hands, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'His fingers' are meant, as in the verse about the moon and stars.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that the handiwork of the righteous is greater than the creation of heaven and earth, citing verses that use singular 'hand' for creation and plural 'hands' for the righteous.
A Babylonian named Rabbi Chiya objects by citing a verse that says 'His hands formed the dry land,' seemingly attributing creation to God's hands in the plural.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by explaining that the plural 'formed' refers to God's fingers, citing a verse about the work of His fingers in the moon and stars.

items.text: Objection and resolution about the heavens declaring God's handiwork
items.text_en: Objection and resolution about the heavens declaring God's handiwork
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a verse that says the heavens declare the work of God's hands. The Gemara explains that the verse means: the work of the righteous, who is it that declares? The firmament, and what is that? Rain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a verse that says the heavens declare the work of God's hands, challenging the claim that God's handiwork is singular.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the verse refers to the handiwork of the righteous, which is attested by the heavens through rain.

items.text: Homily on the verse about a peg and the ear
items.text_en: Homily on the verse about a peg and the ear
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara expounds on the verse 'And you shall have a peg upon your ear', interpreting it as 'upon your ear' — that if a person hears something inappropriate, he should place his finger in his ear.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara expounds on the verse 'וְיָתֵד תִּהְיֶה לְךָ עַל אֲזֵנֶךָ' (And you shall have a peg upon your ear), interpreting it as 'עַל אׇזְנֶךָ' (upon your ear) — that if a person hears something inappropriate, he should place his finger in his ear.

items.text: Why fingers are shaped like pegs and ears are soft
items.text_en: Why fingers are shaped like pegs and ears are soft
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that fingers are shaped like pegs so that one can plug his ears upon hearing something inappropriate, and the ear is hard with a soft lobe so that one can bend the lobe into the ear. A baraita adds that one should not expose his ears to idle talk, as the ears are the first to be burned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why human fingers are shaped like pegs, and rejects the initial answer that each finger has a distinct function.
The Gemara answers that fingers are shaped like pegs so that one can plug his ears upon hearing something inappropriate.
The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that the ear is hard with a soft lobe so that one can bend the lobe into the ear to block inappropriate speech.
The Sages taught in a baraita that one should not expose his ears to idle talk, because the ears are the first to be burned.

items.text: First question: Is blood stored or created?
items.text_en: First question: Is blood stored or created?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question of whether, when engaging in marital relations for the first time on Shabbat, the blood that flows is stored blood (which would be permitted) or created by the wound (which would be prohibited).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question of whether, when engaging in marital relations for the first time on Shabbat, the blood that flows is stored blood (which would be permitted) or created by the wound (which would be prohibited).
Assuming the blood is stored, the Gemara asks whether the man needs the blood itself (permitted) or the opening of the hymen (forbidden).
Assuming he needs the blood and the opening happens automatically, the Gemara asks whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon (who permits an unintended consequence) or Rabbi Yehuda (who forbids it).
Assuming the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, the Gemara asks whether tearing the hymen is destructive (permitted) or constructive (forbidden) with respect to the opening.
An alternative version: assuming the blood is created by the wound, the Gemara asks whether he needs the blood (forbidden) or his own pleasure (permitted).
Assuming he needs his own pleasure and the blood comes automatically, the Gemara asks whether the law follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon.
Assuming the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, the Gemara asks whether making a wound is destructive (permitted) or constructive (forbidden).
Assuming making a wound is destructive, the Gemara asks whether the law follows Rabbi Yehuda in the case of a destructive act.

items.text: If blood is stored: Is the intent for blood or for the opening?
items.text_en: If blood is stored: Is the intent for blood or for the opening?
items.desc_en: Assuming the blood is stored, the Gemara asks whether the man needs the blood (permitted) or the opening of the hymen (prohibited as a wound).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether, assuming the blood is stored, the man needs the blood (permitted) or the opening of the hymen (forbidden as a wound).

items.text: If intent is for blood: Is the opening unintentional?
items.text_en: If intent is for blood: Is the opening unintentional?
items.desc_en: Assuming the intent is for the blood and the opening occurs unintentionally, the Gemara asks whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon (who permits an unintended act) or Rabbi Yehuda (who prohibits it).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara assumes the intent is for the blood and the opening occurs unintentionally, then asks whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon (who permits an unintended act) or Rabbi Yehuda (who prohibits it).

items.text: If like Rabbi Yehuda: Is the opening destructive or constructive?
items.text_en: If like Rabbi Yehuda: Is the opening destructive or constructive?
items.desc_en: Assuming the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, the Gemara asks whether the act of opening the hymen is considered destructive (permitted) or constructive (prohibited) regarding the wound.

sub.desc_en: Assuming the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, the Gemara asks whether the act of opening the hymen is considered destructive (permitted) or constructive (prohibited) regarding the wound.

items.text: Alternative: If blood is created: Is intent for blood or for pleasure?
items.text_en: Alternative: If blood is created: Is intent for blood or for pleasure?
items.desc_en: According to another version, assuming the blood is created by the wound, the Gemara asks whether the man needs the blood (prohibited) or his own pleasure (permitted).

sub.text: Alternative version of the Gemara's question
sub.text_en: Alternative version of the Gemara's question
sub.desc_en: According to an alternative version, assuming the blood is created by the wound, the Gemara asks whether the man needs the blood (prohibited) or his own pleasure (permitted).

items.text: If intent is for pleasure: Is the blood unintentional?
items.text_en: If intent is for pleasure: Is the blood unintentional?
items.desc_en: Assuming the intent is for pleasure and the blood comes unintentionally, the Gemara again asks whether the law follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Assuming the intent is for pleasure and the blood comes unintentionally, the Gemara asks whether the law follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon regarding an unintended consequence.

items.text: If like Rabbi Yehuda: Is the wound destructive or constructive?
items.text_en: If like Rabbi Yehuda: Is the wound destructive or constructive?
items.desc_en: Assuming the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, the Gemara asks whether the act is destructive (permitted) or constructive (prohibited) regarding the wound itself.

sub.desc_en: Assuming the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, the Gemara asks whether the act is destructive (permitted) or constructive (prohibited) regarding the wound itself.

items.text: If destructive: Does Rabbi Yehuda prohibit destruction?
items.text_en: If destructive: Does Rabbi Yehuda prohibit destruction?
items.desc_en: Assuming it is destructive, the Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda prohibits a destructive act, leaving the question unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question: assuming the act is destructive (מקלקל) regarding the wound, does Rabbi Yehuda prohibit destruction, leaving the matter undecided.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous dispute
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits the bride to her husband even if she sees blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, who permits the bride to her husband even if she sees blood.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports conflicting traditions: in Rav's academy they say Rav permits and Shmuel forbids, while in Nehardea they say Rav forbids and Shmuel permits. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports the tradition from Rav's academy: Rav permits and Shmuel forbids.
The Gemara reports the conflicting tradition from Nehardea: Rav forbids and Shmuel permits.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides a mnemonic: 'These are lenient for themselves and those are lenient for themselves' to reconcile the conflicting traditions.

items.text: Challenge to Rav's leniency from the case of a wine press
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav's leniency from the case of a wine press
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's leniency by citing a statement from Rav Shimi bar Chizkiya in Rav's name that one may not tread on a wine press on Yom Tov. The Gemara answers that even Rabbi Shimon would agree in that case, as it is a case of 'פסיק רישיה ולא ימות'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's leniency by citing Rav Shimi bar Chizkiya's statement in Rav's name that treading a wine press is forbidden on Yom Tov.
The Gemara answers that even Rabbi Shimon would agree in that case, as it is a case of 'פסיק רישיה ולא ימות' (an inevitable consequence).

items.text: Contradictory rulings from Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Contradictory rulings from Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Chiyya bar Ashi said Rav ruled like Rabbi Yehuda, while Rav Chanan bar Ami said Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Shimon. Rav Chiyya bar Avin taught the dispute without names, attributing to Rav the ruling like Rabbi Yehuda and to Shmuel like Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites contradictory rulings: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi reported Rav ruled like Rabbi Yehuda, Rav Chanan bar Ami reported Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Shimon, and Rav Chiyya bar Avin taught the dispute without names, attributing to Rav the ruling like Rabbi Yehuda and to Shmuel like Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Resolution of Rav's position
items.text_en: Resolution of Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav consistently holds like Rabbi Yehuda. According to the version that blood is 'stored' (מפקד פקיד), it spoils at the entrance; according to the version that blood is 'attached' (חבורי מיחבר), it spoils in the wound.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rav consistently holds like Rabbi Yehuda, explaining that according to the version that blood is stored (מפקד פקיד) it spoils at the entrance, and according to the version that blood is attached (חבורי מיחבר) it spoils in the wound.

items.text: Supporting baraita from Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Supporting baraita from Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a baraita: For a minor bride who has not yet reached the age of seeing blood, Beit Shammai give four nights, Beit Hillel give until the wound heals. For a bride who has reached the age, Beit Shammai give the first night, Beit Hillel give until after Shabbat, four nights.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's citation of a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's citation of a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a baraita with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's rulings on the blood-checking period for a minor bride who has not yet reached the age of seeing blood.

The baraita concludes with the contrasting ruling for a bride who has reached the age of seeing blood: Beit Shammai give one night, Beit Hillel give from Shabbat eve until Saturday night, four nights.

items.text: Rava's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the Mishnah's allowance for four nights does not include Shabbat, but if he already engaged in intercourse, it is permitted on Shabbat, supporting Shmuel's principle that one may enter a tight alleyway on Shabbat even if it displaces pebbles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah implies that if the groom has not yet engaged in intercourse, he may do so even on Shabbat.
Rava rejects the implication, stating that the allowance excludes Shabbat.
Abaye objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'until after Shabbat, four nights,' implying Shabbat is included.
Rava revises his position, explaining that the Mishnah refers to a case where the groom has already engaged in intercourse.
The Gemara questions what novel teaching Rava's interpretation provides if it refers to a case where intercourse already occurred.

The Gemara explains that Rava's interpretation teaches that intercourse on Shabbat is permitted, supporting Shmuel's principle that one may enter a tight alleyway on Shabbat even if it displaces pebbles.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rava by citing a baraita that a groom is exempt from Shema until after Shabbat if he did not perform the act, implying preoccupation with the act. Abaye counters that the preoccupation is with not having performed it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects by citing a baraita that a groom is exempt from Shema if he did not perform the act, implying preoccupation with the desire to perform it.
Abaye counters that the groom's preoccupation is with not having performed the act, not with the desire to perform it.

items.text: Rava's counter-argument from the mourner's obligation
items.text_en: Rava's counter-argument from the mourner's obligation
items.desc_en: Rava rejects Abaye's explanation, arguing that preoccupation alone cannot exempt one from mitzvot, as a mourner is obligated in all commandments except tefillin, and a shipwrecked person would not be exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's explanation that preoccupation exempts one from the Shema, arguing that if preoccupation were an exemption, a shipwrecked person would also be exempt, which is contradicted by the rule that a mourner is obligated in all commandments except tefillin.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rava cites the ruling that a mourner is obligated in all commandments except tefillin, proving that preoccupation does not exempt one from mitzvot.

items.text: Rava's resolution: a dispute among Tannaim
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: a dispute among Tannaim
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that the exemption depends on a Tannaitic dispute: one opinion exempts the groom for consecutive nights if he did not perform the act, while another exempts only the first two nights. Abaye maintains that both opinions are based on preoccupation.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute by citing two baraitot: one exempts the groom for consecutive nights if he did not perform the act, the other exempts only the first two nights.
Abaye explains that even the Tannaitic dispute is based on preoccupation (טירדא), not on a different principle.
The gemara cites a baraita about a groom who marries a virgin and may not perform the first act on Shabbat, with a dispute between the first Tanna and the Sages who permit it.
Rabba identifies the Sages as Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an unintentional act (דבר שאין מתכוין) is permitted.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Shimon concedes in the case of 'פסיק רישיה ולא ימות' (an inevitable consequence), so the groom's act would be forbidden.
Rabba responds that the case is different because there are experts in deflection (הטייה) who can avoid digging, so it is not an inevitable consequence.
The gemara objects that if deflection is possible, why is there a concern (טורד) at all, and answers that it is for the non-expert, but since most are experts, the concern is dismissed.
Rava bar Rav Chanan objects: if deflection is possible, why are groomsmen and a sheet (מפה) needed for the wedding night?
Abaye answers that the groomsmen and sheet are needed lest the groom see and become aroused, leading to loss of seed.
Rabbi Ammi objects by citing a baraita about lancing a boil on Shabbat, which distinguishes between making an opening (liable) and draining pus (permitted).

items.text: Dispute about initial intercourse on Shabbat
items.text_en: Dispute about initial intercourse on Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who marries a virgin should not initially engage in intercourse on Shabbat, but the Sages permit it. Rabbah identifies the Sages as Rabbi Shimon, who permits an unintended consequence.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who marries a virgin should not engage in initial intercourse on Shabbat, but the Sages permit it.
Rabbah identifies the Sages as Rabbi Shimon, who permits an unintended consequence (דבר שאין מתכוין מותר).

items.text: Abaye's objection and the response about expertise
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and the response about expertise
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbi Shimon admits to the principle of 'psik reishei' (an inevitable consequence). The Gemara answers that experts in 'hatayah' (tilting) can avoid making a wound, and since most are experts, the concern is only for the non-expert, but the groom is preoccupied.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbi Shimon admits to the principle of 'psik reishei' (an inevitable consequence), which would forbid the act.
Rabbah answers that the concern applies only to Babylonians who are not experts in 'hatayah' (tilting), but there are experts in tilting who can avoid making a wound.
The Gemara asks: if experts can avoid the wound, why is the groom still preoccupied (טורד)?
The Gemara answers: the preoccupation is for the non-expert groom who might cause a wound.
The Gemara objects that this would create a problematic distinction: experts are permitted and non-experts are forbidden.
The Gemara resolves that since most people are experts, the concern is only for the minority, and the groom's preoccupation is due to the general concern.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Chanan's question and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's question and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks why groomsmen and a sheet are needed if experts can avoid making a wound. Abaye responds that these are precautions lest the groom see blood and become distressed, leading to loss of seed.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye: if experts can avoid making a wound, why are groomsmen and a sheet needed?
Abaye responds that these precautions are lest the groom see blood and become distressed, leading to loss of seed.

items.text: Rabbi Ammi's objection from lancing a boil
items.text_en: Rabbi Ammi's objection from lancing a boil
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi raises an objection from the case of lancing a boil on Shabbat, where the intent determines liability, implying that the act of intercourse might similarly be prohibited if it inevitably causes a wound.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi raises an objection from the case of lancing a boil on Shabbat, where the intent determines liability, implying that the act of intercourse might similarly be prohibited if it inevitably causes a wound.

items.text: Distinction between a wound that is 'present and not displaced' and one that is 'present and displaced'
items.text_en: Distinction between a wound that is 'present and not displaced' and one that is 'present and displaced'
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between a case where the wound is present and displaced (which is exempt) and the case here where the wound is present but not displaced (which is liable).

items.text: Rabbi Ami and Rav Zevid permit first intercourse on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rav Zevid permit first intercourse on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami permitted first intercourse on Shabbat, and when the rabbis objected that the ketubah was not written, he replied that they should impound movable property. Rav Zevid also permitted it, and some say he himself did so.

items.text: Rav Yehuda permits first intercourse on Yom Tov; Rava's tradition
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda permits first intercourse on Yom Tov; Rava's tradition
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda permitted first intercourse on Yom Tov. Rav Pappi said in the name of Rava that this is not limited to Yom Tov but applies even to Shabbat, and that is how the incident actually occurred.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling and the objection from the principle of 'permitted for need'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling and the objection from the principle of 'permitted for need'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa said in the name of Rava that first intercourse is permitted on Yom Tov but forbidden on Shabbat. Rav Pappi objected: if it is permitted for need, it should also be permitted without need, just as burning incense (mugmar) would be permitted on Yom Tov. Rav Pappa replied that the verse 'akh asher ye'akhel lekhol nefesh' limits permission to something equal for all people.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's challenge and Rav Ashi's response
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's challenge and Rav Ashi's response
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asked Rav Ashi: if a deer happens to be available on Yom Tov, since it is not equal for all people, would it be forbidden to slaughter it? Rav Ashi replied that he meant something needed for all people, and a deer is needed for all people.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling in Tzaidan and the concept of 'ruling for prohibition'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling in Tzaidan and the concept of 'ruling for prohibition'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reported that Rabbi Yochanan ruled in Tzaidan that first intercourse on Shabbat is forbidden. The Gemara questions whether there is such a thing as a ruling for prohibition, and supports it with examples from Beit Hillel and Rabbi's ruling about the spinal cord.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's version: Rabbi Yochanan said 'forbidden', but the halakha is 'permitted'
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's version: Rabbi Yochanan said 'forbidden', but the halakha is 'permitted'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak taught a different version: Rabbi Avahu said that Rabbi Yishmael ben Yaakov asked Rabbi Yochanan in Tzaidan about first intercourse on Shabbat, and he answered that it is forbidden, but the halakha is that it is permitted.

items.text: The blessing for a widow: Rav Huna's apparent contradiction resolved
items.text_en: The blessing for a widow: Rav Huna's apparent contradiction resolved
items.desc_en: Rav Helbo quoted Rav Huna quoting Rav that both a virgin and a widow require a blessing. But Rav Huna himself said a widow does not require a blessing. The Gemara resolves: here it refers to a bachelor who married a widow (requires blessing), there it refers to a widower who married a widow (does not require blessing for seven days, but one day).

items.text: Reconciling the three-day joy with the blessing periods
items.text_en: Reconciling the three-day joy with the blessing periods
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a baraita that the Sages instituted three days of joy: if for a bachelor (seven days of blessing), why only three? If for a widower (one day of blessing), why three? Two answers: for a widower, one day for blessing and three for joy; for a bachelor, seven for blessing and three for joy.

items.text: Duration of blessings for a widow married to a bachelor
items.text_en: Duration of blessings for a widow married to a bachelor
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier statement by citing a baraita that says we bless a virgin for seven days and a widow for one day. It questions whether this applies even to a widow married to a bachelor, and concludes that the baraita refers to a widow married to a widower, implying that a bachelor married to a widow would receive seven days of blessings. The Gemara then refines the baraita's formulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier statement by citing a baraita that says we bless a virgin for seven days and a widow for one day, and questions whether this applies even to a widow married to a bachelor, then refines the baraita's formulation.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita states a fixed rule: no virgin gets less than seven days and no widow gets less than one day, regardless of the spouse's status.

items.text: Source for the requirement of ten for the wedding blessing
items.text_en: Source for the requirement of ten for the wedding blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a tannaitic source deriving the requirement of ten for the wedding blessing from Ruth 4:2. Rabbi Abahu derives it from Psalms 68:27. The Gemara then discusses how each sage interprets the other's verse, leading to a discussion about the need for ten for publicizing a matter, illustrated by Shmuel's instruction to Rav Chana.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Huna bar Natan
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Huna bar Natan
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman, citing Huna bar Natan, introduces a tannaitic source deriving the requirement of ten for the wedding blessing (ברכת חתנים) from Ruth 4:2.
Rabbi Abahu derives the same requirement from Psalms 68:27, using the word 'בְּמַקְהֵלוֹת' (in congregations).
The Gemara asks how Rav Nachman interprets the verse that Rabbi Abahu used.
The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman uses the verse for Rabbi Meir's teaching that even fetuses in their mothers' wombs sang at the sea.

The Gemara objects that if the verse referred to fetuses, it should have said 'מִבֶּטֶן' (from the womb), and explains that 'מִמְּקוֹר' (from the source) refers to the matter of the source (the womb).
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Abahu interprets the verse that Rav Nachman used.

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Abahu uses the verse to derive the rule that an Ammonite man is excluded but not an Ammonite woman, and a Moabite man but not a Moabite woman, since the verse mentions 'זקני העיר' (elders of the city) implying men.
The Gemara objects that if the verse is for a halachic derivation, it still requires ten elders, so the requirement of ten for the blessing is still derived.

The Gemara resolves that the requirement of ten is for publicizing the matter (לפרסומי מילתא), as illustrated by Shmuel's instruction to Rav Chana Bagdata'ah to gather ten people to announce a halachic ruling, though the final ruling is that one who acquires property for a fetus does not acquire it.

items.text: Place for reciting the wedding blessing
items.text_en: Place for reciting the wedding blessing
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the wedding blessing is recited in the house of the groom. Rabbi Yehuda adds that it is also recited in the house of betrothal. Abaye explains that this applies specifically in Judea, because the groom would be secluded with the bride there.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the basic rule: the wedding blessing is recited in the groom's house, and Rabbi Yehuda adds that it is also recited in the house of betrothal.
Abaye explains that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies specifically in Judea, because there the groom would be secluded with the bride in the betrothal house.

items.text: Blessing for betrothal and its formulation
items.text_en: Blessing for betrothal and its formulation
items.desc_en: Another baraita discusses the blessing for betrothal, which is recited in the house of betrothal. Ravin bar Rav Adda and Rabbah bar Rav Adda, both citing Rav Yehuda, state the text of the blessing, which includes a closing formula. Rav Acha bar Rava adds a different closing formula. The Gemara explains the reasoning behind the different versions.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the blessing for grooms is recited in the house of grooms, and the blessing for betrothal in the house of betrothal.
The Gemara asks what blessing is recited for betrothal.

sub.text: Ravin bar Rav Adda and Rabbah bar Rav Adda citing Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda and Rabbah bar Rav Adda citing Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda and Rabbah bar Rav Adda, both citing Rav Yehuda, state the full text of the betrothal blessing without a closing formula.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava citing Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava citing Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava adds a closing formula to the betrothal blessing, citing Rav Yehuda.

The Gemara explains that the version without a closing formula follows the pattern of blessings over fruits and commandments, while the version with a closing formula follows the pattern of the blessing for sanctification (קידוש).

items.text: Requirement of ten for the wedding blessing all seven days and the blessing text
items.text_en: Requirement of ten for the wedding blessing all seven days and the blessing text
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the wedding blessing is recited in the presence of ten for all seven days. Rav Yehuda adds that this applies only when new faces are present. The Gemara then begins to quote Rav Yehuda's formulation of the blessing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita establishes that the wedding blessing (ברכת חתנים) is recited in the presence of ten for all seven days of the wedding feast.
Rav Yehuda qualifies that the seven-day blessing applies only when new faces (פנים חדשות) are present each day.
The Gemara asks what blessing text is recited for the wedding blessing.
Rav Yehuda begins to quote the text of the wedding blessing, starting with 'ברוך אתה ה׳ אלהינו מלך העולם'.

items.text: The seven wedding blessings
items.text_en: The seven wedding blessings
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the text of the seven blessings recited at a wedding feast, starting with 'shehakol bara lichvodo' and ending with 'mesameach chatan im hakallah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the full text of the seven wedding blessings (שבע ברכות), from the first blessing 'shehakol bara lichvodo' to the final blessing 'mesameach chatan im hakallah'.

items.text: Levi and Rav Asi's dispute over the number of blessings
items.text_en: Levi and Rav Asi's dispute over the number of blessings
items.desc_en: Levi recited five blessings at Rabbi Shimon's wedding, while Rav Asi recited six at Mar's wedding. The Gemara initially suggests they disagree about whether there were one or two acts of creation (of Adam), but concludes they both agree there was one creation; they differ on whether the blessing follows the thought or the deed, citing a verse contradiction resolved by Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Levi recited five blessings at Rabbi Shimon's wedding, while Rav Asi recited six at Mar's wedding.
The Gemara suggests that Levi and Rav Asi disagree about whether there was one or two acts of creation of Adam.

The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion, concluding that both agree there was one creation; they differ on whether the blessing follows the thought or the deed, citing Rav Yehuda's resolution of a verse contradiction.

items.text: Rav Ashi's practice regarding new faces
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's practice regarding new faces
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi, when visiting Rav Kahana, recited all seven blessings on the first day of the wedding. Thereafter, if new faces were present, he recited all seven; if not, he only recited 'shehasimcha bim'ono' and 'asher bara'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi visited Rav Kahana's house and on the first day recited all seven wedding blessings.
Thereafter, if new faces were present he recited all seven; if not, he recited only 'shehasimcha bim'ono' and 'asher bara'.

items.text: The time frame for reciting 'shehasimcha bim'ono'
items.text_en: The time frame for reciting 'shehasimcha bim'ono'
items.desc_en: From seven to thirty days, one always recites 'shehasimcha bim'ono'. After thirty days, it depends on whether the gathering is for the wedding. Rav Papi says this applies up to twelve months; Rav Papa says it begins from when barley is thrown at the wedding. Rav Papa's own practice of reciting from engagement is distinguished because he was busy.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the rule: from seven to thirty days after the wedding, one always recites 'shehasimcha bim'ono'; after thirty days, it depends on whether the gathering is for the wedding.
The gemara asks: until when does one recite the blessing if the gathering is for the wedding?

sub.text: Rav Papi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Papi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Papi says in the name of Rava: up to twelve months of the year.
The gemara asks: from when does the obligation begin?
Rav Papa says: from when barley is thrown at the wedding.
The gemara objects: but Rav Papa himself was involved in his son Abba Mar's wedding and recited the blessing from the time of engagement, contradicting his own statement.
The gemara resolves: Rav Papa's case is different because he was busy (and therefore started early to avoid missing the blessing).

items.text: Ravina and Rav Tachlifa's practices; Rav Chaviva's error
items.text_en: Ravina and Rav Tachlifa's practices; Rav Chaviva's error
items.desc_en: Ravina recited blessings from engagement because he was confident the couple would not retract, but they did. Rav Tachlifa recited six long blessings, but the halakha does not follow him. Rav Chaviva recited only 'shehasimcha bim'ono' at a circumcision, but the halakha does not follow him because the baby's pain distracts.

sub.desc_en: Ravina recited blessings from the time of engagement for his son's wedding, confident the couple would not retract, but they did.
Rav Tachlifa recited six long blessings at a wedding, but the halakha does not follow him.
Rav Chaviva recited only 'shehasimcha bim'ono' at a circumcision, but the halakha does not follow him because the baby's pain distracts from the joy.

items.text: Whether bridegrooms and mourners count in a minyan
items.text_en: Whether bridegrooms and mourners count in a minyan
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav says bridegrooms count in a minyan but mourners do not. A baraita objects that both count. The Gemara notes that Rav is a Tanna and can disagree. Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan says the same, and again a baraita objects.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states in Rav's name that bridegrooms count in a minyan but mourners do not.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states both bridegrooms and mourners count in a minyan.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that Rav is a Tanna and may disagree with the baraita.
Rabbi Yitzchak reports in Rabbi Yochanan's name the same ruling that bridegrooms count but mourners do not.
The Gemara again raises the same baraita as an objection against Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about Rabbi Yochanan's statement on blessings in a row
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about Rabbi Yochanan's statement on blessings in a row
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially thought Rabbi Yochanan's statement about blessings in a row referred to Grace after Meals, but then questions it based on another statement by Rabbi Yochanan about bridegroom and mourner blessings requiring ten. It resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a row refers to a broad space, and the blessing of a broad space for seven days is found in the case of new faces.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita about blessings in a row refers to Grace after Meals, while Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers to a row (שורה) of people.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yochanan said that bridegroom and mourner blessings require ten, but a blessing in a row (שורה) is not mentioned there.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about a row actually refers to a broad space (רחבה).
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yochanan said that bridegroom and mourner blessings are recited for seven days, but is there a blessing of a broad space (רחבה) for seven days?
The Gemara resolves that the blessing of a broad space for seven days is found in the case of new faces (פנים חדשות).

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and the eulogy for a child
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and the eulogy for a child
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story where Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba did not attend the funeral of a child on the first day, but the next day sent his translator to deliver a eulogy. The eulogy used a verse to explain that children die because their fathers anger God. An alternative version says the deceased was a young man, and the eulogy used a different verse, followed by a statement from Rav Chanan bar Rav about the severity of speaking obscenely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story about Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba who was teaching the children of Reish Lakish (or some say his own children).
A child died, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba did not attend the funeral on the first day.
The next day, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba sent his translator Yehuda bar Nachmani to deliver a eulogy for the child.
The eulogy cited a verse (Deuteronomy 32:19) to explain that children die because their fathers anger God.
An alternative version says the deceased was a young man, and the eulogy used a different verse (Isaiah 9:16).
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'and still His hand is stretched out' from the verse.

Rav Chanan bar Rav explains that everyone knows why a bride enters the wedding canopy, yet one who speaks obscenely — even if a favorable decree of seventy years was sealed for him — it is overturned for evil.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's rebuke to the translator
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's rebuke to the translator
items.desc_en: When the translator came to console Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Chiyya said he was causing him pain, and that the translator was fit to be seized for the sermon (i.e., he was being too harsh).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba rebukes the translator who came to console him, saying the translator is causing him pain and is fit to be seized for the sermon.

items.text: Series of blessings and consolations delivered by the translator
items.text_en: Series of blessings and consolations delivered by the translator
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba then instructed the translator to deliver a series of blessings: one praising God for reviving the dead, one for the mourners, one for the comforters, and one for all of Israel. Each blessing is quoted in full.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba instructs the translator to recite a blessing praising God's greatness.
The translator recites a blessing praising God as the reviver of the dead.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba instructs the translator to recite a blessing for the mourners.
The translator recites a blessing of consolation for the mourners.
Abaye comments on which phrases in the mourners' blessing should be omitted to avoid inviting misfortune.

sub.text: Supporting baraita and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and a baraita in the name of Rabbi Yosei teach that one should never open his mouth to the Satan (inviting harm).
Rav Yosef cites a verse to support the principle of not opening one's mouth to the Satan.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba instructs the translator to recite a blessing for the comforters of the mourners.
The translator recites a blessing for the comforters, praising them as practitioners of loving-kindness.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba to the translator
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba instructs the translator to recite a blessing for all of Israel.
The translator recites a blessing for all of Israel, asking God to save them from calamities and stop the plague.

items.text: The ten cups of wine in the house of mourning and their later modification
items.text_en: The ten cups of wine in the house of mourning and their later modification
items.desc_en: Ulla or a baraita states that the Sages instituted ten cups of wine in the house of mourning: three before the meal, three during, and four after, corresponding to the blessings of Grace after Meals. Later, four more cups were added for various purposes, but when people became drunk, the practice was reverted to the original ten.

sub.desc_en: Ulla or a baraita states that the Sages instituted ten cups of wine in the house of mourning: three before the meal, three during, and four after, corresponding to the blessings of Grace after Meals.
The baraita reports that four more cups were added for various purposes, but when people became drunk, the practice was reverted to the original ten.

items.text: Explanation of the cup for Rabban Gamliel and the practice of burial in linen
