items.text_en: Explanation of the cup for Rabban Gamliel and the practice of burial in linen
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the cup for Rabban Gamliel: originally, the expense of burial was so great that relatives would abandon the deceased, until Rabban Gamliel set an example by being buried in simple linen garments. Rav Papa notes that now the custom is even to use a cheap shroud worth a zuz. The daf ends with Rabbi Elazar beginning a new statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the reference to Rabban Gamliel in the context of the cups of mourning means.

A baraita explains that originally burial expenses were so burdensome that relatives would abandon the dead, until Rabban Gamliel set a precedent by being buried in simple linen garments, and the people followed his practice.
Rav Papa notes that nowadays the custom is even more modest, using a cheap shroud worth only a zuz.
Rabbi Elazar begins a new statement, marking a transition to a new topic.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband who says 'I found an open entrance' is believed to forbid her to himself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a husband who claims he found an open entrance is believed to forbid her to himself.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the husband is believed, given it is a double doubt (whether she was under him, and if so, whether it was by force or consent). It answers that the case is either a priest's wife, or an Israelite woman whose father accepted betrothal before age three.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the husband is believed, given it is a double doubt (ספק ספיקא): whether she was under him, and if so, whether by force or consent.
The Gemara answers that the case is either a priest's wife, or an Israelite woman whose father accepted betrothal before age three, where no doubt exists.

items.text: Clarifying the novelty
items.text_en: Clarifying the novelty
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's novelty is that even though the husband does not have certain knowledge, he is believed, unlike the case where he says 'I betrothed you' and she denies it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel ruling the Mishnah teaches, since the principle that a man's own claim can render him forbidden is already taught by the case of 'I betrothed you' where she denies it.

The Gemara answers that one might have thought the husband is only believed when he is certain of the facts, but here he may be mistaken about the orifice, so the Mishnah teaches that he is nevertheless believed.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah with Rabbi Elazar's statement that a woman is only forbidden through the process of warning and seclusion, implying that 'open entrance' alone does not forbid. It resolves that Rabbi Elazar meant that from the incident we learn that without warning and seclusion she was not forbidden, but still the Mishnah's case is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar actually holds that a woman is forbidden only through the process of warning and seclusion, citing his statement that this is the only way, as in the incident with David and Bathsheba.
The Gemara objects that the incident with David and Bathsheba did not involve warning and seclusion, and moreover, Bathsheba was not forbidden to her husband.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar meant that from the incident we learn that without warning and seclusion she was not forbidden, but still the Mishnah's case of 'open entrance' is different, leaving a difficulty.

items.text: Refining Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.text_en: Refining Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara further clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's statement was about the number of witnesses: a woman is forbidden only by two witnesses, but warning and seclusion work even with one witness, and 'open entrance' is like two witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Elazar's statement is taken literally, it would absurdly imply that warning and seclusion (קינוי וסתירה) suffice to forbid a woman, but two witnesses do not.

The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's statement actually means: a woman is forbidden only by two witnesses, but warning and seclusion (קינוי וסתירה) work even with one witness, and 'open entrance' (פתח פתוח) is equivalent to two witnesses.

items.text: Explaining the incident and alternative answer
items.text_en: Explaining the incident and alternative answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the incident, she was not forbidden because it was by force, and offers an alternative answer citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the incident, the woman was not forbidden because it was under duress, and then introduces an alternative explanation citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan.
The Gemara answers that in that incident, the intercourse was by force (אונס), so she was not forbidden.
The Gemara introduces an alternative answer.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement by Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan as the basis for the alternative answer.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Soldiers write a get for their wives
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Soldiers write a get for their wives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anyone going to war in David's army writes a bill of divorce for his wife, citing a verse about taking pledges. Rav Yosef explains that 'pledges' refers to matters between husband and wife.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that anyone going to war in David's army writes a bill of divorce for his wife, citing the verse 'ואת ערבתם תקח' (and take their pledge).
Rav Yosef teaches that 'ערבתם' (their pledge) refers to matters that are mixed between husband and wife, i.e., marital relations.

items.text: Abaye's support from the Mishnah of virgin marrying on Wednesday
items.text_en: Abaye's support from the Mishnah of virgin marrying on Wednesday
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that the Mishnah says a virgin marries on Wednesday, not Thursday, due to the husband's ability to prepare a claim. This implies that the husband can make a claim to void the ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites the Mishnah that a virgin marries on Wednesday, not Thursday, to support that the husband can make a claim to void the ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the purpose of the claim?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the purpose of the claim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the husband's claim is to withhold the ketubah or to forbid her to him, and concludes it is to forbid her, as he is making a claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the purpose of the husband's claim is, concluding it is to forbid her to him rather than to withhold the ketubah payment.

items.text: Gemara's suggestion and rejection: Claim of an open entrance vs. blood
items.text_en: Gemara's suggestion and rejection: Claim of an open entrance vs. blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the claim is about finding an open entrance, but rejects this, saying it is about finding blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the claim being cut off is a claim of an open entrance (פתח פתוח).
The Gemara rejects this, stating that the claim being cut off is about finding blood (דמים), not an open entrance.

items.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: One who says 'I found an open entrance' is believed to void her ketubah
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: One who says 'I found an open entrance' is believed to void her ketubah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that a husband claiming an open entrance is believed to void the ketubah. Rav Yosef questions this, citing a Mishnah that in Judea one cannot make such a claim due to seclusion, implying the claim is about blood, not an open entrance.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that a husband who claims 'I found an open entrance' is believed to void her ketubah.

Rav Yosef objects: what new teaching is this? We already have a Mishnah that in Judea one cannot claim virginity if he ate at his father-in-law's without witnesses, implying the claim is about blood, not an open entrance.
Rav Yosef cites the Mishnah's conclusion: in Judea he cannot claim, but in the Galilee he can, showing the claim is about blood, not an open entrance.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: The claim is about blood, not an open entrance
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: The claim is about blood, not an open entrance
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the claim in the Mishnah is about blood, not an open entrance, as in Judea the husband cannot forbid her but can void the ketubah with a blood claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the claim is to forbid her to him, why would it not apply in Judea?
The Gemara answers: rather, the claim is to void her ketubah, and he is claiming about blood, not an open entrance.

items.text: The enactment and the question of its benefit
items.text_en: The enactment and the question of its benefit
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that the Sages enacted the ketubah amounts, and they believed the husband if he claims 'I found an open entrance'. The Gemara asks: if so, what did the Sages accomplish with their enactment? Rava answers: a presumption that a person does not trouble to prepare a feast and then ruin it.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that the Sages enacted the marriage contract amounts: two hundred dinars for a virgin and one hundred for a widow.

sub.text: continuation of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement
sub.text_en: continuation of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement
sub.desc_en: The same statement adds that the Sages deemed the groom credible if he claims he encountered an unobstructed orifice.
The Gemara asks: if the groom is believed to claim she is not a virgin, what did the Sages accomplish with their enactment of the two-hundred-dinar marriage contract?
Rava answers that the enactment is effective due to the presumption that a person does not exert himself to prepare a wedding feast and then cause it to be lost.

items.text: The ketubah is a rabbinic penalty and collected from inferior land
items.text_en: The ketubah is a rabbinic penalty and collected from inferior land
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught: since it is a rabbinic penalty, it is collected only from inferior land. The Gemara objects: what penalty? Rather, say: since it is a rabbinic enactment, it is collected only from inferior land. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: a woman's ketubah is from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that since the ketubah is a rabbinic penalty, it is collected only from the husband's most inferior land.
The Gemara challenges the baraita's use of the word 'penalty,' asking what penalty is involved in a ketubah.
The Gemara emends the baraita: rather than a penalty, the ketubah is a rabbinic enactment, and therefore collected only from inferior land.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissents, holding that a woman's ketubah is an obligation by Torah law.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statements and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statements and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a baraita states that the Sages derived support for the ketubah from the Torah, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the ketubah is not from the Torah but from the Scribes. The Gemara suggests reversing the attribution, but then cites a Mishnah where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the ketubah is from the Torah. Alternatively, the Gemara resolves that the entire baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but it is missing a clause: the ketubah of a virgin is from the Torah, but the ketubah of a widow is from the Scribes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is cited in a baraita saying the ketubah is not from the Torah but from the Scribes, contradicting his earlier statement that it is from the Torah.
The Gemara suggests reversing the attribution in the baraita to resolve the contradiction.
The Gemara objects that we have already heard Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explicitly say the ketubah is from the Torah in a Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but it is missing a clause: the ketubah of a virgin is from the Torah, while the ketubah of a widow is from the Scribes.

items.text: Case of a husband claiming 'open entrance' before Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Case of a husband claiming 'open entrance' before Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: A man came before Rav Nachman claiming 'I found an open entrance'. Rav Nachman said: give him lashes of reeds, you cursed one who struck? The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman himself said he is believed! The Gemara answers: he is believed, but we give him lashes. Rav Achai distinguishes: here it is a bachelor, there it is a married man.

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rav Nachman claiming 'I found an open entrance'; Rav Nachman ordered lashes and called him a cursed one who struck.
The Gemara questions: but Rav Nachman himself said the husband is believed!
The Gemara answers: he is believed, but we still give him lashes.
Rav Achai distinguishes: here it is a bachelor, there it is a married man.

items.text: Case before Rabban Gamliel and the parable of the door
items.text_en: Case before Rabban Gamliel and the parable of the door
items.desc_en: A man came before Rabban Gamliel claiming 'I found an open entrance'. Rabban Gamliel asked: perhaps you tilted it? He gave a parable of a person walking in the dark: if he tilted, he found it open; if not, he found it locked. Another version: perhaps you intentionally tilted and uprooted the door? The parable is similar but with intentional tilting.

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rabban Gamliel claiming he found an open entrance (i.e., the bride was not a virgin).
Rabban Gamliel asks the man: perhaps you tilted the door (i.e., had intercourse at an angle, causing no blood)?
Rabban Gamliel gives a parable of a person walking in the dark: if he tilted the door, he found it open; if not, he found it locked.
An alternative version reports that Rabban Gamliel asked: perhaps you intentionally tilted and uprooted the door (i.e., had intercourse with force, destroying the hymen without blood)?
The alternative version gives a similar parable but with intentional tilting: if he tilted intentionally, he found it open; if not, he found it locked.

items.text: Case before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi and the test with the cloth
items.text_en: Case before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi and the test with the cloth
items.desc_en: A man came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi saying he had intercourse and found no blood. The wife said she was a virgin. Rabban Gamliel asked for the cloth, soaked it in water, washed it, and found many drops of blood. He told the man: go, acquire your purchase. Huna Mar bar Rava from Parzikya asked Rav Ashi: should we also do this? Rav Ashi answered him.

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi claiming he found no blood; the wife insisted she was a virgin; Rabban Gamliel tested the cloth, found blood, and told the man to keep his purchase.

sub.text: Huna Mar bar Rava of Parzikya
sub.text_en: Huna Mar bar Rava of Parzikya
sub.desc_en: Huna Mar bar Rava of Parzikya asked Rav Ashi whether we should also perform this test.

items.text: Transition from previous sugya: glazing vs. laundering
items.text_en: Transition from previous sugya: glazing vs. laundering
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes a prior discussion about glazing (גיהוץ) and laundering, stating that their glazing is like their laundering, and if one were to do glazing it would cause a stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that their pressing is like our laundering, and pressing may damage the garment due to heat.

items.text: First case before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi: the wine barrel test
items.text_en: First case before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi: the wine barrel test
items.desc_en: A man comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi claiming he did not find blood; the woman claims she is still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel tests them by seating them on a wine barrel, and the virgin's scent does not emanate. He tells the man to keep his purchase. The Gemara explains that Rabban Gamliel had heard a tradition about this test but never saw it, and he was careful not to embarrass the daughters of Israel.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi claiming he found no blood, and the woman claims she is still a virgin.
Rabban Gamliel tests the woman by seating her on a wine barrel; her lack of scent proves her virginity, and he tells the man to keep her.
The Gemara asks why Rabban Gamliel did not test the woman directly, and answers that he had heard a tradition but never seen the test, and did not want to demean Jewish women.

items.text: Second case before Rabban Gamliel the Elder: the Dorketi family
items.text_en: Second case before Rabban Gamliel the Elder: the Dorketi family
items.desc_en: A man comes before Rabban Gamliel the Elder with the same claim; the woman says she is from the Dorketi family, which has no menstrual or virginity blood. Rabban Gamliel checks her relatives and confirms her words. He tells the man to keep his purchase, blessing him for marrying into that family. The Gemara explains Dorketi as 'a cut generation,' and Rabbi Chanina criticizes Rabban Gamliel's consolation as vain, citing a tradition that blood is beneficial for a woman, and Rabbi Meir adds that abundant blood leads to many children.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Rabban Gamliel the Elder claiming he found no blood, and the woman claims she is from the Dorketi family, which has no menstrual or virginity blood.
Rabban Gamliel checks the woman's relatives and confirms her claim, then tells the man to keep her and congratulates him on marrying into the Dorketi family.
The Gemara explains that Dorketi means 'a cut-off generation,' and cites Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Meir that blood is beneficial for a woman and promotes many children.

items.text: Dispute about Rabban Gamliel's wording: 'keep' or 'you are liable'
items.text_en: Dispute about Rabban Gamliel's wording: 'keep' or 'you are liable'
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei bar Avin about what Rabban Gamliel said: one says 'keep your purchase' (זְכֵה בְּמִקָּחֶךָ), the other says 'you are liable for your purchase' (נִתְחַיַּיבְתָּ בְּמִקָּחֶךָ). The one who says 'liable' aligns with Rabbi Chanina's criticism; the one who says 'keep' explains the merit is that he avoids uncertainty about niddah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says Rabban Gamliel said 'you have acquired your purchase,' while Rabbi Yosei bar Avin says he said 'you are liable for your purchase.'
The Gemara explains that 'liable' aligns with Rabbi Chanina's criticism, while 'acquired' means the man is spared from the doubt of menstrual impurity.

items.text: Case before Rabbi: fasting couple and the bathhouse
items.text_en: Case before Rabbi: fasting couple and the bathhouse
items.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi with the same claim; the woman says she is still a virgin. Rabbi sees they are emaciated from a fast, so he has them bathe, eat, and drink, then they have intercourse and find blood. Rabbi tells the man to keep his purchase and applies a verse about their skin shriveling.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Rabbi claiming he found no blood, and the woman claims she is still a virgin.
Rabbi sees their faces are black from fasting, has them bathed and fed, then the man finds blood, and Rabbi tells him to keep her.
Rabbi cites the verse 'their skin is shriveled on their bones, it has become dry like wood' to describe their condition.

items.text: Mishnah: basic ketubah amounts and the claim of virginity
items.text_en: Mishnah: basic ketubah amounts and the claim of virginity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a virgin's ketubah is 200 zuz, a widow's is 100. A virgin widow, divorcee, or chalutzah from betrothal also have 200 and are subject to a claim of virginity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the baseline ketubah amounts: a virgin gets 200, a widow gets 100, and a widow, divorcee, or חלוצה (halutzah) from betrothal also gets 200 and has a claim of virginity.

items.text: Gemara: etymology of 'almanah' and its connection to maneh
items.text_en: Gemara: etymology of 'almanah' and its connection to maneh
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'almanah' means. Rav Chana Bagdata'ah says it is named for 'maneh' (100 zuz). The Gemara questions a widow from betrothal and the biblical term, and resolves that the rabbis will later institute a maneh for her, citing a proof from a verse about the future.

items.text: Aggadic and lexicographical digressions: matar, mizbe'ach, tamrei, and more
items.text_en: Aggadic and lexicographical digressions: matar, mizbe'ach, tamrei, and more
items.desc_en: Rav Chana Bagdata'ah explains the word 'matar' (rain) as having five effects. Rava bar Rabbi Yishmael or Rav Yeimar bar Shelemya cites a verse. Rabbi Elazar explains 'mizbe'ach' (altar) as having four effects. Rav Chana Bagdata'ah explains that dates (tamrei) have five properties. Rav says one who eats dates should not teach; a baraisa contradicts this, and the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing before and after bread. Abaye cites his mother's proverb. The section ends with Rava, Rav Pappa, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak giving etymologies for 'dasha', 'darga', and 'purya'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Ketubah of female converts, captives, and slaves
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Ketubah of female converts, captives, and slaves
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a female convert, captive, or slave who was freed or converted before the age of three years and one day has a ketubah of 200 zuz and can claim virginity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a female convert, captive, or slave freed or converted before age three years and one day receives a ketubah of 200 zuz and retains the claim of virginity.

items.text: Gemara: Immersing a minor convert on the court's authority
items.text_en: Gemara: Immersing a minor convert on the court's authority
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a minor convert is immersed on the authority of the court. The Gemara questions what novel point this teaches, given the principle that one can benefit a person in their absence. It explains that a gentile might prefer being ownerless like a slave, but for a minor it is a benefit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a minor convert is immersed on the authority of the court.
The Gemara questions what novel point Rav Huna teaches, given the established principle that one can benefit a person in their absence but cannot harm them.
The Gemara suggests that one might think a gentile prefers being ownerless like a slave, so conversion might not be a clear benefit.
The Gemara resolves that for an adult gentile, the preference for ownerlessness applies, but for a minor, conversion is unequivocally a benefit.

items.text: Attempted support from the Mishnah and its rejection
items.text_en: Attempted support from the Mishnah and its rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Huna from the Mishnah's case of a female convert under three, suggesting she was immersed on court authority. It rejects this, explaining that the case is where she converted with her father, so she consents to his actions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to support Rav Huna from the Mishnah's case of a female convert under three, suggesting that her immersion was performed on court authority (על דעת בית דין).
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that the Mishnah's case is where the minor converted together with her father, so she consents to his actions (ניחא להו במאי דעביד אבוהון).

items.text: Rav Yosef: Minors can protest upon reaching majority
items.text_en: Rav Yosef: Minors can protest upon reaching majority
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that when minor converts reach majority, they can protest their conversion. Abaye objects from the Mishnah that gives a ketubah to a female convert under three, implying she cannot later protest and eat non-kosher food. The Gemara answers that if she does not protest within an hour of reaching majority, she can no longer protest.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that when minor converts reach majority, they can protest their conversion.
Abaye objects from the Mishnah that gives a ketubah of 200 zuz to a female convert under three, implying she cannot later protest and eat non-kosher food.
The Gemara answers that the ketubah is given for when she reaches majority, and if she does not protest within an hour of reaching majority, she can no longer protest.

items.text: Rava's objection from the law of fines
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the law of fines
items.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita that gives a fine for intercourse with a female convert under three, implying she cannot later protest. The Gemara gives the same answer: if she does not protest within an hour of majority, she loses the right.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects from a baraita listing female converts under three who are subject to a fine (קנס), arguing that if they could later protest their conversion, the fine would be paid to a woman who might revert to gentile status.
The Gemara answers that the fine is paid when she reaches majority, but if she does not protest within one hour of majority, she loses the right to protest, so the fine is secure.

items.text: Distinction between ketubah and fine
items.text_en: Distinction between ketubah and fine
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava each explain why they do not accept the other's objection: Abaye says the fine is to prevent the sinner from profiting, so it applies even if she could protest; Rava says the ketubah is to prevent easy divorce, so it applies even if she could protest.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that he does not accept Rava's reasoning because the fine (קנס) is meant to prevent the sinner from profiting, so it applies even if she could protest.
Rava explains that he does not accept Abaye's reasoning because the ketubah (כתובה) is meant to prevent easy divorce, so it applies even if she could protest.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of non-virginity and ketubah amounts
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of non-virginity and ketubah amounts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where a man has intercourse with a minor, a woman with a minor, or a woman injured by wood; Rabbi Meir says their ketubah is 200 zuz, while the Sages say for one injured by wood it is 100. It also states that a widow, divorcee, or חלוצה from marriage has a ketubah of 100.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with cases where a man has intercourse with a minor, a woman with a minor, or a woman injured by wood, and states that Rabbi Meir rules their ketubah is 200 zuz.
The Sages disagree, ruling that for a woman injured by wood the ketubah is only 100 zuz.
The Mishnah concludes that a widow, divorcee, or חלוצה (a woman who performed חליצה) from marriage has a ketubah of 100 zuz.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Exemptions from claims of virginity
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Exemptions from claims of virginity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a convert, captive, or freed slave who is over three years and one day old has a ketubah of one maneh and no claim of virginity can be made against them.

items.text: Gemara: Rav and Shmuel on a minor and a mukkat etz
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav and Shmuel on a minor and a mukkat etz
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that a minor who has intercourse with an adult woman makes her a mukkat etz. Shmuel disagrees, saying there is no concept of mukkat etz in flesh. An alternative version presents this as a direct dispute between Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's objection and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's objection and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir gives a ketubah of 200 for a mukkat etz, while the Sages say 100. Rava explains the baraita: an adult with a minor is nothing, a minor with an adult makes her a mukkat etz, and the dispute is about the mukkat etz itself.

items.text: Rami bar Hama's distinction and the reasoning of Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama's distinction and the reasoning of Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama suggests the dispute is only when he knew she was a mukkat etz: Rabbi Meir compares her to a bogeret (who gets 200), the Sages to a be'ulah (who gets 100). The Gemara questions why each doesn't compare to the other, and explains based on whether a human act was involved.

items.text: Rav Nachman's objection and Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection and Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects with a case where she claims mukkat etz and he claims seduction, and Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer deem her credible. Rava then says that for Rabbi Meir, whether he knew or not, it's 200; for the Sages, if he knew, it's 100, if not, nothing.

items.text: Rava's retraction and the baraita on motzi shem ra
items.text_en: Rava's retraction and the baraita on motzi shem ra
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a husband who claims his wife was not a virgin, distinguishing between adultery after marriage (stoning) and before (ketubah of 100). Rav Chiya bar Avin quotes Rav Sheshet that if he married her presuming virginity and she was not, she gets 100. Rav Nachman objects with a case where she claims rape after betrothal and he claims a mistaken purchase, implying she gets nothing. Rav Chiya bar Avin clarifies that the 'mistaken purchase' refers only to the extra 100, but she still gets the basic 100.

items.text: Rava's resolution and confirmation of retraction
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and confirmation of retraction
items.desc_en: Rava says the objector is correct: 'mistaken purchase' implies nothing at all. He resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita: if she committed adultery before marriage, she gets nothing; if she is a mukkat etz, she gets 100. The Gemara notes that Rava previously said for the Sages, if he didn't know, she gets nothing, so this shows Rava retracted.

items.text: Baraita: First husband's marriage prevents second husband's claim
items.text_en: Baraita: First husband's marriage prevents second husband's claim
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a woman was married to a first husband with witnesses that she was not secluded or not long enough for intercourse, the second husband cannot claim she was not a virgin, since the first husband already married her.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on a woman found non-virgin after marriage
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on a woman found non-virgin after marriage
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Ashi debate whether a woman who was married under the presumption of virginity but found to be non-virgin is entitled to a ketubah of 200 zuz (maneh). Rav Sheravya addresses the concern that she might have committed adultery after betrothal by stating the case involves immediate intercourse after betrothal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states that a woman married under the presumption of virginity who is found to be a non-virgin is entitled to a marriage contract of one hundred dinars.

Rav Ashi counters that generally she would receive nothing, but here she does because the first husband brought her into his house, so the second husband should have anticipated she might not be a virgin.
The Gemara raises a concern that perhaps she committed adultery after betrothal, which would forbid her to the second husband and void her ketubah.
Rav Sherevya answers that the case involves immediate intercourse after betrothal, leaving no opportunity for adultery.
An alternative version applies the same debate to the mishna, explaining how a virgin from a state of marriage is possible: she entered the wedding canopy but did not engage in intercourse.
Rabbah repeats his position in the context of the mishna: a woman married under presumption of virginity who is found non-virgin receives a ketubah of one hundred dinars.
Rav Ashi again distinguishes: generally she gets nothing, but here she entered the wedding canopy, so the husband should have anticipated she might not be a virgin.
The Gemara again raises the concern of adultery after betrothal.
Rav Sherevya repeats that the case involves immediate intercourse after betrothal, eliminating the opportunity for adultery.

items.text: Clarification of the two versions of the statement
items.text_en: Clarification of the two versions of the statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the version of the statement attached to the baraita applies even more so to the mishnah, while the version attached to the mishnah does not apply to the baraita because the husband can claim he relied on witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the two versions: the version attached to the baraita applies all the more so to the mishnah, while the version attached to the mishnah does not apply to the baraita because the husband can claim he relied on witnesses.

items.text: Mishnah: Eating at father-in-law's in Judea without witnesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Eating at father-in-law's in Judea without witnesses
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a man eats at his father-in-law's house in Judea without witnesses, he cannot claim non-virginity because he was secluded with her.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that a man who eats at his father-in-law's house in Judea without witnesses cannot later claim non-virginity, because the couple was secluded together.

items.text: Gemara on the mishnah and the custom of seclusion in Judea
items.text_en: Gemara on the mishnah and the custom of seclusion in Judea
items.desc_en: Abaye infers from the mishnah that there are places in Judea where one does not eat at the father-in-law's. A baraita describes the Judean custom of secluding the groom and bride before the wedding and having attendants. The Gemara resolves a textual difficulty in the baraita regarding the phrase 'one who did not act according to this custom'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the mishnah's phrasing 'the one who eats' that there are places in Judea where one does not eat at the father-in-law's.
Abaye asserts that even in Judea there were different places with different customs.
A baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda describes the Judean custom of secluding the groom and bride an hour before the wedding, which was not done in the Galilee.
The Gemara questions the baraita's phrase 'one who did not act according to this custom' — if it refers to the beginning of the baraita, the text should read 'one who acted'.
If it refers to the end of the baraita, the text should read 'one who was not attended'.
Abaye resolves that the baraita refers to the beginning and should be emended to read 'one who acted'.
Rava objects that the baraita explicitly says 'one who did not act', not 'one who acted'.
Rava explains that the baraita means: one who did not follow the Galilean custom in the Galilee but followed the Judean custom in the Galilee cannot claim virginity.
Rav Ashi resolves that the baraita refers to the end and should be emended to read 'one who was not attended'.

items.text: Mishnah: Ketubah of a widow of an Israelite and a priest
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ketubah of a widow of an Israelite and a priest
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that both a widow of an Israelite and a widow of a priest have a ketubah of 200 zuz (maneh), and that the priestly court would collect 400 zuz for a virgin, and the Sages did not protest.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that both a widow of an Israelite and a widow of a priest have a ketubah of 200 zuz, and the priestly court would collect 400 zuz for a virgin without the Sages protesting.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction regarding widow of a priest's ketubah
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction regarding widow of a priest's ketubah
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a widow of a priest has a ketubah of 400 zuz, contradicting the mishnah. Rav Ashi resolves this by explaining there were two enactments: originally, a virgin received 400 zuz and a widow 200 zuz.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita that says a priest's widow's ketubah is 200 zuz, and questions the contradiction with the mishnah which says both widows have 200 zuz.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that there were two enactments: originally they enacted 400 zuz for a virgin and 200 zuz for a widow, and later they changed it.

Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that there were two enactments: originally, the Sages enacted 400 zuz for a virgin and 100 zuz for a widow, and the baraita reflects the original enactment while the mishnah reflects the later one.

items.text: Enactment of the ketubah for widows of priests
items.text_en: Enactment of the ketubah for widows of priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when the Sages saw that people were disparaging the ketubah of two hundred zuz for widows of priests, they enacted a ketubah of two hundred zuz. When they saw that men were avoiding marrying them, they restored the original enactment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when the Sages saw people disparaging the ketubah of two hundred zuz for widows of priests, they enacted a ketubah of two hundred zuz, and when they saw men avoiding marrying them, they restored the original enactment.

items.text: Priestly court and other families
items.text_en: Priestly court and other families
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that not only a priestly court, but even well-established families in Israel may act in the manner of priests. A challenge is raised from a baraita that limits this practice to cases involving a priestly connection. The Gemara resolves that the baraita is not excluding other cases but rather clarifying that even in cases with a priestly connection, one might think it is not permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that not only a priestly court, but even well-established families in Israel may act in the manner of priests.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that limits the practice to cases involving a priestly connection, implying that a non-priestly Israelite couple cannot do so.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is not excluding other cases but rather clarifying that even in a case with a priestly connection, one might think it is not permitted, so it teaches that it is.

items.text: Mishnah: The husband who did not find virginity
items.text_en: Mishnah: The husband who did not find virginity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a husband claims he did not find virginity, and the wife claims she was raped after betrothal. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer deem her credible, while Rabbi Yehoshua says she is not believed unless she brings proof.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a husband finds no signs of virginity, with the wife claiming she was raped after betrothal and the husband claiming she was not a virgin before betrothal, and records the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer (who deem her credible) and Rabbi Yehoshua (who requires proof).
Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer rule that the wife is believed, accepting her claim of rape after betrothal.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects, ruling that the wife is not believed unless she brings proof, as she is presumed to have been a non-virgin before betrothal.

items.text: Dispute about 'Maneh li b'yadcha'
items.text_en: Dispute about 'Maneh li b'yadcha'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: If one claims 'I have a maneh in your hand' and the other says 'I don't know', Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna say he is liable (because bari is stronger), while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan say he is exempt (because we leave the money in its owner's possession).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about a case where one claims 'I have a maneh in your hand' and the other says 'I don't know', with Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna ruling liable, and Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan ruling exempt.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda explain their ruling: the certainty of the claimant (ברי) is preferable to the uncertainty of the defendant (שמא).

sub.text: Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan explain their ruling: we place the money in the possession of its owner (the defendant) by default.

items.text: Linking the dispute to Rabban Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: Linking the dispute to Rabban Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye says that Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda's view follows Shmuel, who ruled like Rabban Gamliel in the Mishnah. Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda adds that Shmuel ruled like Rabban Gamliel even in the first case, meaning that despite the principle of leaving money in its owner's possession, Rabban Gamliel holds that bari is stronger.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asserts to Rav Yosef that the position of Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda follows Shmuel's ruling.
Abaye cites the Mishnah about a pregnant woman claiming the child is from a priest, where Rabban Gamliel deems her credible, and Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabban Gamliel.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda to Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports to Rav Yehuda that Shmuel ruled like Rabban Gamliel even in the first case, explaining that despite the principle of leaving money in its owner's possession, Rabban Gamliel holds that ברי (the definite claim) is stronger.

items.text: Rejection of the parallel and resolution
items.text_en: Rejection of the parallel and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna follow Rabban Gamliel, while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan follow Rabbi Yehoshua. Rav Nachman rejects this, arguing that Rabban Gamliel's ruling there was based on a migo or a chazaka, which is absent here. The Gemara concludes that Rav Nachman indeed holds like Rabban Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna follow Rabban Gamliel, while Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan follow Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rav Nachman rejects the parallel, arguing that Rabban Gamliel's ruling there relied on a מיגו (a litigant's credible claim that could have been made differently), which is absent here.
Rav Nachman offers an alternative rejection: Rabban Gamliel's ruling there relied on a חזקה (presumption of innocence), which is absent in the monetary case.
The Gemara concludes that the reasoning stands, and Rav Nachman indeed holds like Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction in the previous sugya
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction in the previous sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between the ruling of Rav Nachman in monetary cases and the ruling of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel, concluding that the earlier resolution is correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between Rav Nachman's monetary ruling and Shmuel's ruling that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel, concluding that the earlier resolution is correct.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about a woman's claim of being a virgin
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about a woman's claim of being a virgin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman claims she was a virgin at marriage (and thus entitled to 200 zuz), while the husband claims she was not. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer rule she is believed; Rabbi Yehoshua rules she is not believed and remains in the presumptive state of a non-virgin until she brings proof.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman claims she is a victim of a wooden injury (still a virgin) and the husband claims she was raped, with Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer believing her, while Rabbi Yehoshua says she is presumed raped until she brings proof.

items.text: Gemara: What is the dispute about?
items.text_en: Gemara: What is the dispute about?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the precise claim is. Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute is about 200 vs. 100 (the full ketubah), while Rabbi Elazar says it is about 100 vs. nothing (the basic ketubah). Each is explained as aligning with either Rabbi Meir or the Rabbis regarding the ketubah of a woman whose husband did not know she was a non-virgin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the precise claim in the Mishnah is about.
Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute is about 200 (full ketubah) vs. 100 (basic ketubah).
Rabbi Elazar says the dispute is about 100 (basic ketubah) vs. nothing.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan aligns with Rabbi Meir, who says the ketubah is 200 regardless of whether the husband knew she was a non-virgin.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar aligns with the Rabbis, who say the ketubah is 100 regardless of whether the husband knew she was a non-virgin.

items.text: Why doesn't Rabbi Yochanan agree with Rabbi Elazar?
items.text_en: Why doesn't Rabbi Yochanan agree with Rabbi Elazar?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not adopt Rabbi Elazar's view. It explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds that if a man married a woman presuming she was a virgin and she was found to be a non-virgin, she still gets 100. In this case, both claim 100, so what is the difference between their claims?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not adopt Rabbi Elazar's view, given that Rabbi Elazar's position is consistent with the Rabbis.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds that if a man married a woman presuming she was a virgin and she was found to be a non-virgin, she still gets 100; thus in this case both claim 100, so there is no practical difference between their claims.

items.text: Why two cases in the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Why two cases in the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah includes two cases (the woman's claim and the man's claim). For Rabbi Elazar, one case excludes the view of Rami bar Hama and the other excludes the view of Rav Chiya bar Avin. For Rabbi Yochanan, one case shows the strength of Rabbi Yehoshua (even with a migo she is not believed) and the other shows the strength of Rabban Gamliel (even without a migo she is believed).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for Rabbi Elazar, the Mishnah's two cases are necessary: one to exclude the view of Rami bar Hama.
The Gemara adds that the second case excludes the view of Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rav Sheshet, then asks why Rabbi Yochanan would need two cases.

The Gemara answers that for Rabbi Yochanan, one case demonstrates the strength of Rabbi Yehoshua (even with a migo she is not believed) and the other demonstrates the strength of Rabban Gamliel (even without a migo she is believed).

items.text: Second Mishnah: Cases of a woman seen speaking or pregnant
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Cases of a woman seen speaking or pregnant
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: a woman seen speaking with a man, and a pregnant woman, both claiming the man is a priest. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer believe her, while Rabbi Yehoshua says she is presumed to be with a non-priest (a נתין or ממזר) until she brings proof.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a woman seen speaking with a man claims he is a priest; Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer deem her credible, while Rabbi Yehoshua presumes she is with a נתין or ממזר until she brings proof.
The Mishnah presents the second case: a pregnant woman claims the father is a priest; the same dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer versus Rabbi Yehoshua applies.

items.text: Gemara: What does 'speaking' mean?
items.text_en: Gemara: What does 'speaking' mean?
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the meaning of 'speaking' (מדברת). Ze'iri says it means she was secluded, while Rav Asi says it means she was actually intimate. The Gemara explains why two cases are needed for Rav Asi: one to disqualify her, and one to disqualify her daughter. It also notes that Rav Asi holds the view that one who disqualifies the mother also disqualifies the daughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishna's term מְדַבֶּרֶת (speaking) actually denotes.
Ze'eiri says מְדַבֶּרֶת means she was secluded with the man, not that intercourse occurred.
Rav Asi says מְדַבֶּרֶת means she actually engaged in intercourse.
The Gemara notes that Ze'eiri's reading fits the term מְדַבֶּרֶת, but challenges why Rav Asi's reading would use that term.
The Gemara answers that מְדַבֶּרֶת is a euphemism, citing the verse about the licentious woman who 'eats and wipes her mouth.'
The Gemara asks why the mishna needs both the מְדַבֶּרֶת case and the מְעוּבֶּרֶת case according to Rav Asi.
The Gemara answers that one case deems her fit to marry a priest, and the other deems her daughter fit.
The Gemara objects that this answer only works for the view that deeming the mother fit also deems the daughter fit, but not for the opposing view.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Asi holds the view that one who deems the mother fit also deems her daughter fit.

items.text: Challenge from Rav's ruling on seclusion
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav's ruling on seclusion
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Ze'iri's interpretation: if 'speaking' means seclusion, then Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling contradicts Rav's statement that seclusion is punishable by lashes but does not render a woman forbidden. The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehoshua's stringency is a special enactment regarding lineage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges Abaye: according to Ze'iri who interprets 'speaking' as seclusion, Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling that she is not believed contradicts Rav's principle that seclusion warrants lashes but does not forbid the woman.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehoshua's stringency is a special enactment regarding lineage (מעלה עשו ביוחסין), so it does not contradict Rav's general rule.

items.text: Beginning of a new challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of a new challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita that challenges the previous discussion, describing a case where a woman was seen entering a secluded place with a man.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a woman seen entering a secluded place with a man.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer believe a woman is believed when she says she was raped by a Kohen, while Rabbi Yehoshua says she is not believed and is presumed to have been violated by a Netin or Mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer believe a woman is believed when she says she was raped by a Kohen, while Rabbi Yehoshua says she is not believed and is presumed to have been violated by a Netin or Mamzer.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah mentions two cases (seclusion and ruin) according to Ze'iri and Rav Asi. It then justifies the need for both cases to clarify the positions of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding different majorities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions two scenarios (secret place or ruin), noting that according to Ze'eiri both are needed, but according to Rav Asi who says the woman was violated, only one scenario is needed.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah actually teaches two distinct cases: a ruin in town (where most are kosher) and a ruin in the wilderness (where most are unfit), and both are necessary to show the limits of the dispute.
The Gemara concludes that both cases are necessary to prevent one side from conceding to the other in the opposite scenario.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and the debate about a captive woman
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and the debate about a captive woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yehoshua compares the woman to a captive who claims purity but is not believed. The Sages distinguish between cases with and without witnesses, but Rabbi Yehoshua argues that her belly between her teeth is a witness. The Sages counter that most gentiles are promiscuous, and Rabbi Yehoshua responds that there is no guardian for forbidden relations.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehoshua challenges the Sages: do they not agree that a captive woman who has witnesses to her captivity is not believed to claim she is pure?
The Sages respond that they agree, but distinguish: the captive has witnesses, while this woman has no witnesses.

Rabbi Yehoshua objects that this woman also has witnesses — her pregnant belly — and when the Sages counter that most gentiles are promiscuous, he retorts that there is no guardian for forbidden relations.
Rabbi Yehoshua argues that this woman also has a witness — her belly between her teeth (i.e., her pregnancy).
The Sages counter that most gentiles are promiscuous, and Rabbi Yehoshua responds that there is no guardian for forbidden relations.

items.text: Distinction between the woman's testimony about herself and about her daughter
items.text_en: Distinction between the woman's testimony about herself and about her daughter
items.desc_en: The baraita states that the dispute applies only to the woman's testimony about herself, but regarding her daughter, all agree the child is a shetuki.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara shifts to note that the dispute applies only to the woman's own testimony, but regarding her daughter's status, all agree the child is a שתוקי (silenced one).

items.text: Clarification of the debate and refutation of Rav Asi
items.text_en: Clarification of the debate and refutation of Rav Asi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the exchange between Rabbi Yehoshua and the Sages, distinguishing between a pregnant woman and a non-pregnant one. It concludes that the baraita teaches two cases (speaking and pregnant), which refutes Rav Asi's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehoshua said to the Sages and what they replied.
The Gemara explains that the Sages said to Rabbi Yehoshua: 'You answered us regarding the pregnant woman; what will you answer regarding the speaking woman?'
Rabbi Yehoshua replied that the speaking woman is the same as the captive woman.
The Sages objected that a captive woman is different because most gentiles are promiscuous in sexual matters.
Rabbi Yehoshua rejected this, arguing that here too, since she was secluded, there is no guardian for sexual matters.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita indeed teaches two cases (speaking and pregnant), which is a conclusive refutation of Rav Asi's position.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the distinction between majorities supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that the one who permits permits even with a majority of unfit people, and the one who disqualifies disqualifies even with a majority of fit people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the distinction of majority (רוב) was not raised, and supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that the disputants hold their positions even in the opposite majority scenario.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar about the daughter's status
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar about the daughter's status
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree: Rabbi Yochanan says the one who permits the mother permits the daughter, while Rabbi Elazar says the one who permits the mother disqualifies the daughter. The Gemara explains Rabbi Elazar's reasoning and brings a proof from the baraita, interpreting 'shetuki' as either valid or invalid, and concludes with an explanation of the term 'shetuki' based on Shmuel's statement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that according to the one who permits the mother, the daughter is also permitted.
Rabbi Elazar counters that according to the one who permits the mother, the daughter is disqualified.
Rabbah explains Rabbi Elazar's reasoning: the mother has a presumption of fitness (חזקה דכשרות), but the daughter lacks such a presumption.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects to Rabbi Yochanan by citing the baraita that for a woman's testimony about her daughter, the child is universally a 'shetuki' (silenced one).
The Gemara asks whether 'shetuki' here means invalid (פסול).
The Gemara answers that 'shetuki' here means valid (כשר).
The Gemara questions whether a 'shetuki' can ever be valid.
The Gemara supports the possibility by citing Shmuel's case of ten priests standing where one had relations, making the child a 'shetuki' but still valid.
The Gemara asks for the precise meaning of 'shetuki'.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that 'shetuki' means silenced from inheritance, since the father is unknown.
The Gemara concludes that 'shetuki' means silenced from the law of priesthood, based on the verse that requires lineage for priestly status.

items.text: Introduction of a new case: a betrothed couple
items.text_en: Introduction of a new case: a betrothed couple
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new narrative about a betrothed couple who came before Rav Yosef, where she claims the pregnancy is from him and he denies it.

sub.desc_en: A story is introduced about a betrothed couple who came before Rav Yosef, where she claimed the child was from him and he denied it.

items.text: Rav Yosef's support for Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's support for Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that there is no need to be concerned about the woman's claim because she admits to being raped, and moreover, Shmuel ruled that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rav Yosef's argument that there is no concern about the woman's claim because she admits to being raped.
Rav Yosef states that there is no need to be concerned because the woman admits to being raped.
Rav Yosef adds that Shmuel ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that even Rabban Gamliel requires a majority of kosher people, but here there is a majority of invalid people. The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's ruling applies lechatchilah, while the case at hand is bedi'avad.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that even Rabban Gamliel requires a majority of kosher people, but here there is a majority of invalid people.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's ruling applies לכתחילה (the ideal standard), while the case at hand is בדיעבד (after the fact).

items.text: Abaye's contradiction from the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Abaye's contradiction from the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yehoshua ruled that a woman is not believed, yet he testified that an 'almanat isah' is fit for the priesthood. Rava distinguishes: there the woman investigates before marriage, here she investigates before adultery.

sub.desc_en: Abaye raises a contradiction to Rava: Rabbi Yehoshua ruled that a woman is not believed about her own status, yet he testified that an 'almanat isah' (a widow of a questionable marriage) is fit for the priesthood.
Rava distinguishes: there, a woman investigates before marriage (so the testimony is reliable), but here, a woman does not investigate before adultery (so she is not believed).

items.text: Rava's initial question on Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Rava's initial question on Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rava asks why only Rabbi Yehoshua's contradiction is raised; Rabban Gamliel also appears contradictory, as he accepted testimony but cited Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's decree not to convene a court.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions why only Rabbi Yehoshua's contradiction is raised, pointing out that Rabban Gamliel also appears contradictory: he accepted testimony but cited Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's decree not to convene a court.

items.text: Rava's resolution using bari, shema, and safeik
items.text_en: Rava's resolution using bari, shema, and safeik
items.desc_en: Rava resolves both contradictions: Rabban Gamliel distinguishes between a definite claim (bari) and a possible claim (shema); Rabbi Yehoshua distinguishes between one uncertainty (safeik) and two uncertainties (safeik safeika). The Gemara summarizes the principles for each.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction within Rabban Gamliel by distinguishing between a definite claim (בָּרִי) and a possible claim (שֶׁמָּא), and within Rabbi Yehoshua by distinguishing between one uncertainty (חַד סְפֵיקָא) and two uncertainties (תְּרֵי סְפֵיקֵי).

The Gemara summarizes the halachic principles: for Rabban Gamliel, a definite claim is strong enough to permit even with one uncertainty, while a possible claim is weak enough to disqualify even with two uncertainties; for Rabbi Yehoshua, one uncertainty is strong enough to disqualify even with a definite claim, while two uncertainties are weak enough to permit even with a possible claim.

items.text: Definition of 'almanat isah'
items.text_en: Definition of 'almanat isah'
items.desc_en: The Tanna'im define 'almanat isah' as a woman who is not disqualified due to mamzerut, netinut, or royal slaves. Rabbi Meir begins to speak.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma defines 'almanat isah' as a woman who is not disqualified due to mamzerut, netinut, or royal slaves.
Rabbi Meir begins to speak, introducing his own position on the definition.

items.text: Opening statement: definition of almanat isa
items.text_en: Opening statement: definition of almanat isa
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that any woman who does not have any of these disqualifications (mamzer, netin, or slave) may be married into the priesthood.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that any woman without any of the listed disqualifications may be married into the priesthood.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's definition and additional statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's definition and additional statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya define almanat isa as one who is mixed with a safek challal. They add that Israelites recognize the mamzerim among them but not the challalim.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya define 'almanat isa' as a woman in whom a doubt of חלל (disqualified priest) is mixed, and note that Israel recognizes mamzerim among them but not חללים.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
sub.desc_en: They add that Israelites recognize the ממזרים (bastards) among them but not the חללים (disqualified priests).

items.text: Gemara's question: contradiction between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Gemara's question: contradiction between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the redundancy between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Meir, and points out an internal contradiction in Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement: first it says challal is valid, then it says challalim are not recognized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna Kamma's definition of 'עיסה (mixed) widow' excludes only mamzer, netin, and slave lineages, implying challal is valid, and then notes that Rabbi Meir's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, creating a redundancy.

The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement: the first part defines the widow as one with a ספק חלל (doubtful challal) and says challal is valid, but the second part says challalim are not recognized, implying they are invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: mamzer shouts, challal is silent
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: mamzer shouts, challal is silent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains the dispute: the Tanna Kamma considers any silent person who is called a disqualification as invalid, while Rabbi Meir holds that only a silent mamzer is invalid (since a mamzer would shout), but a silent challal is valid. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that a silent mamzer is valid because he might not care, but a mamzer who shouts and a challal who is silent are invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan introduces the key distinction between a mamzer who shouts and a challal who is silent, explaining that the Tanna Kamma considers any silent person called by a disqualification as invalid.
Rabbi Meir holds that only a silent mamzer is invalid because he would shout if he were not a mamzer, but a silent challal is valid because he might not care about the designation.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar clarifies that Rabbi Meir only validates a silent mamzer (who might not care), but a mamzer who shouts and a challal who is silent are invalid.

items.text: Reconciliation of two baraitot about Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Reconciliation of two baraitot about Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Two contradictory baraitot are cited: one says a silent mamzer is valid and a silent challal is invalid, the other says the opposite. The Gemara resolves that one follows the Tanna Kamma's understanding of Rabbi Meir, and the other follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's understanding of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Yosei rules that a silent mamzer (שתוק ממזר) is כשר (fit for marriage into the community), while a silent challal (שתוק חלל) is פסול (unfit).
A second contradictory baraita is cited, which reverses the ruling: a silent challal is כשר and a silent mamzer is פסול.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita follows the Tanna Kamma's understanding of Rabbi Meir's position, while the second baraita follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's understanding of Rabbi Meir's position.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: case of a raped girl and the principle of majority
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: case of a raped girl and the principle of majority
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yosei's story of a girl who was raped, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules that if most townspeople marry into the priesthood, she may too. The Gemara questions whether this follows Rabban Gamliel (who follows the majority even among disqualifications) or Rabbi Yehoshua (who requires a majority of valid people).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yosei's story of a girl who was raped, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules that if most townspeople marry into the priesthood, she may marry a priest.

Rava asks Rav Nachman whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's ruling aligns with Rabban Gamliel (who follows the majority even among disqualifications) or Rabbi Yehoshua (who requires a majority of valid people).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's answer citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds by citing a tradition from Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, which presumably resolves the question.

items.text: Opening case: the fairs of Tzippori
items.text_en: Opening case: the fairs of Tzippori
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case involving the fairs of Tzippori, citing Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yannai: a woman violated during the fair is fit for the priesthood, but if an individual separated from the city and raped her, the child is a shetuki (of unknown status).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case involving the fairs of Tzippori, linking it to Rabbi Ami's principle.
Rabbi Ami states that the case applies when a group of fit people was passing through.
Rabbi Yannai rules that a woman violated during the fair is fit for the priesthood.
The Gemara objects: can one be violated at the fair itself? It clarifies: violated during the time of the fair.
The Gemara distinguishes: if an individual separated from Tzippori and raped her, the child is a shetuki (of unknown status).

items.text: Ze'iri's ruling: follow majority of city, not majority of group
items.text_en: Ze'iri's ruling: follow majority of city, not majority of group
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Ze'iri quoting Rabbi Chanina: we follow the majority of the city, not the majority of the traveling group.

sub.text: Rav Dimi citing Ze'iri citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi citing Ze'iri citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Ze'iri quoting Rabbi Chanina that we follow the majority of the city, not the majority of the traveling group.

items.text: Refinement: need both majorities
items.text_en: Refinement: need both majorities
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ruling: the group is fixed (kavua) and the city is scattered, so the opposite should apply. It resolves: we follow the majority of the city only when there is also a majority of the group with her, but not either alone, due to a decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the group is fixed (קבוע) and the city is scattered, so the opposite ruling should apply.
The Gemara resolves: we follow the majority of the city only when there is also a majority of the group with her, due to a decree (גזירה) to prevent confusion between the two majorities.

items.text: Application of 'kavua' principle
items.text_en: Application of 'kavua' principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when she goes to them, the situation is fixed (kavua), and Rabbi Zeira states that anything fixed is considered like half-and-half.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the application of the majority principle when the men come to her, since each one who separates from the group is considered to separate from the majority.
The Gemara resolves that the case is when she goes to them, making the situation fixed (קָבוּעַ), and Rabbi Zeira's principle applies: anything fixed is considered like half-and-half.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita of nine stores
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita of nine stores
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the need for two majorities from a baraita about nine stores selling kosher meat and one selling non-kosher: if one buys from an unknown store, the doubt is forbidden, but if the meat is found, follow the majority. Rabbi Zeira notes that even with locked city gates, a stringency was made for lineage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether two majorities are required, citing the baraita of nine stores.
The Gemara raises an objection that even with locked city gates, a stringency was made for lineage, citing Rabbi Zeira.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Zeira's principle of 'kavua'
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Zeira's principle of 'kavua'
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for Rabbi Zeira's rule that 'kavua' is like half-and-half. It considers and rejects the baraita of nine stores and the cases of nine frogs and one reptile, concluding that the source is the biblical verse 'and he lay in wait for him' (Deut. 19:11), excluding one who throws a stone into a group.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Zeira's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Zeira's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Zeira's principle that any 'kavua' (fixed item) is treated as half-and-half, both leniently and stringently.
The Gemara asks for the source of Rabbi Zeira's principle and proposes the baraita of nine stores, but rejects it because that case is only stringent.
The Gemara proposes the case of nine frogs and one reptile, but rejects it as also only stringent.
The Gemara proposes the case of nine reptiles and one frog, which has both lenient and stringent rulings, but this is only a rabbinic enactment.
The Gemara asks for the Torah source, and the school of Rabbi Yannai answers with the verse 'and he lay in wait for him' (Deut. 19:11), excluding one who throws a stone into a group.

items.text: Application of 'kavua' to the case of nine Jews and one gentile
items.text_en: Application of 'kavua' to the case of nine Jews and one gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the case: if there are nine Jews and one gentile, the gentile is fixed, and the principle of 'kavua' applies, making it like half-and-half.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the case is configured, rejecting the possibility of nine gentiles and one Jew because the majority would be gentiles or the case would be a doubt about capital law which is lenient.
The Gemara answers that the case involves nine Jews and one gentile, making the gentile fixed (קבוע), and the principle of 'kavua' applies, treating it as half-and-half.

items.text: Final dispute: halakha vs. hora'at sha'ah
items.text_en: Final dispute: halakha vs. hora'at sha'ah
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi says in the name of Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, while Rav Chanan bar Rava says it was a hora'at sha'ah (emergency ruling). Rabbi Yirmeya challenges whether we need two majorities for lineage, citing a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi reports in the name of Rav that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava counters that Rav's ruling was only a הוראת שעה (emergency directive), not a permanent law.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: do we not require two majorities (תרי רובי) for lineage matters? He cites a mishnah as evidence.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Found infant
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Found infant
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a found infant is in a place where the majority are gentiles, the infant is considered gentile; if the majority are Jews, it is Jewish; if half and half, it is Jewish.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a found infant: follow the majority of the local population to determine whether the infant is Jewish or gentile, and in a tie the infant is treated as Jewish.

items.text: Gemara: Rav and Shmuel's dispute and a difficulty
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav and Shmuel's dispute and a difficulty
items.desc_en: Rav says the Mishnah's ruling applies only for saving the infant's life, not for lineage. Shmuel says it applies for clearing a collapsed pile. The Gemara notes a difficulty from Rav's own statement about an incident in Tzippori, and another from Rav Chanan bar Rava's teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rav limits the Mishnah's ruling: it applies only for saving the infant's life, not for determining lineage.
Shmuel says the Mishnah's ruling applies for clearing a collapsed pile on the infant.

sub.text: Gemara's difficulty from Rav's own statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's difficulty from Rav's own statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a difficulty from Rav's own statement about an incident in Tzippori that seems to contradict his position.

sub.text: Gemara's difficulty from Rav Chanan bar Rava
sub.text_en: Gemara's difficulty from Rav Chanan bar Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty from Rav Chanan bar Rava's teaching that the incident was a temporary ruling.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by noting that the two traditions (Rav's and Rav Chanan bar Rava's) are from different teachers and not necessarily contradictory.

items.text: Repetition of the Mishnah and the dispute
items.text_en: Repetition of the Mishnah and the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the Mishnah and the statements of Rav and Shmuel for clarification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the Mishnah's ruling about a found infant: follow the majority of the city's population.
Rav limits the Mishnah's ruling: it applies only for saving the infant's life, not for establishing lineage.
Shmuel states that the Mishnah's ruling also applies for clearing a debris pile on Shabbat to save the infant.

items.text: Reconciling Shmuel's statements
items.text_en: Reconciling Shmuel's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency, as he elsewhere said we do not follow the majority for saving a life. It resolves that Shmuel's statement was actually about the first clause of the Mishnah (majority gentiles), not about saving life.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency, citing Rav Yosef's report that Shmuel said we do not follow the majority in matters of saving a life (פיקוח נפש).
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement about not following the majority was actually said regarding the first clause of the Mishnah (majority gentiles), not about saving a life.

items.text: Practical applications of the Mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Practical applications of the Mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains the practical halakhic implications: if the majority are gentiles, the infant may be fed neveilot; if the majority are Jews, we return lost property to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halakhic application follows from the Mishnah's ruling that if the majority are gentiles, the found infant is treated as a gentile.
Rav Pappa answers that the ruling applies to feeding the infant neveilot (carrion) — if the majority are gentiles, the infant may be fed non-kosher meat.
The Gemara asks what practical halakhic application follows from the Mishnah's ruling that if the majority are Jews, the found infant is treated as a Jew.
Rav Pappa answers that the ruling applies to returning lost property (אבידה) to the infant — if the majority are Jews, we return lost property to him.

items.text: Half-and-half case: damages
items.text_en: Half-and-half case: damages
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains that in a half-and-half case, the ruling is relevant for damages. The Gemara clarifies the scenario: if the foundling's ox gores our ox, he pays half and says 'bring proof that I am not a Jew and I will pay the rest.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for what practical halachic purpose does the Mishnah rule that a half-and-half foundling is treated as a Jew?
Reish Lakish answers: the ruling is relevant for damages (נזקין).
The Gemara asks: what is the specific scenario?
The Gemara considers and rejects a scenario where our ox gores his ox, because he could demand proof that the foundling is a Jew before paying full damages.
The Gemara resolves: the case is where his ox gores our ox; he pays half and says 'bring proof that I am not a Jew and I will pay the rest.'
