sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that in the divorce case, both witnesses testify about the woman's married status, so the one saying 'divorced' is a single voice against two, and she leaves.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation: woman's ability to contradict
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation: woman's ability to contradict
items.desc_en: Rava says it is two against two, but Rabbi Yochanan accepted Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei's view only for divorce because the woman can contradict the witnesses, whereas for death she cannot. The Gemara questions whether she would be so brazen, citing Rav Hamnuna that a woman is believed when she says 'you divorced me' because she is not brazen, but here witnesses support her, so she is brazen.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yochanan's distinction is not about one vs. two witnesses but about the woman's ability to contradict the witnesses: in death she cannot, in divorce she can.
The Gemara objects that a woman would not be so brazen, citing Rav Hamnuna's principle that a woman is not brazen enough to claim divorce falsely in her husband's presence.
The Gemara resolves that the principle of a woman not being brazen applies only when there are no supporting witnesses, but when witnesses support her claim, she is indeed brazen.

items.text: Rav Asi's explanation: verifiability of divorce
items.text_en: Rav Asi's explanation: verifiability of divorce
items.desc_en: Rav Asi says the witnesses say 'now he died' or 'now he divorced'. Death cannot be verified, but divorce can be verified by asking for the get.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi explains that the witnesses say 'now he died' or 'now he divorced'; death cannot be verified, but divorce can be verified by asking for the get.

items.text: Baraita on betrothal vs. divorce
items.text_en: Baraita on betrothal vs. divorce
items.desc_en: A baraita rules similarly for betrothal: two say 'betrothed' and two say 'not betrothed' — she does not marry, and if she did, she does not leave. For divorce, she leaves.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that when two say 'betrothed' and two say 'not betrothed', she may not marry, and if she married she does not leave; for divorce, she leaves.

items.text: Abaye's resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution of the Mishnah's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah rules differently in the first clause (betrothal) and the last clause (divorce). Abaye explains that the Mishnah is speaking about a case with one witness on each side: in the betrothal case both witnesses testify about a single woman, so the one saying she is betrothed is a single witness against two; in the divorce case both testify about a married woman, so the one saying she is divorced is a single witness against two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah rules differently in the first clause (betrothal) and the last clause (divorce).
Abaye explains the first clause: one witness says she was betrothed and one says she was not, so both testify she is unmarried and the single witness's statement has no validity against two.
Abaye explains the last clause: one witness says she was divorced and one says she was not, so both testify she is a married woman and the single witness's statement has no validity against two.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and the role of קלא
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and the role of קלא
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the Mishnah actually deals with two witnesses on each side, and he reverses the rulings: in the betrothal case she may not marry, and if she did she must leave; in the divorce case she may not marry, but if she did she does not leave. The Gemara explains that in the betrothal case, even though the witnesses live in the same courtyard, we might think there would be a public reputation (קלא) if she were betrothed, but the Mishnah teaches that people sometimes betroth in secret. In the divorce case, we might think divorce always has a קלא, but the Mishnah teaches that people also divorce in secret.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proposes that the Mishnah deals with two witnesses on each side, and reverses the rulings: in the betrothal case she must leave if she marries.
The Gemara questions why the ruling is not obvious, since 'we did not see' is not proof, and answers that it is necessary when they live in the same courtyard.
The Gemara explains that without the Mishnah, one might think betrothal generates a public reputation (קלא), but it teaches that people betroth in secret.
The Gemara presents the second clause of the Mishnah regarding divorce and asks what novel point it teaches, since it seems identical to the first clause.
The Gemara explains that the novel point is that one might think divorce always has a public reputation (קלא), but the Mishnah teaches that people also divorce in secret.

items.text: Dispute over the placement of the clause 'if after she married witnesses came'
items.text_en: Dispute over the placement of the clause 'if after she married witnesses came'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya teaches the clause 'if after she married witnesses came she does not leave' on the first clause (betrothal), while Rabbah bar Avin teaches it on the last clause (divorce). The Gemara explains that the one who places it on the first clause applies it all the more to the last clause, since the Sages were lenient with a captive woman. The one who places it on the last clause does not apply it to the first. The Gemara suggests this dispute relates to Rav Hamnuna's principle, but concludes that all accept Rav Hamnuna; the dispute is whether the principle applies only in the presence of the husband (where she is not brazen) or also in his absence (where she is brazen).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah's clause 'if after she married witnesses came she does not leave' is cited as the basis for the dispute.
The Gemara reports that Rabbi Oshaya teaches this clause on the first clause (betrothal) and Rabbah bar Avin teaches it on the last clause (divorce).

The Gemara explains that the one who places it on the first clause applies it all the more to the last clause, since the Sages were lenient with a captive woman; the one who places it on the last clause does not apply it to the first.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute relates to Rav Hamnuna's principle, where the one who places it on the first clause accepts Rav Hamnuna and the one who places it on the last clause does not.

The Gemara concludes that all accept Rav Hamnuna; the dispute is whether the principle applies only in the presence of the husband (where she is not brazen) or also in his absence (where she is brazen).

items.text: Definition of 'married' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Definition of 'married' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The father of Shmuel explains that 'married' in the Mishnah does not mean actually married, but rather once the court permitted her to marry, even if she has not yet married, she does not leave her permitted status. The Gemara questions the wording 'she does not leave' and answers that it means she does not leave her initial permission.

sub.desc_en: Avuha d'Shmuel explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'if she married' does not mean actual marriage, but once the court permitted her to marry, even if she did not actually marry, she does not leave that permission.
The Gemara questions the wording 'she does not leave' in the Mishnah, implying she was already married.
The Gemara answers that 'she does not leave' means she does not leave her initial permission to marry.

items.text: Baraita on a captive woman who claims purity
items.text_en: Baraita on a captive woman who claims purity
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a captive woman says 'I was captured but I am pure, and I have witnesses that I am pure,' we do not wait for the witnesses but permit her immediately. If after permitting her to marry witnesses come and say 'we do not know,' she does not leave her husband. But if witnesses of impurity come, even if she has many children, she must leave.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a captive woman says she is pure and has witnesses, the court permits her immediately; if witnesses of impurity come later, she must leave even if she has many children.

items.text: Story of the captive women in Nehardea and the ruling of Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Story of the captive women in Nehardea and the ruling of Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Captive women came to Nehardea; the father of Shmuel set guards over them, and Shmuel questioned why they needed guards now. Later, the daughters of Mar Shmuel were captured and brought to the land of Israel, where they said 'I was captured and I am pure,' and Rabbi Chanina permitted them. When their captors later arrived, Rabbi Chanina said they were 'children of masters.' The Gemara discusses whether the presence of witnesses overseas would forbid them, and Rav Ashi clarifies that the discussion is about witnesses of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: captive women arrived in Nehardea, and the father of Shmuel set guards over them; Shmuel questioned why they needed guards now, and his father rebuked him.
The daughters of Mar Shmuel were captured and brought to the land of Israel; they each said 'I was captured and I am pure,' and Rabbi Chanina permitted them.
When the captors later arrived, Rabbi Chanina said they were 'children of masters,' and it was revealed that they were the daughters of Mar Shmuel.

sub.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba's question to Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba's question to Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina told Rav Shemen bar Abba to attend to his relatives, and Rav Shemen bar Abba objected: there are witnesses overseas who might testify to impurity.
Rabbi Chanina answered: since the witnesses are not currently before us, why would the possibility of future witnesses forbid her now?
The Gemara objects: but the father of Shmuel said that once they permitted her to marry, even if she has not yet married, she does not leave the permission — so why would future witnesses matter?
Rav Ashi resolves: the discussion was about witnesses of impurity (עֵדֵי טוּמְאָה), not witnesses of marriage or divorce.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that two captive women who each claim to be pure are not believed, but if they testify for each other they are believed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for two captive women: each alone is not believed, but if they testify for each other they are believed.

items.text: Baraita on various claims
items.text_en: Baraita on various claims
items.desc_en: A baraita presents four cases: a woman claiming she is impure and her friend pure (believed), she is pure and friend impure (not believed), both impure (believed on herself but not friend), both pure (believed on friend but not herself).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting four cases of a woman's claims about her own and her friend's purity status, with rules of belief.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the baraita's first and last cases assume witnesses exist, but the middle case assumes no witnesses. Abaye resolves that indeed the baraita switches between scenarios.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's first case: if there are no witnesses, why is the woman not believed about herself? It concludes that witnesses must exist.
The Gemara questions the baraita's middle case: if witnesses exist, why is the woman not believed about her friend? It concludes that there are no witnesses.
The Gemara questions the baraita's last case: if there are no witnesses, why is the woman not believed about herself? It concludes that witnesses exist.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: the baraita switches between scenarios — the first and last cases assume witnesses exist, the middle case assumes no witnesses.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that all cases have witnesses, but a single witness contradicts the woman's claim. The Gemara then clarifies why additional cases are needed, addressing potential concerns about the woman's motives.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that all cases have witnesses, with one witness contradicting the woman; when she says she is tainted and her counterpart pure, she renders herself prohibited and her counterpart is permitted by her own claim.

Rav Pappa explains the second case: when she claims she is pure and her counterpart tainted, but a witness contradicts her, she cannot permit herself due to witnesses, but her counterpart is permitted by the witness's testimony.

Rav Pappa explains the third case: when she says both are tainted and a witness says both are pure, she renders herself prohibited and her counterpart is permitted by the witness; the Gemara objects that this is identical to the first case.

The Gemara answers that the third case is needed lest one think both are pure and the woman is acting like Samson saying 'Let me die with the Philistines'; the tanna teaches that her claim is not accepted.

Rav Pappa explains the fourth case: when she says both are pure and a witness says both are tainted, she cannot permit herself due to witnesses, but her counterpart is permitted by her claim; the Gemara objects that this is identical to the first part of the first case.

The Gemara answers that the fourth case is needed lest one think she is only credible when she disqualifies herself, but not when she qualifies herself; the tanna teaches that she is credible in both scenarios.

items.text: Second Mishnah on priestly lineage
items.text_en: Second Mishnah on priestly lineage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a parallel case: two men claiming priesthood are not believed unless they testify for each other. Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel debate whether a single witness suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: two men claiming priesthood are not believed unless they testify for each other.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) rules that one does not elevate a man to priesthood based on a single witness.
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) qualifies: the restriction applies only when there are challengers; otherwise, one witness suffices.
רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) states in the name of רבי שמעון בן הסגן (Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan) that one does elevate to priesthood on the basis of a single witness.

items.text: Gemara's question on redundancy
items.text_en: Gemara's question on redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's case is needed, given a prior ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua. It explains that the case of witnesses is distinct from that of the claimant himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's case of witnesses is needed, given the prior ruling of Rabbi Yehoshua.

The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is necessary because the case of witnesses, where there is no monetary aspect (דְּרָרָא דְמָמוֹנָא), might otherwise be thought not to follow Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling.
The Gemara adds that conversely, if only the case of witnesses were taught, one might think the claimant himself is not believed, so both cases are needed.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why list all three cases?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why list all three cases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to list the cases of a woman captured by non-Jews, a woman claiming she is pure, and a woman suspected of adultery. It suggests that if only the first two were taught, one might think they are lenient because they involve money, but the case of a married woman (אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ) involves a prohibition, so one might think she is not believed—hence the third case is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a hypothetical objection: if only the first two cases were taught, one might think the leniency applies only to monetary matters, but not to the prohibition of a married woman.

The Gemara explains that the third case (a married woman claiming she was divorced) is necessary to teach that even in a ritual prohibition, the woman is believed, countering the potential mistaken inference from the first two cases.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah includes the clause 'I was captured but I am pure'—to introduce the case where witnesses come after she married, and she does not leave. It then addresses a dispute about whether this clause is attached to the first or second part of the Mishnah, and explains the need for the case of two captured women and two men, the latter to introduce the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah includes the clause 'I was captured but I am pure,' as it seems redundant.
The Gemara answers that the clause is needed to introduce the case where witnesses come after she married, and she does not leave.
The Gemara objects that this answer works only for one who attaches the clause to the latter part of the Mishnah, but not for one who attaches it to the first part.
The Gemara answers that the clause is needed to introduce the case of two women who were captured.
The Gemara asks why the case of two captured women is needed, as it seems redundant.
The Gemara answers that the case is needed to teach that we are not concerned about collusion between the women.
The Gemara asks why the case of two men is needed, as it seems redundant after the case of two women.
The Gemara answers that the case is needed to introduce the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

items.text: Tosefta: Testimony for priesthood
items.text_en: Tosefta: Testimony for priesthood
items.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited: One who says 'I am a priest and my friend is a priest' is believed to allow him to eat terumah, but not to marry him off, unless there are three witnesses—two testify about each. Rabbi Yehuda says he is not even believed for terumah without three witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta begins: One who says 'I am a priest and my friend is a priest' is believed to allow him to eat תרומה (priestly portion).
The Tosefta states that he is not believed to marry him off unless there are three witnesses—two testify about each.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that he is not even believed for תרומה (priestly portion) without three witnesses.

items.text: Contradiction regarding concern for accomplices
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding concern for accomplices
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: In the Tosefta, Rabbi Yehuda is concerned about accomplices (גוֹמְלִין) while the Rabbis are not, but in a Mishnah about donkey drivers, the opposite appears: Rabbi Yehuda believes them, showing no concern, while the Rabbis do not believe them, showing concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: in the Tosefta Rabbi Yehuda is concerned about accomplices (גוֹמְלִין) while the Rabbis are not, but in the Mishnah about donkey drivers the opposite appears—Rabbi Yehuda believes them (no concern) and the Rabbis do not (concern).

items.text: First resolution: Rav Ada bar Ahava and Abaye
items.text_en: First resolution: Rav Ada bar Ahava and Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava said in the name of Rav that the positions are reversed (מוּחְלֶפֶת הַשִּׁיטָה). Abaye disagrees, saying no reversal is needed: in the case of doubtfully tithed produce (דְּמַאי), the Rabbis were lenient because most amei ha'aretz do tithe.

sub.text: Rav Ada bar Ahava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava reports in Rav's name that the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis are reversed (מוּחְלֶפֶת הַשִּׁיטָה) between the two cases.
Abaye objects, asserting that no reversal is needed; the positions can be reconciled without flipping.

Abaye explains that in the case of doubtfully tithed produce (דְּמַאי), the Rabbis were lenient because most amei ha'aretz (עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ) do tithe, so the apparent contradiction is resolved without reversal.

items.text: Second resolution: Rava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Second resolution: Rava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects: Why is Rabbi Yehuda's contradiction problematic but not the Rabbis'? He resolves both: Rabbi Yehuda's positions are reconciled as previously explained (by Abaye), and the Rabbis' positions are reconciled by Rabbi Chama bar Ukva's principle that the donkey drivers are believed because their tools are in their hands.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: Why is Rabbi Yehuda's internal contradiction considered problematic, but the Rabbis' internal contradiction is not?

Rava resolves both contradictions: Rabbi Yehuda's positions are reconciled as Abaye previously explained, and the Rabbis' positions are reconciled by Rabbi Chama bar Ukva's principle that the donkey drivers are believed because their tools are in their hands.

items.text: The potter's vessels and the dispute of Rabbi Chama bar Ukva
items.text_en: The potter's vessels and the dispute of Rabbi Chama bar Ukva
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the principle of 'when his tools are in his hand' to a case of a potter who left his vessels and went to drink. It resolves contradictions between a Mishnah and two baraitot by distinguishing whether the potter's tools are in his hand or not, and offers an alternative explanation involving public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara applies the principle of 'when his tools are in his hand' to the case of the potter.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah about the potter who left his vessels and went to drink, where inner vessels are pure and outer ones impure.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says both inner and outer vessels are impure.
Rabbi Chama bar Ukva answers that the baraita refers to a case where the potter's tools are in his hand, so everyone touches them.
The Gemara objects by citing another baraita that says both inner and outer vessels are pure.
Rabbi Chama bar Ukva answers that this baraita refers to a case where the potter's tools are not in his hand.
The Gemara asks how to explain the Mishnah's distinction between inner and outer vessels.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with vessels adjacent to the public domain, where passersby brush against the outer ones.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute about elevating from terumah to lineage
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute about elevating from terumah to lineage
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the dispute about the potter's vessels is actually about whether one can elevate from terumah to lineage, a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the dispute about the potter's vessels is actually about whether one can elevate from terumah to lineage, a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

items.text: Inquiry: Can one elevate from documents to lineage?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Can one elevate from documents to lineage?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a document stating 'I, so-and-so the priest, borrowed a maneh' with witnesses can be used to establish priestly lineage. The dispute is between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda, one saying yes and one saying no.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one can elevate from documents to lineage, and clarifies that the case is not where the document says 'I, so-and-so the priest, signed as a witness,' because then who testifies about him?

The Gemara clarifies: rather, the document states 'I, so-and-so the priest, borrowed a maneh from so-and-so' and witnesses signed; the question is whether they testify only about the loan or about the entire statement.
Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute: one says one may elevate from documents to lineage, and one says one may not.

items.text: Inquiry: Can one elevate from priestly blessing to lineage?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Can one elevate from priestly blessing to lineage?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether performing the priestly blessing (נשיאות כפים) can establish lineage. It considers the issue from the perspectives of both those who say one can elevate from terumah and those who say one cannot, raising possible distinctions based on the severity of the prohibition or the public nature of the act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: can one elevate from the priestly blessing (נשיאות כפים) to lineage, and notes that the question applies to both those who say one can elevate from terumah and those who say one cannot.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis for those who say elevate
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis for those who say elevate
sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers the view of those who say one can elevate from terumah: perhaps terumah is different because its violation carries death at the hand of Heaven, while the priestly blessing involves only a positive commandment, so one might not elevate from it; or perhaps there is no difference.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis for those who say do not elevate
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis for those who say do not elevate
sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers the view of those who say one cannot elevate from terumah: perhaps terumah is eaten in private, so a non-priest might risk it, but the priestly blessing is in public, so a non-priest would not be so insolent; or perhaps there is no difference.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Avina, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Avina, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Avina dispute whether one can elevate from priestly blessing to lineage. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava about the matter, and Rava replies that it is the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Avina.

sub.desc_en: The Stam reports the dispute between רב חסדא (Rav Chisda) and רבי אבינא (Rabbi Avina): one says one elevates from נשיאות כפים (the Priestly Benediction) to lineage, and the other says one does not elevate.
רב נחמן בר יצחק (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) asks רבא (Rava): what is the halakha regarding elevating from נשיאות כפים (the Priestly Benediction) to lineage?
רבא (Rava) answers that the matter is the dispute between רב חסדא (Rav Chisda) and רבי אבינא (Rabbi Avina).

items.text: The halakhic conclusion from a baraita of Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: The halakhic conclusion from a baraita of Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says that a 'chazakah' (presumption) is strong, based on the story of the returnees from Babylon who were not allowed to eat from the most holy things until a priest with Urim and Tumim arose. The Gemara argues that if one could elevate from priestly blessing, they would have been elevated, but their presumption was weak. It then defends this by comparing to terumah, where even those who elevate from terumah would not elevate them because their presumption is weak.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava what the halakhic conclusion is regarding elevating from priestly blessing to lineage.

Rava responds by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says that a chazakah (presumption) is strong, based on the biblical story of the returnees from Babylon who were not allowed to eat from the most holy things until a priest with Urim and Tumim arose.
The baraita explains that the returnees were told they remain in their presumption, eating only from lesser sanctities as they did in exile.
The Gemara objects that if one could elevate from priestly blessing to lineage, the returnees would have been elevated when they raised their hands in blessing.
The Gemara resolves that the case is different because their presumption was weak, just as with terumah where even those who elevate from terumah would not elevate them due to weak presumption.

items.text: Clarifying the 'great presumption'
items.text_en: Clarifying the 'great presumption'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what makes the presumption 'great', and offers two explanations: either it allows eating rabbinic terumah initially and now biblical terumah, or it only allows rabbinic terumah but we do not elevate from rabbinic terumah to lineage. The second explanation adds that we do not decree due to biblical terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what makes the presumption 'great'.
First answer: the presumption is great because it allows eating rabbinic terumah initially and now biblical terumah.
Second answer: the presumption is great because even though we do not elevate from rabbinic terumah to lineage, we do not decree due to biblical terumah.

items.text: Objection from the verse about sacred foods
items.text_en: Objection from the verse about sacred foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does the daughter of a priest not eat biblical terumah? A verse implies she does eat biblical terumah. The Gemara clarifies that the verse refers to items called 'kodesh' or 'kodashim', not to terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: does the daughter of a priest not eat biblical terumah? A verse implies she does eat biblical terumah.
The Gemara clarifies that the verse refers to items called 'kodesh' or 'kodashim', not to terumah.

items.text: Proof from the baraita about priestly blessing and challah
items.text_en: Proof from the baraita about priestly blessing and challah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita listing presumptions for priesthood: priestly blessing in Babylonia, eating challah in Syria, and distributing gifts in the cities. It asks whether priestly blessing is for lineage, but answers it is for terumah. The Gemara then challenges the analogy with challah, and explains that challah nowadays is rabbinic while terumah is biblical, and we elevate from rabbinic challah to biblical terumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita listing presumptions for priesthood: priestly blessing in Babylonia, eating challah in Syria, and distributing gifts in the cities.
The Gemara asks whether the priestly blessing listed in the baraita is a presumption for lineage (יוחסין).
The Gemara answers that the presumption is for terumah (תרומה), not for lineage.
The Gemara objects that the baraita pairs priestly blessing with eating challah, which is for lineage, so priestly blessing should also be for lineage.

The Gemara resolves that challah itself is for terumah, because nowadays challah is דרבנן (rabbinic) while terumah is דאורייתא (biblical), and we elevate from rabbinic challah to biblical terumah, as Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua reversed the rabbis' view.

items.text: Another baraita: priestly blessing and threshing-floor distribution
items.text_en: Another baraita: priestly blessing and threshing-floor distribution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: the presumption for priesthood is priestly blessing and threshing-floor distribution in Israel, and in Syria and wherever messengers of the new moon reach, priestly blessing is evidence but not threshing-floor distribution. Babylonia is like Syria. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds Alexandria of Egypt initially because a court was established there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the presumptions for priesthood: priestly blessing and threshing-floor distribution in Israel, and in Syria and wherever new-moon messengers reach, only priestly blessing is evidence.
The baraita adds that Babylonia is like Syria in this regard.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that Alexandria of Egypt was initially included because a court was established there.

items.text: Analysis of the second baraita and the dispute about challah and terumah
items.text_en: Analysis of the second baraita and the dispute about challah and terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes whether priestly blessing is for lineage or for challah, and concludes that threshing-floor distribution is for challah. It then presents a dispute: some hold terumah nowadays is rabbinic and challah biblical, while others hold the opposite. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua found rabbis arguing that even according to the view that terumah is rabbinic, challah is biblical because the land was obligated in challah after the seven years of conquest and seven years of division, but not in terumah. He countered that even according to the view that terumah is biblical, challah is rabbinic, based on a verse about entering the land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mention of priestly blessing (נשיאות כפים) in the baraita is for lineage purposes.
The Gemara answers that the priestly blessing is for challah, not for lineage.
The Gemara objects that since the baraita pairs priestly blessing with threshing-floor distribution (חילוק גרנות), which is for lineage, the blessing should also be for lineage.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that threshing-floor distribution itself is for challah, not for lineage.
The Gemara explains the underlying assumption: one holds that תרומה (terumah) nowadays is rabbinic (דרבנן) and חלה (challah) is biblical (דאורייתא).
The Gemara concludes that one can infer from rabbinic terumah to biblical challah.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's report
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's report
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's encounter with the rabbis.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua reports that the rabbis argued that even according to the view that terumah nowadays is rabbinic, challah is biblical.
The rabbis reason that the land was obligated in challah after the seven years of conquest and seven years of division, but not in terumah.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's counter
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's counter
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua counters that even according to the view that terumah nowadays is biblical, challah is rabbinic.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's proof
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's proof
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua cites a baraita from the verse 'בבואכם אל הארץ' (when you come to the land) to support his position.
The baraita interprets the verse to mean the entire nation's entry, not just a few spies, delaying the obligation of challah.
The baraita concludes that the obligation of challah applies only after the entire nation enters the land, which occurred later.
The baraita continues to discuss the time of Ezra's ascent, which is the end of the section.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that all three practices (priestly blessing, dividing on the threshing floor, and testimony) are independent proofs of priesthood, suggesting that testimony itself is not a separate ḥazakah but rather a form of evidence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that all three practices are independent proofs of priesthood, suggesting testimony is not a separate ḥazakah but a form of evidence.

items.text: Resolution: testimony is like ḥazakah
items.text_en: Resolution: testimony is like ḥazakah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's list means that the ḥazakah for priesthood is established through priestly blessing and dividing on the threshing floor, and testimony is comparable to these: just as testimony establishes lineage, so too priestly blessing establishes lineage. However, testimony that comes from a ḥazakah is as strong as the ḥazakah itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the three proofs of priesthood, then questions whether testimony itself is a ḥazakah.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita means priestly blessing is like testimony: just as testimony establishes lineage, so does priestly blessing.
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that testimony derived from a ḥazakah is itself like a ḥazakah, not a separate category.

items.text: Two cases: priest and Levite by synagogue aliyot
items.text_en: Two cases: priest and Levite by synagogue aliyot
items.desc_en: Two stories illustrate that reading first in the synagogue (followed by a Levite) establishes a ḥazakah for priesthood, and reading second (preceded by a priest) establishes a ḥazakah for Levite status. Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi each accepted such testimony to elevate a person to their respective statuses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi accepted a claim of priesthood based on the witness having seen the person called first to the Torah followed by a Levite, thus establishing a familial presumption (חזקה) for priesthood.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted a claim of being a Levite based on the witness having seen the person called second to the Torah preceded by a priest.

items.text: Dispute about dividing on the threshing floor
items.text_en: Dispute about dividing on the threshing floor
items.desc_en: A case before Reish Lakish raises the question: is dividing on the threshing floor necessary for a ḥazakah of priesthood? Rabbi Elazar argues that if there is no threshing floor, does priesthood become void? Later, when a similar case comes before Rabbi Yochanan, Reish Lakish asks the same question, and Rabbi Yochanan rebukes Rabbi Elazar for not citing the source of this argument from Bar Nafḥa.

sub.desc_en: A man comes before Reish Lakish claiming he is a priest based on being called first to the Torah.
Reish Lakish asks whether the claimant was seen dividing priestly gifts on the threshing floor, a stronger proof of priesthood.
Rabbi Elazar objects: if there is no threshing floor in that town, does that mean priesthood is void?
Later, a similar case comes before Rabbi Yochanan, and Reish Lakish repeats the same question, prompting Rabbi Yochanan to echo Rabbi Elazar's objection.
Rabbi Yochanan sees Rabbi Elazar's embarrassment and rebukes him for not citing the source of this argument from Bar Nafḥa.

items.text: Father and brother testimony for priesthood and Levite status
items.text_en: Father and brother testimony for priesthood and Levite status
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya: Rabbi holds that a father can testify that his son is a priest to allow him to eat terumah but not to marry a woman of priestly lineage, while Rabbi Chiyya argues that if he is believed for terumah, he should be believed for marriage. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi elevated a son based on his father's testimony, and Rabbi Chiyya elevated a brother based on his brother's testimony. A question is raised: why not a son for Rabbi Chiyya? Because a son is too close to his father, but a brother is also close to his brother!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: one sage elevated a son to priesthood based on the father's testimony, and the other elevated a brother to Levite status based on the brother's testimony.

A baraita is cited to prove that Rabbi elevated a son based on the father's testimony: Rabbi rules that a father who says 'this is my son and he is a priest' is believed to allow him to eat תרומה (priestly portion) but not to marry a woman of priestly lineage, while Rabbi Chiyya argues that if believed for תרומה, he should also be believed for marriage.

Rabbi explains the distinction: he believes the father for תרומה because the father can feed his son תרומה himself, but not for marriage because the father cannot marry off his son to a woman of priestly lineage.
The Gemara concludes: since Rabbi elevated a son based on the father's testimony, Rabbi Chiyya must have elevated a brother based on the brother's testimony.

The Gemara questions why Rabbi Chiyya did not elevate a son based on the father's testimony: if the reason is that a son is too close to his father, then a brother is also close to his brother, so why would he elevate a brother?

items.text: The case of mesiach lefi tumo and Rabbi's acceptance
items.text_en: The case of mesiach lefi tumo and Rabbi's acceptance
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where a person, speaking casually, described being immersed as a child to eat terumah, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi relied on this to declare him a priest. Rabbi Chiya adds that his friends distanced themselves from him, calling him 'Yochanan eater of challah'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel brings a story of a person who, speaking casually (מסיח לפי תומו), described being immersed as a child to eat terumah that evening.
Rabbi Chiya adds that the man's friends distanced themselves, calling him 'Yochanan eater of challah', and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi relied on this testimony to declare him a priest.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement on chazakah
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement on chazakah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that just as terumah is a chazakah for priesthood, so too ma'aser rishon is a chazakah for priesthood, but dividing in court is not a chazakah.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that just as terumah is a chazakah for priesthood, so too ma'aser rishon is a chazakah for priesthood, but dividing in court is not a chazakah.

items.text: Challenge: Ma'aser rishon is for Levites
items.text_en: Challenge: Ma'aser rishon is for Levites
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how ma'aser rishon can be a chazakah for priesthood, since it is given to Levites. It cites a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, where Rabbi Elazar says ma'aser rishon is also for priests, but the Gemara asks if he meant exclusively for priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's claim that ma'aser rishon is a chazakah for priesthood, noting that ma'aser rishon is given to Levites, not priests.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who holds that ma'aser rishon is also for priests.
The Gemara cites a baraita recording the dispute: Rabbi Akiva says ma'aser rishon is for Levites, while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says it is also for priests.
The Gemara quotes Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's position that ma'aser rishon is 'also for a priest,' implying it is not exclusively for priests.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya meant that ma'aser rishon is given exclusively to priests and not to Levites, or only that priests may also receive it.

items.text: Resolution: Ezra's decree and the case of a rumor
items.text_en: Resolution: Ezra's decree and the case of a rumor
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that after Ezra penalized the Levites, ma'aser rishon was given to priests. Rav Chisda explains the case: a person whose father was known as a priest but a rumor arose that he was a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah, and he received ma'aser at the granary. Even if ma'aser is permitted to non-priests, they would not give it to him as a portion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that after Ezra penalized the Levites, ma'aser rishon was given to priests.
The Gemara objects: perhaps they happened to give him ma'aser by chance, not as a fixed portion.
Rav Chisda explains the case: a person whose father was known as a priest but a rumor arose that he was a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah, and he received ma'aser at the granary.
The Gemara concludes that even if ma'aser is permitted to non-priests, they would not give it to him as a portion, so receiving it is a valid presumption of priesthood.

items.text: Clarification of 'dividing in court'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'dividing in court'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if dividing in court is not a chazakah, where is it a chazakah? Rav Sheshet explains that the statement refers to one who divides terumah from his father's estate with his brothers in court — that is not a chazakah, because it is for sale, not for eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if dividing in court is not a chazakah, where is it a chazakah?
Rav Sheshet explains that the statement refers to one who divides תרומה (priestly portion) from his father's estate with his brothers in court — that is not a chazakah.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, and then clarifies that the ruling teaches that unlike the other cases which are for eating, this division is for sale.

items.text: Dispute about a single witness for priesthood
items.text_en: Dispute about a single witness for priesthood
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel seem to agree, but Rabbi Yochanan says all agree that a challenge requires two witnesses. The Gemara explains the case: a person whose father was known as a priest but a rumor arose that he was a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah, and he was demoted; then one witness came to restore him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appear identical to that of Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the difference lies in the number of challengers, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that any challenge requires at least two witnesses.

The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining the case: a person whose father was known as a priest but a rumor arose that he was a בן גרושה (offspring of a divorced woman) or בן חלוצה (offspring of a chalutzah), and he was demoted; then one witness came to restore him.

items.text: Dispute about reversing a court ruling due to concern for its dignity
items.text_en: Dispute about reversing a court ruling due to concern for its dignity
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding whether a court can reinstate a priest it had previously disqualified. The Tanna Kamma is concerned about the court's dignity (זילותא דבי דינא) and therefore does not reinstate him, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that since the court itself demoted him, it can also reinstate him without concern for dignity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the case: the court reinstated a priest, then two witnesses disqualified him, and a single witness later testified he is a priest, with the general rule that all witnesses combine for testimony.

The Gemara explains the dispute: the Tanna Kamma fears זילותא דבי דינא (disrespect to the court) and therefore does not reinstate the priest, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that since the court itself demoted him, it can reinstate him without concern for dignity.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to the previous explanation, arguing that if the concern is for dignity, the same logic should apply even when two witnesses come and two witnesses contradict them. He then offers an alternative: the dispute is actually about whether testimony can be combined (מצטרפין לעדות), referencing a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Natan regarding the need for witnesses to see the event simultaneously or sequentially.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: if the concern is for the dignity of the court (זילותא דבי דינא), then even when two witnesses come and two witnesses contradict them, the same logic should apply.

Rav Ashi offers an alternative: the dispute is actually about whether testimony can be combined (מצטרפין לעדות), citing the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Natan regarding the need for witnesses to see the event simultaneously or sequentially.
Rabbi Natan states that the court hears the testimony of each witness on separate days, supporting the view that sequential testimony can be combined.

items.text: Mishnah: A woman imprisoned by gentiles
items.text_en: Mishnah: A woman imprisoned by gentiles
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman was imprisoned by gentiles for financial reasons, she is permitted to her husband, but if imprisoned for capital reasons, she is forbidden to her husband.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a woman imprisoned by gentiles for monetary reasons is permitted to her husband, but for capital reasons she is forbidden.

items.text: Rav's qualification of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav's qualification of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said in the name of Rav that the Mishnah's leniency applies only when Jewish authority is dominant over the gentiles. However, when gentile authority is dominant over themselves, even imprisonment for financial reasons renders the woman forbidden to her husband.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav qualifies the Mishnah: the leniency applies only when Jewish authority is dominant, but when gentile authority is dominant, even a monetary imprisonment renders her forbidden.

items.text: Rava's objection from the case of Ashkelon
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the case of Ashkelon
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a testimony of Rabbi Yosei HaKohen and Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav about a woman who was pawned in Ashkelon, where gentile authority was dominant, yet the Sages did not forbid her outright but required witnesses that she was not secluded or defiled. This challenges Rav's distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises an objection by citing a testimony about a woman pawned in Ashkelon, where gentile authority was dominant, yet the Sages did not forbid her outright but required witnesses that she was not secluded or defiled.

Rava continues the objection, noting that the Sages' response to the family's concern was conditional: if you believe she was pawned, believe she was not secluded; if not, do not believe she was pawned.
Rava concludes the objection by pointing out that Ashkelon was under gentile dominance, yet the Mishnah still requires witnesses about seclusion, contradicting Rav's distinction.

items.text: Distinction between collateral and imprisonment
items.text_en: Distinction between collateral and imprisonment
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially distinguishes between a woman held as collateral (הורהנה) and one imprisoned (נחבשה), but then questions this distinction based on a precedent from Ashkelon. It concludes that the case of collateral is different because it involves money, not life-threatening captivity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially states that a woman held as collateral (הורהנה) is permitted to her husband, but one imprisoned (נחבשה) is not, and notes that the actual case in Ashkelon involved collateral.

Rava cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei the Kohen and Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav testified about a woman from Ashkelon who was held as collateral, and the Sages ruled that if you believe she was collateral, you must also believe she was not secluded or defiled.

The Gemara questions: since Ashkelon was a case of money (collateral), and the ruling depended on witnesses, does this imply that without witnesses, both collateral and imprisonment are treated the same?
The Gemara answers that the case of collateral is different (שאני) because it involves money, not life-threatening captivity.

items.text: Contradiction resolved by political context
items.text_en: Contradiction resolved by political context
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised between the Mishnah's ruling that a woman captured for money is permitted to her husband and the precedent from Ashkelon. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak resolves it by distinguishing between times when Jewish authority is strong versus when non-Jewish authority is strong.

sub.desc_en: Some raise a contradiction: the Mishnah says a woman captured for money is permitted to her husband, but the baraita about Ashkelon implies that without witnesses she is not permitted.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a time when Jewish authority is strong (the Mishnah's case) and when non-Jewish authority is strong (the baraita's case).

items.text: Examples of women captured for life
items.text_en: Examples of women captured for life
items.desc_en: Rav and Levi provide examples of women captured for life-threatening reasons: Rav says the wives of thieves, Levi says the wife of Ben Dunai. Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan debate whether the death sentence must have been finalized for the woman to be forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a woman captured for life-threatening reasons is forbidden to her husband.
Rav gives an example: the wives of thieves who are captured due to their husbands' crimes.
Levi gives another example: the wife of Ben Dunai, a notorious bandit.
Chizkiyah adds the condition that the death sentence must have been finalized for the husband.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and rules that even if the death sentence was not finalized, the wife is still forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: City conquered by siege
items.text_en: Mishnah: City conquered by siege
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that all priestly women found in a city conquered by siege are disqualified, unless they have witnesses (even a slave or maidservant) to their purity. A person cannot testify for themselves.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a city is conquered by a besieging army (כרכום), all priestly women found there are presumed defiled and forbidden to their husbands, unless they have witnesses, even a slave or maidservant, but a person cannot testify for themselves.

items.text: Contradiction with laws of libation and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction with laws of libation and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about a besieged city where wine is permitted in wartime due to lack of time for libation. Rav Mari distinguishes between rape (which has time) and libation (which does not). Rabbi Yitzchak bar Elazar distinguishes between a siege by the same kingdom (where escape is possible) and another kingdom. Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Levi add conditions about guards and barriers. Rabbi Abba bar Zavda reports a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and the Rabbis on this resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about a besieged city, where wine is permitted in wartime due to lack of time for libation, implying leniency.
Rav Mari distinguishes between rape (which has time) and libation (which does not), resolving the contradiction.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Elazar distinguishes between a siege by the same kingdom (where escape is possible) and another kingdom.
The Gemara objects that even in a siege by the same kingdom, it is impossible that no one escapes.
Rav Yehuda answers that the case is when the guards see each other, preventing escape.
The Gemara objects that it is impossible that the guards never sleep.
Rabbi Levi answers that the siege is so tight that even a chain, dog, nut, or goose cannot pass through.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda reports a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and the Rabbis on the resolution of the contradiction.

items.text: Hiding place saves all priestly women
items.text_en: Hiding place saves all priestly women
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin says that if there is one hiding place, it saves all the priestly women. Rabbi Yirmeya questions whether it saves only one woman at a time. The Gemara compares this to a case of two paths (one impure) and applies Rava's principle: if all women are permitted at once, it is like a single case, but the objection is raised that here impurity is uncertain, unlike the path case.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin states in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan that if there is one hiding place, it saves all the priestly women.
Rabbi Yirmeya questions whether the hiding place saves only one woman at a time if it can hold only one, or if each woman can claim it as her hiding place.

sub.text: Gemara's comparison to the case of two paths
sub.text_en: Gemara's comparison to the case of two paths
sub.desc_en: The Gemara compares the question to the dispute about two paths, one impure and one pure, where Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi disagree on the status of pure items prepared by two people who each walked one path.
Rava (or Rabbi Yochanan) explains that when all women are permitted at once, it is like a single case (בבת אחת), so all are permitted, resolving the comparison.
The Gemara objects that the comparison is flawed: in the path case, impurity is certain, whereas here it is uncertain whether the woman was actually defiled.

items.text: Woman's own claim of hiding
items.text_en: Woman's own claim of hiding
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a question: if a woman says she neither hid nor was defiled, what is the ruling? The daf ends with this unresolved query.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks: if a woman says 'I was not hidden and I was not defiled,' what is the ruling?

items.text: The Gemara's question about "מה לי לשקר" in the case of a captive woman
items.text_en: The Gemara's question about "מה לי לשקר" in the case of a captive woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle of "מה לי לשקר" (why would I lie) applies to a captive woman who claims she was not defiled. It compares this to a case brought before Rava where a similar claim was rejected because witnesses were available. Abaye argues that "מה לי לשקר" is not said where witnesses exist, but here there is only a concern, not certainty, so it may apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the principle of מָה לִי לְשַׁקֵּר (why would I lie) applies to a captive woman's claim of purity.
The Gemara cites a case where a man hired a donkey and Rava accepted his claim based on מָה לִי לְשַׁקֵּר, but Abaye objected that the principle is not invoked when witnesses are available.
The Gemara distinguishes: in Rava's case, witnesses definitely existed, but here the woman's defilement is only a concern (חֲשָׁשָׁא), so מָה לִי לְשַׁקֵּר applies.

items.text: The credibility of a maidservant as a witness for a captive woman
items.text_en: The credibility of a maidservant as a witness for a captive woman
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even a slave or maidservant is believed to testify about a captive woman's purity. The Gemara questions whether the woman's own maidservant is believed, citing a baraita that prohibits a woman from being alone with a man except on the testimony of witnesses, excluding her own maidservant. Rav Pappi distinguishes between a captive woman (where leniency applies) and other cases. Rav Papa distinguishes between the woman's maidservant and her husband's maidservant. Rav Ashi explains that the maidservant is believed here because her silence would permit the woman, whereas in the other case her silence would forbid her. The Gemara raises the concern that the maidservant might lie, but concludes she would not do so twice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even a slave or maidservant is believed to testify about a captive woman's purity.
The Gemara asks whether the woman's own maidservant is also believed.
The Gemara cites a baraita that prohibits a woman from being alone with a man except on the testimony of witnesses, excluding her own maidservant because her heart is familiar with her.
Rav Pappi distinguishes that in the case of a captive woman, leniency applies.
Rav Papa distinguishes between the woman's own maidservant and her husband's maidservant.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's ruling that a person cannot testify for himself implies that her own maidservant is like herself and thus should not be believed.
Rav Ashi explains that the maidservant is believed here because her silence would permit the woman, whereas in the other case her silence would forbid her.
The Gemara raises the concern that the maidservant might lie now as well.
The Gemara concludes that the maidservant would not lie twice, so she is believed.

items.text: A parallel case: the brother from Bei Hoza'ah
items.text_en: A parallel case: the brother from Bei Hoza'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Mari bar Isak (or Hana bar Isak) who came to claim his inheritance from his brother, who denied knowing him. Rav Chisda ruled that the brother's denial was valid, citing Joseph's unrecognizability. When the claimant said he had witnesses but they were afraid, Rav Chisda told the defendant to bring witnesses that the claimant was not his brother. The defendant objected that the burden of proof is on the claimant, but Rav Chisda said he would judge thus for all violent men. The Gemara notes that here too, witnesses would not lie twice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story of Mari bar Isak (or Hana bar Isak) whose brother from Bei Hoza'ah came to claim inheritance; the brother denied knowing him, and Rav Chisda supported the denial by citing Joseph's unrecognizability.

Rav Chisda instructs the claimant to bring witnesses, then when the claimant says witnesses are afraid, Rav Chisda tells the defendant to bring witnesses that the claimant is not his brother, overriding the usual burden of proof for violent men, and applies the principle that witnesses would not lie twice.

items.text: The dispute among Tannaim and the resolution via "מסיחה לפי תומה"
items.text_en: The dispute among Tannaim and the resolution via "מסיחה לפי תומה"
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the views of Rav Pappi and Rav Ashi correspond to a Tannaitic dispute about who is believed to testify about a captive woman. One baraita includes the woman's father and mother but not her son or daughter, while another excludes only herself and her husband. Rav Papa's view is also examined, and he explains that his baraita refers to a case where the witness speaks unsolicited (מסיחה לפי תומה). The Gemara supports this with a story of a man who testified unsolicited about his and his mother's captivity, and Rabbi relied on his testimony to marry her to a priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav Pappi and Rav Ashi corresponds to a Tannaitic dispute, citing a baraita listing who may testify about a captive woman, excluding her son, daughter, slave, and maidservant.
A second baraita is cited, stating that everyone is believed to testify except the woman herself and her husband.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Pappa's view also corresponds to a Tannaitic dispute.
Rav Pappa explains that the baraita excluding relatives applies only when the witness speaks unsolicited (מסיחה לפי תומה), not when formally testifying.
A story is brought: a man spoke unsolicited about his and his mother's captivity, and Rabbi relied on his testimony to marry her to a priest, supporting Rav Pappa's distinction.

items.text: The Mishnah of Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav and the Gemara's addition
items.text_en: The Mishnah of Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav and the Gemara's addition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah quotes Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav who swore that his wife's hand never left his during the siege of Jerusalem, but the Sages said a person cannot testify about himself. The Gemara adds a baraita that despite this, he set aside a house for her in his courtyard, and she would go out at the head of her children and come in at the end.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav swears by the Temple that his wife's hand never left his during the siege of Jerusalem.
The Sages object that a person cannot testify about himself.
The Gemara adds a baraita that despite the objection, he set aside a house for her in his courtyard, and she would go out at the head of her children and come in at the end.

items.text: Abaye's question about a divorced woman and the baraita's answer
items.text_en: Abaye's question about a divorced woman and the baraita's answer
items.desc_en: Abaye asks whether the leniency applied to a captive woman (allowing her to live in the same courtyard) applies also to a divorced woman. The Gemara attempts to answer from a baraita that states a man who divorces his wife may not marry her neighbor, implying that proximity is prohibited, thus answering the question.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether the leniency of allowing a captive woman to live in the same courtyard applies also to a divorced woman, or whether the leniency is specific to captives.

The Gemara answers by citing a baraita that a man who divorces his wife may not marry her neighbor, implying that proximity is prohibited, thus resolving that the leniency does not apply to a divorced woman.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rules of residence and priority
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rules of residence and priority
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband is a priest, the wife cannot live with him in the same alleyway. If it is a small village, it is considered a neighborhood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband is a priest, the wife cannot live with him in the same alleyway; if it is a small village, it is considered a neighborhood.

items.text: Gemara: Who is displaced?
items.text_en: Gemara: Who is displaced?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who is displaced from the residence. A baraita teaches that she is displaced from him, not he from her, unless it is her courtyard. A dilemma is raised about a jointly owned courtyard, and the Gemara attempts to resolve it, concluding with a verse about displacement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is displaced from the residence in the case of a priest whose wife is a divorcee or חלוצה (a woman who underwent חליצה).
The Gemara brings a baraita that rules: she is displaced from him, not he from her, unless it is her courtyard, in which case he is displaced from her.
A dilemma is raised: what is the law if the courtyard is jointly owned by both of them?
The Gemara attempts to resolve the dilemma from the baraita, but rejects the proof because the baraita might be referring to a rented courtyard, not a jointly owned one.
The Gemara cites a verse and Rav's statement that a man's displacement is more difficult than a woman's, implying that in a jointly owned courtyard, she is displaced from him.

items.text: Baraita: Collection of ketubah from father's property
items.text_en: Baraita: Collection of ketubah from father's property
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a man borrowed from his wife against her father's property, she can only collect through a third party. Rav Sheshet, Rav Pappa, Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua, and Rav Nachman debate the court's response. Rav Nachman cites a distinction from Eivel Rabbati: if divorced after marriage, she needs a third party; if after betrothal, she collects herself.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught: if a husband borrowed from his wife using her father's property, she may only collect through a third party.
Rav Sheshet says: if they come before us for judgment, we do not engage with them.
Rav Pappa says: we excommunicate them.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua says: we also flog them.
Rav Nachman cites a baraita from Evel Rabbati: the restriction applies only when divorced after marriage, not after betrothal, since he is not familiar with her.

items.text: Story of Rava and the betrothed couple
items.text_en: Story of Rava and the betrothed couple
items.desc_en: A story is told of a betrothed couple who came before Rava. Rava appointed an agent between them. Rav Adda bar Matna questioned this based on Rav Nachman's ruling. Rava responded that he saw they were familiar with each other. An alternative version says Rava did not appoint an agent initially, but Rav Adda suggested it, and Rava explained the distinction.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a betrothed couple who came before Rava, and Rava appointed an agent between them.
Rav Adda bar Matna objects, citing Rav Nachman's ruling from the 'Evel Rabbati' that a betrothed woman collects her ketubah herself, implying no agent is needed.
Rava responds that he saw the couple were familiar with each other, justifying the appointment of an agent.
An alternative version states that Rava did not initially appoint an agent, and Rav Adda bar Matna suggested doing so, citing Rav Nachman's ruling.
Rava explains that Rav Nachman's ruling applies only when the couple are not familiar, but here they are familiar, so an agent is appropriate.

items.text: Mishnah: Who is believed to testify about what they saw as minors
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who is believed to testify about what they saw as minors
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who are believed to testify about what they saw as minors: a person can say 'this is my father's handwriting', 'my rabbi's handwriting', 'my brother's handwriting', or about a woman going out with her head uncovered, a man leaving the school to immerse to eat terumah, dividing the threshing floor, a beit hapras, or the Sabbath boundary. But one is not believed about a path or a eulogy.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing those who are believed to testify as adults about what they saw as minors, beginning with handwriting identification.

The Mishnah continues listing additional testimonies: a woman going out with head uncovered, a man leaving school to immerse for תרומה (priestly portion), dividing the threshing floor, a בית הפרס (plowed-over grave area), and the Sabbath boundary.
The Mishnah concludes by stating what one is not believed to testify about: a path or a eulogy.

items.text: Gemara: Condition for testimony about handwriting
items.text_en: Gemara: Condition for testimony about handwriting
items.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua says that the testimony about handwriting is only valid if there is an adult with him. The Gemara explains why all three cases (father, rabbi, brother) are necessary, and concludes that since document validation is rabbinic, the rabbis relied on this testimony.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua states that the testimony about handwriting is only valid if there is an adult with him.
The Gemara questions why all three cases (father, rabbi, brother) are necessary, suggesting that each alone might be insufficient.
The Gemara resolves that since document validation is rabbinic, the rabbis relied on this testimony even without an adult present.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of testimony about a woman and a man's status
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of testimony about a woman and a man's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why testimony about a woman going out with her head uncovered is believed: most women are married. Regarding a man leaving the school to immerse for terumah, the Gemara questions if he might be a Canaanite slave, and cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that one may not teach a slave Torah. The Gemara then challenges this with a baraita about a slave studying Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why testimony about a woman going out with her head uncovered is believed, and answers that since most women are married, it is merely revealing an obvious fact.
The Gemara questions whether the man leaving the school to immerse for terumah might be a Canaanite slave, and notes that this supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's position.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that it is forbidden for a person to teach his slave Torah.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement by citing a baraita that implies a slave may have studied Torah.

items.text: Slave who performed mitzvot does not go free
items.text_en: Slave who performed mitzvot does not go free
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that a slave who acted as an apostate, put on tefillin in front of his master, or read three verses in the synagogue does not thereby go free, because he did so of his own accord, not as a sign of freedom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a slave who acted as an apostate, put on tefillin, or read three verses in the synagogue does not go free, because he did so of his own accord, not as a sign of freedom.

items.text: Terumah distribution to a slave and lineage
items.text_en: Terumah distribution to a slave and lineage
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case of a slave who immersed to eat terumah refers to rabbinic terumah, and that the case of one who divided with us on the threshing floor is explained by the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei: Rabbi Yehuda holds that terumah is not given to a slave unless his master is with him, while Rabbi Yosei holds the slave can claim for himself if he is a priest or for his master if he is a slave. In Rabbi Yehuda's place, they would elevate lineage based on terumah distribution; in Rabbi Yosei's place, they would not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the case of a slave who immerses to eat תרומה (priestly portion) and answers that it refers to rabbinic תרומה.
The Gemara questions the case of one who divided with us on the threshing floor, asking whether he might be a priest's slave.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that תרומה is not given to a slave unless his master is with him.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's position that a slave can claim תרומה for himself if he is a priest or for his master if he is a slave.
The Gemara concludes that in Rabbi Yehuda's place they would elevate lineage based on תרומה distribution, but in Rabbi Yosei's place they would not.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's testimony about a slave
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's testimony about a slave
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei saying he never testified, but once he did and they elevated a slave to the priesthood based on his testimony. The Gemara objects that this cannot be, as God does not bring calamity through the righteous. It corrects: they sought to elevate a slave, but he saw in Rabbi Yosei's place and went and testified in Rabbi Yehuda's place.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei stating that he never testified, but once he did and they elevated a slave to the priesthood based on his testimony.
The Gemara objects that it is impossible for a righteous person's testimony to cause a slave to be elevated to the priesthood, since God does not bring calamity through the righteous.
The Gemara corrects the baraita: they only sought to elevate a slave, but Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei saw in Rabbi Yosei's place and went and testified in Rabbi Yehuda's place.

items.text: Testimony about a beit haperas
items.text_en: Testimony about a beit haperas
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that testimony that a place is a beit haperas is believed because beit haperas is a rabbinic impurity, as Rav Yehuda said Shmuel said: one may sift a beit haperas and walk, and Rav Yehuda bar Ami said in the name of Rav Yehuda: a trodden beit haperas is pure, since it is impossible for a barley-sized bone not to be crushed by foot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a בית הפרס (a field with scattered bones) is considered impure only by rabbinic law.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that one may sift a בית הפרס (field with scattered bones) and walk through it, indicating its impurity is rabbinic.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Ammi in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Ammi in the name of Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Ammi in the name of Rav Yehuda adds that a בית הפרס (field with scattered bones) that was trampled is pure, because any bone the size of a barley grain would have been crushed.

items.text: Testimony about Shabbat boundaries
items.text_en: Testimony about Shabbat boundaries
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that testimony that 'we came up to here on Shabbat' is believed because Shabbat boundaries are rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case of traveling on Shabbat is permitted because the laws of תחומין (Sabbath boundaries) are rabbinic.

items.text: Testimony about a path or eulogy is not believed
items.text_en: Testimony about a path or eulogy is not believed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one is not believed to say 'there was a path for so-and-so in this place' or 'there was a eulogy for so-and-so in this place' because this would extract money, and we do not extract money based on such testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one is not believed to testify about a path or funeral because that would extract money, which requires stronger evidence.
The Gemara explains the reason: such testimony would extract money, and we do not extract money based on this level of testimony.

items.text: Child's testimony about family purity and the dispute about converts and freed slaves
items.text_en: Child's testimony about family purity and the dispute about converts and freed slaves
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a child is believed to say 'this family is pure' or 'this family is impure' (corrected to 'fit' or 'unfit'), and about eating at a betrothal meal or bringing hallah and gifts to a priest. This is only for himself, not for others. All these, if the person was a gentile and converted or a slave and freed, they are not believed. Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka says they are believed. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka disputes the first clause (about converts and freed slaves), not the latter. The dispute is: the first tanna holds that since he was a gentile, he was not precise, while Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka holds that since he intended to convert, he was precise.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a child is believed to say 'this family is fit' or 'this family is unfit' (correcting the original 'pure'/'impure' as impossible).

The baraita continues listing additional testimonies a child is believed about (betrothal meal, bringing hallah and gifts to a priest), but only for himself, and adds that converts and freed slaves are not believed.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka states that converts and freed slaves are believed, disputing the first tanna's position.

The Gemara asks which clause of the baraita Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka disputes, rejecting the possibility that he disputes the final clause (about 'way' and 'eulogy') because that involves monetary loss.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka disputes the first clause regarding converts and freed slaves.
The Gemara explains the dispute: the first tanna holds that as a gentile he was not precise, while Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka holds that since he intended to convert, he was precise.

items.text: Explanation of 'ketzatzah'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'ketzatzah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what 'ketzatzah' is: when one brother married a woman unfit for him, the family brings a barrel of fruit, breaks it in the public square, and declares that they fear his seed will mix with theirs, calling on the community to take a lesson. This is the ketzatzah about which a child is believed to testify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the meaning of the term 'קצצה' (family separation ceremony).

A baraita explains that a קצצה (family separation ceremony) occurs when a family member marries an unsuitable woman, and the family breaks a barrel of fruit in the street to publicly separate from him, and a child is believed to testify about it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: listing of girls with kenas
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: listing of girls with kenas
