items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates two groups: first, girls who are disqualified (mamzeret, netinah, kutit, convert, captive, slave) who were under three years old; second, relatives (sister, etc.) who have kenas despite being subject to karet, but not to court execution.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the first group of girls who have a fine (קנס): those who are disqualified (mamzeret, netinah, kutit, convert, captive, slave) who were under three years old.
The Mishnah lists the second group of girls who have a fine (קנס): relatives (sister, etc.) who are subject to karet but not to court execution.

items.text: Gemara's question and clarification
items.text_en: Gemara's question and clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: does the Mishnah imply that only disqualified girls have kenas, but kosher girls do not? It answers that the Mishnah means: these are the disqualified girls who have kenas.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication: do only disqualified girls have a fine, but not qualified ones?
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah means: 'These are the disqualified girls who have a fine' — it does not exclude qualified girls.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna: Rabbi Meir's view on kenas for a minor
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna: Rabbi Meir's view on kenas for a minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'na'arah' (girl from 12 to 12.5) but not 'ketanah' (under 3). It asks which Tanna holds this. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says it is Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that a ketanah has no kenas until she brings two pubic hairs, while a na'arah has kenas but no sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds the view that only a na'arah (girl from 12 to 12.5) has kenas (fine), but a ketanah (minor under 3) does not.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that a ketanah has no kenas until she brings two pubic hairs, while a na'arah has kenas but no sale.

items.text: Sages' objection and correction
items.text_en: Sages' objection and correction
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that a ketanah from age three onward has kenas, but the Gemara objects: if she has kenas, does she not have sale? The Gemara then corrects the text to say that the Sages hold she has both kenas and sale.

sub.desc_en: The Chachamim state that a minor from three years and one day until she reaches majority has a fine.
The Gemara questions the implication of the Chachamim's statement: does a minor have a fine but no sale? It then begins to correct the text.
The Gemara corrects the text, implying that the Sages actually hold she has both קנס (fine) and מכר (sale), and the original wording should be read differently.

items.text: Opening statement: The penalty applies where the sale would apply
items.text_en: Opening statement: The penalty applies where the sale would apply
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the penalty (kenas) applies in a case where the sale (of the daughter) would apply, implying that the woman must be eligible for marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the penalty (kenas) applies where the sale (of the daughter) would apply, implying the woman must be eligible for marriage.

items.text: Two derivations from extra scriptural terms
items.text_en: Two derivations from extra scriptural terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for extra verses, then presents Resh Lakish's derivation from three occurrences of 'na'arah' and Rav Pappa's derivation from three occurrences of 'betulah', each using one for the basic law, one for those liable to lashes, and one for those liable to karet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how young women of flawed lineage can be entitled to the fine, since the verse 'והיתה לו לאשה' implies only a woman suitable for him.
Reish Lakish derives from the three mentions of 'נערה' that the fine applies also to those liable for prohibitions and those liable for karet.
Rav Pappa derives the same inclusion from the three mentions of 'בתולה' in the passage of the seducer.

items.text: Why each Amora didn't adopt the other's derivation
items.text_en: Why each Amora didn't adopt the other's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Resh Lakish and Rav Pappa each did not use the other's set of verses: Rav Pappa needed 'na'arah' for Abaye's ruling (exempt if the girl died), and Resh Lakish needed 'betulah' for a gezeirah shavah (comparing the mohar). The Gemara then notes that both actually need both derivations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Pappa did not use the derivation from the term 'na'arah' like Resh Lakish.
The Gemara answers that Rav Pappa needed the term 'na'arah' for Abaye's ruling that if the girl died, the rapist is exempt from the fine.
The Gemara asks why Resh Lakish did not use the derivation from the term 'betulah' like Rav Pappa.
The Gemara answers that Resh Lakish needed the term 'betulah' for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) comparing the fine of the seducer to that of the rapist.
The Gemara objects that both Resh Lakish and Rav Pappa actually need both derivations, so the earlier answers are insufficient.

items.text: Resolution: Six verses suffice for all needs
items.text_en: Resolution: Six verses suffice for all needs
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that there are six verses (three 'na'arah' and three 'betulah'): two for the basic law, one for Abaye's ruling, one for the gezeirah shavah, and the remaining two for those liable to lashes and karet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that there are six scriptural terms total, allowing two for the basic laws, one for Abaye's ruling, one for the verbal analogy, and the remaining two for the inclusions of those liable to lashes and karet.

items.text: Rejecting another Tanna's interpretation
items.text_en: Rejecting another Tanna's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa where Shimon HaTimni and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya interpret 'ishah ha'ru'uyah lo' differently: one says a woman with whom intercourse is possible, the other says a woman fit to sustain the marriage. Rabbi Zeira explains the practical difference is a mamzeret or netinah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita (תניא) that records two Tannaic interpretations of the phrase 'ולו תהיה לאשה' (and she shall be his wife): Shimon HaTimni says it means a woman with whom intercourse is possible (יש בה הויה), while Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says it means a woman fit to sustain the marriage (ראויה לקיימה).

Rabbi Zeira explains the practical difference between the two opinions: a mamzeret (ממזרת) or netinah (נתינה) — according to the first opinion, such a woman is fit for intercourse (יש בה הויה), so the rapist must marry her; according to the second, she is not fit to sustain the marriage (אינה ראויה לקיימה), so he does not.

items.text: Further differences according to Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yeshevav
items.text_en: Further differences according to Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yeshevav
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the difference is according to Rabbi Akiva (who holds that kiddushin does not take effect for those liable to lashes), and answers that it is a widow for a Kohen Gadol, citing Rabbi Simai. It then asks the same for Rabbi Yeshevav, who says any forbidden union produces a mamzer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference remains between the two tannaitic positions according to רבי עקיבא (Rabbi Akiva), who holds that קידושין (betrothal) does not take effect for those liable to lashes.

The Gemara answers that the difference is the case of an אלמנה (widow) to a כהן גדול (High Priest), citing the baraita of רבי סימאי (Rabbi Simai) that רבי עקיבא (Rabbi Akiva) deems offspring mamzerim from all forbidden unions except a widow to a High Priest, where the Torah says 'לא יקח ... ולא יחלל' — he creates חילולין (profaned offspring) but not mamzerim.

The Gemara asks what the practical difference is according to רבי ישבב (Rabbi Yeshevav), who said 'come and let us cry out against עקיבא בן יוסף (Akiva ben Yosef)' because he would say that any union lacking permitted ביאה (intercourse) in Israel produces a ממזר (mamzer).
The Gemara begins to answer that there is a difference between them, but the answer continues beyond this daf.

items.text: Opening statement: חייבי עשה, מצרי ואדומי
items.text_en: Opening statement: חייבי עשה, מצרי ואדומי
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the category of those liable for positive commandments, specifically a Egyptian or Edomite convert, as a basis for discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the category of those liable for positive commandments, specifically an Egyptian or Edomite convert, as a basis for discussion.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yeshevav and Rabbi Simai's views
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yeshevav and Rabbi Simai's views
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yeshevav's ruling follows Rabbi Simai's reasoning or his own, and identifies the practical difference as a woman who had intercourse with a High Priest, which is a non-universal positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rabbi Yeshevav adopting Rabbi Simai's reasoning versus stating his own view, since both would include חייבי עשה (those liable for positive commandments).
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in a woman who had intercourse with a High Priest, which is a positive commandment that is not universal (אינו שוה בכל).

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on one who has intercourse with a niddah
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on one who has intercourse with a niddah
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree that one who has intercourse with a niddah pays a fine, whether one holds that there is potential for conception or that she is fit for procreation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree one who has relations with a menstruating woman pays a fine, whether the reasoning is based on conception or suitability for fulfillment.

items.text: Excluding Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah's view
items.text_en: Excluding Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Chisda's statement excludes the view of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, who equates Yom Kippur with Shabbat for exempting from payment when liable for death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana treats Yom Kippur like Shabbat for fines, exempting from payment when liable for capital punishment.

items.text: Abaye explains Rabbi Nechunya's reasoning
items.text_en: Abaye explains Rabbi Nechunya's reasoning
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that Rabbi Nechunya derives from a verbal analogy of the word 'ason' (mishap) used both for human-inflicted and divine-inflicted harm, that one is exempt from payment in both cases.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains Rabbi Nechunya's reasoning by deriving a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'אסון' (misfortune) used for both human and divine agency.

Abaye explains that Rabbi Nechunya derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'אסון' (mishap) used both for human-inflicted and divine-inflicted harm, concluding that one is exempt from payment in both cases.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects to Abaye's proof, questioning whether Jacob's warning about 'thorns and snares' refers to divine or human agency, and the Gemara resolves with a baraita that thorns and snares are not in heaven's hands, and that lions and thieves are not in human hands, citing Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects to Abaye's proof, questioning whether Jacob's warning about 'thorns and snares' refers to divine agency or human agency (lions and thieves).
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that Jacob warned his sons about all dangers, both divine and human, so the objection is irrelevant.
The Gemara questions whether thorns and snares are really in heaven's hands, citing a baraita that everything is in heaven's hands except thorns and snares, as per the verse.

The Gemara further questions whether lions and thieves are really in human hands, citing Rav Yosef (and a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya) that since the Temple's destruction, the four death penalties have not ceased.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by noting that the statement 'they have not ceased' is itself problematic, and the discussion continues with an explanation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Four death penalties not nullified
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Four death penalties not nullified
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the four court-imposed death penalties are not nullified; one liable for stoning falls from a roof or is mauled by a beast, etc. The Gemara then notes a textual issue and suggests reversing the attributions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the four court-imposed death penalties are not nullified, listing for each penalty a natural or accidental death that substitutes for it.
The Gemara notes a textual inconsistency and reverses the attributions: wild beasts and thieves are by Heaven's hand, thorns and traps are by human hand.

items.text: Rava's proof from the verse
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the verse
items.desc_en: Rava derives Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's principle from a verse: just as court-imposed death exempts from payment, so too karet exempts from payment.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana's principle from a verse: just as court-imposed death exempts from payment, so too karet exempts from payment.

items.text: Difference between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Difference between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Abaye and Rava, and answers: a non-priest who ate terumah — according to Abaye he is exempt from payment, according to Rava he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the positions of Rava and Abaye.
The Gemara answers: the difference is a non-priest (זר) who ate תרומה (priestly portion) — according to Abaye he is exempt from payment, according to Rava he is liable.

items.text: Objection from Rav Chisda's ruling
items.text_en: Objection from Rav Chisda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can Abaye exempt him? Rav Chisda said that Rabbi Nechunya agrees one who steals another's forbidden fat and eats it is liable, because the theft precedes the prohibition. Here too, the acquisition precedes the capital liability. The Gemara resolves: the case is where another shoved the terumah into his mouth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can Abaye exempt the priest? Rav Chisda said Rabbi Nechunya agrees one who steals another's forbidden fat and eats it is liable, because the theft precedes the prohibition; here too, the acquisition precedes the capital liability.
The Gemara resolves: the case is where another shoved the terumah into his mouth, so the priest never acquired it.

items.text: Further refinement of the case
items.text_en: Further refinement of the case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions: once he chews it, he acquires it, but capital liability only comes at swallowing. The case is where he shoved it into his gullet. If he can spit it out, why is he liable? If not, why is he liable? The answer: he can spit it out with difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: once he chews the terumah, he acquires it, but capital liability only comes at swallowing, so how can he be liable for both?
The Gemara answers: the case is where he shoved the terumah directly into his gullet.
The Gemara questions: if he can spit it out, why is he liable for theft? If he cannot, why is he liable for the death penalty?
The Gemara resolves: he can spit it out only with difficulty, so he is liable for theft (since he could theoretically return it) and for the death penalty (since it is effectively swallowed).

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi's alternative cases
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi's alternative cases
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says the case is where another shoved liquids of terumah into his mouth. Rav Ashi says it is a non-priest who ate his own terumah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa proposes that the case involves a non-priest whose friend shoved liquids of תרומה (priestly portion) into his mouth, so he never acquired them.
Rav Ashi counters that the case is a non-priest (זר) who ate his own תרומה (priestly portion), which he never acquired for consumption.

items.text: Opening citation
items.text_en: Opening citation
items.desc_en: The segment cites the case of tearing silk garments, which is the context for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the case of tearing silk garments belonging to another.

items.text: Rav Chisda's statement and the objection from Rabbi Avin
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statement and the objection from Rabbi Avin
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asserts that Rabbi Nechunya would hold a thief liable for eating forbidden fat because the theft was already committed before the prohibition of eating fat. The Gemara raises an objection from Rabbi Avin's principle that lifting is necessary for eating, but then distinguishes the cases: here eating is possible without lifting, and the thief could return the item.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asserts that Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana would hold a thief liable for eating forbidden fat because the theft was already committed before the prohibition of eating fat.
The Gemara raises an objection from Rabbi Avin's principle that lifting is necessary for eating, implying that the thief should be exempt.
The Gemara distinguishes the cases: here eating is possible without lifting, and the thief could return the item, unlike the arrow case.

items.text: Distinction between the two versions of the answer
items.text_en: Distinction between the two versions of the answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations given, and answers with the case of moving a knife in the public domain that tears silk: one version focuses on the impossibility of placing without lifting, the other on the inability to retrieve the item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two formulations of the rejection.

The Gemara answers that the difference lies in the case of one who carries a knife in the public domain and tears silk in its path: according to the first formulation, he is liable because placement is impossible without lifting; according to the second, he is exempt because he can retrieve the knife.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's principle and Rav Bibi's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's principle and Rav Bibi's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Avin's statement that one who shoots an arrow and tears silk is exempt because lifting is necessary for placing. Rav Bibi bar Abaye objects from the case of a thief who steals a purse on Shabbat: he is liable because the theft precedes the Shabbat violation, but if he drags it out, he is exempt because both prohibitions occur simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Avin's statement that one who shoots an arrow and tears silk is exempt because the lifting is a prerequisite for placement.

Rav Beivai bar Abaye objects with a baraita: one who steals a purse on Shabbat is liable because theft liability precedes the capital prohibition, but if he drags it out, he is exempt because both prohibitions arise simultaneously.

items.text: Gemara's answer to Rav Bibi's objection
items.text_en: Gemara's answer to Rav Bibi's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case of dragging is different because the thief lifted the purse with intent to hide it, and later decided to take it out, so the lifting was not for the sake of carrying out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the dragging case is exempt; here too, one could argue that the lifting is a prerequisite for the carrying out.
The Gemara answers that the case involves one who lifted the purse with intent to hide it, and then changed his mind and carried it out.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yohanan's principle
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yohanan's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even with intent to hide, if one later decides to take it out, he should be exempt, as Rabbi Yohanan ruled that moving objects from corner to corner and then taking them out is exempt because the initial lifting was not for that purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects based on Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who moves objects from corner to corner and then changes his mind and carries them out is exempt, because the initial lifting was not for that purpose.

items.text: Resolution: the case of standing to rest
items.text_en: Resolution: the case of standing to rest
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises the case: the thief lifted the purse with intent to take it out, and the discussion is about when he stood still. If he stood to rest, he is liable; if he stood to adjust his load, he is exempt because that is his normal way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the earlier explanation: the thief lifted the purse with intent to take it out, not to hide it.
The Gemara specifies that the case involves the thief standing still after lifting the purse.
The Gemara asks: for what purpose did he stand?
The Gemara answers: if he stood to adjust his load, that is his normal way and he is exempt.
The Gemara concludes: the case is when he stood to rest, making him liable.
The Gemara asks: but what about the case of standing to adjust his load?

items.text: Analysis of the case of dragging out on Shabbat
items.text_en: Analysis of the case of dragging out on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one who drags out an object is exempt, suggesting it should have taught the case of one who throws. It explains that the case of dragging was necessary to teach that dragging is a normal method of carrying out, and then identifies the anonymous Mishnah as following Ben Azzai who considers walking like standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah teaches the case of dragging out (מגרר ויוצא) rather than the more common case of throwing (זורק), and suggests it should have distinguished within the same case.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Ben Azzai, who considers walking like standing, so throwing would also be exempt; the case of dragging was necessary to teach that dragging is a normal method of carrying out.
The Gemara explains that the case of dragging was necessary because one might have thought that dragging is not a normal way of carrying out, so the Mishnah teaches that it is.

items.text: בירור גודל הכיס: בינוני
items.text_en: Determining the size of the object
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what size object is being discussed, concluding it must be a medium-sized object, as a large one is normally carried and a small one is not typically carried out.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת באיזה גודל כיס מדובר – לא גדול (שדרכו להיגרר) ולא קטן (שלא דרכו), אלא בינוני, שיש חידוש בכך שהוא חייב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what size object is being dragged, concluding it must be medium-sized, since large objects are normally dragged and small ones are not.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת באיזה גודל כיס מדובר, ומבררת שלכיסים גדולים דרכם להיגרר ולקטנים לא, ולכן מדובר בבינוני.

items.text: בירור הרשות: צידי רשות הרבים
items.text_en: Where the object was taken and the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions where the object was taken: if to the public domain, there is a Shabbat prohibition but no theft; if to a private domain, theft but no Shabbat. It resolves that it was taken to the sides of the public domain, and then discusses the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer (who considers the sides like the public domain for Shabbat) and the Rabbis (who do not). The Gemara concludes that even according to Rabbi Eliezer, for acquisition purposes the sides are considered private.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת לאיזו רשות הוצא הכיס – לא לרשות הרבים (שם איסור גניבה ליכא) ולא לרשות היחיד (שם איסור שבת ליכא), אלא לצידי רשות הרבים. לפי רבי אליעזר, צידי רשות הרבים כרשות הרבים לעניין שבת, אבל לעניין קניין קונה משום שהרבים אינם מצויים שם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the object was taken, noting that if to the public domain there is a Shabbat prohibition but no theft, and if to a private domain there is theft but no Shabbat prohibition.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה לאיזו רשות הוציא הגנב את הכיס: לרשות הרבים – איסור גניבה ליכא, לרשות היחיד – איסור שבת ליכא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the object was taken to the sides of the public domain (צידי רשות הרבים).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה לאיזו רשות הוציא הגנב את הכיס: לרשות הרבים – איסור גניבה ליכא, לרשות היחיד – איסור שבת ליכא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion this follows, noting that according to Rabbi Eliezer the sides are like the public domain for Shabbat (so Shabbat prohibition exists but no theft), while according to the Rabbis they are not (so theft exists but no Shabbat).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: לפי רבי אליעזר – איסור שבת איכא ואיסור גניבה ליכא; לפי רבנן – איסור גניבה איכא ואיסור שבת ליכא; בשני המקרים אין חילוק בין איסורים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the case follows Rabbi Eliezer, but his ruling that the sides are like the public domain applies only to Shabbat liability (since crowds sometimes push in there), not to acquisition, where the sides are considered private because the public is not commonly found there.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת: לעולם כרבי אליעזר, שדבריו מוגבלים לעניין חיוב שבת, אבל לעניין קניין – קונה בצידי רשות הרבים, כי הרבים אינם מצויים שם.

items.text: תירוץ רב אשי: צירוף ידו למטה משלשה
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case is where the thief cupped his hand below three handbreadths and received the object, citing Rava's principle that a person's hand is considered like a four-by-four handbreadth area.
items.desc: רב אשי מתרץ שהשעור הוא במקרה שצירוף ידו למטה משלשה וקיבל, כדברי רבא שידו של אדם חשובה כארבעה על ארבעה. באופן זה גם קונה וגם מחלל שבת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers an alternative answer: the case is where the thief cupped his hand below three handbreadths and caught the object, applying Rava's principle that a person's hand is considered four by four handbreadths.
sub.desc: רב אשי מתרץ שמדובר במקרה שצירף ידו למטה משלושה טפחים וקיבל את החפץ, ובכך גם קונה וגם מחלל שבת, כדברי רבא שידו של אדם חשובה כארבעה על ארבעה.

items.text: מחלוקת רבינא ורב אחא בהוצאה לרשות הרבים
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative explanation and the dispute with Rav Acha
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the object was taken to the public domain and acquired there, and both Rav Acha and Ravina derive their positions from the Mishnah about one who pulls out an animal. Ravina infers from the first clause that if the animal died in the owner's domain he is exempt, implying that if he took it out he is liable. Rav Acha infers from the latter clause that the act of taking out must be similar to lifting, i.e., bringing it into his domain. The Gemara resolves the difficulties each faces with the other's proof.
items.desc: רבינא סובר שהגבהה בלבד קונה אפילו ברשות הרבים, ואילו רב אחא סובר שצריך שיבוא לרשותו. שניהם דנים במשנה בבבא קמא, ומתרצים את הקושיות.

sub.desc_en: Ravina presents an alternative version of the sugya: the object was taken to the public domain and acquired there, and both Rav Acha and Ravina derive their positions from the Mishnah about one who pulls out an animal.
sub.desc: רבינא מציג את עמדתו: גם בהוצאה לרשות הרבים הגנב קונה, והמחלוקת עם רב אחא תלויה בדרך הדיוק במשנה בבבא קמא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about one who pulls out an animal: if it died in the owner's domain he is exempt, but if he lifted it or took it out of the owner's domain and it died, he is liable.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה: רבינא דייק מהרישא (שפטור רק כשמת ברשות בעלים) ורב אחא דייק מהסיפא (שההגבהה וההוצאה אמורות לבוא לרשותו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Ravina infers from the first clause and Rav Acha infers from the latter clause of the Mishnah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה: רבינא דייק מהרישא (שפטור רק כשמת ברשות בעלים) ורב אחא דייק מהסיפא (שההגבהה וההוצאה אמורות לבוא לרשותו).

sub.desc_en: Ravina infers from the first clause that if the animal died in the owner's domain he is exempt, implying that if he took it out he is liable.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה: רבינא דייק מהרישא (שפטור רק כשמת ברשות בעלים) ורב אחא דייק מהסיפא (שההגבהה וההוצאה אמורות לבוא לרשותו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha infers from the latter clause that the act of taking out must be similar to lifting, i.e., bringing it into his domain.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותרת את הקושיות: לרב אחא הרישא מתורצת בכך שעדיין נקרא 'רשות בעלים' כל עוד לא בא לרשותו, ולרבינא הסיפא מתורצת בכך שאין דורשים 'הוצאה דומיא דהגבהה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: Rav Acha's position is difficult with the first clause, and Ravina's position is difficult with the latter clause.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותרת את הקושיות: לרב אחא הרישא מתורצת בכך שעדיין נקרא 'רשות בעלים' כל עוד לא בא לרשותו, ולרבינא הסיפא מתורצת בכך שאין דורשים 'הוצאה דומיא דהגבהה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulties: for Rav Acha, as long as the animal has not entered his domain, it is still considered the owner's domain; for Ravina, the requirement that taking out be similar to lifting is not applied.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותרת את הקושיות: לרב אחא הרישא מתורצת בכך שעדיין נקרא 'רשות בעלים' כל עוד לא בא לרשותו, ולרבינא הסיפא מתורצת בכך שאין דורשים 'הוצאה דומיא דהגבהה'.

items.text: קושיה ממשנת הלוקין
items.text_en: Transition to the list of those liable for lashes
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic, citing a Mishnah about one who has relations with his sister and other relatives, and raises a contradiction with a baraita listing those who are lashed, which includes the same cases.
items.desc: הגמרא מעלה סתירה בין משנתנו (שמזכירה עריות שבהן קנס) למשנה במכות (שמזכירה עריות הלוקות), ומצביעה על כך שאותן עריות מופיעות בשתי הרשימות.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those liable for lashes: one who has relations with his sister, his father's sister, his mother's sister, his wife's sister, his brother's wife, his father's brother's wife, and a menstruating woman.
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה סתירה בין משנתנו (שמזכירה עריות שבהן קנס) לבין משנה במכות (שמזכירה עריות הלוקות), שכן אותן עריות מופיעות בשתי הרשימות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita listing those who are lashed, which includes the same cases.
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה סתירה בין משנתנו (שמזכירה עריות שבהן קנס) לבין משנה במכות (שמזכירה עריות הלוקות), שכן אותן עריות מופיעות בשתי הרשימות.

items.text: Ulla's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Ulla's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Ulla resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one's sister who is a na'arah and one's sister who is a bogeret. The Gemara then questions the case of a bogeret, where there is still boshet and pegam, and answers that it refers to a shoteh; it then questions tza'ar and answers that it refers to a mefutah. Finally, the Gemara suggests that even if it is one's sister who is a na'arah, it could be a yetomah and mefutah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that it is established that one does not receive both lashes and payment.
Ulla resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one's sister who is a na'arah and one's sister who is a bogeret.
The Gemara questions that even in the case of one's sister who is a bogeret, there is still boshet (shame) and pegam (blemish).
The Gemara answers that it refers to a shoteh (an insane woman), who has no boshet or pegam.
The Gemara further questions that there is still tza'ar (pain).
The Gemara answers that it refers to a mefutah (a seduced woman), who does not experience tza'ar.
The Gemara concludes that even if it is one's sister who is a na'arah, it could be a yetomah (orphan) and mefutah, thus avoiding the contradiction.

items.text: Ulla's principle and its source from Chovel ba-Chaveiro
items.text_en: Ulla's principle and its source from Chovel ba-Chaveiro
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Ulla holds the principle that wherever there is both monetary payment and lashes, he pays and is not flogged. It asks where Ulla derives this from and answers that he learns it from one who injures his fellow: just as there, he pays and is not flogged, so too here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Ulla holds the principle that wherever there is both monetary payment and lashes, he pays and is not flogged.
The Gemara asks from where Ulla derives this principle.
The Gemara answers that Ulla learns it from the case of one who injures his fellow: just as there he pays and is not flogged, so too here.

items.text: Rejection of the analogy to Chovel ba-Chaveiro
items.text_en: Rejection of the analogy to Chovel ba-Chaveiro
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy to one who injures his fellow because that case involves liability for five items, and the monetary payment is lenient since it is permitted in court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy to one who injures his fellow because that case involves liability for five items, and the monetary payment is lenient since it is permitted in court.

items.text: Alternative source from Edim Zomemim
items.text_en: Alternative source from Edim Zomemim
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests deriving the principle from conspiring witnesses, where there is both monetary payment and lashes, and he pays and is not flogged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the principle that one pays and is not flogged from the case of conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין), where both monetary payment and lashes apply, yet the witnesses pay and are not flogged.

items.text: Rejection of the analogy to Edim Zomemim
items.text_en: Rejection of the analogy to Edim Zomemim
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this analogy because conspiring witnesses do not require warning, and the monetary payment is lenient since they did not perform an action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy to conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין) because they require no warning (התראה) and their monetary payment is lenient, as they performed no action.

items.text: Derivation from the common element of both sources
items.text_en: Derivation from the common element of both sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the principle is derived from the common element of both cases, despite each having a stringent aspect and a lenient aspect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation by combining both sources through a common element (צד השוה), noting that despite each having a stringent aspect and a lenient aspect, the principle of paying monetary compensation instead of lashes applies wherever both money and lashes are possible.

items.text: Ulla's position: payment, not lashes
items.text_en: Ulla's position: payment, not lashes
items.desc_en: Ulla argues via a גזירה שווה from 'תחת' that wherever there is both monetary and lashes liability, the offender pays and does not receive lashes.

sub.desc_en: Ulla argues via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'תחת' that wherever there is both monetary and lashes liability, the offender pays and does not receive lashes.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction: warning determines lashes
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction: warning determines lashes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between cases where the offender was warned (lashes, no payment) and where not (payment, no lashes), deriving from the verse 'כדי רשעתו' that one is not punished for two wrongdoings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between a case where the offender was warned (lashes, no payment) and where not (payment, no lashes), even regarding one's sister who is a נערה (a young woman).

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds that when there is both monetary payment and lashes and the offender was warned, he receives lashes and does not pay, deriving this from the verse 'כְּדֵי רִשְׁעָתוֹ' (according to his wickedness) and the adjacent verse 'אַרְבָּעִים יַכֶּנּוּ' (forty lashes he shall strike him).

items.text: Objection from the case of one who injures another
items.text_en: Objection from the case of one who injures another
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the case of one who injures another, where even if warned, he pays and does not receive lashes, as per Rabbi Ami's statement about a blow worth less than a perutah.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the case of one who injures another
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the case of one who injures another
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: in the case of one who injures another, where there is both monetary and lashes liability, he pays and does not receive lashes, even with warning, as Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Yochanan states that one who strikes a blow worth less than a פרוטה (a small coin) receives lashes, implying that if it were worth a פרוטה he would pay and not receive lashes.

items.text: Resolution: explicit Torah verses for payment
items.text_en: Resolution: explicit Torah verses for payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Ila'a's principle that the Torah explicitly prescribed payment for conspiring witnesses and for one who injures another, so they pay even when lashes apply. Rabbi Yochanan rejects Ulla's position because it would nullify the prohibition against incest.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a cites the principle that the Torah explicitly prescribed payment for conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין) and for one who injures another (חובל בחבירו), deriving from the extra phrase 'יָד בְּיָד' (hand to hand) and 'כֵּן יִנָּתֵן בּוֹ' (so shall be given in him) that these are monetary payments, not lashes.

The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not accept Ulla's position, and answers that accepting it would nullify the prohibition against incest (ערוות אחותך לא תגלה), since the Torah's explicit prohibition would be undermined by the principle of 'two wrongdoings' (שתי רשעיות).

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution for the cases of חובל and עדים זוממין
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution for the cases of חובל and עדים זוממין
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one who injures his fellow and conspiring witnesses are liable for both payment and lashes, then the verses 'לא יוסיף' and 'והיה אם בן הכות הרשע' would be nullified. It resolves that conspiring witnesses can be applied to a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה, and one who injures can be applied to a blow worth less than a perutah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one who injures his fellow and conspiring witnesses are liable for both payment and lashes, the verses 'לֹא יוֹסִיף' and 'וְהָיָה אִם בִּן הַכּוֹת הָרָשָׁע' would be nullified.
The Gemara resolves that conspiring witnesses can be applied to a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה, and one who injures can be applied to a blow worth less than a perutah.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Ulla's derivations for בושת ופגם
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Ulla's derivations for בושת ופגם
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the case of one's sister, resolving it with a bogeret. Rabbi Yochanan explains that the phrase 'תחת אשר עינה' is needed for Abaye's derivation that it implies there is also בושת ופגם. Ulla derives the same from Rava's teaching about the fifty silver shekels for the father, which implies there is also בושת ופגם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: the case of one's sister can also be fulfilled with a בוגרת (grown woman), so the verse is not rendered moot.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) answers that he needs the phrase 'תחת אשר עינה' for Abaye's derivation.
Abaye cites the verse 'תחת אשר עינה' to infer that there is also בושת ופגם (humiliation and degradation).
The Gemara asks: and Ulla, who uses that verse for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), from where does he derive Abaye's halakha?
Rava cites the verse about the fifty silver shekels to infer that there is also בושת ופגם (humiliation and degradation).

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and Rava's support
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and Rava's support
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says that conspiring witnesses pay monetary compensation but do not receive lashes because they are not subject to warning. Rava supports this by arguing that warning them at any stage is impractical: before the testimony they might claim forgetfulness, during the testimony they would refrain, and after the testimony it is too late.

sub.desc_en: רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) states that conspiring witnesses pay monetary compensation but are not flogged because they are not subject to forewarning.
רבא (Rava) supports this by arguing that forewarning is impractical at any stage: initially they might claim forgetfulness, during testimony they would refrain, and after testimony it is too late.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Acha's counter-arguments
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Acha's counter-arguments
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's reasoning, suggesting that warning could be given within 'within the time it takes to speak' (בתוך כדי דיבור). Rav Acha bar Rav Ika further suggests that warning could be given beforehand with a hint (רמזי).

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: why not warn them within the time it takes to say a short phrase (בתוך כדי דיבור)?
Rav Acha bar Rav Ika objects: why not warn them initially and hint to them?

items.text: Abaye's retraction and final argument
items.text_en: Abaye's retraction and final argument
items.desc_en: Abaye retracts his objection, arguing that if conspiring witnesses required warning, then they would be killed without warning while they themselves require warning, contradicting the principle 'ועשיתם לו כאשר זמם לעשות לאחיו'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye retracts his objection, saying his statement was nothing.

Abaye argues that if conspiring witnesses needed warning, they would require warning to be killed, but they seek to kill others without warning, violating the principle 'וַעֲשִׂיתֶם לוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם'.

items.text: Rav Sama's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sama's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Yirmeya objects that if the requirement for warning is derived from 'כאשר זמם', then a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה, who are included from a different verse, should also require warning. The Gemara answers with the verse 'משפט אחד יהיה לכם', indicating a uniform law for all.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Yirmeya objects: if so, a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה, who are not derived from 'כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם', should require warning.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'מִשְׁפַּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם' establishes a uniform law for all.

items.text: Rav Shisha's derivation for חובל and the principle of warning for a severe matter
items.text_en: Rav Shisha's derivation for חובל and the principle of warning for a severe matter
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi derives that one who injures his fellow pays compensation but does not receive lashes from the verse about a pregnant woman. Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse speaks of a fight involving potential death, where warning was given for a severe matter (death) and thus serves as a warning for a light matter (injury). Rav Ashi challenges whether a warning for a severe matter indeed serves for a light matter, and whether death is indeed more severe.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi derives from the verse about a pregnant woman that one who injures his fellow pays compensation but does not receive lashes.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse speaks of a fight involving potential death, as indicated by the penalty of capital punishment.
The gemara asks: if no warning was given, why would the assailant be executed? It must be that warning was given.
The gemara resolves that warning for a severe matter (death) serves as warning for a light matter (injury), and the Torah imposes monetary payment when no death occurs.
Rav Ashi challenges whether a warning for a severe matter indeed serves for a light matter, and whether death is indeed more severe.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is lashes more severe?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is lashes more severe?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether lashes might be considered more severe than death, citing Rav's statement that if Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah had been flogged they would have worshipped the idol. Rav Sama bar Rav Asi challenges Rav Ashi, asking whether there is a distinction between a flogging with a fixed number of lashes and one without a fixed number.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility that lashes might be more severe than death, citing Rav's statement that if Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah had been flogged they would have worshipped the idol.

sub.text: Rav Sama bar Rav Asi's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Asi's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Asi challenges Rav Ashi, questioning whether there is a distinction between a flogging with a fixed number of lashes and one without a fixed number.

items.text: Rav Yaakov's objection: According to Rabbi's view
items.text_en: Rav Yaakov's objection: According to Rabbi's view
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod objects: This works according to the Rabbis who hold that 'nefesh' means actual capital punishment, but according to Rabbi who holds it means monetary compensation, what can be said?

sub.text: Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov objects: This works according to the Rabbis who hold that 'נפש' (nefesh) means actual capital punishment, but according to Rabbi who holds it means monetary compensation, what can be said?

items.text: Rav Yaakov's answer: Proof from the verse
items.text_en: Rav Yaakov's answer: Proof from the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod cites a proof from the verse 'If he rises and walks outside on his staff, then the striker shall be acquitted.' The Gemara explains that this teaches that the assailant is imprisoned, and if the victim dies, he is executed; if not, he pays for lost time and medical expenses. The Gemara clarifies that this must be a case where warning was given for a severe matter, which serves as a warning for a light matter.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod cites a proof from the verse 'If he rises and walks outside on his staff, then the striker shall be acquitted,' explaining that the assailant is imprisoned and if the victim dies he is executed, otherwise he pays for lost time and medical expenses.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and Rav Sama's response
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and Rav Sama's response
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: How do we know that warning for a severe matter is a warning for a light matter? And even if it is, how do we know death is more severe? Perhaps lashes are more severe, as Rav said. Rav Sama bar Rav Asi responds by asking whether there is a distinction between a flogging with a fixed number and one without.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: How do we know that warning for a severe matter constitutes warning for a light matter, and even if so, how do we know death is more severe — perhaps lashes are more severe, as Rav said that if Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah had been flogged they would have worshipped the idol.

sub.text: Rav Sama bar Rav Asi's response
sub.text_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Asi's response
sub.desc_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Asi responds: Is there no distinction between a flogging with a fixed number of lashes and one without a fixed number (i.e., death)?

items.text: Rav Mari's objection: Intentional vs. unintentional
items.text_en: Rav Mari's objection: Intentional vs. unintentional
items.desc_en: Rav Mari objects: How do we know that the verse 'and he shall be acquitted' refers to acquittal from death in an intentional case? Perhaps it refers to acquittal from exile in an unintentional case. The Gemara notes this is a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari objects that the verse 'וְנִקָּה' (and he shall be acquitted) might refer to acquittal from exile in an unintentional case, not from death in an intentional case, and the Gemara notes this is a difficulty.

items.text: Resh Lakish's identification: Rabbi Meir's view
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's identification: Rabbi Meir's view
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says: This ruling is in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can be both flogged and pay. The Gemara objects: If it is Rabbi Meir, then even for his daughter (i.e., in the case of seduction) he would also hold that he is flogged and pays?

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish identifies the anonymous ruling as following Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can be both flogged and pay monetary compensation.

The Gemara objects that if the ruling follows Rabbi Meir, then even in the case of seducing one's daughter (where the Torah prescribes death) he would also hold that the offender is flogged and pays, which is not the case.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution: The case of slaughtering through an agent
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution: The case of slaughtering through an agent
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Does Rabbi Meir hold that one who is executed does not pay? But there is a baraita where Rabbi Meir says one who steals and slaughters on Shabbat, or for idolatry, or a goring ox, pays the four or five-fold penalty, while the Sages exempt him. The Gemara resolves that this refers to slaughtering through an agent, as explained by Rabbi Yochanan and others. Rava derives this from the verse 'or sells it' — just as selling can be through an agent, so too slaughtering. The schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah also derive this from the words 'or' and 'under'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Does Rabbi Meir really hold that one who is executed does not pay, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir obligates payment for stealing and slaughtering on Shabbat or for idolatry, while the Sages exempt him.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to slaughtering through an agent, as stated by Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan and others.
Rava derives from the verse 'וּטְבָחוֹ אוֹ מְכָרוֹ' (and slaughters it or sells it) that just as selling can be through an agent, so too slaughtering.

sub.text: Schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah
sub.text_en: Schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah
sub.desc_en: The schools of Rabbi Yishmael and Hezekiah derive from the words 'אוֹ' (or) and 'תַּחַת' (under) respectively that the law includes an agent.

items.text: Mar Zutra's objection and the identity of the Sages
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's objection and the identity of the Sages
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra objects: Is there any case where if the person himself did it he would not be liable, but if an agent did it he would be liable? The Gemara answers that the person himself is not liable because he is subject to a more severe penalty (death). The Gemara then asks: If it is through an agent, what is the reason of the Sages who exempt? Who are these Sages?

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra objects: Is there any case where the principal would not be liable if he did it himself, but an agent would be liable?
The Gemara answers that the principal is not exempt because he is not liable, but because he is subject to a more severe penalty (death).
The Gemara asks: If the case involves slaughter through an agent, what is the reason of the Sages who exempt? Who are these Sages?

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Shabbat slaughter is fit for consumption, citing a Mishnah that even though one is liable for capital punishment, the slaughter is valid. It then resolves that the earlier statement follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that slaughter not fit for consumption is not considered slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the earlier statement follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that slaughter not fit for consumption is not considered slaughter.
The Gemara objects that Shabbat slaughter is fit for consumption, citing a Mishnah that even though one is liable for capital punishment, the slaughter is valid.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar's position on Shabbat cooking
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar's position on Shabbat cooking
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier statement follows Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, who holds that Shabbat labor products are forbidden in benefit for the one who acted intentionally. A baraita cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar regarding eating food cooked on Shabbat. Rabbi Chiya derives from a verse that Shabbat labor products are like consecrated items, but the word 'lachem' permits benefit for others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the earlier anonymous position follows Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar.
A baraita is cited presenting the dispute between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar regarding eating food cooked on Shabbat, whether intentionally or unintentionally.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar's position.
Rabbi Chiya derives from the verse 'ושמרתם את השבת כי קדש היא לכם' that Shabbat labor products are like consecrated items, forbidden in benefit, but the word 'לכם' permits benefit for others.
The Gemara resolves that the prohibition applies only to intentional acts (מזיד), not to unintentional ones (שוגג), based on the verse 'מחלליה מות יומת'.

items.text: Dispute over the status of Shabbat labor products
items.text_en: Dispute over the status of Shabbat labor products
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina dispute whether the prohibition of Shabbat labor products is biblical or rabbinic. One holds it is biblical based on the earlier derivation, while the other holds it is rabbinic, interpreting the verse to mean that only Shabbat itself is holy, not its products.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina over whether the prohibition of Shabbat labor products is biblical (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא) or rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן).

sub.text: Stam's explanation of the biblical position
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of the biblical position
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that the one who holds it is biblical relies on the earlier derivation from the verse.

sub.text: Stam's explanation of the rabbinic position
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of the rabbinic position
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that the one who holds it is rabbinic interprets the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ הִיא' (it is holy) to mean that only Shabbat itself is holy, not its products.

items.text: Explanation of the Sages' exemption
items.text_en: Explanation of the Sages' exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the view that Shabbat labor products are rabbinic, the Sages who exempt from liability for slaughtering such an animal do so only for the remaining meat, not for the initial act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that Shabbat labor products are only rabbinically prohibited (דרבנן), what is the reasoning of the Sages who exempt from liability for slaughtering such an animal?
The Gemara answers: the Sages exempt only for the remaining meat (אשארא), not for the initial act of slaughter.

items.text: Slaughter for idolatry and the owner's loss
items.text_en: Slaughter for idolatry and the owner's loss
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the case of slaughtering for idolatry: once a small cut is made, the animal becomes forbidden, so the rest of the slaughter is not of the owner's property. Rava explains that one worships the idol through the completion of the slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how slaughter for idolatry can be considered the owner's property, since once a small cut is made the animal becomes forbidden and the rest is not the owner's.
Rava answers that the case is where one worships the idol through the completion of the slaughter, so the entire act is considered worship and the owner's loss applies.

items.text: The stoned ox and Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.text_en: The stoned ox and Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the stoned ox, which is not the owner's property. Rabbah explains the case involves a bailee whose ox was condemned and then stolen. Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yaakov, who holds that the bailee returns the ox to the owner after sentencing, and Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a matter causing monetary loss is considered like money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a stoned ox is not the owner's property, so how can the thief be liable for slaughtering it?
Rabbah explains the case involves a bailee whose ox was condemned and then stolen from the bailee's house.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yaakov, who holds the bailee returns the ox to the owner after sentencing, and Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a matter causing monetary loss is considered like money.

items.text: Rabbah's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbah's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbah offers an alternative explanation: the case involves slaughtering with one's own hands, implying that the liability is for the act itself rather than the property status.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that the case always involves slaughtering with one's own hands, shifting the focus to the act itself rather than the property status.

items.text: Rabbah's principle: liability for theft before Shabbat or burglary
items.text_en: Rabbah's principle: liability for theft before Shabbat or burglary
items.desc_en: Rabbah establishes that if one already possessed a stolen animal and then slaughtered it on Shabbat or in a burglary, he is liable for the fine because the theft liability preceded the capital offense. However, if the theft and slaughter occur simultaneously on Shabbat or in a burglary, he is exempt from the fine. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbah's principle: liability for theft before Shabbat or burglary leads to a fine, but simultaneous theft and slaughter exempts.
Rabbah applies the same principle to burglary: prior possession of a stolen goat leads to liability, but simultaneous theft and slaughter exempts.
The Gemara explains why both cases (Shabbat and burglary) are necessary to teach, as each has a unique feature that might otherwise lead to a different ruling.

items.text: Rav Pappa's case: a borrowed cow slaughtered on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's case: a borrowed cow slaughtered on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa adds a case where one had a borrowed cow and slaughtered it on Shabbat, teaching that he is exempt from the fine. Rav Acha bar Rava questions Rav Pappa, and Rav Pappa explains that he needed to teach that despite the borrower's liability for accidents from the time of borrowing, here he is exempt because the Shabbat violation overrides.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that if one had a stolen cow and slaughtered it on Shabbat, he is liable; but if it was a borrowed cow, he is exempt.
Rav Acha bar Rava objects to Rav Pappa's statement, questioning why he needed to teach about a cow specifically.

Rav Ashi explains that Rav Pappa's novelty is about the borrowed cow, teaching that despite a potential argument from Rav Pappa's own principle, the borrower is exempt from liability for the cow's value on Shabbat.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a borrowed cow left by a father
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a borrowed cow left by a father
items.desc_en: Rava discusses a case where a father left a borrowed cow to his sons; they may use it during the loan period, but if it dies they are not liable for accidents. If they mistakenly thought it was their father's and slaughtered it, they pay only the cheap meat price. If the father left assets for liability, they must pay full value. The Gemara notes two versions of this teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules on a case where a father left a borrowed cow to his sons: they may use it during the loan period, but if it dies they are not liable for its value; if they mistakenly slaughter and eat it, they pay only the cheap meat price; but if the father left assets for liability, they must pay full value.
The Gemara notes two versions of Rava's statement: one attached to the first part (implying disagreement with Rav Pappa) and one attached to the latter part (aligning with Rav Pappa).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on liability without warning
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on liability without warning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's position: since if warned the offender would be exempt (due to capital punishment), even without warning he is exempt. This is supported by a tradition from Rav Dimi about unintentional capital and lashes offenses. Reish Lakish then cites a verse to challenge Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan does not adopt Reish Lakish's position because he interprets the Mishnah according to the Rabbis.
The Gemara asks why Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's position.
Reish Lakish argues that since if warned the offender would be exempt (due to capital punishment), even without warning he is exempt.
The Gemara cites Rav Dimi's tradition about unintentional capital and lashes offenses, showing that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish follow their respective principles.
Reish Lakish cites a verse to challenge Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and two versions of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and two versions of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish regarding the interpretation of 'ason' (calamity) in Exodus 21:22-23. One version holds that Rabbi Yochanan argued 'ason' means actual death (ason mamash), while the other holds he argued it means a court-imposed death penalty (din ason).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the verse 'ason' means actual death (ason mamash).
The first version answers that 'ason' refers to a court-imposed death penalty (din ason).
The second version presents Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Resh Lakish.
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse and asks whether 'ason' means a court-imposed death penalty.
The second version answers that 'ason' means actual death.

items.text: Rava's objection from the baraita of the school of Hezekiah
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the baraita of the school of Hezekiah
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the premise that unintentional capital offenders are liable to pay, citing a baraita from the school of Hezekiah that draws an analogy between striking a person and striking an animal. Just as for striking an animal one is always liable for payment regardless of intent, so for striking a person one is always exempt from payment, implying that unintentional capital offenders are exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether anyone holds that unintentional capital offenders are liable to pay compensation.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from the school of Hezekiah
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from the school of Hezekiah
sub.desc_en: Rava cites the baraita of the school of Hezekiah that draws an analogy between striking a person and striking an animal, concluding that in both cases one is exempt from payment for unintentional acts.

items.text: Ravin's resolution: dispute is about unintentional flogging offenses
items.text_en: Ravin's resolution: dispute is about unintentional flogging offenses
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that all agree unintentional capital offenders are exempt from payment; the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish concerns unintentional flogging offenses (חייבי מלקות שוגגין). Rabbi Yochanan holds them liable because capital offenses are linked to payment by analogy, but flogging offenses are not; Resh Lakish holds them exempt because the Torah explicitly equates flogging offenses with capital offenses.

sub.desc_en: Ravin clarifies that all agree unintentional capital offenders are exempt; the dispute is about unintentional lashes (חייבי מלקות שוגגין).
Rabbi Yochanan holds that unintentional lashes are liable because the Torah juxtaposed capital and lashes only for intentional cases, not for unintentional ones.
Resh Lakish holds that unintentional lashes are exempt because the Torah explicitly included lashes with capital cases, making them equivalent.

items.text: Scriptural sources for the analogy: Abaye, Rava, and Rav Pappa's objection
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the analogy: Abaye, Rava, and Rav Pappa's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava propose different scriptural analogies to equate flogging offenses with capital offenses: Abaye uses a verbal analogy from 'rasha' (wicked), while Rava uses 'makeh' (striker). Rav Pappa challenges Rava's source, noting that the verse 'makeh adam yumat' deals with killing, not wounding. Rava then clarifies that the analogy is from 'makeh nefesh behemah' and the adjacent verse about wounding, and the Gemara explains that this verse applies to wounding without monetary value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the Torah explicitly equated liability for lashes with liability for capital punishment.
Abaye proposes a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'rasha' (wicked) used in both contexts.
Rava proposes a different verbal analogy from the word 'makeh' (striker) used in both contexts.
Rav Pappa challenges Rava's source, arguing that the verse 'וּמַכֵּה אָדָם יוּמָת' deals with killing, not wounding.
Rava clarifies that the analogy is from 'מַכֵּה נֶפֶשׁ בְּהֵמָה' (striking an animal) and the adjacent verse about wounding a person.
The Gemara objects that the verse about wounding is not about 'makeh' but about 'hakkah' (striking), and that the wounder is liable for monetary compensation.
The Gemara resolves that since the verse cannot apply to a wounding that has monetary value (שווה פרוטה), it is applied to a wounding without monetary value, establishing the analogy for lashes.

items.text: Rava's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the apparent contradiction about one who kills and pays, explaining that the case is where the blow simultaneously tore the victim's garments, so the payment is for the garment, not for the person.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involves a blow that simultaneously tore the victim's garments, so the payment is for the garment, not for the person.

items.text: Rav Chiyya's challenge from the school of Chizkiya
items.text_en: Rav Chiyya's challenge from the school of Chizkiya
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya challenges Rava: according to the school of Chizkiya, who compares striking a person to striking an animal, perhaps the verse about striking a person refers to Shabbat, where one could argue about the animal itself. The Gemara rejects this, showing the verse must refer to a weekday because on Shabbat the animal payment would not apply.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya challenges Rava: according to the school of Chizkiya, who compares 'מכה אדם' (striking a person) to 'מכה בהמה' (striking an animal), perhaps the verse about striking a person refers to Shabbat, where one could argue about the animal itself.
The Gemara rejects this, showing the verse must refer to a weekday because on Shabbat the animal payment would not apply.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about Raba's view
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about Raba's view
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to Raba, who says that a fine is a novel enactment and one pays even if executed, with which Tanna does the Mishnah align? He notes difficulties with Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana, and Rabbi Yitzchak. The Gemara concludes that Raba must hold like Rabbi Yochanan, not Resh Lakish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to Raba, who holds that a fine (קנס) is a novel enactment (חידוש) and one pays even if executed, with which Tanna does the Mishnah align? He notes difficulties with Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana, and Rabbi Yitzchak.
The Gemara resolves that if Raba holds like Rabbi Yochanan he can reconcile the Mishnah, but if he holds like Resh Lakish he cannot; therefore Raba must hold like Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Rav Mattana's question about Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Rav Mattana's question about Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana asks Abaye: according to Resh Lakish, who says the Torah explicitly equated those liable to lashes with those liable to death, which Tanna disputes Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana? The options are Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yitzchak.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana asks Abaye: according to Resh Lakish, who holds that the Torah explicitly equated those liable to lashes with those liable to death, which Tanna disputes Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana — Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yitzchak?

items.text: Baraita listing women without fine or seduction payment
items.text_en: Baraita listing women without fine or seduction payment
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught: For forbidden relations (arayot) and secondary forbidden relations (sheniyot), a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet), an aylonit, and a woman who leaves due to a bad name — none receive a fine or seduction payment. The Gemara begins to clarify the terms 'arayot' and 'sheniyot'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is taught listing categories of women who receive neither a fine (קנס) nor seduction payment (פיתוי): forbidden relations (עריות), secondary forbidden relations (שניות לעריות), a minor who refuses marriage (ממאנת), an aylonit (איילונית), and a woman who leaves due to a bad name (יוצאת משום שם רע).

The Gemara asks: What is meant by 'עריות' (forbidden relations) and 'שניות לעריות' (secondary forbidden relations) in the baraita? It begins to consider the possibility that 'עריות' refers to the standard biblical prohibitions.

items.text: Dispute over which forbidden relations are subject to the fine
items.text_en: Dispute over which forbidden relations are subject to the fine
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Tannaitic dispute: one version holds that 'arayot' refers to capital offenses and 'sheniyot' to karet offenses, while those liable for negative commandments have a fine, attributed to Shimon HaTimni. Another version holds that 'arayot' includes both capital and karet offenses, and 'sheniyot' are negative commandments, attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how 'arayot' (forbidden relations) could refer to actual forbidden relations and 'sheniyot' (secondary forbidden relations) to rabbinic enactments, since if the woman is Biblically permitted, why would she have no fine?

The Gemara resolves that 'arayot' refers to capital offenses (חייבי מיתות בית דין) and 'sheniyot' to karet offenses (חייבי כריתות), while those liable for negative commandments have a fine, and this is the position of Shimon HaTimni.
An alternative version holds that 'arayot' includes both capital and karet offenses, and 'sheniyot' are negative commandments, attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.

items.text: Contradiction in the mishnah regarding a minor who refuses marriage
items.text_en: Contradiction in the mishnah regarding a minor who refuses marriage
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a me'anes (a minor who refuses marriage) has no fine, implying that a regular minor does have a fine. This matches the Rabbis' view. However, the continuation says an aylonit has no fine, which aligns with Rabbi Meir, who holds that a minor has no fine. This creates a contradiction: the first part follows the Rabbis, the second part follows Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction in the mishnah: the first clause (about a minor who refuses marriage) follows the Rabbis, but the second clause (about an aylonit) follows Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Attempt to attribute the entire mishnah to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Attempt to attribute the entire mishnah to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the entire mishnah might be Rabbi Meir, who holds regarding a me'anes like Rabbi Yehuda. But a baraita shows Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree about the age of refusal: Rabbi Meir says until two pubic hairs, Rabbi Yehuda says until black hair exceeds white. This refutes the suggestion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the entire mishnah might be Rabbi Meir, who holds regarding a me'anes like Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree about the age of refusal, showing Rabbi Meir does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Attempt to attribute the entire mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Attempt to attribute the entire mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, who holds regarding a minor like Rabbi Meir. But Rav Yehuda said in Rav's name that the view that a minor has no fine is only Rabbi Meir's. If Rabbi Yehuda agreed, the statement would say 'Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda'. The Gemara concludes that this Tanna agrees with Rabbi Meir on one matter and disagrees on another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, who holds regarding a minor like Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara objects: Rav Yehuda said in Rav's name that the view that a minor has no fine is only Rabbi Meir's; if Rabbi Yehuda agreed, the statement would say 'Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda'.
The Gemara concludes that this Tanna agrees with Rabbi Meir on one matter and disagrees on another.

items.text: Rafram's interpretation of 'me'anes'
items.text_en: Rafram's interpretation of 'me'anes'
items.desc_en: Rafram explains that 'me'anes' in the mishnah means one who is eligible to refuse (i.e., a minor). The Gemara objects: why not just say 'minor'? The difficulty remains.

sub.desc_en: Rafram explains that the term 'me'anes' in the mishnah refers to a girl who is eligible to refuse (i.e., a minor).
The Gemara objects: if the mishnah means a minor, why not simply say 'minor'? The difficulty remains unresolved.

items.text: Contradiction regarding an aylonit's fine and the resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding an aylonit's fine and the resolution
items.desc_en: The mishnah says an aylonit has no fine, but a baraita says a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and an aylonit have a fine. The Gemara initially dismisses the contradiction as a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis. However, it then notes a more precise contradiction: a baraita states that a deaf-mute, imbecile, and bogeret (adult) and one injured by wood have no claim of virginity, while a blind woman and an aylonit do have such a claim. Sumchus adds in Rabbi Meir's name that a blind woman has no claim.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that an aylonit (a woman with male-like physical traits) has no fine (קנס) and no seduction payment (פיתוי).
The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and an aylonit do have a fine and a claim of virginity.
The Gemara objects that the contradiction is not strong, since the mishnah could follow the Rabbis and the baraita could follow Rabbi Meir, so why raise it?

The Gemara explains that the real contradiction is with a different baraita: a deaf-mute, imbecile, bogeret (adult), and one injured by wood have no claim of virginity, while a blind woman and an aylonit do have such a claim.

sub.text: Sumchus in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Sumchus in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Sumchus adds in Rabbi Meir's name that a blind woman has no claim of virginity, providing an additional position on the matter.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's resolution of the aylonit contradiction
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's resolution of the aylonit contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by attributing the sources to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua. The objection is raised that Rabban Gamliel only believes her when she claims, but here she does not claim. The Gemara answers that since Rabban Gamliel deems her credible, it is like 'open your mouth for the mute' — he speaks on her behalf.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction by attributing the conflicting sources to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Gemara objects that Rabban Gamliel's credibility rule applies only when the woman herself claims, but here she does not claim.
The Gemara answers that since Rabban Gamliel deems her credible, it is like 'open your mouth for the mute' — he speaks on her behalf.

items.text: Contradiction regarding a bogeret's claim of virginity
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding a bogeret's claim of virginity
items.desc_en: The baraita states that a bogeret has no claim of virginity, but Rav says a bogeret is given the first night (to claim virginity). This sets up a contradiction that will be addressed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraita states that a bogeret (a girl who has passed the age of na'arus) has no claim of virginity, but Rav says that a bogeret is given the first night (to claim virginity).

items.text: Clarifying the case of a claim of blood
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of a claim of blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between a claim of blood (טענת דמים) and a claim of an open entrance (טענת פתח פתוח). It explains that the current discussion deals with a claim of an open entrance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case involves a claim of an open entrance (טענת פתח פתוח), not a claim of blood (טענת דמים).

items.text: Sumchos' reason for a blind girl having no claim of virginity
items.text_en: Sumchos' reason for a blind girl having no claim of virginity
items.desc_en: Sumchos says in the name of Rabbi Meir that a blind girl has no claim of virginity. Rabbi Zeira explains that this is because she is likely to be injured by falling on the ground. The Gemara questions why other girls are not similarly injured, and answers that they can see and show their injuries to their mothers, but a blind girl cannot.

sub.text: Sumchos in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Sumchos in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Sumchos states in the name of Rabbi Meir that a blind girl has no claim of virginity.
The Gemara asks what Sumchos' reason is for this ruling.
Rabbi Zeira explains that it is because she is likely to be injured by falling on the ground.
The Gemara objects that all girls are similarly injured by falling.
The Gemara resolves that other girls can see and show their injuries to their mothers, but a blind girl cannot.

items.text: A girl with a bad reputation has no fine or seduction payment
items.text_en: A girl with a bad reputation has no fine or seduction payment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a girl who leaves due to a bad reputation has no fine or seduction payment. The Gemara questions how this can be, since such a girl is subject to stoning. Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah refers to a girl who had a bad reputation in her youth, before she was betrothed.
