sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a girl who leaves due to a bad reputation has no fine or seduction payment.
The Gemara objects: a girl who leaves due to a bad reputation is subject to stoning, so how can she lack a fine?
Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah refers to a girl who had a bad reputation in her youth, before she was betrothed.

items.text: Rav Pappa's inference about a problematic document
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's inference about a problematic document
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa infers from the Mishnah that a problematic document (שטרא ריעא) is not collected in court. He compares the case of a girl with a bad reputation to a document suspected of being forged. The Gemara distinguishes between a rumor of promiscuity (which is not heeded) and testimony that the man asked witnesses to forge the document (which is heeded).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa infers from the Mishnah that a problematic document (שטרא ריעא) is not collected in court.
The Gemara asks what case Rav Pappa is referring to, suggesting it might be a rumor that the document is forged.
The Gemara objects that just as Rava ruled a rumor of promiscuity is not heeded, a rumor about a document being forged should also not be heeded.
The Gemara resolves that the case is when two witnesses testify that the man asked them to forge the document, and since he sought forgery, he likely forged it himself.

items.text: Mishnah: Those who have no fine
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who have no fine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who have no fine: one who has relations with a convert, captive, or maidservant who were redeemed, converted, or freed after the age of three; and one who has relations with close relatives, because they are liable for capital punishment, and one liable for death does not pay monetary compensation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who have no fine: one who has relations with a convert, captive, or maidservant who were redeemed, converted, or freed after the age of three, and Rabbi Yehuda adds that a captive who was redeemed retains her sanctity even if she is an adult.

The Mishnah continues listing those who have no fine: one who has relations with close relatives, because they are liable for capital punishment, and one liable for death does not pay monetary compensation, as derived from the verse.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan links Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan links Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa said the same thing. Rabbi Yehuda's view is that a captive woman retains her sanctity. Rabbi Dosa's view is that a captive woman may eat terumah, as the Arab did not actually render her unfit for the priesthood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan declares that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa said the same thing.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda's view from the Mishnah that a captive woman retains her sanctity.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Dosa rules that a captive woman may eat תרומה (priestly portion).
Rabbi Dosa asks rhetorically what the Arab actually did to her, implying no real damage.
Rabbi Dosa concludes that mere fondling does not disqualify her from the priesthood.

items.text: Rabbah challenges the link between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa
items.text_en: Rabbah challenges the link between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa
items.desc_en: Rabbah suggests that Rabbi Yehuda's leniency regarding a captive woman might be only to prevent the sinner from profiting, while he agrees with the Rabbis regarding terumah. Alternatively, Rabbi Dosa's leniency might be only regarding rabbinic terumah, while he agrees with the Rabbis regarding the biblical fine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah questions the link between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa, suggesting each might agree with the Rabbis in the other case.

items.text: Abaye questions Rabbah's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Abaye questions Rabbah's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah, pointing out that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning for a captive woman is not just to prevent the sinner from profiting, as evidenced by a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a captive woman as young as ten has a ketubah of 200. Abaye asks what profit is there in that case, and suggests it is to prevent men from refraining from marrying her.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah's explanation that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is only to prevent the sinner from profiting, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda grants a ketubah of 200 to a captive woman as young as ten, and asks what profit exists there, suggesting it is to prevent men from refraining from marrying her.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's view regarding a captive woman
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's view regarding a captive woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that one who redeems a captive woman may marry her, but if he testifies about her, he may not. Rabbi Yehuda says in either case he may not marry her. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by emending the text: Rav Pappa says Rabbi Yehuda says in either case he may marry her. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua says Rabbi Yehuda was speaking to the Rabbis according to their reasoning. The Rabbis explain their own view: one who redeems and testifies may marry her, but one who merely testifies may not, lest he be motivated by lust.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda holds that a captive woman retains her sanctity, citing a baraita that contradicts his position.
The Gemara resolves the internal contradiction in the baraita by explaining that it refers to one who both redeems and testifies, versus one who merely testifies.
The Gemara notes that even with this resolution, the baraita still contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's position.
Rav Pappa emends the text of the baraita to say that Rabbi Yehuda permits marriage in both cases.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that Rabbi Yehuda was speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning, while in his own view he permits marriage.
The Rabbis explain their own view: one who redeems and testifies may marry her to avoid financial loss, but one who merely testifies may not, lest he be motivated by lust.

items.text: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel raises a contradiction to Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel raises a contradiction to Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new section where Rav Pappa bar Shmuel raises a contradiction to Rav Yosef, but the content is cut off at the end of the daf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rav Pappa bar Shmuel raises a contradiction to Rav Yosef, but the content is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda from the convert case
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yehuda from the convert case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Does Rabbi Yehuda really hold that a captive woman is presumed to have been violated? It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a convert who sees blood after conversion only needs to count from that time, implying she is not presumed to have had relations. Rabbi Yosei disagrees. The Gemara distinguishes: a convert guards herself, a captive does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehuda's position that a captive woman is presumed violated, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a convert who sees blood after conversion only counts from that time, implying she is not presumed to have had relations, while Rabbi Yosei disagrees.
The Gemara distinguishes between a convert, who does not guard herself, and a captive woman, who does guard herself, thus resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Contradiction between captive cases resolved by silence
items.text_en: Contradiction between captive cases resolved by silence
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two baraitot about captives: one requires a three-month wait, another permits immediate marriage. Rabbi Yehuda's student is silent, unable to resolve it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two baraitot about captives: one requires a three-month wait, another permits immediate marriage. Rabbi Yehuda's student is silent, unable to resolve it.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's resolution: she was seen being violated
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's resolution: she was seen being violated
items.desc_en: The student is asked if he heard anything about this. He reports Rav Sheshet's statement: the case is where she was seen being violated. The Gemara then asks: if so, why does Rabbi Yosei permit immediate marriage? Rabba answers that Rabbi Yosei holds a promiscuous woman uses a contraceptive sponge to avoid pregnancy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the student if he has heard any tradition regarding this matter.
Rav Sheshet answers that the case is where the woman was seen being violated.
The Gemara questions: if so, what is Rabbi Yosei's reasoning for permitting immediate marriage?
Rabba answers that Rabbi Yosei holds a promiscuous woman uses a contraceptive sponge (מוך) to avoid pregnancy.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yosei from other cases
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yosei from other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei's leniency: for a convert, captive, or slave, they guard themselves, but what about a maidservant freed for losing a tooth or eye? And even if Rabbi Yosei says only voluntary acts require waiting, the cases of a raped or seduced woman are involuntary, yet a baraita shows Rabbi Yosei permits immediate marriage there too.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei's leniency by noting that while a convert, captive, or slave has reason to guard herself, a maidservant freed for losing a tooth or eye has no such reason, so why would Rabbi Yosei permit immediate marriage?

The Gemara objects that even if Rabbi Yosei only permits immediate marriage for voluntary acts, the cases of a raped or seduced woman are involuntary, yet a baraita shows Rabbi Yosei permits immediate marriage there too.

items.text: Rabba's revised explanation: she turns over to avoid pregnancy
items.text_en: Rabba's revised explanation: she turns over to avoid pregnancy
items.desc_en: Rabba offers a new explanation: Rabbi Yosei holds that a promiscuous woman turns over during intercourse to prevent pregnancy. The Gemara asks: and the other opinion? It answers: we are concerned she may not have turned over properly.

sub.desc_en: Rabba revises his explanation: Rabbi Yosei holds that a promiscuous woman turns over during intercourse to prevent pregnancy.
The Gemara asks: and the other opinion (Rabbi Yehuda) — what does he hold?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yehuda is concerned that she may not have turned over properly, so she must wait.

items.text: Derivation of the principle: no double punishment
items.text_en: Derivation of the principle: no double punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse and explains that from it we derive that one is not punished for two offenses simultaneously. It then shows the necessity of teaching this principle for both death+monetary and lashes+monetary cases, as each alone might be insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse (Exodus 21:22) and the principle of 'כדי רשעתו' (according to his wickedness) to derive that one is not punished for two offenses simultaneously.
The Gemara questions whether the principle is derived from this verse or from another source.
The Gemara explains that both derivations are necessary: one for the case of death and monetary punishment, and one for lashes and monetary punishment, as each alone might be insufficient.

items.text: Question for Rabbi Meir: why two cases?
items.text_en: Question for Rabbi Meir: why two cases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can be flogged and pay, why are two cases (death+monetary and lashes+monetary) needed?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can be flogged and pay, why are two cases (death+monetary and lashes+monetary) needed?

items.text: Need for both cases: death+property and death+lashes
items.text_en: Need for both cases: death+property and death+lashes
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases (death+property and death+lashes) are necessary to teach that multiple penalties are not applied. If only death+property were stated, one might think it is because one penalty is on the body and one on property, but death+lashes (both on the body) might be considered a single extended death and applied. Conversely, if only death+lashes were stated, one might think death+property (body and property) could be applied. Therefore both are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that both cases (death+property and death+lashes) are necessary, explaining that if only death+property were taught, one might think death+lashes (both bodily) could be applied as a single extended death.
The Gemara concludes that both cases are necessary: if only death+lashes were taught, one might think death+property (one bodily, one monetary) could be applied, so both are needed.

items.text: Verses prohibiting ransom for murderer and accidental killer
items.text_en: Verses prohibiting ransom for murderer and accidental killer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah needs two verses: 'Do not take a ransom for the life of a murderer' and 'Do not take a ransom for one who flees to a city of refuge'. It explains that one is for an intentional murderer and one for an accidental killer, and both are necessary: for the intentional, because his sin is severe, one might think ransom is allowed; for the accidental, because there is no loss of life, one might think ransom is allowed. Therefore both verses are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'Do not take a ransom for the life of a murderer' is needed.
The Gemara explains that the verse teaches not to accept money from a murderer to exempt him from execution.
The Gemara asks why the verse 'Do not take a ransom for one who flees to a city of refuge' is needed.
The Gemara explains that the verse teaches not to accept money from an accidental killer to exempt him from exile.
The Gemara asks why both verses are needed.
The Gemara answers that one verse applies to an accidental killer and one to an intentional murderer.

The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: for the intentional murderer, because his sin is severe, one might think ransom is allowed; for the accidental killer, because there is no loss of life, one might think ransom is allowed.

items.text: Verse: land cannot be atoned except by blood of the murderer
items.text_en: Verse: land cannot be atoned except by blood of the murderer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'And the land cannot be atoned for the blood that is shed therein except by the blood of him who shed it' teaches. It answers that it teaches that if the heifer was beheaded and then the murderer was found, he is not exempt, as the verse indicates that only the murderer's blood atones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'וְלָאָרֶץ לֹא יְכוּפַּר לַדָּם אֲשֶׁר שׁוּפַּךְ בָּהּ כִּי אִם בְּדַם שׁוֹפְכוֹ' is needed.

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for a baraita: if the heifer's neck was broken and then the murderer was found, he is not exempt, as the verse teaches that the land is not atoned except by the blood of the shedder.

items.text: Execution by sword at the neck, and choosing a good death
items.text_en: Execution by sword at the neck, and choosing a good death
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'And you shall remove the innocent blood from your midst' teaches. It answers that it teaches that those executed by the sword are killed from the neck, as all shedders of blood are compared to the heifer whose neck is broken. The Gemara then asks if it is also with a cleaver from the back of the neck, and Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah answers that the verse 'Love your neighbor as yourself' teaches to choose a good death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'ואתה תבער הדם הנקי מקרבך' (And you shall remove the innocent blood from your midst) teaches.

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for a baraita teaching that those executed by the sword (מוּמָתִים בְּסַיִיף) are killed from the neck, based on a verbal analogy to the heifer whose neck is broken (עֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה).
The Gemara objects: just as the heifer is killed with a cleaver (קוֹפִיץ) from the back of the neck (מִמּוּל עוֹרֶף), so too should those executed by the sword be killed from the back of the neck?

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah resolves the objection by citing the verse 'ואהבת לרעך כמוך' (Love your neighbor as yourself), teaching that one must choose a good death (ברור לו מיתה יפה), i.e., a quick and less painful death from the front of the neck with a sword, not a cleaver from the back.

items.text: One sentenced to death cannot be redeemed
items.text_en: One sentenced to death cannot be redeemed
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'Any devoted thing that is devoted from among men shall not be redeemed' teaches. It answers that it teaches that if one is led out to be executed and someone says 'I vow his valuation upon me', he has said nothing, as the verse says 'shall not be redeemed'. One might think this applies even before his verdict is finalized, so the verse says 'from among men' — not all men, implying only after the verdict.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'כׇּל חֵרֶם אֲשֶׁר יׇחֳרַם מִן הָאָדָם לֹא יִפָּדֶה' is needed.

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for a baraita: one condemned to death who says 'ערכי עלי' (my valuation is upon me) says nothing, but before the verdict is finalized, the verse 'מִן הָאָדָם' excludes some cases.

items.text: Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's view and the verse for light deaths
items.text_en: Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's view and the verse for light deaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya, who holds that one sentenced to death can be valued because his value is fixed, interprets the verse 'Any devoted thing'. It answers that the verse is needed for a teaching of Rabbi Yishmael: since we find that those executed by Heaven give money and are atoned, one might think the same applies to those executed by man, so the verse says 'devoted from among men shall not be redeemed'. And from this we derive that even light death penalties (where accidental killing is atoned) also cannot be redeemed, as the verse says 'any devoted thing'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya, who holds that a condemned man can be valued because his value is fixed, interprets the verse 'כׇּל חֵרֶם' (any devoted thing).

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for a teaching of Rabbi Yishmael: since those executed by Heaven give money and are atoned, one might think the same applies to those executed by man, so the verse says 'חֵרֶם מִן הָאָדָם לֹא יִפָּדֶה' (a devoted thing from man shall not be redeemed).
The baraita extends the teaching: from 'כׇּל חֵרֶם' (any devoted thing) we derive that even light death penalties, where accidental killing is atoned, also cannot be redeemed.

items.text: Question: why not derive from 'Do not take a ransom'?
items.text_en: Question: why not derive from 'Do not take a ransom'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Could we not derive from the verse 'Do not take a ransom' that one cannot pay money to be exempt? Why then is the verse 'Any devoted thing' needed? Rami bar Chama answers that it is necessary, because one might think that since the verse says 'Do not take a ransom' only for intentional murder, but for other capital offenses one might allow redemption, so the verse 'Any devoted thing' teaches that no one sentenced to death can be redeemed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: is this not already derived from the verse 'לֹא תִקְחוּ כּוֹפֶר' that one cannot take money and exempt him?
Rami bar Chama answers that the verse is necessary, because one might have thought otherwise, though the explanation is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's initial statement on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's initial statement on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling that a killer does not pay compensation applies only when he killed in an upward manner, where his inadvertence is not atoned for. But if he killed in a downward manner, where his inadvertence is atoned for, one might think he should pay and be exempt from death; the Mishnah therefore teaches that he does not pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the killer struck upward (דרך עלייה), where his inadvertence is not atoned for, but if he struck downward (דרך ירידה), one might think he should pay and be exempt, so the Mishnah teaches he does not pay.

items.text: Rava's objection from the Tanna of the school of Hezekiah
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the Tanna of the school of Hezekiah
items.desc_en: Rava objects that this distinction is already derived from the Tanna of the school of Hezekiah, who compares 'one who strikes a person' to 'one who strikes an animal': just as for an animal there is no distinction between intentional and unintentional, etc., regarding liability for payment, so too for a person there is no distinction—he is always liable to pay, not exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the distinction between intentional and unintentional killing is already derived from the Tanna of the school of Hezekiah's comparison of striking a person to striking an animal.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Hezekiah's baraita
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Hezekiah's baraita
sub.desc_en: The baraita of the school of Hezekiah cites the verses 'one who strikes a person' and 'one who strikes an animal' to derive that for both, there is no distinction between intentional and unintentional regarding monetary liability.

items.text: Rami bar Hama's alternative necessity
items.text_en: Rami bar Hama's alternative necessity
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama suggests that the Mishnah's ruling is needed for a case where the killer blinded the victim's eye and then killed him with a different object, where one might think he should pay. Rava again objects that this too is derived from the Tanna of the school of Hezekiah's teaching on 'eye for an eye'—not 'eye and life for an eye'.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Hama suggests the Mishnah's ruling is needed for a case where the killer blinded the victim's eye and then killed him with a different object, where one might think he should pay.
Rava objects that this case too is derived from the Tanna of the school of Hezekiah's teaching on 'eye for an eye'—not 'eye and life for an eye'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's final necessity and Rabba's view
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's final necessity and Rabba's view
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah is needed because one might think that since the penalty is a novel enactment (chiddush), even if he is executed he should still pay. The Mishnah teaches otherwise. The Gemara then notes that Rabba, who holds that a chiddush requires payment even when executed, interprets the verse 'all herem' according to the first Tanna of Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah is needed because one might think that since the penalty is a novel enactment (חידוש), even if he is executed he should still pay; the Mishnah teaches otherwise.
The Gemara asks how Rabba, who holds that a novel enactment requires payment even when executed, interprets the verse 'כל חרם' (all devoted property).
The Gemara answers that Rabba follows the first Tanna of Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya, who interprets the verse differently.

items.text: Mishnah: Betrothed and divorced maiden
items.text_en: Mishnah: Betrothed and divorced maiden
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a maiden who was betrothed and then divorced, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says she has no fine (if seduced), while Rabbi Akiva says she has a fine and it is for herself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says a betrothed and divorced maiden has no fine, while Rabbi Akiva says she has a fine and it belongs to herself.

items.text: Gemara: Reasons for the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasons for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from the verse 'asher lo orasah' (who was not betrothed) that if she was betrothed, she has no fine. Rabbi Akiva interprets the same phrase to mean that the fine goes to her father only when she was not betrothed, but if betrothed, it is for herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reasoning of each sage: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from 'אשר לא אורשה' (who was not betrothed) that a betrothed maiden has no fine, while Rabbi Akiva interprets the same phrase to mean the fine goes to herself.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from the verse 'אשר לא אורשה' (who was not betrothed) that if she was betrothed, she has no fine.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi Akiva's reasoning.
Rabbi Akiva interprets the same phrase to mean that the fine goes to her father only when she was not betrothed, but if betrothed, it is for herself.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Akiva's interpretation
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Akiva's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the phrase 'na'arah' excludes a bogeret, and 'betulah' excludes a non-virgin, would those also go to herself? Rather, they exclude entirely. So too here, 'lo orasah' should exclude entirely, not give to herself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if 'אשר לא אורשה' is interpreted as 'to herself', then similarly 'na'arah' (maiden) and 'betulah' (virgin) would also imply 'to herself', which is absurd — so the phrase must be for exclusion, not allocation.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's response and the gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's response and the gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva responds that the phrase 'asher lo orasah' is needed for a different teaching: it excludes a betrothed and divorced maiden from having a fine (according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili), but Rabbi Akiva himself holds she has a fine and it goes to her father, based on a kal vachomer from betrothal money. The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Akiva uses 'asher lo orasah' for a gezerah shavah and 'betulah' to exclude a non-virgin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva explains that the phrase 'אשר לא אורשה' (who is not betrothed) is needed for a baraita: it excludes a betrothed and divorced maiden from a fine according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, but Rabbi Akiva himself holds she has a fine and it goes to her father, based on a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) from betrothal money.

The baraita explains that since the phrase 'אשר לא אורשה' is superfluous (מופנה), it is used for a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) to teach that the fine is fifty shekels of silver, just as in the parallel case.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva uses 'אשר לא אורשה' for the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) and 'בתולה' (virgin) to exclude a non-virgin, rather than the reverse.

items.text: Debate over which phrase is used for a gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Debate over which phrase is used for a gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the phrase 'betulah' or 'asher lo orasah' should be used for a gezeirah shavah to include a betrothed maiden who was divorced. It concludes that 'asher lo orasah' is more appropriate because it refers to a change in status, not a change in the body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes using the word 'בתולה' (virgin) for a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) and 'אשר לא אורשה' (who was not betrothed) to exclude a betrothed maiden who was divorced.
The Gemara concludes that 'אשר לא אורשה' (who was not betrothed) is more appropriate for the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) because it refers to a change in status, not a change in the body.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's source for his reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's source for his reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives his reasoning from a baraita that compares the fine to the mohar of betulah, indicating a parallel between the two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives his reasoning that the fine is parallel to the mohar of betulah.
The Gemara cites a baraita that teaches the fine must be like the mohar of betulah and vice versa, providing Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's source.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's positions
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between Rabbi Akiva's view in the Mishnah and his view in a baraita. It explains that in the Mishnah, he does not allow a gezeirah shavah to uproot the plain meaning of the verse, but in the baraita, he does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rabbi Akiva's position in the Mishnah and his position in a baraita, and suggests they represent two different Tannaic traditions in his name.
The Gemara explains the distinction: in the Mishnah, Rabbi Akiva does not allow a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) to uproot the plain meaning of the verse entirely, but in the baraita, he does.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution and Rabba's view
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution and Rabba's view
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by reading the verse as 'asher lo arusah', implying she is liable for execution, but the Gemara suggests one might think she still pays. Rabba, who holds that a novelty of the Torah allows payment despite execution, aligns with Rabbi Akiva of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the verse as referring to an arusah (betrothed woman) who is liable for execution, yet one might think she still pays because the Torah's novelty in fines allows payment despite execution.
The Gemara concludes that Rabba, who holds that the Torah's novelty in fines allows payment despite execution, aligns with Rabbi Akiva of the Mishnah.

items.text: Dispute over who receives the fine
items.text_en: Dispute over who receives the fine
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: one opinion says the fine goes to the father, another says to herself. Rav Chisda explains that this refers to a betrothed maiden who was divorced, and the dispute mirrors the disagreement between Rabbi Akiva of the Mishnah and Rabbi Akiva of the baraita.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: one opinion says the fine goes to the father, another says to herself.
The gemara questions how the fine could go to herself, since the father normally receives it.
Rav Chisda explains that the baraita refers to a betrothed maiden who was divorced, and the dispute mirrors the disagreement between Rabbi Akiva of the Mishnah and Rabbi Akiva of the baraita.

items.text: Payment if the maiden dies
items.text_en: Payment if the maiden dies
items.desc_en: Abaye states that if the seducer had relations with her and she died, he is exempt, as the verse says 'to the father of the maiden' and not to the father of a dead maiden. Rava questions whether there is 'beger in the grave' (i.e., does the fetus become the child of the father or the seducer?), affecting who receives the fine.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if the seducer had relations with the maiden and she died, he is exempt from the fine, citing the verse 'and he shall give to the father of the maiden' — not to the father of a dead maiden.

Rava questions whether there is 'בֶּגֶר בַּקֶּבֶר' (a child in the grave) — i.e., does the fetus become the child of the seducer, affecting who receives the fine, or does it remain the father's child.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Can a na'arah become pregnant?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Can a na'arah become pregnant?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a na'arah can become pregnant, citing a baraita about three women who use a mokh (absorbent cloth) to prevent pregnancy: a minor, a pregnant woman, and a nursing mother. The baraita defines a minor as between 11 and 12 years old, but Rabbi Meir and the Sages disagree about the age range.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a na'arah can become pregnant, citing Rav Bibi's baraita before Rav Nachman about three women who use a mokh (absorbent cloth): a minor, a pregnant woman, and a nursing mother.
The baraita defines a minor as from 11 to 12 years old, according to Rabbi Meir, with those younger or older using normally.
The Sages disagree, saying that all such women use normally and Heaven will have mercy, citing the verse 'שומר פתאים ה׳' (the Lord protects the simple).

items.text: Gemara's objection: Can she give birth within six months?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Can she give birth within six months?
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that the girl became pregnant as a na'arah and gave birth while still a na'arah, but objects that Shmuel said there are only six months between na'arut and bagrut, making a full-term pregnancy impossible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the girl became pregnant as a na'arah and gave birth as a na'arah, Shmuel's statement that there are only six months between na'arut and bagrut makes a full-term pregnancy impossible, and rejects the possibility of a shorter pregnancy because Shmuel said 'אלא' (only).

items.text: Reframing the question: Yesh beger ba'kevar?
items.text_en: Reframing the question: Yesh beger ba'kevar?
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the original inquiry: does death create majority status (bogeret) and thereby remove the father's authority, or not? Mar bar Rav Ashi raises a similar question, concluding with teiku.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the original inquiry: does death create majority status (bogeret) and thereby remove the father's authority, or not?
Mar bar Rav Ashi raises a parallel question: does death itself effect majority status (bagrut) or not?
The sugya concludes with תיקו (teiku — the question stands unresolved).

items.text: Rava's inquiry: Betrothal after intercourse
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry: Betrothal after intercourse
items.desc_en: Rava asks Abaye: if a man has intercourse with a na'arah and then betroths her, to whom does the fine go? Abaye argues that the verse implies the father receives the fine only if she is not betrothed. The Gemara distinguishes betrothal from marriage, noting that betrothal does not fully remove her from her father's authority.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Abaye: if a man has intercourse with a na'arah and then betroths her, to whom does the fine go?
Abaye argues that the verse implies the father receives the fine only if she is not betrothed, and similarly for marriage.
The Gemara objects that marriage fully removes her from her father's authority, unlike betrothal.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that betrothal does not fully remove her from her father's authority, as both father and husband annul her vows.

items.text: Mishnah: Distinctions between the seducer and the rapist
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distinctions between the seducer and the rapist
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the payments: the seducer pays three (boshet, pegam, knas), the rapist adds tza'ar. It details differences: the rapist pays immediately and must marry her (if she is fit), while the seducer pays upon divorce and may divorce her if he wishes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the seducer pays three types of compensation (boshet, pegam, knas) while the rapist adds a fourth (tza'ar).

The Mishnah enumerates three differences between the rapist and the seducer: the rapist pays tza'ar, pays immediately, and must marry her (if fit), while the seducer pays only upon divorce and may divorce her if he wishes.

sub.text: Mishnah's clarification of 'drinks from his pot'
sub.text_en: Mishnah's clarification of 'drinks from his pot'
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah clarifies that the rapist must marry her even if she is disabled, but if she is forbidden to marry a Jew (e.g., due to a sexual offense or disqualification), he may not keep her, as the verse requires a wife 'fit for him'.

items.text: Gemara: What is the tza'ar?
items.text_en: Gemara: What is the tza'ar?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the tza'ar payment covers. Avuh deShmuel says it is for being thrown to the ground. Rabbi Zeira objects: if she were thrown on cushions, would he be exempt? He cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon that the rapist does not pay tza'ar because... (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the tza'ar (pain) payment in the Mishnah covers.
Avuh deShmuel answers that the tza'ar payment is for the pain of being thrown to the ground during the rape.
Rabbi Zeira objects: if he threw her onto cushions, would he be exempt from tza'ar?

Rabbi Zeira cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon that the rapist does not pay tza'ar, implying that tza'ar is not for the ground-throwing but for something else.

items.text: The nature of the pain of rape vs. seduction
items.text_en: The nature of the pain of rape vs. seduction
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the pain of rape is the future suffering under her husband, but the Sages object that a raped woman is not like a willing one. Rav Nachman bar Abbuha explains that the pain is specifically the pain of spreading the legs, citing a verse. The Gemara then questions whether a seduced woman also has such pain, and Rav Nachman bar Abbuha gives a parable that a seduced woman has no pain, as she is like one who says 'tear my silk garments and be exempt.' The Gemara then questions the parable, and Rav Nachman bar Abbuha clarifies that the wise women among them say a seduced woman has no pain. The Gemara then asks how we can see that she does have pain, and Abaye, Rava, and Rav Papa each cite a woman's description of the sensation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the pain of rape is the future suffering under her husband.
The Sages object that a raped woman is not comparable to a willing one.
Rav Nachman bar Abbuha explains that the pain is specifically the pain of spreading the legs, citing a verse.
The Gemara questions whether a seduced woman also has such pain.
Rav Nachman bar Abbuha gives a parable that a seduced woman has no pain, like one who says 'tear my silk garments and be exempt.'
The Gemara objects that the silk garments belong to her father, not to her.
Rav Nachman bar Abbuha clarifies that the wise women among them say a seduced woman has no pain.
The Gemara asks how we can see that she does have pain.
Abaye cites his mother's description that the pain is like hot water on a bald head.
Rava cites the daughter of Rav Chisda's description that it is like the pressure of a cucumber.
Rav Papa cites the daughter of Abba Sura'a's description that it is like hard bread in the jaws.

items.text: Timing of payment for the rapist and seducer
items.text_en: Timing of payment for the rapist and seducer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the rapist pays immediately, while the seducer pays when he divorces. The Gemara questions how the seducer can pay when he divorces, since she is his wife. Abaye explains that the text should read 'when he does not marry her.' A baraita supports this, stating that the seducer pays the fine when he does not marry her, but the shame and damage are paid immediately. Both the rapist and seducer, and both the woman and her father, can prevent the marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the rapist pays immediately, while the seducer pays when he divorces her.
The Gemara questions how the seducer can divorce her if she is already his wife.
Abaye explains that the Mishnah means 'when he does not marry her' rather than 'when he divorces her.'
A baraita supports Abaye's reading, stating that the seducer pays when he does not marry, and both the woman and her father can delay the marriage.
The baraita concludes that both the rapist and seducer, and both the woman and her father, can prevent the marriage.

items.text: Source for the father's ability to prevent marriage in rape
items.text_en: Source for the father's ability to prevent marriage in rape
items.desc_en: The Gemara first notes that for a seduced woman, the father's ability to prevent marriage is derived from the verse 'if her father refuses.' For the woman herself, it is derived from the repetition of 'refuse.' For a raped woman, the woman's consent is derived from 'and she shall be his wife' (implying with her consent), but the father's ability is questioned. Abaye says it is so that the sinner should not profit, while Rava derives it via a kal vachomer from the seducer. The Gemara then explains why each rejects the other's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that for a seduced woman, the father's ability to prevent marriage is derived from the verse 'if her father refuses,' and the woman's own ability from the repetition of 'refuse.'
The Gemara asks: for a raped woman, the woman's consent is derived from 'and she shall be his wife,' but from where is the father's ability to prevent marriage derived?
Abaye answers that the father can prevent marriage so that the sinner should not profit, while Rava derives it via a kal vachomer from the seducer.

The Gemara explains why Rava rejects Abaye's reasoning (the rapist pays a fine, so he does not profit) and why Abaye rejects Rava's kal vachomer (the seducer himself can be prevented from marrying, unlike the rapist).

items.text: Dispute about the rapist's ketubah obligation
items.text_en: Dispute about the rapist's ketubah obligation
items.desc_en: A baraita states that although the rapist pays immediately, when she leaves (divorce or death) she has nothing from him. If he dies, the fine is included in her ketubah. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says she has a ketubah of one hundred dinars. The Gemara explains the dispute: the Rabbis hold that the ketubah was instituted so that divorce would not be easy, but since he cannot divorce her, there is no need for a ketubah. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds that he can still cause her distress until she says she does not want him.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that although the rapist pays immediately, when she leaves she has nothing from him; if he dies, the fine is included in her ketubah.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds that the raped woman has a ketubah of one hundred dinars.
The Gemara asks what is the basis of the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis hold the ketubah was instituted to make divorce difficult, but since he cannot divorce her, no ketubah is needed.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda holds he can still cause her distress until she says she does not want him.

items.text: The rapist drinks from his vessel
items.text_en: The rapist drinks from his vessel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the rapist drinks from his vessel (i.e., he must marry her). Rava of Parzikya asks Rav Ashi: since they learn from each other (the rapist and seducer), why is the seducer not also required to marry her? The Gemara is cut off here.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the rapist drinks from his own barrel (i.e., he must marry her).

sub.text: Rava of Parzikya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rava of Parzikya's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rava of Parzikya asks Rav Ashi: since they learn from each other, what is the halacha?

items.text: Gemara's question on the positive commandment overriding a prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the positive commandment overriding a prohibition
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana suggests that the positive commandment to marry a seduced woman should override the prohibition against marrying a divorcee, but Rav Zevid objects: the positive commandment only applies if the woman consents, so it cannot override a prohibition when the woman refuses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana proposes that the positive commandment to marry a seduced woman should override the prohibition against marrying a divorcee, based on a parallel from the Mishnah.
Rav Zevid objects that the positive commandment only applies if the woman consents, so when she refuses, there is no positive commandment to override the prohibition.

items.text: Mishnah: Orphan who was betrothed and divorced
items.text_en: Mishnah: Orphan who was betrothed and divorced
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an orphan who was betrothed and then divorced is raped or seduced, Rabbi Elazar rules that the rapist is liable but the seducer is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for an orphaned girl who was betrothed and divorced, Rabbi Elazar rules the rapist is liable but the seducer is exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says Rabbi Elazar's ruling aligns with Rabbi Akiva's view that a betrothed and divorced maiden has her own fine. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah teaches that such a maiden is like an orphan, with the fine going to herself.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation via Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation via Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Akiva's view that the girl has a fine and it belongs to herself, and the term 'יתומה' (orphan) teaches that a betrothed and divorced girl is like an orphan — her fine goes to herself.
The Gemara infers this from the Mishnah's wording 'an orphan (יתומה)', which implies that the maiden is like an orphan and the fine goes to herself.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's term 'יתומה' is not obvious but teaches that a betrothed and divorced maiden is like an orphan, with the fine going to herself.

items.text: Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: A chain of Amoraim transmits that Rav ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar, and Rav praised Rabbi Elazar as 'the best of the sages'.

sub.text: Rav's ruling via chain of transmission
sub.text_en: Rav's ruling via chain of transmission
sub.desc_en: Rav rules the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Elazar, and calls him 'the best of the sages'.

items.text: Mishnah: Definitions of boshet and pegam
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definitions of boshet and pegam
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines boshet (humiliation) as depending on the parties involved, and pegam (depreciation) as assessed by comparing the woman's value as a slave before and after the incident. The fine (kenas) is uniform for all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines בושת (humiliation) as depending on the parties, פגם (damage) as assessed by the girl's market value as a slave, and קנס (fine) as a fixed amount equal for all.

items.text: Gemara: Question on the uniformity of the fine
items.text_en: Gemara: Question on the uniformity of the fine
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the fine is uniform (fifty sela) regardless of the woman's status, and Abaye objects that the same logic would apply to a slave's value, which varies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the fine is not uniform for all cases, since the Torah says fifty silver shekels for any seduced girl.
Rabbi Zeira answers that a uniform fine would lead to absurdity — a king's daughter and a commoner's daughter would both get fifty, which is unreasonable.
Abaye objects that the same logic would apply to a slave — a slave who pierces pearls and a slave who does menial work would both be valued at thirty, which is also unreasonable.

items.text: Question on the fine amount for a damaged girl
items.text_en: Question on the fine amount for a damaged girl
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the fine for seducing a na'arah is fifty regardless of her physical state, using the analogy of a slave. Rabbi Zeira suggests that if two men raped her, one normally and one abnormally, the fine would still be fifty, which seems inconsistent. Abaye objects with the parallel of a healthy slave versus a sick slave both valued at thirty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the fine for seducing a na'arah is fifty regardless of her physical state, using the analogy of a slave.
Rabbi Zeira suggests that if two men raped her, one normally and one abnormally, the fine would still be fifty, which seems inconsistent.
Abaye objects with the parallel of a healthy slave versus a sick slave both valued at thirty.

items.text: Scriptural derivation that the fine covers only the sexual benefit
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation that the fine covers only the sexual benefit
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava each derive from the verse that the fifty-coin fine is specifically for the sexual benefit (הנאת שכיבה), implying that there is also compensation for shame and damage (בושת ופגם) separately. This explains why the fine is uniform.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves by citing the verse 'תחת אשר עינה' (because he violated her), implying that the fifty covers only the violation, while shame and damage are separate.
Rava resolves by citing the verse 'ונתן האיש השוכב עמה' (and the man who lay with her shall give), indicating the fifty is for the pleasure of lying, implying shame and damage are separate.

items.text: Why the fine goes to the father
items.text_en: Why the fine goes to the father
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the fine is given to the father and not to the daughter herself. It answers with the verse 'בִּנְעוּרֶיהָ בֵּית אָבִיהָ', indicating that all the benefit of her youth belongs to her father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the fine should go to the father rather than to the daughter herself.
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'בנעוריה בית אביה' (in her youth, in her father's house), implying all the benefit of her youth belongs to her father.

items.text: Alternative derivation for the daughter's earnings going to the father
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for the daughter's earnings going to the father
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Huna derived from the law of an amah that a daughter's earnings go to her father, but questions why this is needed given the verse 'בִּנְעוּרֶיהָ'. It explains that verse refers to annulling vows, and one cannot learn monetary law from prohibitions or fines. Instead, it is logical that the father gets her earnings because he can marry her off to a leper.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav derives from the sale of a daughter as a maidservant that her earnings belong to her father.
The Gemara asks why this derivation is needed, given the verse 'בנעוריה בית אביה'.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'בנעוריה בית אביה' is written in the context of annulling vows, not earnings.
The Gemara objects that one cannot derive monetary law from a prohibition context.
The Gemara objects that one cannot derive monetary law from a penalty context.
The Gemara resolves that it is logical the earnings belong to the father, since he can marry her off to a leprous man.

items.text: How to assess the damage (פגם)
items.text_en: How to assess the damage (פגם)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that to assess the damage, the girl is evaluated as if she were a maidservant. The father of Shmuel says we estimate how much a person would pay between a virgin maidservant and a non-virgin maidservant for his use. The Gemara clarifies that the comparison is for marrying her to his slave, where the slave's satisfaction matters.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for damage, the girl is assessed as if she were a maidservant being sold.
The Gemara asks how the assessment is made.
Avuh deShmuel answers that one assesses how much a person would pay for a virgin maidservant versus a non-virgin maidservant for his service.
The Gemara asks what difference it makes to him whether she is a virgin or not.
The Gemara answers that the difference is for marrying her to his slave.
The Gemara asks what difference it makes to his slave whether she is a virgin or not.
The Gemara answers that it matters for a slave from whom his master derives satisfaction.

items.text: Mishnah and dispute on the relationship between sale and fine
items.text_en: Mishnah and dispute on the relationship between sale and fine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that where there is sale (of a minor daughter) there is no fine, and where there is fine there is no sale. A ketanah has sale but no fine, a na'arah has fine but no sale, and a bogeret has neither. The Gemara cites a beraita where Rabbi Meir holds this view, but the Sages say a ketanah from age three and up has a fine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that where there is sale (of a minor daughter) there is no fine, and where there is fine there is no sale, specifying the stages of ketanah, na'arah, and bogeret.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav attributes the Mishnah's view to Rabbi Meir.
Rav Yehuda reports that the Sages disagree and hold that a ketanah does have a fine in the place of sale.

A baraita is cited detailing Rabbi Meir's position that a ketanah from birth to two pubic hairs has sale but no fine, and a na'arah has fine but no sale, while the Sages say a ketanah from age three and up has a fine.

items.text: Reason for Rabbi Meir's and the Sages' positions
items.text_en: Reason for Rabbi Meir's and the Sages' positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Sages say a ketanah has a fine, not sale. Rav Chisda explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the verse 'וְלוֹ תִּהְיֶה לְאִשָּׁה' speaks of one who is fit for marriage (a na'arah). Reish Lakish explains the Sages' view: the word 'נַעֲרָ' can include even a minor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Sages' position: does a minor have a fine but no sale?
The Gemara corrects: say 'also a fine in place of sale'.

sub.text: Rav Chisda's explanation of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda's explanation of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: the verse 'ולו תהיה לאשה' (and she shall be his wife) speaks of one who can effect marriage herself (a na'arah).

sub.text: Reish Lakish's explanation of the Rabbis
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's explanation of the Rabbis
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish explains the Rabbis' reasoning: the verse 'נער' (girl) includes even a minor.

items.text: Reish Lakish's statement on motzi shem ra for a minor
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's statement on motzi shem ra for a minor
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports that Reish Lakish said one who slanders a minor is exempt because the verse says 'נַעֲרָה' (full spelling), implying specifically a na'arah. Rav Adda bar Ahava objects, noting that the context of stoning shows a minor is not liable, so the verse must mean that wherever 'נַעֲרָ' is written, it includes a minor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports to Rav Shimi bar Ashi that Reish Lakish ruled one who slanders a minor is exempt because the verse writes 'נַעֲרָה' (full spelling), implying specifically a na'arah.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that the context of stoning shows a minor is not liable, so the verse's full spelling is unnecessary for exclusion.
Rav Adda bar Ahava resolves that the full spelling 'נַעֲרָה' teaches that wherever 'נַעֲרָ' is written without the 'ה', it includes a minor.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one who admits liability pays compensation on his own testimony but not the fine: seduction (boshet and pegam but not the fine), theft (principal but not double or four/five), and goring (full damages but not the fine for a slave). The general rule is that one who pays more than the damage does not pay on his own admission.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not include the case of rape (אָנַסְתִּי). It answers that the Mishnah is not necessary for rape, since there is no degradation (פגם), but for seduction, which involves degradation, one might think he does not pay on his own testimony—so the Mishnah teaches that he does.

items.text: A dissenting opinion on boshet and pegam
items.text_en: A dissenting opinion on boshet and pegam
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah quoting Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one does not pay boshet and pegam on his own testimony, because he should not be allowed to degrade another's daughter.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about consent
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about consent
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if the daughter is pleased with the admission, what then? Perhaps the father is not pleased. If the father is pleased, perhaps the family is not pleased. If the family is pleased, there might be someone overseas who is not pleased—so the admission is never fully acceptable.

items.text: Debate on half-damages: monetary or fine
items.text_en: Debate on half-damages: monetary or fine
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav Pappa says half-damages (for a tam ox) are monetary, because oxen are not presumed guarded, so the Torah reduced liability out of mercy. Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua says half-damages are a fine, because oxen are presumed guarded, so the Torah penalizes the owner to ensure better guarding.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about nizak and mazik
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about nizak and mazik
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that states the injured party and the injurer are both involved in payment. For Rav Pappa (monetary), this fits. For Rav Huna (fine), how can the injured party be involved if he receives not his own?

items.text: Resolution: the baraita refers to depreciation of the carcass
items.text_en: Resolution: the baraita refers to depreciation of the carcass
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the baraita is needed only for the depreciation of the carcass (פחת נבילה), which is monetary even according to Rav Huna. But this is already taught elsewhere—so the Gemara questions the necessity.

items.text: Distinction between tam and mu'ad
items.text_en: Distinction between tam and mu'ad
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that two separate teachings are needed: one for tam (where the animal is not yet forewarned) and one for mu'ad (where it is forewarned), because each case might otherwise be thought different.

items.text: Attempted proof from a baraita listing differences
items.text_en: Attempted proof from a baraita listing differences
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from a baraita that lists differences between tam and mu'ad but does not mention that tam does not pay on his own testimony while mu'ad does—implying that half-damages are monetary (so both pay on admission).

items.text: Rejection: the baraita omitted other items
items.text_en: Rejection: the baraita omitted other items
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, noting that the baraita also omitted half of the kofer payment (for a mu'ad that kills a person), so it is not exhaustive.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling that a tam pays half-damages only on his own admission aligns with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that a tam pays half a kofer (fine).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds that a tam pays half a kofer (fine).

items.text: Proof from a Baraita about paying on admission
items.text_en: Proof from a Baraita about paying on admission
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who says 'my ox killed so-and-so' paying on his own admission. It initially assumes this refers to a tam, but rejects this, saying it refers to a mu'ad. It then questions whether a tam would not pay on his own admission, and resolves that the entire baraita deals with a mu'ad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who says 'my ox killed so-and-so' paying on his own admission, initially assuming it refers to a tam, but then rejecting this and saying it refers to a mu'ad.
The Gemara objects that if the baraita deals with a mu'ad, then a tam would not pay on his own admission, and resolves that the entire baraita deals with a mu'ad.

items.text: Proof from the rule 'all who pay more than the damage'
items.text_en: Proof from the rule 'all who pay more than the damage'
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a rule: one who pays more than the damage does not pay on his own admission, implying one who pays less does. It corrects this to 'one who pays like the damage' pays on his own admission. It then questions what about paying less, and concludes that the rule should have said 'one who does not pay like the damage' to include both less and more. This is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a rule: one who pays more than the damage does not pay on his own admission, implying one who pays less does.
The Gemara corrects the inference: not 'less than the damage', but 'like the damage' pays on his own admission.
The Gemara questions what about paying less — does he not pay on his own admission?
The Gemara concludes that the rule should have said 'one who does not pay like the damage' to include both less and more, and declares this a refutation.

items.text: Reconciling the refutation with the halakha
items.text_en: Reconciling the refutation with the halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that half-damages are a fine, but notes the contradiction with the refutation. It explains that the refutation was only because the rule did not say 'like the damage', but this does not decide the matter, since there is the case of half-damages for pebbles (צרורות) which is a halakha from Sinai and monetary, so the rule omitted it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that half-damages (פַּלְגָא נִזְקָא) are a fine (קְנָסָא).
The Gemara questions how the halakha can stand given the refutation (תְּיוּבְתָּא) that was just raised.
The Gemara explains that the refutation was only because the rule did not say 'like the damage' (כְּמָה שֶׁהִזִּיק), but this does not decide the matter definitively.

The Gemara notes that since there is the case of half-damages for pebbles (צְרוֹרוֹת), which is a halakha from Sinai and monetary, the rule omitted it, so the refutation does not overturn the halakha.

items.text: Enforcement of fines in Babylonia
items.text_en: Enforcement of fines in Babylonia
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses practical enforcement: a dog that eats large lambs or a cat that eats large roosters is an anomaly (מושנה) and we do not collect such fines in Babylonia, but for small ones it is normal and we collect. If one seized property, we do not take it away. If he requests a court date to go to Israel, we set it, and if he does not go, we excommunicate him. In any case, we excommunicate him to remove the damage, based on Rabbi Natan's teaching not to keep a dangerous dog or rickety ladder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that now that we have established that half-damage is a fine (קנס), a dog that eats large lambs or a cat that eats large roosters is an anomaly (מושנה) and we do not collect such fines in Babylonia, but for small ones it is normal and we collect.
The Gemara rules that if one seized property for such a fine, we do not take it away; if he requests a court date to go to Israel, we set it, and if he does not go, we excommunicate him.

The Gemara concludes that in any case we excommunicate him to remove the damage, based on Rabbi Natan's teaching not to keep a dangerous dog or rickety ladder, as derived from the verse 'וְלֹא תָשִׂים דָּמִים בְּבֵיתֶךָ' (and you shall not put blood in your house).

items.text: Mishnah: Payments for a seduced girl
items.text_en: Mishnah: Payments for a seduced girl
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for a seduced girl, shame, degradation, and fine belong to her father, and pain is in the seizure. If she stood in court before the father died, they belong to the father; if he died, to the brothers. If she did not stand in court before the father died, they are hers. Rabbi Shimon says if she did not collect before the father died, they are hers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that for a seduced girl, shame, degradation, and fine belong to her father, pain is in the seizure, and if she stood in court before the father died, they belong to the father; if he died, to the brothers.
The Mishnah continues that if she did not stand in court before the father died, the payments are hers, and adds a parallel case regarding reaching majority.
Rabbi Shimon states that if she did not collect before the father died, the payments are hers.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even if the father has not yet collected the earnings or finds of his daughter, if he dies they belong to the brothers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that even if the father has not yet collected his daughter's earnings or finds, upon his death they belong to the brothers.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the father's right
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the father's right
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah is necessary, since we already know the father receives the fines. It answers that the Mishnah teaches the case where the daughter stood in court before the father died, which is a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah is necessary, since we already know the fines from the Mishnah in the fourth chapter.

The Gemara initially answers that the Mishnah is needed to teach that the father receives the fines, but then rejects this because the father's right is obvious from the fact that the seducer pays the father.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is necessary for the case where the daughter stood in court before the father died, which is a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah in Shevuot teaches that if a man says 'You raped my daughter' and the defendant denies it, then admits after an oath, he is liable. Rabbi Shimon exempts him from the fine because one does not pay a fine on his own admission, but the Rabbis say he pays shame and damage on his own admission.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah in Shevuot states the case: a man claims rape or seduction of his daughter, the defendant denies, takes an oath, and then admits — he is liable.
Rabbi Shimon exempts him from the fine because one does not pay a fine on his own admission, but the Rabbis say he pays shame and damage on his own admission.

items.text: Abaye's question to Rabbah
items.text_en: Abaye's question to Rabbah
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah: if a father says 'You raped my daughter, I stood you in court, and you were liable to pay me money,' and the defendant denies everything, then swears and admits, what is the law according to Rabbi Shimon? Rabbah answers that since he stood in court, it is a monetary debt and he is liable for a guilt-offering for the false oath.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah about the case where a father claims the defendant stood trial and was liable for money, and the defendant denies everything, swears, and admits — what is the law according to Rabbi Shimon?
Rabbah answers that since the defendant stood in court, it is a monetary debt and he is liable for a guilt-offering for the false oath.

items.text: Objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says that for claims of rape, goring, or injury, if the defendant swore and admitted, he is exempt from a guilt-offering because they are fines, not monetary debts. This contradicts Rabbah's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon lists cases of rape, goring, and injury, and the defendant swore and admitted, suggesting he might be liable for a guilt-offering.

The baraita concludes with a דרשה (derivation) from the verse that only monetary claims (ממון) obligate a guilt-offering, excluding these cases because they are קנס (fines), thus contradicting Rabbah's ruling that after standing in court the claim becomes monetary.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and answer
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case involves one who stood trial, and answers that it does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case involves one who stood trial.
The Gemara answers that it does not involve one who stood trial.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah's structure
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah's structure
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the first clause (רישא) deals with standing trial, the latter clause (סיפא) must also deal with standing trial, as the Mishnah's opening lists cases where fines apply after trial.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that since the first clause of the baraita deals with standing trial, the latter clause must also deal with standing trial, contradicting Rabba's interpretation.
The Gemara supports Abaye by analyzing that if the case were without trial, double payment would not apply, so the baraita must refer to standing trial.

items.text: Rejected forced distinction
items.text_en: Rejected forced distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers distinguishing between the clauses by attributing them to Rabbi Shimon, but rejects this as forced because the Mishnah would then need to explicitly name Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Rabba proposes a forced answer: the first clause deals with one who stood trial, the latter clause with one who did not, and the entire baraita follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara rejects this as forced, arguing that if the entire baraita were Rabbi Shimon, the tanna would have explicitly named him in the first or latter clause.

items.text: Final resolution: both clauses after trial, different authorities
items.text_en: Final resolution: both clauses after trial, different authorities
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that both clauses deal with standing trial: the first clause follows the Rabbis, the latter follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that both clauses refer to standing trial, with the first clause following the Rabbis and the latter following Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Distinction between guilt-offering and inheritance
items.text_en: Distinction between guilt-offering and inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara concedes that regarding the guilt-offering of a false oath, the Torah exempts one who admits before trial, but maintains that the fine is considered monetary property for inheritance purposes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concedes that regarding the guilt-offering of a false oath, the Torah exempts one who admits before trial.
The Gemara maintains that the fine is considered monetary property for inheritance purposes.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's ruling
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from Rabbi Shimon's statement that if the father dies before collection, the fine belongs to the daughter herself, contradicting the idea that it is inheritable property.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from Rabbi Shimon's ruling that if the father dies before collection, the fine belongs to the daughter herself, contradicting the claim that the fine is inheritable property.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Torah grants only from time of giving
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Torah grants only from time of giving
items.desc_en: Rava reports that Rabbah and Rav Yosef struggled with this for 22 years until Rav Yosef resolved it: regarding the seducer's fine, the Torah grants the father only from the time of giving, not before. Rabbah's ruling about inheritance applies to other fines.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rabbah and Rav Yosef struggled with this matter for 22 years until Rav Yosef resolved it.
Rav Yosef resolves that regarding the seducer's fine, the Torah grants the father ownership only from the time of giving (נתינה), not before.
Rabbah's ruling that the fine is considered property (ממון) for inheritance applies only to other fines, not the seducer's fine.

items.text: Challenge from the case of a slave
items.text_en: Challenge from the case of a slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the distinction between 'give' (יתן) and 'and give' (ונתן) by comparing to the slave's fine, and questions the need for the verse 'and denied' (וכחש).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the distinction between 'יתן' (he shall give) and 'ונתן' (and he shall give) by applying the same logic to the case of a slave, where the verse says 'יתן' (he shall give), and questions whether the Torah only grants the master rights from the time of giving.
The Gemara objects that if the slave's case is analogous, then the verse 'וכחש' (and denied) is superfluous, and the verse 'ונתן' (and he shall give) should have been used instead.

items.text: Rava's explanation of 'and denied'
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of 'and denied'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse 'and denied' is needed for a case where the daughter stood trial, then matured or died, so the father inherits from her, not directly from the fine.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse 'וכחש' (and denied) is necessary for a case where the daughter stood trial and then matured or died, so the father inherits from her, not directly from the fine.

items.text: Distinguishing fines from monetary payment
items.text_en: Distinguishing fines from monetary payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why fines are exempt from the guilt-offering if they are monetary, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that they are exempt because their essence is a fine, not monetary compensation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why fines are exempt from the guilt-offering if they are monetary, pointing out the contradiction in the mishnah's language.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that fines are exempt because their essence is a fine (קנס), not monetary compensation.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's response to the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's response to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: An objection is raised that Rabbi Shimon exempts one who admits before trial, implying that after trial he would be liable for a guilt-offering. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon is speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon exempts one who admits before trial, implying that after trial he would be liable for a guilt-offering.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon is speaking to the Rabbis according to their own reasoning, conceding that if they hold that admission after trial triggers liability, he disagrees fundamentally.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis regarding a daughter who claims support from her brothers. Rabbi Shimon holds that she would not forgo a fixed claim (the ketubah) for a non-fixed one (support), while the Rabbis hold she would not forgo a claim that is not discharged by admission for one that is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: Rabbi Shimon holds that one who admits to a fine is exempt, while the Rabbis hold that the claimant is actually suing for shame and damage.
The Gemara asks: on what principle do they disagree?

Rav Pappa explains: Rabbi Shimon holds that a person would not forgo a fixed claim (the ketubah) for a non-fixed one (support), while the Rabbis hold that a person would not forgo a claim that is not discharged by admission for one that is.

items.text: Question about a daughter supported by brothers
items.text_en: Question about a daughter supported by brothers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avina asks Rav Sheshet whether a daughter who is supported by her brothers retains her earnings. Rav Sheshet responds by citing a mishnah that a widow supported by orphans has her earnings belong to them, implying the same for the daughter.

sub.text: Rabbi Avina's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avina's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avina asks Rav Sheshet: a daughter supported by the brothers — to whom do her earnings belong?

The gemara clarifies the two sides of the dilemma: do the brothers stand in place of the father, so her earnings go to them, or is it different because the father supported her from his own resources while the brothers support her from the father's estate?
Rav Sheshet answers by citing a mishnah: a widow supported by orphans — her earnings belong to them, implying the same for the daughter.

items.text: Distinction between widow and daughter
items.text_en: Distinction between widow and daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the comparison, noting that a widow's earnings are not desired by the husband, while a daughter's earnings are desired by the father. It then cites a statement by Rabbi Yossi that a widow is prioritized over a daughter in terms of dignity, but a daughter is prioritized in terms of earnings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the comparison between a widow and a daughter, arguing that a husband does not desire the widow's earnings while a father does desire his daughter's earnings.
Rabbi Abba objects in the name of Rabbi Yossi, citing a ruling that a widow takes precedence over a daughter in dignity with limited assets.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between dignity, where the widow is prioritized, and earnings, where the daughter is prioritized.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef raises an objection from a baraita that states a daughter's earnings belong to her brothers only if she was supported by her father, implying that if she is supported by brothers, they belong to her. The Gemara initially resolves that the baraita refers to a daughter who is not supported, but then distinguishes between a Canaanite slave and a Hebrew slave, concluding that a daughter is even more entitled.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef raises an objection from a baraita stating that a daughter's earnings and finds belong to the brothers even if she did not collect them before the father's death, implying that after the father's death they are hers.
The Gemara infers that the baraita must refer to a daughter who is supported by the brothers, challenging the earlier position.
The Gemara initially resolves that the baraita refers to a daughter who is not supported by the brothers.
The Gemara objects that if she is not supported, the baraita's statement is obvious and unnecessary.
