The Gemara resolves by distinguishing between a Canaanite slave (עבד כנעני) and a Hebrew slave (עבד עברי), concluding that a daughter is even more entitled than a Hebrew slave to keep her earnings when not supported.

items.text: Rava's explanation of Rav Yosef's difficulty
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of Rav Yosef's difficulty
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rav Yosef's difficulty was not with the substance but with the wording of the baraita, which compares earnings to a found object. The Gemara concludes that the baraita teaches that a daughter's earnings belong to her father during his lifetime and to herself after his death.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla answers that the baraita was only necessary to teach about the surplus earnings (העדפה) beyond the daughter's basic support.
Rava objects that a great man like Rav Yosef would certainly know about the concept of surplus earnings, so his difficulty must have been about something else.
Rava resolves that Rav Yosef's difficulty was with the wording of the baraita itself, which compares earnings to a found object, but a found object is not something one collects from anyone.

Rava explains that the baraita means earnings are like a found object: during the father's lifetime they belong to him, after his death they belong to her, and the Gemara concludes that this is the correct understanding.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling and Rav Kahana's proof
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling and Rav Kahana's proof
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that a daughter supported by brothers retains her earnings. Rav Kahana provides a scriptural proof from Leviticus 25:46, indicating that a father does not bequeath the right to his daughter's earnings to his son.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that a daughter supported by the brothers keeps her own earnings.
Rav Kahana provides a scriptural proof from Leviticus 25:46, showing that a father does not bequeath the right to his daughter's earnings to his son.

items.text: Rabba's objection and Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina's response
items.text_en: Rabba's objection and Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina's response
items.desc_en: Rabba objects that the verse might refer to seduction, fines, and damages. Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina responds that damages are for bodily pain, not earnings, leaving the matter unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rabba objects that the verse might be speaking about seduction of the daughter, fines, and damages, and cites a supporting baraita from Rabbi Chanina.
Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina responds that damages (חבלות) are for bodily pain, not earnings, leaving the objection unresolved.

items.text: A daughter supported by brothers keeps her earnings
items.text_en: A daughter supported by brothers keeps her earnings
items.desc_en: Rav Zera quotes Rav Matna quoting Rav that a daughter who is supported by her brothers keeps the earnings of her hands for herself, based on a biblical verse indicating that a father does not bequeath the right to his daughter's earnings to his son.

sub.text: Rav Zera quoting Rav Matna quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zera quoting Rav Matna quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zera quotes Rav Matna quoting Rav that a daughter supported by her brothers keeps her earnings for herself.
Rav derives from the verse 'וְהִתְנַחַלְתֶּם אוֹתָם לִבְנֵיכֶם' that a father does not bequeath the right to his daughter's earnings to his son.

items.text: Attribution of the ruling and halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Attribution of the ruling and halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Avimi bar Papi questions whether the ruling was said by Rav or by Shmuel (called Shakud), and Mar bar Ameimar reports that the Nehardeans rule like Rav Sheshet, while Rav Ashi rules like Rav.

sub.desc_en: Avimi bar Papi questions whether the ruling was said by Rav or by Shmuel (called Shakud), noting that Rav himself said it.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel also said the ruling, not only Rav.
Mar bar Ameimar reports that the Nehardeans rule like Rav Sheshet, but Rav Ashi rules like Rav, and the halakhic conclusion follows Rav.

items.text: Mishnah: Father's rights to his daughter's ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Father's rights to his daughter's ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a father betroths his daughter and she is divorced or widowed, the ketubah belongs to the father; but if he marries her off and she is divorced or widowed, the ketubah belongs to her. Rabbi Yehuda says the first ketubah belongs to the father, but the Sages disagree once she is married.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: if a father betroths his daughter and she is divorced or widowed, the ketubah belongs to the father.
The Mishnah states the exception: if the father marries her off and she is divorced or widowed, the ketubah belongs to her.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the first ketubah (from betrothal) belongs to the father.
The Sages object to Rabbi Yehuda, arguing that once she is married, the father has no authority over her ketubah.

items.text: Gemara: Inference about a widow twice and support for Rabbi's view
items.text_en: Gemara: Inference about a widow twice and support for Rabbi's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that only if she is divorced or widowed after marriage does the ketubah belong to her, but if she is widowed twice, she is no longer fit to marry, and incidentally the Tanna rules like Rabbi that two occurrences establish a presumption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that only if a daughter is married and then divorced or widowed does the ketubah belong to her, but if she is widowed twice, she is no longer fit to marry.
The Gemara notes that incidentally the Tanna rules like Rabbi that two occurrences establish a presumption (חזקה).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: Since he acquired from betrothal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: Since he acquired from betrothal
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that Rabbi Yehuda holds the first ketubah belongs to the father because from the time of betrothal the father acquired the rights to it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda's position that the first ketubah belongs to the father.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's position.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain that Rabbi Yehuda holds the father acquired the ketubah from the time of betrothal.

items.text: Rava's objection and revised explanation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and revised explanation
items.desc_en: Rava objects that Rabbi Yehuda admits that if a daughter was betrothed as a minor and then matured before marriage, the father has no rights, contradicting the earlier reasoning. The Gemara revises the explanation: the father's right is because the ketubah is written under his authority.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda admits that if a daughter was betrothed as a minor and then matured before marriage, the father has no rights, contradicting the earlier reasoning that the father acquires the ketubah from the time of betrothal.

The Gemara revises the explanation: Rabbah and Rav Yosef actually said the father's right is because the ketubah is written under his authority (בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ), not because he acquired it from the time of betrothal.

items.text: When is the ketubah collected?
items.text_en: When is the ketubah collected?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when the ketubah is collected. Rav Huna says the basic 100/200 from betrothal and the additional amount from marriage; Rav Asi says both from marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from what point the ketubah is collected.
Rav Huna rules that the basic 100/200 zuz are collected from the time of betrothal, and the additional amount from the time of marriage.
Rav Asi disagrees and holds that both the basic amount and the additional amount are collected only from the time of marriage.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Huna from a case of two ketubot
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Huna from a case of two ketubot
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from a case where a woman has two ketubot, and Rav Huna ruled she collects 200 from the first date and 300 from the second, but not a mix. The Gemara explains that since the husband did not write a clause linking them, she cannot collect 200 from the first and 100 from the second.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna by citing a case where a woman has two ketubot (כתובות) and Rav Huna ruled she collects 200 from the first date and 300 from the second, not a mix.
The Gemara objects that if Rav Huna's principle were correct, she should be able to collect 200 from the first date and 100 from the second.
The Gemara further objects that by the same logic, she should collect all 500 — 200 from the first date and 300 from the second.

The Gemara resolves that since the husband did not write a clause linking the two ketubot (כתובות), she cannot combine them; she collects either 200 from the first date or 300 from the second, not both.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the ketubah case with added property
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the ketubah case with added property
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the woman cannot collect from the added property, invoking Rav Nachman's rule that a second document nullifies the first. Rav Pappa qualifies that if the second document adds something, it is written for the addition, and here the husband added something.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the woman cannot collect from the added property because she waived her prior lien by not writing 'I added one hundred cubits' in the second document.
The Gemara questions whether this contradicts Rav Nachman's rule that a second document nullifies the first.
Rav Pappa resolves that Rav Nachman agrees: if the second document adds something, it is written only for the addition, and here the husband added something, so the first lien remains.

items.text: Rav Nachman's principle and its application to sales and gifts
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's principle and its application to sales and gifts
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rav Nachman's statement that a second document nullifies the first, with Rav Pappa's qualification about additions. It then discusses cases where the first document is a sale and the second a gift, or vice versa, and concludes that when both are sales or both gifts, the second nullifies the first, with two explanations from Rafram and Rav Acha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Nachman's principle that when two documents are issued one after the other, the second nullifies the first.
Rav Pappa qualifies that Rav Nachman concedes if the second document adds a date tree, it is written for the addition.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of sale vs. gift
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of sale vs. gift
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the first document is a sale and the second a gift, the second is written to enhance the recipient's power due to the law of the neighbor's right of preemption.

sub.text: Gemara's extension to gift then sale
sub.text_en: Gemara's extension to gift then sale
sub.desc_en: The Gemara extends that all the more so if the first is a gift and the second a sale, the second is written due to the creditor's law.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion for same type documents
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion for same type documents
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that when both documents are sales or both gifts, the second indeed nullifies the first.
The Gemara asks for the reason why the second nullifies the first.
Rafram explains that the second document indicates the seller admitted to the buyer that the first sale was invalid.
Rav Acha explains that the second document shows the seller waived his lien on the property.

items.text: Difference between the two explanations
items.text_en: Difference between the two explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rafram's and Rav Acha's explanations, and answers that it lies in the case of undermining witnesses, and also regarding payment of produce and tax.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Rafram's and Rav Acha's explanations.
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in the case of undermining witnesses and also regarding payment of produce and tax.

items.text: Ruling on when the ketubah and tosefet are collected
items.text_en: Ruling on when the ketubah and tosefet are collected
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says the basic ketubah (maneh or two hundred) is collected from the time of betrothal, while the tosefet is from the time of marriage. The Sages say both are from the time of marriage, and the halakha follows the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the ruling is regarding when the ketubah and tosefet are collected, and cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon who says the basic ketubah (maneh or two hundred) is collected from the time of betrothal, while the tosefet is from the time of marriage.
The Sages say both the basic ketubah and the tosefet are collected from the time of marriage.
The Gemara rules that the halakha follows the Sages: both the basic ketubah and the tosefet are collected from the time of marriage.

items.text: Mishnah: The female convert's daughter who commits adultery
items.text_en: Mishnah: The female convert's daughter who commits adultery
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a female convert whose daughter was conceived or born at different times relative to conversion. If both conception and birth were after conversion, the daughter is like a full Israelite; otherwise, she is punished by strangulation or stoning, and lacks the father's house opening and the hundred selah fine.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a female convert whose daughter converted with her and then committed adultery, stating she is executed by strangulation and lacks the father's house opening and the hundred selah fine.

The Mishnah adds two subcases: if conception was before conversion but birth after, she is stoned and lacks the opening and fine; if both conception and birth were after conversion, she is like a full Israelite daughter.
The Mishnah concludes that if she has a father but no father's house opening, or vice versa, she is stoned, and the father's house opening is only a מצוה (commandment) requirement.

items.text: Derivation of the law from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the law from the verse
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish derives from the word 'ומתה' that the defamer is liable only if the girl dies, not for a fine, and that the verse includes a girl whose conception was not in holiness but whose birth was in holiness. The Gemara questions why this does not also imply a flogging or the hundred-sela fine, and answers that the verse limits it to death. It then considers alternative interpretations and rejects them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived? Reish Lakish answers that the verse 'ומתה' (and she shall die) includes a girl whose conception was not in holiness but whose birth was in holiness.
The Gemara objects: If so, let the defamer also be flogged and pay the hundred-sela fine.
The Gemara answers: The verse 'ומתה' (and she shall die) includes her only for the death penalty, not for the fine.
The Gemara proposes: Perhaps the verse includes only a girl whose conception and birth were both in holiness? The Gemara rejects this: That is a full-fledged Jewish woman, no need for inclusion.
The Gemara proposes: Perhaps the verse includes even a girl whose conception and birth were both not in holiness? The Gemara rejects: If so, what purpose does the phrase 'בישראל' (in Israel) serve?

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: Orphaned girl exempts the defamer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: Orphaned girl exempts the defamer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that one who defames an orphaned girl is exempt, because the verse says 'ונתנו לאבי הנערה', excluding one who has no father.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוסי בר חנינא (Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina) states that one who defames an orphaned girl is exempt, because the verse 'ונתנו לאבי הנערה' (and they shall give to the father of the young woman) excludes one who has no father.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin (or bar Zevida) raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from 'ואם מאן ימאן אביה' that an orphaned girl is included for the fine. The same rabbi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case is where the man had relations with her and she later became orphaned.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin (or some say Rabbi Yosei bar Zevida) objects: the verse 'ואם מאן ימאן אביה' (and if her father refuses) includes an orphan for the fine, according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
He himself resolves the objection: the case is where the man had relations with her and then she became an orphan.

items.text: Rava: Defamer is liable for an orphaned girl
items.text_en: Rava: Defamer is liable for an orphaned girl
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the defamer is liable for an orphaned girl, based on a baraita that distinguishes between a Jewish girl and a convert's girl. He reasons that if the defamer were exempt for an orphaned Jewish girl, the verse would not need to exclude converts.

sub.desc_en: Rava says: the defamer is liable; from where? From the baraita that teaches 'בתולת ישראל' (a virgin of Israel), excluding a virgin of converts.

The Gemara supports Rava: if you say that in such a case an Israelite is liable, then the verse is needed to exclude converts; but if an Israelite is exempt, then certainly converts are exempt, making the exclusion superfluous.

items.text: Reish Lakish: Defamer of a minor is exempt
items.text_en: Reish Lakish: Defamer of a minor is exempt
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that one who defames a minor girl is exempt, because the verse says 'הנערה' with a full spelling, implying a maiden (na'arah) and not a minor. Rav Acha bar Abba objects, noting that elsewhere 'נערה' includes a minor, but the Gemara concludes that here the full spelling teaches that only a maiden is included.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that one who defames a minor girl is exempt, citing the full spelling of 'הנערה' in the verse.
Rav Acha bar Abba objects that the full spelling is not decisive, because elsewhere 'נערה' in the stoning passage cannot apply to a minor who is not liable for punishment.
The Gemara resolves that here the full spelling 'נערה' teaches exclusion of a minor, but elsewhere 'נער' includes even a minor.

items.text: Tanna of the house of Sheilah: Three categories of a na'arah
items.text_en: Tanna of the house of Sheilah: Three categories of a na'arah
items.desc_en: A baraita from the house of Sheilah begins to list three legal categories regarding a na'arah, starting with the case where witnesses testify that she committed adultery in her father's house after she was married.

sub.desc_en: Sheila teaches a baraita: there are three categories regarding a girl: if witnesses came against her in her father-in-law's house that she committed adultery in her father's house —

items.text: Opening Mishnah: execution locations and method for a betrothed young woman who committed adultery
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: execution locations and method for a betrothed young woman who committed adultery
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a betrothed young woman who committed adultery is stoned at her father's door; if witnesses came after she left her father's house, she is stoned at the city gate; if she committed adultery and then reached bagrut, she is executed by strangulation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a betrothed young woman who committed adultery is stoned at her father's door, or at the city gate if witnesses came after she left her father's house, and if she reached bagrut (physical maturity) after the sin, she is executed by strangulation.

items.text: Gemara's question and contradiction from the defamed bride case
items.text_en: Gemara's question and contradiction from the defamed bride case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: does a change in the body (bagrut) change the execution method? It raises a contradiction from a baraita: a betrothed young woman who committed adultery, and after bagrut her husband brought a false defamation claim, he is not flogged and does not pay 100 sela, but she and her conspiring witnesses are brought to stoning. The Gemara corrects the baraita: either she or her witnesses are brought to stoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a change in the body (bagrut) changes the execution method.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about a betrothed young woman who committed adultery and after bagrut was defamed, showing she is still stoned.
The Gemara corrects the baraita: either she or her conspiring witnesses are brought to stoning, not both.

items.text: Rava's answer: the defamed bride is a novelty
items.text_en: Rava's answer: the defamed bride is a novelty
items.desc_en: Rava answers: the case of the defamed bride (motzi shem ra) is a novelty, because normally a woman who entered the chuppah but was not yet intimate and then committed adultery is executed by strangulation, yet the Torah prescribed stoning for the defamed bride. Therefore, the novelty applies only where the body has not changed, but where the body has changed, the novelty does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the case of the defamer (מוציא שם רע) is a novelty, because normally a woman who entered the wedding canopy but was not yet intimate and then committed adultery is executed by strangulation, yet the Torah prescribed stoning for the defamed bride, so the novelty applies only where the body has not changed.

items.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection
items.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua objects to Rava: perhaps the Torah innovated only where the body has not changed, but where the body has changed, the Torah did not innovate, so the defamed bride after bagrut should still be stoned?

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua objects to Rava: perhaps the Torah innovated only where the body has not changed (i.e., before bagrut), but where the body has changed (after bagrut), the Torah did not innovate, so the defamed bride after bagrut should still be stoned.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: a Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: a Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says: the question of whether a change in status changes the law is a dispute among Tannaim, as taught in a baraita: if priests sinned before appointment, they are like commoners; Rabbi Shimon says if their sin was known before appointment they are liable, but after appointment they are exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the question by asserting that the issue of whether a change in status changes the law is a dispute among Tannaim.

The baraita cites the Tanna Kamma's position that priests who sinned before appointment are treated as commoners, and Rabbi Shimon's position that if their sin was known before appointment they are liable, but after appointment they are exempt.

items.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Shimon follows awareness (ידיעה) rather than the sin, then the sinner should bring a korban like the present case, but the anointed priest brings a bull and the prince a goat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Shimon follows awareness (ידיעה) rather than the sin, then the sinner should bring a korban like the present case, but the anointed priest brings a bull and the prince a goat.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and Rabbi Ila'a's derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and Rabbi Ila'a's derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan instructs the tanna to teach that the woman is judged by stoning, despite being a bogeret, because the verse says 'the young woman' (הנערה) meaning she was previously a young woman.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's instruction to the Tanna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's instruction to the Tanna
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan instructs the Tanna to teach that the betrothed girl is judged by stoning, and Rabbi Il'a explains that the verse 'הַנַּעֲרָה' (the girl) refers to one who was previously a girl (i.e., a bogeret).
The gemara questions why the woman is stoned, since the Torah says 'na'arah hame'urasah' but she is a bogeret.
Rabbi Ila'a answers that the verse says 'הנערה' (the young woman) meaning she was previously a young woman.

items.text: Exchange between Rabbi Chananya and Rabbi Ila'a, and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin's explanation
items.text_en: Exchange between Rabbi Chananya and Rabbi Ila'a, and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chananya asks why she should not also receive lashes and pay the fine; Rabbi Ila'a rejects this. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin explains that her actions caused her punishment (she sinned as a na'arah) and his words caused his (he slandered when she was a bogeret).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chananya asks Rabbi Ila'a: if the girl is judged as a na'arah, why should she not also receive lashes and the slanderer pay the fine?
Rabbi Ila'a rejects Rabbi Chananya's suggestion, saying 'May Heaven save us from that opinion' and retorts 'May Heaven save us from your opinion.'
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin explains the rationale: the girl's actions caused her punishment (she sinned as a na'arah) and the slanderer's words caused his (he slandered when she was a bogeret).

items.text: Baraita on the location of stoning
items.text_en: Baraita on the location of stoning
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a betrothed young woman who committed adultery is stoned at the entrance of her father's house; if she has none, at the city gate; if the city is mostly gentiles, at the court entrance. Similarly, an idolater is stoned at the gate where he worshipped.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a betrothed girl who committed adultery is stoned at the door of her father's house; if no such door, at the city gate; if a mostly gentile city, at the court door; similarly for an idolater.

items.text: Derivation of the location for idolatry
items.text_en: Derivation of the location for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for these laws. It cites a baraita that interprets 'your gates' (שְׁעָרֶיךָ) as the gate where he worshipped, derived from a verbal analogy between 'your gates' above and below. Another interpretation excludes gentile gates, and the extra word teaches both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the law that an idolater is stoned at the gate where he worshipped, and raises the alternative possibility that it means the gate where he is judged.

The baraita derives via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) that 'your gates' below (Deut. 17:5) refers to the gate where he worshipped, just as 'your gates' above (Deut. 13:17) refers to the gate of the idolatrous city.
Another interpretation excludes gentile gates, and the extra word 'שְׁעָרֶיךָ' (your gates) rather than 'שַׁעַר' (gate) teaches both meanings.

items.text: Derivation for the betrothed young woman
items.text_en: Derivation for the betrothed young woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we derive the location for the betrothed young woman. Rabbi Avahu says we learn 'opening' (פתח) from 'opening', and 'opening' from 'gate', and 'gate' from 'your gates'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for idolatry, but from where do we derive the location for the betrothed young woman?
Rabbi Avahu answers by deriving 'opening' (פתח) from 'opening', and 'opening' from 'gate', and 'gate' from 'your gates'.

items.text: Dispute about lashes and the fine for a slanderer
items.text_en: Dispute about lashes and the fine for a slanderer
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a slanderer (מוציא שם רע) receives lashes and pays 100 sela. Rabbi Yehuda says he always receives lashes, but pays only if he had intercourse. The Gemara explains the dispute as between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis, and notes a contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's view, resolved by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that the lashes are rabbinic lashes of rebellion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the ruling that a slanderer (מוציא שם רע) receives lashes and pays 100 sela.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the slanderer always receives lashes, but pays the 100 sela only if he actually had intercourse.

The Gemara explains that the dispute in the baraita aligns with the earlier dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis, interpreting the Tanna Kamma as following the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda as following Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

An alternative version holds that the entire baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, with the Tanna Kamma requiring both lashes and payment only if he had intercourse, while Rabbi Yehuda adds that lashes are always given.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda himself says that lashes apply only if he had intercourse, contradicting his statement here that he always receives lashes.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by explaining that the lashes Rabbi Yehuda always mandates are rabbinic lashes of rebellion (מכת מרדות), not the Torah lashes.

items.text: Rav Papa's explanation of 'ba'al lokeh'
items.text_en: Rav Papa's explanation of 'ba'al lokeh'
items.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that the term 'ba'al lokeh' in the Mishnah refers to a monetary penalty, not lashes. He supports this by citing a parallel case where 'lokeh' means paying a full valuation, due to a decree to prevent confusion between similar phrases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa opens by identifying that the Mishnah's term 'ba'al lokeh' refers to a monetary penalty, not lashes, and raises the question of why money is called 'lashes'.
Rav Papa supports his claim by citing a baraita where 'lokeh' in the context of valuations means paying a full valuation, not lashes.
Rav Papa answers that the term 'lokeh' there means he pays the full valuation, explaining the usage.

Rav Papa resolves the difficulty by explaining that the decree was enacted to prevent confusion between the phrases 'half his valuation' and 'valuation of half', where the latter refers to a vital limb.

items.text: Source for lashes in motzi shem ra
items.text_en: Source for lashes in motzi shem ra
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives both monetary fine and lashes from the verse 've'anshu oto' and 'veyisru'. It then questions the source for lashes, and Rabbi Avahu provides a gezerah shavah linking 'yisru' to the verse about lashes for a rebellious son.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, deriving the monetary fine from 've'anshu oto' and lashes from 'veyisru'.
The Gemara questions the source for lashes, noting the monetary fine is explicit in the verse.
Rabbi Avahu provides a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) linking 'yisru' to the verse about lashes for a rebellious son.

items.text: Source for the prohibition against slander
items.text_en: Source for the prohibition against slander
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the negative commandment against slander. Rabbi Elazar derives it from 'lo telech rachil', while Rabbi Nathan derives it from 'venishmarta mikol davar ra'. The Gemara explains why each rejects the other's source, citing other uses of those verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the negative commandment (אזהרה) against a slanderer (מוציא שם רע).
Rabbi Elazar derives the prohibition from the verse 'לֹא תֵלֵךְ רָכִיל' (Do not go as a talebearer).
Rabbi Nathan derives the prohibition from the verse 'וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ מִכֹּל דָּבָר רָע' (And you shall guard yourself from every evil thing).
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Elazar does not use Rabbi Nathan's verse as the source.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar rejects that verse because it is needed for Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's teaching that one should not entertain improper thoughts by day that lead to טומאה (impurity) by night.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Nathan does not use Rabbi Elazar's verse as the source.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Nathan rejects that verse because it is needed as a warning to the court (בית דין) not to be lenient to one party and harsh to the other.

items.text: The case of unsolicited witnesses and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: The case of unsolicited witnesses and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the husband did not ask witnesses to testify, he is exempt from fine and lashes. The Gemara clarifies that this excludes Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that he must hire witnesses. Rabbi Avahu and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derive this from a gezerah shavah on 'simah'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if the husband did not ask witnesses to testify, he is exempt from flogging and the fine, and either she or the conspiring witnesses are brought to stoning.
The Gemara objects that it is impossible for both her and the conspiring witnesses to be stoned together, and corrects the baraita to mean either she or the witnesses are stoned.
The Gemara infers that if the husband did ask witnesses to testify, even without hiring them, he is liable, which excludes the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda who requires hiring.

The Gemara asks for the reason of Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Avahu answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שימה' (placing) in the defamer verse to the interest verse, teaching that it involves money.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak confirms that Rav Yosef Tzidoni taught in the school of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai the same גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'שימה' (placing).

items.text: Unresolved questions about hiring witnesses and yavam
items.text_en: Unresolved questions about hiring witnesses and yavam
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rav Ashi raise unresolved questions about hiring witnesses with land or less than a perutah, and about slandering a wife after first marriage or yibbum. A partial resolution is found from Rabbi Yona's teaching that the verse excludes a yavam.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya raises three unresolved questions about hiring witnesses with land, less than a perutah, or both with a perutah.
Rav Ashi raises two unresolved questions about slandering a wife regarding first marriage or levirate marriage.
The Gemara resolves at least one dilemma by citing Rabbi Yona's teaching that the verse 'I gave my daughter to this man' excludes a yavam, so slandering a yevama does not apply.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov on the definition of motzi shem ra
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov on the definition of motzi shem ra
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita where the Rabbis hold that the slanderer is liable even without intercourse, while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires intercourse. The Gemara analyzes how each interprets the relevant verses, including 'uva eleha', 'lo matzati', 've'eleh betulai', and 'ufarsu hasimlah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is, and introduces a baraita describing the case of motzi shem ra.
The Gemara objects that if there are witnesses to adultery under him, she should be stoned, not receive a ketubah.
The Gemara clarifies: if she committed adultery after betrothal, she is stoned; if before, she receives a ketubah of a maneh.
The baraita states that for a false motzi shem ra, the slanderer is flogged and pays 100 selaim whether or not he had intercourse, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov requires intercourse.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the verse 'וּבָא אֵלֶיהָ' (and he came to her) fits, but for the Rabbis, what do these verses mean?
The Gemara answers: for the Rabbis, 'וּבָא אֵלֶיהָ' refers to accusations, and 'וָאֶקְרַב אֵלֶיהָ' refers to words.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the verse 'לֹא מָצָאתִי לְבִתְּךָ בְּתוּלִים' (I did not find your daughter a virgin) fits, but for the Rabbis, what does it mean?
The Gemara answers: for the Rabbis, it means 'I did not find your daughter's valid virginity.'
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the verse 'וְאֵלֶּה בְּתוּלֵי בִתִּי' (and these are my daughter's virginity tokens) fits, but for the Rabbis, what does it mean?
The Gemara answers: for the Rabbis, it means 'and these are my daughter's valid virginity tokens.'
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the verse 'וּפָרְשׂוּ הַשִּׂמְלָה' (and they shall spread the garment) fits, but for the Rabbis, what does it mean?

Rabbi Avahu answers: for the Rabbis, 'וּפָרְשׂוּ הַשִּׂמְלָה' means they spread out what he accused her of, and a baraita explains that witnesses from both sides clarify the matter like a new garment, while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds it literally as a garment.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the unique case of motzi shem ra
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the unique case of motzi shem ra
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that motzi shem ra is unique in that the Torah distinguishes between normal and abnormal intercourse for liability: the slanderer is only liable if he engaged in abnormal intercourse and slandered regarding normal intercourse. The Gemara questions which opinion this follows.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rav Yaakov bar Giyorei)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rav Yaakov bar Giyorei)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the Torah uniquely distinguishes between normal and abnormal intercourse for liability in the case of motzi shem ra: the slanderer is liable only if he engaged in abnormal intercourse and slandered regarding normal intercourse.

The Gemara asks which opinion this ruling follows: if it follows the Rabbis, the slanderer is liable even without intercourse, contradicting the requirement of abnormal intercourse; if it follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, the slanderer is liable only when he actually engaged in intercourse.

items.text: Clarification of the earlier statement about normal intercourse
items.text_en: Clarification of the earlier statement about normal intercourse
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a previous difficulty by citing Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a husband is only liable for a bad name if he both had normal intercourse and spread the bad name in a normal manner.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier difficulty by citing Rav Kahana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a husband is only liable for a bad name if he both had normal intercourse and spread the bad name in a normal manner.

items.text: Mishnah: Father's rights and husband's additional rights
items.text_en: Mishnah: Father's rights and husband's additional rights
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the father's rights over his daughter: to receive her betrothal money, find her lost object, her earnings, annul her vows, and accept her divorce. After marriage, the husband gains rights to her produce, is obligated for her sustenance, ransom, and burial. Rabbi Yehuda adds that even a poor man must provide at least two flutes and a wailing woman for her burial.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the father's rights over his daughter: he receives her betrothal money, finds, earnings, and annuls her vows, but does not enjoy her produce during her lifetime.

The Mishnah continues: when the daughter is married, the husband gains additional rights (enjoying her produce) and obligations (support, ransom, burial), with Rabbi Yehuda adding a requirement for even the poorest to provide two flutes and a wailing woman.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that even a poor man must provide at least two flutes and a wailing woman for her burial.

items.text: Source for betrothal by money: father receives the money
items.text_en: Source for betrothal by money: father receives the money
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda derives from the verse 'and she shall go out for nothing, without money' that the father receives the betrothal money. The Gemara challenges that perhaps the daughter herself should receive it, but responds that since the father gives her away, he takes the money. A further challenge about a נערה who has legal capacity is answered by the verse 'in her youth, in her father's house' — all the benefit of her youth belongs to her father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that betrothal can be effected by money?
Rav Yehuda cites the verse 'וְיָצְאָה חִנָּם אֵין כָּסֶף' (and she shall go out for nothing, without money), interpreting that the money goes to another master — her father.
The Gemara objects: Perhaps the daughter herself should receive the betrothal money, since she is the one being betrothed.
The Gemara responds: Since the father gives her away in betrothal (as per the verse 'אֶת בִּתִּי נָתַתִּי לָאִישׁ הַזֶּה'), it is logical that he receives the money, not she.
The Gemara objects further: Perhaps this applies only to a minor (קְטַנָּה) who lacks legal capacity, but a נערה (adolescent girl) who has legal capacity should betroth herself and take the money.
The Gemara resolves: The verse 'בִּנְעוּרֶיהָ בֵּית אָבִיהָ' (in her youth, in her father's house) teaches that all benefit of her youth belongs to her father, including betrothal money.

items.text: Source for daughter's earnings belonging to father
items.text_en: Source for daughter's earnings belonging to father
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a verse comparing a daughter to a maidservant to teach that her earnings belong to her father. The Gemara questions why this verse is needed, since the earlier verse 'in her youth' could teach this. It answers that verse is for annulling vows. Attempts to derive monetary matters from prohibitions or fines are rejected, and the case of בושת ופגם is distinguished because the father is also affected.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a verse comparing a daughter to a maidservant to prove that her earnings belong to her father.
The Gemara questions why this verse is needed, since the verse 'in her youth' could already teach this.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'in her youth' is used for the law of annulling vows, not for monetary matters.
The Gemara rejects deriving monetary law from prohibitions or fines, stating that one cannot learn monetary matters from איסורא (prohibitions) or קנסא (fines).
The Gemara distinguishes the case of בושת ופגם (shame and depreciation) because the father is also affected, so it cannot serve as a precedent for the daughter's earnings.

items.text: Resolution: the verse excludes a comparable departure
items.text_en: Resolution: the verse excludes a comparable departure
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse excludes a departure similar to that from a master, but the daughter's departure from her father is not complete until she enters the chuppah. However, from the perspective of annulling vows, she does leave his authority, as per the Mishnah that a betrothed maiden's vows are annulled by both father and husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse excludes only a departure comparable to that from a master, not the daughter's partial departure from her father.
The Gemara objects that the daughter's departure from her father is not complete like a slave's, since she still requires entry into the chuppah.

The Gemara resolves that from the perspective of annulling vows, the daughter does leave her father's authority, as the Mishnah states that a betrothed maiden's vows are annulled by both father and husband.

items.text: Source for betrothal by document and intercourse
items.text_en: Source for betrothal by document and intercourse
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives betrothal by document and intercourse from the verse 'and she shall be for another man', teaching that all modes of betrothal are equated to each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that betrothal by document (שטר) and by intercourse (ביאה) also give the father the money?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'וְהָיְתָה לְאִישׁ אַחֵר' teaches that all modes of betrothal (הוויות) are equated to each other.

items.text: Beginning of discussion on found object
items.text_en: Beginning of discussion on found object
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss the father's right to his daughter's found object, but the segment ends abruptly, indicating the continuation of the sugya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins discussing the Mishnah's statement that the father is entitled to his daughter's finds (מציאה).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Father's rights over daughter's earnings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Father's rights over daughter's earnings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father is entitled to his daughter's earnings, but the Gemara questions the source for this law.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a father is entitled to his daughter's earnings, but the Gemara will question the source.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of father's right to earnings
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of father's right to earnings
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a verse to derive that a daughter's earnings belong to her father, but the Gemara questions whether this applies only to a minor or also to a נערה. Rav Achai objects with alternative scenarios, and the Gemara concludes that the verse is needed specifically for a נערה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is it derived that a daughter's earnings belong to her father?

Rav Huna in the name of Rav derives from the verse about selling a daughter as a maidservant that just as a maidservant's earnings belong to her master, so too a daughter's earnings belong to her father.
The Gemara objects: perhaps this applies only to a minor daughter, whom the father can sell, but not to a נערה (adolescent daughter), whom he cannot sell.
The Gemara argues that the earnings must belong to the father, because otherwise the father's right to give her in marriage would be undermined, as he would be depriving her of her earnings.
Rav Achai objects that the father could compensate her for lost earnings, or marry her at night or on Shabbat and festivals when she is not working.
The Gemara concludes that the verse is not needed for a minor, whose earnings obviously belong to her father, but is needed specifically for a נערה (adolescent daughter).

items.text: Father's right to annul vows
items.text_en: Father's right to annul vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the father's right to annul his daughter's vows from the verse 'בִּנְעוּרֶיהָ בֵּית אָבִיהָ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a father has the power to annul his daughter's vows?
The Gemara answers: it is derived from the verse 'בִּנְעוּרֶיהָ בֵּית אָבִיהָ' (in her youth, in her father's house), implying the father's authority over her vows.

items.text: Father's right to accept her get
items.text_en: Father's right to accept her get
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the father's right to accept his daughter's get from the juxtaposition of 'וְיָצְאָה' and 'וְהָיְתָה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a father receives his daughter's bill of divorce (גט)?

The Gemara answers: it is derived from the verses 'וְיָצְאָה ... וְהָיְתָה' (she shall go out... and she shall be), linking the act of divorce (יציאה) to the act of betrothal (הויה), so just as the father accepts betrothal, he accepts the divorce.

items.text: Dispute over father's usufruct during daughter's lifetime
items.text_en: Dispute over father's usufruct during daughter's lifetime
items.desc_en: A Tannaitic dispute: the Tanna Kamma holds that a father does not eat the produce of his daughter's property during her lifetime, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds he does. The Gemara explains their reasoning: the husband was given usufruct to encourage him to redeem his wife, but the father would redeem her anyway, so no such enactment was needed; Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda argues the father might refrain from redeeming her if he has no usufruct.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that a father does not eat the produce (פירות) of his daughter's property during her lifetime, reasoning that a husband was granted this right to encourage him to redeem her, but a father would redeem her anyway.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda argues that the father does eat the produce, because otherwise he might refrain from redeeming her, thinking she has a purse of money and can redeem herself.
The Gemara asks: on what principle do they disagree?

The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's reasoning: the husband was granted usufruct (פֵּירֵי) by rabbinic enactment to encourage him to redeem his wife, but the father would redeem her anyway without such incentive.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's reasoning: the father might refrain from redeeming her, thinking 'I have a purse of money over her, let her go and redeem herself.'

items.text: Dispute over husband's inheritance of property brought from father's house
items.text_en: Dispute over husband's inheritance of property brought from father's house
items.desc_en: A Tannaitic dispute: if a husband wrote to his wife that property from her father's house would come with her, and she dies, does the husband acquire it? The Sages say no, Rabbi Natan says yes. The Gemara suggests this dispute parallels the dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah and the Rabbis regarding whether a widow or divorcee collects all or only the ketubah amount.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the Sages' position: if a husband wrote to his wife that property from her father's house would come with her, and she dies, he does not acquire it.
The baraita records Rabbi Natan's dissenting opinion: the husband does acquire the property.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Natan parallels the dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah and the Rabbis.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah: a widow or divorcee collects all property; Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah limits collection from betrothal to the ketubah amount.

items.text: Dispute over acquisition of wife's property
items.text_en: Dispute over acquisition of wife's property
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the positions of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and the Rabbis regarding whether a husband acquires property written for his wife on condition of marriage. It distinguishes between property from the husband to the wife and from the wife to the husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: one who says the husband does not acquire the property follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and one who says he does acquire follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara refines the dispute: everyone agrees with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, but the disagreement is only about property from the husband to the wife, which was written conditionally.

The Gemara concludes that regarding property from the wife to the husband, even Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya agrees the husband acquires it, because it is given for the sake of marriage and the marriage has already occurred.

items.text: Tannaitic enactment linking maintenance, earnings, ransom, and usufruct
items.text_en: Tannaitic enactment linking maintenance, earnings, ransom, and usufruct
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the Sages enacted a wife's maintenance in exchange for her earnings, her burial in exchange for her ketubah, and therefore the husband eats the produce of her property. The Gemara corrects the text to include that her ransom is in exchange for the produce.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the Sages enacted a wife's maintenance in exchange for her earnings, her burial in exchange for her ketubah, and therefore the husband eats the produce of her property.
The Gemara objects that the baraita never mentioned produce before concluding that the husband eats it, so the text must be incomplete.
The Gemara corrects the baraita to include that her ransom is in exchange for the produce, and then the husband eats the produce.

items.text: Explanation of 'therefore'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'therefore'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'therefore' teaches, and explains that it precludes the possibility that the husband might set aside the produce without eating it, which would discourage him from ransoming her. It teaches that eating the produce is preferable, and sometimes he ransoms her from his own funds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'therefore' in the baraita teaches.

The Gemara explains that 'therefore' precludes the possibility that the husband might set aside the produce without eating it, which would discourage him from ransoming her; it teaches that eating the produce is preferable, and sometimes he ransoms her from his own funds.

items.text: Objection and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Objection and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: An anonymous objection is raised: why not reverse the enactments? Abaye answers that the Sages matched what is common (maintenance and earnings) with what is common, and what is uncommon (ransom and produce) with what is uncommon.

sub.desc_en: An anonymous voice objects: why not reverse the pairings of the enactments?
Abaye answers that the Sages matched what is common (maintenance and earnings) with what is common, and what is uncommon (ransom and produce) with what is uncommon.

items.text: Biblical derivation of maintenance and other obligations
items.text_en: Biblical derivation of maintenance and other obligations
items.desc_en: Rava asserts that the tanna holds maintenance is from the Torah, citing verses for 'her flesh' (maintenance), 'her clothing', and 'her conjugal rights'. Rabbi Elazar interprets the same verses differently: 'her flesh' as conjugal rights, 'her clothing' as clothing, and 'her conjugal rights' as maintenance.

sub.desc_en: Rava asserts that the tanna holds maintenance is from the Torah, citing verses for 'her flesh' (maintenance), 'her clothing', and 'her conjugal rights'.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the same verses differently: 'her flesh' as conjugal rights, 'her clothing' as clothing, and 'her conjugal rights' as maintenance.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov explains that the verse "her flesh, her clothing, and her conjugal rights" means that the husband must provide clothing appropriate to the wife's age and season, ensuring that an old woman does not receive a young woman's clothes or vice versa, and that new clothes are not given in summer nor worn-out clothes in winter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov interprets the verse 'שארה כסותה ועונתה' (her flesh, her clothing, and her conjugal rights) to mean that the husband must provide clothing appropriate to the wife's age and season.

items.text: Rav Yosef's teaching on "she'er" as physical closeness
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's teaching on "she'er" as physical closeness
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that "she'er" refers to physical closeness, meaning the husband should not behave like Persians who have marital relations while clothed. This supports Rav Huna's ruling that if a husband says he will only be intimate with his wife while both are clothed, he must divorce her and pay her ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that 'she'er' refers to physical closeness, prohibiting the Persian practice of marital relations while clothed.
The gemara notes that Rav Yosef's teaching supports Rav Huna's ruling that a husband who insists on clothed relations must divorce and pay the ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on burial
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on burial
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda regarding whether a wife's burial expenses are covered by her husband's estate. It clarifies that the case is where the husband's standard of living is higher than the wife's; the Tanna Kamma holds that the principle 'she ascends with him but does not descend with him' applies only during his lifetime, not after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda, asking how the case could be such that the Tanna Kamma would deny burial expenses or Rabbi Yehuda would grant them.

The Gemara resolves the question by explaining that the case is where the husband's standard of living is higher than the wife's; the Tanna Kamma holds that the principle 'she ascends with him but does not descend with him' applies only during his lifetime, not after death.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling in the name of Mar Ukva
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling in the name of Mar Ukva
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports in the name of Mar Ukva that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, meaning that even after death, the wife's burial is according to her husband's honor, as she ascends with him.

sub.text: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports in the name of Mar Ukva that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, meaning that even after death, the wife's burial is according to her husband's honor, as she ascends with him.

items.text: Court's authority over a mentally incapacitated person's assets
items.text_en: Court's authority over a mentally incapacitated person's assets
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda further states in Mar Ukva's name that if a man becomes mentally incapacitated, the court may use his assets to support his wife, children, and 'something else.' Ravina questions why this differs from the case of a man who traveled overseas, where the court supports only the wife, not the children. Rav Ashi answers that there is a distinction between one who leaves intentionally and one who leaves unintentionally.

sub.text: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states in Mar Ukva's name that if a man becomes mentally incapacitated, the court may use his assets to support his wife, children, and 'something else.'
Ravina questions why this differs from the case of a man who traveled overseas, where the court supports only the wife, not the children or 'something else.'
Rav Ashi answers that there is a distinction between one who leaves intentionally and one who leaves unintentionally.

items.text: Dispute over the meaning of 'something else'
items.text_en: Dispute over the meaning of 'something else'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'something else' is disputed: Rav Chisda says it refers to jewelry, while Rav Yosef says it refers to charity. The one who says jewelry certainly includes charity, but the one who says charity excludes jewelry because the husband would not want his wife to become unattractive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'דבר אחר' (something else) refers to in the context of the husband's obligations.
Rav Chisda says 'דבר אחר' refers to תכשיט (jewelry) for the wife.
Rav Yosef says 'דבר אחר' refers to צדקה (charity) given on behalf of the husband.
The Gemara notes that according to Rav Chisda, jewelry certainly includes charity, since jewelry is a greater expense.
The Gemara explains that according to Rav Yosef, charity is given but jewelry is not, because the husband would not want his wife to become unattractive (by lacking jewelry).

items.text: Burial of a wife who died while husband was overseas
items.text_en: Burial of a wife who died while husband was overseas
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin quotes Rav Huna: if a man went overseas and his wife died, the court uses his assets to bury her according to his honor. The Gemara clarifies that this means 'also according to his honor,' teaching that the principle 'she ascends with him but does not descend with him' applies even after death.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin reports Rav Huna's ruling: if a man went overseas and his wife died, the court uses his assets to bury her according to his honor.
The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'according to his honor' implies that her honor is disregarded.
The Gemara resolves that the intended meaning is 'also according to his honor,' not exclusively.
The Gemara concludes that the ruling teaches the principle 'she ascends with him but does not descend with him' applies even after death.

items.text: Rav Mattana's ruling on a husband's stipulation about burial
items.text_en: Rav Mattana's ruling on a husband's stipulation about burial
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana rules that if a husband says 'if she dies, do not bury her from my assets,' we listen to him, because the assets will go to the heirs. However, if he says 'if I die, do not bury me from my assets,' we do not listen to him, as he cannot enrich his children at the public's expense.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana rules that if a husband stipulates that his wife not be buried from his assets, we listen to him.
The Gemara questions why the husband's stipulation matters, since even without it the assets would go to the heirs.

The Gemara clarifies that the ruling actually applies to a husband who says 'if I die, do not bury me from my assets,' and we do not listen to him because he cannot enrich his children at the public's expense.

items.text: Beginning of the Mishnah on a daughter's status
items.text_en: Beginning of the Mishnah on a daughter's status
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins: 'A daughter is always under her father's authority until she enters [the marriage canopy].'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins by stating that a daughter is always under her father's authority until she enters the marriage canopy.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a betrothed woman is always under her father's authority until she enters the chuppah, but if the father hands her over to the husband's agents, she enters the husband's authority. Various scenarios of accompaniment are detailed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a betrothed woman is under her father's authority until she enters the husband's domain for marriage, and then details scenarios of transfer of authority.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of 'always'
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of 'always'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's use of 'always' excludes an earlier Mishnah which allowed the betrothed to eat terumah once the wedding time arrived, even without marriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'לעולם' (always) in the Mishnah excludes, and answers that it excludes the earlier Mishnah's ruling.
The Gemara cites a baraita that when the time for marriage arrives but the wedding has not occurred, the betrothed woman eats from her husband's property and eats תרומה (priestly portion).
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah teaches that the father's authority persists 'always' until the chuppah, countering the earlier baraita.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rav Asi on the scope of 'handing over'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rav Asi on the scope of 'handing over'
items.desc_en: Rav and Rav Asi debate whether handing over to the husband's agents grants authority for all matters except terumah (Rav) or even for terumah (Rav Asi). Rav Asi is challenged from the Mishnah, and Rav defends him by reinterpreting 'handing over' as entry into the chuppah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that when the father hands over the daughter to the husband's agents, she enters the husband's domain.
Rav states that the handing over grants the husband authority over all matters except for eating תרומה (priestly portion).
Rav Asi argues that the handing over grants authority even for eating תרומה (priestly portion).

sub.text: Rav Huna's objection to Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's objection to Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna (or Ḥiyya bar Rav) objects to Rav Asi by citing the Mishnah's statement that the daughter remains in the father's domain until she enters the chuppah.
Rav defends Rav Asi by reinterpreting the Mishnah: the 'handing over' itself is considered her entry into the chuppah.

items.text: Shmuel and Resh Lakish on inheritance and ketubah
items.text_en: Shmuel and Resh Lakish on inheritance and ketubah
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that 'handing over' grants authority for inheritance, while Resh Lakish says it grants authority for the ketubah. The Gemara questions the difference, and Ravina explains that Resh Lakish means the ketubah is collected from the most superior property.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the father's authority over his daughter after she is handed over to the husband's agents is limited to matters of inheritance (ירושה).
Resh Lakish states that the father's authority after handing over is limited to matters of the ketubah (כתובה).
The Gemara asks: what does Resh Lakish mean by 'for her ketubah' — if it means inheritance, that is the same as Shmuel's position.
Ravina explains that Resh Lakish means the ketubah is collected from the most superior property (אחר מנה), not that the husband inherits her.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina's view refuted by a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina's view refuted by a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina agree with Rav Asi that handing over grants authority even for terumah. A baraita is brought that distinguishes between inheritance (where handing over suffices) and terumah (which requires entry into the chuppah), refuting all opinions that allow terumah upon mere handing over.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina both state that handing over the daughter grants authority for everything, even for eating תרומה (priestly portion).

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes between inheritance (where handing over suffices) and תרומה (which requires entry into the chuppah), refuting all opinions that allow תרומה upon mere handing over.

items.text: Resolution of internal contradiction in the baraita
items.text_en: Resolution of internal contradiction in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction within the baraita: one clause implies that entering to lodge is not for marriage, while another implies the opposite. Rav Ashi resolves that the baraita refers to two different courtyards: her courtyard (for lodging) and his courtyard (for marriage).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: the first clause implies that entering to lodge is not for marriage, but the second clause implies that entering without specification is for marriage.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to two different courtyards: her courtyard (for lodging) and his courtyard (for marriage).

items.text: Source for the law of a betrothed who committed adultery after being handed over
items.text_en: Source for the law of a betrothed who committed adultery after being handed over
items.desc_en: A Tanna states that if the father handed over the daughter to the husband's agents and she committed adultery, she is executed by strangulation. Rabbi Ami bar Chama derives this from a verse. The Gemara questions whether the verse excludes a woman who entered the chuppah but was not yet intimate, and Rava clarifies that the verse already excludes such a case.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states that if the father handed over the daughter to the husband's agents and she committed adultery, she is executed by strangulation.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this law.
Rabbi Ami bar Chama derives the law from the verse 'לִזְנוֹת בֵּית אָבִיהָ' (to commit adultery in her father's house), excluding a woman handed over to the husband's agents.
The Gemara objects that the verse might exclude a woman who entered the chuppah (bridal canopy) but was not yet intimate, rather than one handed over to agents.
Rava explains that the verse itself already excludes a woman who entered the chuppah but was not intimate, by the phrase 'מְאוֹרָשָׂה' (betrothed) and not 'נְשׂוּאָה' (married).

The Gemara clarifies that 'נְשׂוּאָה' cannot mean fully married (since that is already excluded by 'בְּתוּלָה'), so it must refer to a woman who entered the chuppah but was not yet intimate, confirming that the verse in question excludes only the case of handing over to agents.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: father loses annulment rights once daughter leaves his domain
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: father loses annulment rights once daughter leaves his domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman who returns to her father's house after being widowed or divorced reverts to her father's authority for vow annulment. Rava cites a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that once she has left her father's domain (e.g., by being handed to the husband's agents), the father can no longer annul her vows.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman who returns to her father's house after being widowed or divorced reverts to her father's authority for vow annulment.
Rava cites a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that once she has left her father's domain (e.g., by being handed to the husband's agents), the father can no longer annul her vows.

items.text: Supporting proofs from Mishnayot
items.text_en: Supporting proofs from Mishnayot
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak each bring a Mishnah to support the principle that once a woman enters the husband's domain (even via agents), she is considered under his authority. Rav Pappa cites the case of a betrothed maiden, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the case of a married woman who is liable for capital punishment upon entering the husband's domain for marriage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa supports Rava's ruling by citing a Mishnah that excludes a girl handed to the husband's agents from the category of 'in her father's house' for the law of the one who seduces a betrothed maiden.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's supporting evidence
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's supporting evidence
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds further support from a Mishnah that once a woman enters the husband's domain for marriage, even without intercourse, she is considered fully married for the law of adultery.

items.text: Mishnah: Father not obligated for daughter's sustenance
items.text_en: Mishnah: Father not obligated for daughter's sustenance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father is not obligated to support his daughter. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya derived this from the verse that sons inherit and daughters are supported: just as sons inherit only after the father's death, so too daughters are supported only after the father's death.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father is not obligated to support his daughter, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya derives from the inheritance laws that daughters are supported only after the father's death.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that while there is no obligation for a daughter, there is at least a mitzvah. It then asks which Tanna holds this view, ruling out Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka based on a baraita where each has a different position on the obligation or mitzvah to support children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that while there is no obligation for a daughter, there is at least a mitzvah (commandment) to support her.
The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, ruling out Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

A baraita is cited showing the positions of Rabbi Meir (mitzvah for daughters, kal vachomer for sons), Rabbi Yehuda (mitzvah for sons, kal vachomer for daughters due to their shame), and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka (obligation for daughters after the father's death, but no support during his lifetime).

The Gemara objects that none of the three Tannaim match the Mishnah: Rabbi Meir says there is a mitzvah for sons, Rabbi Yehuda says there is a mitzvah for sons as well, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says there is not even a mitzvah.

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah can align with any Tanna
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah can align with any Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah could be attributed to Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, or Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. It then explains how it aligns with Rabbi Meir: the Mishnah states that a father is not obligated for his daughter, and the same applies to his son; there is a mitzvah for the daughter, and a fortiori for the son. The Mishnah specifically mentions the daughter to teach this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers three possible attributions for the Mishnah: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, or Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.

The Gemara explains how the Mishnah aligns with Rabbi Meir: the father is not obligated for his daughter, and the same applies to his son; there is a mitzvah for the daughter, and a fortiori for the son, so the Mishnah mentions the daughter to teach this.

items.text: Three interpretations of the Mishnah's phrase 'he is not obligated for his daughter's sustenance'
items.text_en: Three interpretations of the Mishnah's phrase 'he is not obligated for his daughter's sustenance'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers three alternative explanations of the Mishnah's statement that a father is not obligated for his daughter's sustenance. The first suggests that even for a daughter there is no obligation, but there is a mitzvah; the second attributes the view to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds there is no obligation even for a son, but a mitzvah; the third attributes it to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds there is neither obligation nor mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers the first interpretation: the Mishnah means that even for a daughter there is no obligation (חובה), but there is a mitzvah (מצוה).

The Gemara offers the second interpretation: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that there is no obligation even for a son, only a mitzvah, and the mention of a daughter teaches that even for her there is no obligation.

sub.text: Gemara's third answer (Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka)
sub.text_en: Gemara's third answer (Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers the third interpretation: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who holds that there is neither obligation nor mitzvah for a daughter, and the same applies to a son.

items.text: The Usha enactment: a person must support his minor children
items.text_en: The Usha enactment: a person must support his minor children
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a quotes Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina that in Usha they enacted that a person must support his minor sons and daughters. The Gemara then raises the question of whether this is binding law.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a citing Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a citing Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a reports in the name of Resh Lakish citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina that in Usha they enacted that a person must support his minor sons and daughters.
The Gemara raises a question: is the halacha (binding law) in accordance with this enactment or not?
The Gemara brings a supporting anecdote: when people came before Rav Yehuda, he rebuked them, implying that a father must support his children.

items.text: Rav Chisda's response: coercion through public shame
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's response: coercion through public shame
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda, when people came before him, would instruct them to publicly shame the father by saying that even a raven wants its children, but this man does not. The Gemara questions the raven's desire for its children, citing a verse, and resolves the contradiction between white and black ravens.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda instructs those who come before him to coerce the father by publicly shaming him, saying that even a raven wants its children but this man does not.
The Gemara objects: does a raven really desire its children, citing the verse that God provides for the raven's young who cry out, implying they are abandoned?
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the verse refers to white ravens which abandon their young, while Rav Chisda spoke of black ravens which care for their offspring.

items.text: Rava's approach: coercion only when the father is not well-off
items.text_en: Rava's approach: coercion only when the father is not well-off
items.desc_en: Rava would ask the father if he is content with his children receiving charity. The Gemara clarifies that coercion applies only when the father is not wealthy; if he is wealthy, we force him against his will, as Rava did to Rav Nathan bar Ami, extracting four hundred zuz for charity.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks the father if he is content with his children receiving charity.

The Gemara clarifies that coercion applies only when the father is not well-off; if he is wealthy, we force him against his will, as Rava did to Rav Nathan bar Ami, extracting four hundred zuz for charity.

items.text: The Usha enactment: one who writes all property to his sons, he and his wife are supported from it
items.text_en: The Usha enactment: one who writes all property to his sons, he and his wife are supported from it
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a quotes Resh Lakish about another Usha enactment: if a man writes all his property to his sons, he and his wife are supported from those assets. Rabbi Zeira objects that even a widow is supported from the estate, so surely he and his wife should be. The Gemara cites a case of a man who died leaving a widow and daughter, and the widow is supported even after the daughter marries or dies. The Gemara explains that the enactment is necessary to teach that even though the father himself toiled for both himself and his wife, he still retains support.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a quotes Resh Lakish that in Usha they enacted: one who writes all his property to his sons, he and his wife are supported from those assets.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects: they already said a greater case — a widow is supported from the estate; surely he and his wife should be supported without needing a special enactment.
Ravin's letter cites a case: if a man died leaving a widow and daughter, the widow is supported from the estate even after the daughter marries.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben achoto shel Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben achoto shel Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
