sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben achoto shel Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that even if the daughter dies, the widow continues to be supported from the estate.

The Gemara resolves the objection: the enactment is necessary because one might think that since the father toiled for both himself and his wife, he would not retain support, so the enactment teaches that he does.

items.text: Inquiry into the law of the enactment and a supporting story
items.text_en: Inquiry into the law of the enactment and a supporting story
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the law follows this enactment. It brings a story where Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan were standing, and a man came and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot. Rabbi Chanina asked what this was about, and Rabbi Yonatan explained that the man was one who wrote his property to his sons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the halacha follows the enactment that a person supports his minor children.

The Gemara brings a story where Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yonatan were standing, and a man kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot; Rabbi Yonatan explained that the man was one who wrote his property to his sons, implying the enactment is followed.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's enactment
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that the court made the daughters into a trust for the sons, asking whether this was a proper legal decision or an extraordinary measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the court's action of making the daughters a trust for the sons was a proper legal decision (דינא) or an extraordinary measure, since if it was law, they would need to do it.

items.text: The enactment of Usha on charitable giving
items.text_en: The enactment of Usha on charitable giving
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila states that in Usha they enacted that one should not spend more than one-fifth of his assets on charity, citing a supporting baraita and a verse from Jacob's vow. Rav Ashi explains the verse to equate the second tithe with the first.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila states that in Usha they enacted that one should not spend more than one-fifth of his assets on charity.
A baraita supports the enactment, recounting a story where Rabbi Yeshevav (or Rabbi Akiva) prevented someone from spending more than one-fifth.

sub.text: Rav Nachman / Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman / Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman (or Rav Acha bar Yaakov) cites a verse from Jacob's vow as a biblical source for the one-fifth limit.
The Gemara objects that the second tithe (one-tenth of the remainder) is not equivalent to the first tithe (one-tenth of the whole).
Rav Ashi resolves the objection by interpreting the verse 'אֲעַשְּׂרֶנּוּ' to mean that the second tithe is treated like the first, equating them.

items.text: Diminishing traditions
items.text_en: Diminishing traditions
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi notes that these traditions are diminishing, with a mnemonic: 'small ones wrote and spent.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi notes that these traditions are diminishing, with the mnemonic 'small ones wrote and squandered'.

items.text: The age for teaching a child and supporting him
items.text_en: The age for teaching a child and supporting him
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak states that in Usha they enacted that a father should be lenient with his son until age twelve, after which he must support him. The Gemara reconciles this with Rav's instruction to accept a student at age six, distinguishing between teaching Scripture and Mishnah. Abaye and Rav Katina add details about the ages for learning and the danger of scorpion stings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak states that in Usha they enacted that a father should be lenient with his son until age twelve, and thereafter must support him.
The Gemara objects: Rav instructed Rav Shmuel bar Shilat to accept a student at age six and feed him like an ox, contradicting the leniency until twelve.
The Gemara answers: one feeds him like an ox from age six, but does not support him fully until after twelve.
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves: the leniency until twelve applies to Mishnah study, while age six applies to Scripture study.
Abaye cites his mother's tradition: age six for Scripture, ten for Mishnah, thirteen for a full-day fast, and twelve for girls.
Abaye digresses with his mother's folk remedies for a six-year-old stung by a scorpion and a one-year-old stung by a wasp.
Rav Katina warns against sending a child to school before age six, with two versions of the warning and a resolution distinguishing weak from strong children.

items.text: The enactment of Usha on a wife selling melog property
items.text_en: The enactment of Usha on a wife selling melog property
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that in Usha they enacted that if a wife sold her melog property during her husband's lifetime and then died, the husband can reclaim it from the buyers. Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef found Rabbi Avahu in the crowd of Usha and learned this tradition from him forty times.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina states that in Usha they enacted that if a wife sold her melog property during her husband's lifetime and then died, the husband may reclaim it from the buyers.

sub.text: Story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef and Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: A story: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef found Rabbi Avahu in the crowd of Usha, asked who was the master of the Usha tradition, learned it from Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina forty times, and it was as clear as if placed in his pocket.

items.text: Aggadic interpretations of verses on charity and grandchildren
items.text_en: Aggadic interpretations of verses on charity and grandchildren
items.desc_en: The rabbis in Yavneh and Rabbi Eliezer interpret 'doing charity at all times' as supporting one's minor children, while Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it refers to raising orphans. Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate whether 'wealth and riches in his house' refers to one who learns and teaches Torah or one who writes and lends scrolls. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani interpret 'seeing children's children' as bringing peace to Israel or to its judges.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'אַשְׁרֵי שׁוֹמְרֵי מִשְׁפָּט עוֹשֵׂה צְדָקָה בְכׇל עֵת' (Happy are those who keep justice, who do charity at all times) and questions how charity can be done at all times.
The Rabbis of Yavneh (or Rabbi Eliezer) interpret 'doing charity at all times' as referring to one who supports his minor sons and daughters.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani interprets the verse as referring to one who raises an orphan boy or girl in his home and marries them off.
The Gemara cites the verse 'הוֹן וָעוֹשֶׁר בְּבֵיתוֹ וְצִדְקָתוֹ עוֹמֶדֶת לָעַד' (Wealth and riches are in his house, and his charity endures forever).
Rav Huna (one of the two) says the verse refers to one who learns Torah and teaches it.
Rav Chisda (the other) says the verse refers to one who writes Torah, Prophets, and Writings and lends them to others.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וּרְאֵה בָנִים לְבָנֶיךָ שָׁלוֹם עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל' (And see your children's children, peace upon Israel).
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that when one sees children's children, there is peace upon Israel because it avoids the need for חליצה (levirate release) and יבום (levirate marriage).
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that when one sees children's children, there is peace upon the judges of Israel because it avoids them being insulted.
The Gemara notes that this is the midrash that Rabbi Elazar taught before the Sages, and the rest of the passage is abbreviated.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's statement and Rav Yosef's clarification
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's statement and Rav Yosef's clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that just as sons inherit only from land, so too daughters are sustained only from land. The world objects that this would mean if a man leaves no land, his sons inherit nothing. Rav Yosef suggests Rav Hamnuna might be referring to the ketubah of sons (כתובת בנין דכרין), and Rav Hamnuna confirms that Rav Yosef understands his intent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that just as sons inherit only from land, so too daughters are sustained only from land.
The world objects that if a man leaves no land, his sons would inherit nothing.
Rav Yosef suggests that Rav Hamnuna might be referring to the ketubah of sons (כתובת בנין דכרין).
Rav Hamnuna confirms that Rav Yosef understands his intent.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef's report and the doubt about its meaning
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef's report and the doubt about its meaning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef reports that Rav provided sustenance from wheat of the upper chamber. The Gemara raises a doubt: was this for regular sustenance (פרנסה), in which case the 'upper chamber' refers to the father's elevated status, consistent with Shmuel's ruling that for sustenance we assess based on the father's standing? Or was it for actual food (מזונות), in which case the 'upper chamber' refers to the good things said in the upper chamber, where Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef instituted that daughters are sustained from movables.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef reports that Rav provided sustenance from wheat of the upper chamber.

The Gemara raises a doubt: was this for regular sustenance (פרנסה), in which case 'upper chamber' refers to the father's elevated status, consistent with Shmuel's ruling that for sustenance we assess based on the father's standing?
Or was it for actual food (מזונות), in which case 'upper chamber' refers to the good things said in the upper chamber.

sub.text: Citation of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's enactment
sub.text_en: Citation of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's enactment
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's statement that in the upper chamber they instituted that daughters are sustained from movables.

items.text: Attempt to resolve from the case of Rabbi Bannai's orphans
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve from the case of Rabbi Bannai's orphans
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where Rabbi Bannai held movables of orphans and came before Shmuel, who told him to provide sustenance. The Gemara initially thinks this refers to food (מזונות), supporting Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef. But it rejects this: it was for regular sustenance (פרנסה), consistent with Shmuel's own view that for sustenance we assess based on the father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where Rabbi Bannai held movables of orphans and Shmuel told him to provide sustenance (זון), attempting to prove that Shmuel supports sustenance from movables.
The Gemara infers that Shmuel's instruction was for food (מזונות), aligning with Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's view that daughters are sustained from movables.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the case involved regular sustenance (פרנסה), not food (מזונות), consistent with Shmuel's own view that for sustenance we assess based on the father.

items.text: Precedents in Nehardea and Pumpedita
items.text_en: Precedents in Nehardea and Pumpedita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites that an incident occurred in Nehardea where the judges of Nehardea ruled accordingly, and in Pumpedita where Rav Chana bar Bizna collected sustenance from movables. Rav Nachman threatened to seize their property if they did not reverse their ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites that an incident occurred in Nehardea where the local judges ruled that daughters may collect sustenance from movables.
The Gemara cites that in Pumpedita, Rav Chana bar Bizna collected sustenance for daughters from movables.
Rav Nachman threatened to seize the judges' property if they did not reverse their ruling allowing collection from movables.

items.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's attempt and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's attempt and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi considered providing sustenance from movables, but Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi objected: a matter that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish did not act upon, you would act upon?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi considered providing sustenance for daughters from movable property.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi objected: a matter that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish did not act upon, you would act upon?

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's intention and Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's warning
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's intention and Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's warning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar considered providing sustenance from movables. Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim warned him that he was acting out of mercy, not strict law, and that students might see and establish the halakha for generations.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that Rabbi Elazar intended to provide sustenance from movables.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim warns Rabbi Elazar that he is acting out of mercy, not strict law.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim expresses concern that students might see and establish the halakha for generations.

items.text: Case before Rav Yosef and Abaye's question
items.text_en: Case before Rav Yosef and Abaye's question
items.desc_en: A man came before Rav Yosef, who ordered to give the woman from dates on a palm branch. Abaye asked: if it were a creditor, would the Master give in such a manner? Rav Yosef replied that he was referring to dates fit for the branch (i.e., already harvested).

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rav Yosef, who ordered to give the woman from dates on a palm branch.
Abaye asked Rav Yosef: if it were a creditor, would the Master give in such a manner (i.e., from unharvested dates)?
Rav Yosef replied that he was referring to dates already fit for the branch (i.e., harvested and suitable for use).

items.text: Rava's ruling on supporting an orphan from a date palm
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on supporting an orphan from a date palm
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier principle that standing crops are considered as already cut, and then recounts a case where Rava ruled to support an orphan from a date palm for the sake of an orphan girl. The rabbis object, citing Rava's own rule that sustenance is collected only from land, not movables. Rava responds that if the orphan could hire a maidservant from the palm's value, certainly here where there are two benefits (the palm and the girl) it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier principle, noting that everything standing to be cut is considered as already cut, and clarifies that the discussion refers to a case where the date palm itself is needed.
The Gemara recounts a case where an orphan boy and orphan girl came before Rava, and Rava ruled to support the orphan boy from the date palm for the sake of the orphan girl.
The rabbis object to Rava, citing his own rule that sustenance is collected only from land (מקרקעי) and not from movables (מטלטלי), whether for maintenance, ketubah, or support.
Rava responds that if the orphan could hire a maidservant from the palm's value, certainly here where there are two benefits (the palm and the orphan girl) it is permitted.

items.text: Baraita on collecting for daughters from different property types and the halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Baraita on collecting for daughters from different property types and the halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar regarding collecting for daughters' sustenance from various heirs using different types of property. Rabbi allows collection from both land and movables, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes between them. The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing Rava's ruling that sustenance, ketubah, and support are collected only from land, not movables.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi (Tanna Kamma) allows collecting for daughters' sustenance from both land and movables, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes between them, allowing collection from land for all but restricting movables.

The Gemara rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, citing Rava's principle that collection for sustenance, ketubah, and support is only from land (מקרקעי) and not from movables (מטלטלי).

items.text: Mishnah: Ketubah stipulations and obligations for ransom and medical care
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ketubah stipulations and obligations for ransom and medical care
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even if a husband did not write a ketubah, the wife collects the standard amounts due to the court's stipulation. If he wrote a field worth a maneh instead of two hundred zuz but did not include the standard lien clause, he is still liable. Similarly, if he did not write the clause about ransoming her if captured, he is liable. If she is captured, he must ransom her; he cannot simply give her a get and ketubah and let her ransom herself. If she becomes ill, he must provide medical care, but if he gives her a get and ketubah, he is permitted to let her pay for her own care.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if a husband did not write a ketubah, the wife collects the standard amounts due to the court's stipulation, and if he wrote a field worth a maneh instead of two hundred zuz without a lien clause, he is still liable.
The Mishnah continues that if the husband did not write the clause about ransoming her if captured, he is still liable due to the court's stipulation.

The Mishnah concludes that if the wife is captured, the husband must ransom her and cannot give her a get and ketubah to ransom herself, but if she becomes ill, he must provide medical care, though he may give her a get and ketubah and let her pay for her own care.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author and the dispute about the lien clause
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author and the dispute about the lien clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's first clause as following Rabbi Meir, who holds that reducing the ketubah amount renders the marriage a licentious act. It then questions the second clause, which implies that the lien clause is a court stipulation, suggesting it follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says that the lien is a scribal error. The Gemara notes that if it were Rabbi Meir, he would not require the clause since the lien is not a scribal error. The discussion is cut off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's first clause as following Rabbi Meir, who holds that reducing the ketubah amount renders the marriage a licentious act.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Yehuda, he would allow reducing the ketubah amount by writing a receipt, contradicting the Mishnah's implication.
The Gemara turns to the second clause of the Mishnah, which states that even without writing the lien clause, the husband is liable because it is a court stipulation.
The Gemara answers that the second clause follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the lien clause is a scribal error and thus the court stipulation applies.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi Meir, he would not require the lien clause since the lien is not a scribal error, citing a baraita about finding debt documents.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Return of documents without lien
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Return of documents without lien
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a document has a property lien, it is not returned; if it lacks a lien, Rabbi Meir says it is returned, but the Sages say it is not returned in either case because the court can collect from the debtor's property.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a document includes a property guarantee, it is not returned to the lender.
Rabbi Meir says that if the document lacks a property guarantee, it is returned.
The Sages say that in both cases the document is not returned, because the court collects from the debtor's property.

items.text: Gemara's question: Contradiction between Mishnah and Baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Contradiction between Mishnah and Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah's first clause follows Rabbi Meir and the latter clause follows Rabbi Judah. It then cites a Baraita listing five items that are collected from encumbered property, including a ketubah without a lien, which seems to contradict Rabbi Meir's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah's first clause follows Rabbi Meir and the latter clause follows Rabbi Judah, and questions whether Rabbi Meir distinguishes between a marriage contract and other documents.
The Gemara cites a Baraita listing five items collected from free assets, including a marriage contract without a lien, to challenge the proposed distinction.

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir, who holds that omission of a property guarantee is not a scribal error, is the authority for the Baraita, proving he does not distinguish between a marriage contract and other documents.

items.text: Two answers resolving the contradiction
items.text_en: Two answers resolving the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two resolutions: either the Baraita follows Rabbi Judah, who distinguishes between a ketubah where the wife wrote 'I accepted' and one where she did not; or it follows Rabbi Meir, who interprets 'liable' in the Baraita as meaning from encumbered property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces two alternative resolutions, one attributing the Baraita to רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) and one to רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda).
The first resolution: the Baraita follows רבי יהודה, and the distinction is that there she wrote him 'הִתְקַבַּלְתִּי' (I have received it) whereas here she did not.
The second resolution: the Baraita follows רבי מאיר, and 'חייב' (liable) in the Baraita means only from מְחוֹרָרִין (free, unencumbered property).

items.text: Avuh deShmuel's ruling on a raped woman
items.text_en: Avuh deShmuel's ruling on a raped woman
items.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel rules that an Israelite woman who was raped is forbidden to her husband due to concern that the rape began under duress but ended willingly. Rav challenges him with a Mishnah about a captive woman, and Avuh deShmuel is silent. Rav then cites a verse about placing a hand over the mouth.

sub.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel rules that an Israelite woman who was raped is forbidden to her husband due to concern that the rape began under duress but ended willingly.
Rav challenges Avuh deShmuel by citing a Mishnah that permits a captive woman to her husband, and Avuh deShmuel is silent.
Rav cites the verse 'שָׂרִים עָצְרוּ בְמִלִּים' (Job 29:9) about Avuh deShmuel's silence, and explains that the leniency applies only to a captive woman, not a raped one.

items.text: Rava's lenient view on rape that ends willingly
items.text_en: Rava's lenient view on rape that ends willingly
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Avuh deShmuel would find a case of permitted rape, answering only when witnesses testify she screamed throughout. This disagrees with Rava, who rules that if the act began under duress and ended willingly, even if she says 'leave him,' she is permitted because her desire overcame her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Avuh deShmuel would find a case of permitted rape, answering only when witnesses testify she screamed throughout.
Rava disagrees, ruling that if the act began under duress and ended willingly, even if she says 'leave him,' she is permitted because her desire overcame her.

items.text: Supporting Baraitot and Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.text_en: Supporting Baraitot and Rabbi Yishmael's statement
items.desc_en: Two Baraitot support Rava: one says if she was not seized she is forbidden, but if seized she is permitted, and another adds a case where even if seized she is forbidden (a priest's wife). Rabbi Yishmael adds a case where even if not seized she is permitted: a woman with mistaken kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava: if she was not seized she is forbidden, but if seized she is permitted, and another case where even if not seized she is permitted — one whose beginning was coercion and end was consent.
Another baraita adds a case where even if seized she is forbidden: a priest's wife.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael's statement via Rav Yehuda and Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's statement via Rav Yehuda and Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael adds a case where even if not seized she is permitted: a woman with mistaken kiddushin (קידושי טעות), who may refuse even if her child is on her shoulder.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on women captured by bandits and distinctions among captors
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on women captured by bandits and distinctions among captors
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that women captured by bandits are permitted to their husbands, despite bringing them food and arrows, because they act out of fear. The Rabbis distinguish: if they voluntarily stay, they are forbidden. A Baraita distinguishes between royal captives (treated as captives) and bandit captives (not), with further distinctions between different kingdoms and bandits.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that women captured by bandits are permitted to their husbands.
The Rabbis object that the women bring food to the bandits, but Rav Yehuda explains it is out of fear.
The Rabbis further object that the women send arrows to the bandits, but Rav Yehuda again explains it is out of fear.
Rav Yehuda distinguishes: if the women voluntarily stay with the bandits, they are forbidden.
A baraita distinguishes between royal captives (treated as captives) and bandit captives (not).
The Gemara objects that another baraita states the opposite.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the baraitot regarding kingdoms: one refers to the kingdom of Achashverosh, the other to the kingdom of Ben Netzar.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding bandits: one refers to Ben Netzar (considered a king relative to ordinary bandits), the other to ordinary bandits.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on redeeming a widow of a High Priest
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on redeeming a widow of a High Priest
items.desc_en: Abaye states that a widow of a High Priest must be redeemed, as the verse 'and to a priestess I will return you to your land' applies to her.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that a high priest is obligated to ransom a widow, based on the verse 'and to a priestess I will return you to your land'.

items.text: Rava's principle on ransom obligation
items.text_en: Rava's principle on ransom obligation
items.desc_en: Rava states that a husband is obligated to ransom his wife only if the prohibition of her being captured is caused by the captivity itself, not by another prohibition. This introduces the key distinction for the sugya.

sub.desc_en: The stam states that a husband is not obligated to ransom a mamzeret or netinah wife, because the verse 'ואותבינך לי לאינתו' does not apply to her.
Rava articulates the principle: if the prohibition of captivity itself causes her capture, he must ransom her; if another prohibition causes it, he is not obligated.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about a husband who vowed and his wife was captured
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about a husband who vowed and his wife was captured
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding a husband who vowed (prohibited his wife from benefit) and she was subsequently captured. Rabbi Eliezer says he must ransom her and give her ketubah; Rabbi Yehoshua says he gives her ketubah but does not ransom her. Rabbi Nathan asks Sumchos whether the order matters, and Sumchos says he hasn't heard but it seems the vow preceded the captivity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about a husband who vowed (prohibited his wife from benefit) and she was subsequently captured.
Rabbi Nathan asks Sumchos whether Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling applies when the vow preceded the captivity or when the captivity preceded the vow.
Sumchos says he hasn't heard a tradition but reasons that the vow must have preceded the captivity, because if the captivity came first the husband might be suspected of strategic evasion.

items.text: Initial attempt to align Abaye and Rava with the Tannaim
items.text_en: Initial attempt to align Abaye and Rava with the Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Tannaim are disputing about a wife of a priest who was vowed, and that Abaye follows Rabbi Eliezer (obligated to ransom) while Rava follows Rabbi Yehoshua (not obligated).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Tannaim dispute about a wife of a priest who was vowed, aligning Abaye with Rabbi Eliezer (obligated to ransom) and Rava with Rabbi Yehoshua (not obligated).

items.text: Rejection: The dispute is about a wife who vowed herself
items.text_en: Rejection: The dispute is about a wife who vowed herself
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the alignment, explaining that the case is where the wife vowed and the husband ratified it. Rabbi Eliezer holds the husband is responsible (put his finger between her teeth), while Rabbi Yehoshua holds she is responsible. The Gemara raises difficulties: if she is responsible, why does she get a ketubah? And why would Rabbi Nathan ask about the order if the wife vowed?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous alignment, explaining that the case is where the wife vowed and the husband ratified it.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds the husband is responsible (put his finger between her teeth), while Rabbi Yehoshua holds she is responsible.
The Gemara raises a difficulty: if she is responsible, why does she get a ketubah?
The Gemara raises another difficulty: why would Rabbi Nathan ask about the order if the wife vowed, since the order would be irrelevant?
The Gemara concludes the objection: if she vowed, what difference does the order make?

items.text: Abaye and Rava each reconcile the Tannaitic dispute with their principles
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava each reconcile the Tannaitic dispute with their principles
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the case is indeed where the husband vowed. Abaye reconciles: all agree that a widow to a High Priest and a mamzeret/netinah to an Israelite are clear cases; the dispute is about a wife of a priest who was vowed, which is like a widow to a High Priest (obligated). Rava reconciles: all agree that a widow to a High Priest and a mamzeret/netinah are not obligated; the dispute is about a vowed wife, whether of a priest or Israelite. Both agree the dispute hinges on whether we follow the initial state (Rabbi Eliezer) or the final state (Rabbi Yehoshua).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the case is indeed where the husband vowed.
Abaye reconciles: all agree that a widow to a High Priest is obligated, a mamzeret/netinah to an Israelite is not, and a vowed wife of a priest is like a widow to a High Priest (obligated).
Abaye explains that the dispute is about a vowed wife of an Israelite, where Rabbi Eliezer follows the initial state and Rabbi Yehoshua follows the final state.
Rava reconciles: all agree that a widow to a High Priest and a mamzeret/netinah are not obligated; the dispute is about a vowed wife, whether of a priest or an Israelite.
Rava concludes that both agree the dispute hinges on whether we follow the initial state (Rabbi Eliezer) or the final state (Rabbi Yehoshua).

items.text: Baraita on ransom after husband's death and Levi's ruling
items.text_en: Baraita on ransom after husband's death and Levi's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if the wife was captured during her husband's lifetime and he recognized her, the heirs must ransom her; if not, they are exempt. Levi wanted to rule accordingly, but Rav said the halakha follows another baraita: if captured after the husband's death, or even during his lifetime but he died, the orphans are not obligated, because the verse 'and to take you as a wife' does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches: if a wife was captured during her husband's lifetime and he recognized her, the heirs must ransom her; if not, they are exempt.

Levi wanted to rule according to the first baraita, but Rav told him that the halakha follows a different baraita: the orphans are never obligated to ransom her, because the clause 'and I will restore you to me as a wife' does not apply.

items.text: Baraita on multiple ransom demands
items.text_en: Baraita on multiple ransom demands
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if the wife is captured and they demand up to ten times her value, the first time he must ransom her; thereafter, he may choose. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers a different opinion (cut off).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states a baraita: if a wife is captured and the ransom is up to ten times her value, the first time he must ransom her; thereafter, he may choose.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel begins to offer a different opinion, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Contradiction in redeeming a captive wife
items.text_en: Contradiction in redeeming a captive wife
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that captives are not redeemed for more than their value, but a wife may be redeemed up to her ketubah. A baraita is cited that limits the husband's obligation to redeem her to the first time, with Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel adding that redemption is only required if the ransom equals the ketubah. This creates a contradiction with the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that captives are not redeemed for more than their value, but a wife may be redeemed even if her ransom exceeds her ketubah.

The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that limits the husband's obligation to redeem his wife to the first time, with Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel adding that redemption is only required if the ransom equals the ketubah.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel holds two leniencies: he allows redemption up to the ketubah and also allows the husband to choose not to redeem after the first time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel holds two leniencies.

items.text: Medical expenses for a widow
items.text_en: Medical expenses for a widow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a husband must heal his wife. A baraita discusses a widow's medical expenses: some say they are like sustenance, while Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between fixed-cost and variable-cost treatments. Rabbi Yochanan rules that bloodletting in Eretz Yisrael is considered a variable-cost treatment, and he initially advised relatives to pay a doctor a lump sum, later reconsidering due to his status.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband is obligated to heal his wife if she falls ill.
The baraita rules that a widow's medical expenses are treated like her sustenance, paid from the orphans' estate.
Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between fixed-cost treatments (paid from her ketubah) and variable-cost treatments (treated like sustenance).
Rabbi Yochanan rules that bloodletting in Eretz Yisrael is considered a variable-cost treatment (אין לה קצבה).
Rabbi Yochanan's relatives had a mother-in-law needing daily medical care, and he advised them to pay the doctor a lump sum.
Rabbi Yochanan initially thought he was acting like a judge's assessor, but later reconsidered because he is a distinguished person (אדם חשוב שאני).

items.text: Mishnah: Clauses of the ketubah for sons and daughters
items.text_en: Mishnah: Clauses of the ketubah for sons and daughters
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the standard clauses of the ketubah: that sons inherit the ketubah, that daughters are supported from the estate until marriage, and that the widow lives in the husband's house and is supported. It notes the different customs of Jerusalem, Galilee, and Judea regarding the widow's residence.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband did not write the clause about sons inheriting the ketubah, he is still obligated because it is a תנאי בית דין (court-imposed condition).

The Mishnah states that if a husband did not write the clause about daughters being supported from the estate until marriage, he is still obligated because it is a תנאי בית דין (court-imposed condition).

items.text: Reason for the enactment of the sons' clause
items.text_en: Reason for the enactment of the sons' clause
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the enactment of the sons' clause was to encourage a man to give his daughter a dowry like his son. The Gemara questions why rabbis would override Torah law, and answers that it is based on the verse about providing for daughters. Abaye and Rava set the limit at one-tenth of the estate.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the enactment of the sons' clause (כתובת בנין דכרין) was instituted so that a man would be motivated to give his daughter a dowry like his son.
The Gemara questions how the rabbis could override Torah law, which grants inheritance only to sons, by enacting that daughters inherit.

The Gemara answers that this too is based on Torah, citing the verse 'Take wives and bear sons and daughters, and give your daughters to husbands' (Jeremiah 29:6), which implies an obligation to provide for daughters.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution and Abaye and Rava's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution and Abaye and Rava's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the verse teaches to clothe, cover, and give something to the daughter so that men will marry her, and Abaye and Rava set the limit at one-tenth of the estate.

items.text: Scope and limitations of the enactment
items.text_en: Scope and limitations of the enactment
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether the enactment applies only to the father or also to the husband, and whether a daughter inherits among sons or among daughters. It concludes that the rabbis treated it like inheritance (so a daughter does not inherit among sons) and like a ketubah (so she collects from movable property and from liened property, but only if there is a surplus of a dinar).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the enactment should apply only to the father's inheritance (so the daughter inherits from the father) but not to the husband's inheritance (so the daughter does not inherit from the husband).
The Gemara answers that if the enactment applied only to the father, the father would refrain from writing the clause, undermining the purpose of the enactment.
The Gemara proposes an alternative: let the husband write the clause only where the father wrote it, but not where the father did not write it.
The Gemara rejects this proposal, stating that the rabbis did not differentiate between cases.
The Gemara asks whether a daughter should inherit among sons as well.
The Gemara answers that the rabbis treated the enactment like inheritance, so a daughter does not inherit among sons.
The Gemara asks whether a daughter should inherit among daughters.
The Gemara rejects this, stating that the rabbis did not differentiate between cases.
The Gemara asks whether the daughter should collect from movable property.
The Gemara answers that the rabbis treated the enactment like a כתובה (ketubah), so she collects from movable property.
The Gemara asks whether she should collect from liened property.
The Gemara answers that the mishna uses the term 'יִרְתוּן' (they shall inherit), implying inheritance law, so she does not collect from liened property.
The Gemara asks whether the daughter should collect even when there is no surplus of a dinar.
The Gemara answers that where it would uproot Torah inheritance law, the rabbis did not institute the enactment, so she collects only if there is a surplus of a dinar.

items.text: Anecdote: Rav Papa and Yehudah bar Marimar
items.text_en: Anecdote: Rav Papa and Yehudah bar Marimar
items.desc_en: Rav Papa went to write a ketubah for his son's marriage, and Yehudah bar Marimar came to meet him. When Rav Papa tried to leave, Yehudah bar Marimar invited him to enter with him, implying a discussion about the ketubah clauses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa went to write a ketubah for his son's marriage in the academy of Abba Sura.
Yehudah bar Marimar heard and came out to meet Rav Papa.
When they reached the entrance, Rav Papa began to take his leave from Yehudah bar Marimar.
Yehudah bar Marimar said to him: Let the master enter with me.

items.text: Story of Rav Yosef and the inheritance transfer
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yosef and the inheritance transfer
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef is pressured to transfer his property to his son-in-law, but he resists, citing Shmuel's warning against transferring inheritances. He eventually writes all his property to his son-in-law, but the son-in-law refuses to accept it, and Rav Yosef declines to retract the gift.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's question to his son-in-law
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's question to his son-in-law
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks his son-in-law why he is pressuring him, citing Shmuel's warning against transferring inheritances even from a bad son to a good son, and certainly not from a son to a daughter.
The son-in-law argues that this is a rabbinic enactment (תקנתא דרבנן) and that Rav Yosef's own merit is in the transfer.
Rav Yosef is pressured and writes all his property to his son-in-law, but the son-in-law later complains that Rav Yosef left nothing for himself.
The son-in-law refuses the gift, and Rav Yosef declines to retract it, saying he will not make himself a retractor.

items.text: Question about a woman who sells her ketubah to her husband
items.text_en: Question about a woman who sells her ketubah to her husband
items.desc_en: Rav Yeimar Sava asks Rav Nachman whether a woman who sells her ketubah to her husband retains the right to ketubat banin dikhran. Rava interjects, asking whether the same question applies to a woman who forgives her ketubah.

sub.text: Rav Yeimar Sava's question to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yeimar Sava's question to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yeimar Sava asks Rav Nachman whether a woman who sells her ketubah to her husband retains the right to ketubat banin dikhran (the sons' inheritance clause).
Rava interjects, asking whether the same question applies to a woman who forgives (forgoes) her ketubah.

sub.text: Rav Yeimar Sava's response to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Yeimar Sava's response to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Yeimar Sava responds that his question about a seller is more pressing, since one might argue she was pressured by money, whereas a forgiver clearly acts voluntarily.

items.text: Rava's clear ruling on seller vs. forgiver
items.text_en: Rava's clear ruling on seller vs. forgiver
items.desc_en: Rava states that it is obvious: a woman who sells her ketubah to others retains ketubat banin dikhran because the money pressured her, but one who forgives her ketubah to her husband loses it because she willingly relinquished it.

sub.desc_en: Rava states his clear ruling: a woman who sells her ketubah to others retains the right of ketubat banin dikhran because the money pressured her, but one who forgives her ketubah to her husband loses it because she willingly relinquished it.

items.text: Rava's unresolved question and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's unresolved question and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava questions whether a woman who sells her ketubah to her husband is like a seller to others or like a forgiver to her husband. He later resolves it: she is like a seller to others.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises an unresolved question: whether a woman who sells her ketubah to her husband is treated like a seller to others or like a forgiver to her husband.
Rava resolves his own question: a woman who sells her ketubah to her husband is like a seller to others, not like a forgiver.

items.text: Objection from Rav Idi bar Avin and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rav Idi bar Avin and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin raises an objection from a mishnah about a woman who dies and whose heirs inherit her ketubah, which is interpreted as ketubat banin dikhran. The Gemara explains that there the Sages penalized her, so the rule differs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin raises an objection from a mishnah about a woman who dies and whose heirs inherit her ketubah, questioning why the rule of 'יצר אנסא' (desire compelled her) does not apply.
Rav Pappa explains that the mishnah refers to 'כתובת בנין דכרין' (the sons' inheritance of the ketubah) and questions why the same reasoning of compulsion does not apply here.
The Gemara resolves that in that case, the Sages imposed a penalty (קנס) on the woman, so the rule is different and the objection is deflected.

items.text: Rav Chisda's reaction to a ruling about a forgiver's sustenance
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's reaction to a ruling about a forgiver's sustenance
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Chanina reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a woman who forgives her ketubah to her husband loses her right to sustenance. Rav Chisda objects, citing a verse about returning evil for good.

sub.text: Ravin bar Chanina's statement in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Chanina's statement in the name of Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Chanina reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that a woman who forgives her ketubah to her husband loses her right to מזונות (sustenance), and Rav Chisda reacts with a verse about returning evil for good.
Rav Chisda objects, saying that were it not for the authority of Rabbi Elazar, he would cite the verse 'One who returns evil for good—evil shall not depart from his house' against the ruling.

items.text: Discussion of an arusah who dies and her ketubah
items.text_en: Discussion of an arusah who dies and her ketubah
items.desc_en: A case arises of a man whose arusah died, and the Sages tell him to bury her or pay her ketubah. Rav Chiya cites a baraita that an arusah who dies has no ketubah. Rav Hoshaya explains the reason: the condition in the ketubah is not met. Reish Lakish later rules similarly.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rav Nachman, Ulla, Avimi bar Rav Papi, and Rav Chiya bar Ami are sitting together when a man whose arusah died approaches, and the Sages tell him to bury her or pay her ketubah.
Rav Chiya bar Ami cites a baraita stating that an arusah does not mourn or become impure for each other, and if he dies she collects her ketubah, implying that if she dies she has no ketubah.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that only if the husband dies does she collect her ketubah, but if she dies she has no ketubah.
Rav Hoshaya explains the reason: the condition in the ketubah that she will collect when she marries another is not fulfilled, so she has no claim.
When Ravin arrived, he reported that Reish Lakish also rules that an arusah who dies has no ketubah.
Abaye instructs them to go and tell the man this ruling.

items.text: Opening statement: Rav Hoshaya's interpretation in Babylonia
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rav Hoshaya's interpretation in Babylonia
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a statement about a woman's sustenance being taken and thrown to the vegetables, which Rav Hoshaya already interpreted in Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a folk saying about a woman's sustenance being thrown to the vegetables, noting that Rav Hoshaya already interpreted this statement in Babylonia.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Levi on the condition for daughters' sustenance
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Levi on the condition for daughters' sustenance
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav teaches that daughters are sustained 'until they are taken by husbands,' while Levi teaches 'until they reach puberty.' The Gemara clarifies that both agree on cases of puberty without marriage or marriage without puberty; the dispute is about a betrothed woman who has not yet reached puberty. Levi's baraita includes both conditions as alternatives.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav teaches that daughters are sustained until they are taken by husbands, while Levi teaches until they reach puberty.
The Gemara questions whether Rav's position applies even after puberty, and whether Levi's applies even after marriage.
The Gemara clarifies that both agree on cases of puberty without marriage or marriage without puberty; the dispute is about a betrothed woman who has not yet reached puberty.
The Gemara cites Levi's baraita which includes both conditions as alternatives, supporting the interpretation that the dispute is about a betrothed minor.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: until betrothal or until puberty
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: until betrothal or until puberty
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: the first Tanna says a daughter is sustained until she is betrothed, while Rabbi Elazar says until she reaches puberty. Rav Yosef teaches a version with the term 'הֲוָיָה', and the Gemara questions whether this refers to betrothal or marriage, leaving it unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: the first Tanna says a daughter is sustained until she is betrothed, while Rabbi Elazar says until she reaches puberty.
Rav Yosef teaches a version of the dispute using the term 'עַד דִּיהֶוְויָין' (until they become).
The Gemara questions whether 'הֲוָיָה' (becoming) refers to betrothal or marriage.
The question remains unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rav Yosef debate whether a betrothed woman has sustenance
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Yosef debate whether a betrothed woman has sustenance
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Yosef whether a betrothed woman has sustenance. Rav Yosef initially says no, because the husband does not want her to be degraded. Rav Chisda counters that since the husband is not yet certain of her, he would not waste money. An alternative version reverses their positions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Yosef whether he has heard from Rav Yehuda whether a betrothed woman has sustenance.
Rav Yosef answers that he has not heard a tradition, but by logic she does not have sustenance because the husband does not want her to be degraded.
Rav Chisda objects that by logic she does have sustenance, because the husband is not certain of her and will not waste money.
An alternative version reverses the positions: Rav Yosef first says she has sustenance, and Rav Chisda objects that she does not.

items.text: Mnemonic sign for the list of cases
items.text_en: Mnemonic sign for the list of cases
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is given for the list of women discussed: a minor who refuses marriage, a yevamah, a second wife, a betrothed woman, and a raped woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic sign listing the cases of women to be discussed: a minor who refuses marriage, a yevamah, a second wife, a betrothed woman, and a raped woman.

items.text: Rav Sheshet rules on a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet)
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet rules on a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet) has sustenance. Rav Sheshet cites a baraita: a widow, divorcee, and shomeret yavam in her father's house have sustenance; Rabbi Yehuda adds that if she is not in her father's house, she does not. The Gemara notes that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda is about the mema'enet: the first Tanna holds she has sustenance, Rabbi Yehuda holds she does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet) has sustenance rights.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita: a widow, divorcee, and shomeret yavam in her father's house have sustenance; Rabbi Yehuda says if she is not in her father's house, she does not.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda concerns the mema'enet: the first Tanna holds she has sustenance, Rabbi Yehuda holds she does not.

items.text: Reish Lakish's question about the daughter of a yevamah
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's question about the daughter of a yevamah
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks whether the daughter of a yevamah (a woman who falls to yibbum) has sustenance. The Gemara considers: since her ketubah is on the first husband's property, she may not have sustenance; or perhaps because if she has none from the first, the Sages instituted it from the second. The question remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks whether the daughter of a yevamah (a woman who falls to yibbum) has sustenance from the estate.
The Gemara raises a consideration: since the master said her ketubah is on the first husband's property, she may have no sustenance.
The Gemara offers the opposite possibility: since if she has none from the first, the Sages instituted sustenance from the second husband.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question about the daughter of a second wife
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question about the daughter of a second wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether the daughter of a woman married to a second husband (a 'second wife') has sustenance.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether the daughter of a second wife (שנייה) has sustenance (מזונות) from the father's estate.

items.text: Rava's question about a daughter who committed adultery
items.text_en: Rava's question about a daughter who committed adultery
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a daughter who committed adultery loses her right to sustenance because she has no ketubah, or whether she retains it since she did not commit the sin herself. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a betrothed daughter has sustenance rights, given she has a ketubah but it was not yet enacted at betrothal, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rava's question about a betrothed daughter
items.text_en: Rava's question about a betrothed daughter
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a betrothed daughter (בת ארוסה) has a right to sustenance, given that her ketubah is not yet established until marriage. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether a betrothed daughter (בת ארוסה) has a right to sustenance, given that her ketubah is not yet established until marriage, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about a raped daughter
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about a raped daughter
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether a raped daughter (בת אנוסה) has sustenance. He distinguishes between Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's view (who grants her a ketubah of a maneh) and the Rabbis' view (who say her fine is absorbed into her ketubah). The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether a raped daughter (בת אנוסה) has sustenance (מזונות) from her father's estate.
The Gemara clarifies that the question does not arise according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who grants her a ketubah of a maneh.
The question is refined: according to the Rabbis, who say her fine is absorbed into her ketubah (יצא כסף קנסה בכתובתה), what is the law?

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the two sides
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the two sides
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two possible rationales: either since she has no ketubah she has no sustenance, or the purpose of the ketubah is to prevent easy divorce, and since he cannot divorce her (as a rapist), she should still receive sustenance.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute about a widow living in her husband's house
items.text_en: Dispute about a widow living in her husband's house
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a widow who says 'You shall dwell in my house' has no right to the house but does have sustenance. Mar bar Rav Ashi argues she has no sustenance either, but the halakha rejects his view.

sub.desc_en: The baraita is cited: a widow who says 'You shall dwell in my house' has no right to the house itself but does have sustenance.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects that the widow has no sustenance either.
The halakha rejects Mar bar Rav Ashi's view, affirming the baraita's position.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a widow who was asked to remarry
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a widow who was asked to remarry
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel: if a widow was asked to remarry and agreed, she loses her sustenance. Rav Anan clarifies that if she says 'because of my husband' she retains sustenance, but if she says 'because of unsuitable men' she loses it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel's ruling: if a widow was asked to remarry and agreed, she loses her sustenance.
The Gemara infers a question: if she was not persuaded, does she retain her sustenance?
Rav Anan clarifies from Shmuel himself: if she says 'because of my husband' she retains sustenance, but if she says 'because of unsuitable men' she loses it.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rav Yosef on a widow's misconduct
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Yosef on a widow's misconduct
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a widow who committed adultery loses sustenance. Rav Yosef adds that even cosmetic adornment (כיחלה ופירכסה) suffices. The Gemara notes a dispute: one who says adultery certainly includes adornment, but one who says adornment might still grant sustenance for adultery due to overwhelming desire.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a widow who committed adultery loses her sustenance.
Rav Yosef adds that even cosmetic adornment (כיחלה ופירכסה) suffices to lose sustenance.
The Gemara notes a dispute: one who says adultery certainly includes adornment, but one who says adornment might still grant sustenance for adultery due to overwhelming desire.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a widow who claims her ketubah in court
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a widow who claims her ketubah in court
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: a widow who claims her ketubah in court loses her sustenance. The Gemara questions this from a baraita that lists selling, mortgaging, or assigning her ketubah as causes for losing sustenance, implying that mere claiming does not. The resolution distinguishes between court and non-court contexts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel's ruling that a widow who claims her ketubah in court loses her sustenance.
The Gemara objects from a baraita that lists selling, mortgaging, or assigning her ketubah as causes for losing sustenance, implying that mere claiming does not.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between court and non-court contexts: the baraita's cases apply in both, while Shmuel's ruling applies only when the claim is made in court.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on local customs
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on local customs
items.desc_en: Rav rules like the people of Yehuda, Shmuel like the people of Galil. The Gemara recounts a case where a woman from Mehoza married a man from Nehardea, and Rav Nachman ruled according to the custom of the husband's place, defined by the reach of a Nehardean kab.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav rules like the people of Yehuda and Shmuel rules like the people of Galil regarding local customs of ketubah payment.
The Gemara reports the established practice: Bavel and its environs follow Rav, while Nehardea and its environs follow Shmuel.
Rav Nachman rules in a case of a woman from Mehoza married to a man from Nehardea that the custom of the husband's place applies, defined by the reach of a Nehardean kab (measure).

items.text: Dispute about assessing a widow's clothing
items.text_en: Dispute about assessing a widow's clothing
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether a widow's clothing is assessed (שמין) for the heirs. Rav Chiyya bar Avin notes the opposite applies to a hired laborer (לקיט). Rav Nachman rules like Rav despite the Mishnah seeming to support Shmuel, because the husband's intent was for her to remain, not to leave.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the dispute: Rav says a widow's clothing is assessed (שמין) for the heirs, while Shmuel says it is not assessed.
Rav Chiyya bar Avin notes that the opposite ruling applies to a hired laborer (לקיט): his clothing is not assessed for the employer, but the widow's is.
Rav Kahana teaches the opposite version: the same rule (assessment) applies to a hired laborer (לקיט) as to a widow.
A mnemonic sign is placed on Rav Kahana's version: 'the orphan and the widow — send and release' (implying the same rule for both).
Rav Nachman rules like Rav, even though the Mishnah appears to support Shmuel, citing the Mishnah about one who consecrates property (where the wife's clothing is exempt).
Rava objects: since the Mishnah supports Shmuel, why does Rav Nachman rule like Rav?
Rav Nachman answers: at first glance the Mishnah runs like Shmuel, but upon deeper analysis the law follows Rav.
The gemara explains Rav's reasoning: the husband granted her the clothing only for her to remain with him, not for her to take and leave.

items.text: Case of the daughter-in-law of Bar Elyashiv
items.text_en: Case of the daughter-in-law of Bar Elyashiv
items.desc_en: A daughter-in-law of Bar Elyashiv claimed her ketubah from orphans. They found it degrading that she came to court, so she went and wore all her garments. Ravina ruled like Rav that a widow's clothing is assessed.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces the case of the daughter-in-law of Bar Elyashiv who claimed her ketubah from orphans.
The narrator describes that the orphans found it degrading that she came to court.
The narrator recounts that she went and wore all her garments.
Ravina rules like Rav that a widow's clothing is assessed.

items.text: Case of a dowry for a daughter
items.text_en: Case of a dowry for a daughter
items.desc_en: A man said 'the dowry for my daughter' and the dowry was lost. Rav Idi bar Avin rules that the loss falls on the orphans (פורנא ליתמי).

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a man said 'the dowry for my daughter' and the dowry was lost.
Rav Idi bar Avin rules that the loss falls on the orphans (פורנא ליתמי).

items.text: Case of wine appreciation for orphans
items.text_en: Case of wine appreciation for orphans
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef comments on a case where a father wrote a ketubah for his daughter with wine worth 400 zuz, and the wine appreciated in value. He rules that the profit goes to the orphans.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that when a father wrote a ketubah for his daughter with wine worth 400 zuz and the wine appreciated, the profit belongs to the orphans.
Rav Yosef rules that the profit from the price increase belongs to the orphans.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about a widow's maintenance
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about a widow's maintenance
items.desc_en: A widow was wasting her maintenance, and Rabbi Yochanan advised setting aside land for her. Reish Lakish disagreed, arguing that this increases her maintenance, and threatened to bring Rabbi Yochanan out from behind them. Rabbi Yochanan conceded that Reish Lakish opposed him.

sub.desc_en: A relative of Rabbi Yochanan had a widow wasting her maintenance, and Rabbi Yochanan advised setting aside land for her.
Reish Lakish objected that setting aside land increases her maintenance, threatened to bring Rabbi Yochanan out from behind them, and Rabbi Yochanan conceded that Reish Lakish opposed him.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that Rabbi Yochanan's statement 'for maintenance' means he increased her maintenance, while 'in maintenance' means he fixed her maintenance. This resolves the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu clarifies the distinction: if Rabbi Yochanan said 'לִמְזוֹנוֹת' (for support), it means he increased her support; if he said 'בִּמְזוֹנוֹת' (in support), it means he fixed her support.
Rabbi Avahu completes his clarification: when Rabbi Yochanan said 'בִּמְזוֹנוֹת' (in maintenance), it means he fixed her maintenance at a set amount, resolving the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah with the phrase 'Hadran alach Na'arah'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara marks the end of the chapter 'Na'arah' with the formulaic 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ' (we return to you).

items.text: Mishnah: Adding to the ketubah and disputes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Adding to the ketubah and disputes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband may add to the basic ketubah amount. If the wife is widowed or divorced, she collects the entire amount. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya distinguishes between marriage and betrothal. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir discuss writing a receipt for part of the ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the basic rule: a husband may add to the ketubah, and the wife collects the entire amount upon widowhood or divorce.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya distinguishes between marriage and betrothal: from marriage she collects the entire added amount, but from betrothal only the basic ketubah, since the addition was conditional on marriage.
Rabbi Yehuda permits writing a receipt for part of the ketubah: the husband writes the full amount, and the wife acknowledges receiving a portion.
Rabbi Meir rules that anyone who reduces the ketubah below the standard amounts renders the marriage a בעילת זנות (licentious intercourse).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's necessity
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to state that a husband may add, as it seems obvious. It answers that one might think the Sages fixed the amounts to avoid embarrassing the poor, so the Mishnah teaches that adding is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the Mishnah states the obvious, and answers that it teaches that the rabbis' fixed amounts were not absolute but to avoid embarrassing the poor.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that the fixed amounts are not an absolute limit, countering a possible assumption that they were set to avoid embarrassing the poor.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yannai's principle about ketubah conditions
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yannai's principle about ketubah conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'wants to add' not 'wants to write', supporting Rabbi Ayvu citing Rabbi Yannai that a condition in the ketubah is like the ketubah itself. Practical differences include a woman who sells, forgives, rebels, impairs, claims, or violates religious law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'wants to add' (רָצָה לְהוֹסִיף) and not 'wants to write' (רָצָה לִכְתּוֹב לָהּ), implying a distinction.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Ayvu in the name of Rabbi Yannai that a condition in the ketubah (תְּנַאי כְּתוּבָּה) is like the ketubah itself (כִּכְתוּבָּה דָּמֵי), supporting the Mishnah's phrasing.

The Gemara lists practical halachic differences that follow from this principle: a woman who sells (מוֹכֶרֶת), forgives (מוֹחֶלֶת), rebels (מוֹרֶדֶת), impairs (פּוֹגֶמֶת), claims (תּוֹבַעַת), or violates religious law (עוֹבֶרֶת עַל דָּת).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: List of cases where a woman collects from the lowest quality land
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: List of cases where a woman collects from the lowest quality land
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several situations where a woman collects her ketubah from the lowest quality land, including for improvement, oath, Sabbatical year, and when a man writes all his property to his sons. It also mentions the clause of 'benin dichrin' (sons' inheritance).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a woman collects her ketubah from the lowest quality land, including for improvement, oath, Sabbatical year, writing all property to sons, and the clause of sons' inheritance.

items.text: Dispute over 'benin dichrin': Pumbedita vs. Meḥasya
items.text_en: Dispute over 'benin dichrin': Pumbedita vs. Meḥasya
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Pumbedita says the daughters do not collect from encumbered property because the clause uses 'yirtun' (they shall inherit), while the people of Meḥasya say they do collect because it uses 'yisbun' (they shall take). The halakha follows Pumbedita that they do not collect from encumbered property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about whether the sons' inheritance clause (כתובת בנין דכרין) is collected from liened property, with Pumbedita saying no because the Mishnah uses 'יִרְתוּן' (they shall inherit).
Bnei Mata Machseya argue that she does collect from liened property because the Mishnah uses 'יִסְּבוּן' (they shall take).
The Gemara rules that she does not collect from liened property, as the Mishnah uses 'יִרְתוּן' (they shall inherit).

items.text: Dispute over movable property: whether an oath is required
items.text_en: Dispute over movable property: whether an oath is required
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses movable property: if the movables are extant, no oath is required. If they are not extant, Pumbedita says no oath, while Meḥasya says an oath is required. The halakha follows Pumbedita that no oath is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that for movable property that still exists, the daughters collect without an oath.
Pumbedita says that even if the property no longer exists, the daughters collect without an oath.
Bnei Mata Machseya say that if the property no longer exists, the daughters must take an oath.
The Gemara rules that the daughters collect without an oath even when the property no longer exists.

items.text: Dispute over designated land: with four boundaries vs. one
items.text_en: Dispute over designated land: with four boundaries vs. one
items.desc_en: If a husband designated land for his wife with four boundaries, no oath is required. If with one boundary, Pumbedita says no oath, Meḥasya says an oath is required. The halakha follows Pumbedita that no oath is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the father designated a specific field with four boundaries for the daughters, they collect without an oath.
Pumbedita says that even if only one boundary was designated, the daughters collect without an oath.
Bnei Mata Machseya say that with only one boundary, the daughters must take an oath.
The Gemara rules that even with one boundary, the daughters collect without an oath.

items.text: Dispute over whether the husband must consult the wife when instructing witnesses
items.text_en: Dispute over whether the husband must consult the wife when instructing witnesses
items.desc_en: If a husband told witnesses 'write, sign, and give' and they acquired from him, he need not consult her. If they did not acquire, Pumbedita says he need not consult, Meḥasya says he must. The halakha follows Meḥasya that he must consult.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the father told witnesses to write, sign, and give the document, and they acquired from him, no further consultation is needed.
Pumbedita says that even without acquisition, no further consultation is needed.
Bnei Mata Machseya say that without acquisition, consultation with the father is required.
The Gemara rules that without acquisition, consultation with the father is required.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Natan regarding Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's ruling
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Natan regarding Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: one says the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, the other says it does not. It concludes that Rabbi Natan is the one who said the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, as he follows estimation, citing his ruling on Rabbi Shimon Shezuri regarding a dangerous situation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav and Rabbi Natan: one says the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, the other says it does not.

The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Natan is the one who said the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, because he follows estimation (אומדנא), as evidenced by his ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri in a dangerous situation.

items.text: Opening citation of the Mishnah's rule
items.text_en: Opening citation of the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: The segment cites the Mishnah's law regarding terumat ma'aser of demai, setting the context for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating the rule regarding terumat ma'aser (תרומת מעשר) of demai (דמאי, produce of uncertain tithing).

items.text: Gemara's question about Rav and estimation
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rav and estimation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav follows estimation (אומדנא), citing a known dispute about a dying man's gift with a kinyan, where Rav's school holds a dual status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav follows אומדנא (estimation), citing a known dispute about a dying man's gift with a kinyan.
The Gemara cites that Rav's school holds the gift has a dual status (ארכביה אתרי רכשי), while Shmuel says he does not know how to judge it.

items.text: Explanation of Rav's school's position
items.text_en: Explanation of Rav's school's position
items.desc_en: Rav's school explains that the gift is treated both as a healthy person's gift (irrevocable if he recovers) and as a dying person's gift (allowing verbal transfer of a loan).

sub.desc_en: Rav's school declares that a dying person's gift which includes a formal kinyan (acquisition) is treated as having dual nature: both a healthy person's gift and a dying person's gift.
Rav's school explains the dual nature: like a healthy person's gift it is irrevocable if he recovers, and like a dying person's gift it allows verbal transfer of a loan without a formal kinyan.

items.text: Shmuel's uncertainty about the gift
items.text_en: Shmuel's uncertainty about the gift
items.desc_en: Shmuel expresses uncertainty about the gift's validity, suggesting the donor may have intended to transfer only through a document, which cannot take effect after death.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel expresses uncertainty about the gift's validity, suggesting the donor may have intended to transfer only through a document, which cannot take effect after death.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rav and Shmuel base their rulings on estimation (אומדנא). The one who says the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya does so because the husband's estimation is that he will not need to write a receipt, while the one who says the halakha does not follow him holds that the husband's estimation is that he will need to write a receipt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute between Rav and Shmuel by explaining that both base their rulings on estimation (אומדנא), differing only in their assessment of the husband's likely concern about needing a receipt.

items.text: Dispute over the halakha regarding Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
items.text_en: Dispute over the halakha regarding Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina stated that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, but Rabbi Yannai rejected this. Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi and Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel ruled that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, while Rav Nachman himself ruled against it. Ultimately, the Gemara concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, even for practical application.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina states before Rabbi Yannai that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, but Rabbi Yannai dismisses him, saying the halakha does not follow Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi in the name of Rabbeinu
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi in the name of Rabbeinu
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi cites Rabbeinu that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and Rav Nachman cites Shmuel to the same effect.

Rav Nachman himself rules against Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, but the Nehardeans report in his name that the halakha follows him; despite Rav Nachman's curse on judges who rule accordingly, the Gemara concludes that the halakha for practice follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

items.text: Ravin's question: Does the wedding canopy or marital relations acquire the ketubah?
items.text_en: Ravin's question: Does the wedding canopy or marital relations acquire the ketubah?
items.desc_en: Ravin asks whether a woman who entered the wedding canopy but was not yet married is acquired by the canopy or by marital relations. The Gemara attempts to resolve this from a baraita taught by Rav Yosef, but the proof is rejected. Ultimately, the Gemara explains that the baraita merely teaches proper conduct, not a legal ruling.

sub.desc_en: Ravin asks whether a woman who entered the wedding canopy (חופה) but was not yet sexually intimate is acquired by the act of חופה or by the act of intimacy (ביאה).

The Gemara cites a baraita taught by Rav Yosef about a husband who wrote a ketubah only for the obligation of the first night, and argues that this supports the view that חופת חופה (canopy) is the acquiring act, not intimacy.
The Gemara objects that if חופה is the acquiring act, it can occur by day as well, and resolves that the baraita merely teaches proper conduct — that intimacy is at night.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty about חופה by explaining that since the standard חופה is for intimacy, the baraita merely teaches proper conduct that intimacy is at night.

items.text: Rav Ashi's question: A woman who entered the canopy and then became a niddah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question: A woman who entered the canopy and then became a niddah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks about a woman who entered the wedding canopy and then became a niddah. If the canopy acquires, perhaps it only acquires when it is fit for marital relations, but if not, it does not. The Gemara concludes with תיקו (the question stands unresolved).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether a woman who entered the canopy but then menstruated (נידה) is acquired by חופה, and the Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara concludes the question stands unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on writing a receipt for the ketubah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on writing a receipt for the ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehuda can allow writing a receipt for the ketubah, given that he generally does not allow writing a receipt for a debt. Rabbi Yirmeya and Abaye offer different explanations: Rabbi Yirmeya says the receipt is written from within the ketubah itself, while Abaye says that even without that, the case is different because the husband is not at risk of being defrauded. The Gemara explains why each sage rejects the other's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yehuda can allow writing a receipt for the ketubah, given that in the Mishnah he forbids writing a receipt for a partial debt payment.
