Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the receipt is written from within the ketubah itself, so it is not a separate document.
Abaye answers that even without writing from within the ketubah, the case is different because the husband is not at risk of being defrauded—the wife's claim is merely a matter of her own vigilance.

The Gemara explains why each sage rejects the other's view: Abaye rejects Rabbi Yirmeya because the Mishnah does not mention writing from within; Rabbi Yirmeya rejects Abaye due to a decree against writing a receipt here, lest it be confused with a regular receipt.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view on stipulations regarding monetary matters
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view on stipulations regarding monetary matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that a stipulation regarding a monetary matter is valid, as seen in a baraita about a man who betroths a woman on condition that he is not obligated for her food, clothing, or marital relations. However, the Gemara questions why the rabbis strengthened the ketubah more than Torah law, given that they did not do so for other rabbinic enactments like the right to eat the produce of her property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a written receipt is required for the ketubah, but an oral statement is insufficient, given that it is a monetary matter.
The Gemara answers that since it is a monetary matter, Rabbi Yehuda's principle that a stipulation regarding money is valid would apply, so an oral condition should suffice.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir rules that a betrothal conditioned on exemption from food, clothing, and marital relations is valid but the condition is void.
The baraita concludes with Rabbi Yehuda's view that in a monetary matter, the stipulation is valid.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds the ketubah is a rabbinic enactment, and the rabbis strengthened their enactments more than Torah law, requiring a written receipt.
The Gemara objects that the rabbis did not strengthen their enactment regarding the right to eat the produce of the wife's property, which is also rabbinic.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a husband may eat the produce of his wife's property forever unless he writes a formal waiver, showing that an oral statement suffices for rabbinic produce rights.

items.text: Opening statement: clarification of 'kotev'
items.text_en: Opening statement: clarification of 'kotev'
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that 'kotev' (writes) in the context of ketubah means 'says' (orally stipulates). This sets the stage for the discussion of conditional reductions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that the term 'kotev' (writes) in the context of ketubah means 'omer' (orally stipulates).

items.text: Abaye and Rava on chizuk for common vs. uncommon matters
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava on chizuk for common vs. uncommon matters
items.desc_en: Abaye states that the rabbis applied chizuk (strengthening) only to common matters, not uncommon ones. The Gemara objects with the case of donkey drivers (chamarin) who are common yet no chizuk was applied. Abaye clarifies that chizuk applies to certainties (vadai) but not doubts (safeik), while Rava explains the leniency is due to demai (doubtfully tithed produce).

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the rabbis applied chizuk (strengthening) only to common matters, not uncommon ones.
The Gemara objects that donkey drivers (chamarin) are common yet no chizuk was applied.
The Gemara cites a baraita about donkey drivers who claim their wine is new or old, and Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that they are believed.
Abaye clarifies that chizuk applies to certainties (vadai) but not doubts (safeik), while Rava explains the leniency is due to demai (doubtfully tithed produce).

items.text: Rabbi Meir's view: reducing ketubah invalidates the condition
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's view: reducing ketubah invalidates the condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir holds that any reduction in ketubah, even by condition, is void because the woman does not rely on the stipulation, making the intercourse a zenut relationship. The Gemara questions this, noting that Rabbi Meir elsewhere rules that conditions against Torah law are void but rabbinic conditions stand; the answer is that Rabbi Meir considers ketubah to be Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Meir's ruling that anyone who reduces the ketubah amount, even conditionally, invalidates the condition, and the intercourse becomes a zenut relationship because the woman does not rely on the stipulation.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's position, noting that he elsewhere rules that conditions against Torah law are void but conditions against rabbinic law are valid.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Meir considers the ketubah to be a Torah law, so the condition against it is void.

items.text: Baraita: Tannaitic dispute on reducing ketubah
items.text_en: Baraita: Tannaitic dispute on reducing ketubah
items.desc_en: A baraita presents three opinions: Rabbi Meir says reducing the ketubah makes the intercourse zenut; Rabbi Yosei permits it; Rabbi Yehuda allows a written receipt acknowledging partial payment.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting the positions of Rabbi Meir (any reduction makes the marriage a forbidden union), Rabbi Yosei (permitted), and Rabbi Yehuda (he may write the full amount and she writes a receipt for less).
Rabbi Yosei permits reducing the ketubah.
Rabbi Yehuda allows a practical compromise: the husband writes the full ketubah amount, and the wife writes a receipt acknowledging partial payment.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabbi Yosei's leniency
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabbi Yosei's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yosei elsewhere objects to making ketubah from movable property because they are not fixed and depreciate, implying he is concerned about reduction. The Gemara resolves that in that case the woman does not know the value will decrease, but here she knowingly forgives the reduction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yosei holds that a husband may reduce the ketubah, yet elsewhere he objects to making a ketubah from movable property because they are not fixed and depreciate.
The Gemara clarifies that the Tanna Kamma's statement is about a case without liability, and Rabbi Yosei's objection is that even with liability, the property is not fixed and depreciates.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: there the woman does not know the value will decrease, but here she knowingly forgives the reduction.

items.text: Transition to a new narrative
items.text_en: Transition to a new narrative
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story about the sister of Rami bar Chama who was married to Rav Avya, serving as a segue to the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara digresses with a brief note about the sister of Rami bar Chama who was married to Rav Avya.

items.text: The case of the woman who delayed her ketubah and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: The case of the woman who delayed her ketubah and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: A woman delayed claiming her ketubah. Rav Yosef cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the ruling follows Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say a man can delay his wife for two or three years without a ketubah. Abaye objects that Shmuel ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees, so the woman must be given her ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a woman delayed claiming her ketubah, and Rav Yosef cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that the ruling follows Rabbi Meir.
The Sages object that a man may delay his wife for two or three years without a ketubah.
Abaye objects that Shmuel ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees.
Rav Yosef concedes and instructs to write the ketubah for the woman.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan about the nature of the machloket
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan about the nature of the machloket
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi and Ravin bring conflicting traditions from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan about whether the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies at the beginning or end of the marriage. Rabbi Avahu reconciles them, explaining that they do not actually disagree: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi refers to the beginning and end of the chuppah, while Rabbi Yochanan refers to the beginning and end of intercourse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies only at the beginning of the marriage, but at the end all agree she does not waive her ketubah.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the dispute applies both at the beginning and at the end.
Rabbi Avahu declares that he has a clear tradition from Rabbi Yochanan that he and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi do not actually disagree.

Rabbi Avahu explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's 'beginning' means the beginning of the chuppah and his 'end' means the end of intercourse, while Rabbi Yochanan's 'both' refers to the beginning and end of the chuppah, which is the beginning of intercourse.
Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the dispute applies only at the end, but at the beginning all agree she waives her ketubah.
Rabbi Yochanan again states that the dispute applies both at the beginning and at the end.
Rabbi Avahu again declares that he has a clear tradition that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi do not disagree.

Rabbi Avahu explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's 'end' means the end of the chuppah and his 'beginning' means the beginning of the chuppah, while Rabbi Yochanan's 'both' refers to the beginning and end of intercourse.

items.text: Rav Pappa's analysis of the traditions
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's analysis of the traditions
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that without Rabbi Avahu's clarification, one would think Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree, while Rav Dimi and Ravin do not. He clarifies that Rav Dimi's 'beginning' refers to the beginning of intercourse, and Ravin's 'end' refers to the end of the chuppah. The Gemara concludes that this teaches that two Amoraim can disagree about the reasoning of another Amora without disagreeing with that Amora himself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that without Rabbi Avahu's clarification, one would mistakenly think Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree, while Rav Dimi and Ravin do not.
Rav Pappa clarifies that Ravin's 'end' refers to the end of the chuppah, and Rav Dimi's 'beginning' refers to the beginning of intercourse.
The Gemara asks what practical lesson is being taught by this analysis.
The Gemara concludes that this teaches that two Amoraim can disagree about the reasoning of another Amora without disagreeing with that Amora himself.

items.text: The Mishnah on the time allotted for a bride and the laws of terumah
items.text_en: The Mishnah on the time allotted for a bride and the laws of terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a virgin is given twelve months from the time the husband demands to prepare herself, and a widow thirty days. If the time passes and they are not married, they eat from his food and eat terumah. Rabbi Tarfon says she is given all terumah, Rabbi Akiva says half chullin and half terumah. A yavam does not enable her to eat terumah. If she spent six months with the husband and six with the yavam, or even one day less, she does not eat terumah. This is the first Mishnah; a later court said otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the time allotted for a virgin (12 months) and a widow (30 days) from the husband's demand, and that after the time passes they eat from his food and eat terumah.
Rabbi Tarfon rules that she is given all terumah, while Rabbi Akiva rules half chullin and half terumah.
The Mishnah rules that a yavam does not enable her to eat terumah, and if she spent six months with the husband and six with the yavam, or even one day less, she does not eat terumah.
The Mishnah notes that this is the first Mishnah, and a later court said otherwise.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman does not eat terumah until she enters the wedding canopy.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman does not eat תרומה (priestly portion) until she enters the wedding canopy.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of the twelve-month period
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of the twelve-month period
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda derives the waiting period from the verse about Rebecca, where 'days' means a year. The Gemara rejects a month as the meaning, using a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the twelve-month waiting period) derived?
Rav Chisda answers by citing the verse about Rebecca: 'Let the maiden stay with us יָמִים (days) or ten'.
The Gemara objects: if 'יָמִים' means two days, that would be absurd; rather it must mean a year, as derived from the verse 'יָמִים תִּהְיֶה גְּאוּלָּתוֹ' (days shall be its redemption).
The Gemara objects further: perhaps 'יָמִים' means a month, as the verse says 'עַד חֹדֶשׁ יָמִים' (until a month of days).
The Gemara resolves: we derive 'יָמִים' stated without qualification from another 'יָמִים' stated without qualification, and we do not derive from 'יָמִים' where a month is specified.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's baraita on a minor's delay
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's baraita on a minor's delay
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira teaches that a minor girl or her father can delay the marriage, and explains the father's concern about future rebellion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a baraita that a minor girl or her father can delay the marriage.
The Gemara questions why the father would delay if the daughter is willing.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the father fears the daughter will later rebel and become a burden on him.

items.text: Rabbi Abba bar Levi on betrothing a minor
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Levi on betrothing a minor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Levi rules that one may not arrange a marriage for a minor while she is still a minor, but may do so for when she becomes an adult, dispelling a concern about fear causing weakness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Levi rules that one may not arrange a marriage for a minor while she is a minor, but may do so for when she becomes an adult.
The Gemara asks whether this ruling is obvious.

The Gemara explains that the ruling is not obvious because one might have been concerned that fear from the current arrangement would cause weakness, so Rabbi Abba bar Levi teaches that this concern is unfounded.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a bogeret and its refutation
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a bogeret and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says a bogeret who is betrothed gets thirty days like a widow. The Gemara brings two challenges, ultimately refuting Rav Huna's position.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a bogeret (mature maiden) who was betrothed receives thirty days to prepare for marriage, like a widow.
The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from a baraita that says a bogeret is like a 'tevu'ah' (a claimed party), implying she gets twelve months like a betrothed virgin, not thirty days.
The Gemara deflects by reinterpreting 'tevu'ah' as referring to a widow's claim (thirty days), not a virgin's.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer discusses a bogeret who waited twelve months, implying the standard period for a bogeret is twelve months, not thirty days.
The Gemara rejects the objection by reinterpreting the baraita as referring to a bogeret who already waited twelve months from the time of betrothal, not that she is given twelve months.
The Gemara brings a definitive baraita stating that a bogeret is like a 'tevu'ah' and receives twelve months, directly contradicting Rav Huna.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Huna's position is conclusively refuted (תיוּבְתָּא).

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the baraita refers to a bogeret who already waited twelve months in her bogeret status and then got betrothed, receiving thirty days like a widow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita means by 'and for an arusah (betrothed woman) thirty days'.
Rav Pappa explains that the baraita refers to a bogeret (matured maiden) who already waited twelve months in her bogeret status and then got betrothed, receiving thirty days like a widow.

items.text: Ulla's reason for the Mishnah's rule and subsequent discussion
items.text_en: Ulla's reason for the Mishnah's rule and subsequent discussion
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that by Torah law an arusah eats terumah, but the Sages forbade it due to concern she might feed her relatives. The Gemara questions why the concern doesn't apply after the time has passed, and discusses other cases like a Levite's son or a slave.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that by Torah law an arusah (betrothed woman) eats terumah, but the Sages forbade it lest she feed her relatives.
The Gemara asks why the same concern does not apply when the time for marriage has passed but they have not yet married.
The Gemara answers that in that case the husband designates a separate place for her, reducing the concern.
The Gemara objects that if the concern applies, a kohen's dependent (לקיט) living with an Israelite should also be forbidden to eat terumah, but that is not the case.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda offers a different reason: the prohibition is due to simpon (a potential hidden defect that could void the betrothal).
The Gemara asks why the same simpon concern does not apply to a woman who entered the chuppah but was not yet intimate.
The Gemara answers that there the husband examines her before bringing her in, so simpon is not a concern.
The Gemara objects that if simpon is the reason, a kohen's slave bought from an Israelite should also be forbidden to eat terumah, but the Gemara rejects this because simpon does not apply to slaves.
The Gemara begins a new topic about a found thief, but the section ends here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of kubiyustus and bandits
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of kubiyustus and bandits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a woman does not eat terumah: if her husband is a kubiyustus (a tax collector) or if bandits or a royal decree intervene. The Gemara notes that in these cases there is a public outcry (kala).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where a woman does not eat terumah: if her husband is a kubiyustus (tax collector) or if bandits or a royal decree intervene, noting that these have public outcry (kala).

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the practical difference?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the practical difference?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since in all these cases the woman does not eat terumah, what is the difference between them? It answers: the difference lies in whether the husband accepted, handed over, or went (i.e., the timing of the event).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since according to both opinions the woman does not eat terumah, what is the practical difference between them?
The Gemara answers: the difference lies in whether the husband accepted, handed over, or went (i.e., the timing of the event).

items.text: Abaye's distinctions regarding terumah division
items.text_en: Abaye's distinctions regarding terumah division
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva applies only to a bat kohen married to a kohen, but for a bat Yisrael married to a kohen, all agree it is half chullin and half terumah. Similarly, the dispute applies only to an arusah (betrothed), but for a nesuah (married), all agree it is half and half. A baraisa supports this.

sub.desc_en: The mishna's position of רבי טרפון (Rabbi Tarfon) is cited: he may give her everything from תרומה (priestly portion).

אביי (Abaye) limits the מחלוקת (dispute) to a בת כהן (priest's daughter) betrothed to a כהן (priest), while a בת ישראל (Israelite woman) betrothed to a כהן receives half חולין (non-sacred food) and half תרומה by all opinions.
אביי (Abaye) further limits the מחלוקת (dispute) to an ארוסה (betrothed woman), while a נשואה (married woman) receives half חולין and half תרומה by all opinions.
A ברייתא (baraita) is cited that supports אביי's distinctions, recording the dispute of רבי טרפון and רבי עקיבא and the qualifications regarding בת כהן לכהן and ארוסה versus נשואה.

items.text: Additional opinions on terumah division
items.text_en: Additional opinions on terumah division
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offer alternative views on how to divide terumah and chullin. The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between them and answers: the effort (tircha) involved.

sub.desc_en: רבי יהודה בן בתירא (Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira) rules that the husband gives her two portions of תרומה (priestly portion) and one portion of חולין (non-sacred food).
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) rules that he may give her everything in תרומה (priestly portion), and she sells it and buys חולין (non-sacred food) with the money.
רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) rules that wherever תרומה (priestly portion) is mentioned, he gives her double the amount in חולין (non-sacred food).
The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the opinions of רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel).
The Gemara answers that the practical difference between them is the effort (טירחא) involved in selling the תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: Yavam does not feed terumah
items.text_en: Yavam does not feed terumah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a yavam does not enable his yevamah to eat terumah. The Gemara explains the reason: the Torah says 'his acquisition' (kinyan kaspo), but this woman is the acquisition of his brother.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: the yavam (levir) does not enable his yevamah (levirate widow) to eat תרומה.
The Gemara explains the reason: the Torah said 'קנין כספו' (acquisition of his money), and this yavam's acquisition is that of his brother (not his own).
The Gemara explains that the Torah says 'his acquisition' (קִנְיַן כַּסְפּוֹ), but this woman is the acquisition of his brother.

items.text: Clarification: six months in the husband's presence
items.text_en: Clarification: six months in the husband's presence
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says she worked six months in the husband's presence. The Gemara notes that this is obvious: if she does not eat in the husband's presence, certainly not in the yavam's. It explains that the Mishnah uses the style 'this and needless to say that'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: now you say she does not eat in the presence of the husband (after six months), is it necessary to mention that she does not eat in the presence of the yavam?
The Gemara answers: the Mishnah teaches in the style of 'this and needless to say that' (a fortiori).

items.text: Reason for the later Mishnah: simpon
items.text_en: Reason for the later Mishnah: simpon
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says 'this is the first Mishnah' and then gives a later ruling. Ulla (or Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda) explains the reason is simpon (a condition or pretext). The Gemara elaborates: the first case is because they might mix a cup for her in her father's house, and the later case is due to simpon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the distinction between the first and later Mishnah rulings.
Ulla (or alternatively Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda) answers that the reason is due to simpon (a condition or pretext).
The Gemara elaborates that the first case is due to concern they might mix a cup for her in her father's house, and the later case is due to simpon.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute between Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and the earlier Tanna
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute between Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and the earlier Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the two opinions attributed to Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, both based on simpon (a condition). The difference is whether external examination (bedikat chutz) is considered a valid examination.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the two opinions of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, both based on simpon (a condition).
The Gemara answers that the difference is whether external examination (בדיקת חוץ) is considered a valid examination.

items.text: Mishnah: Consecrating a wife's handiwork
items.text_en: Mishnah: Consecrating a wife's handiwork
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband consecrates his wife's handiwork, she may still work and eat. The surplus is disputed: Rabbi Meir says it is consecrated, Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar says it is non-sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if a husband consecrates his wife's handiwork, she may still work and eat.
Rabbi Meir rules that the surplus of the wife's handiwork is consecrated.
Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar rules that the surplus is non-sacred (חולין).

items.text: Rav Huna's statement: A wife can refuse sustenance and work
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement: A wife can refuse sustenance and work
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says in the name of Rav that a wife can say to her husband, 'I will not be sustained and I will not work.' The rationale is that the rabbis instituted sustenance as primary, and her work is only to prevent enmity; she may waive both.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states in Rav's name that a wife may tell her husband she will not accept sustenance and will not work, because the rabbis instituted sustenance as primary and her work only to prevent enmity, so she may waive both.

items.text: Challenges and support for Rav Huna's view
items.text_en: Challenges and support for Rav Huna's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says 'they instituted sustenance in exchange for her handiwork,' implying a fixed exchange. It then attempts to support Rav Huna from the Mishnah, but deflects that the Mishnah refers to a wife who is not sustained. A comparison to a Canaanite slave and a Hebrew slave is made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states 'they instituted sustenance in exchange for her handiwork,' implying a fixed exchange that contradicts Rav Huna's view.
The Gemara deflects the objection by reinterpreting the baraita: 'they instituted her handiwork in exchange for sustenance,' not the reverse.
The Gemara attempts to support Rav Huna from the Mishnah, which says a husband who consecrates his wife's handiwork leaves her to work and eat.
The Gemara deflects the support by clarifying that the Mishnah refers to a wife who is not sustained by her husband.

The Gemara explains that even for one who says a master can tell a Canaanite slave 'work with me and I will not feed you,' a Hebrew slave (with whom the master must dwell) cannot be treated thus, and certainly not a wife.

items.text: Resolving the Mishnah's surplus dispute with Reish Lakish's explanation
items.text_en: Resolving the Mishnah's surplus dispute with Reish Lakish's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's surplus case is necessary for the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar. Reish Lakish says Rabbi Meir's reasoning is not that one can consecrate something not yet in the world, but because he can compel her to work, it is as if he said 'let your hands be consecrated to their Maker.' Since Rabbi Meir holds that words are not in vain, this is effective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the latter clause of the Mishnah, regarding the surplus, was necessary to present the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar.

Reish Lakish explains that Rabbi Meir's reasoning is not that one can consecrate something not yet in the world, but because he can compel her to work, it is as if he said 'let your hands be consecrated to their Maker.'
The Gemara objects that he did not actually say this to her, and answers that since Rabbi Meir holds that a person does not say things in vain, it is considered as if he said it.

items.text: Questioning whether Rabbi Meir holds that one cannot consecrate future objects
items.text_en: Questioning whether Rabbi Meir holds that one cannot consecrate future objects
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Reish Lakish's assumption that Rabbi Meir does not allow consecration of future objects, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir says a woman is betrothed after conversion, etc. The Gemara concludes that the baraita does not prove the point about consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Meir holds that one cannot consecrate a future object, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir rules that betrothal after a future event (e.g., conversion) is valid.
The Gemara resolves that from that baraita one can learn that Rabbi Meir holds this view, but from this mishna no inference is to be learned.

items.text: Dispute about when the surplus becomes consecrated
items.text_en: Dispute about when the surplus becomes consecrated
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel say the surplus is consecrated only after the wife's death, while Rav Adda bar Ahava says it is consecrated during her lifetime. Rav Pappa analyzes the dispute: if the husband provides both sustenance and spending money, why would it be after death? If he provides neither, why would it be during life? The resolution is that he provides sustenance but not spending money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when the surplus becomes consecrated, and cites Rav and Shmuel (after death) versus Rav Adda bar Ahava (during her lifetime).

Rav Pappa analyzes the dispute: if the husband provides both sustenance and spending money, why would the surplus be consecrated only after death? If he provides neither, why would it be consecrated during life?
The Gemara resolves that the husband provides sustenance but not spending money, so Rav and Shmuel hold the surplus is consecrated only after death.

items.text: Dispute over surplus earnings
items.text_en: Dispute over surplus earnings
items.desc_en: Rav Yochanan HaSandlar holds that the husband's provision of sustenance is in exchange for the wife's handiwork, and the ma'ah kesef is in exchange for the surplus; since he does not give the ma'ah kesef, the surplus is hers. Rav Adda bar Ahava reverses the pairings, holding that sustenance is in exchange for the surplus, so the surplus is the husband's. The Gemara explains their dispute as revolving around whether the more common item (sustenance) should be exchanged for the more common item (handiwork) or the fixed item (ma'ah kesef) for the fixed item (surplus).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yochanan HaSandlar holds that sustenance is in exchange for handiwork and the ma'ah kesef for the surplus, so since the husband does not give the ma'ah kesef, the surplus belongs to the wife.
Rav Adda bar Ahava reverses the pairings, holding that sustenance is in exchange for the surplus and the ma'ah kesef for handiwork, so since the husband provides sustenance, the surplus is his.

The Gemara explains that the dispute revolves around whether the more common item (sustenance) should be exchanged for the more common item (handiwork) or the fixed item (ma'ah kesef) for the fixed item (surplus).

items.text: Challenges and resolution regarding the surplus
items.text_en: Challenges and resolution regarding the surplus
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita that states sustenance is in exchange for handiwork, implying the surplus is the husband's. The Gemara deflects by reinterpreting it as 'in exchange for the surplus of her handiwork'. Another challenge from a mishnah states that if he does not give her the ma'ah kesef, her handiwork is hers; the Gemara again reinterprets it as 'the surplus of her handiwork is hers'. The Gemara explains that the mishnah's listing of her work (five selas of wool) is to calculate the surplus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita that states sustenance was instituted in exchange for handiwork, implying the surplus belongs to the husband.
The Gemara deflects by reinterpreting the baraita as saying sustenance is in exchange for the surplus of her handiwork.
The Gemara raises another challenge from a mishnah that states if he does not give her the ma'ah kesef, her handiwork is hers, implying the surplus is hers.
The Gemara again reinterprets the mishnah as referring to the surplus of her handiwork being hers.
The Gemara explains that the mishnah's listing of her work (five selas of wool in Judea) is to calculate the surplus.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules in accordance with Rav Yochanan HaSandlar, meaning the surplus belongs to the wife when the husband fails to give the ma'ah kesef.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, meaning the surplus of the wife's earnings belongs to her when the husband fails to give the ma'ah kesef.

items.text: Contradiction from Shmuel's other ruling
items.text_en: Contradiction from Shmuel's other ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Shmuel elsewhere ruled like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding a wife's vow not to work for her husband, which implies the surplus belongs to the husband. The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's ruling there was specifically about the surplus (העדפה), not the basic handiwork. The Gemara questions why Shmuel did not explicitly say 'halakha like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding the surplus', and suggests alternative formulations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency by citing a baraita where Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding a wife's vow not to work for her husband.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's ruling there was specifically about the surplus (העדפה), not the basic handiwork.
The Gemara questions why Shmuel did not explicitly say 'halakha like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding the surplus', and suggests alternative formulations.

items.text: Rav Yosef's distinction regarding vows
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's distinction regarding vows
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the case of vows (קונמות) is different because a person can prohibit another's produce upon himself, and thus can consecrate something not yet in existence. This distinguishes the vow case from the earlier dispute about surplus earnings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef distinguishes vows (קונמות) from the earlier case, explaining that through a vow a person can prohibit another's produce upon himself and thereby consecrate something not yet in existence.

items.text: Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's reasoning: while a person can prohibit his own produce upon his friend, can he prohibit something not yet in existence upon his friend? The analogy fails because one cannot prohibit another's produce upon that other.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's reasoning: while a person can prohibit his own produce upon his friend, can he prohibit something not yet in existence upon his friend? The analogy fails because one cannot prohibit another's produce upon that other.

items.text: Rav Huna's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Huna's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua explains that the wife says 'my hands shall be consecrated to their Maker', and since her hands already exist in the world, the vow is valid. The Gemara questions how she can consecrate her hands when they are already mortgaged to her husband; the answer is that she means after divorce.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that the wife says 'my hands shall be consecrated to their Maker', and since her hands already exist in the world, the vow is valid.
The Gemara objects: how can she consecrate her hands when they are already mortgaged to her husband?
The Gemara resolves that she means the consecration takes effect after divorce.

items.text: Discussion on consecrating future property
items.text_en: Discussion on consecrating future property
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether something that is not currently consecrated can become consecrated later. Rabbi Ilai gives an example of a field sold with a condition that when repurchased it becomes consecrated, which is valid. Rabbi Yirmeya objects that in that case the seller can consecrate it, but here the wife cannot divorce herself. Rav Pappa further objects that in the field case the buyer has both the body and produce, while here the wife has control over her body. The discussion is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether something that is not consecrated now can become consecrated later.
Rabbi Ilai gives an example of a field sold with a condition that when repurchased it becomes consecrated, which is valid.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects that in the field case the seller can consecrate it, but here the wife cannot divorce herself.
Rav Pappa further objects that in the field case the buyer has both the body and produce, while here the wife has control over her body.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the woman's vow
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the woman's vow
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha and Rav Ashi challenge the earlier analogy between a woman's vow and a mortgaged field, arguing that the woman cannot divorce herself. Rav Ashi resolves by invoking konamot (vows of consecration), which are sanctified objects that can override liens, citing Rava's principle that consecration, leaven, and manumission nullify liens. The Gemara then explains that the husband's lien is strengthened by the Sages to prevent immediate consecration.

sub.text: Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi objects that the analogy between a woman's vow and a mortgaged field is flawed because the woman cannot divorce herself, unlike the borrower who can redeem the field.
Rav Ashi objects further that even the modified analogy of a ten-year mortgage fails because the woman can never divorce herself.

Rav Ashi resolves that the case involves קונמות (vows of consecration), which are sanctified objects (קדושת הגוף) that override liens, citing Rava's principle that consecration, leaven, and manumission nullify liens.
The Gemara explains that the Sages strengthened the husband's lien to prevent immediate consecration of the property.

items.text: Mishnah: List of a wife's obligatory labors
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of a wife's obligatory labors
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates the labors a wife must perform for her husband: grinding, baking, laundering, cooking, nursing her child, making the bed, and working in wool. It then details how many labors are exempted based on the number of maidservants she brings into the marriage, culminating in the case of four maidservants where she may sit in a chair.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the seven labors a wife must perform for her husband and specifies exemptions based on the number of maidservants she brings.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's additions
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's additions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that even if she brings a hundred maidservants, he can compel her to work in wool because idleness leads to promiscuity. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that if a man vows to prevent his wife from working, he must divorce her and pay her ketubah, as idleness leads to boredom.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that even if a wife brings a hundred maidservants, he can compel her to work in wool because idleness leads to promiscuity.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that if a man vows to prevent his wife from working, he must divorce her and pay her ketubah, because idleness leads to boredom.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of 'grinding'
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of 'grinding'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the term 'grinding' (טוחנת) since it is typically done by a mill, and suggests it means 'supervising the grinding' (מטחנת) or refers to a hand-mill (בריחיא דידא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's use of the term 'טוחנת' (grinding), since grinding is typically done by a mill, not a person.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah means 'מטחנת' (supervising the grinding) rather than doing the grinding herself.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the Mishnah refers to grinding with a hand-mill (בריחיא דידא), which a woman can operate.

items.text: Mishnah not in accord with Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Mishnah not in accord with Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's requirement of labors contradicts Rabbi Chiyya's statements that a woman is only for beauty, for children, and for adornments. Rabbi Chiyya also advises that to pamper one's wife, dress her in linen, and to whiten one's daughter, feed her chicks and milk near her maturity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's requirement of labors contradicts Rabbi Chiyya's view.
Rabbi Chiyya teaches that a woman is only for beauty.
Rabbi Chiyya teaches that a woman is only for children.
Rabbi Chiyya teaches that a woman is only for adornments.
Rabbi Chiyya advises that to pamper one's wife, dress her in linen garments.
Rabbi Chiyya advises that to whiten one's daughter, feed her chicks and milk near her maturity.

items.text: Debate about nursing and Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Debate about nursing and Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that a wife must nurse aligns with Beit Shammai, who in a baraita say that if she vowed not to nurse, she may remove the baby from her breast. Beit Hillel say she is compelled to nurse. The Gemara initially suggests the Mishnah is not like Beit Shammai, but then reinterprets the case as one where the husband ratified her vow, and Beit Shammai hold that he is responsible (puts his finger between her teeth), while Beit Hillel hold she is responsible. The Gemara then rejects this and concludes the Mishnah is indeed not like Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that a wife must nurse aligns with Beit Shammai, citing a baraita where Beit Shammai say she may remove the baby from her breast if she vowed not to nurse, while Beit Hillel say she is compelled.

The Gemara reinterprets the case as one where the wife vowed and the husband ratified her vow, explaining that Beit Shammai hold the husband is responsible (puts his finger between her teeth), while Beit Hillel hold she is responsible.
The Gemara objects that the dispute should be about the marriage contract (כתובה) alone, and cites a baraita where Beit Shammai explicitly say she does not nurse.
The Gemara concludes definitively that the Mishnah is not like Beit Shammai.

items.text: Dispute over the waiting period for a nursing widow
items.text_en: Dispute over the waiting period for a nursing widow
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan argue about how long a nursing widow must wait before remarrying: three months, thirty days, or fifty days. Rav Shimi bar Abbaye rules like Rabbi Yitzchak, and the Gemara questions Shmuel's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how long a nursing widow must wait before remarrying.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Yirmeya bar Abba citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the waiting period is three months.
Shmuel rules that the waiting period is thirty days.
Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan rules that the waiting period is fifty days.
Rav Shimi bar Abbaye rules the halacha follows Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara questions Shmuel's position, noting that while Rav and Rabbi Yochanan's periods align with the seasons, Shmuel's thirty-day period does not correspond to any natural cycle.

items.text: Shmuel's actual ruling and a test case
items.text_en: Shmuel's actual ruling and a test case
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel reports that Shmuel actually said the widow may remarry as long as she recognizes the child. A story illustrates this: Shmuel tests a woman by having her child brought before her, and she recognizes him by smell and taste.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel reports that Shmuel's actual ruling is that the widow may remarry as long as she recognizes the child.
A story illustrates Shmuel's test: a woman recognizes her child by smell and taste, confirming the ruling.

items.text: Baraita on the duration of nursing
items.text_en: Baraita on the duration of nursing
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a child may nurse until twenty-four months; after that, nursing is considered repulsive. Rabbi Eliezer holds this view, while Rabbi Yehoshua permits nursing even up to four or five years. If the child stopped after twenty-four months and resumed, it is repulsive.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that a child may nurse until twenty-four months.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that after twenty-four months, nursing is considered repulsive (כְּיוֹנֵק שֶׁקֶץ).
Rabbi Yehoshua permits nursing even up to four or five years.
The baraita adds that if the child stopped after twenty-four months and resumed, it is repulsive.

items.text: Contradiction regarding human milk and blood
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding human milk and blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita teaches that human milk is pure, but a kal vachomer would suggest it is impure. The Torah excludes human milk and blood from impurity. Rav Sheishet says there is no obligation to abstain from it. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the child stopped nursing and when it did not, and applies a similar distinction to blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita teaches that after 24 months nursing is like sucking an abomination, yet another baraita rules human milk is pure, using a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that would suggest it should be impure.
The baraita resolves the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'את הגמל' (the camel) to exclude human milk and blood from טומאה (ritual impurity), declaring them pure.
Rav Sheishet states that even the obligation to abstain from such milk does not apply, emphasizing its permissibility.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the child has stopped nursing (פָּרֵישׁ) and when it has not (לָא פָּרֵישׁ), applying different rules accordingly.
The Gemara applies the same distinction to blood: blood on bread is scraped off and eaten, but blood between the teeth is sucked without concern.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's lenient ruling and its measure
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's lenient ruling and its measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehoshua says even if the child carries his bundle on his shoulders, he may nurse. This is the same measure as before. Rav Yosef rules like Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the earlier baraita that Rabbi Yehoshua permits nursing even up to four or five years.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita says Rabbi Yehoshua permits even if the child carries his bundle on his shoulders, implying a different measure.
The Gemara resolves that both formulations refer to the same measure.
Rav Yosef rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehoshua's lenient position.

items.text: Permissibility of nursing on Shabbat and other leniencies
items.text_en: Permissibility of nursing on Shabbat and other leniencies
items.desc_en: Rabbi Marinus permits a child to nurse on Shabbat because it is an indirect act of separating, and the Sages did not decree in a case of pain. Rav Yosef rules like him. Nachum Ish Galya permits crushing scales in a pipe on Shabbat because it is an indirect repair, and the Sages did not decree in a case of loss.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Marinus permits a child to nurse on Shabbat because it is an indirect act of separating.
The Gemara explains that the Sages did not decree in a case of pain.
Rav Yosef rules the halacha follows Rabbi Marinus.

items.text: Duration of repulsiveness after stopping
items.text_en: Duration of repulsiveness after stopping
items.desc_en: The baraita says that if a child stopped nursing after twenty-four months and resumed, it is repulsive. The Gemara asks how long this repulsiveness lasts. Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva citing Shmuel says three days.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that if a child stopped nursing after twenty-four months and resumed, it is repulsive, and the Gemara asks how long this repulsiveness lasts.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva in the name of Shmuel answers that the repulsiveness lasts three days.
An alternative version reports that Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva recited this teaching before Shmuel as a baraita.

items.text: Restriction on a nursing widow remarrying
items.text_en: Restriction on a nursing widow remarrying
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a nursing widow whose husband died within twenty-four months of childbirth may not become engaged or married.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a nursing widow whose husband died within twenty-four months of childbirth may not become engaged or married.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the waiting period
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the waiting period
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir (24 months) and Rabbi Yehuda (18 months) regarding how long a woman must wait after giving birth before remarrying. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel proposes a compromise: subtract three months from each opinion because milk does not curdle until three months after weaning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir requires a 24-month waiting period, while Rabbi Yehuda permits remarriage after 18 months.
Rabbi Natan bar Yosef identifies the dispute as parallel to the earlier dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel proposes a compromise: subtract three months from each opinion because milk does not curdle until three months after weaning.

items.text: Amoraic rulings and a practical question
items.text_en: Amoraic rulings and a practical question
items.desc_en: Ulla rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda. Mar Ukva reports that Rabbi Chanina permitted marriage after 15 months. Abaye's tenant asks about betrothal at 15 months, and Abaye supports leniency based on multiple precedents.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion regarding the waiting period for a widow to remarry.
Mar Ukva reports that Rabbi Chanina personally permitted a widow to marry after fifteen months, supporting the lenient view.
Abaye's tenant comes before him and asks whether it is permitted to become betrothed (לֵיאָרֵס) after fifteen months.

Abaye answers leniently, citing multiple precedents: the הלכה follows Rabbi Yehuda, the הלכה follows Beit Hillel, Ulla's ruling, and Mar Ukva's report, concluding that betrothal (לֵיאָרֵס) is certainly permitted.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and Abaye's lesson
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and Abaye's lesson
items.desc_en: When the tenant comes before Rav Yosef, he cites Rav and Shmuel who require a 24-month waiting period excluding the birth and betrothal days. The tenant runs after Rav Yosef but cannot catch him. Abaye explains that one should not rule in the presence of one's teacher, not out of disrespect, but because the matter may not be successful.

sub.desc_en: The tenant comes before Rav Yosef, who cites Rav and Shmuel requiring a 24-month waiting period excluding the birth and betrothal days.
The tenant runs after Rav Yosef for three parasangs but cannot catch him.

Abaye explains that one should not rule in the presence of one's teacher, not out of disrespect, but because the matter may not be successful, citing his own experience with the teaching of Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Exceptions for weaning or death of the child
items.text_en: Exceptions for weaning or death of the child
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if a woman gave her child to a wet nurse, weaned it, or the child died, she may remarry immediately. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua wanted to act accordingly, but an old woman told them that Rav Nachman forbade it. The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman permitted the house of the Exilarch, but that is different because they do not return to their husbands.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that if a woman gave her child to a wet nurse, weaned it, or the child died, she may remarry immediately.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua wanted to act in accordance with this baraita.
An old woman told them that she had a case and Rav Nachman forbade it.
The Gemara objects: But Rav Nachman permitted the house of the Exilarch to remarry immediately!
The Gemara answers: The house of the Exilarch is different because they do not return to their husbands, so there is no concern about confusion of parentage.

items.text: Further exceptions and Rabbi Meir's decree
items.text_en: Further exceptions and Rabbi Meir's decree
items.desc_en: Rav Pappi cites a baraita listing various cases (e.g., woman fleeing to father's house, husband in prison, etc.) where all require a three-month waiting period according to Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Yosei permits immediate betrothal and marriage. Rav Nachman cites Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi cites a baraita listing various cases (woman fleeing, husband in prison, etc.) where Rabbi Meir requires a three-month waiting period.
The baraita records that Rabbi Yosei permits immediate betrothal and marriage in these cases.
Rav Nachman cites Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees.

items.text: Final ruling and a tragic case
items.text_en: Final ruling and a tragic case
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: if the child died, she is permitted; if she weaned it, she is prohibited. Mar bar Rav Ashi says even if the child died she is prohibited, lest she kill it and remarry. A case occurred where a woman strangled her child, but that was a madwoman, and women do not normally strangle their children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the final ruling: if the child died she is permitted to remarry immediately; if she weaned it, she is prohibited.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects that even if the child died she is prohibited, lest she kill the child and remarry.
A case occurred where a woman strangled her child, but the Gemara dismisses it as the act of a madwoman, since women do not normally strangle their children.

items.text: Laws of nursing and dietary effects
items.text_en: Laws of nursing and dietary effects
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a woman who is given a child to nurse: she may not nurse her own child or another's alongside it. If her milk supply is low, she should eat more, but not foods harmful to milk. The Gemara specifies which foods are harmful (e.g., leeks, cress, small fish, earth) and lists various foods and their effects on children's health.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that a woman given a child to nurse may not nurse her own child or another's alongside it; if her milk supply is low, she should eat more, but not foods harmful to milk.
The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions both 'her son' and 'another's son' when the latter is obviously included in the former.
The Gemara explains that the baraita needed to specify both cases to counter a possible assumption that she would only nurse her own child excessively, but not another's.
The Gemara asks from whose resources the woman should eat more when her milk supply is low.
Rav Sheishet answers that she should eat from her own resources.
The Gemara asks which foods are considered harmful to milk.
Rav Kahana lists leeks, cress, small fish, and earth as harmful foods.
Abaye adds pumpkin and fenugreek to the list of harmful foods.
Rav Pappa adds gourd and safflower to the list.
Rav Ashi adds purslane and a type of vegetable to the list.
The Gemara concludes that some of these foods stop milk production and others spoil the milk.
The Gemara lists various maternal behaviors and their effects on children's health, such as using a mill causing epileptic children.

items.text: Opening anecdote about foods and children's traits
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about foods and children's traits
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists foods that affect the appearance of a woman's children, citing the example of Shapur's daughter who ate an etrog and gave birth to fragrant children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists foods that affect children's traits, concluding with the anecdote of Shapur's daughter who ate an etrog and bore fragrant children.

items.text: Dispute about nursing: whose opinion prevails
items.text_en: Dispute about nursing: whose opinion prevails
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks whether the husband or wife's wish regarding nursing is followed. The Gemara resolves it from the principle that a wife ascends with her husband but does not descend with him, citing verses from Rav Huna and Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks whether the husband's or wife's preference regarding nursing is followed when both have or lack the custom.
The Gemara resolves the question from the principle that a wife ascends with her husband but does not descend, citing verses from Rav Huna and Rabbi Elazar.

items.text: One maidservant: the wife's claim and the husband's response
items.text_en: One maidservant: the wife's claim and the husband's response
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a wife brings one maidservant, she does not grind or bake. The Gemara questions why she cannot claim she brought a maidservant for herself, and answers that the husband says the maidservant is busy for both of them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the wife cannot claim she brought a maidservant for herself, exempting her from other work.
The Gemara answers that the husband can respond that the maidservant is busy for both of them, so who will work for the wife alone?

items.text: Two maidservants: the wife's claim and the husband's response
items.text_en: Two maidservants: the wife's claim and the husband's response
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says with two maidservants she does not cook or nurse. The Gemara asks why she cannot claim she brought a maidservant for herself and one for him, and answers that the husband says the second is for guests.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that with two maidservants, the wife does not cook or nurse.
The Gemara infers that with two maidservants she still does other work, and asks why she cannot claim she brought one maidservant for herself and one for him.
The Gemara answers that the husband can respond: the second maidservant is for guests, and who will serve them if she does nothing?

items.text: Three maidservants: the wife's claim and the limit of four
items.text_en: Three maidservants: the wife's claim and the limit of four
items.desc_en: With three maidservants she does not make the bed. The Gemara asks why she cannot claim she brought one for guests, and the husband says more household members mean more guests. The Gemara then asks why not four, and answers that four help each other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that with three maidservants the wife does not make the bed, implying she does other work.
The Gemara asks why the wife cannot claim she brought a fourth maidservant for guests.
The husband answers that more household members mean more guests, so the extra maidservant is needed for them.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not allow four maidservants, since the same logic would apply.
The Gemara answers that with four maidservants they help each other, so the wife is exempt from bed-making.

items.text: The principle of being 'fit to bring' maidservants
items.text_en: The principle of being 'fit to bring' maidservants
items.desc_en: Rav Hana or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani states that the Mishnah's rule applies even if she did not actually bring maidservants but is fit to bring them. A baraisa supports this, saying it applies whether she brought them or provided them from her own funds.

sub.text: Rav Hana / Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.text_en: Rav Hana / Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.desc_en: Rav Hana or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani states that the Mishnah's rule applies even if she did not actually bring maidservants but is merely fit to bring them.
A baraita supports this, stating that the rule applies whether she brought maidservants or provided them from her own funds.

items.text: Wife with four maidservants and the niddah's exceptions
items.text_en: Wife with four maidservants and the niddah's exceptions
items.desc_en: With four maidservants she sits in a chair, but still pours wine and makes the bed. Rav Huna lists tasks a niddah may not do for her husband. Rava limits the bed-making to in his presence, and various Amoraim demonstrate how they received the cup.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that with four maidservants the wife sits in a chair, but Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya quoting Rav Huna adds that she still pours wine, makes the bed, and washes his face, hands, and feet.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya quoting Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya quoting Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a niddah may perform all household tasks for her husband except pouring wine, making the bed, and washing his face, hands, and feet.
Rava limits the bed-making prohibition to in his presence, and various Amoraim demonstrate how they received the cup from their wives to avoid direct contact.

items.text: Delaying before a servant and the danger of fragrant foods
items.text_en: Delaying before a servant and the danger of fragrant foods
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says one may delay before a servant except for meat and wine. Rav Chisda specifies fatty meat and old wine, and Rava adds seasonal details. Rav Anan and Rav Ashi recount near-death experiences from not receiving such foods, and Rav Pappa includes a sweet date. The rule: anything with smell and substance.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Chananya citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one may delay before a servant for any food except meat and wine.
Rav Chisda specifies that the dangerous foods are fatty meat and old wine.
Rava adds that fatty meat is dangerous all year, but old wine only during the summer solstice (תקופת תמוז).
Rav Anan recounts that he stood before Mar Shmuel and was in danger when not given a dish of beets.
Rav Ashi recounts that he stood before Rav Kahana and was in danger when not given turnip stalks in bread.
Rav Pappa adds that even a sweet date can be dangerous.
The gemara concludes the general rule: anything with smell and substance is dangerous.

items.text: Stories about eating early and Elijah's revelation
items.text_en: Stories about eating early and Elijah's revelation
items.desc_en: Two sons of Ihi differed: one ate from every dish, the other from one dish; Elijah spoke only to the one who ate from every dish. Similarly, two pious men or Rav Mari and Rav Pinchas: the one who ate early merited Elijah's conversation. The daf ends with Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi sitting at the king's gate and seeing the king's guard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that two sons of Ihi differed in their eating habits, and Elijah spoke only to the one who ate from every dish.
The Gemara brings a parallel story about two pious men (or Rav Mari and Rav Pinchas) where the one who ate early merited Elijah's conversation.
The daf ends with a brief scene of Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi sitting at the king's gate and seeing the king's guard.

items.text: Stories of miraculous detection
items.text_en: Stories of miraculous detection
items.desc_en: Two stories illustrate how sages detected hidden flaws: one about a Roman who spoiled a king's feast and was found to have leprosy, and another about a Roman who tricked a woman into eating pomegranate seeds to cure her illness.

items.text: Mishnah: Wife works in wool, not linen
items.text_en: Mishnah: Wife works in wool, not linen
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a wife works in wool, not linen. The Gemara identifies this as Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, who holds that a husband cannot force his wife to do degrading work like standing before his father or son, but can force her to give straw to his cattle; linen work is forbidden because it damages the mouth and lips.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that the Mishnah permits only wool work, not flax, and identifies the Mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a husband cannot force his wife to work with flax because it damages the mouth and lips.
The gemara adds that this applies specifically to Roman flax, which is particularly harsh.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that he cannot force her to work in linen because it damages the mouth and lips.
The Gemara qualifies that this applies only to Roman linen, which is particularly harsh.

items.text: Halakha like Rabbi Eliezer; distinction between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya
items.text_en: Halakha like Rabbi Eliezer; distinction between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya
items.desc_en: Rav Malkiyo in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, who says a wife cannot be forced to work even if she brought many maidservants. The Gemara then distinguishes between Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya regarding their rulings on spit, maidservants, and pits, with Rav Pappa noting that Mishnayot and baraitot are attributed to Rav Malkiya while halakhic traditions are attributed to Rav Malkiyo.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that a wife cannot be forced to work even if she brought a hundred maidservants.

sub.text: Rav Malkiyo citing Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Rav Malkiyo citing Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: Rav Malkiyo in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Chanina brei d'Rav Ika attributes the rulings on spit (שפוד), maidservants (שפחות), and pits (גומות) to Rav Malkiyo.
The rulings on a lock of hair (בלורית), ash from a kiln (אפר מקלה), and cheese (גבינה) are attributed to Rav Malkiya.
Rav Pappa distinguishes: Mishnayot and baraitot (מתניתין ומתניתא) are attributed to Rav Malkiya, while halakhic traditions (שמעתתא) are attributed to Rav Malkiyo.
Rav Pappa provides a mnemonic: 'מתניתא מלכתא' (the baraita is the queen), linking the Aramaic word for queen (מלכתא) to the name Malkiya.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two attributions and answers: the case of maidservants (שפחות) is the point of dispute.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion and the difference from Tanna Kamma
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion and the difference from Tanna Kamma
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, but explains the difference lies in a case where the wife is accustomed to small cats and dogs (i.e., luxury items).

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks how Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion differs from the first Tanna's.
The difference lies in cases involving small cats and a type of fabric (נדרשיר).

items.text: Mishnah: Vowing to withhold marital relations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vowing to withhold marital relations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a husband who vows to withhold marital relations from his wife: Beit Shammai says he may wait two weeks, Beit Hillel says one week. It also lists the frequency of marital relations based on occupation: idlers daily, laborers twice a week, donkey drivers once a week, camel drivers once every 30 days, sailors once every six months.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding a husband who vows to withhold marital relations: Beit Shammai permits a two-week wait, Beit Hillel permits one week.

The Mishnah lists the frequency of marital relations based on occupation: idlers daily, laborers twice a week, donkey drivers once a week, camel drivers once every 30 days, sailors once every six months, as stated by Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Gemara: Source of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Gemara: Source of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai derives the waiting period from a woman who gives birth to a female (two weeks of impurity), while Beit Hillel derives it from a woman who gives birth to a male (one week). Beit Hillel actually learns from niddah (menstruation), not from childbirth. The dispute is about whether we learn from a common case or from a case where the husband causes the separation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reason for Beit Shammai's position and answers that they derive the waiting period from a woman who gives birth to a female, while Beit Hillel derive it from a woman who gives birth to a male.
The Gemara objects that Beit Hillel could also derive from a female birth, and then answers that Beit Hillel actually derives from the laws of נִדָּה (menstruation), not from childbirth.

The Gemara resolves the dispute: Beit Shammai learns from a common case (female birth, which is common), while Beit Hillel learns from a case where the husband causes the separation (menstruation, where the husband's actions cause the separation).

items.text: Rav and Shmuel debate: explicit vs. implicit vow
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel debate: explicit vs. implicit vow
items.desc_en: Rav holds that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel applies only when the vow is explicit; if implicit, all agree he must divorce immediately and pay the ketubah. Shmuel argues that even with an implicit vow, he may wait, hoping to find a way to annul the vow. The Gemara notes this same dispute appears elsewhere regarding a vow of benefit, and explains why both cases are necessary.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel applies only when the vow is explicit, but if implicit, all agree he must divorce immediately and pay the ketubah.
Shmuel argues that even with an implicit vow, he may wait, hoping to find a way to annul the vow.
The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel already disputed this same point elsewhere regarding a vow of benefit, citing the Mishnah and their respective positions.
The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: each case highlights a unique reason why one might think the other opinion would concede, so both disputes are needed to fully clarify the positions.

items.text: Students leaving with permission
items.text_en: Students leaving with permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that students who leave to study Torah with permission may do so for as long as they wish.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: if the husband gives permission, how long may the student be away? Answer: as long as he wishes.
The Gemara answers that with permission, students may leave for as long as they wish.

items.text: Debate on the frequency of visits for Torah scholars
items.text_en: Debate on the frequency of visits for Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan debate how often a Torah scholar should be with his wife: Rav says one month away and one month home, citing a verse about the Temple guard; Rabbi Yochanan says one month away and two months home, citing a different verse. The Gemara explains why each rejects the other's proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how often a Torah scholar should visit his wife, and Rav answers with a verse: one month away and one month home.
Rabbi Yochanan counters with a different verse: one month away and two months home.
The Gemara explains why Rav rejects Rabbi Yochanan's proof: the Temple construction could be done by others, so it is not analogous.
The Gemara explains why Rabbi Yochanan rejects Rav's proof: the Temple guard had a break period, so it is not comparable.

items.text: Debate on the effect of sighing
items.text_en: Debate on the effect of sighing
items.desc_en: Rav says a sigh breaks half a person's body, citing a verse; Rabbi Yochanan says it breaks the whole body, citing another verse. The Gemara reconciles the verses: Rabbi Yochanan's verse describes the start from the loins, while Rav's verse refers to a particularly strong news (the Temple destruction).

sub.desc_en: Rav states that a sigh breaks half a person's body, citing the verse 'הֵאָנַח בְּשִׁבְרוֹן מׇתְנַיִם' (sigh with broken loins).
Rabbi Yochanan argues that a sigh breaks the entire body, citing the verse 'וְנָמֵס כׇּל לֵב...' (every heart melts).
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Yochanan: does not Rav's verse explicitly mention broken loins, implying only half the body?
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yochanan's verse describes the start from the loins, but the sigh then spreads to the whole body.
The Gemara objects to Rav: does not Rabbi Yochanan's verse mention melting of the entire heart and weakening of all limbs, implying the whole body?
The Gemara resolves: the news of the Temple's destruction was particularly strong, so it breaks the whole body even according to Rav.

items.text: Story illustrating the power of a fresh sigh
items.text_en: Story illustrating the power of a fresh sigh
items.desc_en: A Jew and a gentile walking together; the gentile cannot keep up. The Jew mentions the Temple destruction and sighs, but the gentile still cannot keep up. The gentile questions the claim that a sigh breaks half the body, and the Jew explains that a fresh sigh is powerful, but an old one (like a worn-out garment) does not.

sub.desc_en: A Jew and a gentile are walking together; the gentile cannot keep pace with the Jew.
The Jew sighs upon recalling the Temple destruction, yet the gentile still cannot keep up; the gentile challenges the claim that a sigh breaks half the body.
The Jew explains that a fresh sigh is powerful, but an old one, like a worn-out garment, does not affect the body.

items.text: Definition of 'day-travelers' (טַיָּילִין)
items.text_en: Definition of 'day-travelers' (טַיָּילִין)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions 'day-travelers' who visit their wives daily. Rava defines them as 'students of the study periods' (בני פירקי). Abaye objects, citing a verse about the wives of Torah scholars who sacrifice sleep in this world for the World to Come, implying they are not home daily. Abaye then offers an alternative definition: like Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, who is independent and not disturbed by royal messengers. Ravin says they are like the pampered ones of the West.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'day-travelers' (טַיָּילִין).
Rava defines 'day-travelers' as 'students of the study periods' (בני פירקי) who visit their wives daily.
Abaye objects, citing a verse and Rav Yitzchak's interpretation that the wives of Torah scholars sacrifice sleep in this world for the World to Come, implying the scholars are not home daily.
Abaye offers an alternative definition: like Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, who is independent, self-sufficient, and not disturbed by royal messengers.
Ravin adds that 'day-travelers' are like the pampered ones of the West (ארץ ישראל).

items.text: Stories of Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Yochanan's strength
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Yochanan's strength
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu was in a bathhouse with two slaves supporting him; the floor collapsed, but he grabbed a pillar and lifted them up. Similarly, Rabbi Yochanan was on a staircase with Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi supporting him; the step collapsed, and he lifted them. The rabbis asked why he needed support if he was so strong; he replied that otherwise he would have nothing for old age.

sub.desc_en: The gemara tells a story of Rabbi Avahu in a bathhouse, where the floor collapsed and he lifted two slaves supporting him.
A parallel story is told about Rabbi Yochanan on a staircase, where the step collapsed and he lifted Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi.
The rabbis ask Rabbi Yochanan why he needed support if he was so strong.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that he needs support now so that he will have something to rely on in old age.

items.text: Frequency for laborers: twice or once a week?
items.text_en: Frequency for laborers: twice or once a week?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says laborers visit twice a week, but a baraita says once a week. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina resolves the contradiction: if they work in their own city, twice; if in another city, once. A baraita supports this distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah states laborers visit twice a week, but a baraita says once a week.

Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to laborers working in their own city (twice a week), while the baraita refers to those working in another city (once a week).

A baraita is cited that explicitly supports Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Chanina's distinction, stating that laborers working in their own city visit twice a week, while those in another city visit once a week.

items.text: Question about the order of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Question about the order of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye why the Tanna taught the categories of 'day-traveler' and 'laborer' (which are more frequent) before 'camel-drivers' (which is less frequent). Abaye responds that the Tanna did not need to teach them in order of frequency.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye why the Tanna bothered to teach the categories of 'day-traveler' and 'laborer' (which are more frequent) before 'camel-drivers' (which is less frequent), implying the order is not by frequency.
Abaye responds that the Tanna did not need to teach them in order of frequency, implying the Mishnah's order is not based on how often the husband visits.

items.text: Gemara's question on the six-month allowance
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the six-month allowance
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement about six months, noting that having bread in one's basket is not comparable to not having it, implying a distinction in the quality of marital relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement about six months, noting that having bread in one's basket is not comparable to not having it, implying a distinction in the quality of marital relations.

items.text: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
items.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye about a man who changes from a donkey driver to a camel driver, and Abaye responds that a woman prefers a small portion with companionship over a large portion with abstinence.
