sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye about a man who changes from a donkey driver to a camel driver, and Abaye answers that a woman prefers a smaller portion with intimacy over a larger portion with separation.
Abaye responds that a woman prefers a small portion (קב) with companionship over ten portions with abstinence.

items.text: Dispute on sailors' onah and the halachic ruling
items.text_en: Dispute on sailors' onah and the halachic ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that sailors visit their wives once every six months. Rav Brona cites Rav that the halacha follows Rabbi Eliezer, but Rav Adda bar Ahava cites Rav that the Sages allow students to leave for two or three years without permission, and Rava notes that the rabbis relied on this and acted accordingly.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that sailors visit their wives once every six months; Rav Berona in Rav's name rules like Rabbi Eliezer, but Rav Adda bar Ahava in Rav's name reports that the Sages say students may leave for Torah study for two or three years without permission, and Rava notes that the rabbis relied on Rav Adda bar Ahava's version and acted accordingly.
Rav Brona cites Rav that the halacha follows Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava cites Rav that Rabbi Eliezer's statement is his individual view, but the Sages permit students to leave for two or three years without permission.
Rava concludes that the rabbis relied on Rav Adda bar Ahava's version and acted accordingly in practice.

items.text: Story of Rav Rechumi's tragic death
items.text_en: Story of Rav Rechumi's tragic death
items.desc_en: Rav Rechumi, who studied before Rava in Mechoza, used to come home every Yom Kippur eve. One day he was delayed by his studies, and his wife, expecting him, became distressed and wept. He was sitting on a roof that collapsed, killing him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story about Rav Rechumi, who studied by Rava and came home every Yom Kippur eve; one time his study delayed him, his wife despaired and cried, the roof collapsed, and he died.

items.text: The onah of Torah scholars
items.text_en: The onah of Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that the onah of Torah scholars is from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve, and Rav Yehuda (or others) identifies the verse 'which gives its fruit in its season' as referring to one who fulfills this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when is the marital duty (עונה) for Torah scholars, and Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name answers: from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's interpretation of a verse
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's interpretation of a verse
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda (or some say Rav Huna or Rav Nachman) interprets the verse 'which gives its fruit in its season' as referring to one who fulfills the marital duty from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda (or Rav Huna or Rav Nachman) citing a verse
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda (or Rav Huna or Rav Nachman) citing a verse
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda (or alternatively Rav Huna or Rav Nachman) identifies the verse 'which gives its fruit in its season' as referring to one who fulfills the onah from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve.

items.text: Story of Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's death
items.text_en: Story of Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's death
items.desc_en: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiyya and son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai, would study and come home every twilight, preceded by a pillar of fire. One day he was delayed, and Rabbi Yannai, seeing no sign, ordered his bed to be turned, saying that if Yehuda were alive he would not neglect his onah. Yehuda died, fulfilling 'an error that proceeds from the ruler.'

sub.text: Story about Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Story about Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells of Yehuda son of Rabbi Chiyya, who studied at the academy and came home every twilight; one time his study delayed him, the sign of a pillar of fire disappeared, Rabbi Yannai ordered his bed overturned, and Yehuda died as a 'mistake that goes out from the ruler.'

items.text: Stories of Rabbi's son and Rabbi Yose ben Zimra's son-in-law
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi's son and Rabbi Yose ben Zimra's son-in-law
items.desc_en: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Chiyya's daughter, but she died. They investigated lineages and found both were of noble descent. Rabbi then arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Yose ben Zimra's daughter, stipulating twelve years of study. The son reduced it to six, then insisted on marrying first. He was embarrassed before his father, who consoled him with a verse. He studied for twelve years, and his wife became barren. Rabbi debated whether to divorce her or marry another, but prayed and she was healed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Chiyya's daughter, but she died at the time of writing the ketubah; they investigated the lineages and found both were of noble descent.

Rabbi arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Yose ben Zimra's daughter, stipulating twelve years of study; the son reduced it to six, then insisted on marrying first, and was embarrassed before his father.

Rabbi consoled his son with a verse: initially it says 'You will bring them and plant them,' and later it says 'They shall make Me a sanctuary and I will dwell among them,' implying that study precedes marriage.
The son studied for twelve years, his wife became barren, Rabbi debated whether to divorce her or marry another, but prayed for her and she was healed.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chananya ben Chachinai
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chananya ben Chachinai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chananya ben Chachinai left for study right after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's wedding, despite being asked to wait. He studied for twelve years. When he returned, the paths had changed and he couldn't find his home. He followed a girl calling 'Bat Chachinai' and found his wife grinding flour. She saw him, her heart gave out, and she died. He prayed and revived her.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that Rabbi Chananya ben Chachinai left for the study hall right after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's wedding, ignoring a request to wait, and studied for twelve years.
Upon returning, the paths had changed and he could not find his home; he followed a girl calling 'Bat Chachinai', found his wife grinding flour, she died from shock, and he prayed and revived her.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chama bar Bisa and his son Rabbi Oshaya
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chama bar Bisa and his son Rabbi Oshaya
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Bisa studied for twelve years. Upon returning, he sent word home and his son Rabbi Oshaya came to him. Seeing his son's sharp scholarship, he felt distressed that he had missed raising such a son. At home, his son stood before him, and his wife rebuked him for standing before his son. Rami bar Chama applied the verse 'a threefold cord is not quickly broken' to Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens: Rabbi Chama bar Bisa went and sat for twelve years in the study hall, and upon returning he sent word home rather than surprising his wife.
Rabbi Oshayaa, his son, came and sat before him; when Rabbi Chama saw his son's sharp scholarship, he became distressed that he had missed raising such a son.
At home, Rabbi Chama's wife rebuked him for standing before his son, and Rami bar Chama applied the verse 'a threefold cord is not quickly broken' to Rabbi Oshayaa.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Akiva's marriage and study
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Akiva's marriage and study
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva was a shepherd for Ben Kalba Savua. His daughter saw his modesty and worth, and proposed marriage on condition he go study. He agreed, and they married secretly. Her father disowned her. Akiva studied for twelve years and returned with 12,000 students. He heard an old man telling her how long she waited.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva was a shepherd for ben Kalba Savua; his daughter saw his modesty and worth, proposed marriage on condition he go to the academy, he agreed, they married secretly, her father banished her, Akiva studied twelve years and returned with twelve thousand students.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Akiva's wife and daughter
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Akiva's wife and daughter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva returns after 24 years with many students; his wife goes out to meet him, and his daughter later acts similarly with Ben Azzai. The story illustrates the reward of patience and the saying that daughters follow their mothers' ways.

sub.text: Neighbors' question to Rabbi Akiva's wife
sub.text_en: Neighbors' question to Rabbi Akiva's wife
sub.desc_en: The neighbors ask Rabbi Akiva's wife why she lives like a widow while her husband is alive.
She tells the neighbors that if they listen to her, Rabbi Akiva should sit another twelve years, and he agrees to do so with her permission.
Rabbi Akiva returns after twelve more years with 24,000 students; his wife goes out to meet him in rags, and he declares that both his learning and theirs belong to her.

Rabbi Akiva's father-in-law seeks to annul his vow, discovers Rabbi Akiva is the great man, and gives him half his wealth; the story concludes with the proverb that a daughter follows her mother's ways, as Rabbi Akiva's daughter did with Ben Azzai.

items.text: Story of Rav Yosef son of Rava
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yosef son of Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef, son of Rava, was sent to study by his father. After three years, he tried to visit home on Yom Kippur eve, but his father rebuked him, causing both to be distressed.

sub.text: Narrator's introduction of the story of Rav Yosef bar Rava
sub.text_en: Narrator's introduction of the story of Rav Yosef bar Rava
sub.desc_en: Rava sends his son Rav Yosef to study before Rav Yosef, and they set a six-year term for him.
After three years, on Yom Kippur eve, Rav Yosef bar Rava goes to visit his family; his father Rava confronts him with a harsh question, and both are distressed and unable to resume their studies.
Rava hears of his son's plan, goes out to meet him, and rebukes him with a harsh question: 'Have you remembered your prostitute?' (or 'your dove').
Both father and son were distressed and did not complete their studies.

items.text: Mishnah: The rebellious wife and husband
items.text_en: Mishnah: The rebellious wife and husband
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a rebellious wife (מורדת) loses seven dinars per week from her ketubah; Rabbi Yehuda says seven tropaics. The reduction continues until the ketubah is exhausted. Rabbi Yosei says it continues indefinitely, and if she later inherits, he collects from that. Similarly, a rebellious husband has three dinars added to her ketubah each week.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a wife who rebels against her husband has seven dinars deducted from her ketubah each week.
Rabbi Yehuda says the deduction is seven טרפעיקין (a smaller coin) instead of dinars.

sub.text: Mishnah's continuation on the limit of deduction
sub.text_en: Mishnah's continuation on the limit of deduction
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the deduction continues only until it reaches the value of her ketubah.
Rabbi Yosei says the deduction continues indefinitely, so that if she later inherits property, the husband can collect from it.

sub.text: Mishnah's ruling on a rebellious husband
sub.text_en: Mishnah's ruling on a rebellious husband
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a husband who rebels against his wife has three dinars added to her ketubah each week.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative opinion on the husband's addition
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative opinion on the husband's addition
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says the addition is three טרפעיקין instead of dinars.

items.text: Gemara: What does 'rebellious' mean?
items.text_en: Gemara: What does 'rebellious' mean?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from what does she rebel? Rav Huna says from marital relations; Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says from work. The Gemara questions the latter: is a husband obligated to work for her? It answers: when he says 'I will not support or provide.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from what does she rebel — what is the specific marital duty she refuses?
Rav Huna says she rebels against marital relations.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina says she rebels against performing household work.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yosei's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yosei's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: according to the view that she rebels against work, is a husband really obligated to work for his wife?
The Gemara answers: yes, the husband is obligated to provide sustenance, and the rebellion is when he says 'I will not feed nor support.'

items.text: Objection from Rav's statement
items.text_en: Objection from Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rav said that one who says 'I will not support or provide' must divorce and pay the ketubah, implying he is not obligated to support. So how can the husband be considered rebellious for refusing work?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rav said that a husband who says 'I will not feed nor support' must divorce and pay the ketubah, not just have additions made.
The Gemara asks: does this not require consultation (i.e., is it not a case where the court must first advise the husband)?

items.text: Supporting baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing cases where the husband is liable: for an arusah, nesuah, niddah, ill woman, and yevamah. The Gemara analyzes: for the view that rebellion is from work, all fit; for the view that it is from relations, a niddah is not fit for relations. The answer: one who has bread in his basket is different from one who does not (i.e., the prohibition does not remove the desire).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing cases where the husband is liable for the wife's rebellion: arusah, nesuah, niddah, ill woman, and yevamah.
The Gemara questions: according to the view that rebellion is from relations, how can a niddah be included, since she is forbidden for relations?
The Gemara answers: one who has bread in his basket is different from one who does not — the prohibition does not remove the desire for relations.

items.text: Alternative version of the analysis
items.text_en: Alternative version of the analysis
items.desc_en: An alternative version: for the view that rebellion is from relations, the baraita's mention of a sick woman fits, as she is exempt from work but not from relations.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version: according to the view that she rebels against relations, that is why the baraita includes a sick woman (who cannot have relations).

items.text: Clarifying the dispute: refusal of labor vs. marital relations
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute: refusal of labor vs. marital relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all agree refusal of marital relations makes a woman a מורדת; the dispute is only about refusal of labor. One opinion holds that refusal of labor does not make her a מורדת, while another holds it does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that a woman can rebel by refusing labor, how can a sick woman be considered a מורדת (rebellious wife) if she is exempt from labor?
The Gemara resolves: all agree that refusal of marital relations (תשמיש) makes her a מורדת; the dispute is only about refusal of labor.
The Gemara states the two opinions: one holds that refusal of labor does not make her a מורדת, the other holds that it does.

items.text: The Mishnah: penalties and procedure for a מורדת
items.text_en: The Mishnah: penalties and procedure for a מורדת
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a rebellious wife loses seven dinars per week from her ketubah. Rabbi Yehuda says seven טרפעיקין. The Sages later ruled that the court announces her rebellion for four consecutive weeks and sends her a warning that she forfeits even a large ketubah. This applies to an arusah, a nesu'ah, a niddah, a sick woman, and a yevamah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a rebellious wife (מורדת) loses seven dinars per week from her ketubah.
Rabbi Yehuda gives an alternative measure: seven טרפעיקין (a smaller coin) per week.
The Sages later ruled that the court announces her rebellion for four consecutive weeks and warns her that she forfeits even a large ketubah, applying to all types of wives.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef's question to Shmuel about a niddah
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef's question to Shmuel about a niddah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel: Is a niddah fit for marital relations? Shmuel answers with a metaphor: one who has bread in his basket is not comparable to one who does not, implying that even if relations are impossible, the desire remains.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel whether a niddah (menstruant) is fit for marital relations.
Shmuel answers with a metaphor: one who has bread in his basket is not comparable to one who does not, implying that even if relations are impossible, the desire remains.

items.text: Rami bar Chama: details of the announcement procedure
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama: details of the announcement procedure
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that the announcement is made only in synagogues and study halls. Rava confirms this from the Mishnah's wording 'four consecutive weeks.' Rami bar Chama adds that the court sends two notices: one before the announcement and one after.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that the announcement about a rebellious wife is made only in synagogues and study halls.
Rava confirms Rami bar Chama's ruling from the Mishnah's wording 'four consecutive weeks,' implying the announcement is made in public places.
Rami bar Chama adds that the court sends two notices to the wife: one before the announcement and one after.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda taught that the halakha follows the Sages. Rava called this a 'blessing' (בורכה). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak defended it, saying he stated it in the name of a great man, Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda teaches that the binding law (הלכה) follows the Sages (רבותינו) regarding the rebellious wife.
Rava dismisses the ruling as a 'blessing' (בורכה), implying it is worthless or a mere platitude.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak defends the ruling, stating he transmitted it in the name of a great man, Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina.

items.text: Dispute about consulting the wife before the announcement
items.text_en: Dispute about consulting the wife before the announcement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With whom does Rava agree? It cites a dispute: Rava said in the name of Rav Sheshet that the halakha is that we consult her; Rav Huna bar Yehuda said in the name of Rav Sheshet that we do not consult her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With whom does Rava agree in the dispute about consulting the wife before the announcement?
Rava says in the name of Rav Sheshet that the halakha is that we consult her.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda says in the name of Rav Sheshet that the halakha is that we do not consult her.

items.text: Definition of a מורדת and a case of coercion
items.text_en: Definition of a מורדת and a case of coercion
items.desc_en: Ameimar defines a מורדת as one who says 'I want him and I will torment him.' But if she says 'he is repulsive to me,' we do not coerce her. Mar Zutra says we do coerce her. A case occurred where Mar Zutra coerced her, and Rabbi Chanina from Sura was born from that union, but that was due to heavenly assistance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of a מורדת (rebellious wife).
Ameimar defines a מורדת as one who says 'I want him and I will torment him,' but if she says 'he is repulsive to me,' we do not coerce her.
Mar Zutra disagrees and says we do coerce her even if she says 'he is repulsive to me.'
A case occurred where Mar Zutra coerced her, and Rabbi Chanina from Sura was born from that union.
The Gemara resolves that the case is not a precedent because it was due to heavenly assistance.

items.text: Case of Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law and the dispute about lost embellishments
items.text_en: Case of Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law and the dispute about lost embellishments
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled. Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi sat with Rav Gamda. They said she lost her embellishments (בלאות). Rav Gamda challenged them, citing Rava's unresolved question. An alternative version says they said she did not lose her embellishments, and Rav Gamda again challenged them.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces the case of Rav Zevid's rebellious daughter-in-law, who was holding a silk garment, and the sages Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi, with Rav Gamda present, who ruled that a rebellious woman loses her embellishments.
Rav Gamda objects, accusing them of flattering Rav Zevid because he is a great man, and cites Rav Kahana that Rava raised this question and it was never resolved.
An alternative version reports that the sages ruled the rebellious woman does not lose her embellishments, and Rav Gamda again objects.

items.text: Ruling on the rebellious wife's maintenance during the twelve-month waiting period
items.text_en: Ruling on the rebellious wife's maintenance during the twelve-month waiting period
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if a wife seizes property during the twelve-month period after the get, we do not take it from her; if she did not seize, we do not give it to her. During those twelve months, she has no maintenance from her husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that because Rav Zevid is a great man, the court reversed the ruling against him, citing Rav Kahana's report that Rava's question remained unresolved.

The Gemara concludes that since no definitive ruling was stated either way, if the wife seized property during the twelve-month period we do not take it from her, and if she did not seize we do not give it to her.
The Gemara rules that the wife is delayed twelve months after the get, and during those twelve months she has no maintenance from her husband.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on writing a letter of rebellion for an arusah but not for a shomeret yavam
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on writing a letter of rebellion for an arusah but not for a shomeret yavam
items.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna quotes Shmuel: we write a letter of rebellion for an arusah but not for a shomeret yavam. A challenge is raised from a baraita that includes shomeret yavam in the list of women for whom a letter of rebellion is written. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to when the husband claims, while Shmuel's ruling applies when the wife claims.

sub.text: Rav Tovi bar Kisna citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tovi bar Kisna quotes Shmuel: we write a letter of rebellion (איגרת מרד) for an arusah (betrothed woman) but not for a shomeret yavam (a yevamah awaiting yibbum).
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists shomeret yavam among those for whom a letter of rebellion is written, contradicting Shmuel's exclusion.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the cases: the baraita applies when the husband claims (תבע הוא), while Shmuel's ruling applies when the wife claims (תבעה היא), as Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi quotes Shmuel.

items.text: Clarification of Shmuel's ruling and the reason for the distinction
items.text_en: Clarification of Shmuel's ruling and the reason for the distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the wording of Shmuel's statement and suggests it should read 'for an arusah' (לַאֲרוּסָה) rather than 'on an arusah' (עַל אֲרוּסָה). It then asks why a shomeret yavam is different, and answers that in the case of an arusah who comes with a claim (e.g., she wants a staff in her hand and a spade for burial), we write the letter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's wording, arguing that if his ruling applies when she initiated the claim, the phrase should be 'for an arusah' (לַאֲרוּסָה) rather than 'on an arusah' (עַל אֲרוּסָה).
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that the text should be emended to read 'לַאֲרוּסָה' (for an arusah).
The Gemara asks why a shomeret yavam is treated differently from an arusah, since both could be told 'go, you are not commanded' (to marry).
The Gemara explains that the case involves a woman who comes with a claim, saying she wants a staff in her hand and a spade for burial (i.e., she needs support and a proper burial).

items.text: Distinction between claiming for halitzah and claiming for yibbum
items.text_en: Distinction between claiming for halitzah and claiming for yibbum
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially tries to apply the same logic to a shomeret yavam, but then reinterprets the case: both are when the husband claims, and the distinction is between claiming for halitzah and claiming for yibbum. Rabbi Pedat quotes Rabbi Yochanan: if he claims for halitzah, we respond; if for yibbum, we do not. The reason is that for yibbum we tell him to marry another woman, but for halitzah he claims that because he is bound to her, no one else will marry him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the same logic of a woman claiming for sustenance applies to a shomeret yavam (waiting yevamah).
The Gemara reinterprets the case: both are when the husband claims, and the distinction is between claiming for halitzah and claiming for yibbum.
Rabbi Pedat cites Rabbi Yochanan: if he claims for halitzah we respond; if for yibbum we do not.
The Gemara questions why the court does not respond to a claim for yibbum, suggesting the same reasoning (marry another woman) could apply to halitzah.
The Gemara explains that for halitzah, the yavam claims that because he is bound to her, no one else will marry him, so the court must respond.

items.text: Distinction between the first and later Mishnah regarding yibbum and halitzah
items.text_en: Distinction between the first and later Mishnah regarding yibbum and halitzah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous distinction and instead explains that both cases are when he claims for yibbum, but the difference is between the first Mishnah (where yibbum is preferred) and the later Mishnah (where halitzah is preferred). The baraita is cited: originally the mitzvah of yibbum preceded halitzah, but now halitzah precedes yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the same argument applies to chalitzah, and resolves by distinguishing between the first Mishnah (where yibbum is preferred) and the later Mishnah (where chalitzah is preferred).
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that originally the mitzvah of yibbum preceded chalitzah, but now that they no longer intend for the mitzvah, chalitzah precedes yibbum.

items.text: Definition of tarpe'ikin and Rabbi Yehudah's statement
items.text_en: Definition of tarpe'ikin and Rabbi Yehudah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the term 'tarpe'ikin' from the Mishnah: Rav Sheshet says it is an 'istera', and how much is an 'istera'? Half a zuz. A baraita supports this: Rabbi Yehudah says three tarpe'ikin, which are nine ma'ah, i.e., a ma'ah and a half per day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'tarp'ikin' means, and Rav Sheshet answers that it is an 'istira', which is half a zuz.
A baraita supports this, with Rabbi Yehuda stating that three tarp'ikin equal nine ma'ah, which is a ma'ah and a half per day.
A baraita supports this: Rabbi Yehudah says three טַרְפְּעִיקִין are nine ma'ah, i.e., a ma'ah and a half per day.

items.text: Question about Shabbat allowance for the husband versus the wife
items.text_en: Question about Shabbat allowance for the husband versus the wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel: why do we give the husband Shabbat allowance but not the wife? The answer is that the wife is decreasing (her allowance), so it does not appear as Shabbat wages, while the husband is increasing (his allowance).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef to Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef to Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef asks Shmuel why the husband is given Shabbat allowance but the wife is not, and answers that since the wife is decreasing her allowance, it does not appear as Shabbat wages, while the husband is increasing his allowance.
Shmuel answers that the wife is decreasing her allowance, so it does not appear as Shabbat wages, while the husband is increasing his allowance.

items.text: Distinction between a rebellious husband and wife
items.text_en: Distinction between a rebellious husband and wife
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Yosef asks Shmuel what is the difference between a rebellious husband (moreid) and a rebellious wife (moredet). Shmuel answers with a parable from the marketplace of prostitutes, and adds that a man's yetzer is outside while a woman's yetzer is inside.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Yosef asks Shmuel what is the difference between a rebellious husband (מורד) and a rebellious wife (מורדת).
Shmuel answers with a parable from the marketplace of prostitutes and adds that a man's yetzer is outside while a woman's yetzer is inside.

items.text: Mishnah: Minimum provisions for a wife supported through a third party
items.text_en: Mishnah: Minimum provisions for a wife supported through a third party
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband who leaves his wife supported by a third party must provide her with specific minimum amounts of food, oil, dried figs, and other items. It also details her clothing allotment, her spending money, and the work she must do for him, with adjustments for a nursing mother and according to his honor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the minimum food provisions a husband must provide when supporting his wife through a third party, including wheat, barley, legumes, oil, and dried figs, with a note from Rabbi Yosi about barley.
Rabbi Yosi adds that the allowance of barley was only instituted by Rabbi Yishmael, who lived near Edom where barley was common.
The Mishnah lists the household items and clothing the husband must provide, including a bed, mat, head covering, belt, shoes, and annual clothing worth fifty zuz, with seasonal adjustments.
The Mishnah states that the husband gives her a ma'ah of silver for her expenses, and if he fails to do so, her earnings belong to her.
The Mishnah details the work the wife must do for her husband, with adjustments for a nursing mother and according to his honor.

items.text: Gemara's question: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Who is the Tanna of the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, noting it is neither Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka nor Rabbi Shimon, based on a baraita about the shiur of a meal for a poor person. The baraita records disputes between Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, and Rabbi Shimon about the size of a kikar. The Gemara calculates that the Mishnah's two kav of wheat would yield a number of loaves that does not match either opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authored the Mishnah, noting it is neither Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka nor Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara cites a baraita that records disputes about the shiur of a meal for a poor person, involving Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, and Rabbi Shimon.
The baraita continues with a digression about the halachic uses of half-loaves for leprous houses, disqualification of the body, and susceptibility to food impurity.

The Gemara calculates that the Mishnah's two kav of wheat would yield eight loaves according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka or eighteen according to Rabbi Shimon, neither matching the Mishnah's implied number.

items.text: First resolution: Rav Chisda's deduction for the shopkeeper
items.text_en: First resolution: Rav Chisda's deduction for the shopkeeper
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially resolves the difficulty by applying Rav Chisda's principle that one must deduct a third for the shopkeeper's profit. However, this still yields too many loaves. The Gemara then considers that the Mishnah's clause 'she eats with him on Shabbat nights' might mean actual eating or marital relations, and adjusts the calculation accordingly, leading to a different deduction of half for the shopkeeper.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, and applies Rav Chisda's principle of deducting a third for the shopkeeper's profit to the calculation.

The Gemara objects that even after deducting a third, the result is twelve loaves, not the required number, and notes that the Mishnah's clause 'she eats with him on Shabbat nights' might adjust the count.
The Gemara questions whether the clause 'she eats with him' refers to actual eating or to marital relations, and notes that even with that adjustment, the count would be thirteen loaves.
The Gemara revises the application of Rav Chisda's principle, now deducting half for the shopkeeper's profit instead of a third, to yield the correct number of loaves.

items.text: Reconciling Rav Chisda's statements and further adjustments
items.text_en: Reconciling Rav Chisda's statements and further adjustments
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between Rav Chisda's two statements (deduct a third vs. deduct half) and resolves it based on whether the place provides firewood. It then calculates that even with the deduction, the number of loaves is sixteen, which matches Rabbi Chidka's opinion of four Shabbat meals. Alternatively, it can be reconciled with the Rabbis by deducting one meal for guests, and with Rabbi Shimon by deducting three or two meals for guests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rav Chisda's two statements (deduct a third vs. deduct half).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a place that provides firewood (deduct a third) and a place that does not (deduct half).
The Gemara calculates that even with the deduction, the number of loaves is sixteen, and asks whose opinion this matches.
The Gemara answers that this matches Rabbi Chidka's opinion that one must eat four Shabbat meals.
The Gemara alternatively reconciles the calculation with the Rabbis by deducting one meal for guests.
The Gemara further reconciles with Rabbi Shimon by deducting three meals for guests, and with Rabbi Chidka by deducting two meals for guests.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yosi's statement and the omission of wine
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yosi's statement and the omission of wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosi's statement about barley was not that only in Edom do they eat barley, but that only Rabbi Yishmael, who was near Edom, would double the barley portion because Edomite barley is poor. The Gemara then notes that the Mishnah does not mention wine, which supports Rabbi Elazar's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosi's statement, asking whether it implies that only in Edom do people eat barley, but not elsewhere.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yosi meant that only Rabbi Yishmael, who was near Edom, doubled the barley portion because Edomite barley is poor.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not mention wine among the provisions, which supports Rabbi Elazar's view.
The Gemara concludes that the omission of wine supports Rabbi Elazar's position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: No fixed wine for a woman
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: No fixed wine for a woman
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not fix a wine allowance for a woman, but if she says 'I will go after my lovers who give me my bread and water, my wool and flax, my oil and drink,' these are things a woman craves, namely jewelry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one does not fix a wine allowance for a woman, but if she demands it, it is considered jewelry, which she craves.

items.text: Derivation from Hannah: No wine for a woman
items.text_en: Derivation from Hannah: No wine for a woman
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda of Kfar Neburya derives from Hannah that one does not fix wine for a woman, as the verse says 'after she ate and after she drank' (singular), implying she drank alone. The Gemara questions why the same logic doesn't apply to eating, and answers that the change in language indicates a special point.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda of Kfar Neburya derives from the verse about Hannah that one does not fix wine for a woman, because the verse says 'after she drank' (שָׁתָה) in the singular, not 'after they drank' (שָׁתָת).
The Gemara questions why the same logic does not apply to eating, since the verse also says 'after she ate' (אָכְלָה) in the singular.
The Gemara answers that the derivation is based on the change in the verse's language, which indicates a special point about drinking, not eating.

items.text: Challenge and resolution: Accustomed woman gets wine
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution: Accustomed woman gets wine
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from a baraita that an accustomed woman is given wine. The Gemara resolves that an accustomed woman is different, citing Rav Chinana bar Kahana quoting Shmuel: an accustomed woman gets one cup, an unaccustomed woman gets two cups. Abaye explains: accustomed, in her husband's presence – two cups; not in his presence – one cup. Unaccustomed, in his presence – one cup; not in his presence – none at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that an accustomed woman is given wine, contradicting the earlier ruling that wine is not allotted to women.
The Gemara resolves that an accustomed woman is different, citing Rav Chinana bar Kahana quoting Shmuel: an accustomed woman gets one cup, an unaccustomed woman gets two cups.

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Kahana quoting Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Kahana quoting Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Kahana reports in the name of Shmuel that an accustomed woman receives one cup of wine, while an unaccustomed woman receives two cups.

Abaye clarifies the statement: an accustomed woman in her husband's presence gets two cups, not in his presence gets one cup; an unaccustomed woman in his presence gets one cup, not in his presence gets none at all.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Wine for cooking
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Wine for cooking
items.desc_en: Alternatively, 'accustomed' refers to wine for cooking (ציקי קדירה). Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Yochanan relates a story about the daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Gurion, for whom the Sages fixed two se'ah of wine for cooking from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve. She said: 'Thus may you fix for your daughters.' It was taught: She was a yevamah, and they did not answer 'Amen' after her.

sub.desc_en: An alternative explanation states that 'accustomed' refers to wine for cooking, citing a story of Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter-in-law who was allotted two se'ah of wine weekly for cooking, and she cursed the judges.
Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan relates a story about the daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Gurion, for whom the Sages fixed two se'ah of wine for cooking from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve.
The daughter-in-law responds: 'Thus may you fix for your daughters.'
It was taught in a baraita: She was a yevamah (שמרת יבם), and they did not answer 'Amen' after her.

items.text: Effects of wine on women and the case of Hannah
items.text_en: Effects of wine on women and the case of Hannah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: One cup is good for a woman, two is degrading, three leads to public solicitation, four even a donkey solicits in the market and she is not embarrassed. Rava says: This applies only when her husband is not with her, but when her husband is with her, we have no concern. The Gemara questions Hannah, whose husband was with her, and answers that a guest is different, as Rav Huna derives from the verse that a guest is forbidden in marital relations.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches the effects of wine on a woman: one cup is beneficial, two cups are degrading, three lead to public solicitation, and four cause her to solicit even a donkey without embarrassment.
Rava qualifies the baraita: the concern applies only when her husband is not with her, but when her husband is present, there is no concern.
The Gemara objects: Hannah drank wine while her husband Elkana was with her, contradicting Rava's qualification.
The Gemara resolves: a guest (אכסנאי) is different, as Rav Huna derives from the verse that a guest is forbidden in marital relations, so Hannah's case does not apply.

items.text: Story of Huma, wife of Abaye, seeking wine
items.text_en: Story of Huma, wife of Abaye, seeking wine
items.desc_en: Huma, wife of Abaye, came before Rava and asked for sustenance; he granted it. She then asked for wine. Rava said: I know that Nachmani (Abaye) did not drink wine. She replied: By the life of my master, he would give me wine in large goblets like this. While showing him, her arm was revealed, and light fell in the court. Rava went home and sought his wife, daughter of Rav Chisda. She asked who was in court; he said Huma. She went after her, struck her with the bolts of a chest until she drove her out of all Mechoza, saying: You killed three, and you come to kill another?

sub.desc_en: Huma, wife of Abaye, comes before Rava and requests sustenance; he grants it.
Huma asks for wine; Rava objects that Abaye did not drink wine.
Huma swears that Abaye gave her wine in large goblets, and while demonstrating, her arm is revealed and light falls in the court.
Rava goes home and seeks his wife, daughter of Rav Chisda; she asks who was in court.
Bat Rav Chisda pursues Huma, strikes her with chest bolts, drives her out of Mechoza, and accuses her of killing three and seeking to kill another.

items.text: Stories of other women seeking wine and silk
items.text_en: Stories of other women seeking wine and silk
items.desc_en: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Nechemya son of Rav Yosef, who granted her sustenance and wine, noting that the people of Mechoza drink wine. The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Devil came before Rav Yosef, who granted her sustenance and wine. When she asked for silk (שיראי), he asked why, and she replied: For you, your colleague, and your colleague's colleague.

sub.text: Story: Wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava before Rav Nechemya
sub.text_en: Story: Wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava before Rav Nechemya
sub.desc_en: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Nechemya son of Rav Yosef, who granted her sustenance and wine, noting that the people of Mechoza drink wine.

sub.text: Story: Wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya before Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Story: Wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya before Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Devil came before Rav Yosef, who granted her sustenance and wine; when she asked for silk (שיראי), he questioned why, and she replied: For you, your colleague, and your colleague's colleague.

items.text: Provision of bed, mat, and pillows
items.text_en: Provision of bed, mat, and pillows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: He gives her a bed and a mat. The Gemara asks: Why does she need a mat and a rush mat? Rav Papa answers: In a place where they fill the bed with ropes, he provides it. The Rabbis taught: They do not give her a pillow or a bolster. In the name of Rabbi Natan they said: They give her a pillow and a bolster. The Gemara clarifies: If it is her custom, why does the first Tanna disagree? If not her custom, why does Rabbi Natan disagree? The resolution: It is his custom but not hers. The first Tanna says he can take them when he goes and bring them when he returns; Rabbi Natan says she might need them at twilight and he cannot bring them, so she would sleep on the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband provides his wife with a bed and a mat.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions both a mat (מפץ) and a rush mat (מחצלת) as separate items.
Rav Papa answers that in a place where they fill the bed frame with ropes, the mat is provided to cover the ropes.
A baraita is cited: the Rabbis taught that a pillow and bolster are not provided, but Rabbi Natan says they are provided.
The Gemara asks: if it is her custom to use pillows, why does the first Tanna (תנא קמא) disagree; if it is not her custom, why does Rabbi Natan disagree?

The Gemara resolves: it is his custom but not hers; the first Tanna (תנא קמא) says he can take them when he goes and bring them back, while Rabbi Natan says she might need them at twilight and he cannot bring them, so she would sleep on the ground.

items.text: Provision of a cap (כיפה)
items.text_en: Provision of a cap (כיפה)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: He gives her a cap (כיפה). Rav Papa said to Abaye: ... (the text breaks off).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye about the Mishnah's ruling that a husband gives his wife a head covering (כִּפָּה).
Rav Papa begins to ask Abaye a question about the cap mentioned in the Mishnah, but the text breaks off.

items.text: Clarification of the Tanna's statement about shoes
items.text_en: Clarification of the Tanna's statement about shoes
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Tanna who requires three pairs of shoes for a woman, explaining that this applies in a mountainous region where shoes wear out quickly. The Tanna also teaches that these should be given during the festival to bring her joy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Tanna can require three pairs of shoes for a woman, as if he is a messenger who also throws in shoes.
The answer explains that the Tanna refers to a mountainous region where shoes wear out quickly, and also teaches that the shoes should be given during the festival to bring her joy.

items.text: Interpretation of 'fifty zuz' for clothing
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'fifty zuz' for clothing
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the fifty zuz mentioned for clothing refers to small coins (prutot), not actual zuzim, because a poor woman would not have fifty actual zuzim. This is derived from the mishnah's distinction between a poor and honored woman.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the fifty zuz mentioned in the Mishnah are simple (low-quality) coins, not actual fifty zuz.
Abaye proves his point from the Mishnah's distinction between a poor person and a respected one, arguing that a truly poor person could not afford fifty actual zuz.
The gemara infers from the mishnah's distinction between a poor and honored woman that the fifty zuz must be small coins, since a poor woman would not have fifty actual zuzim.

items.text: Surplus of worn-out garments
items.text_en: Surplus of worn-out garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the rule that surplus food money goes to the husband, but surplus worn-out garments go to the wife. Rachaba explains that the wife uses them during her menstrual period to avoid being repulsive to her husband. Abaye adds that for a widow, the surplus goes to her husband's heirs, as she no longer needs to avoid being repulsive to him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule: surplus food money goes to the husband, surplus worn-out garments go to the wife.
The Gemara asks: what purpose does the surplus of worn-out garments serve for the wife?
Rachaba explains that the wife uses them during her menstrual period to avoid being repulsive to her husband.
Abaye adds that for a widow, the surplus goes to her husband's heirs, as she no longer needs to avoid being repulsive to him.

items.text: Dispute over the meaning of 'ochellet'
items.text_en: Dispute over the meaning of 'ochellet'
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether 'ochellet' in the mishnah means eating or marital relations. Rav Nachman says it means eating, while Rav Ashi says it means relations. The Gemara brings support from the mishnah's phrase 'ochellet with him on Shabbat nights' and a challenge from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement about Shabbat day, which Rava resolves by allowing relations in a dark house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'ochellet' means in the mishnah.
Rav Nachman says 'ochellet' means literal eating.
Rav Ashi says 'ochellet' means marital relations.

The Gemara cites the mishnah's phrase 'ochellet with him on Shabbat nights' and explains that for Rav Ashi, 'ochellet' is a euphemism for relations, as in the verse 'אכלה ומחתה פיה' (she ate and wiped her mouth).

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement that she eats on Shabbat nights and Shabbat day, challenging Rav Ashi's view since relations are not permitted during the day.
Rava resolves the objection by noting that relations are permitted in a dark house even during the day, so Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement can still refer to relations.

items.text: Support for a nursing mother
items.text_en: Support for a nursing mother
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the obligation to support a nursing mother's children. Rabbi Ulla taught that one must support even very young children. The Gemara determines the age as up to six, based on Rav Asi's ruling about a child going out with his mother's eruv. It then explains that a nursing mother receives extra food because she needs to eat with the child, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that she should receive wine, which is good for milk.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ulla taught at the entrance of the Nasi's house that although one is not obligated to support older minor children, one must support very young children.
The Gemara defines the age as up to six, based on Rav Asi's ruling that a child of six may rely on his mother's eruv.
The Gemara asks: what is the source for the extra food? It suggests it is because the child needs to eat with her.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the extra food is because the nursing mother is ill, not because of the child's needs.
The Gemara rejects the objection: if it were about illness, the mishnah would say 'if she is ill'; it says 'nursing' to teach that nursing mothers are generally ill.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that a nursing mother should receive extra wine, because wine is beneficial for milk production.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the wife's earnings and inheritance
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the wife's earnings and inheritance
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a wife's found object and earnings belong to her husband, and he eats the produce of her inheritance during her lifetime, but her shame and blemish are hers. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira distinguishes between private and public cases. The Gemara questions what is new, noting that the father's rights were already taught, and explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis is necessary for the laws of shame and blemish.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that a wife's found object and earnings belong to her husband, he eats the produce of her inheritance during her lifetime, but her shame and blemish are hers.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira distinguishes between private and public cases regarding the division of shame and blemish compensation.
The Gemara questions what is new in the mishnah, noting that the father's rights regarding his daughter were already taught in a previous mishnah.
The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis is necessary specifically for the laws of shame and blemish.

items.text: Dispute about the wife's found object
items.text_en: Dispute about the wife's found object
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rava that a wife's found object is hers, but Rabbi Akiva says it belongs to her husband. Rava begins to question this based on the principle of 'ha'adafa' (surplus).

sub.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rava that a wife's found object belongs to herself.
Rabbi Akiva says the found object belongs to her husband.
Rava questions the Tanna, comparing the found object to the surplus earnings.

items.text: Ownership of the wife's earnings and finds
items.text_en: Ownership of the wife's earnings and finds
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that a wife's earnings belong to her husband, but Rabbi Akiva argues that her finds are hers. The Gemara then reinterprets the Mishnah, distinguishing between surplus earned without pressure (husband's) and surplus earned under pressure (disputed). Rav Papa equates her finds to surplus under pressure, aligning with the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that a wife's earnings belong to her husband, and Rabbi Akiva argues that her finds are certainly hers.

A baraita is cited: a woman who vows not to work for her husband does not require annulment, but Rabbi Akiva requires it due to possible surplus; the Gemara then reverses the Mishnah's ruling, stating that a wife's finds belong to her husband, while Rabbi Akiva says they are hers.

Rav Yohanan resolves that all agree surplus earned without pressure belongs to the husband, and the dispute is only over surplus earned under pressure; Rav Papa equates her finds to surplus under pressure, aligning with the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Papa and Ravina's queries on multiple items at once
items.text_en: Rav Papa and Ravina's queries on multiple items at once
items.desc_en: Rav Papa asks whether the rule applies if she made two items at once, and Ravina asks about three or four. The Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand unresolved).

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa asks: if a wife produced two surplus items at once, what is the halacha?
Ravina asks: if a wife produced three or four surplus items at once, what is the halacha?
The Gemara leaves both questions unresolved with 'תיקו' (let it stand).

items.text: Embarrassment payment for a wife
items.text_en: Embarrassment payment for a wife
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Hanan challenges the Mishnah's ruling that a husband receives embarrassment payment for his wife, arguing that embarrassing a horse or spitting on a garment does not require payment. Ravina extends the question to embarrassing a poor man of good family. Rav Ashi distinguishes: the wife is his own body, unlike other cases.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan objects: if one shames his friend's horse, is he liable for embarrassment? A horse has no sense of shame.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Chanan's second objection
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's second objection
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan further objects: if one spits on his friend's garment, is he liable for embarrassment?

The Gemara rejects the objection by citing a baraita: one who spits on a person is liable for 400 zuz, but Rav Papa clarifies that this applies only to the person, not his garment, because a garment has no shame, whereas a wife has shame.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: if one shames a poor man of good family, should he pay embarrassment to all family members?
Rav Ashi answers: there, the family members are not the man's own body, but a wife is considered her husband's own body.

items.text: Mishnah: Dowry pledges and valuations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dowry pledges and valuations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a man pledged money to his son-in-law and the son-in-law died, he can refuse to give it to the brother. It details the valuation of dowry: for 1000 dinars, the husband pledges 15 maneh; for items valued at a maneh, she adds a fifth; for 400, she gives 500.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one who pledges money to his son-in-law and the son-in-law dies may say, 'I intended to give to your brother, but to you I cannot give.'
The Mishnah rules: if a woman pledged to bring 1000 dinars, the husband pledges 15 maneh against it, and against the appraisal he deducts one-fifth.
The Mishnah rules: if an item is appraised at a maneh and worth a maneh, she receives only a maneh; if appraised at a maneh, she gives 31 selas and a dinar; if at 400, she gives 500.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Groom adds a fifth
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Groom adds a fifth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when a groom sets a dowry, he must add a fifth (i.e., one-fifth more than the bride's contribution).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule that a groom adds a fifth to the dowry he sets.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that even if the first husband was an ignoramus and the second a scholar, the widow can refuse the second. It then questions the redundancy of the Mishnah's phrasing about setting a dowry, resolving it by distinguishing between the groom's valuation and the bride's.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, stating that even if the first husband was an ignoramus and the second a scholar, the widow can refuse the second, saying she was willing to give to the first but not to the second.
The Gemara questions the redundancy of the Mishnah's phrasing about setting a dowry, noting it seems to repeat the earlier clause.

The Gemara resolves the redundancy by explaining that the Mishnah teaches both a large valuation (the groom's) and a small valuation (the bride's), and both the groom's valuation and the bride's valuation.

items.text: Mishnah: Coin valuation and groom's expenses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Coin valuation and groom's expenses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that when a bride brings in coins, each Sela is valued at six dinars, and the groom accepts ten dinars per maneh for the spice box. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says everything follows local custom.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules on coin valuation and the groom's spice box expenses, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel deferring to local custom.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the coin valuation
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the coin valuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the math: if a Sela is four dinars, how is it six? It answers that the Mishnah discusses a large business (where profit is high) and a small business (where profit is low), and both cases are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the math: if a Sela is valued at six dinars, the total should be fifteen maneh, not the stated amount.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah discusses both a large business (עסקה רבה) with high profit and a small business (עסקה זוטא) with low profit, and both cases are necessary to teach the law.

items.text: Gemara: Defining the spice box
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining the spice box
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the 'kupa' refers to a spice box, and that this ruling applies only in Jerusalem, where spices were expensive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the 'kupa' (box) mentioned in the Mishnah refers to.
Rav Ashi answers that the 'kupa' is a spice box.
Rav Ashi adds that this ruling applies only in Jerusalem, where spices were expensive.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Ashi's unresolved queries
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Ashi's unresolved queries
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises a series of unresolved questions about whether the ten dinars per maneh apply to a fixed sum or a received sum, and whether it is per day, per week, per month, or per year. The questions remain unanswered (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether the ten dinars per maneh are calculated based on the fixed sum (הנישום) or the sum actually received (המתקבל).
Rav Ashi raises a chain of unresolved conditional questions about whether the payment applies per day, per week, per month, or per year, all left unanswered (תיקו).

items.text: Story: Nakdimon's daughter's dowry
items.text_en: Story: Nakdimon's daughter's dowry
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav recounts that the Sages set a dowry of 400 gold coins for the spice box for Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter, and she blessed them that they should do the same for their daughters, to which they answered Amen.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav recounts that the Sages set a dowry of 400 gold coins for the spice box for Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter.
Nakdimon's daughter blesses the Sages that they should set the same dowry for their own daughters, and they respond with Amen.

items.text: Story: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and the fallen daughter
items.text_en: Story: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and the fallen daughter
items.desc_en: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai encounters Nakdimon's daughter gathering barley from animal dung. She asks for sustenance, and he recalls signing her ketubah for a million gold dinars. He weeps, teaching that when Israel does God's will, no nation rules over them; when not, they are delivered into the hands of a lowly nation, even their animals.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a story: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, riding out of Jerusalem with his disciples, sees a woman gathering barley from among the dung of Arab animals.

The woman asks Rabban Yochanan for sustenance; he asks who she is, and she identifies herself as Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter, explaining that her father's wealth was lost due to lack of charity and her father-in-law's wealth was consumed by the other loss.

The woman asks Rabban Yochanan to recall signing her ketubah for a million gold dinars; he weeps and teaches that when Israel does God's will, no nation rules over them, but when not, they are delivered into the hands of a lowly nation, even their animals.

items.text: Gemara: Questioning Nakdimon's charity
items.text_en: Gemara: Questioning Nakdimon's charity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Did Nakdimon ben Gurion not give charity? It cites a baraita that when he went to the study hall, he had luxurious garments, implying he was wealthy but perhaps not charitable enough.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Nakdimon ben Gurion did not give charity, citing a baraita that he wore luxurious garments when going to the study hall, implying he was wealthy but perhaps not charitable enough.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the earlier contradiction about spreading mats
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the earlier contradiction about spreading mats
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative answers to resolve the contradiction about spreading mats for the poor: either it was done for the rich man's honor, or he did not do what he should have done, as the proverb says 'according to the camel is the burden.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the earlier baraita about spreading mats for the poor and raises the contradiction.
The Gemara offers the first answer: the mats were spread for the rich man's honor, not for the poor.
The Gemara offers the second answer: the rich man did not do what he should have done, as per the proverb.
The Gemara cites the proverb 'according to the camel is the burden' to support the second answer.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony about a wealthy woman's degradation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony about a wealthy woman's degradation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok testifies that he saw a wealthy woman gathering barley from under horses' hooves in Akko, and he applied a verse to her, interpreting 'your kids' as 'your bodies' to indicate her fallen state.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok testifies that he saw a wealthy woman reduced to gathering barley from under horses' hooves in Akko, and he applied the verse 'go in the footsteps of the flock and graze your kids' to her, interpreting 'kids' as 'bodies' to show her degradation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on gold and the objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on gold and the objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if a woman brought gold into the marriage, it is appraised and considered at its value. The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says gold is like vessels, questioning whether this means silver vessels that depreciate. The Gemara deflects that it means gold vessels that do not depreciate, but then objects that it should say 'like his vessels.'

sub.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that if a woman brought gold into the marriage, it is appraised and considered at its value.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says gold is like vessels, questioning whether this means silver vessels that depreciate.
The Gemara deflects that the baraita means gold vessels, which do not depreciate.
The Gemara objects that if it means gold vessels, the baraita should have said 'like his vessels' rather than 'like vessels.'

items.text: Analysis of the baraita about gold and dinars with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita about gold and dinars with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that gold is like vessels and gold dinars are like silver. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that where it is not customary to change them, they are appraised at their value. The Gemara questions which part of the baraita Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is addressing. It first considers the latter clause, but rejects it because the first tanna would then permit changing even where not customary. It then considers the first clause, interpreting 'vessels' as silver vessels. Finally, it suggests that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is addressing the latter clause, and they dispute whether the dinars can be changed with difficulty, with one holding that since they can be changed, we enhance her value, and the other holding that since they can only be changed with difficulty, we do not enhance her value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that gold is like vessels, gold dinars are like silver, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that where it is not customary to change them, they are appraised at their value.
The Gemara asks which clause of the baraita Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is addressing.

The Gemara considers that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel addresses the latter clause, but rejects this because the first tanna would then permit changing even where not customary, which is impossible since the dinars cannot be changed there.
The Gemara suggests that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel addresses the first clause, interpreting 'vessels' as silver vessels, and he says gold is like gold dinars where not customary to change.

The Gemara resolves that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel addresses the latter clause, and the dispute is whether the dinars can be changed with difficulty; one holds that since they can be changed, we enhance her value, and the other holds that since they can only be changed with difficulty, we do not enhance her value.

items.text: Alternative resolution: the entire baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel with a missing clause
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: the entire baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel with a missing clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the entire baraita is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion, and it is missing a clause. The full text would state that gold is like vessels and gold dinars are like silver, but this applies only where it is customary to change them; where it is not customary, they are appraised at their value, according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative resolution: the entire baraita is the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and it is missing a clause; the full text would state that gold is like vessels and gold dinars are like silver, but this applies only where it is customary to change them, while where it is not customary, they are appraised at their value.

items.text: Resolution of the difficulty with 'like his vessels' and Rav Ashi's answer
items.text_en: Resolution of the difficulty with 'like his vessels' and Rav Ashi's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the difficulty that the baraita should say 'like his vessels' and declares it a difficulty. It then offers two answers: either we are dealing with crushed gold, or Rav Ashi says it is about a mold (for making vessels).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the baraita should have said 'like his vessels' (כְּכֵלָיו) rather than 'like vessels' (כְּכֵלִים), and declares it a difficulty.
The Gemara offers a first answer: the case involves crushed gold (דהבא פריכא), which is not made into vessels, so it is compared to vessels in general.
Rav Ashi gives a second answer: the baraita refers to a mold (ממלא) for making vessels, so it is called 'like vessels' because it is a tool for vessels.

items.text: Rulings on other assets: spices, camels, tax-collection rights, and sacks
items.text_en: Rulings on other assets: spices, camels, tax-collection rights, and sacks
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai rules that spices of Antioch are like silver. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yochanan that a woman can collect her ketubah from Arabian camels. Rav Pappi rules that tax-collection seats and sacks of flour and bran are collectible. Rava initially thought that money-bags of Mehoza are collectible because they are a security, but later retracted because they are used to buy land.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai rules that spices of Antioch are treated like silver for collection.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a woman can collect her ketubah from Arabian camels.
Rav Pappi rules that tax-collection seats are collectible for a woman's ketubah.
Rav Pappi rules that sacks of flour and bran are collectible for a woman's ketubah.
Rava initially thought money-bags of Mehoza are collectible as a security, but retracted because they are used to buy land.

items.text: Mishnah: Dowry obligations for a daughter and an orphan
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dowry obligations for a daughter and an orphan
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who marries off his daughter without stipulation must not give less than fifty zuz. If he stipulated to bring her in naked, the husband cannot say he will clothe her when she enters his house, but rather he must clothe her while she is still in her father's house. Similarly, one who marries off an orphan must not give less than fifty zuz. If there is money in the fund, they provide for her according to her honor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who marries off his daughter without stipulation must not give less than fifty zuz.
The Mishnah rules that if a father stipulated to bring his daughter in naked, the husband must clothe her while she is still in her father's house, not after she enters his home.
The Mishnah extends the same minimum of fifty zuz to one who marries off an orphan.
The Mishnah concludes that if there is money in the fund, they provide for the orphan according to her honor.

items.text: Abaye's interpretation: the fifty zuz are small coins
items.text_en: Abaye's interpretation: the fifty zuz are small coins
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the fifty zuz mentioned in the Mishnah are small coins (prutot). He proves this from the later clause that says if there is money in the fund, they provide according to her honor, and Rav Chaba explains that 'fund' refers to the charity purse. If the fifty zuz were actual coins, how much would they give her if there is money? Rather, they are small coins.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asserts that the fifty zuz mentioned in the Mishnah are small coins (פשיטי), not full-value zuzim.

sub.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah's continuation
sub.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah's continuation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's later clause about the charity purse (ארנקי של צדקה) as evidence for Abaye's interpretation.
The Gemara asks: if the fifty zuz were actual coins, how much would they give her from the charity purse?
The Gemara concludes that the fifty zuz must be small coins (פשיטי), as otherwise the Mishnah's later clause would be incoherent.

items.text: Baraita: priority of supporting an orphan girl over an orphan boy
items.text_en: Baraita: priority of supporting an orphan girl over an orphan boy
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if an orphan boy and orphan girl come to be supported, they support the girl first, because a man is accustomed to go door-to-door (to beg), but a woman is not accustomed to do so.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that when an orphan boy and orphan girl come to be supported, the girl is supported first because a man is accustomed to beg door-to-door but a woman is not.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Priority of marrying off the orphan girl
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Priority of marrying off the orphan girl
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when orphans come to be married, the community marries off the orphan girl before the orphan boy, because a woman's shame is greater than a man's.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that when orphans come to marry, the community marries off the orphan girl before the orphan boy because a woman's shame is greater.

items.text: Baraita: Providing a home and wife for an orphan
items.text_en: Baraita: Providing a home and wife for an orphan
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for an orphan who comes to marry, the community rents a house, prepares a bed and all utensils, and then marries him off, based on the verse 'די מחסורו אשר יחסר לו'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that for an orphan who comes to marry, the community hires a house, prepares a bed and utensils, and then marries him off, citing the verse 'די מחסורו' (enough for his lack) to include house, bed, table, and wife.

items.text: Baraita: Extent of provision – even a horse and slave
items.text_en: Baraita: Extent of provision – even a horse and slave
items.desc_en: Another baraita expounds 'די מחסורו' to mean you are commanded to support him but not to enrich him, and 'אשר יחסר לו' includes even a horse to ride and a slave to run before him, as illustrated by Hillel the Elder who bought such for a poor man of good lineage.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds 'די מחסורו' (enough for his lack) to mean you are commanded to support him but not to enrich him, and 'אשר יחסר לו' (what he lacks) includes even a horse to ride and a slave to run before him, illustrated by Hillel the Elder who bought a horse and slave for a poor man of good lineage and once ran before him three miles.
The baraita expounds 'אשר יחסר לו' (that which he lacks) to include even a horse to ride and a slave to run before him, expanding the scope of provision.
The baraita cites a story about Hillel the Elder who bought a horse and a slave for a poor man of good lineage, and once ran before him three miles when no slave was available.

items.text: Story: A litra of meat daily for a poor man of good lineage
items.text_en: Story: A litra of meat daily for a poor man of good lineage
items.desc_en: A story is told of the people of Upper Galilee who bought a litra of meat daily for a poor man of good lineage. Rav Huna explains it was poultry, and Rav Ashi says it was a small village where they would lose an animal daily for him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that the people of Upper Galilee bought a litra of meat daily for a poor man of good lineage from Tzippori, and the gemara discusses the significance of this amount, with Rav Huna saying it was poultry and Rav Ashi explaining it was a small village where the meat caused a loss of wild game.
The gemara questions what is so remarkable about a litra of meat daily.
Rav Huna answers that the meat was poultry, which was expensive.
An alternative answer suggests it was a litra of actual meat, not poultry.
Rav Ashi explains that it was a small village where they would lose an animal daily for him, making the expense understandable.

items.text: Story: Rabbi Nechemya and the poor man who died from lentils
items.text_en: Story: Rabbi Nechemya and the poor man who died from lentils
items.desc_en: A poor man came before Rabbi Nechemya, who asked what he ate. The man said fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nechemya suggested he subsist on lentils, the man agreed and died. The Gemara clarifies that the man himself was at fault for not adjusting his expectations.

sub.desc_en: A poor man came before Rabbi Nechemya, who asked what he ate; the man said fatty meat and aged wine, and when Rabbi Nechemya suggested lentils, the man agreed and died, leading Rabbi Nechemya to lament that he killed him.
The gemara objects that Rabbi Nechemya should have said 'woe to Nechemya who killed him,' but resolves that the man himself should not have indulged so much.
The Gemara resolves that the poor man himself was at fault for not adjusting his expectations, so Rabbi Nechemya's lament was appropriate.

items.text: Story: Rava and the poor man who ate a fattened chicken
items.text_en: Story: Rava and the poor man who ate a fattened chicken
items.desc_en: Another poor man came before Rava, who asked what he ate. The man said a fattened chicken and aged wine. Rava questioned his concern for the public burden, and the man replied that he eats from God, not from them, citing the verse 'עיני כל אליך ישברו'.

sub.desc_en: A poor man came before Rava, who asked what he ate; the man said a fattened chicken and aged wine, and when Rava questioned concern for the public burden, the man cited the verse 'עיני כל אליך ישברו' (the eyes of all look to You) to argue that God provides each person's sustenance at its proper time.
The poor man answers that he eats a fattened chicken and aged wine.
Rava questions whether the poor man is concerned about burdening the public.
The poor man retorts that he eats from God, not from the public.
The poor man cites a baraita from the verse 'עיני כל אליך ישברו' to prove that God provides each person's sustenance at the right time.

items.text: Rava's sister arrives with the same food
items.text_en: Rava's sister arrives with the same food
items.desc_en: While they were speaking, Rava's sister, whom he hadn't seen in thirteen years, arrived with a fattened chicken and aged wine. Rava invited the poor man to eat, saying he had been answered.

sub.desc_en: Meanwhile, Rava's sister, who had not seen him for thirteen years, arrived with a fattened chicken and aged wine, and Rava, realizing the man's request was justified, invited him to eat.
Rava asks the poor man what is before him, and the poor man replies that Rava has been answered; Rava invites him to eat.

items.text: Dispute: How to give to one who refuses charity
