items.text_en: Dispute: How to give to one who refuses charity
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute about one who has nothing and refuses to be supported. Rabbi Meir says give as a loan then as a gift; the Sages say give as a gift then as a loan. Rava explains 'as a gift' means to open for him as a gift. For one who has but refuses, Rabbi Meir says give as a gift and collect after death; Rabbi Shimon says do not give at all; for one who has nothing, demand a pledge to preserve dignity.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a dispute: for one who has nothing and refuses support, Rabbi Meir says give as a loan then as a gift.
The Sages counter: give as a gift first, then as a loan.
The gemara objects: if offered as a gift, the poor person will not accept it.
Rava resolves: 'give as a gift' means to open the hand for him as a gift (so he takes it as a loan in his mind).
The baraita shifts to the case of one who has but refuses: give as a gift and collect after death.
The gemara objects: if they collect from him, he will not accept the gift.
Rav Pappa resolves: the collection is after death, so the recipient does not know.
Rabbi Shimon says: for one who has but refuses, do not give at all.
Rabbi Shimon adds: for one who has nothing and refuses, demand a pledge to preserve his dignity.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation of 'העבט' and 'תעביטנו'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation of 'העבט' and 'תעביטנו'
items.desc_en: Another baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda, who interprets 'העבט' as referring to one who has nothing and refuses, giving as a loan then as a gift, and 'תעביטנו' as one who has and refuses, giving as a gift and collecting after death. The Sages say that for one who has and refuses, we do not give at all, and 'תעביטנו' is just the Torah's manner of speech.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation of 'העבט' as referring to one who has nothing and refuses, given as a loan then a gift, and 'תעביטנו' as one who has and refuses, given as a gift then collected after death.
The Sages object that for one who has and refuses, we do not give at all, and 'תעביטנו' is merely the Torah's manner of speech.

items.text: Story: Mar Ukva and the poor neighbor – avoiding embarrassment
items.text_en: Story: Mar Ukva and the poor neighbor – avoiding embarrassment
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva had a poor neighbor to whom he would throw four zuzim daily through a door hinge. One day the neighbor tried to see who was doing it, and Mar Ukva and his wife fled into a furnace that was still hot. His wife's feet were less burned because she was more frequently at home. The Gemara explains that it is better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to embarrass someone publicly, as learned from Tamar.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Mar Ukva's practice of secretly giving four zuzim daily to a poor neighbor through a door hinge, and the day the neighbor tried to discover the benefactor.
Describes how Mar Ukva and his wife fled into a hot furnace to avoid being identified, and his wife's feet were less burned because she was more frequently at home.
Explains that it is better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to embarrass someone publicly, citing the precedent of Tamar.

items.text: Mar Ukva's charity and his deathbed distribution
items.text_en: Mar Ukva's charity and his deathbed distribution
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva would send four hundred zuz to a poor neighbor every Yom Kippur eve. Once his son reported that the neighbor was being served aged wine, so Mar Ukva increased the amount. On his deathbed, he found he had given away seven thousand dinars, and distributed half his wealth, despite the rule not to give more than a fifth, because that rule applies only during life, not after death.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes Mar Ukva's regular practice of sending four hundred zuz to a poor neighbor every Yom Kippur eve, and how one year, upon learning the neighbor was being served aged wine, he doubled the amount.

On his deathbed, Mar Ukva reviewed his charity accounts, found he had given away seven thousand dinars, and distributed half his wealth, justifying this by citing Rabbi Ila'i's rule that the limit of one-fifth applies only during life, not after death.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's method of giving charity
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's method of giving charity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba would tie coins in his scarf and throw it behind him, then go to the poor people's doorways, and avert his eyes from swindlers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba would tie coins in his scarf and throw it behind him, making himself available to the poor while avoiding deceivers.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's regular charity and the poor man's refusal
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's regular charity and the poor man's refusal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina would send four zuz to a poor man every Friday. One week his wife reported that the poor man said he didn't need it. She heard them asking him what he eats, implying he was being supported elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina regularly sent four zuz to a poor man before Shabbat; one week his wife reported the man said he didn't need it, and when asked why, she heard people asking him what he eats.

items.text: Gemara's opening: praise for deceivers and the severity of ignoring charity
items.text_en: Gemara's opening: praise for deceivers and the severity of ignoring charity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'silver coins' or 'gold coins' are meant, then cites Rabbi Elazar praising deceivers for preventing sin. A baraita from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha equates ignoring charity to idolatry through a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the 'silver coins' or 'gold coins' are meant in the Mishnah.
Rabbi Elazar praises deceivers (רמאין) for preventing sin, citing a verse about calling out to God.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: A baraita equates ignoring charity to idolatry through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'בליעל'.

items.text: Baraita on the consequences of feigning disability and receiving charity unnecessarily
items.text_en: Baraita on the consequences of feigning disability and receiving charity unnecessarily
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who blinds his eye, distends his belly, or cripples his leg will not die before actually needing such aid. Similarly, one who accepts charity unnecessarily will eventually come to need it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one who feigns blindness, a distended belly, or a crippled leg will not die before actually needing such aid, and one who accepts charity unnecessarily will eventually come to need it.

items.text: Contradiction about selling household items for charity and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction about selling household items for charity and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: a mishnah says one is not forced to sell his house or utensils, but a baraita says one must downgrade from gold to silver to copper vessels. Rav Zevid resolves by distinguishing between beds/tables (not sold) and cups/dishes (sold due to disgust). Rava bar Rabbah adds a case of a silver plow. Rav Pappa resolves differently: before collection, one is not forced; after collection, one is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a mishnah says one is not forced to sell his house or utensils, but a baraita says one must downgrade from gold to silver to copper vessels.
Rav Zevid resolves by distinguishing between beds/tables (not sold) and cups/dishes (sold due to disgust), and Rava bar Rabbah adds a case of a silver plow.
Rav Pappa resolves differently: before collection, one is not forced; after collection, one is.

items.text: Mishnah: Orphaned daughter married with consent can later claim her due
items.text_en: Mishnah: Orphaned daughter married with consent can later claim her due
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if an orphaned daughter was married by her mother or brothers with her consent and they wrote her a dowry of 100 or 50 zuz, she can later claim what she was entitled to. Rabbi Yehuda says if they married off the first daughter, they must give the second similarly. The Sages say circumstances change, so the court assesses the estate and gives accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that an orphaned daughter married with consent by her mother or brothers can later claim what she was entitled to.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that if the father married off the first daughter, the second must receive similarly.
The Sages argue that circumstances change, so the court assesses the estate and gives accordingly.

items.text: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling on assessing for sustenance and its challenge
items.text_en: Gemara: Shmuel's ruling on assessing for sustenance and its challenge
items.desc_en: Shmuel says for 'sustenance' (parnasa), we assess based on the father's estimation. A baraita is cited that says daughters are sustained and provided for from the father's estate, and we assess the estate. The Gemara initially thinks this refers to the husband's sustenance, but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it means her own sustenance. The Gemara then distinguishes between food/drink and clothing/covering.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that for 'sustenance' (פרנסה), we assess based on the father's estimation.
The Gemara challenges Shmuel by citing a baraita that says daughters are sustained and provided for from the father's estate, and we assess the estate.
The Gemara initially assumes the baraita refers to the husband's sustenance.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that the baraita refers to her own sustenance, not the husband's.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita's two terms 'ניזונות' (sustained) and 'מתפרנסות' (provided for) refer to two different types of sustenance.
The Gemara resolves that both terms refer to her own sustenance, distinguishing between food/drink and clothing/covering.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel from the mishnah and resolution: he follows Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel from the mishnah and resolution: he follows Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Sages' statement about 'poor' and 'rich', concluding it refers to mental state, not wealth. This contradicts Shmuel's view that we follow the father's estimation. The Gemara resolves that Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who says if he married off the first daughter, he gives to the second as he gave to the first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah's statement that sometimes a person is poor and becomes rich, and asks what 'poor' and 'rich' mean in this context.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that 'poor' and 'rich' refer to financial status, since the first Tanna would then have no case of a rich man who became poor.
The Gemara concludes that 'poor' and 'rich' refer to mental state, and this contradicts Shmuel's view that we follow the father's estimation.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yehuda, who says that if he married off the first daughter, he gives to the second as he gave to the first.

items.text: Clarification of Shmuel's statement and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of Shmuel's statement and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement was necessary to teach that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning applies even without marrying off, and the mishnah's case of marrying off shows the Sages' strength. Rava asks Rav Chisda to rule like Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Chisda blesses him for teaching good things.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shmuel did not simply rule explicitly that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara explains that Shmuel's statement was necessary to teach that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning applies even without marrying off, not only when he actually married her off.
The Gemara adds that the mishnah's case of marrying off was only to demonstrate the strength of the Sages, who do not follow estimation even when the father's intent is revealed.
Rava asks Rav Chisda to rule like Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Chisda blesses him for teaching good things.

items.text: Contradiction in Rava's rulings and resolution: assessed vs. not assessed
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rava's rulings and resolution: assessed vs. not assessed
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rava ruled like Rabbi Yehuda, but also ruled like Rabbi who says a daughter supported by brothers takes a tenth of the estate. The resolution is that one case is where the father's estimation is known, the other where it is not. This is supported by a story of Rabbi giving one-twelfth. The Gemara then cites Rabbi's statement and a challenge about ten daughters and one son, with Rabbi's response that they take tenths in order and then divide equally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rava can rule like Rabbi Yehuda (following the father's estimation) when he also ruled like Rabbi, who gives a daughter a fixed tenth of the estate.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one case is where the father's estimation is known (אומדנא), the other where it is not.
Rav Adda bar Ahava cites a story where Rabbi gave only one-twelfth, supporting the distinction between assessed and unassessed cases.
The Gemara confirms that the contradiction in Rabbi's own practice is resolved by the same distinction, concluding definitively.
The Gemara cites Rabbi's original ruling that a daughter supported by brothers takes a tenth of the estate.
The Sages challenge Rabbi: if each daughter takes a tenth, a man with ten daughters and one son would leave nothing for the son.
Rabbi explains that the daughters take tenths sequentially from the remaining estate, then divide the remainder equally, so the son always receives something.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on daughters marrying simultaneously
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's ruling on daughters marrying simultaneously
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's statement about daughters dividing equally applies when they all marry at once. Rav Mattanah supports this, explaining that they take one tithe together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether each daughter takes a tithe for herself individually.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means they divide equally only if they all marry simultaneously.
Rav Mattanah supports this interpretation, stating that if all come to marry at once, they take one tithe together.
The Gemara objects that taking one tithe (a single tithe) is absurd.
The Gemara corrects: they take a tithe together (i.e., one tithe divided among them).

items.text: Baraita on loss of sustenance and parnasah for daughters
items.text_en: Baraita on loss of sustenance and parnasah for daughters
items.desc_en: A baraita states that daughters who married before maturity or matured before marriage lose their sustenance but not their parnasah, according to Rabbi. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says they also lose parnasah, and they hire husbands to receive it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that daughters who matured before marriage or married before maturity lose their sustenance (מזונות) but not their parnasah (פרנסה), according to Rabbi.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar argues that daughters also lose their parnasah, and they hire husbands to receive it.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi. Rava objects from a baraita about an orphan who married with consent, which implies that only a minor can later claim her due, but an adult waives it. The Gemara resolves that the distinction is whether she protested.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Huna that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi's position regarding the daughters' sustenance.
Rava objects by citing a baraita about an orphan who married with consent, which implies that only a minor can later claim her due, but an adult waives it — contradicting Rav Nachman's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where she protested (מחאי) and one where she did not protest (לא מחאי).

items.text: Support for the distinction from Rabbi's own teaching
items.text_en: Support for the distinction from Rabbi's own teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports the distinction by noting that Rabbi himself says a daughter who is supported by brothers takes a tithe, but one who is not supported does not. This confirms the difference between protesting and not protesting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the distinction is logically necessary, because otherwise Rabbi's own statements would contradict each other: he rules that a daughter supported by brothers takes a tithe, but one not supported does not.
The Gemara concludes that the distinction between protesting and not protesting is indeed correct, as demonstrated by Rabbi's own teaching.

items.text: Ravina's report and Rava's apparent contradiction
items.text_en: Ravina's report and Rava's apparent contradiction
items.desc_en: Ravina reports that Rava said a daughter who matured or married does not need to protest, but if both occurred she must. Rava's earlier objection seems to contradict this, but the Gemara resolves that the difference is whether she was being supported by them.

sub.desc_en: Ravina reports to Rava that Rav Adda bar Ahavah said in Rava's name: a daughter who matured (בגרה) or married (נשאת) does not need to protest (למחות), but if both occurred she must protest.
The Gemara questions whether Rava actually said this, given that Rava earlier objected to Rav Nachman and was answered with the distinction between protesting and not protesting.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the case where she must protest is when she is being supported by them (מיתזנא מינייהו), and the case where she does not need to protest is when she is not being supported by them.

items.text: The nature of parnasah compared to the ketubah's condition
items.text_en: The nature of parnasah compared to the ketubah's condition
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says parnasah is not like the ketubah's condition. The Gemara explores possible meanings: parnasah is collected from encumbered property or from movables, but Rabbi holds both are collectible. Ultimately, the difference is that a father can stipulate that daughters not receive parnasah, but not that they not receive sustenance.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna reports in the name of Rabbi that parnasah (the daughters' portion from the father's estate) is not like the condition of the ketubah.
The Gemara asks what the statement that parnasah is not like the ketubah's condition means.

The Gemara suggests that the difference is that parnasah is collected from encumbered property (משועבדים) while the ketubah's condition is not, but rejects this because it is well-known that parnasah is collected and sustenance is not.
The Gemara alternatively suggests that parnasah is collected even from movables (מטלטלי) while the ketubah's condition is collected only from land (מקרקעי).

The Gemara objects that for Rabbi, both parnasah and the ketubah's condition are collected from both land and movables, citing a baraita where Rabbi rules that both types of property are used for the woman's sustenance and daughters' portion.

The Gemara resolves that the difference is that a father can stipulate that his daughters not receive parnasah (אל יתפרנסו) and his instruction is followed, but he cannot stipulate that they not receive sustenance (אל יזונו), because parnasah is not like the ketubah's condition.

items.text: Rav's ambiguous query to Rabbi and its resolution
items.text_en: Rav's ambiguous query to Rabbi and its resolution
items.desc_en: Rav asks Rabbi about brothers who 'shiyabdu' (mortgaged or sold) property for a daughter's needs. Rabbi Chiyya clarifies whether they sold or mortgaged, but Rav intentionally wrote ambiguously to cover both possibilities, reasoning that a clear answer on one would imply the other.

sub.desc_en: Rav sends an ambiguous query to Rabbi about brothers who 'שיעבוד' (mortgaged or sold) property for a daughter's needs.
Rabbi Chiyya asks Rav whether they sold or mortgaged, and Rabbi answers that in either case, the court may seize property for a daughter's support (פרנסה) but not for her maintenance (מזונות).
The Gemara objects: if Rav only needed to know about one case, why didn't he write the specific term?
The Gemara explains that Rav needed to know both cases and intentionally wrote the ambiguous term 'שיעבוד' to cover both possibilities, reasoning that a clear answer on one would imply the other.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the unresolved question
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the unresolved question
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that in both cases (sale or mortgage) the property is not taken back. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan was unaware of Rabbi's ruling or rejected it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that in both cases (sale or mortgage) the property is not taken back.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan was unaware of Rabbi's ruling or rejected it.

items.text: Proof from a case of two daughters and a son
items.text_en: Proof from a case of two daughters and a son
items.desc_en: A case is brought where a man died leaving two daughters and a son; the first daughter took her tenth, then the son died. Rabbi Yochanan says the second daughter forfeited. Rabbi Chanina objects, citing the principle that property is taken for sustenance but not maintenance. The Gemara deflects, suggesting Rabbi Yochanan may have accepted Rabbi's ruling, but the case differs due to 'profit for the house'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case where a man died leaving two daughters and a son; the first daughter took her tenth, then the son died before the second daughter could collect.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that the second daughter forfeited her right to the tenth.
Rabbi Chanina objects, citing the principle that property is taken for sustenance (פרנסה) but not for maintenance (מזונות), implying the second daughter should still collect.
The Gemara deflects, suggesting that Rabbi Yochanan may not have heard Rabbi's ruling, but if he had, he would accept it; the case differs because there is 'profit for the house' (רווח ביתא).

items.text: Rav Yemar's challenge to Rav Ashi about 'profit for the house'
items.text_en: Rav Yemar's challenge to Rav Ashi about 'profit for the house'
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar asks Rav Ashi if any profit for the house would exempt a daughter from her tenth. Rav Ashi clarifies he meant profit from these specific assets.

sub.text: Rav Yemar's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar challenges Rav Ashi: if any profit for the house exempts a daughter from her tenth, then even a found object would exempt her.
Rav Ashi clarifies that he meant profit specifically from these assets, not any general profit.

items.text: Amemar and Rav Ashi debate: daughter as heir or creditor
items.text_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi debate: daughter as heir or creditor
items.desc_en: Amemar says the daughter is an heir, so she cannot be paid off with money. Rav Ashi argues she is a creditor, and Amemar later retracts, as shown by a case where he allowed payment with money.

sub.desc_en: Amemar asserts that the daughter is an heir (יורשת), so the brother cannot pay her off with money or land.
Rav Ashi argues that the daughter is a creditor (בעלת חוב), and cites a case where Amemar himself allowed payment with money, showing he retracted.

items.text: Practical difference: collection from medium or poor quality land
items.text_en: Practical difference: collection from medium or poor quality land
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical difference between the daughter being a creditor or heir: as a creditor, she collects from medium-quality land without an oath, or from poor-quality land with an oath. A case with Rav Ashi's daughter confirms this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: now that the daughter is considered a creditor, what practical difference does it make whether she collects from the father's estate or the brothers' estate?
The Gemara answers: the difference is that as a creditor she collects from medium-quality land without an oath, or from poor-quality land with an oath.
The Gemara cites a case where Ravina collected for Rav Ashi's daughter from medium-quality land without an oath, and from poor-quality land with an oath, confirming the practical difference.

items.text: Correspondence about collecting the tenth from various assets
items.text_en: Correspondence about collecting the tenth from various assets
items.desc_en: Rav Nechemya instructs Rabbah bar Rav Huna to collect the tenth even from a cloak. Rav Ashi adds from house rent. Rav Anan sends a vague message to Rav Huna, leading to a dispute about whether from land or movables, and who sits first at the mourners' feast. Mar Ukva resolves the matter.

sub.text: Rav Nechemya bar Rav Yosef's instruction
sub.text_en: Rav Nechemya bar Rav Yosef's instruction
sub.desc_en: Rav Nechemya bar Rav Yosef sends a message to Rabbah bar Rav Huna instructing him to collect the tenth of assets even from a cloak.
Rav Ashi adds that when he was in the house of Rav Kahana, they would collect even from house rent.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's challenge to Rav Anan's vague message
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's challenge to Rav Anan's vague message
sub.desc_en: Rav Anan sends a vague message to Rav Huna about collecting the tenth; Rav Sheshet, sitting before Rav Huna, tells him to respond by demanding clarification whether from land or movables and who sits first at the mourners' feast.
Rav Sheshet goes to Rav Anan and reports the exchange; Rav Anan then goes to Mar Ukva, who resolves the matter by explaining the meaning of 'marzeicha'.

items.text: Definition of 'marzeach' and the mourner's seating
items.text_en: Definition of 'marzeach' and the mourner's seating
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the meaning of 'marzeach' as mourning, citing a verse. Rabbi Abahu derives from a verse that a mourner sits at the head, but a correction is made that the verse reads 'yinnachem' (will be comforted). Mar Zutra offers an alternative derivation from another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the actual incident and criticizes the messenger for not knowing the meaning of 'marzeach'.
The Gemara explains that 'marzeach' means mourning, citing a verse from Jeremiah.
Rabbi Abahu derives from a verse that a mourner sits at the head.
The Gemara objects that the verse reads 'yenachem' (will comfort others), not about the mourner himself.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak corrects that the verse actually reads 'yinnachem' (will be comforted), referring to the mourner.
Mar Zutra offers an alternative derivation from another verse about 'marzeach'.

items.text: Rava's ruling on collecting from land
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on collecting from land
items.desc_en: Rava states a halakha: collection is made from land (מקרקעי) and not from movable property (מטלטלי), whether for sustenance, ketubah, or support.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that collection is made from land (מקרקעי) and not from movable property (מטלטלי), whether for sustenance, ketubah, or support.

items.text: Mishnah: Depositing money for a daughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: Depositing money for a daughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a father deposits money for his daughter. If she says her husband is trustworthy, Rabbi Meir rules the trustee does as instructed; Rabbi Yosei compares it to a field she can sell. The distinction is made between a grown daughter and a minor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a father depositing money for his daughter; Rabbi Meir rules that if she declares her husband trustworthy, the trustee follows the deposit instructions.
Rabbi Yosei objects, comparing the daughter's declaration to a field she can sell immediately, implying her statement is effective.
The Mishnah distinguishes between a grown daughter, whose statement is valid, and a minor, whose action is meaningless.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah and baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah and baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on the Mishnah, distinguishing between a grown daughter and a minor, and between after marriage and after betrothal. The Gemara questions what the dispute is about, initially suggesting a minor after marriage, then reinterprets the Mishnah as Rabbi Meir's view with missing details, concluding the dispute is about a grown daughter after betrothal.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited, elaborating on the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei regarding a father who deposits money with a third party for his daughter, distinguishing between a grown daughter and a minor, and between after marriage and after betrothal.
The Gemara asks what the practical difference is between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei, initially suggesting it is a minor daughter after marriage.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's clause about a minor having no legal capacity is redundant if attributed to Rabbi Yosei, since his earlier statement already implies it.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is actually Rabbi Meir's view, but it is missing details: the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei is specifically about a grown daughter after betrothal.

items.text: Ruling on the halakha
items.text_en: Ruling on the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yosei, while Rava in the name of Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi Meir.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava reports in the name of Rav Nachman that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Ilfa's challenge and the baraita about giving shekels
items.text_en: Ilfa's challenge and the baraita about giving shekels
items.desc_en: Ilfa puts himself in danger, vowing to jump if he cannot resolve a difficulty from the Mishnah. An old sage teaches him a baraita about a man who says 'give a shekel to my sons on Shabbat' and the rules when they are entitled to a sela. Ilfa asks whose opinion it is.

sub.desc_en: Ilfa puts himself in danger, vowing to jump from a ship's mast if he cannot resolve a difficulty from the Mishnah with a baraita from the school of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya.

An old sage teaches Ilfa a baraita about a man who says 'give a shekel to my sons on Shabbat' and the rules when they are entitled to a sela, including the exception when the father specifies 'if they die, others shall inherit'.
Ilfa asks whose opinion the baraita represents, seeking to resolve his difficulty.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's ruling and the halakha
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's ruling and the halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous mishna as Rabbi Meir's view that one must fulfill the words of the deceased. Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva states the halakha: whether the dying person said 'give' or 'do not give,' the court provides for the children's needs. The Gemara questions this, noting that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir, and resolves that in other matters one must fulfill the deceased's words, but here the deceased's intent was to spur the children to action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous mishna as Rabbi Meir's view that one must fulfill the words of the deceased.
Rav Chisda citing Mar Ukva states the halakha: whether the dying person said 'give' or 'do not give,' the court provides for the children's needs.
The Gemara questions how the halakha can contradict Rabbi Meir's principle that one must fulfill the deceased's words.
The Gemara resolves that in other matters one must fulfill the deceased's words, but here the deceased's intent was to spur the children to action.

items.text: The ruling on minors' transactions and the role of a guardian
items.text_en: The ruling on minors' transactions and the role of a guardian
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna that minors' purchases and sales of movable property are valid. Rafram limits this to cases without a guardian; if there is a guardian, their transactions are invalid. The Gemara proves this from a baraita stating that a minor girl's actions are void, and rejects the possibility that the presence of a third party changes the ruling, concluding that even in general cases the minor's actions are void when a guardian exists.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna stating that minors' purchases and sales of movable property are valid.
Rafram limits the mishna's ruling to cases without a guardian; if a guardian exists, the minor's transactions are invalid.
The Gemara proves Rafram's position from a baraita stating that a minor girl's actions are void, implying the same for a minor with a guardian.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might be limited to a case with a third-party trustee (שליש), not a general guardian.
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that if the baraita were only about a trustee, it would have said 'but for a minor girl, the trustee should do as instructed'.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita's blanket statement 'a minor's actions are void' implies the same even in general cases with a guardian.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, The Finding of the Woman,' indicating a return to the main topic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the phrase 'We have returned to you, The Finding of the Woman,' indicating a return to the main topic.

items.text: Mishna: Vows that restrict the wife
items.text_en: Mishna: Vows that restrict the wife
items.desc_en: The mishna presents cases where a husband vows to prevent his wife from benefiting from him, or from tasting certain foods, or from adorning herself. The time limits for keeping the wife without divorce vary: for general benefit, up to thirty days; for food, immediate divorce; for adornment, Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between poor and wealthy women. Rabbi Yehuda adds distinctions between Israelites and priests.

sub.desc_en: The mishna opens with the case of a husband who vows to prevent his wife from benefiting from him, setting a 30-day limit before he must divorce and pay her ketubah.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between an Israelite husband (one month to keep, two to divorce) and a priest (two months to keep, three to divorce).
The mishna presents the case of a husband who vows to prevent his wife from tasting any fruit, requiring immediate divorce.
Rabbi Yehuda again distinguishes between an Israelite (one day to keep, two to divorce) and a priest (two days to keep, three to divorce).
The mishna presents the case of a husband who vows to prevent his wife from adorning herself, requiring immediate divorce.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between a poor woman (no fixed time limit) and a wealthy woman (30 days).

items.text: Gemara's question: How can a husband vow against his wife's benefit?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: How can a husband vow against his wife's benefit?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a husband can vow to prevent his wife from benefiting from him, given that he is legally obligated to support her. It cites a mishna where a wife's vow not to work for her husband is not annulled, showing she cannot void his right to her earnings. The Gemara answers that the husband can say to her, 'Go out with your earnings in exchange for your maintenance,' thereby offsetting his obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a husband can vow to prevent his wife from benefiting from him, given that he is legally obligated to support her.
The Gemara cites a mishna where a wife's vow not to work for her husband is not annulled, showing she cannot void his right to her earnings.
The Gemara answers that the husband can say to her, 'Go out with your earnings in exchange for your maintenance,' thereby offsetting his obligation.

items.text: Initial challenge: why no need to annul the vow?
items.text_en: Initial challenge: why no need to annul the vow?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a husband who vowed his wife's handiwork as a konam does not need to annul the vow, given that she could say 'I will not be supported and I will not work,' making it as if she said so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges why a husband who vowed his wife's handiwork as a konam does not need to annul the vow, given that she could say 'I will not be supported and I will not work,' making it as if she said so.

items.text: Revised explanation: he actually says it
items.text_en: Revised explanation: he actually says it
items.desc_en: The Gemara retracts the previous assumption and states that the husband actually says to her 'Go out, your handiwork is for your sustenance.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: it does not mean the husband's statement is treated as if he said 'go out with your handiwork for your sustenance,' but rather he explicitly says so.

items.text: Clarifying the steward's role
items.text_en: Clarifying the steward's role
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the steward is needed when the wife can afford large items but not small ones, and the Gemara specifies that this applies when she was accustomed to receiving small items from her father's house and now cannot due to the vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the husband says 'go out with your handiwork for your sustenance,' why does he need a steward (פרנס) at all? And if she cannot afford it, the difficulty returns.
Rav Ashi answers: the case is where she can afford large items but not small ones, so the steward provides the small items.
The Gemara asks: what are these small items? If she was accustomed to them, she already has them; if not, why does she need a steward?
The Gemara resolves: she was accustomed to receiving small items from her father's house, and she would rely on him; now that he vowed, she cannot rely on him, so the steward provides them.

items.text: Reason for the 30-day limit
items.text_en: Reason for the 30-day limit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that within 30 days, people have not heard about the vow and there is no disgrace, but beyond that, it becomes known and causes disgrace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the thirty-day limit: within thirty days, people have not heard and there is no disgrace; beyond that, they hear and it causes disgrace.
The Gemara answers that within 30 days people have not heard of the vow and there is no disgrace, but beyond that it becomes known and causes disgrace.

items.text: Alternative: when she was betrothed and time arrived
items.text_en: Alternative: when she was betrothed and time arrived
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case is when he vowed while she was betrothed and the wedding time arrived but they were not married, as per the mishnah that such a woman eats from his food and terumah. The 30-day limit is because within that time the agent fulfills his mission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative scenario: the husband vowed when she was betrothed and the wedding time arrived but they were not yet married.
The Gemara cites a mishnah that when the wedding time arrived and they were not married, the betrothed woman eats from her husband's food and terumah.
The Gemara explains that the 30-day limit is because within that time the agent fulfills his mission, but beyond that he does not.

items.text: Another alternative: betrothed and then married
items.text_en: Another alternative: betrothed and then married
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests she was betrothed and then married, but the objection is raised that she accepted the vow upon marriage. The Gemara concludes that the original explanation stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative explanation: the husband vowed when she was betrothed and then she married.
The Gemara objects: once she married, she accepted the vow knowingly, so why would he need to annul it?
The Gemara answers: she can claim she thought she could endure the vow but now finds she cannot.
The Gemara objects: this reasoning applies to physical defects (מוּמִין), but regarding sustenance (מְזוֹנֵי) do we say the same?
The Gemara concludes: rather, the original explanation (that she was betrothed and the time arrived but they had not married) is the clarified version.

items.text: The steward and the statement 'whoever provides does not lose'
items.text_en: The steward and the statement 'whoever provides does not lose'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the steward acts based on the husband's statement 'whoever provides does not lose,' which is not a direct command. The Gemara distinguishes this from a case of a man in a pit asking someone to write a get, and from Rabbi Ami's ruling about fire, where the statement is permitted only to avoid Sabbath violations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the steward can act without being a direct agent of the husband, given the husband's vow.
Rav Huna explains that the husband says 'whoever provides does not lose,' which is not a direct command but a general statement.
The Gemara objects that even a general statement like 'whoever hears my voice shall write a get' is considered an agency, citing a baraita about a man in a pit.
The Gemara rejects the objection, distinguishing that the man in the pit said 'let them write' (a directive), whereas here the husband only says 'whoever provides' (a descriptive statement).

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Ami's ruling about fire permits only 'whoever extinguishes does not lose' to avoid Sabbath violations, implying that normally such a statement would be forbidden as agency.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Ami's leniency is specifically to exclude other Sabbath prohibitions, not to permit agency in general.

items.text: Baraita on a person prohibited from benefiting
items.text_en: Baraita on a person prohibited from benefiting
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita where a person prohibited from benefiting from another can go to a regular storekeeper and hint, but cannot say 'whoever provides does not lose.' The Gemara explains that the baraita is not needed for the latter case, as it teaches that even the hint is permitted only because it is not a direct command.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita where a person prohibited from benefiting from another can hint to a regular storekeeper, but cannot say 'whoever provides does not lose'.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is not needed for the latter case, as it teaches that even the hint is permitted only because it is not a direct command.

items.text: Full baraita and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Full baraita and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the complete baraita detailing how a person prohibited from benefiting can obtain food, building, and other services through intermediaries, and concludes with Rava explaining Rabbi Yosei's stringency regarding declaring property ownerless.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the first case: a person prohibited from benefiting can obtain food from a familiar storekeeper by stating the situation, and the storekeeper gives and collects from the prohibitor.
The baraita continues with the second case: for building, fencing, or harvesting, the prohibitor can hire familiar workers through the same indirect method.
The baraita concludes with the third case: when traveling without food, one may give to another as a gift or declare the food ownerless, but Rabbi Yosei prohibits the ownerless declaration.
Rava explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: the prohibition is a גזירה (decree) lest one come to benefit directly.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The mishnah of the incident of Beit Horon is cited, setting the context for the discussion of vows and divorce.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah cites the incident of Beit Horon, introducing the context of vows and divorce.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the difference between Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and the Tanna Kamma, with Abaye and Rava offering explanations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda's statement differs from the Tanna Kamma's position.
Abaye explains that Rabbi Yehuda's statement teaches a new halacha regarding a priest's daughter (כֹּהֶנֶת).
Rava explains that the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and the Tanna Kamma is whether the month is full (30 days) or deficient (29 days).

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on explicit vs. implicit vows
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on explicit vs. implicit vows
items.desc_en: Rav rules that only an explicit vow requires immediate divorce, while Shmuel holds that even an implicit vow does not require immediate divorce lest a loophole be found.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the Mishnah's requirement of immediate divorce applies only to an explicit vow, but for an implicit vow the husband divorces immediately and pays the ketubah.
Shmuel holds that even an implicit vow does not require immediate divorce, lest a halachic loophole be found to annul the vow.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution of redundancy
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution of redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel already disputed in a similar case (vow against marital relations) and explains why both statements are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav and Shmuel already disputed this same issue in the context of a vow against marital relations, citing the Mishnah from Nedarim.

The Gemara resolves that both statements are necessary, because each case has a unique feature that might have led one to think the other Amora would agree, so both rulings are needed to clarify the full dispute.

items.text: Challenge from the mishnah on tasting fruit
items.text_en: Challenge from the mishnah on tasting fruit
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a husband who vows his wife may not taste any fruit must divorce her and pay her ketubah. This challenges Shmuel's view that an implicit vow does not require immediate divorce.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the mishnah that a husband who vows his wife may not taste any fruit must divorce her and pay her ketubah, and notes that while this is consistent with Rav's distinction between explicit and implicit vows, it poses a difficulty for Shmuel's view that an implicit vow does not require immediate divorce.

items.text: Gemara's answer: the case where she vowed and he confirmed
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: the case where she vowed and he confirmed
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the mishnah deals with a case where the wife vowed and the husband confirmed it, and Rabbi Meir holds that he is responsible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the mishnah deals with a case where the wife vowed and the husband confirmed it, and Rabbi Meir holds that he is responsible.

items.text: Extended debate on the principle of 'he puts a finger between her teeth'
items.text_en: Extended debate on the principle of 'he puts a finger between her teeth'
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the tannaitic dispute about who is responsible for a wife's vow, citing and reinterpreting baraitot to align the opinions of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Meir holds the principle 'he puts a finger between her teeth' by citing a contradictory baraita.
The baraita states that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda say 'she puts a finger between her teeth,' contradicting the earlier assumption.
The baraita continues that Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar say 'he puts a finger between her teeth,' but the Gemara notes the text should be reversed.
The Gemara reverses the attributions: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda now say 'he puts a finger,' and Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar say 'she puts a finger.'
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei cannot hold 'she puts a finger,' citing a mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says the husband may annul vows of poverty without a fixed limit.
The Gemara proposes a new pairing: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei say 'he puts a finger,' while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar say 'she puts a finger.'
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda cannot hold 'she puts a finger,' citing a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda says the husband may keep the wife for one day.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei all say 'he puts a finger,' and only Rabbi Elazar says 'she puts a finger.'
The Gemara offers an alternative: if the baraita lists pairs, then Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar say 'she puts a finger,' while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei say 'he puts a finger.'
The Gemara concludes that the anonymous mishnah (segments 5-6) does not follow Rabbi Meir's opinion.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's view on vows of affliction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's view on vows of affliction
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between vows of affliction (e.g., not eating meat or drinking wine) and other vows, implying the husband can annul only the former.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei's position, noting that he holds a husband can annul a vow of affliction without a fixed duration, implying the husband can annul.
The Gemara cites a baraita listing the vows a husband can annul, including those of affliction like washing or adorning.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between vows of affliction (e.g., not eating meat or drinking wine) and other vows (e.g., washing or adorning), implying the husband can annul only the former.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'in colored garments'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'in colored garments'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's mention of 'colored garments' and clarifies that the discussion here is about matters between husband and wife (דברים שבינו לבינה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's mention of 'colored garments' and clarifies that the discussion here is about matters between husband and wife (דברים שבינו לבינה).

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahavah on annulment of such vows
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahavah on annulment of such vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for the opinion that the husband can annul matters between them, but for the opinion that he cannot, there is a problem. It cites the dispute: Rav Huna says the husband annuls, Rav Adda bar Ahavah says he does not, because 'we never found a fox that died in the dust of a pit' (a proverb meaning such a case never occurs).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for the opinion that the husband can annul vows about matters between them, but asks what can be said for the opposing opinion.
The Gemara cites the dispute: Rav Huna says the husband annuls, Rav Adda bar Ahavah says he does not, with the aphorism 'we never found a fox that died in the dust of a pit.'
Rav Adda bar Ahavah argues that the husband does not annul, using a proverb that such a case never occurs.

items.text: Resolution: the case involves a vow linking adornment to marital relations
items.text_en: Resolution: the case involves a vow linking adornment to marital relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is where she tied her adornment to marital relations, saying 'Let marital relations be forbidden to me if I adorn myself,' as per Rav Kahana's ruling: if she says 'my marital relations are forbidden to you,' he can force her to serve him; if she says 'your marital relations are forbidden to me,' he can annul, because one does not feed a person something forbidden to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case involves a vow linking adornment to marital relations, as per Rav Kahana's ruling.

Rav Kahana rules that if she says 'my marital relations are forbidden to you,' he can force her to serve him; if she says 'your marital relations are forbidden to me,' he can annul, because one does not feed a person something forbidden to him.

items.text: Objection and resolution: why not let her adorn and be forbidden?
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: why not let her adorn and be forbidden?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not let her adorn and be forbidden? If she does not adorn, she becomes repulsive. If she adorns and is forbidden, according to Beit Shammai it would be two weeks, according to Beit Hillel one week. But that applies when he vowed, as she thinks he is angry and will calm down; here, she vowed and he was silent, so she thinks he hates her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not let her adorn and be forbidden? If she does not adorn, she becomes repulsive.

The Gemara answers: if she adorns and is forbidden, according to Beit Shammai it would be two weeks, according to Beit Hillel one week, but that applies when he vowed; here she vowed and he was silent, so she thinks he hates her.

items.text: Dispute on the time limit for poverty and wealth
items.text_en: Dispute on the time limit for poverty and wealth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says in poverty without a fixed time. The Gemara asks: what is the fixed time? Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says twelve months; Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says ten years; Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi says a festival, because Jewish women adorn themselves on the festival. For wealth, the time is thirty days, as Abaye explains because a distinguished woman enjoys the scent of her adornments for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that in a case of poverty, no fixed time was given for the husband to provide adornments.
The Gemara asks: what is the fixed time for poverty?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel answers: twelve months.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan answers: ten years.

sub.text: Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Avimi answers: a festival (רֶגֶל), because Jewish women adorn themselves on the festival.
The Mishnah states: for wealth, the time is thirty days.
The Gemara asks: what is special about thirty days?
Abaye answers: because a distinguished woman enjoys the scent of her adornments for thirty days.

items.text: Mishnah: vows preventing visiting father's house, mourning, or feasting
items.text_en: Mishnah: vows preventing visiting father's house, mourning, or feasting
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If a husband vows that his wife not go to her father's house, when he is in the same city, he can maintain the vow for one month, after two months he must divorce and pay the ketubah. When he is in another city, one festival is allowed, after three he must divorce. If he vows she not go to a house of mourning or feasting, he must divorce and pay the ketubah, because he locks her out. If he has another reason, he is permitted. Also, if he says 'on condition that you tell so-and-so what you said to me' or 'what I said to you' or that she fill and pour into the garbage, he must divorce and pay the ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a husband who vows his wife may not visit her father's house may maintain the vow for one month when he is in the same city, but must divorce after two; when he is in another city, one festival is allowed, but three require divorce with ketubah payment.

The Mishnah rules that a husband who vows his wife may not go to a house of mourning or a house of feasting must divorce and pay the ketubah, because he locks her out, but if he has another reason he is permitted.
The Mishnah rules that if a husband conditions the vow on her telling so-and-so what was said, or on her filling and pouring into the garbage, he must divorce and pay the ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction in the Mishnah and resolutions
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction in the Mishnah and resolutions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the first clause says one festival he may maintain, implying two he must divorce; the latter clause says three he must divorce, implying two he may maintain. Abaye resolves that the latter clause refers to a priest's daughter and follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbah bar Ulla resolves that here it is a woman who is 'pursued' (רדופה) to go, there it is one who is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the Mishnah: the first clause implies two festivals require divorce, but the latter clause implies two festivals permit maintenance.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the latter clause refers to a priest's wife, following Rabbi Yehuda's stricter view.
Rabbah bar Ulla offers an alternative resolution: the first clause deals with a woman eager to visit her father, the latter with one who is not eager.

items.text: Supporting verses and continuation of the Mishnah discussion
items.text_en: Supporting verses and continuation of the Mishnah discussion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets a verse about a bride found complete in her father-in-law's house and pursued to tell her praise in her father's house, and another verse about calling Him 'my husband' not 'my master', like a bride in her father-in-law's house not in her father's house. The Gemara then begins to analyze the Mishnah's case of vowing not to go to a feasting house.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'Then I was in his eyes like one who finds peace' as a bride found complete in her father-in-law's house, pursued to tell her praise in her father's house.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'You will call me my husband and no longer call me my master' as a bride in her father-in-law's house, not in her father's house.
The Gemara transitions to analyzing the Mishnah's case of vowing not to go to a feasting house.

items.text: Gemara's question about 'locking the door' at a mourner's house
items.text_en: Gemara's question about 'locking the door' at a mourner's house
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'locking the door in her face' means in the context of a mourner's house, and cites a baraita explaining that if a woman is not mourned, it is as if she is locked out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'locking the door in her face' means in the context of a mourner's house.
A baraita explains that locking the door means that tomorrow she will die and no one will eulogize or care for her.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's exposition on Ecclesiastes
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's exposition on Ecclesiastes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir explains the verse 'It is better to go to a house of mourning...' and derives that one should reflect on matters of death, as what one does for others will be done for oneself.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Rabbi Meir's exposition of the verse from Ecclesiastes.
Rabbi Meir asks the meaning of the phrase 'and the living will take to heart'.
Rabbi Meir explains that one should reflect on matters of death, as what one does for others will be done for oneself.

items.text: Permissibility of a different reason for a vow
items.text_en: Permissibility of a different reason for a vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses when a husband may vow for a different reason, and Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says it is due to 'loose people' present. Rav Ashi limits this to when it is established that such people are there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'a different reason' in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel answers that it refers to loose people present at the location.
Rav Ashi limits the ruling to when it is established that such people are present; otherwise, the husband cannot claim this reason.

items.text: Vows about speaking and pouring water
items.text_en: Vows about speaking and pouring water
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's cases: if he vows that she speak certain words, Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says these are words of shame. If he vows that she pour water into the trash, Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says she must fill and strain, and a baraita says she fills ten jugs and pours them out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if he vows that she speak certain words, what is the problem — she can just speak them?
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel answers that the vow refers to words of shame (קלון), which are inherently degrading.
The Gemara asks: if he vows that she pour water into the trash, what is the problem — she can just do it?
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel answers that she must fill and strain (נופצת), a demeaning task.
A baraita specifies that she must fill ten jugs of water and pour them into the trash, confirming the demeaning nature.

items.text: Why the wife must be divorced for the pouring vow
items.text_en: Why the wife must be divorced for the pouring vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Shmuel's explanation makes sense but the baraita's does not, and Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan answers that it makes her appear insane.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Shmuel's explanation makes sense but the baraita's does not, asking what the wife gains from the pouring vow.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that the pouring vow makes her appear insane, justifying the divorce.

items.text: Vows about borrowing utensils
items.text_en: Vows about borrowing utensils
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that if a husband vows that his wife not borrow or lend certain household items, he must divorce her and pay the ketubah because it gives her a bad name. A baraita supports this and adds that if she vows similarly, she goes out without a ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that a husband who vows to prevent his wife from borrowing or lending household items must divorce her and pay the ketubah, because it gives her a bad reputation among neighbors.
A baraita supports Rav Kahana's ruling and adds that if the wife makes a similar vow, she goes out without a ketubah.

items.text: Mishnah: Those who go out without a ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those who go out without a ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists women who go out without a ketubah: those who violate the law of Moses (feeding untithed food, serving during her period, not separating challah, vowing and not fulfilling) and Jewish custom (going out with uncovered head, spinning in the market, speaking with everyone). Abba Shaul adds cursing his parents, and Rabbi Tarfon adds a loud voice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing women who go out without a ketubah, specifying the violations of דת משה (the law of Moses): feeding untithed food, serving during her period, not separating challah, and vowing without fulfilling.
The Mishnah defines דת יהודית (Jewish custom) as going out with uncovered head, spinning in the market, and speaking with everyone.
Abba Shaul adds that a woman who curses her husband's parents in his presence also goes out without a ketubah.
Rabbi Tarfon adds the קולנית (a loud-voiced woman) whose voice is heard by neighbors when she speaks in her house.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of 'law of Moses' violations
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of 'law of Moses' violations
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes each case: feeding untithed food is when she falsely claims a priest tithed it; serving during her period is when she falsely claims a sage permitted the blood; not separating challah is when she falsely claims a baker prepared the dough; vowing and not fulfilling is explained by the verse that vows cause children to die, with Rav Nachman citing a proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a case of a wife feeding untithed food is possible, since if the husband knows he would separate himself, and if he doesn't know how would he discover it.
The Gemara answers that the case is where she falsely claims a priest tithed the produce for her, and he investigates and finds it false.
The Gemara asks how a case of a wife serving her husband during her menstrual period is possible, since if he knows he would separate, and if he doesn't know he relies on her.

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Kahana citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Kahana citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Kahana cites Shmuel's proof that a menstruating woman counts her clean days for herself, based on the verse 'וְסָפְרָה לָּהּ' (she shall count for herself).
The Gemara answers that the case is where she falsely claims a sage permitted the blood, and he investigates and finds it false.

Alternatively, the Gemara cites Rav Yehuda's ruling that if a woman is established as a menstruant among her neighbors, her husband is liable for relations with her due to the presumption of her state.
The Gemara asks how a case of a wife not separating challah is possible, since if he knows he would separate, and if he doesn't know how would he discover it.
The Gemara answers that the case is where she falsely claims a baker prepared the dough for her, and he investigates and finds it false.

The Gemara explains that a wife who vows and does not fulfill is a violation because Mar taught that the sin of vows causes children to die, citing the verse 'אַל תִּתֵּן אֶת פִּיךָ לַחֲטִיא אֶת בְּשָׂרֶךָ' (do not let your mouth bring guilt upon your flesh), interpreted as referring to one's children.
Rav Nachman cites a different verse, 'לַשָּׁוְא הִכֵּיתִי אֶת בְּנֵיכֶם' (in vain I struck your children), interpreting 'לַשָּׁוְא' as referring to matters of vanity (vows).

items.text: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on dealing with a wife who vows
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on dealing with a wife who vows
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir says a husband who knows his wife vows and does not fulfill should provoke her to vow in his presence so he can annul it; the Sages say one cannot live with a snake in a basket. Rabbi Yehuda says he should separate challah after her; the Sages respond similarly. The Gemara notes the different versions of the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Meir's position: a husband who knows his wife vows and does not fulfill should provoke her to vow in his presence so he can annul it.
The Sages reject Rabbi Meir's proposal, saying one cannot live with a snake in a basket — i.e., one cannot tolerate a wife who habitually vows.
The baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's position: a husband who knows his wife does not separate חלה (the priestly portion of dough) should separate it after her.
The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda's proposal with the same metaphor: one cannot live with a snake in a basket.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the baraita versions
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the baraita versions
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the different versions of the baraita: one who teaches the Sages' response on Rabbi Yehuda's case applies it all the more to Rabbi Meir's case, but one who teaches it only on Rabbi Meir's case holds that Rabbi Yehuda's case is different because sometimes the husband might eat the dough after her separation.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'Jewish custom' – uncovered head
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'Jewish custom' – uncovered head
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why going out with uncovered head is considered Jewish custom when it is a Torah prohibition, citing the verse about the sotah and Rabbi Yishmael's school that warns Jewish women not to go out with uncovered head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why going out with uncovered head is listed as 'Jewish custom' (דת יהודית) when it is a Torah prohibition, citing the verse about the sotah and the school of Rabbi Yishmael's warning.

items.text: Opening Mishnah segment on loose hair
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah segment on loose hair
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who goes out with her head uncovered (loose hair) violates Jewish law (dat Yehudit) and is considered a transgression.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a woman going out with loose hair violates dat Yehudit (Jewish law), and even a קלתה (light head-covering) is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of loose hair
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of loose hair
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that loose hair is not considered 'peruah rosh' (uncovered head). Rabbi Zeira questions where this applies: in the market it is dat Yehudit, in the courtyard no woman would be allowed. Abaye or Rav Kahana answer: from one courtyard to another via an alleyway.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that loose hair (קלתה) does not constitute the prohibition of פְּרוּעַ רֹאשׁ (uncovered head).
Rabbi Zeira questions in which context this applies: if in the market, it violates דָּת יְהוּדִית (Jewish custom); if in the courtyard, no woman would be allowed to sit under her husband.
Abaye (or alternatively Rav Kahana) answers that the case is when she goes from one courtyard to another via an alleyway (מבוי), where the hair is visible but not in the public market.

items.text: Definitions of 'spinning in the market'
items.text_en: Definitions of 'spinning in the market'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that it means showing her arms to people. Rav Chisda quotes Avimi that it means spinning wool in front of her face and talking to everyone. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel again that it means playing with young men.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists 'spinning in the market' as a disqualifying behavior for a woman.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that 'spinning in the market' means showing her arms to people.
Rav Chisda cites Avimi that it means spinning wool in front of her face and talking to everyone.
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel again that it means playing with young men.

items.text: Story of Rabba bar bar Chana and the Arab woman
items.text_en: Story of Rabba bar bar Chana and the Arab woman
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana recounts following Rav Ukva and seeing an Arab woman spinning wool in front of her face. When she saw them, she stopped and asked for the spindle. Rav Ukva commented on her. Ravina says he said 'spinning in the market,' while the Rabbis say he said 'talking to everyone.'

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana recounts following Rav Ukva and seeing an Arab woman sitting and spinning wool in front of her face.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana's story continues
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana's story continues
sub.desc_en: The woman stops spinning when she sees them and asks Rabba bar bar Chana for the spindle.
The gemara asks what Rav Ukva said about the woman.
Ravina says Rav Ukva said she was 'spinning in the market.'
The Rabbis say Rav Ukva said she was 'talking to everyone.'

items.text: Definition of 'cursing her husband's parents'
items.text_en: Definition of 'cursing her husband's parents'
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul adds the case of a woman who curses her husband's parents. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that it means cursing his parents in his presence. Rabba gives an example: she says 'may a lion eat the old man in front of his son.'

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul adds the case of a woman who curses her husband's parents to the list of transgressors.
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the curse must be directed at the husband's parents in his presence.
The gemara provides a mnemonic from the verse 'Ephraim and Menashe shall be like Reuben and Shimon' to illustrate the relationship of parents and children.
Rabba gives an example of the curse: the woman says 'may a lion eat the old man in front of his son.'

items.text: Definition of 'loud voice' (kolanit)
items.text_en: Definition of 'loud voice' (kolanit)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon adds the case of a loud-voiced woman. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that it means her voice is heard concerning marital matters. A baraita teaches: she engages in intimacy in this courtyard and her voice is heard in another courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon adds the case of a loud-voiced woman (קולנית) to the list of women who go out without a ketubah.
The Gemara asks for the definition of the term קולנית (loud-voiced woman).
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that a קולנית is one whose voice is heard concerning marital matters (תשמיש).
A baraita teaches that a קולנית is one who engages in intimacy in one courtyard and her voice is heard in another courtyard.

items.text: Gemara's question about listing these with blemishes
items.text_en: Gemara's question about listing these with blemishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why these cases (loose hair, etc.) were not listed together with the blemishes in the Mishnah. It answers: the Mishnah is a clarification (mechavarta) as originally taught.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why these cases (loose hair, etc.) were not listed together with the blemishes in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is a clarification (מחוורתא) as originally taught, not a new list.

items.text: Mishnah on betrothal with conditions about vows and blemishes
items.text_en: Mishnah on betrothal with conditions about vows and blemishes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If a man betroths a woman on condition that she has no vows and she has vows, she is not betrothed. If he married her unconditionally and vows are found, she leaves without a ketubah. The same applies to blemishes. All blemishes that disqualify priests disqualify women.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of betrothal and marriage when vows or blemishes are discovered, including the rule that all blemishes disqualifying priests also disqualify women.

items.text: Gemara's question about duplication with Kiddushin
items.text_en: Gemara's question about duplication with Kiddushin
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a similar Mishnah appears in Kiddushin. It explains: here the Tanna needed to teach about Ketubot, so he taught Kiddushin in the context of Ketubot; there he needed to teach about Kiddushin, so he taught Ketubot in the context of Kiddushin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a similar Mishnah appears in Kiddushin, questioning the duplication.
The Gemara explains that in each tractate the Tanna taught the other topic incidentally because the primary topic was needed.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's definition of 'these vows'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's definition of 'these vows'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak says: 'These vows' refer to vows that cause affliction of the soul: not eating meat, not drinking wine, and not adorning herself with colored garments. A baraita supports this.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines 'these vows' as vows that cause affliction of the soul: not eating meat, not drinking wine, and not adorning herself with colored garments.
A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's definition, listing the same three vows.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question on the scope of vows
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question on the scope of vows
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks: to which part of the Mishnah does Rabbi Yochanan's statement refer? If it refers to the first clause (betrothal on condition), since he is particular, even any vow would invalidate. Rather, it refers to the latter clause (unconditional marriage).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers to the first clause (betrothal on condition) or the latter clause (unconditional marriage), concluding it must refer to the latter.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative answer
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative answer
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says: the statement always refers to the first clause, but only matters that people are particular about are considered a valid condition; matters people are not particular about are not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by asserting that the statement always refers to the first clause, but only matters people are particular about constitute a valid condition, while matters people are not particular about do not.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on conditional betrothal followed by unconditional marriage
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on conditional betrothal followed by unconditional marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara reports: If he betrothed her conditionally and then married her unconditionally, Rav says she needs a get from him, Shmuel says she does not need a get. Abaye begins to analyze.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports the dispute: If he betrothed her conditionally and then married her unconditionally, Rav says she needs a get from him, Shmuel says she does not need a get.
Abaye begins to analyze the dispute, presumably raising a question or challenge.

items.text: Rav's true reasoning
items.text_en: Rav's true reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav's position is not that cohabitation unconditionally nullifies the condition, but rather that a person does not make his cohabitation an act of licentiousness, so the marriage is valid despite the condition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the initial assumption that Rav's reasoning is that unconditional cohabitation nullifies the condition, and instead states that Rav's true reasoning is that a person does not make his cohabitation an act of licentiousness (בְּעִילַת זְנוּת).

items.text: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel in a different case
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav and Shmuel in a different case
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav and Shmuel already disagreed in a case of a minor who did not refuse and later married. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary to teach, to avoid assuming each would concede to the other in the other case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav and Shmuel have already disputed this matter in a different case.
The Gemara cites a case of a minor who did not refuse and later married, where Rav says she does not need a get from the second husband and Shmuel says she does.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary to teach, because each rabbi might concede to the other in the other case if only one case were stated.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: if a man married a woman unconditionally and found she had vows, she leaves without a ketubah but needs a get. This implies that even if he married her unconditionally after a conditional betrothal, a get is required, contradicting Shmuel's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a woman married unconditionally who is found to have vows leaves without a ketubah but requires a get, and infers that this applies even after a conditional betrothal, thereby challenging Shmuel's position.

items.text: Opening statement: betrothed unconditionally and married unconditionally
items.text_en: Opening statement: betrothed unconditionally and married unconditionally
