items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a man betrothed a woman unconditionally and married her unconditionally, she does not require a get when flaws are found.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a man betrothed a woman unconditionally and married her unconditionally, she does not require a get when flaws are found.

items.text: Gemara's question: conditional betrothal and unconditional marriage
items.text_en: Gemara's question: conditional betrothal and unconditional marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman betrothed conditionally but married unconditionally also does not require a get, and challenges the Mishnah's formulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a woman betrothed conditionally but married unconditionally also does not require a get, and challenges the Mishnah's formulation.

items.text: Gemara's answer: the Mishnah's true case
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: the Mishnah's true case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah actually refers to a case where the betrothal was conditional but the marriage was unconditional, and she is not betrothed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah actually refers to a case where the betrothal was conditional but the marriage was unconditional, and she is not betrothed.

items.text: Gemara's objection: why require a get?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: why require a get?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if she does not require a ketubah, she should also not require a get, since the husband can claim he does not want a vow-prone woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if she does not require a ketubah, she should also not require a get, since the husband can claim he does not want a vow-prone woman.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Chisda's resolution: rabbinic get
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Chisda's resolution: rabbinic get
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Chisda rule that she requires a get by rabbinic law, while Rava suggests the Tanna is uncertain and rules stringently for prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that she requires a get by rabbinic law (מדבריהם).
Rav Chisda agrees with Rabbah that she requires a rabbinic get.
Rava explains that the Tanna is uncertain, so he rules leniently for monetary matters and stringently for prohibitions.

items.text: Rabbah's first distinction: error of two women vs. one woman
items.text_en: Rabbah's first distinction: error of two women vs. one woman
items.desc_en: Rabbah initially states that the dispute applies only to an error involving two women, but for an error of a single woman, all agree she does not require a get.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah distinguishes the dispute: it applies only to an error involving two women, but for an error of a single woman, all agree she does not require a get.

items.text: Abaye's objection: the Mishnah is a single woman error
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: the Mishnah is a single woman error
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the Mishnah itself involves an error of a single woman, yet it was challenged.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the Mishnah itself involves an error of a single woman, yet it was challenged with a refutation.

items.text: Rabbah's revised distinction: error of a single woman akin to two
items.text_en: Rabbah's revised distinction: error of a single woman akin to two
items.desc_en: Rabbah revises his statement: the dispute is about an error of a single woman that is similar to two women, but a pure single woman error requires no get.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah revises his position: the dispute applies only to an error of a single woman that is akin to two women, but a pure single-woman error requires no get.

items.text: Abaye's challenge from a baraita on error of betrothal
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge from a baraita on error of betrothal
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about betrothal by error with less than a perutah, where there is a dispute, and the Gemara explains the dispute is about the nature of the error, not vows.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about betrothal by error with less than a perutah, where there is a dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda citing Rabbi Yishmael.
Abaye infers that since this is a case of error regarding one woman and they dispute, the error must be about vows, challenging Rava's position.
The Gemara rejects Abaye's inference, explaining that the error is about less than a perutah, not about vows, and the baraita is merely clarifying the nature of the error.

The Gemara resolves the dispute: one opinion holds that a person knows betrothal does not take effect with less than a perutah and therefore intends new betrothal through intercourse, while the other holds he does not know and intends the original betrothal.

items.text: Abaye's second challenge: conditional betrothal on father's will
items.text_en: Abaye's second challenge: conditional betrothal on father's will
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about betrothal conditional on the father's will, where there is a dispute, and the Gemara explains the dispute is about the interpretation of the condition.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about conditional betrothal on the father's will, where there is a dispute, to challenge the position that there is no dispute in a single-woman error case.

The Gemara explains that the dispute in the baraita is not about the error itself but about the interpretation of the condition: one opinion holds 'on condition that father consents' means silence suffices, while the other holds it requires explicit verbal consent.

items.text: Final baraita: a minor girl returned after divorce
items.text_en: Final baraita: a minor girl returned after divorce
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a minor girl who was divorced and returned, and the conditions under which she must perform chalitzah or yibbum.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding a minor girl who was married by her father, divorced, and then returned, that she must perform חליצה (the release ceremony) and not יבום (levirate marriage).
The baraita explains the reason: her divorce is a complete divorce, but her return is not a complete return.

The baraita qualifies that this applies only when she was divorced and returned while still a minor; but if she was divorced as a minor and returned as an adult, or returned as a minor and grew up with him and he died, she may either perform חליצה or יבום.

items.text: Gemara's question on the dispute about mistaken betrothal
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the dispute about mistaken betrothal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier dispute about a woman who was betrothed in error (where one opinion says she must undergo chalitzah but cannot enter yibbum) is relevant, given that the case involves a mistaken woman. It explains that the dispute actually revolves around whether a man knows that a minor's betrothal is invalid and intends his intercourse as a new betrothal, or whether he acts based on the original betrothal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the earlier dispute about a woman betrothed in error (where one opinion says she must undergo חליצה (chalitzah) but cannot enter יבום (yibbum)) is relevant, given that the case involves a mistaken woman, and yet they dispute.

The Gemara explains that the dispute actually revolves around whether a man knows that a minor's betrothal is invalid and intends his intercourse as a new betrothal, or whether he acts based on the original betrothal.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on conditional betrothal and intercourse, with an objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on conditional betrothal and intercourse, with an objection
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who betroths conditionally and then has intercourse does not require a get. An objection is raised from the case of mistaken chalitzah, where Reish Lakish says it is valid if the brother was told 'chalitz for her and thereby you will marry her.' Rabbi Yochanan initially distinguishes, but then redefines mistaken chalitzah as a case where the brother is promised money, implying that the act nullifies the condition. The Gemara applies this logic to conditional betrothal.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who betroths conditionally and then has intercourse does not require a get.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika objects by citing the case of mistaken chalitzah, where Reish Lakish defines it as when the brother is told 'chalitz for her and thereby you will marry her.'

Rabbi Yochanan initially distinguishes by citing his own teaching that mistaken chalitzah is invalid unless both parties intend it, then redefines the case as one where the brother is promised money, implying the act nullifies the condition.
The Gemara concludes that since the brother performed the act (chalitzah), he nullified his condition, and similarly, since the betrothed man had intercourse, he nullified his condition.

items.text: Bar Bei Rav's challenge from the laws of conditions
items.text_en: Bar Bei Rav's challenge from the laws of conditions
items.desc_en: Bar Bei Rav challenges the previous conclusion by citing the general rule that conditions are derived from the condition of the tribes of Gad and Reuven. A condition that can be fulfilled through an agent is valid, but one that cannot (like intercourse) is not. The Gemara answers that intercourse is an exception because 'havayot' (acts of creation) are equated to each other.

sub.desc_en: Bar Bei Rav challenges the previous conclusion by asking whether the rule is well-founded, noting that all conditions are derived from the condition of the tribes of Gad and Reuven.
Bar Bei Rav states the general principle: a condition that can be fulfilled through an agent is valid, but one that cannot (like intercourse) is not.
Bar Bei Rav objects that intercourse, which cannot be fulfilled through an agent, is nevertheless treated as a valid condition in the earlier case.
The Gemara resolves that intercourse is an exception because 'havayot' (acts of creation) are equated to each other by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

items.text: Rav Ulla bar Abba and Rav Kahana's rulings on conditional betrothal
items.text_en: Rav Ulla bar Abba and Rav Kahana's rulings on conditional betrothal
items.desc_en: Rav Ulla bar Abba quotes Ulla quoting Rabbi Elazar that in cases of betrothal with a loan, conditional betrothal, or betrothal with less than a perutah's worth, followed by intercourse, all agree she requires a get. Rav Yosef bar Abba quotes Rabbi Ami that specifically for less than a perutah she needs a get because there is no mistake, but in the other cases there is a mistake. Rav Kahana in the name of Ulla rules that conditional betrothal followed by intercourse requires a get, citing a precedent where the sages could not release her without a get.

sub.text: Rav Ulla bar Abba citing Ulla citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rav Ulla bar Abba citing Ulla citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Ulla bar Abba reports in the name of Ulla citing Rabbi Elazar that in three cases of betrothal followed by intercourse — with a loan, on a condition, or with less than a perutah's value — all agree she requires a get.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Abba citing Rabbi Menachem citing Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Abba citing Rabbi Menachem citing Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Abba quotes Rabbi Ami that only in the case of less than a perutah does she need a get because there is no mistake, but in the other two cases there is a mistake and she does not need a get.

sub.text: Rav Kahana in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules in the name of Ulla that conditional betrothal followed by intercourse requires a get, citing a precedent where the sages could not release her without a get.

items.text: Exclusion of a contrary Tanna
items.text_en: Exclusion of a contrary Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana's ruling excludes the opinion of a Tanna cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel quoting Rabbi Yishmael, who derives from a verse that a woman who was seized (by captors) is permitted, but one not seized is forbidden, and there is another case where even if not seized she is permitted: when her betrothal was a mistaken betrothal, such that even if her child is on her shoulder, she is permitted.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a contrary Tanna
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a contrary Tanna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a contrary Tanna who, via Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel quoting Rabbi Yishmael, derives from the verse that a woman who was seized (by captors) is permitted, but one not seized is forbidden, and adds that there is another case where even if not seized she is permitted: when her betrothal was a mistaken betrothal (קידושי טעות), such that even if her child is on her shoulder, she is permitted.

items.text: Opening statement
items.text_en: Opening statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman who was a minor may continue to refuse (מְמָאֶנֶת) and go her own way, implying that her refusal is effective.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a minor woman may refuse her marriage and leave, implying her refusal is effective.

items.text: Baraita on sage vs. doctor
items.text_en: Baraita on sage vs. doctor
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if a woman went to a sage and he annulled her vow, she is betrothed; if she went to a doctor and he cured her, she is not betrothed. The difference is that a sage uproots the vow from its root, while a doctor only cures from now onward.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if a woman went to a sage (חכם) who annulled her vow, she is betrothed (מקודשת), but if she went to a doctor (רופא) who cured her, she is not betrothed, because the sage uproots the vow from its root (עוקר את הנדר מעיקרו) while the doctor only cures from now onward (מכאן ולהבא).

items.text: Contradiction and resolution by Rava
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution by Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: another baraita states that whether she went to a sage or a doctor, she is not betrothed. Rava resolves this by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Meir, who holds that a man wants his wife to be degraded in court, and the second to Rabbi Elazar, who holds that a man does not want his wife degraded in court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that states that whether she went to a sage or a doctor, she is not betrothed.
Rava resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Meir and the second to Rabbi Elazar.
Rava explains that Rabbi Meir holds that a man wants his wife to be degraded in court, while Rabbi Elazar holds that a man does not want his wife degraded in court.

items.text: Introduction to the Mishnah of divorcing due to a vow
items.text_en: Introduction to the Mishnah of divorcing due to a vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the source of this dispute? It cites a Mishnah: one who divorces his wife because of a vow may not remarry her; similarly, if because of a bad name, he may not remarry her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the source of the dispute is.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah: one who divorces his wife because of a vow or a bad name may not remarry her.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: Rabbi Yehuda says any vow known to the public prevents remarriage; if not known, he may remarry. Rabbi Meir says any vow requiring a sage's inquiry prevents remarriage; if not, he may remarry. Rabbi Elazar says both types prevent remarriage, and explains that they only prohibited the requiring type because of the non-requiring type. The Gemara then begins to explain Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning with a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that a vow known to the public prevents remarriage, but if not known, he may remarry.
Rabbi Meir states that a vow requiring a sage's inquiry prevents remarriage, but if not, he may remarry.
Rabbi Elazar states that both types of vows prevent remarriage.
Rabbi Elazar explains that they only prohibited the requiring type because of the non-requiring type.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda, citing a verse.

items.text: Definition of 'many' in the verse
items.text_en: Definition of 'many' in the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'And the children of Israel did not strike them because the princes of the congregation had sworn to them' and asks how many constitute 'many'. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says three, based on the principle that 'days' is two and 'many' is three. Rabbi Yitzchak says ten, because the word 'congregation' is written regarding them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the Gibeonites and asks how many constitute 'many'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that 'many' means three, based on the hermeneutic principle that 'days' is two and 'many' is three.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that 'many' means ten, because the word 'עֵדָה' (congregation) is written regarding them, and a congregation is ten.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir says any vow that requires the examination of a Sage, he should not take her back. Rabbi Elazar says they did not forbid it except because it does not require examination. The Gemara explains their dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that a man wants his wife to be humiliated in court, while Rabbi Elazar holds that a man does not want his wife to be humiliated in court.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir says any vow requiring a Sage's examination invalidates return; Rabbi Elazar says the prohibition applies only to vows that do not require examination.
The Gemara asks: On what principle do they disagree?

The Gemara explains: Rabbi Meir holds that a man wants his wife to be humiliated in court (so he would not have released the vow himself), while Rabbi Elazar holds that a man does not want his wife to be humiliated in court (so he would have released it, making the vow a pretext for divorce).

items.text: Rava's resolution and the case of a prominent woman
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and the case of a prominent woman
items.desc_en: Rava says we are dealing with a prominent woman, where the husband says he does not want to be prohibited from her relatives. The Gemara objects: if so, in the latter clause where it says 'but if he went to a Sage and he released it, or to a doctor and he healed him, she is betrothed', let it teach 'she is not betrothed' and say we are dealing with a prominent man, where she says she does not want to be prohibited from his relatives! The Gemara answers: she is content with any man, as Resh Lakish said: 'It is better to sit as two than to sit as a widow'. Abaye says: 'A sesame-sized man, her seat is in the garbage dump'. Rav Pappa says: 'A flax-beater man, call him at the doorposts and she will sit'. Rav Ashi says: 'A fuller man, she does not need a pot cover'. A baraisa teaches: And all of them commit adultery and blame their husbands.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the Mishnah by saying it deals with a prominent woman, where the husband says he does not want to be prohibited from her relatives.

The Gemara objects: if so, in the latter clause where it says 'but if he went to a Sage and he released it, she is betrothed', let it teach 'she is not betrothed' and say we are dealing with a prominent man.
The Gemara answers: she is content with any man, as Resh Lakish said: 'It is better to sit as two than to sit as a widow'.
Abaye adds: 'A sesame-sized man, her seat is in the garbage dump'.
Rav Pappa adds: 'A flax-beater man, call him at the doorposts and she will sit'.
Rav Ashi adds: 'A fuller man, she does not need a pot cover'.
A baraisa teaches: And all of them commit adultery and blame their husbands.

items.text: Additional blemishes: sweat, mole, bad breath
items.text_en: Additional blemishes: sweat, mole, bad breath
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches: They added to them sweat, a mole, and bad breath. The Gemara questions: Are these not disqualifying for priests? But we learned: 'The old, the sick, and the foul-smelling' and we learned: 'These blemishes, whether permanent or temporary, disqualify a person'.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa adds sweat, a mole, and bad breath to the list of blemishes that disqualify a woman.
The Gemara asks: Are these blemishes not disqualifying for priests? This challenges the novelty of the baraisa.
The Gemara cites a baraita that lists 'the old, the sick, and the foul-smelling' as disqualifying blemishes for priests.
The Gemara cites another baraita that these blemishes, whether permanent or temporary, disqualify a person (including priests).

items.text: Resolution for sweat: temporary vs. permanent
items.text_en: Resolution for sweat: temporary vs. permanent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina says it is not difficult: here it refers to temporary sweat, there it refers to permanent sweat. Rav Ashi says: Do you compare sweat to foul-smelling? There, regarding priests, it is possible to pass it with wine sediment. And regarding bad breath, it is possible to hold pepper in his mouth and perform the service. But regarding a woman, it is not possible.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina resolves the contradiction between the baraita listing sweat as a disqualifying blemish for women and the Mishnah listing it as a disqualifying blemish for priests by distinguishing between temporary sweat (עוברת) and permanent sweat (שאינה עוברת).

Rav Ashi objects that sweat is not comparable to the blemish of 'מזוהם' (foul-smelling person) listed in the Mishnah for priests, because for priests the sweat can be removed with wine sediment and bad breath can be masked with pepper, but for a woman such remedies are not possible.

items.text: Definition of a mole as a blemish
items.text_en: Definition of a mole as a blemish
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the case of this mole? If it has hair, here and there it disqualifies. If it does not have hair, if it is a large mole, here and there it disqualifies; if it is a small mole, here and there it does not disqualify. As it was taught: A mole that has hair is a blemish; if it does not have hair, a large one is a blemish, a small one is not a blemish. And what is a large one? Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explained: up to an Italian issar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of mole is under discussion, distinguishing between a mole with hair (always a blemish), a large mole without hair (always a blemish), and a small mole without hair (never a blemish).
A baraita is cited to support the distinction: a mole with hair is a blemish, a large one without hair is a blemish, a small one without hair is not a blemish.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel defines a large mole as one up to the size of an Italian issar coin.

items.text: Location of the mole: on the forehead vs. under the hair
items.text_en: Location of the mole: on the forehead vs. under the hair
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina says: When it stands on her forehead. The Gemara objects: On her forehead, he sees and is appeased! Rav Pappa says: When it stands for her under the cap of her head, and sometimes it is seen and sometimes it is not seen.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that the mole is disqualifying when it stands on her forehead.
The Gemara objects: If the mole is on her forehead, he sees it and is appeased (so it cannot be a hidden defect).
Rav Pappa answers: The mole is under the cap of her head, sometimes seen and sometimes not, so it qualifies as a hidden defect.

items.text: Additional blemishes: dog bite scar, thick voice, gap between breasts
items.text_en: Additional blemishes: dog bite scar, thick voice, gap between breasts
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: I heard this matter from a great man, and who is he? Rabbi Sheila: If a dog bit her and the place became a scar, this is a blemish. Rav Chisda says: A thick voice in a woman is a blemish, as it is stated: 'For your voice is sweet and your appearance is lovely'. Rabbi Natan the Babylonian taught: The gap between a woman's breasts is a handbreadth. Rav Acha the son of Rava thought to say before Rav Ashi: A handbreadth for superiority. Rav Ashi said to him: It was taught regarding blemishes, and how much? Abaye said: Three fingerbreadths.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reports from Rabbi Sheila that a dog bite scar is a blemish.
Rav Chisda adds that a thick voice in a woman is a blemish, citing the verse 'For your voice is sweet and your appearance is lovely'.
Rabbi Natan the Babylonian teaches that a handbreadth gap between a woman's breasts is a blemish.

sub.text: Rav Acha the son of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha the son of Rava suggests the handbreadth is for superiority, but Rav Ashi corrects that it was taught regarding blemishes.
Abaye specifies the measure of the gap as three fingerbreadths.

items.text: Large breasts as a blemish
items.text_en: Large breasts as a blemish
items.desc_en: It was taught: Rabbi Natan says: Any woman whose breasts are larger than those of her friends, this is a blemish. And how much? Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, said in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: A handbreadth. The Gemara asks: Is there such a thing? Yes, for Rabbah bar bar Chanah said: I saw one Arab woman who slung her breasts behind her and nursed her son.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Natan rules that a woman whose breasts are larger than her friends' has a blemish.

sub.text: Rabbi Meyasha in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Meyasha in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, specifies the measure: a handbreadth (טפח).
The Gemara questions whether such large breasts actually exist.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah testifies that he saw an Arab woman sling her breasts behind her and nurse her son, confirming such a size is possible.

items.text: Praise of those born in or aspiring to see Zion
items.text_en: Praise of those born in or aspiring to see Zion
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds the verse: 'And of Zion it shall be said: This and that man was born in her, and He, the Most High, will establish her.' Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, says: Both one born in her and one who aspires to see her. Abaye says: One of them is better than two of us. Rava says: One of us, when he goes up there, is better than two of them. For Rabbi Yirmeya, when he was here, did not know what the Rabbis were saying; when he went up there, he called us 'foolish Babylonians'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the verse about Zion, setting the stage for the praise that follows.
Rabbi Meyasha explains that the verse praises both one born in Zion and one who aspires to see her.
Abaye asserts that one of those praised (born in or aspiring to Zion) is better than two of the Babylonians.
Rava counters that one of the Babylonians who ascends to Eretz Yisrael is better than two of those born there.
The Gemara supports Rava's claim with the example of Rabbi Yirmeya, who was ignorant in Babylonia but after ascending to Eretz Yisrael called the Babylonians foolish.

items.text: Mishnah: Burden of proof for blemishes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Burden of proof for blemishes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If she had blemishes while still in her father's house, the father must bring proof that after she was betrothed these blemishes appeared, and his field was flooded. If she entered the husband's domain, the husband must bring proof that before she was betrothed these blemishes existed, and his purchase was a mistaken purchase. These are the words of Rabbi Meir. And the Sages say: In what case are these words said? Regarding hidden blemishes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: if she had blemishes while in her father's house, the father must bring proof they appeared after betrothal.
The Mishnah states the reverse rule: if she entered the husband's domain, the husband must bring proof the blemishes existed before betrothal.
The Mishnah attributes the preceding ruling to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages qualify the dispute: the ruling applies only to hidden blemishes.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that for visible blemishes the husband cannot claim, and if there is a bathhouse in the city, even hidden blemishes cannot be claimed because he can have her examined by relatives.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that for visible blemishes the husband cannot claim fraud, and if there is a bathhouse in the city, even hidden blemishes cannot be claimed because he can have her examined by relatives.

items.text: Gemara's Contradiction Between Reisha and Seifa
items.text_en: Gemara's Contradiction Between Reisha and Seifa
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the reisha implies the husband is believed unless the father brings proof, aligning with Rabbi Yehoshua, while the seifa implies the father is believed unless the husband brings proof, aligning with Rabban Gamliel. Rabbi Elazar resolves this by saying the one who taught this did not teach that.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the reisha that the husband is believed unless the father brings proof, identifying this with Rabbi Yehoshua's position.
The Gemara notes that the seifa implies the father is believed unless the husband brings proof, aligning with Rabban Gamliel's position.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction by stating that the one who taught the reisha did not teach the seifa.

items.text: Rava's Reinterpretation: Rabbi Yehoshua Follows Chazaka Only When No Monetary Chazaka
items.text_en: Rava's Reinterpretation: Rabbi Yehoshua Follows Chazaka Only When No Monetary Chazaka
items.desc_en: Rava argues that Rabbi Yehoshua does follow a חזקת הגוף, but only when there is no countervailing monetary chazaka. He supports this from a baraita where Rabbi Yehoshua rules a doubtful נגע as טהור, showing he relies on the body's presumptive status.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by rejecting the assumption that Rabbi Yehoshua never follows a chazaka of the body, and asserts that he does so when there is no countervailing monetary chazaka.
Rava cites a baraita about a doubtful נגע (skin affliction) where Rabbi Yehoshua rules it טהור (pure), showing he follows the body's presumptive status.
Rabba explains that Rabbi Yehoshua's term 'כֵּהָה' (dimmed) means the doubtful case is ruled טהור (pure), confirming reliance on the body's chazaka.

items.text: Rava's Alternative Resolution: Here They Were Found, Here They Were
items.text_en: Rava's Alternative Resolution: Here They Were Found, Here They Were
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different resolution: both the reisha and seifa can be consistent with one authority, because the distinction is whether the blemishes were found after betrothal (where we say they were there all along) or after marriage (where we say they arose later).

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by asserting that in both the reisha and seifa, the blemishes were found after betrothal or marriage but were present all along, so the distinction is based on timing of discovery relative to the legal status.

items.text: Abaye's Objection and Rava's First Answer
items.text_en: Abaye's Objection and Rava's First Answer
items.desc_en: Abaye objects from the seifa: the husband must bring proof only if the blemishes were before betrothal, but not after betrothal. Why not say 'here they were found, here they were'? Rava answers that after betrothal we apply the principle that a person does not drink from a cup without inspecting it, so he saw and was appeased.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects from the seifa of the Mishnah: the husband must bring proof only for blemishes before betrothal, but not after betrothal; why not apply the principle 'here they were found, here they were'?
Rava answers that after betrothal we apply the principle that a person does not drink from a cup without inspecting it, so he saw the blemishes and was appeased.

items.text: Refinement: Two Chazakot Override the Single Chazaka of Appeasement
items.text_en: Refinement: Two Chazakot Override the Single Chazaka of Appeasement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the same logic does not apply before betrothal, and answers that there we say a person is not appeased by blemishes. The final resolution is that after betrothal, two chazakot (body's presumptive status and inspection) override the single chazaka of non-appeasement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the logic of appeasement applies after betrothal, it should also apply before betrothal, but the previous answer invoked the principle that a person is not appeased by blemishes (חזקה אין אדם מיפייס במומין).

The Gemara resolves that after betrothal, two chazakot (חזקות) — the body's presumptive status (העמד הגוף על חזקתו) and the principle that one does not drink from a cup without inspecting it (חזקה אין אדם שותה בכוס אלא אם כן בודקו) — override the single chazaka that a person is not appeased by blemishes (חזקה אין אדם מיפייס במומין).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's ruling about a bride's blemishes, considering whether the principle of 'one claim in place of two' applies. It weighs two presumptions: that a person checks a cup before drinking (implying the husband knew of the blemish) and that a person does not become appeased regarding blemishes (implying he would not have married her if he knew).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle of 'one claim in place of two' (חֲדָא בִּמְקוֹם תַּרְתֵּי) applies here, concluding that it does not.
The Gemara notes that before betrothal, one cannot apply the presumption of bodily integrity (העמד הגוף על חזקתו).
The Gemara asks what presumption does apply, and answers: the presumption that a person checks a cup before drinking (אין אדם שותה בכוס אלא אם כן בודקו).
The Gemara objects that perhaps the husband saw the blemish and was appeased, but counters with the presumption that a person is not appeased regarding blemishes (אין אדם מיפייס במומין).
The Gemara resolves that the presumption of not being appeased, combined with the principle of 'stand the money on its presumption' (העמד ממון על חזקתו), supports the husband's claim.

items.text: Rav Ashi's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains the Mishnah by distinguishing between the beginning and end of the clause: the beginning is like 'I have a maneh of your father in your hand' (a claim against the father), while the end is like 'I have a maneh of yours in your hand' (a claim against the husband).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the Mishnah by distinguishing the beginning of the clause as a claim against the father (מנה לאבא בידך) and the end as a claim against the husband (מנה לי בידך).

items.text: Rav Acha's objection
items.text_en: Rav Acha's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Acha, son of Rav Avya, objects to Rav Ashi: Rabbi Meir agrees that for blemishes that could have come from her father's house, the father must bring proof. But why? That is like 'I have a maneh of yours in your hand' (the husband is the claimant), so the father should not be required to bring proof.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha objects to Rav Ashi: Rabbi Meir agrees that for blemishes that could have come from her father's house, the father must bring proof, but this is analogous to 'I have a maneh of yours in your hand' (the husband is the claimant), so the father should not be required to bring proof.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: dealing with an additional blemish
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: dealing with an additional blemish
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection: the case involves an additional blemish (יתרת) that appeared after betrothal. The father can bring proof that the husband saw it and was appeased, shifting the burden to the husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by specifying that the case involves an additional blemish (יתרת) that appeared after betrothal, and the father can bring proof that the husband saw it and was appeased.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: a barter case
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: a barter case
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: if one exchanges a cow for a donkey, and the donkey's owner pulls the cow but the cow's owner does not pull the donkey before it dies, the donkey's owner must bring proof that the donkey was alive at the time of the cow's pulling. This illustrates the burden of proof in a similar exchange.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel's ruling that in a barter exchange where one party pulled the cow but the other did not yet pull the donkey before it died, the burden of proof falls on the donkey's owner to prove the donkey was alive at the time of the cow's pulling.

items.text: Introduction of a baraita about a bride
items.text_en: Introduction of a baraita about a bride
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that discusses a bride, but the text is cut off, asking which bride is being referred to.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about a bride (כלה) and then asks which bride is being referred to, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Initial comparison of bride and found defect
items.text_en: Initial comparison of bride and found defect
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the case of a bride in her father's house is comparable to a found defect, noting that in the former the father brings proof, while here the donkey owner brings proof to establish his claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the case of a bride in her father's house is comparable to a found defect, noting that in the former the father brings proof, while here the donkey owner brings proof to establish his claim.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's alternative comparison
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's alternative comparison
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba suggests comparing to a bride in her father-in-law's house, but the Gemara notes the difference: there the husband brings proof to weaken the father's presumption, while here the donkey owner brings proof to strengthen his own presumption.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba proposes comparing to a bride in her father-in-law's house, but the Gemara objects that there the husband brings proof to weaken the father's presumption, while here the donkey owner brings proof to strengthen his own presumption.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution via betrothal
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution via betrothal
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the issue by comparing to a bride in her father's house regarding betrothal. He explains that even according to the view that betrothal is for actual marriage, this applies only to valid betrothal, but for mistaken betrothal, proof is required.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes a new comparison: the case is like a bride in her father's house regarding betrothal (קידושין), shifting the framework.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that even according to the view that betrothal is for actual marriage (קידושין לטיבועין ניתנו), this applies only to valid betrothal; for mistaken betrothal (קידושי טעות), proof is required to establish the claim.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about a needle in the rumen
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about a needle in the rumen
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a needle found in the thickness of the rumen: if found on one side it is kosher, on two sides it is treifa. If blood is found, it is known to be before slaughter; if not, after. If the wound is healed, it is known to be three days before slaughter; if not, the burden of proof is on the claimant. And if the butcher paid, he must bring proof to extract money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a needle found in the thickness of the rumen, detailing the rules for determining kosher status and timing relative to slaughter.
The baraita continues with rules about a healed wound indicating three days before slaughter, and the burden of proof on the butcher if he paid money.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the animal owner doesn't bring proof to establish his claim, and answers that it is when the butcher has not paid. But then it questions what the ruling is in that case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the animal owner does not bring proof to establish his claim, given the principle that the burden of proof is on the claimant.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the butcher has not yet paid the animal owner, so the animal owner is not a claimant.
The Gemara questions what the ruling is in that case, implying that the answer is unclear.

items.text: Rami bar Yechezkel's report of Shmuel's rule
items.text_en: Rami bar Yechezkel's report of Shmuel's rule
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel reports that Shmuel said: Anyone for whom a doubt arose in his domain, the burden of proof is on him. And a tanna taught similarly regarding a bride.

sub.text: Rami bar Yechezkel's report of Shmuel's rule
sub.text_en: Rami bar Yechezkel's report of Shmuel's rule
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel reports that Shmuel ruled: anyone for whom a doubt arose in his domain bears the burden of proof, and a tanna taught similarly regarding a bride.

items.text: Objection resolved and conclusion
items.text_en: Objection resolved and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the baraita: if the butcher didn't pay, the animal owner must bring proof, but the doubt arose in the butcher's domain. It resolves that the butcher did pay, and the default assumption is that one does not give an animal without receiving money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the baraita about a needle found in the stomach wall: if the butcher did not pay, the animal owner must bring proof, but the doubt arose in the butcher's domain, contradicting the rule that the doubt is resolved against the one in whose domain it arose.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the butcher did pay, and the default assumption is that one does not give an animal without receiving money, so the doubt arose in the animal owner's domain.

items.text: Rav Nachman's statement on hidden blemishes
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement on hidden blemishes
items.desc_en: The daf ends with the beginning of a statement by Rav Nachman about the Sages' ruling regarding hidden blemishes, which is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the Sages' ruling that the distinction between hidden and visible blemishes applies only to hidden blemishes.
Rav Nachman begins a statement about the Sages' ruling, but the text is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Opening distinction on epileptic fits
items.text_en: Opening distinction on epileptic fits
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between fixed and non-fixed epileptic fits: a fixed fit is like hidden blemishes (the wife can claim she did not know), while a non-fixed fit is like visible blemishes (she is presumed to have known).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between fixed epileptic fits, treated as hidden blemishes, and non-fixed fits, treated as visible blemishes.

items.text: Mishnah: Blemishes that do and do not compel divorce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blemishes that do and do not compel divorce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man was born with blemishes, he is not forced to divorce. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies: this applies only to minor blemishes, but for major blemishes he is forced to divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a man with congenital blemishes is not forced to divorce, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes between minor and major blemishes.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies the Mishnah: the leniency applies only to minor blemishes, but for major blemishes the husband is forced to divorce.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over the Mishnah's wording and its implication
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over the Mishnah's wording and its implication
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Chiyya bar Rav dispute whether the Mishnah says 'were born' (נולדו) or 'were' (היו). The Gemara then questions how the distinction between major and minor blemishes works according to the version 'were', since the wife presumably accepted them. The answer: she thought she could tolerate them but now cannot. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel lists examples of major blemishes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Yehuda teaches the Mishnah as 'were born' (נולדו) and Chiyya bar Rav as 'were' (היו), and explains the logical relationship between the two versions.
The Gemara questions how the version 'were' (היו) can distinguish between major and minor blemishes, since the wife presumably accepted them all.
The Gemara answers that she thought she could tolerate them but now cannot, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel lists examples of major blemishes.

items.text: Ruling on the halakha and a contradiction
items.text_en: Ruling on the halakha and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; Rava in the name of Rav Nachman rules like the Sages. The Gemara notes a contradiction from Rabbi Yochanan's general principle that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel except in three cases. The resolution: the amoraim differ in their traditions of Rabbi Yochanan's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, while Rava in the name of Rav Nachman rules like the Sages.
The Gemara objects: Did Rabbi Yochanan really say that? He stated a general rule that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel everywhere except in three cases.
The Gemara resolves: The amoraim differ in their traditions of Rabbi Yochanan's opinion.

items.text: Mishnah: Those forced to divorce and the dispute about acceptance
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those forced to divorce and the dispute about acceptance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those forced to divorce: one with boils, polypus, a gatherer of dog feces, a copper smelter, and a tanner. Rabbi Meir says even if she agreed beforehand, she can later claim she cannot tolerate it. The Sages say she must accept it except for one with boils because it causes him to rot. A case in Sidon: a tanner died and his brother was a tanner; the Sages ruled she can refuse the brother.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the types of men whom the court forces to divorce their wives: one with boils, polypus, a gatherer of dog feces, a copper smelter, and a tanner.
The Mishnah notes that the rule applies whether the condition existed before marriage or developed after marriage.
Rabbi Meir states that even if she agreed beforehand, she can later claim she cannot tolerate the condition.
The Sages rule that she must accept the condition against her will, except for one with boils because it causes him to rot.
The Mishnah cites a case in Sidon where a tanner died and his brother was a tanner; the Sages ruled she can refuse the brother.

items.text: Gemara: Definitions of the terms in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Definitions of the terms in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'ba'al polypus' as either bad breath or bad smell from the nose, with a dispute between Rav Yehuda/Shmuel and a baraisa. It defines 'mekametz' as either a tanner or a gatherer of dog feces, resolving a contradiction by distinguishing large vs. small tanners. It defines 'metzaref nechoshet' as either a smelter of copper vessels or a cutter of copper from its source, with a supporting baraisa.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of the term 'ba'al polypus' in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel defines it as bad breath from the nose.
A baraita defines it as bad breath from the mouth.
Rav Asi reverses the attributions, teaching the opposite version.
The Gemara notes a mnemonic: Shmuel's mouth never stops from all the chapters, linking him to the nose (mouth-related) version.
The Gemara asks for the definition of the term 'mekametz' in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda defines 'mekametz' as a gatherer of dog feces.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that defines 'mekametz' as a tanner (bursi).
The Gemara retorts that the Mishnah itself lists 'mekametz' and 'bursi' separately, so the baraita's equation is problematic.
The Gemara resolves the Mishnah's listing: one refers to a large tanner, the other to a small tanner.
The Gemara objects that Rav Yehuda's definition still contradicts the baraita.
The Gemara resolves that there is a Tannaitic dispute: one Tanna says it is a tanner, another says it is a gatherer of dog feces.
The Gemara asks for the definition of the term 'metzaref nechoshet' in the Mishnah.
Rav Ashi defines 'metzaref nechoshet' as a smelter of copper vessels.
Rabba bar bar Chana defines it as a cutter of copper from its source.
A baraita supports Rabba bar bar Chana's definition, identifying 'metzaref' as a cutter of copper from its source.

items.text: Rav's ruling on one who refuses to support his wife
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on one who refuses to support his wife
items.desc_en: Rav rules that if a man says 'I will not support or provide for my wife,' he must divorce and pay the ketubah. Shmuel objects, saying he should be forced to support first. Rav defends his position: a person cannot live with a snake in a basket. Rabbi Zeira later reports that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rav, and notes that Shmuel's criticism was unjustified.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a man who says 'I will not support or provide for my wife' must divorce her and pay the ketubah.
Shmuel objects, arguing that before forcing him to divorce, the court should force him to support her.
Rav defends his position with the principle that a person cannot live with a snake in a basket, meaning the marriage is intolerable.
Rabbi Zeira reports that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rav, and notes that Shmuel's criticism of Rabbi Elazar was unjustified.

items.text: Coercion to divorce for invalid marriages and childlessness
items.text_en: Coercion to divorce for invalid marriages and childlessness
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi says coercion to divorce applies only to invalid marriages (e.g., a widow to a High Priest). Shmuel lists examples. But if a man married a woman and lived with her ten years without children, he is not forced to divorce. Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel disagrees and says he is forced. The Gemara questions this from the Mishnah's list. Rav Nachman resolves: the Mishnah lists rabbinic cases, not Torah ones. Rabbi Abba objects with a verse, then concludes both are with lashes.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi states that coercion to divorce applies only to invalid marriages, and Shmuel lists examples.
Shmuel adds that a man who married and lived with his wife for ten years without children is not forced to divorce.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel disagrees and says that even in the case of ten years without children, he is forced to divorce.
The Gemara questions Rav Tachlifa's position from the Mishnah's list of forced divorces, which does not include the childlessness case.
Rav Nachman resolves that the Mishnah lists cases of rabbinic coercion (במילי), while the childlessness case requires physical coercion (בשוטי).
Rabbi Abba objects with the verse 'A slave will not be disciplined with words,' implying that verbal coercion is ineffective.
Rabbi Abba concludes that both cases (invalid marriages and childlessness) require physical coercion (בשוטי) with lashes.

items.text: Distinction between מוכה שחין and other cases
items.text_en: Distinction between מוכה שחין and other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts the case of a woman who claims she was willing to live with her husband (and is believed) with the case of a מוכה שחין, where even if she claims willingness, she is not believed because the disease causes him to rot. It further distinguishes between the two cases regarding the woman's offer to live with witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: in the case of a husband afflicted with boils (מוכה שחין), even if she says she wants to stay, we do not leave her, as taught in the mishna.
The Gemara resolves: in the boils case, if she offers to live with witnesses, we leave her; but in the barren woman case, even with witnesses, we do not leave her.

items.text: Twenty-four types of מוכה שחין and the severity of בעלי ראתן
items.text_en: Twenty-four types of מוכה שחין and the severity of בעלי ראתן
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei reporting an elder from Jerusalem who said there are twenty-four types of מוכה שחין, and the Sages said intercourse is difficult for them, but בעלי ראתן is the most severe. The Gemara explains the cause: if a couple both bled and then had intercourse, they produce children with ראתן. Rav Pappa qualifies that this applies only if they did not eat anything.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei reports an elder from Jerusalem who said there are twenty-four types of מוכה שחין (boil-afflicted), and the Sages said intercourse is difficult for them, but בעלי ראתן (those afflicted with ra'atan) is the most severe.
The Gemara asks: From where does this disease come about?

The Gemara answers with a baraita: If one let blood and then engaged in intercourse, he has weak children; if both let blood and then engaged in intercourse, they have children afflicted with ראתן (ra'atan).
Rav Pappa qualifies: this applies only if they did not taste anything between bloodletting and intercourse, but if they tasted something, there is no problem.

items.text: Symptoms and cure for בעלי ראתן
items.text_en: Symptoms and cure for בעלי ראתן
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the symptoms of בעלי ראתן: eyes drip, nose runs, and saliva flows from the mouth, with flies gathering. Abaye prescribes a cure involving various ingredients boiled together, placed in a marble house, and a procedure of pouring cups on the head until the brain softens, then cutting and applying myrtle leaves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the symptoms of בעלי ראתן are, and describes them: eyes drip, nose runs, saliva flows from the mouth, and flies gather on them.
Abaye prescribes a cure: various ingredients boiled together, placed in a marble house (or a house of brick and beam).
Abaye details the procedure: pour three hundred cups on the head until the brain softens, then cut and apply myrtle leaves, otherwise the condition returns.

items.text: Rabbinic attitudes toward בעלי ראתן
items.text_en: Rabbinic attitudes toward בעלי ראתן
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan warns against the flies of בעלי ראתן. Various rabbis take precautions: Rabbi Zeira avoids sitting in their direction, Rabbi Elazar avoids their tent, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi avoid eggs from that alley. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, however, wraps himself with them and engages in Torah study, arguing that Torah protects its students.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan publicly warns people to beware of the flies of בעלי ראתן (those afflicted with a certain skin disease).
Rabbi Zeira would not sit in the direction of the wind coming from בעלי ראתן.
Rabbi Elazar would not enter the tent of a בעל ראתן.

sub.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi's precaution
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi's precaution
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi would not eat eggs from the alley where a בעל ראתן lived.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would wrap himself with בעלי ראתן and engage in Torah study.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites the verse 'אילת אהבים ויעלת חן' (a loving doe and a graceful mountain goat) to argue that if Torah bestows charm on its students, surely it protects them from harm.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and the Angel of Death
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and the Angel of Death
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was instructed to fulfill his wish. He asked to see his place in the Garden of Eden, and then took the angel's knife. He jumped to the other side, and the angel grabbed his cloak. Rabbi Yehoshua swore not to return, and a heavenly voice confirmed his oath. Elijah announced to make way for him. He then met Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who questioned whether he was truly worthy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was instructed to fulfill his wish; Rabbi Yehoshua asked to see his place in the Garden of Eden, took the angel's knife, and jumped to the other side.
The Angel of Death grabbed Rabbi Yehoshua's cloak; Rabbi Yehoshua swore not to return, a heavenly voice confirmed his oath, and Elijah announced to make way for him.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai questioned whether Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was truly worthy, based on whether a rainbow appeared in his lifetime.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi actually did see a rainbow but denied it to avoid taking credit for himself.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa and the Angel of Death
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa and the Angel of Death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, the groomsman of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, asked the Angel of Death for thirty days to review his Torah. Afterward, the angel appeared again. Rabbi Chanina asked for the knife, but the angel refused, suspecting he would do as his friend did. Rabbi Chanina then asked to see a Torah scroll to prove his observance. The angel noted that he had wrapped himself with בעלי ראתן and studied Torah. At his death, a pillar of fire separated him from the world, a rare honor. Rabbi Alexandri pleaded for him, but he did not relent until asked for his own honor. Abaye and Rav Adda bar Matna explained the pillar's purpose.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa as the groomsman of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and recounts that at his death the Angel of Death was told to fulfill his wish; Rabbi Chanina requested thirty days to review his Torah, citing the maxim that one is fortunate to arrive in the next world with his learning in hand.

After thirty days the Angel of Death appeared again; when Rabbi Chanina asked to see his place and requested the knife, the angel refused, suspecting he would do as his friend (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) did.

Rabbi Chanina asked to bring a Torah scroll to prove he fulfilled all its commandments; the angel noted that he had wrapped himself with בעלי ראתן (those afflicted with raatan) and studied Torah, yet at his death a pillar of fire separated him from the world.
The gemara notes a tradition that such a pillar of fire appears only for one or two individuals per generation.
Rabbi Alexandri pleaded with the pillar of fire to depart for the honor of the sages, then for the honor of Rabbi Chanina's father, and finally for his own honor, at which point the pillar withdrew.
Abaye explains that the pillar of fire was to exclude someone who did not fulfill even a single letter of the Torah.
Rav Adda bar Matna objects that the pillar was to exclude a certain master who lacked a parapet on his roof.
The gemara resolves that the master did have a parapet, but at that moment a spark had dislodged it.

items.text: Why there are no בעלי ראתן or lepers in Babylonia
items.text_en: Why there are no בעלי ראתן or lepers in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that there are no בעלי ראתן in Babylonia because they eat תרדין (beets) and drink beer of היזמי (a type of plant). Rabbi Yochanan adds that there are no lepers there because they eat תרדין, drink beer, and bathe in the Euphrates.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that there are no בעלי ראתן (a skin disease) in Babylonia because they eat תרדין (beets) and drink beer of היזמי (a type of plant).
Rabbi Yochanan adds that there are no lepers (מצורעין) in Babylonia because they eat תרדין (beets), drink beer, and bathe in the Euphrates.

items.text: Mishnah: Disputes over a woman's property rights at different stages
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disputes over a woman's property rights at different stages
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents the laws of a woman who acquires property before betrothal, after betrothal, and after marriage. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree she may sell property acquired before betrothal, but disagree on property acquired after betrothal. After marriage, all agree the husband can reclaim sold property. Rabban Gamliel rules that if she sold property acquired between betrothal and marriage, the sale is valid, but the Sages question this. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between property known to the husband and unknown property.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the law of a woman who acquires property before betrothal: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree she may sell it and the sale is valid, but for property acquired after betrothal they disagree.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda citing the Sages' question and Rabban Gamliel's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda citing the Sages' question and Rabban Gamliel's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda reports that the Sages asked Rabban Gamliel: since the husband acquired the woman, should he not also acquire her property? Rabban Gamliel rebukes them for raising old issues.

sub.text: Mishnah continuing with property after marriage and Rabban Gamliel's second ruling
sub.text_en: Mishnah continuing with property after marriage and Rabban Gamliel's second ruling
sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that for property acquired after marriage, all agree the husband can reclaim it from buyers; for property acquired between betrothal and marriage, Rabban Gamliel rules the sale is valid, and Rabbi Chanina ben Akavya reports a similar exchange with the Sages.
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between property known to the husband (sale is void) and property unknown to the husband (sale is valid).

items.text: Gemara's question: Why the difference between the first and last clauses?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why the difference between the first and last clauses?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel do not dispute in the first case (property before betrothal) but do dispute in the later case (property after betrothal).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel do not dispute in the first case (property before betrothal) but do dispute in the later case (property after betrothal).

items.text: Answer and refinement from the school of Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: Answer and refinement from the school of Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that in the first case, the property fell to her in her own merit, so she has full rights. In the later case, it might have fallen in her merit or in his merit, so initially she may not sell, but if she did, the sale is valid. The Gemara then questions why the sale would be valid if it fell in his merit, and refines the answer.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that in the first case (before betrothal) the property fell to her in her own merit, while in the later case (after betrothal) it fell in his merit.
The Gemara objects: if the property fell in his merit, why should her sale be valid at all?

The Gemara refines: in the first case it definitely fell in her merit; in the later case it is uncertain whether it fell in her merit or his merit, so לכתחילה (the ideal standard) she may not sell, but if she sold or gave, the sale is valid.

items.text: Inquiry about Rabbi Yehuda's statement: initial or retroactive?
items.text_en: Inquiry about Rabbi Yehuda's statement: initial or retroactive?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about Rabbi Yehuda's report of the Sages' question to Rabban Gamliel: whether the Sages' question was about the initial ruling (le-chatchila) or about the retroactive validity (di-avad).

sub.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: The gemara raises an inquiry: does Rabbi Yehuda's statement refer to the לכתחילה (ideal standard) ruling or to the בדיעבד (after the fact) ruling?

items.text: Baraita: Rabban Gamliel's first response
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabban Gamliel's first response
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda reports that the Sages asked Rabban Gamliel: since both women are his wives, why is the sale of one void and not the other? Rabban Gamliel replied: 'Are we ashamed of the new matters that you force us to deal with the old?' The Gemara concludes that this implies he was speaking of a case that already happened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita to support its position.
The Sages ask Rabban Gamliel: since both women are his wives, why is the sale of one void and not the other?
Rabban Gamliel replies: 'Are we ashamed of the new matters that you force us to deal with the old?'
The Gemara concludes that this implies Rabban Gamliel was speaking of a case that already happened.

items.text: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya's version of Rabban Gamliel's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya's version of Rabban Gamliel's response
items.desc_en: A second baraita records Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya's version: Rabban Gamliel responded with a logical distinction between a married woman (whose husband has rights to her findings, earnings, and annulment of vows) and an arusah (whose husband has none of these).

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya
sub.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya's version: Rabban Gamliel responded to the sages with a logical distinction between a married woman (whose husband has rights to her findings, earnings, and annulment of vows) and an arusah (whose husband has none of these).

items.text: Question about sale before and after marriage, and the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Question about sale before and after marriage, and the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Sages asked Rabban Gamliel about a woman who sold property before marriage and then married, or sold after marriage. He replied that her sale is valid. They objected: since he acquired the woman, should he not acquire the property? He repeated his earlier retort. The Gemara notes that our Mishnah states that Rabban Gamliel rules her sale is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Sages ask Rabban Gamliel about the validity of a woman's sale of property before marriage and after marriage.
Rabban Gamliel rules that even in these cases her sale is valid.
The Sages object: since the husband acquired the woman, should he not also acquire her property?
Rabban Gamliel rebukes them, saying they are shamed by new matters and dredge up old ones.
The Gemara notes that our Mishnah supports Rabban Gamliel's ruling that her sale is valid.

items.text: Reconciling the two versions of Rabban Gamliel's response
items.text_en: Reconciling the two versions of Rabban Gamliel's response
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid teaches that the Mishnah's version says 'her sale is valid' (קַיָּים), while Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction: the first baraita (Rabbi Yehuda) reports Rabban Gamliel's response in a case that already happened, while the second (Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya) reports his logical argument. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya follows Beit Shammai, and answers that he says Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not dispute this point.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid teaches that the Mishnah's version should read 'she sells and gives and it is valid' (קַיָּים), reconciling the text.

Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction: the first baraita (Rabbi Yehuda) reports Rabban Gamliel's response in a case that already happened, while the second (Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya) reports his logical argument.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya's position follows Beit Shammai.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya says Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not dispute this point.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's ruling and its source
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's ruling and its source
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both rule that whether the property fell to her before or after betrothal, once she marries, the husband can reclaim it from the buyers. The Gemara asks: whose opinion is this? It is neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya, but rather the later Rabbis (רבותינו) who voted that the husband reclaims the property in both cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel rule that whether property fell before or after betrothal, once married the husband reclaims it from buyers.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this ruling follows, noting it is neither Rabbi Yehuda nor Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya.
The Gemara answers that Rav and Shmuel follow the later Rabbis (רבותינו) who voted that the husband reclaims the property in both cases.

items.text: The enactment of Usha and its distinction from the Mishnah
items.text_en: The enactment of Usha and its distinction from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that after marriage, all agree. It asks whether this is the enactment of Usha, where Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina said they instituted that if a woman sold melog property during her husband's lifetime and died, the husband reclaims it from the buyers. The Gemara distinguishes: the Mishnah deals with her lifetime and for the produce, while the enactment of Usha deals with the land itself after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that after marriage, both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree the husband repossesses the property.
The Gemara asks whether this ruling is the same as the ordinance of Usha.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina cites the ordinance of Usha: if a woman sold melog property during her husband's lifetime and died, the husband reclaims it from the buyers.
The Gemara distinguishes: the Mishnah deals with her lifetime and only for the produce, while the ordinance of Usha deals with the land itself after her death.

items.text: Definition of known and unknown properties
items.text_en: Definition of known and unknown properties
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between known and unknown properties. Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina defines known as land and unknown as movables. Rabbi Yoḥanan says both are known; unknown refers to property that falls to her while she is in one place and the property is overseas. A baraita supports Rabbi Yoḥanan's definition.

sub.desc_en: The mishna states that Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between known and unknown properties, and the Gemara asks for definitions.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina defines known properties as land and unknown properties as movable goods.
Rabbi Yoḥanan disagrees, stating that both land and movables are known; unknown properties are those that fall to her while she resides here and the property is overseas.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yoḥanan's definition, stating that unknown properties are those where she resides here and the property falls to her overseas.

items.text: Story of a woman who transferred property to her daughter
items.text_en: Story of a woman who transferred property to her daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of a woman who wanted to hide her property from her husband, so she wrote it over to her daughter. She then married and was divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of a woman who transferred her property to her daughter to hide it from her husband, then married and was divorced.

items.text: Rav Nachman tears the delivery deed; Mar Ukva and Rava defend the ruling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman tears the delivery deed; Mar Ukva and Rava defend the ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman tears a deed brought before him. Rav Anan complains to Mar Ukva, who asks for details and then cites Shmuel's ruling that a 'delivery deed' (שטר מברחת) should be torn. Rava asks Rav Nachman for the reasoning: a person would not give away their own property to others, but to a daughter they might; however, even then, the woman prefers herself over her daughter.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav Nachman tears the deed
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav Nachman tears the deed
sub.desc_en: A woman came before Rav Nachman with a deed, and Rav Nachman tore it.

sub.text: Rav Anan complains to Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Rav Anan complains to Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva about Rav Nachman's tearing of deeds, and Mar Ukva asked for the details of the case.
Rav Anan described the case to Mar Ukva.
Mar Ukva identified the deed as a 'delivery deed' (שטר מברחת) and cited Shmuel's ruling that such a deed should be torn.

sub.text: Rava asks Rav Nachman for the reasoning
sub.text_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman for the reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rava asked Rav Nachman for the reasoning behind the ruling: a person would not give away their own property to others.

sub.text: Rava's objection: but to a daughter?
sub.text_en: Rava's objection: but to a daughter?
sub.desc_en: Rava objected that while a person would not give to others, they might give to their daughter.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's resolution: even to a daughter, she prefers herself
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: even to a daughter, she prefers herself
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolved that even regarding a daughter, the woman prefers herself over her daughter.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah of a woman hiding assets from her husband
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah of a woman hiding assets from her husband
items.desc_en: A baraisa is cited: a woman who wants to hide assets from her husband writes a 'deed of division' (שטר פסים) to others, according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. The Sages say she must write 'from today and when I wish' to avoid the gift being absolute. The Gemara infers that without such a condition, the recipient acquires the property, contradicting the earlier ruling that a delivery deed is invalid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a woman who wants to hide assets from her husband writes a 'deed of division' (שטר פסים) to others, according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The Sages say she must write 'from today and when I wish' to avoid the gift being absolute.
The Gemara infers that without such a condition, the recipient acquires the property, contradicting the earlier ruling that a delivery deed is invalid.

items.text: Resolution: distinction between full and partial transfer; the husband does not acquire
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction between full and partial transfer; the husband does not acquire
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction: the baraisa refers to transferring all property, while the delivery deed refers to part. Abaye adds that the Sages treated such property as unknown to the husband, following Rabbi Shimon's view, so the husband does not acquire it even if the recipient does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a full transfer (כולה) and a partial transfer (מקצתה), explaining that the baraisa refers to transferring all property, while the delivery deed refers to part.
The Gemara objects: if the recipient does not acquire the property, why should the husband not acquire it?

Abaye answers that the Sages treated such property as נכסים שאין ידועין לבעל (property unknown to the husband), following Rabbi Shimon's view, so the husband does not acquire it even if the recipient does not.

items.text: Mishnah: rules for a wife's melog property and its produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: rules for a wife's melog property and its produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a wife receives cash, land is purchased with it and the husband eats the produce. For detached produce, the same applies. For attached produce, Rabbi Meir assesses the land's value with and without produce, and the surplus is used to buy land. The Sages say attached produce belongs to the husband, detached to the wife. Rabbi Shimon adds a principle: where the husband's power is greater at entry, it is weaker at exit, and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if a wife receives cash or detached produce, land is purchased with it and the husband eats the produce.
Rabbi Meir states that for attached produce, the land is assessed with and without the produce, and the surplus is used to buy land for the husband's produce consumption.
The Sages rule that attached produce belongs to the husband and detached produce belongs to the wife, with detached produce used to buy land for the husband's produce.

Rabbi Shimon states a general principle: where the husband's power is greater at entry, it is weaker at exit, and vice versa, illustrating with attached produce (his at entry, hers at exit) and detached produce (hers at entry, his at exit).

items.text: Gemara: defining what constitutes 'produce' (פירי) vs. 'principal' (קרנא)
items.text_en: Gemara: defining what constitutes 'produce' (פירי) vs. 'principal' (קרנא)
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that when land and houses are involved, the land is the principal; houses and palm trees — houses; palm trees and other trees — palm trees; trees and vines — trees. For certain plants like אבא, זרדתא, and פירא דכוורי, there is a dispute whether they are produce or principal. The rule: if the stem renews, it is produce; if not, it is principal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the obvious hierarchy: when land and houses are involved, land is the principal; houses and palm trees — houses; palm trees and other trees — palm trees; trees and vines — trees.
The Gemara presents a dispute about certain plants (אבא, זרדתא, פירא דכוורי) whether they are produce or principal, and gives the rule: if the stem renews, it is produce; if not, it is principal.

items.text: Beginning of a new sugya: a thief's liability
items.text_en: Beginning of a new sugya: a thief's liability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a tradition in the name of Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yannai about a thief, but the text is cut off here.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira citing Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira introduces a tradition in the names of Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yannai (with an alternate transmission via Rabbi Abba) about a thief, but the text is cut off here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a melog animal gives birth, the husband pays double payment to the wife.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a melog animal gives birth, the husband pays double payment to the wife.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah
