items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whose opinion the Mishnah follows, citing a Tannaic dispute between the Rabbis and Chananya about the ownership of offspring from melog property. It resolves the issue by distinguishing between primary produce and secondary produce, and explains the Rabbis' concern for the animal's death versus its hide.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows, citing the Tannaic dispute between the Rabbis and Chananya.
The Gemara resolves that even according to both opinions, the Rabbis instituted primary produce for the husband but not secondary produce.
The Gemara explains Chananya's position that we do not worry about the animal's death.

The Gemara challenges the Rabbis: if they worry about death, why not give the offspring of a melog animal to the wife as well; if they don't worry, why not give the offspring of a melog maidservant to the husband?
The Gemara resolves that the Rabbis do worry about death, but an animal's hide offsets the loss, unlike a maidservant.

items.text: Ruling of Shmuel and Rava
items.text_en: Ruling of Shmuel and Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya quotes Shmuel that the halakha follows Chananya, but Rava quotes Rav Nachman that Chananya agrees that if the wife is divorced, she pays the value and takes the offspring, due to the enhancement of her father's house.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiya reports that Shmuel rules the law follows Chananya, and Rava adds that Chananya concedes that if the wife is divorced, she pays the value and takes the offspring, due to the enhancement of her father's house.
Rav Nachman adds that even Chananya concedes that if the wife is divorced, she may pay the value and take the produce, due to the enhancement of her father's house.

items.text: Consuming produce that diminishes the principal
items.text_en: Consuming produce that diminishes the principal
items.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that if a wife brought a goat for its milk, a sheep for its wool, a hen for its eggs, or a palm tree for its dates, the husband may consume the produce until the principal is exhausted. Rav Nachman adds that a cloak is considered produce, and the husband may use it until it wears out. The Gemara identifies this view with a Tanna who considers salt and sand as produce, and distinguishes between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding a sulfur pit and a lime pit.

sub.desc_en: Rava quotes Rav Nachman that if a wife brought a goat for its milk, a sheep for its wool, a hen for its eggs, or a palm tree for its dates, the husband may consume the produce until the principal is exhausted.
Rav Nachman adds that a cloak is considered produce, and the husband may use it until it wears out.
The Gemara asks whose view this ruling aligns with, and identifies it with a specific Tanna.
A baraita is cited: salt and sand are considered produce; regarding a sulfur pit and a lime pit, Rabbi Meir says it is principal, while the Sages say it is produce.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon's statement seems identical to the Tanna Kamma, raising an objection.
Rava resolves the objection by explaining that the difference between Rabbi Shimon and the Tanna Kamma lies in whether items are considered attached at the time of extraction.

items.text: Mishnah on selling worn-out property
items.text_en: Mishnah on selling worn-out property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where a wife inherits old slaves or old olive trees and grapevines, and whether they should be sold to buy land from which the husband eats the produce. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehuda argue that they should not be sold due to the enhancement of her father's house. The Gemara cites Rav Kahana's interpretation of the dispute, which is challenged by Rav Yosef and then corrected.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: old slaves and old trees that fall to a wife, with a dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehuda who argue they should not be sold due to the enhancement of her father's house.
Rav Kahana citing Rav explains that the Mishnah's dispute applies only when the property fell in her own field, but in a field not hers all agree she may sell because the capital is being consumed.
Rav Yosef objects that slaves and maidservants are like a field not hers, yet the Mishnah shows they are disputed.
The Gemara corrects Rav Kahana's statement: the dispute is actually in a field not hers, but in her own field all agree she should not sell due to the enhancement of her father's house.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on husband's expenses
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on husband's expenses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a husband spent much on his wife's property but consumed little, or vice versa, he accounts for what he spent and what he consumed. If he spent but did not consume, he swears how much he spent and takes it. The Gemara asks how much is 'little,' and Rabbi Asi answers that even one fig is considered little, provided it was eaten in a dignified manner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if a husband spent much on his wife's property but consumed little, or vice versa, he accounts for what he spent and what he consumed; if he spent but did not consume, he swears how much he spent and takes it.
The Gemara asks: how much is considered 'little' (קִימְעָא) in the Mishnah's ruling?
Rabbi Asi answers that even one fig is considered little, provided it was eaten in a dignified manner (דֶּרֶךְ כָּבוֹד).

items.text: Opening question about inferior produce
items.text_en: Opening question about inferior produce
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi asks whether a cake of dates (חובצא דתמרי) is considered like the lowest grade of produce (שיגרא דתמרי) for the husband's usufruct rights. The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi asks whether a cake of dates (חובצא דתמרי) is considered like the lowest grade of produce (שיגרא דתמרי) for the husband's usufruct rights, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute over the measure of honor
items.text_en: Dispute over the measure of honor
items.desc_en: Ulla reports a dispute between two Amoraim in the West: one says the husband must provide an issar's worth of food, the other says a dinar's worth, when the wife does not eat in a dignified manner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the husband must provide if the wife does not eat in a dignified manner.
Ulla reports that two Amoraim in the West dispute: one says an issar's worth, the other says a dinar's worth.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's precedent with bundles of branches
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's precedent with bundles of branches
items.desc_en: The judges of Pumbedita report that Rav Yehuda ruled practically with bundles of branches (חבבילי זמורות), consistent with his own view that if the wife ate orlah, shevi'it, or kilayim produce, that establishes a chazakah (presumption of ownership).

sub.desc_en: The judges of Pumbedita report that Rav Yehuda ruled practically with bundles of branches (חבבילי זמורות), consistent with his own view that if the wife ate orlah, shevi'it, or kilayim produce, that establishes a chazakah (presumption of ownership).

items.text: Rule for a minor wife's property
items.text_en: Rule for a minor wife's property
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov quoting Rav Chisda states that one who spends on his minor wife's property is like one who spends on another's property, because the Sages enacted a safeguard to prevent him from losing it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov in the name of Rav Chisda states that one who spends on his minor wife's property is like one who spends on another's property.
The Gemara explains the reason: the Sages enacted a safeguard (תקנתא) so that the husband would not lose the property.

items.text: Case of a husband who spent on his wife's property
items.text_en: Case of a husband who spent on his wife's property
items.desc_en: A story is told of a woman who inherited 400 zuz; her husband spent 600 to bring them, but took one zuz from them. Rabbi Ammi ruled that what he spent is spent and what he ate is eaten. The Rabbis object that he consumed the principal, not just the produce, so he should be treated as one who spent without eating and should take an oath and collect.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a woman who inherited 400 zuz in Bei Hozai; her husband spent 600 to bring them, but took one zuz from them during the journey.
Rabbi Ammi rules that what the husband spent is spent and what he ate is eaten, implying no further claim.
The Rabbis object that the husband consumed the principal (קרנא), not just the produce, so he should be treated as one who spent without eating and should take an oath and collect.

items.text: Dispute about oath and the measure of improvement
items.text_en: Dispute about oath and the measure of improvement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Assi adds that the oath applies only when there is improvement equal to the expenditure. Abaye explains that if the improvement exceeds the expenditure, he takes the expenditure without an oath. Rava objects that this would lead to evasion, and instead rules that if the expenditure exceeds the improvement, he only gets up to the value of the improvement, with an oath.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that the husband swears how much he spent and then takes that amount.
Rabbi Assi adds that the oath applies only when there is improvement (שבח) equal to the expenditure.
The gemara asks: what practical halachic conclusion follows from Rabbi Assi's statement?
Abaye explains that if the improvement exceeds the expenditure, the husband takes his expenditure without an oath.
Rava objects that Abaye's ruling would lead to evasion (הערמה) by the husband.
Rava rules instead that if the expenditure exceeds the improvement, the husband only receives up to the value of the improvement, and must take an oath.

items.text: Inquiry about a husband who appointed sharecroppers
items.text_en: Inquiry about a husband who appointed sharecroppers
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether sharecroppers appointed by the husband remain after his death or divorce. Rava bar Rav Chanan compares it to the case of an unauthorized planter, but the Gemara distinguishes because here the husband toiled. Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua resolves: if the husband is a sharecropper himself, the sharecroppers leave; if not, the land remains for them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether sharecroppers appointed by the husband remain on the land after his death or divorce, or whether they leave with him.
Rava bar Rav Chanan objects by comparing the case to an unauthorized planter, who is assessed and receives the lower amount.
The Gemara rejects the comparison because in the unauthorized case no one toiled, whereas here the husband toiled.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua resolves: if the husband is himself a sharecropper, the sharecroppers leave with him; if not, the land remains for them.

items.text: Inquiry about a husband who sold land for its produce
items.text_en: Inquiry about a husband who sold land for its produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband who sold land for its produce (i.e., the buyer gets the produce) has effectively transferred what he acquired, or whether the Sages only granted produce to the husband for himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband who sold land for its produce has effectively transferred what he acquired, or whether the Sages only granted produce to the husband for himself.

items.text: Dispute over husband's sale of wife's property for usufruct
items.text_en: Dispute over husband's sale of wife's property for usufruct
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a dispute between Yehudah Mar bar Mareimar and Rav Pappa in the name of Rava: whether a husband who sold his wife's land for usufruct has any legal effect. Rav Pappa clarifies that Yehudah Mar's ruling was not explicit but inferred from a case where a woman brought two maidservants and her husband gave one to a second wife; Rava ignored her complaint, not because the sale was valid, but because the house was already spacious.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle of רווח ביתא (household benefit) applies only to giving property for use, not to selling it.

sub.text: Yehudah Mar bar Mareimar in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Yehudah Mar bar Mareimar in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Yehudah Mar bar Mareimar reports in Rava's name that a husband's sale of his wife's land for usufruct is valid (מה שעשה עשוי).

sub.text: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports in Rava's name that the sale has no legal effect (לא עשה ולא כלום).
Rav Pappa clarifies that Yehudah Mar's ruling was not explicit but inferred from a case.
Rav Pappa recounts the case: a woman brought two maidservants, and her husband gave one to a second wife.
The Gemara explains that Rava ignored the woman's complaint not because the sale was valid, but because the house was already spacious (רווח ביתא).

items.text: Halakhic ruling and rationale for husband's sale
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and rationale for husband's sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha: a husband who sold land for usufruct has done nothing. Abaye and Rava debate the reason: Abaye fears the land might depreciate, while Rava cites the need for household income. The practical difference between them is whether the land is near town, the husband is a sharecropper, or he uses the money for business.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakhic ruling: a husband who sold land for its usufruct (פירות) has done nothing (the sale is void).
The Gemara asks for the rationale behind the ruling.
Abaye explains the reason: we fear the land might depreciate (תַּכְסִיף) in value, harming the wife's eventual claim.
Rava gives a different reason: the husband needs household income (רווח ביתא) from the land, so selling the usufruct would deprive the household.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between Abaye's and Rava's rationales.
The Gemara lists three practical differences: land near town (where depreciation is unlikely), the husband being a sharecropper (אריס), or the husband using the money for business (עיסקא).

items.text: Mishnah: Yevamah's assets and inheritance dispute
items.text_en: Mishnah: Yevamah's assets and inheritance dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a shomeret yavam (waiting yevamah) who receives assets may sell and give them away, and the transaction stands. If she dies, Beit Shammai say the husband's heirs and the father's heirs divide the ketubah and the property that goes in and out with her. Beit Hillel rule that property remains in its presumptive ownership: the ketubah goes to the husband's heirs, and the property that goes in and out with her goes to the father's heirs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a shomeret yavam (waiting yevamah) who receives assets may sell and give them away, and the transaction stands.
The Mishnah raises the question of what happens to the ketubah and the property that goes in and out with her if she dies.
Beit Shammai rule that the husband's heirs and the father's heirs divide the ketubah and the property.
Beit Hillel rule that property remains in its presumptive ownership: the ketubah goes to the husband's heirs, and the property that goes in and out with her goes to the father's heirs.

items.text: Mishnah: Handling of yavam's assets and produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Handling of yavam's assets and produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details how assets left by the deceased brother are handled: money is used to buy land, and the yavam eats the produce. For detached produce, land is bought; for attached produce, Rabbi Meir assesses their value with and without produce, and the surplus buys land. The Sages rule that attached produce belongs to the yavam, and detached produce is acquired by whoever takes it first; if the yavam takes it, he keeps it; if the yevamah takes it, it is used to buy land for usufruct.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that money left by the deceased brother is used to purchase land, and the yavam consumes the produce; the same applies to detached produce.
Rabbi Meir says that attached produce is evaluated for its value with and without produce, and the surplus is used to purchase land while the yavam eats the produce.

The Sages rule that attached produce belongs to the yavam, detached produce is acquired by whoever takes it first, and if the yevamah takes it first, land is purchased with it and the yavam eats the produce.

items.text: Mishnah: Yavam's marriage and ketubah obligations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Yavam's marriage and ketubah obligations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that once the yavam marries the yevamah, she is like his wife in all respects, except her ketubah is on the first husband's property. He cannot say her ketubah is set aside; all his property is liable for it. If he divorces her, she gets only her ketubah; if he remarries her, she is like any other woman with only a ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that once the yavam marries the yevamah she is like his wife in every respect, except that her ketubah is charged against the first husband's property.
The yavam may not tell her that her ketubah is set aside on the table; rather all his property remains mortgaged for it, and the same applies to any man and his wife.
If the yavam divorces her she has only her ketubah, and if he remarries her she is like all other women with only her ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's question: Who buries the deceased yevamah?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Who buries the deceased yevamah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if a shomeret yavam dies, who is responsible for her burial? The husband's heirs, who inherit the ketubah, or the father's heirs, who inherit the property that goes in and out with her? Rav Amram cites a baraitha that addresses this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a shomeret yavam dies, who buries her — the husband's heirs who inherit the ketubah, or the father's heirs who inherit the property that goes in and out with her?
Rav Amram cites a baraitha to resolve the question, beginning: 'A shomeret yavam who died...'

items.text: Abaye's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a Mishnah that an almanah supported by orphans' property is not buried by them, but her ketubah heirs are obligated, identifying this as a shomeret yavam.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a Mishnah that an almanah supported by orphans' property is not buried by them, but her ketubah heirs are obligated, identifying this as a shomeret yavam.

items.text: Rava's objection and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Rava's objection and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: Rava objects that a yavam could claim he inherits as a brother but is not obligated to bury the wife; Abaye counters that the yavam faces a dilemma: if he inherits, he must bury, and if he does not bury, he must pay the ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the yavam could claim he inherits as a brother but is not obligated to bury the wife.
Abaye counters that the yavam faces a dilemma: if he inherits, he must bury, and if he does not bury, he must pay the ketubah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Beit Shammai's view on a standing debt
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Beit Shammai's view on a standing debt
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that only Beit Shammai holds that a ketubah can be collected from the living, as they consider a document ready for collection as already collected, citing a Mishnah about sotah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that the marriage contract can be expounded, identifying Beit Shammai, who consider a document ready for collection as already collected.
The Gemara cites a mishna about sotah where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether widows take their marriage contract.
The Gemara questions the wording of Beit Hillel's statement, clarifying that since the husband is dead, the women cannot drink, so they do not take the marriage contract.
The Gemara questions why Beit Shammai allows collection of the marriage contract despite the uncertainty of adultery, noting that an uncertain claim would supersede a certain one.
The Gemara concludes that Beit Shammai consider a document ready for collection as already collected, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Objection and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Objection and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the ketubah condition requires marriage to another, but Rav Ashi answers that a yavam is considered like another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the ketubah condition requires marriage to another, and this is not the case with a yavam.
Rav Ashi answers that a yavam is considered like another, so the condition is fulfilled.

items.text: Rava's question and the baraita from Rabbi Abba
items.text_en: Rava's question and the baraita from Rabbi Abba
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether a ketubah can be collected from the living, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Abba asked Sumchos about selling a brother's property, implying that a yavam can circumvent the obligation.

sub.desc_en: Rava sends a question to Abaye via Rav Shemayah bar Zeira: Is a ketubah given to be collected from the living (i.e., from the yavam while he is alive)?

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Abba asked Sumchos about a brother who wants to sell the deceased brother's property: if a kohen, he appeases with a meal; if an Israelite, he divorces with a גט (bill of divorce) and remarries, implying that the yavam can circumvent the obligation by divorcing, thus the ketubah is not collected from the living.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding selling property
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding selling property
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if a ketubah could be collected from the husband's lifetime, why not designate her ketubah amount and sell the rest? It answers that the Mishnah merely offers good advice, as the parallel case of not saying 'your ketubah is on the table' also teaches advice, not law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if a ketubah could be collected from the husband's lifetime, why not designate her ketubah amount and sell the rest?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah merely offers good advice (עצה טובה), as shown by the parallel case of not saying 'your ketubah is on the table'.

items.text: Resolving Rabbi Abba's difficulty due to enmity
items.text_en: Resolving Rabbi Abba's difficulty due to enmity
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Abba's earlier statement is not problematic because it was motivated by concern for enmity (eivah) between the yavam and yevama.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: Rabbi Abba's earlier statement still seems problematic.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Abba's statement is not difficult because it was motivated by concern for enmity (איבה) between the yavam and yevama.

items.text: Story of a yavam and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.text_en: Story of a yavam and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.desc_en: A man had a yevama in Pumbedita; his brother sought to disqualify her with a get. The first brother offered to share property. Rav Yosef ruled that since the Sages said not to sell, even if sold the sale is void, citing a baraita about a yavam who inherited property.

sub.desc_en: The storyteller introduces a case: a man had a yevama (levirate widow) in Pumbedita, and his brother sought to disqualify her with a get (bill of divorce).
The first brother asks the second brother why he wants to disqualify the yevama, and offers to share the property with him.
Rav Yosef rules that since the Sages said not to sell, even if sold the sale is void, citing a baraita about a yavam who inherited property.

items.text: Abaye's objection and the response from Rabbi Chanina bar Papi
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and the response from Rabbi Chanina bar Papi
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: is every sale prohibited by the Sages void? The Mishnah about a widow selling shows that Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai agree that if she sold, it is valid. They sent to Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, who ruled like Rav Yosef. Abaye questions this, and they sent to Rav Minyomi, who ruled like Abaye but asked for Rav Yosef's alternative reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rav Yosef's principle that any sale prohibited by the Sages is void, citing the Mishnah where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that a widow's sale is valid even though they prohibited it.

sub.text: Response from Rabbi Chanina bar Papi
sub.text_en: Response from Rabbi Chanina bar Papi
sub.desc_en: They sent the question to Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, who ruled in accordance with Rav Yosef's position that the sale is void.
Abaye challenges the authority of Rabbi Chanina bar Papi's ruling, implying it was not a decisive resolution.
They sent to Rav Minyomi, who ruled like Abaye but requested that if Rav Yosef has an alternative reasoning, they should send it to him.

items.text: Rav Yosef finds a supporting baraita and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Yosef finds a supporting baraita and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef found a baraita stating that if one was owed by his brother who died leaving a yevama, the debt is collected from the yavam to buy land. Abaye suggests this might be for the yavam's benefit, but Rav Yosef retorts that the baraita says 'they take out' (forcefully), not merely advise.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's citation of a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's citation of a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef finds a baraita stating that a creditor of a deceased brother who left a יבמה (yevama) may collect the debt from the יבם (yavam) to purchase land, from which the creditor eats the produce.
Abaye suggests that the baraita might only be advising for the יבם's (yavam's) benefit, not compelling him.
Rav Yosef retorts that the baraita uses the term 'מוֹצִיאִין' (they take out forcefully), indicating compulsion, not mere advice.

items.text: Rav Minyomi's rejection of the baraita and explanation
items.text_en: Rav Minyomi's rejection of the baraita and explanation
items.desc_en: They sent again to Rav Minyomi, who said Rav Nachman ruled that this baraita is not a Mishnah (i.e., not authoritative). The Gemara explores reasons: perhaps because it involved movables (which are not liened for ketubah), but that would align with Rabbi Meir; rather, the reason is that the creditor cannot claim from the yavam directly since the yevama is not his debtor.

sub.desc_en: They sent again to Rav Minyomi, who reported in the name of Rav Nachman that this baraita is not a Mishnah (i.e., not authoritative).
The Gemara asks for the reason, suggesting it might be because the property involved was movables (מִטַּלְטְלִי), which are not liened for the ketubah.
The Gemara rejects that explanation, noting that it would align only with Rabbi Meir's view that movables are liened for the ketubah.
The Gemara concludes that the true reason is that the yavam can say to the yevama: 'You are not my litigant' (the creditor cannot claim from the yavam directly since the yevama is not his debtor).

items.text: Identifying the Tanna behind the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna behind the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah might follow Rabbi Nathan, who holds that a creditor can collect from a debtor's debtor. It then concludes that no Tanna combines both stringencies of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Nathan regarding a ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah might follow Rabbi Nathan, citing his baraita that a creditor can collect from a debtor's debtor based on the verse 'וְנָתַן לַאֲשֶׁר אָשַׁם לוֹ'.
The Gemara concludes that no Tanna combines both stringencies of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Nathan regarding a ketubah; it is either one or the other.

items.text: Rava's clarification of Abaye's statement
items.text_en: Rava's clarification of Abaye's statement
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Abaye's cryptic remark 'This is not a Mishnah' refers to the difficulty of finding a Tanna who holds both stringencies.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves that Abaye's cryptic statement 'This is not a Mishnah' refers to the impossibility of finding a Tanna who holds both stringencies.

items.text: Story of a yavam and property dispute
items.text_en: Story of a yavam and property dispute
items.desc_en: A man had a yevamah and his brother sought to disqualify her with a get. The yavam offered to divide the property, but the brother feared being tricked like the Pumbeditan. The yavam then offered an immediate division.

sub.desc_en: The storyteller introduces a case of a man who had a yevamah (a sister-in-law awaiting yibbum) in the town of Machseya.
The brother sought to disqualify the yevamah from the yavam by giving her a get (bill of divorce).
The yavam asks the brother what he intends, and offers to divide the property with him.
The brother objects, saying he fears being tricked like the deceitful Pumbeditan.
The yavam resolves the objection by offering to divide the property immediately.

items.text: Acquisition after thirty days and its application
items.text_en: Acquisition after thirty days and its application
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who says 'pull this cow but it will be acquired only after thirty days' acquires it after thirty days, even if it stands in a marsh. The Gemara distinguishes between cases where the item is in the giver's domain versus not, and resolves a contradiction between Rabbi Yochanan's statements by distinguishing whether the giver said 'acquire from now'.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who says 'pull this cow but it will be acquired only after thirty days' acquires it after thirty days, even if it stands in a marsh.
The Gemara distinguishes between the case where the item is in the giver's domain (there) versus not (here).
The Gemara resolves a contradiction between two versions of Rabbi Yochanan's statement by distinguishing whether the giver said 'acquire from now' or not.

items.text: Yibbum and division of property: order matters
items.text_en: Yibbum and division of property: order matters
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a yavam who performed yibbum and then divided the estate, or divided and then performed yibbum. Rav Sheshet challenges the need to ask both, as the result is the same. Resh Lakish rules that in either case, the division is void, and the halakhah follows this.

sub.desc_en: Ulla asks two cases: if a yavam performed yibbum and then divided the estate, or divided and then performed yibbum, what is the law? The Gemara answers both: he has done nothing.
Rav Sheshet objects: if the first case (yibbum then division) already yields 'he has done nothing,' why ask the second case? The two are distinct acts.
Resh Lakish rules that in both cases the division is void, and the halakhah follows this.

items.text: Dispute over attached produce and the ketubah
items.text_en: Dispute over attached produce and the ketubah
items.desc_en: The Sages say that attached produce belongs to the husband, but the Gemara questions this because all his property is liable for the ketubah. Resh Lakish corrects the text to say 'belongs to her'.

sub.desc_en: The Sages rule that attached produce belongs to the husband.
The Gemara questions why the husband retains attached produce, since all his property is liable for the ketubah.
Resh Lakish resolves the difficulty by correcting the Mishnah text to read that the produce belongs to her.

items.text: Status of a yevamah after yibbum
items.text_en: Status of a yevamah after yibbum
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that after yibbum, the woman is like a full wife, meaning he can divorce her with a get and remarry her. The Gemara clarifies that this teaches she does not require chalitzah, and that remarriage is obvious.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after yibbum (levirate marriage), the woman is like a full wife.
The Gemara asks: what practical halachic implication does this teach?
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers: to teach that he can divorce her with a גט (bill of divorce) and remarry her.
The Gemara objects: that he can divorce her with a גט is obvious — why would it need to be stated?

The Gemara resolves: one might have thought that since the Torah said 'וְיִבְּמָהּ' (and he shall perform yibbum), the original yibbum bond remains, so she cannot be released by a גט but only by חליצה (release); the Mishnah teaches otherwise.
The Gemara objects: that he can remarry her is also obvious — why is it stated?

items.text: Yevamah's ketubah is like a wife's
items.text_en: Yevamah's ketubah is like a wife's
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that a yevamah's ketubah is not merely a mitzvah obligation but becomes like a wife's ketubah, as the verse says 'and he takes her as a wife'—once he takes her, she is like his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: one might think the yevamah's ketubah is merely a mitzvah obligation imposed by the Torah, and she would remain under the prohibition of אשת אח (the brother's wife), so the mishnah teaches otherwise.
The Gemara counters: one might still argue the opposite, but the verse 'וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה' (and he takes her as a wife) teaches that once he takes her, she becomes like his wife.

items.text: Ketubah lien on first husband's property
items.text_en: Ketubah lien on first husband's property
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the yevamah's ketubah is specifically on the property of her first husband (the deceased brother), as she was 'acquired from heaven' for the yavam. If she has no property from the first husband, she collects from the second, to prevent him from easily divorcing her.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the yevamah's ketubah is specifically a lien on the property of her first husband.
The Gemara explains the reason: the yevamah was 'acquired from heaven' for the yavam, so her ketubah is on the first husband's property.
The Mishnah adds that if she has no property from the first husband, she collects from the second, to prevent him from easily divorcing her.

items.text: The yavam cannot say 'here is your ketubah'
items.text_en: The yavam cannot say 'here is your ketubah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'and so' (וְכֵן) from the mishnah: the yavam cannot say 'here is your ketubah' and dismiss her, even though he wrote 'I acquire and I will acquire' (דִּקְנַאי וּדְקָנֵינָא), which might make her rely on his property. The mishnah teaches that she still has a claim on the first husband's property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'and so' (וְכֵן) in the mishnah adds, given the statement that the yavam cannot say 'here is your ketubah'.

The Gemara explains that the mishnah teaches that even though the yavam wrote 'I acquire and I will acquire' (דִּקְנַאי וּדְקָנֵינָא), which might make her rely on his property, she still has a claim on the first husband's property.

items.text: If he divorces her, she has only her ketubah
items.text_en: If he divorces her, she has only her ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the yavam divorces the yevamah, she has only her ketubah (from the first husband), not from him. This teaches like Rabbi Abba's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the yavam divorces the yevamah, she has only her ketubah from the first husband, not from him, teaching like Rabbi Abba's principle.

items.text: If he remarries her, she is like all women
items.text_en: If he remarries her, she is like all women
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if the yavam divorces the yevamah and then remarries her, she is like all other women and has only her ketubah (from the first husband). This teaches that even though he wrote her a ketubah himself (unlike the first marriage), she still does not collect from him if he divorces and remarries.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if the yavam divorces the yevamah and then remarries her, she is like all other women and has only her marriage contract.
The Gemara asks what novel point the mishnah teaches by mentioning the case of remarriage, since the general rule is already known.
The Gemara cites a baraita that one who divorces a woman and remarries her does so on the basis of her first marriage contract.

The Gemara explains that the mishnah is necessary lest one think that for a yevamah, where the yavam did not write the marriage contract himself, a new marriage contract from him would be required upon remarriage; the mishnah teaches that this is not the case.

items.text: Shimon ben Shataḥ's enactment on ketubah lien
items.text_en: Shimon ben Shataḥ's enactment on ketubah lien
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda recounts that originally, ketubot were written for fixed amounts (200 for a virgin, 100 for a widow), but men would grow old and not marry. Shimon ben Shataḥ enacted that all a man's property is liened to the ketubah. A baraita elaborates: earlier enactments (leaving her in her father's or father-in-law's house) failed because the husband could still say 'take your ketubah and leave.' Shimon ben Shataḥ's enactment made all property liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that originally fixed ketubah amounts caused men to delay marriage until Shimon ben Shataḥ enacted that all property is liened.
A baraita confirms the initial practice and adds that the Sages first enacted placing the ketubah in her father's house, but the husband could still say 'go to your ketubah.'
The baraita describes a further enactment placing the ketubah in the father-in-law's house, with wealthy women making silver or gold baskets and poor women a urine vessel.

The baraita concludes that even after these enactments the husband could still say 'take your ketubah and leave,' until Shimon ben Shataḥ instituted that he writes 'all my property is guaranteed for her ketubah.'

items.text: Mishnah: Renunciation of rights to wife's property
items.text_en: Mishnah: Renunciation of rights to wife's property
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: a husband who writes 'I have no claim to your property' still eats the produce during her lifetime and inherits her; if he adds 'and to their produce,' he does not eat produce but inherits; Rabbi Yehuda requires an additional clause to exclude him from produce of produce. The third case adds 'in your life and after your death,' where he neither eats produce nor inherits, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues he inherits because the condition contradicts Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: a husband who writes 'I have no claim to your property' still eats the produce during her lifetime and inherits her, but the clause validates her sales.
The Mishnah presents the second case: if he adds 'and to their produce,' he does not eat produce but inherits; Rabbi Yehuda requires an additional clause to exclude him from produce of produce.

The Mishnah presents the third case: if he adds 'in your life and after your death,' he neither eats produce nor inherits, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues he inherits because the condition contradicts Torah law.

items.text: Gemara's opening: Citation of a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's opening: Citation of a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a baraita from Rabbi Chiyya that uses the phrase 'one who says to his wife' instead of 'one who writes,' suggesting a different formulation.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of a baraita from Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of a baraita from Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Rabbi Chiyya that uses the phrase 'one who says to his wife' instead of 'one who writes,' suggesting a different formulation.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why is the deed effective?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is the deed effective?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the deed is effective at all, citing a baraita that if one says to another 'I have no claim to this field,' it is meaningless, implying a verbal renunciation without transfer is void.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the deed is effective at all, citing a baraita that if one says to another 'I have no claim to this field,' it is meaningless, implying a verbal renunciation without transfer is void.

items.text: Answer: The case is when she is still an arusah
items.text_en: Answer: The case is when she is still an arusah
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that the Mishnah deals with a husband writing to his wife while she is still an arusah (betrothed), not yet fully married. This is supported by Rav Kahana's principle that one can stipulate not to inherit property that comes from another source, and by Rava's principle that one may opt out of rabbinic enactments, like a wife saying she will not be supported nor work.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that the Mishnah deals with a husband writing to his wife while she is still an arusah (betrothed), not yet fully married.
Rav Kahana's principle is cited: one can stipulate not to inherit property that comes from another source.
Rava's principle is cited: one may opt out of rabbinic enactments, like a wife saying she will not be supported nor work.
Rav Huna citing Rav provides an example of opting out: a wife can say she will not be supported nor work.

items.text: Objection and resolution: Even a nesu'ah?
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: Even a nesu'ah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if so, even a married woman (nesu'ah) should be able to renounce rights. Abaye and Rava disagree: Abaye says the husband's hand is like hers (so renunciation is effective), Rava says his hand is superior (so it is not). The practical difference is for a shomeret yavam (a yevamah awaiting levirate marriage).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the renunciation works for an arusah, it should also work for a nesu'ah (married woman).
Abaye answers that for a nesu'ah, the husband's hand is like hers, so her renunciation is effective.
Rava answers that the husband's hand is superior to hers, so her renunciation is ineffective.
The Gemara notes that the practical difference between Abaye and Rava applies to a shomeret yavam (a yevamah awaiting levirate marriage).

items.text: Inquiry: If a kinyan was performed from him
items.text_en: Inquiry: If a kinyan was performed from him
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: if a formal acquisition (kinyan) was performed from the husband, what is the law? Rav Yosef says it is effective from the matter of 'din u'devarim' (the renunciation itself), while Rav Nachman says it is effective from the body of the land itself. Abaye supports Rav Yosef's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a formal acquisition (קִנְיָן) was performed from the husband, what is the law regarding the renunciation of his rights?
Rav Yosef answers that the acquisition is effective from the matter of 'דין ודברים' (the renunciation itself), meaning the husband's statement alone suffices.
Rav Nachman answers that the acquisition is effective from the body of the land itself, meaning the husband must transfer ownership of the land.
Abaye states that Rav Yosef's view is logically preferable, though the reasoning is not fully elaborated here.

items.text: Amemar's ruling on the husband's acquisition from the land itself
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling on the husband's acquisition from the land itself
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that the husband acquires from the land itself immediately. Rav Ashi asks whether this applies when the wife is still alive or only after her death, and Amemar responds that he has not heard of this distinction, meaning he does not accept it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the distinction between movable property (עורר) and standing land (עומד), stating that for land the husband acquires from the land itself immediately.
Amemar rules that the halacha is that the husband acquires from the land itself immediately.
Rav Ashi asks Amemar whether this applies to movable property (עורר) or standing land (עומד), explaining the practical difference relates to Rav Yosef's principle.
Amemar responds that he has not heard of this distinction, meaning he does not accept it.

items.text: Abaye's principle: the hand of the holder of the document is on the bottom
items.text_en: Abaye's principle: the hand of the holder of the document is on the bottom
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the husband would not be considered to have waived all rights. Abaye answers that the principle is that the hand of the holder of the document is on the bottom, meaning the document is interpreted in the most limited way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the husband should not be considered to have waived all rights to his wife's property.
Abaye answers that the principle is 'the hand of the holder of the document is on the bottom,' meaning the document is interpreted in the most limited way.

items.text: Distinction between produce and inheritance
items.text_en: Distinction between produce and inheritance
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the husband waives rights to produce. Abaye answers with a proverb that a lamp is better than a radish, meaning the husband would not waive common benefits. Regarding inheritance, Abaye explains that death is common while sale is not, so one does not waive rights to a common occurrence. Rav Ashi derives from the phrase 'your property' that the husband waives neither produce nor posthumous rights.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the husband waives rights to produce (פירות) as well.
Abaye answers with a proverb that a lamp (בוצינא) is better than a radish (קרא), meaning the husband would not waive common benefits like produce.
The Gemara asks whether the husband waives rights to inheritance (ירושה) as well.
Abaye explains that death is common (שכיחא) while sale is not (לא שכיחא), so one does not waive rights to a common occurrence like inheritance.
Rav Ashi derives from the phrase 'your property' (בנכסייך) that the husband waives neither produce nor posthumous rights.

items.text: Definition of produce and secondary produce according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Definition of produce and secondary produce according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma defines produce as fruit from land the wife brought, and secondary produce as fruit from land purchased with the original produce. This sets up the discussion of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the husband always eats secondary produce, and a baraita defines produce and secondary produce.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's statement: 'secondary produce' or 'forever'
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's statement: 'secondary produce' or 'forever'
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether Rabbi Yehuda's phrase 'forever he eats secondary produce' means that only secondary produce is eaten, or that he eats forever, or both. It then explores the necessity of each phrase: 'secondary produce' indicates that he eats even secondary produce, while 'forever' prevents him from eating tertiary produce, and together they clarify the full scope.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a three-way inquiry about Rabbi Yehuda's statement: whether 'secondary produce' is precise, or 'forever' is precise, or both are precise.
The Gemara considers the possibility that 'secondary produce' is precise, explaining that 'forever' then teaches that writing 'secondary produce' is equivalent to writing 'forever'.
The Gemara considers the possibility that 'forever' is precise, explaining that 'secondary produce' then teaches that only if both terms are written does the husband eat secondary produce.
The Gemara resolves that both terms are precise: 'forever' prevents eating tertiary produce, and 'secondary produce' prevents eating primary produce, each term being necessary.

items.text: Question about a document waiving 'rights and words' in property and secondary produce
items.text_en: Question about a document waiving 'rights and words' in property and secondary produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband who writes that he has no rights in his wife's property and secondary produce has waived only secondary produce or all produce. It initially suggests he must have waived all, since otherwise secondary produce could not exist. The Gemara then refutes this by citing Rabbi Yehuda's case where produce is consumed but secondary produce remains from what is left over.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a husband who writes that he has no rights in his wife's property and secondary produce has waived only secondary produce or all produce.
The Gemara initially asserts that he must have waived all produce, since otherwise secondary produce could not exist after the primary produce is consumed.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yehuda's case, where the husband eats secondary produce even though primary produce is consumed, and asks how that is possible.
The Gemara resolves that in Rabbi Yehuda's case, the wife left over some produce, and here too she left over some produce, so the husband can eat secondary produce from what remains.

items.text: Rav's ruling on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but not for his reasoning. The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a condition contradicting Torah law is void, while Rav holds it is valid, but Rav agrees with the outcome because the husband's inheritance is rabbinic, and the Sages strengthened their decrees more than Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion that if the wife dies, her husband inherits from her despite his waiver.
Rav rules that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but not for his reasoning.
The Gemara asks: what does it mean that the law follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel but not for his reasoning?

The Gemara explains: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a condition contradicting Torah law is void, while Rav holds it is valid, but Rav agrees with the outcome because the husband's inheritance is rabbinic (דרבנן), and the Sages strengthened their decrees more than Torah law.

items.text: Rav's position on inheritance and conditions
items.text_en: Rav's position on inheritance and conditions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's ruling that a condition to waive inheritance is void, contrasting it with his view on ona'ah. It proposes that Rav follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's principle that a condition contradicting Torah law is void, but not for the same reason, as Rabban Shimon holds the husband inherits his wife, while Rav does not. The Gemara then refines this, suggesting Rav follows the halakha but not the reasoning, and later that Rav adds his own stringency even to rabbinic laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's consistency: if he holds that a condition to waive inheritance is void, why does he also hold that a condition to waive ona'ah (overcharge) is void, contradicting his own principle?

items.text: Rav's view that husband's inheritance is rabbinic
items.text_en: Rav's view that husband's inheritance is rabbinic
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a third explanation: Rav holds that a husband's inheritance is rabbinic, and the Sages fortified their decrees like Torah law. This is challenged by a Mishnah of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, which implies inheritance is Torah law. Rav resolves this by interpreting the Mishnah as referring to a cemetery inheritance, where the Sages require compensation due to family disgrace, but Rav himself does not accept this reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rav rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel but not for his reason, since Rabban Shimon holds a husband inherits his wife, while Rav holds he does not.
The Gemara objects that this would mean Rav follows Rabban Shimon's reasoning but not his halacha, which is contradictory.
The Gemara revises: Rav follows Rabban Shimon's halacha (a husband inherits) but not his reason, because Rabban Shimon voids only Torah conditions, while Rav voids even rabbinic conditions.
The Gemara objects that this actually makes Rav follow both Rabban Shimon's reason and halacha, merely adding his own stringency, which does not explain the original statement.

The Gemara concludes: Rav follows Rabban Shimon's halacha but not his reason, because Rabban Shimon holds a husband's inheritance is Torah law, while Rav holds it is rabbinic, and the Sages fortified their decrees like Torah law.

The Gemara challenges Rav's view by citing a Mishnah of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka about a husband inheriting and compensating the family, and questions whether it assumes Torah or rabbinic inheritance.
Rav explains that Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's Mishnah refers to a cemetery inheritance, where the Sages require compensation due to family disgrace, but the inheritance itself is Torah law.
The Gemara supports Rav's interpretation by citing a baraita that family members can force a buyer of a grave to let them bury there due to family disgrace.
The Gemara concludes that Rav stated this explanation for Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's position, but Rav himself does not accept it.

items.text: Mishnah: Distribution among competing claimants
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distribution among competing claimants
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a man dies leaving a wife, a creditor, and heirs, with a deposit or loan held by others. Rabbi Tarfon says the assets go to the weakest claimant, while Rabbi Akiva says they go to the heirs, as all others require an oath but heirs do not. The Gemara explains why both a loan and a deposit are mentioned, to show that Rabbi Tarfon's reasoning applies only to loans, and Rabbi Akiva's to deposits.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man who died leaving a wife, a creditor, and heirs, with a deposit or loan held by others, and records the dispute between Rabbi Tarfon (give to the weakest) and Rabbi Akiva (give to the heirs, who alone are exempt from an oath).
The Mishnah adds a second clause about detached produce, where the first taker acquires it, and the same dispute applies to any surplus.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to mention both a loan and a deposit, since the same dispute applies to both.

The Gemara explains that both are necessary: without the deposit case, one might think Rabbi Tarfon only rules for loans (given for spending), but for deposits (still intact) he would agree with Rabbi Akiva; and without the loan case, one might think Rabbi Akiva only rules for deposits, but for loans he would agree with Rabbi Tarfon.

items.text: Interpretation of 'the weakest' and the Mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'the weakest' and the Mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the meaning of 'the weakest' (הכושל): Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says it means the weakest in evidence, while Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to the wife's ketubah, due to favor. This is supported by a Tannaitic dispute. The Gemara then questions why the Mishnah mentions 'the remainder' in the case of detached produce, and explains that Rabbi Akiva holds all produce belongs to the heirs, but the Mishnah uses 'remainder' because Rabbi Tarfon did.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'the weakest' (הכושל) in the Mishnah means.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that 'the weakest' means the weakest in evidence (i.e., the one with the weakest claim).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'the weakest' refers to the wife's ketubah, because of favor (חינא).
A Tannaitic dispute is cited: Rabbi Binyamin says 'the weakest' means the weakest in evidence, while Rabbi Elazar says it refers to the wife's ketubah, due to favor.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions 'the remainder' (מוֹתָר) in the case of detached produce, since according to Rabbi Akiva all the produce belongs to the heirs.
The Gemara answers that indeed all produce belongs to the heirs according to Rabbi Akiva, but the Mishnah uses 'remainder' because Rabbi Tarfon used that term.

items.text: Rava's qualification of Rabbi Akiva's position
items.text_en: Rava's qualification of Rabbi Akiva's position
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman clarifies that Rabbi Akiva's view that seizure (תפיסה) is ineffective applies only if the seizure occurred after death; if it occurred during the debtor's lifetime, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva's position that seizure (תפיסה) is completely ineffective applies universally.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava citing Rav Nachman answers that Rabbi Akiva's rule applies only if the seizure occurred after the debtor's death, not during his lifetime.

items.text: Dispute about the location of the seized property
items.text_en: Dispute about the location of the seized property
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel hold that Rabbi Tarfon's ruling applies only when the property is in the public domain (רשות הרבים), but not in a semi-public domain (סימטא). Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue that it applies even in a semi-public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Tarfon, where is the property located that allows seizure?
Rav and Shmuel both answer that Rabbi Tarfon's ruling applies only when the property is piled in the public domain (רשות הרבים), but not in a semi-public domain (סימטא).
Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both answer that Rabbi Tarfon's ruling applies even in a semi-public domain (סימטא).

items.text: Reish Lakish retracts the ruling
items.text_en: Reish Lakish retracts the ruling
items.desc_en: The judges ruled according to Rabbi Tarfon, but Reish Lakish forced them to retract. Rabbi Yochanan praised him, saying he acted in accordance with the Torah.

sub.text: Narrative: Reish Lakish retracts the ruling
sub.text_en: Narrative: Reish Lakish retracts the ruling
sub.desc_en: The judges ruled according to Rabbi Tarfon, but Reish Lakish forced them to retract; Rabbi Yochanan praised him, saying he acted in accordance with the Torah.

items.text: First explanation of the dispute: error in a Mishnah
items.text_en: First explanation of the dispute: error in a Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree about whether one who errs in a Mishnah matter must retract. One holds that he must, the other that he need not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree about whether one who errs in a Mishnah matter must retract.

items.text: Rejection and second explanation: halakha like Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rejection and second explanation: halakha like Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the first explanation, as all agree that an error in a Mishnah requires retraction. Instead, the dispute is about whether the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva over his colleague but not over his teacher, or even over his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the first explanation, asserting that all agree an error in a Mishnah requires retraction, and instead frames the dispute as whether the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva over his colleague but not over his teacher, or even over his teacher.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Tarfon's status
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Tarfon's status
items.desc_en: Another explanation: all agree that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva over a colleague but not over a teacher. The dispute is whether Rabbi Tarfon was Rabbi Yochanan's teacher or colleague.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation: everyone agrees that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva over a colleague but not over a teacher.
One opinion holds that the dispute is about whether Rabbi Tarfon was Rabbi Yochanan's teacher.
The other opinion holds that Rabbi Tarfon was Rabbi Yochanan's colleague, not his teacher.

items.text: Final explanation: halakha vs. mattin
items.text_en: Final explanation: halakha vs. mattin
items.desc_en: A third explanation: all agree Rabbi Tarfon was a colleague. The dispute is whether the ruling was stated as a definitive halakha or as a leaning (מטין).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a third explanation: everyone agrees Rabbi Tarfon was a colleague of Rabbi Akiva.
The dispute is whether the ruling was stated as a definitive הלכה (binding law) or as מטין (a leaning opinion).

items.text: Case of Rabbi Yochanan's relative seizing a cow
items.text_en: Case of Rabbi Yochanan's relative seizing a cow
items.desc_en: A relative of Rabbi Yochanan seized an orphan's cow from a semi-public domain. Rabbi Yochanan approved, but Reish Lakish ordered its return. Rabbi Yochanan deferred to Reish Lakish's opposition.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a relative of Rabbi Yochanan seized an orphan's cow from a semi-public domain (סימטא).
When the parties came before Rabbi Yochanan, he ruled that the seizure was valid (שפיר תפסתוה).
When they came before Reish Lakish, he ordered them to return the cow.
When they returned to Rabbi Yochanan, he deferred to Reish Lakish's opposition, saying 'What can I do? One who stands against me disagrees.'

items.text: Case of the ox seized from a herdsman
items.text_en: Case of the ox seized from a herdsman
items.desc_en: A creditor claimed he seized an ox during the debtor's lifetime, while the orphan's herdsman claimed it was after death. Rav Nachman ruled that since the creditor could claim it was purchased, he can also claim seizure during life. The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's principle about fences does not apply because the ox was entrusted to a herdsman.

sub.desc_en: The narrator presents a case: a herdsman of orphans seized an ox from a creditor, and each party claims a different timing for the seizure.

Rav Nachman rules that since the creditor could claim the ox was purchased (and thus validly held), he can also claim it was seized during the debtor's lifetime, applying the principle of מיגו (since he could have made a stronger claim, his actual claim is credible).
The Gemara objects that Reish Lakish's principle — that fences (items in public domain) have no presumption of ownership — should undermine the creditor's claim.
The Gemara resolves that the case is different because the ox was entrusted to a herdsman, so the presumption of ownership does not apply.

items.text: Case of the house of the Nasi seizing a maidservant
items.text_en: Case of the house of the Nasi seizing a maidservant
items.desc_en: The house of the Nasi seized an orphan's maidservant from a semi-public domain. Rabbi Avahu and others approved, but Rabbi Abba criticized them for flattery, citing the precedent of Reish Lakish's retraction.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens with the house of the Nasi seizing an orphan's maidservant from a semi-public domain (סימטא), with Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Chanina bar Papi, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha present.
Rabbi Abba sits with them, and Rabbi Avahu and his colleagues declare that the seizure was valid (שפיר תפסיתוה).
Rabbi Abba objects, accusing them of flattery (חנופה) because the defendants are from the house of the Nasi.
Rabbi Abba cites the precedent of the judges who ruled like Rabbi Tarfon and Reish Lakish retracted the ruling, implying that the current ruling is also wrong.

items.text: Case of seizing a ship for a debt
items.text_en: Case of seizing a ship for a debt
items.desc_en: A creditor sent his agent to seize a ship from the estate. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objected, citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle that seizing property in a way that harms other creditors is invalid. The text breaks off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the case: a creditor named Bar Ḥashu sent his agent to seize a ship from the debtor's estate.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua object to the seizure, citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle that seizing property in a way that harms other creditors is invalid.

items.text: Dispute over seizure of fish from a river
items.text_en: Dispute over seizure of fish from a river
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua seize fish from a river, each claiming full ownership. Rav Pinchas bar Ami cites Rav and Shmuel that seizure is valid only if the items are in the public domain. They respond that they seized due to the swift current. Rava rebukes them and cites Rav Nachman that seizure must be from life.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua seized a fish from a river, each claiming full ownership.
Rav Pinchas bar Ami objects, citing Rav and Shmuel that seizure is valid only if the items are gathered in the public domain.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's response
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's response
sub.desc_en: They respond that they seized due to the swift current of the river, which effectively makes the fish like items in the public domain.
Rava rebukes them and cites Rav Nachman that seizure is valid only if the fish was seized while still alive, rejecting their claim.

items.text: Agent repays debt without returning the document
items.text_en: Agent repays debt without returning the document
items.desc_en: Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu sends money through Chama bar Rabbah bar Avahu to repay a debt. The creditors claim the document is a 'side document' (not the original). Rabbi Avahu rules that since the creditors could deny the debt entirely, they can also claim it is a side document.

sub.desc_en: Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu sends money through Chama bar Rabbah bar Avahu to repay a debt, but the creditors claim the document is a 'side document' (not the original).
Rabbi Avahu rules that since the creditors could deny the debt entirely (מיגו), they can also claim it is a side document.

items.text: Liability of an agent who pays before receiving the document
items.text_en: Liability of an agent who pays before receiving the document
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi discusses whether an agent who pays the debt before taking the document is liable if the creditor later claims the document. Initially, if the agent was told 'take the document and give the money' he is liable; if 'give the money and take the document' he is not. The Gemara concludes that in either case he is liable, because he was sent to fix, not to ruin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the law regarding an agent's liability to pay back the creditor if he pays before receiving the document?
Rav Ashi initially distinguishes: if the agent was told 'take the document and give the money' he is liable; if 'give the money and take the document' he is not.
The Gemara concludes that in either case the agent is liable, because he was sent לתקוני (to fix) and not לעוותי (to ruin).

items.text: Woman claims she seized documents during the debtor's lifetime
items.text_en: Woman claims she seized documents during the debtor's lifetime
items.desc_en: A woman holding deposited documents is sued by heirs. She claims she seized them during the debtor's lifetime. Rav Nachman rules that since she has no witnesses that they demanded them from her during his lifetime, it is a seizure after death and invalid.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a woman held deposited documents, and the heirs sued her for them.
The woman claims she seized the documents during the debtor's lifetime.
Rav Nachman rules that since she has no witnesses that the heirs demanded the documents during the debtor's lifetime, her seizure is after death and invalid.

items.text: Oath transferred due to suspicion, and testimony of a single witness
items.text_en: Oath transferred due to suspicion, and testimony of a single witness
items.desc_en: A woman suspected of swearing falsely has the oath transferred to the opposing party. Later, Rav Pappa testifies that a document is paid. Rav Adda bar Mattana argues that Rav Pappa is like Bat Rav Chisda, but since Rav Pappa is not as well-known to the court, his testimony is insufficient. Rav Pappa then says that for someone he knows well, like his son Abba Mar, he would tear up the document. The Gemara corrects that he would only weaken it.

sub.desc_en: A woman was liable to take an oath before Rava's court, but Bat Rav Chisda testified that she was suspected of swearing falsely, so Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
Rav Pappa testified before Rav Adda bar Mattana that a certain document was paid, but Rav Adda bar Mattana rejected his testimony because a single witness is insufficient.
Rav Adda bar Mattana objects that Rav Pappa should be treated like Bat Rav Chisda, but distinguishes that Bat Rav Chisda was well-known to the court while Rav Pappa is not.

Rav Pappa concedes that the principle of 'קים לי בגויה' (the court's personal knowledge) is valid, and states that for someone he knows well, like his son Abba Mar, he would tear up the document based on that testimony.
The Gemara rejects the idea of tearing the document and corrects that Rav Pappa would only weaken it (מרע) based on his testimony.

items.text: Writing a document of rights before an oath, and the validity of court endorsements
items.text_en: Writing a document of rights before an oath, and the validity of court endorsements
items.desc_en: A woman required to swear asks for a document granting her rights before she swears. Rav Bibi bar Abaye orders it written. Rav Pappi criticizes this as a 'swollen' ruling. The Gemara compares it to Rava's rule that a court endorsement written before witnesses sign is invalid, as it appears false. However, it rejects this, citing Rav Nachman that Rabbi Meir allows even a found and signed document, and the Sages only disagree regarding divorce documents.

sub.desc_en: A woman required to swear in Rav Bibi bar Abaye's court asks for a document of rights to be written for her before she swears, and Rav Bibi orders it written.
Rav Pappi criticizes Rav Bibi's ruling as a 'swollen' (invalid) ruling, implying it is improper.
The Gemara attempts to support Rav Pappi by citing Rava's rule that a court endorsement written before witnesses sign is invalid because it appears false, suggesting the same applies here.
The Gemara rejects the comparison, citing Rav Nachman that Rabbi Meir permits even a found and signed document, and the Sages only disagree regarding divorce documents, not other documents.

items.text: A paid loan document cannot be reused
items.text_en: A paid loan document cannot be reused
items.desc_en: Rav Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan states that a document used for a loan that was repaid cannot be used again for another loan, because its lien has been extinguished. The Gemara notes that the reason is the lien is void, not that it appears false.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that a document used for a loan that was repaid cannot be reused for another loan because its lien has been extinguished.
The Gemara infers that the reason is the lien is void, not that the document appears false.

items.text: Opening principle: No concern for falsehood
items.text_en: Opening principle: No concern for falsehood
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general principle: we do not suspect that a claimant is lying when they provide identifying marks for a deposit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general principle: we do not suspect that a claimant is lying when they provide identifying marks for a deposit.

items.text: First case: pearls deposited with Rabbi Miyasha
items.text_en: First case: pearls deposited with Rabbi Miyasha
items.desc_en: A man deposited seven pearls wrapped in a cloth with Rabbi Miyasha, who died without instructions. Rabbi Ami ruled to return them to the depositor because he knew Rabbi Miyasha was not a liar and the depositor gave a identifying mark. The Gemara adds that this applies only if the depositor was not a frequent visitor; otherwise, he might have seen the deposit.

sub.desc_en: A man deposited seven pearls with Rabbi Miyasha; after his death, Rabbi Ammi ruled that the claimant may retrieve them because the depositor was not dishonest and provided identifying marks.
The Gemara qualifies that this leniency applies only when the claimant was not a frequent visitor; otherwise, we suspect he may have seen the item and falsely claimed it.
The Gemara qualifies that this ruling applies only if the depositor was not a frequent visitor; otherwise, he might have seen the deposit and claimed it falsely.

items.text: Second case: silver cup deposited with Chasa
items.text_en: Second case: silver cup deposited with Chasa
items.desc_en: A man deposited a silver cup with Chasa, who died without instructions. Rav Nachman ruled similarly: he knew Chasa was not a liar, and the depositor gave a identifying mark. The same qualification about frequent visitors applies.

sub.desc_en: A man deposited a silver cup with Chasa; after his death, Rav Nachman ruled similarly that the claimant may retrieve it because the depositor was not dishonest and provided identifying marks.
The Gemara repeats the same qualification: the leniency applies only when the claimant was not a frequent visitor.
The gemara qualifies that this ruling applies only if the depositor was not a frequent visitor; otherwise, the mark could have been learned by observation.

items.text: Third case: garment deposited with Rav Dimi
items.text_en: Third case: garment deposited with Rav Dimi
items.desc_en: A man deposited a garment with Rav Dimi, who died without instructions. Rabbi Abba ruled similarly: he knew Rav Dimi was not a liar, and the depositor gave a identifying mark. The same qualification applies.

sub.desc_en: A man deposited a garment with Rav Dimi; after his death, Rabbi Abba ruled similarly that the claimant may retrieve it because the depositor was not dishonest and provided identifying marks.
The Gemara repeats the same qualification: the leniency applies only when the claimant was not a frequent visitor.
The gemara qualifies that this ruling applies only if the depositor was not a frequent visitor; otherwise, one might suspect he saw the item and claimed it falsely.

items.text: Case of ambiguous inheritance: 'To Toviyah'
items.text_en: Case of ambiguous inheritance: 'To Toviyah'
items.desc_en: A man said 'My property to Toviyah' and died. Rabbi Yochanan ruled that if a Toviyah comes, he receives it. The Gemara clarifies: if he said 'Toviyah' and Rav Toviyah came, it goes to Toviyah, not Rav Toviyah, unless he was familiar with him. If two Toviyahs come, one a neighbor and one a Torah scholar, the scholar precedes; if a relative and a scholar, the scholar precedes.

sub.desc_en: A man declared 'My property to Toviyah' and died; Toviyah came, and Rabbi Yochanan ruled that he receives it.

The Gemara clarifies: if he said 'Toviyah' and Rav Toviyah came, it goes to Toviyah, not Rav Toviyah, unless he was familiar with him; if two Toviyahs come, a neighbor and a Torah scholar, the scholar precedes; if a relative and a scholar, the scholar precedes.

items.text: Query: neighbor vs. relative
items.text_en: Query: neighbor vs. relative
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one is a neighbor and the other a relative, which takes precedence? It answers with a verse: 'Better a near neighbor than a distant brother.' If both are relatives, both neighbors, and both scholars, the decision is left to the judges' discretion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the two claimants are a neighbor and a relative, which takes precedence?
The Gemara answers with a verse: 'A close neighbor is better than a distant brother', but if both are close relatives, neighbors, and scholars, the decision is left to the discretion of the judges.

items.text: Rava's teaching: seller of a debt who cancels it
items.text_en: Rava's teaching: seller of a debt who cancels it
items.desc_en: Rava reports his father's teaching: Shmuel said that if one sells a promissory note to another and then cancels the debt, it is cancelled, even if the heir cancels it. However, Shmuel concedes that if a woman brings a note into her husband's property and then cancels it, it is not cancelled, because her hand is like his hand.

sub.desc_en: Rava tells the son of Rav Chiyya bar Avin that he will teach him an excellent principle that his father used to say.

Shmuel ruled that if one sells a debt document and then forgives the debt, it is forgiven; but if a woman brings a debt document into her marriage and then forgives it, it is not forgiven because her hand is like her husband's hand.

sub.text: Shmuel's concession via Rav Chiyya bar Avin
sub.text_en: Shmuel's concession via Rav Chiyya bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Shmuel concedes that if a woman brings a note into her husband's property and then cancels it, it is not cancelled, because her hand is like his hand.

items.text: Case: relative of Rav Nachman sells her ketubah
items.text_en: Case: relative of Rav Nachman sells her ketubah
items.desc_en: A relative of Rav Nachman sold her ketubah for a benefit, then was divorced and died. Claimants came to collect from her daughter. Rav Nachman asked: is there no one to advise her?

sub.desc_en: A relative of Rav Nachman sold her ketubah for a benefit; she was divorced and died, and then creditors came to claim from her daughter.
Rav Nachman responded: is there no one to advise her (the daughter) properly?

items.text: The daughter forgives her mother's ketubah
items.text_en: The daughter forgives her mother's ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a daughter forgave her mother's ketubah debt to her father, and then inherited from him. Rav Nachman comments that they acted as if they were judges, and explains the initial and final reasoning: initially, they thought one must not ignore one's own flesh, but later they considered that a prominent person is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a daughter was advised to forgive her mother's ketubah debt to her father and then inherit from him, and she did so.
Rav Nachman comments that they acted as if they were judges, and explains the initial reasoning (not ignoring one's own flesh) and the final reasoning (a prominent person is different).

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on selling and forgiving a promissory note
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on selling and forgiving a promissory note
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that if one sells a promissory note to another and then forgives the debt, it is forgiven, and even an heir can forgive. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua adds that if the buyer is clever, he can secure his payment by having the debtor write a new note in his name.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if one sells a promissory note and then forgives the debt, the forgiveness is effective, and even an heir can forgive.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's advice
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's advice
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua adds that if the buyer is clever, he can secure his payment by having the debtor write a new note in his name.

items.text: Damages for causing loss of a promissory note
items.text_en: Damages for causing loss of a promissory note
