items.desc_en: Ameimar distinguishes between judges who adjudicate cases of indirect damage (גרמי) and those who do not: the former award the full value of the note, the latter only the paper. A story is told where Rafram compelled Rav Ashi to pay the full value.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar states a rule: a judge who adjudicates cases of indirect damage (גרמי) awards the full value of the promissory note, while one who does not awards only the value of the paper.
A story is told where Rafram compelled Rav Ashi to pay the full value of the note, like a beam for an idol, illustrating the application of Ameimar's rule.

items.text: Priority between a wife's ketubah and a creditor
items.text_en: Priority between a wife's ketubah and a creditor
items.desc_en: Ameimar in the name of Rav Chama rules that when a debtor has both land and cash, the creditor is paid with cash and the wife with land, each according to their due. If only one piece of land is available, the creditor takes it, not the wife, because a woman is more eager to marry than a man is to marry.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar in the name of Rav Chama rules that when a debtor has both land and cash, the creditor is paid with cash and the wife with land, each according to their due.
If only one piece of land is available, the creditor takes it, not the wife, because a woman is more eager to marry than a man is to marry.

items.text: Debtor with land told to sell it to pay
items.text_en: Debtor with land told to sell it to pay
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rav Chama whether a debtor who has land can be told to sell it to pay his creditor. Rav Chama answers no, and explains the case: the debtor had lent money to a gentile, and since he acted improperly, they treated him improperly.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's question to Rav Chama
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's question to Rav Chama
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rav Chama whether a debtor who has land can be told to sell it to pay his creditor.
Rav Chama answers no, and explains the case: the debtor had lent money to a gentile, and since he acted improperly, they treated him improperly.

items.text: Can one refuse to perform a positive commandment?
items.text_en: Can one refuse to perform a positive commandment?
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Pappa: if one says he does not want to perform the mitzvah of repaying a debt, what is the law? Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah distinguishes between negative and positive commandments; for positive ones like building a sukkah or taking a lulav, one is compelled.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's question to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's question to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Pappa: according to your view that repaying a debt is a מצוה (commandment), if one says 'I do not want to perform the commandment,' what is the law?

Rav Pappa answers by citing the Mishnah: the distinction applies only to negative commandments, but for positive commandments like building a sukkah or taking a lulav, one is compelled to perform them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband who appoints his wife as a shopkeeper or agent may administer an oath to her whenever he wishes. Rabbi Eliezer adds that this applies even to her spinning and baking.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband who appoints his wife as a shopkeeper or agent may administer an oath to her whenever he wishes, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that this applies even to her spinning and baking.

items.text: Question about a get placed in a semi-public domain
items.text_en: Question about a get placed in a semi-public domain
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda about a get given conditionally after thirty days, where the wife placed it in a semi-public domain (צידי רשות הרבים). Rav Chisda rules she is not divorced, citing Rav and Shmuel that such a domain is like the public domain. An alternative version has Rav Chisda ruling she is divorced based on Rav Nachman's analogy to an animal in a marsh, but the Gemara rejects the equation.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda about a get (bill of divorce) given conditionally, where the wife placed it in a side alley of the public domain.
Rav Chisda answers that she is not divorced, citing Rav and Shmuel's principle that a side alley is like the public domain.
The Gemara objects that she should be divorced based on Rav Nachman's ruling about a cow in a marsh, but then distinguishes between a marsh and a side alley.

An alternate version of the discussion reverses the positions, with Rav Chisda initially ruling she is divorced, and the Gemara objecting based on Rav and Shmuel, but ultimately distinguishing the public domain from its side alley.
An alternative version has Rav Chisda ruling she is divorced based on Rav Nachman, but the Gemara again rejects the equation of public domain and semi-public domain.

items.text: Mishnah: Oaths for a wife who is a shopkeeper or agent
items.text_en: Mishnah: Oaths for a wife who is a shopkeeper or agent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a husband who appoints his wife as a shopkeeper or agent may administer an oath to her whenever he wishes. Rabbi Eliezer extends this even to her spinning and baking.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a husband who appoints his wife as a shopkeeper or agent may administer an oath to her whenever he wishes, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that this applies even to her spinning and baking.

items.text: Gemara: Is Rabbi Eliezer's oath initial or via gilgul?
items.text_en: Gemara: Is Rabbi Eliezer's oath initial or via gilgul?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Eliezer permits the oath initially (לכתחילה) or only through gilgul (when already under oath). A proof from the Sages' response 'No one lives with a snake in a basket' suggests it is initial, as otherwise the wife could simply leave. A second proof from a baraita confirms that Rabbi Eliezer's position is initial.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer's statement is only through גלגול (incidental extension of an oath) or לכתחילה (as an independent right).
The Gemara cites the Sages' objection to Rabbi Eliezer that 'no one lives with a snake in a basket,' arguing that if it were only through גלגול, the wife would have no complaint.
The Gemara explains that even through גלגול, the wife could complain that the constant suspicion makes cohabitation impossible.
The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between a wife appointed as agent and one not appointed, to clarify the scope of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is לכתחילה (an independent right), not merely through גלגול.

items.text: Mishnah: Varying formulations of oath waivers
items.text_en: Mishnah: Varying formulations of oath waivers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details how different formulations of a husband's waiver of 'vow and oath' affect who can administer oaths: the husband, his heirs, or the wife's heirs. It also addresses the case of a widow who returns to her father's or father-in-law's home.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the first formulation: if a husband writes 'I have no vow or oath against you,' he cannot administer an oath to her, but he can to her heirs and those who enter her authority.

The Mishnah presents the second formulation: if the husband adds 'and on your heirs and those who enter your authority,' he cannot administer an oath to her, her heirs, or those who enter her authority, but his heirs can administer oaths to her, her heirs, and those who enter her authority.

The Mishnah presents the third formulation: if the husband writes 'I have no vow or oath, nor my heirs nor those who enter my authority, against you, your heirs, and those who enter your authority,' neither he, his heirs, nor those who enter his authority can administer an oath to her, her heirs, or those who enter her authority.

The Mishnah concludes with the case of a widow who returns to her father's or father-in-law's home: if she was not appointed an administrator, the heirs cannot administer an oath to her; if she was appointed, they administer an oath regarding the future but not the past.

items.text: Gemara: Why an oath?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why an oath?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why an oath is relevant in this context, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav begins to explain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why an oath is relevant here, and begins to cite Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav begins to explain the relevance of the oath.

items.text: Dispute over the reason for the oath
items.text_en: Dispute over the reason for the oath
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh says the oath is because she impugns her ketubah (claims it was not fully paid). Rav Mordechai questions this: if the oath is because she was appointed an executor during her husband's lifetime, how would she know to ask for a waiver of the oath?

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh states that the oath mentioned in the Mishnah is because she impugns her ketubah (claims it was not fully paid).

sub.text: Rav Mordechai's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai questions Rav Ashi: according to the view that the oath is because she was appointed an executor during her husband's lifetime, how could she have known to ask for a waiver of the oath in advance?

items.text: The source of the dispute: a baraita about an executor
items.text_en: The source of the dispute: a baraita about an executor
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi responds that they learn the law from a different baraita: a widow who goes to her father's house and is not appointed an executor is not sworn; if she is appointed, she is sworn for the future but not the past. Rav Yehuda explains that 'the past' refers to executorship during the husband's lifetime, but between death and burial she is sworn. Rav Mattana disagrees, citing the Nehardeans that property can be sold without proclamation for burial expenses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi tells the questioner that they (the questioners) learn the law from one baraita, but we (Rav Ashi's academy) learn it from a different baraita.
The baraita states that a widow who goes to her father's house without being appointed an executor is not sworn; if appointed, she is sworn for the future but not the past.
The gemara asks: what is the meaning of 'the past' in this context?
Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains that 'the past' refers to executorship during the husband's lifetime.
Rav Yehuda adds that between death and burial she is sworn.
Rav Mattana disagrees, saying that even between death and burial she is not sworn.
Rav Mattana supports his view by citing the Nehardean rule that property can be sold without proclamation for burial expenses.

items.text: Dispute between Rava and Rav Yosef about the meaning of the husband's waiver
items.text_en: Dispute between Rava and Rav Yosef about the meaning of the husband's waiver
items.desc_en: Rava says that if the husband wrote 'without vow and without oath', he cannot swear her, but heirs can; if he wrote 'free of vow and free of oath', neither he nor heirs can swear her. Rav Yosef disagrees: in the latter case, both he and heirs can swear her, as the phrase means 'purify yourself with an oath'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah, citing Rabbi Chiyya, distinguishes between two formulations: 'without vow and without oath' (heirs can swear her) and 'free of vow and free of oath' (neither he nor heirs can swear her), interpreting the latter as 'you are purified from an oath'.
Rav Yosef, also citing Rabbi Chiyya, disagrees: in the 'free of vow and free of oath' case, both he and heirs can swear her, interpreting the phrase as 'purify yourself with an oath'.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Zakkai and Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Zakkai and Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zakkai rules that if the husband wrote 'from my property', he cannot swear her but heirs can; if 'from these properties', neither he nor heirs can swear her. Rav Nachman cites Shmuel in the name of Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam that all these formulations exempt both husband and heirs, but the Sages require an oath for collecting from orphans. An alternative version attributes this directly to Abba Shaul, and Rav Nachman rules the law follows him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zakkai sends to Mar Ukva a ruling distinguishing between 'from my property' formulations (husband exempt, heirs swear) and 'from these properties' formulations (both exempt).

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel in the name of Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel in the name of Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel in the name of Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam that all formulations exempt both husband and heirs, but the Sages require an oath for collecting from orphans.

sub.text: Alternative version and Rav Nachman's ruling
sub.text_en: Alternative version and Rav Nachman's ruling
sub.desc_en: An alternative version attributes the same ruling directly to Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam, and Rav Nachman rules the law follows him.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases where a woman must swear to collect her ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases where a woman must swear to collect her ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five cases: when she impugns her ketubah, when a single witness testifies it was paid, when collecting from encumbered property, from orphans' property, or in the husband's absence. Each case requires an oath before collection.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a woman who impugns her ketubah may only collect with an oath.
The Mishnah adds that a single witness testifying the ketubah was paid also requires an oath.
The Mishnah lists that collecting from orphans' property or encumbered property requires an oath.
The Mishnah concludes that collecting in the husband's absence also requires an oath.
The Mishnah illustrates the case of impugning the ketubah with a specific example of a woman claiming only part payment.
The Mishnah illustrates the case of a single witness with an example of a woman denying full payment.
The Mishnah illustrates collecting from encumbered property with an example of the husband selling assets.
The Mishnah illustrates collecting from orphans' property with an example of the husband dying and leaving assets to orphans.
The Mishnah illustrates collecting in the husband's absence with an example of him traveling overseas.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that if a widow claims her ketubah, the heirs can impose an oath on her; if she does not claim it, they cannot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states the Mishnah rule: if a widow claims her ketubah, the heirs impose an oath; if she does not claim it, they do not.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the oath's nature
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the oath's nature
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama initially thinks the oath is Torah-level, based on partial admission. Rava refutes this with two objections: the oath here is for taking, not paying, and it involves land. Rava concludes it is a rabbinic oath to ensure the widow investigates properly.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Hama initially thinks the widow's oath is Torah-level, based on the principle of partial admission (הודאה במקצת הטענה).
Rava raises two objections: the Torah's oaths are for those who swear and do not pay, but she swears and takes; and one does not swear regarding denial of lien on land.
Rava concludes the oath is rabbinic (מדרבנן), instituted to ensure the widow investigates carefully whether she was paid.

items.text: Case of impairing the ketubah with witnesses
items.text_en: Case of impairing the ketubah with witnesses
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if a widow impairs her ketubah by claiming partial payment with witnesses, does she need an oath? The Gemara cites a baraita listing those who swear and collect, including one who impairs his document without witnesses, implying that with witnesses she does not need an oath. The Gemara clarifies that the baraita means she certainly needs an oath with witnesses, but without witnesses one might think she collects without oath, so it teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if a widow impairs her ketubah with witnesses, does she need an oath, or do we suspect the witnesses were mistaken?
The Gemara cites a baraita listing those who swear and collect, including one who impairs his document without witnesses, implying that with witnesses she does not need an oath.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita means she certainly needs an oath with witnesses, but without witnesses one might think she collects without oath, so it teaches otherwise.

items.text: Case of impairing less than a perutah
items.text_en: Case of impairing less than a perutah
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if a widow impairs her ketubah by less than a perutah, do we say she is precise and truthful, or is she scheming? The Gemara leaves it unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a widow impugns her ketubah by claiming a deficiency of less than a perutah (פחות משוה פרוטה), is she considered meticulous (דייקה) or cunning (מערמא)? The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Case of reducing the ketubah
items.text_en: Case of reducing the ketubah
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: is reducing the ketubah the same as impairing it? The Gemara cites a baraita that a woman who reduces her ketubah collects without an oath, and explains that she claims an oral loan (amana) between them, so the document is valid for the reduced amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: is reducing the ketubah (פּוֹחֶתֶת) the same as impairing it (פּוֹגֶמֶת), or is it different because the woman does not admit to partial payment?
The Gemara cites a baraita that a woman who reduces her ketubah collects without an oath, illustrating the case where she claims only a portion was owed.
Rava brei d'Rabbah resolves the difficulty by explaining that the woman claims an oral loan (אמנה) between them, so the document remains valid for the reduced amount.
Rava bar Rabba answers: she says there was a private trust arrangement (אמנה) between her and her husband, so the document is valid.

items.text: Case of one witness testifying it is paid
items.text_en: Case of one witness testifying it is paid
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama thinks one witness obligates a Torah oath, citing the verse that a single witness stands for an oath. Rava refutes with the same two objections as before, concluding it is a rabbinic oath to appease the husband.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Hama argues that a single witness testifying the ketubah was paid obligates a Torah oath, citing the verse that a single witness stands for an oath and the principle that wherever two witnesses would obligate payment, one obligates an oath.
Rava raises two objections: first, all Torah oaths are sworn and not paid, but here she swears and takes money; second, oaths are not taken on denial of lien on land.
Rava concludes that the oath is only rabbinic, instituted to appease the husband's mind.

items.text: Rav Pappa's statement
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa begins to speak, but the text is cut off; this marks the start of a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa begins a statement (the content is cut off in the source).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case of a clever husband
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case of a clever husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the husband can rely on a later witness to establish the first witness as a loan witness, and offers two alternative explanations: either he gives the ketubah in front of both witnesses simultaneously, or he informs them of his intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the clever husband's strategy: he gives the ketubah in front of one witness, then relies on a second witness to establish the first as a loan witness, thereby subjecting the wife to a Torah oath.

sub.text: Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi objects: how can the husband rely on the second witness to retroactively establish the first? He offers an alternative: the husband gives the ketubah in front of both witnesses simultaneously, designating them as loan witnesses.
Rav Ashi objects: even with both witnesses present, the wife could claim she received two ketubot; he resolves that the husband informs the witnesses of his intent.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase 'from encumbered property'
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase 'from encumbered property'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about orphans not collecting without an oath refers to orphans collecting from other orphans, not from the original borrower.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: orphans may only collect from encumbered property with an oath.
The Gemara questions: from whom do the orphans collect? If from the borrower, it would be absurd that their father collected without an oath but they need one.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means orphans collecting from other orphans require an oath.

items.text: Rav Zrika's ruling on orphans' claims and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Zrika's ruling on orphans' claims and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Zrika initially distinguishes between orphans who say their father said 'I borrowed and repaid' (require oath) and those who say 'I never borrowed' (no oath needed). Rava objects that 'I never borrowed' is like 'I never repaid', so the same rule should apply. The Gemara then corrects the tradition: if they say 'I never borrowed', they collect without an oath.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zerika quoting Rav Yehuda limits the baraita: the oath applies only when orphans say 'father borrowed and repaid,' but if they say 'father never borrowed,' they cannot collect even with an oath.
Rava objects: on the contrary, one who says 'I never borrowed' is like one who says 'I never repaid,' so the orphans should collect without an oath.
The Gemara corrects the tradition: if the orphans say 'father never borrowed,' they collect without an oath, because one who denies borrowing is deemed to deny repayment.

items.text: Dispute about collecting without the debtor present
items.text_en: Dispute about collecting without the debtor present
items.desc_en: Rav Acha Sar HaBira reports that Rabbi Yitzchak in Antioch ruled that the Mishnah's requirement of an oath for collecting without the debtor present applies only to a ketubah (due to charm), but not to a regular debt. Rava citing Rav Nachman disagrees, applying the rule to all debts to prevent people from taking loans and fleeing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a woman collecting her ketubah not in the husband's presence may only collect with an oath.
Rav Acha Sar HaBirah reports a case before Rabbi Yitzchak in Antioch, who ruled that the oath requirement applies only to a ketubah, due to חינא (favor), but not to a regular creditor.
Rava quoting Rav Nachman disagrees: even a regular creditor requires an oath, to prevent people from taking loans and fleeing, which would lock the door before borrowers.

items.text: Identifying Rabbi Shimon's statement in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying Rabbi Shimon's statement in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that Rabbi Shimon's ruling that heirs make the widow swear applies to the earlier Mishnah's case of collecting without the debtor present, and applies to both maintenance and ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Shimon's statement: as long as she claims her ketubah, her heirs may impose an oath upon her.
The Gemara asks: to which clause does Rabbi Shimon refer?
Rabbi Yirmeya explains: Rabbi Shimon refers to the clause about collecting not in his presence, teaching that whether for sustenance or ketubah, her heirs may impose an oath.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a widow does not claim her ketubah, heirs do not impose an oath upon her. The Gemara explains that this follows the dispute between Ḥanan and the sons of the High Priests regarding whether a woman claiming sustenance must swear at the end or both at the beginning and end. Rabbi Shimon sides with Ḥanan, the Rabbis with the sons of the High Priests.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a widow does not claim her ketubah, the heirs do not impose an oath upon her.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling follows the dispute between Ḥanan and the sons of the High Priests.
A baraita is cited: Ḥanan says a woman claiming sustenance swears at the end but not at the beginning.
The sons of the High Priests disagree and say she swears both at the beginning and at the end.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon follows Ḥanan, while the Rabbis follow the sons of the High Priests.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects: the Mishnah says 'heirs impose an oath upon her,' but it should say 'the court imposes an oath upon her'! He resolves by reinterpreting the Mishnah as referring to a case where the widow went to her father's house or her father-in-law's house and did not become an administrator; then heirs do not impose an oath. But if she became an administrator, heirs impose an oath regarding future matters, not past. Rabbi Shimon's statement is then about when she claims her ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects that the Mishnah should say 'the court imposes an oath upon her' rather than 'heirs impose an oath upon her.'

Rav Sheshet resolves by reinterpreting the Mishnah: if the widow went to her father's house or father-in-law's house and did not become an administrator, heirs do not impose an oath; but if she became an administrator, heirs impose an oath regarding future matters, and Rabbi Shimon's statement applies when she claims her ketubah.

items.text: Second tannaitic dispute: Abba Shaul and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Second tannaitic dispute: Abba Shaul and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis aligns with the dispute between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis regarding an administrator appointed by the father versus by the court. Rabbi Shimon follows Abba Shaul, the Rabbis follow the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis regarding whether an administrator appointed by the father or by the court must swear.
The baraita cites Abba Shaul's position that an administrator appointed by the court must swear, while one appointed by the father does not.
The Gemara aligns Rabbi Shimon with Abba Shaul and the Rabbis with the opposing Rabbis.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: the phrase 'all the time that she claims her ketubah' should be 'if she claims'! He resolves by reinterpreting the Mishnah as referring to a case where the husband wrote to her 'I have no vow or oath upon you' and similar clauses, which exempt her from oaths by him, his heirs, and her heirs. Rabbi Shimon's statement then applies only when she claims her ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'all the time that she claims her ketubah' should read 'if she claims', since the condition is binary.
Abaye resolves by reinterpreting the Mishnah as referring to a case where the husband wrote a clause exempting her from oaths, so Rabbi Shimon's statement applies only when she claims her ketubah.

items.text: Third tannaitic dispute: Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam
items.text_en: Third tannaitic dispute: Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis aligns with the dispute between Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam and the Rabbis. Rabbi Shimon follows Abba Shaul, the Rabbis follow the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis by aligning it with the tannaitic dispute between Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam and the Rabbis regarding the oath of an appointed guardian.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: the Mishnah's phrase 'all the time that she claims her ketubah' works, but what about when she does not claim it? He resolves that the Mishnah comes to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants, who hold that even without claiming, heirs impose an oath.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: the Mishnah's phrase 'all the time that she claims her ketubah' works, but what about when she does not claim it?
Rav Pappa resolves that the Mishnah comes to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer and his disputants, who hold that even without claiming, heirs impose an oath.

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The next Mishnah begins: 'If she produced a get but no ketubah with it...' This introduces a new topic about a widow who has a get but no ketubah document.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a new case: a widow produces a get (bill of divorce) but no ketubah (marriage contract) document.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a woman produces a ketubah without a get, and the husband claims he has a receipt. Similarly, a creditor produces a debt document without a prozbul. In both cases, they cannot collect. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that from the time of danger onward, a woman can collect her ketubah without a get, and a creditor without a prozbul.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case: a woman produces a ketubah without a get, and a creditor produces a debt document without a prozbul — in both cases they cannot collect.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that from the time of danger onward, a woman can collect her ketubah without a get, and a creditor without a prozbul.

items.text: Gemara's inference about writing a receipt
items.text_en: Gemara's inference about writing a receipt
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a receipt is written, because if not, the woman could produce her ketubah and collect without concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a receipt (שובר) is written, because otherwise the woman could produce her ketubah and collect without concern.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on the Mishnah's context
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute on the Mishnah's context
items.desc_en: Rav says the Mishnah deals with a place where a ketubah is not written, while Shmuel says even where it is written. This affects the interpretation of the case.

sub.desc_en: Rav asserts that the Mishnah deals with a place where a ketubah is not customarily written.
Shmuel counters that the Mishnah applies even where a ketubah is customarily written.

items.text: Clarification of Shmuel's position by Rav Anan
items.text_en: Clarification of Shmuel's position by Rav Anan
items.desc_en: Rav Anan explains Shmuel's view: in a place where a ketubah is not written and the husband says he wrote one, he must bring proof; where it is written and she says he did not write, she must bring proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Shmuel, does one write a receipt (שובר) for a ketubah?

Rav Anan explains Shmuel's position: in a place where a ketubah is not written and the husband claims he wrote one, he must bring proof; where it is written and she claims he did not write, she must bring proof.

items.text: Rav's retraction and final ruling
items.text_en: Rav's retraction and final ruling
items.desc_en: Rav retracts his earlier statement and rules that in all places, a get allows collection of the principal, and a ketubah allows collection of the additional amount. He challenges anyone who disagrees to respond.

sub.desc_en: Rav retracts his earlier position and rules that a get (bill of divorce) allows collection of the principal (עיקר) of the ketubah, while the ketubah itself allows collection of the additional amount (תוספת), and challenges anyone to dispute this.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah according to Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah according to Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah: for Shmuel, it fits his view that the husband must bring proof. For Rav, the question arises why the additional amount is not collected. Rav Yosef answers that the case involves no witnesses to the divorce, so the husband can claim he never divorced her.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about a woman with a ketubah but no get, and the husband claims he lost a receipt.
The Gemara notes that for Shmuel, the Mishnah fits his view that in a place where no ketubah is written, the husband must bring proof.
The Gemara asks: for Rav, even if the basic ketubah is not collected, why should the additional amount (תוספת) not be collected?
Rav Yosef answers that the case involves no witnesses to the divorce, so the husband can claim he never divorced her, preventing collection of the additional amount.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge to Rav's position
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge to Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's statement that a get alone allows collection of the principal (עיקר) of the ketubah. It argues that the Mishnah's later clause, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows collection without a get during a period of danger, implies that normally a get is needed, and that the Mishnah deals with a case where there are witnesses to the divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's position by noting that the Mishnah's later clause, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows collection without a get during danger, implies that normally a get is needed, and the Mishnah must deal with a case where there are witnesses to the divorce.

items.text: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the entire Mishnah as the view of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, explaining that it is missing a clause. The correct reading is that without witnesses to the divorce, the woman cannot collect; with witnesses, she collects the additional amount (תוספת); and the principal requires a get. During a period of danger, she collects even without a get.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and it is missing a clause: normally, with witnesses to divorce, she collects the additional amount (תוספת) with a get, but the principal (עיקר) requires a get; during danger, even without a get, she collects.

The Gemara cites the continuation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement: from the period of danger onward, a woman collects her ketubah without a get, and a creditor collects without a פרוזבול (prosbul).

items.text: Question about a widow from marriage
items.text_en: Question about a widow from marriage
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav: according to your view that a get allows collection of the principal, how does a widow from marriage collect her ketubah? She collects based on witnesses of death. But we should be concerned that she might have been divorced and then uses the get to collect again? The answer is that we are dealing with a woman who is sitting under her husband (i.e., she was not divorced). And if he divorced her close to death, he brought the loss upon himself.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question to Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question to Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav: according to your view that a get allows collection of the principal, how does a widow from marriage collect her ketubah based on witnesses of death, given the concern that she might have been divorced and then use the get to collect again?
The gemara answers that the case involves a woman who was sitting under her husband (i.e., she was not divorced).
The gemara objects: perhaps he divorced her close to death, and she could still use the get fraudulently.
The gemara resolves that if he divorced her close to death, he brought the loss upon himself.

items.text: Question about a widow from betrothal and the solution of a receipt
items.text_en: Question about a widow from betrothal and the solution of a receipt
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a widow from betrothal: she collects based on witnesses of death, but we should be concerned that she might have been divorced and then uses the get to collect again? The answer is that in a place where it is impossible to write a receipt (שובר), we write one. Otherwise, we would be concerned about double collection even with witnesses of death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: A widow from betrothal collects her ketubah based on witnesses of death, but we should be concerned that she might have been divorced and then uses the get to collect again.
The Gemara answers: In a place where it is impossible to write a receipt (שובר), we write one, otherwise we would be concerned about double collection even with witnesses of death.

items.text: Source that a widow from betrothal has a ketubah
items.text_en: Source that a widow from betrothal has a ketubah
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi: from where do we derive that a widow from betrothal has a ketubah? He suggests a Mishnah and a baraita, but each is challenged because the ketubah might have been written explicitly. The Gemara concludes that the baraita of Rav Chiya bar Avin is needed to teach that he does not inherit her, implying she has a ketubah.

sub.text: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha asks Rav Ashi: from where do we derive that a widow from betrothal (אלמנה מן האירוסין) has a ketubah?

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the first suggested source
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the first suggested source
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah (נתארמלה או נתגרשה) as a source, but objects: perhaps the ketubah was explicitly written for her.

sub.text: Gemara's counter-argument about Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah
sub.text_en: Gemara's counter-argument about Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara counters: if it were written, why state it? The Mishnah comes to exclude Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah's view that he writes only on condition of marriage.

sub.text: Gemara's proof from the Mishnah's wording
sub.text_en: Gemara's proof from the Mishnah's wording
sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves from the Mishnah's phrase 'גובה את הכל' (she collects everything) that it must refer to a written ketubah, otherwise she would only collect the basic מנה מאתיים.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Chiya bar Avin's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Chiya bar Avin's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara instead cites the baraita of Rav Chiya bar Avin, which states that a betrothed wife collects her ketubah when her husband dies.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the baraita also refers to a case where he wrote a ketubah, but concludes that the baraita is needed to teach that he does not inherit her, implying she has a ketubah.

items.text: Concern of double collection with a get and the solution of tearing
items.text_en: Concern of double collection with a get and the solution of tearing
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna: according to Rav who says a get allows collection of the principal, we should be concerned that she might collect in one court and then again in another? If you say we tear the get, she might say she wants to remarry with it. The solution is to tear it and write on it that it was torn not because it is invalid, but to prevent double collection.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna: according to Rav who says a get allows collection of the principal, we should be concerned that she might collect in one court and then again in another?
Rav Nachman anticipates the solution of tearing the get, but objects that she might want to remarry with it.
The gemara resolves: we tear the get and write on it that it was torn not because it is invalid, but to prevent double collection.

items.text: Mishnah: Two gittin and two ketubot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two gittin and two ketubot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If a woman has two gittin and two ketubot, she collects both ketubot. If she has two ketubot and one get, or one ketubah and two gittin, or one ketubah, one get, and a death, she collects only one ketubah. This is because one who divorces his wife and remarries her does so on the condition of the first ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if a woman has two gittin and two ketubot, she collects both ketubot; but with two ketubot and one get, or one ketubah and two gittin, or one ketubah, one get, and death, she collects only one ketubah, because one who divorces and remarries does so on the condition of the first ketubah.

items.text: Gemara on the Mishnah and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara on the Mishnah and Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the woman can choose which ketubah to collect. It suggests this is a refutation of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel, who said that two documents issued one after the other, the second nullifies the first. Rav Papa explains that Rav Nachman admits that if the second adds a date tree, it is written for the addition. Here too, the second ketubah adds something.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that a woman with two ketubot collects both means she can choose which one to collect.
The Gemara suggests this is a refutation of Rav Nachman citing Shmuel, who ruled that two documents issued one after the other, the second nullifies the first.
Rav Papa explains that Rav Nachman admits that if the second document adds a date tree, it is written for the addition; here too, the second ketubah adds something, so both are valid.

items.text: Beginning of a baraita on get, ketubah, and death
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita on get, ketubah, and death
items.desc_en: The baraita begins: If a woman produced a get, a ketubah, and a death (document), it sets up a case for further discussion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins: the Sages taught: if she produced a get, a ketubah, and a death certificate...

items.text: Opening Mishnah and related cases
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and related cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a get precedes a ketubah, the woman collects two ketubot; if the ketubah precedes the get, she collects only one. It then adds that a minor whose father married him off has a valid ketubah, as does a convert's wife who converted with him, because they were established on that condition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if a get precedes a ketubah, she collects two ketubot; if the ketubah precedes the get, she collects only one, because remarriage is on condition of the first ketubah.
The Mishnah adds that a minor whose father married him off has a valid ketubah, as does a convert's wife who converted with him, because they were established on that condition.

items.text: Dispute about whether the ketubah includes additional payment (תוספת)
items.text_en: Dispute about whether the ketubah includes additional payment (תוספת)
items.desc_en: Rav Huna limits the Mishnah's 'ketubah' to the basic 100 or 200 zuz, excluding additional payment (תוספת). Rav Yehuda argues that even תוספת is included. A baraita is brought against Rav Yehuda, showing that only if they renewed the ketubah does she get the renewal; otherwise, she gets only the basic amount. The Gemara concludes this is a refutation of Rav Yehuda, explaining that he was misled by the Mishnah's phrasing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav Huna limits the Mishnah's rule to the basic ketubah of מנה מאתיים (one or two hundred zuz), but not תוספת (additional amount); Rav Yehuda says even תוספת is included.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if they renewed the ketubah, she takes what they renewed — implying that without renewal, she does not take the תוספת.

The Gemara rejects the objection by reinterpreting the baraita as 'even what they renewed', but then cites a fuller version that explicitly distinguishes between renewal and non-renewal, concluding that this is a refutation of Rav Yehuda.

The Gemara explains that Rav Yehuda was misled by the Mishnah's phrasing 'כתובתה קיימת' (her ketubah stands), which he thought applied to the entire ketubah, but it actually refers only to the basic ketubah.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita is a refutation of Rav Yehuda.
The Gemara explains that Rav Yehuda was misled by the Mishnah's phrasing, thinking it referred to the entire ketubah, but it actually refers only to the basic amount.

items.text: Mishnah on precedence of wives' ketubot
items.text_en: Mishnah on precedence of wives' ketubot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if a man married two women and died, the first wife's ketubah takes precedence over the second's. If the first wife died and he married a second, then the second wife and her heirs precede the first wife's heirs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man married two women and died, the first wife takes precedence over the second, and her heirs precede the second's heirs; if the first died and he married a second and then died, the second and her heirs precede the first's heirs.

items.text: First inference: later creditor who collected keeps it
items.text_en: First inference: later creditor who collected keeps it
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrasing 'first precedes the second' (not 'first has, second has not') that if the second wife collected first, we do not take it from her. This implies that a later creditor who collected before an earlier one keeps what he collected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrasing 'first precedes the second' (not 'first has, second has not') that if the second wife collected first, we do not take it from her, implying that a later creditor who collected before an earlier one keeps what he collected.

items.text: Rejection of first inference
items.text_en: Rejection of first inference
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that 'precedes' might mean 'precedes for the entire amount' (like 'a son precedes a daughter'), and the later creditor's collection is not valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps the Mishnah's 'precedes' only means precedence for collection, not that a later collection is irreversible, citing the parallel of 'a son precedes a daughter' where the son does not actually take the daughter's share.

items.text: Alternative inference and its rejection
items.text_en: Alternative inference and its rejection
items.desc_en: Some say the opposite inference: since the Mishnah does not explicitly say 'if the second collected we do not take it', it implies that if she collected, we do take it. This would mean a later creditor's collection is invalid. The Gemara rejects this too, suggesting that the Mishnah's later clause about the second wife preceding the first's heirs shows that the second's collection is valid.

sub.desc_en: The alternative view infers from the Mishnah's silence about not taking from the second wife that if she collected first, we do take it from her, implying that a later creditor's collection is invalid.
The Gemara concludes from this inference that a later creditor who collected before the earlier one has not acquired the property (מה שגבה לא גבה).

The Gemara rejects the alternative inference, arguing that the Mishnah's later clause about the second wife and her heirs preceding the first wife's heirs shows that the second wife's collection is valid (מה שגבה גבה).

items.text: Opening Tanna statement
items.text_en: Opening Tanna statement
items.desc_en: The Tanna states that the first wife takes precedence over the second wife in collecting her ketubah from the estate.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the first wife takes precedence over the second wife in collecting her ketubah from the estate.

items.text: Gemara's three inferences from the Tanna
items.text_en: Gemara's three inferences from the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers three halakhot from the Tanna's statement: that children from both marriages have ketubat banin dikhrin, that a ketubah becomes a surplus for another ketubah, and that ketubat banin dikhrin does not collect from liened property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that three halakhot are inferred from the Tanna's statement: that children from both marriages have ketubat banin dikhrin, that a ketubah becomes a surplus for another ketubah, and that ketubat banin dikhrin does not collect from liened property.

The Gemara provides the source for the first inference: from the Tanna's phrasing that the second wife and her heirs precede the heirs of the first, implying that if there is a surplus, the first wife's children also take.
The Gemara provides the source for the second inference: the Tanna did not condition the ruling on a surplus of a dinar, implying that a ketubah can become a surplus for another ketubah.

The Gemara provides the source for the third inference: if ketubat banin dikhrin collected from liened property, the children of the first wife could collect from the children of the second wife, which the Tanna does not allow.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge to the inferences
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge to the inferences
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges each inference, suggesting alternative interpretations: the precedence may be for inheritance only, the surplus may exist, and the Tanna may hold that ketubah does not become a surplus.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges the inference that the first wife's sons inherit the father's estate, suggesting the precedence may only apply to inheritance (נחלה), not to the full ketubah claim.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's objection to the surplus inference
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to the surplus inference
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the mention of 'heirs of the first' is merely parallel to 'second and her heirs', not a substantive legal point.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's objection to the surplus rule
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to the surplus rule
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the Tanna may hold that a ketubah does not become a surplus for another, and the case here simply involves a surplus of a dinar.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute between Ben Nannas and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute between Ben Nannas and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute between Ben Nannas and Rabbi Akiva regarding the rights of children from two marriages when one wife predeceased and the other survived. The Gemara suggests they argue about whether children have ketubat banin dikhrin in such a case.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Ben Nannas says children of the first wife can tell the second wife's children 'you are creditors, take your mother's ketubah and leave'; Rabbi Akiva says the inheritance has already jumped from the first wife's children to the second wife's children.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about whether children from two marriages have the right of ketubat banin dikhrin when one wife predeceased and the other survived.

items.text: Rabbah's alternative explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbah's alternative explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbah reports that the rabbis of the school of Rav hold that all agree children have ketubat banin dikhrin, and the dispute is about whether a ketubah becomes a surplus for another ketubah and by extension for a creditor. Rabbah himself argues that regarding a creditor all agree it is a surplus, and the dispute is only about ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah reports that the rabbis of the school of Rav hold that all agree children have ketubat banin dikhrin, and the dispute is about whether a ketubah becomes a surplus for another ketubah and by extension for a creditor.
Rabbah elaborates that one opinion holds that a ketubah becomes a surplus for another ketubah and likewise for a creditor.
Rabbah argues that regarding a creditor all agree it is a surplus, and the dispute is only about ketubah.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to Rabbah's explanation, arguing that if the dispute were about surplus, Rabbi Akiva should have mentioned 'if there is a surplus of a dinar.' He concludes that the dispute is indeed about whether children have ketubat banin dikhrin when one wife predeceased and the other survived.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects to Rabbah's explanation: if the dispute were about surplus, Rabbi Akiva should have said 'if there is a surplus of a dinar.'
Rav Yosef concludes that the dispute between Ben Nanas and Rabbi Akiva is about whether children inherit (כתובת בנין דכרין) when one wife predeceased and the other survived.

items.text: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Shimon's opinion
items.text_en: Supporting baraita with Rabbi Shimon's opinion
items.desc_en: A second baraita is brought involving Rabbi Shimon, who requires a surplus of a dinar for children to take their mother's ketubah. The Gemara initially suggests this parallels the earlier dispute, but then concludes that all agree children have ketubat banin dikhrin, and the dispute is about the surplus requirement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting Rabbi Shimon's opinion that children divide the estate equally unless there is a surplus of a dinar.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the baraita parallels the earlier dispute about whether children inherit ketubat banin dikhrin when one wife predeceased the husband.
The Gemara rejects the parallel and concludes that all agree children have ketubat banin dikhrin; the dispute is about the requirement of a surplus of a dinar.

items.text: First explanation: dispute over movable property
items.text_en: First explanation: dispute over movable property
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Shimon is about whether the surplus must be specifically from land (מקרקעי) or can include movable property (מטלטלי). One holds only land counts, the other even movables.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether the surplus must be from land (מקרקעי) or can include movable property (מטלטלי).

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Shimon explicitly requires property with אחריות (land) exceeding two ketubot by a dinar, implying movables are worthless. This contradicts the idea that movables could count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's explicit requirement of property with אחריות (land) exceeding two ketubot by a dinar proves movables are worthless, contradicting the earlier suggestion.

items.text: Second explanation: dispute over liened property
items.text_en: Second explanation: dispute over liened property
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises: the dispute is about whether the surplus can come from property that is liened (משועבדי) or only from free property (בני חורין). One says only free property counts, the other even liened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the dispute: the disagreement is about whether the surplus of a dinar can come from liened property (משועבדי) or only from free property (בני חורין).

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's wording
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Shimon says 'if there is a surplus of a dinar' (אִם יֵשׁ), implying a conditional, not a given. If the dispute were about liened property, he should say 'since there is a surplus' (כֵּיוָן שֶׁיֵּשׁ).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon's wording 'אִם יֵשׁ' (if there is) is conditional, whereas if the dispute were about liened property he should have said 'כֵּיוָן שֶׁיֵּשׁ' (since there is).

items.text: Third explanation: dispute over less than a dinar
items.text_en: Third explanation: dispute over less than a dinar
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether a surplus of less than a dinar counts. One says only a full dinar works, the other even less. But both Tannaim mention 'dinar', so the Gemara considers inverting the opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute is about whether a surplus of less than a dinar (דינר) suffices: one Tanna requires a full dinar, the other accepts even less.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon explicitly says 'dinar', so he cannot be the one who accepts less than a dinar.
The Gemara notes that even if one inverts the opinions, the first Tanna also says 'dinar', so the inversion does not resolve the problem.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute follows the earlier two versions, and the opinions are inverted relative to the initial suggestion.

items.text: Rejection and return to earlier explanations
items.text_en: Rejection and return to earlier explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the third explanation and returns to the first two formulations, but inverts the opinions (i.e., the first Tanna is more lenient, Rabbi Shimon more strict).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the third explanation and returns to the first two formulations, but inverts the opinions, making the first Tanna more lenient and Rabbi Shimon more strict.

items.text: Halakhic ruling by Mar Zutra
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling by Mar Zutra
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa rules: if one wife died during the husband's lifetime and another after his death, the daughters have the right of כתובת בנין דכרין, and one ketubah can serve as surplus for the other. The Gemara explains the necessity of this ruling, clarifying that it applies even when the later wife bore a son (who might inherit), precluding concern of collusion.

sub.text: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa rules that if one wife died during the husband's lifetime and another after his death, the daughters have the right of כתובת בנין דכרין, and one ketubah can serve as surplus for the other.
The Gemara explains that if only the first clause had been stated, one might think the surplus diner requirement applies.
The Gemara notes that the second clause alone would have been sufficient, as it implies the first.
The Gemara raises a concern: if only the second clause were stated, one might think it applies only when the later wife bore a daughter, who does not inherit.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling teaches that even when the later wife bore a son (who inherits), there is no concern of collusion, and the daughters still receive their mother's ketubah.

items.text: Mishnah: division of assets among orphans
items.text_en: Mishnah: division of assets among orphans
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case: a man married two women, both died before him, then he died. The orphans seek their mothers' ketubot but only two ketubot worth of assets exist. They divide equally. If there is a surplus of a dinar, each takes their mother's ketubah. Orphans cannot inflate the estate's value; the court appraises. Property that is ראוי (not yet in hand) is not like מוחזק. Rabbi Shimon requires land exceeding the two ketubot by a dinar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case of a man married to two women, both predecease him, and the orphans divide the estate equally if only two ketubot exist.
The Mishnah states that if there is a surplus of a dinar, each group takes its mother's ketubah.
The Mishnah rules that orphans cannot inflate the estate's value; the court appraises the property.
The Mishnah states that property that is ראוי (not yet in hand) is not like מוחזק (property in hand).
Rabbi Shimon requires land exceeding the two ketubot by a dinar for the surplus rule to apply.

items.text: Baraita: unequal ketubot
items.text_en: Baraita: unequal ketubot
items.desc_en: A Baraita teaches: if one wife's ketubah is 1000 and the other's 500, if there is a surplus of a dinar, each takes her ketubah; otherwise, they divide equally.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the rule for unequal ketubot: if there is a surplus of a dinar, each takes her ketubah; otherwise, they divide equally.

items.text: Gemara: case of property increase or decrease
items.text_en: Gemara: case of property increase or decrease
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the estate was large and then diminished, the heirs have already acquired it. But if it was small and then increased, what is the law? It cites a case from the house of Bar Tzartzur where property was small and then increased. Rav Amram told them to appease the orphans; when they didn't, he threatened punishment. They went to Rav Nachman, who ruled similarly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the estate was large and then diminished, the heirs have already acquired it; but if it was small and then increased, what is the law?
The Gemara cites a case from the house of Bar Tzartzur where property was small and then increased, and the litigants came before Rav Amram.
Rav Amram threatened punishment if they did not appease the orphans, and when they refused, he sent them to Rav Nachman, who ruled similarly.

items.text: Opening statement from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening statement from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's rule: if orphans say they will appraise their father's property at a higher value, they gain the rights to it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if orphans say they will appraise their father's property at a higher value, they gain the rights to it.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided to help remember the following cases.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic (סימן) is provided to help remember the sequence of cases on this daf.

items.text: First case: debtor sells two properties for 1000 zuz
items.text_en: First case: debtor sells two properties for 1000 zuz
items.desc_en: A man owes 1000 zuz and sells two estates for 500 each. The creditor seizes one, and the debtor offers 1000 zuz to redeem it. Rami bar Hama compares this to the Mishnah, but Rava rejects the comparison because here the debtor suffers no loss.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man owes 1000 zuz, sells two estates for 500 each, and the creditor seizes one and then the other.
The debtor takes 1000 zuz to the creditor and offers to redeem the seized estate, saying if it's worth 1000 zuz to you, fine; otherwise take the 1000 and withdraw.
Rami bar Hama thought this case is identical to the Mishnah where orphans say they will pay a dinar more for the property.
Rava rejects the comparison: there the orphans suffer a loss, but here the debtor gives 1000 and takes 1000, so he suffers no loss.

items.text: Dispute over the amount of the receipt
items.text_en: Dispute over the amount of the receipt
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for how much the creditor writes a receipt. Ravina says 1000, Rav Avira says 500, and the halakha follows Rav Avira.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks at what value the deed of seizure should be written.
Ravina says the deed should be written for 1000 zuz.
Rav Avira says the deed should be written for 500 zuz.
The halacha is ruled in accordance with Rav Avira: the deed is written for 500 zuz.

items.text: Second case: debtor sells two fields for 100 zuz
items.text_en: Second case: debtor sells two fields for 100 zuz
items.desc_en: A man owes 100 zuz and sells two small fields for 50 each. The creditor seizes one, and the debtor offers 100 zuz to redeem it. Rav Yosef compares this to the Mishnah, but Abaye rejects it. The halakha for the receipt is 50.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a second case: a man owes 100 zuz, sells two small fields for 50 each, and the creditor seizes one and then the other.
The debtor takes 100 zuz to the creditor and offers: if the field is worth 100 to you, fine; otherwise take the 100 and withdraw.
Rav Yosef thought this case is identical to the Mishnah's rule, but Abaye rejects it, noting that here the debtor suffers no loss since he pays 100 and receives 100.
The gemara asks how much to write in the receipt; Ravina says 100, Rav Avira says 50, and the halakha (הלכה) is 50.

items.text: Third case: orphans pay and then creditor seizes again
items.text_en: Third case: orphans pay and then creditor seizes again
items.desc_en: A man dies owing 100 zuz, leaving a field worth 50. The creditor seizes it, the orphans pay 50, and then the creditor seizes again. Abaye rules that the first payment was a mitzvah, but the second seizure is lawful, unless the orphans specified the payment was for the field's value.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a man dies owing 100 zuz, leaving a field worth 50; the creditor seizes it, the orphans pay 50, and then the creditor seizes again.

Abaye rules that the first payment was a מצוה (fulfillment of the mitzvah to pay the father's debt), but the second seizure is lawful, as the orphans did not specify the payment was for the field's value.
The gemara qualifies that if the orphans had specified the payment was for the field's value, the creditor would be permanently removed from the field.

items.text: Case of selling mother's ketubah with a stipulation
items.text_en: Case of selling mother's ketubah with a stipulation
items.desc_en: A man sells his mother's ketubah rights with a stipulation that if she objects, he will not compensate. The mother dies without objecting, but the son objects. Rami bar Hama says he stands in his mother's place, but Rava says he accepted liability for himself.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a man sold his mother's ketubah rights with a stipulation that if she objects, he will not compensate the buyer.
The mother died without objecting, but the son himself came to object to the sale.
Rami bar Hama thought to say that the son stands in his mother's place, so his objection is ineffective.
Rava objects: although the seller did not accept liability for the mother's objection, he certainly accepted liability for his own objection, so the son must compensate the buyer.

items.text: Principle: selling a field without warranty
items.text_en: Principle: selling a field without warranty
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama states a principle: if Reuven sells a field to Shimon without warranty, and Shimon sells it back to Reuven with warranty, the law is discussed.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama begins a new halachic statement: Reuven sold a field to Shimon without אחריות (guarantee), and Shimon then sold it back to Reuven with אחריות.

items.text: Rava's objection to Shimon compensating Reuven's creditor
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Shimon compensating Reuven's creditor
items.desc_en: Rava questions whether Shimon, who bought land from Reuven with אחריות, must compensate Reuven when Reuven's creditor seizes the land. Rava argues that Shimon accepted responsibility for external debts but not for Reuven's own debt.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: Reuven's creditor seizes land from Shimon, and the law is that Shimon must compensate Reuven.
Rava objects: Shimon accepted responsibility for external debts (אחריות דעלמא) but did he accept responsibility for Reuven's own debt (אחריות דנפשיה)?

items.text: Rava's concession in a case of inherited land
items.text_en: Rava's concession in a case of inherited land
items.desc_en: Rava concedes that if Reuven inherited land from Yaakov and sold it to Shimon without אחריות, and Shimon later sold it back to Reuven with אחריות, then when Yaakov's creditor seizes it, Shimon must compensate Reuven. The creditor of Yaakov is considered an external creditor.

sub.desc_en: Rava concedes a case: if Reuven inherited a field from Jacob and sold it to Shimon without אחריות, and Shimon sold it back to Reuven with אחריות, then when Jacob's creditor seizes it, Shimon must compensate Reuven.
The gemara explains the reason: Jacob's creditor is like an external creditor (בעל חוב דעלמא), not Reuven's own debt.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's case: heirs exempt from movables
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's case: heirs exempt from movables
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama presents a case where Reuven sold a field to Shimon with אחריות, then borrowed money from Shimon and died. When Reuven's creditor seizes the field and Shimon pays him off, Reuven's sons claim that their father left movables with Shimon, which are not subject to creditor collection from orphans.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama presents a case: Reuven sold a field to Shimon with אחריות, then borrowed money from Shimon, and Reuven died; Reuven's creditor seizes the field from Shimon, and Shimon appeases him with money.
The law is that Reuven's sons can say to Shimon: our father left movable property (מטלטלי) with you, and movables of orphans are not subject to creditors' liens.

items.text: Rava's advice: convert movables to land
items.text_en: Rava's advice: convert movables to land
items.desc_en: Rava advises the creditor, if clever, to have the court give the orphans land in lieu of their movables, then seize that land, following Rav Nachman's ruling that creditors can reclaim land that orphans collected for their father's debt.

sub.desc_en: Rava advises: if the other party (Shimon) is clever, he should give them land (as payment) and then collect it back from them.
Rava's advice follows Rav Nachman's principle: orphans who collected land for their father's debt can have that land re-collected by a creditor.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling: creditor may choose which buyer to collect from
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling: creditor may choose which buyer to collect from
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if Reuven sold all his fields to Shimon, and Shimon sold one field to Levi, Reuven's creditor may collect from either Shimon or Levi. However, this applies only if Shimon sold a בינונית field; if he sold עידית or זיבורית, he can claim he bought land unsuitable for the creditor. Even with בינונית, this applies only if Shimon left no comparable בינונית for himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if Reuven sold all his fields to Shimon, and Shimon sold one field to Levi, Reuven's creditor may collect from either Shimon or Levi.
Rabbah qualifies that this applies only if Shimon sold a בינונית (medium-quality) field; if he sold עידית (superior) or זיבורית (inferior), he can claim he bought land unsuitable for the creditor.
Rabbah further qualifies that even with a בינונית field, the ruling applies only if Shimon left no comparable בינונית field for himself.

items.text: Opening principle: seller's right to designate inferior land
items.text_en: Opening principle: seller's right to designate inferior land
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a seller left medium-quality land of equal value, the buyer cannot force him to pay from better land, as the seller can say 'I left you a place to collect from it.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that if a seller left medium-quality land of equal value, the buyer cannot demand payment from better land, as the seller can claim he left a place for collection.

items.text: Abaye's first ruling: sale with warranty
items.text_en: Abaye's first ruling: sale with warranty
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if Reuven sold a field to Shimon with warranty (אחריות) and a creditor of Reuven seizes it, Reuven must compensate Shimon and cannot claim Shimon is not his litigant, because the creditor's claim ultimately falls back on Reuven.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if Reuven sold a field to Shimon with אחריות (guarantee) and a creditor of Reuven seizes it, Reuven must compensate Shimon and cannot claim Shimon is not his litigant, because Shimon can say 'whatever you extract from him comes back upon me.'

items.text: Alternative version: even without warranty
items.text_en: Alternative version: even without warranty
items.desc_en: Some say that even without warranty, Reuven must compensate Shimon, because Shimon can say 'I do not want Shimon to have a complaint against me.'

sub.desc_en: Some say that even without אחריות (guarantee), Reuven must compensate, because Shimon can say 'I do not want Shimon to have a complaint against me.'

items.text: Abaye's second ruling: sale without warranty and claimants emerge
items.text_en: Abaye's second ruling: sale without warranty and claimants emerge
items.desc_en: Abaye introduces a new case: Reuven sold a field to Shimon without warranty, and then claimants (creditors) emerge against it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces a new case: Reuven sold a field to Shimon without אחריות (guarantee), and claimants arose against it.

items.text: Opening discussion on acquisition of a field
items.text_en: Opening discussion on acquisition of a field
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the point at which a buyer acquires a field and cannot retract, citing the principle of 'חייתא דקיטרי' and an alternative opinion regarding responsibility.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that until a buyer takes possession of a field, he can retract; after possession, he cannot, because the seller says 'you saw the knots and accepted,' and possession is defined as when he plows the borders.
An alternative opinion holds that even regarding responsibility for liens, the seller says 'show your seizure and I will pay you.'

items.text: Mishnah: Division among three wives
items.text_en: Mishnah: Division among three wives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man who married three women with different ketubah amounts and died, leaving an estate insufficient to cover all. It details how the estate is divided proportionally, and extends the principle to partners in a fund.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a man married to three women with different ketubah amounts, and when the estate is only one hundred zuz, they divide equally.
The Mishnah details the proportional division when the estate is two hundred or three hundred zuz.
The Mishnah extends the same proportional division principle to three partners who invested in a fund.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Shmuel's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Shmuel's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the wife with a 100-zuz ketubah receives 50 when the estate is 200, as she should get only 33⅓. Shmuel explains that the wife with 200 writes a waiver to the wife with 100, renouncing her claim to the first 100. The Gemara then challenges this from the continuation, and the answer is that the waiver only applies to the 'din v'devarim' claim.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the division of 200 and 300 dinars among the three wives.
The mishnah adds that the same rule applies to three partners in a business venture.
The Gemara questions why the wife with a 100-zuz ketubah receives 50 when the estate is 200, as she should get only 33⅓.
Shmuel explains that the wife with 200 writes a waiver to the wife with 100, renouncing her claim to the first 100.
The Gemara objects from the continuation: if the waiver is total, the wife with 300 should take 100, not 75.
The Gemara answers that the waiver only applies to the 'din v'devarim' claim, not to the actual right to the money.
The Gemara transitions to the next case of the mishnah where the estate has 300 dinars.

items.text: Second question and Shmuel's second answer
items.text_en: Second question and Shmuel's second answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the wife with 200 receives 100 when the estate is 300, as she should get 75. Shmuel explains that the wife with 300 writes a waiver to both others, renouncing her claim to the first 100.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the wife with 200 receives 100 when the estate is 300, as she should get 75.
Shmuel explains that the wife with 300 writes a waiver to both others, renouncing her claim to the first 100.

items.text: Rav Yaakov's alternative explanation: two seizures
items.text_en: Rav Yaakov's alternative explanation: two seizures
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod explains in the name of Ravina that the Mishnah's distribution is based on two separate seizures of the estate: in the first case, 75 and 125 are seized at different times; in the second case, 75 and 225 are seized at different times.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod in the name of Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod in the name of Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov introduces the explanation that both the first and second cases of the Mishnah involve two separate seizures of the estate.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov's explanation of the first case
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov's explanation of the first case
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov explains the first case: 75 and 125 were seized at two different times, producing the Mishnah's distribution.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov's explanation of the second case
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov's explanation of the second case
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov explains the second case: 75 and 225 were seized at two different times, producing the Mishnah's distribution.

items.text: Tosefta dispute and extension to partners
items.text_en: Tosefta dispute and extension to partners
items.desc_en: A Tosefta records that this Mishnah is according to Rabbi Natan, but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagrees and says they divide equally. The Gemara then begins to discuss the parallel case of partners in a fund, with Shmuel's statement about two partners.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited, stating that the Mishnah's ruling follows Rabbi Natan.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects, saying he does not accept Rabbi Natan's view in these cases.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules instead that the wives divide the estate equally.
The Gemara transitions to the parallel case of partners in a fund, citing the Mishnah's extension.
Shmuel begins to discuss the case of two partners who contributed different amounts to a common fund.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when two partners invest unequal amounts, the profit is divided equally (השכר לאמצע).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when two partners invest unequal amounts, the profit is divided equally (השכר לאמצע).

items.text: Rava and Rav Hamnuna's dispute
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Hamnuna's dispute
items.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah's rule to cases where the investment is in an ox for plowing, but if it is for slaughter, each takes profit proportionally. Rav Hamnuna argues that even for slaughter, profit is split equally.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that Shmuel's ruling applies only when the ox is fit for plowing and remains for plowing, but if it was fit for plowing and stands for slaughter, each partner takes according to his investment.
Rav Hamnuna disagrees and holds that even if the ox was fit for plowing and stands for slaughter, the profit is still divided equally.

items.text: Objection against Rava
items.text_en: Objection against Rava
