items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a Mishnah about two who put money into a purse, one 100 and one 200, where profit is split equally. It suggests this refutes Rava, but answers that it refers to an ox for plowing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: two who put money into a purse, one a maneh and one two hundred, the profit is divided equally — does this not refer to an ox fit for plowing and standing for slaughter, refuting Rabbah?
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the baraita refers to an ox fit for plowing and remaining for plowing.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not explicitly distinguish between the two cases. It explains that the Mishnah's second clause (each takes according to his investment) applies to the case of an ox for slaughter, treating it as if they bought separately and mixed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's ruling would be for an ox purchased for plowing but used for slaughter, suggesting it would be that each takes according to his investment.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah should have distinguished within its own first clause rather than relying on the second clause.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah indeed implies the distinction: for an ox for slaughter, it is treated as if they bought separately and mixed, so each takes according to his investment.

items.text: Interpretation of 'increased' and 'decreased'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'increased' and 'decreased'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says that if three partners' investment increased or decreased, they divide equally. Rav Nachman bar Abba explains that 'increased' refers to new coins and 'decreased' to worn coins, not actual profit or loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: three partners who invested together divide equally whether they decreased or increased.
The Gemara asks: does 'decreased' mean actual loss and 'increased' mean actual profit, implying proportional division, contradicting Shmuel?
Rav Nachman bar Abba explains that 'increased' refers to new coins and 'decreased' to worn coins, not actual profit or loss, so the Mishnah does not contradict Shmuel.

items.text: Mishnah on multiple widows' precedence
items.text_en: Mishnah on multiple widows' precedence
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when a man married four wives and died, the first wife takes precedence over the second, and so on. The first must swear to the second, etc., but the last collects without an oath. Ben Nannas disagrees, requiring an oath for the last as well. If all divorces were on the same day, the one who recorded the earlier hour wins; if at the same hour with only one maneh, they divide equally.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the precedence of widows: the first wife collects first, each swears to the next, and the last collects without an oath.
Ben Nannas objects that the last widow should not be exempt from an oath merely because she is last, and requires her to swear as well.
The Mishnah rules that if all divorces were on the same day, the earlier hour prevails; if the same hour with only one maneh, they divide equally.

items.text: Gemara's opening question
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between the Sages and Ben Nannas is based on, and Shmuel begins to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: over what principle do they disagree?
Shmuel begins to answer the question (the continuation is in the next daf).

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Ben Nannas on later creditor's collection
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Ben Nannas on later creditor's collection
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case involves a creditor who collected from property that was not the debtor's. Tanna Kamma holds that what he collected is not collected (he must return it), while Ben Nannas holds that it is collected (he keeps it).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case involves a creditor who collected from property that was not the debtor's, and the dispute is about a later creditor who collected first.
Tanna Kamma holds that what the later creditor collected is not collected (he must return it).
Ben Nannas holds that what the later creditor collected is collected (he keeps it).

items.text: Rav Nachman's explanation: concern about embarrassment
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's explanation: concern about embarrassment
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha says that everyone agrees the later creditor does not keep the proceeds; the dispute is about whether we fear that the woman will be embarrassed (if she must swear). One opinion fears embarrassment, the other does not.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha explains that everyone agrees what was collected is not collected, and the dispute is about whether we suspect the debtor's property might be devalued (תכסיף).
One authority (Tanna Kamma) suspects devaluation, while the other (Ben Nannas) does not.

items.text: Abaye's explanation: the baraita of Abaye the Elder
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation: the baraita of Abaye the Elder
items.desc_en: Abaye says the dispute is about the baraita of Abaye the Elder, which states that orphans who said they are adults (to avoid swearing) are believed, and needless to say minors. Tanna Kamma does not accept this baraita, while Ben Nannas does.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the dispute is about the baraita of Abaye the Elder regarding orphans who said they are adults.
Tanna Kamma rejects Abaye the Elder's baraita, while Ben Nannas accepts it.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on partners in litigation
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on partners in litigation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if two brothers or partners have a case with one person, and one of them goes to court with him, the other cannot claim he is not a party; the one who went acted as his agent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that when two brothers or partners have a case against one person, and one of them goes to court with him, the other cannot claim he is not a party; the first acted as his agent.

items.text: Rav Nachman's application and limitation of the agency principle
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's application and limitation of the agency principle
items.desc_en: When Rav Nachman visited Sura, they asked him about a similar case. He cited the Mishnah where the first wife swears to the second, etc., but not the first to the third, implying agency. They object that the Mishnah involves oaths to many, while here one claims he could have argued more. The Gemara limits the ruling to when the absent party is not in town; if he is, he must come.

sub.text: Sura sages' question to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Sura sages' question to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: When Rav Nachman visited Sura, the sages there asked him about a similar case to the one just discussed.
Rav Nachman cited the Mishnah where the first wife swears to the second, etc., but not the first to the third, implying that the second acts as the first's agent.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah involves oaths to many, while here the claimant says he could have argued more.
The Gemara limits the ruling to when the absent party is not in town; if he is, he must come.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on two documents issued the same day
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on two documents issued the same day
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: if two documents (e.g., deeds of sale) are issued on the same day, Rav says the claimants divide the property, while Shmuel says it depends on the judges' discretion. The Gemara suggests Rav follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that witnesses' signatures are what effect the document.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding two documents issued on the same day: Rav says the claimants divide the property, while Shmuel says it depends on the judges' discretion.
The Gemara suggests that Rav's position aligns with Rabbi Meir, who holds that the witnesses' signatures are what effect the document.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute over the principle of חלוקה vs. שודא דדייני
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute over the principle of חלוקה vs. שודא דדייני
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav and Shmuel both agree with Rabbi Elazar that witnesses of delivery are decisive, but they disagree about how to divide property between two competing deeds: Rav holds that חלוקה (equal division) is preferable, while Shmuel holds that שודא דדייני (the judges' discretion) is preferable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel aligns with Rabbi Elazar's view that witnesses of delivery are decisive, and that Rav and Shmuel disagree on the preferred method of dividing property between competing deeds: Rav holds that חלוקה (equal division) is preferable, while Shmuel holds that שודא דדייני (judges' discretion) is preferable.

items.text: Challenge to Rav's alignment with Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav's alignment with Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav can be aligned with Rabbi Elazar, citing Rav Yehuda's report that Rav ruled like Rabbi Elazar only in גיטין (divorce documents), but Shmuel extended it to שטרות (deeds). This implies Rav disagreed regarding שטרות. The Gemara resolves that Rav actually follows Rabbi Meir, while Shmuel follows Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav cannot be aligned with Rabbi Elazar regarding deeds, because Rav Yehuda said in Rav's name that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Elazar only for גיטין (bills of divorce), not for שטרות (deeds), so the dispute must be recharacterized: Rav follows Rabbi Meir and Shmuel follows Rabbi Elazar.
The Gemara resolves that Rav actually follows Rabbi Meir, while Shmuel follows Rabbi Elazar, reconciling the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Shmuel's defense
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Shmuel's defense
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says two deeds issued on the same day are divided equally, which contradicts Shmuel's view. Shmuel deflects by attributing the baraita to Rabbi Meir. The Gemara then challenges this by citing the baraita's continuation: if one wrote a deed for one person and delivered it to another, the recipient acquires it, which contradicts Rabbi Meir's view that witnesses of signature are decisive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says two deeds issued on the same day are divided equally, which contradicts Shmuel's view.
Shmuel deflects the objection by attributing the baraita to Rabbi Meir, while he himself follows Rabbi Elazar.

The Gemara challenges Shmuel's attribution by citing the baraita's continuation: if one wrote a deed for one person and delivered it to another, the recipient acquires it, which contradicts Rabbi Meir's view that witnesses of signature are decisive.

items.text: Resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita reflects a dispute among Tannaim: the Sages say the property is divided, but another opinion says the third party (the one holding the property) may do as he wishes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita reflects a dispute among Tannaim, citing a beraita where חכמים (the Sages) say the heirs divide equally, while another opinion says the third party may do as he wishes.

items.text: Case of Rami bar Hama and Mar Ukva bar Hama
items.text_en: Case of Rami bar Hama and Mar Ukva bar Hama
items.desc_en: The mother of Rami bar Hama wrote deeds granting her property to Rami in the morning and to Mar Ukva in the evening. Rami appeared before Rav Sheshet, who awarded him the property; Mar Ukva appeared before Rav Nachman, who awarded him the property. Rav Sheshet confronted Rav Nachman, who justified his ruling based on שודא דדייני. Rav Sheshet claimed he also used שודא דדייני, but Rav Nachman countered that he is a judge and Rav Sheshet is not, and that Rav Sheshet originally came to court as a litigant.

sub.desc_en: The mother of Rami bar Hama wrote deeds granting her property to Rami in the morning and to Mar Ukva bar Hama in the evening.
Rami bar Hama appeared before Rav Sheshet, who awarded him the property; Mar Ukva appeared before Rav Nachman, who awarded him the property.
Rav Sheshet confronted Rav Nachman, asking why he ruled for Mar Ukva, and Rav Nachman countered by asking why Rav Sheshet ruled for Rami.
Rav Sheshet justified his ruling by saying Rami's deed was earlier, but Rav Nachman rejected this because they are not in Jerusalem where hours are recorded.
Rav Nachman justified his ruling based on שודא דדייני (the judge's discretion to decide which deed is more credible).
Rav Sheshet claimed he also used שודא דדייני in his ruling.
Rav Nachman rejected Rav Sheshet's claim, arguing that Rav Sheshet is not a qualified judge and originally came to court as a litigant, not a judge.

items.text: Case of two deeds before Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Case of two deeds before Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Two deeds came before Rav Yosef: one dated the 5th of Nisan, the other simply 'Nisan'. Rav Yosef awarded the property to the holder of the 5th of Nisan deed. The other claimant protested, and Rav Yosef told him he could claim a later date. The claimant then asked Rav Yosef to write him a document, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case of two deeds that came before Rav Yosef, one dated the 5th of Nisan and the other simply 'Nisan'.
Rav Yosef awards the property to the holder of the 5th of Nisan deed.
The other claimant protests that he will lose out, and Rav Yosef tells him he can claim a later date (e.g., the 29th of Nisan).
The second claimant asks Rav Yosef to write him a document, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening question about a creditor's remedy
items.text_en: Opening question about a creditor's remedy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what remedy a creditor has if the debtor sold land after Nisan, and the buyer can claim the debt was incurred after the sale. The solution is to write authorization to each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what remedy a creditor has if the debtor sold land after Iyar, and the buyer can claim the debt was incurred after Nisan.
The Gemara answers that the solution is for the creditor and buyer to write authorization (הרשאה) to each other.

items.text: Mishnah: Two wives and a sale
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two wives and a sale
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a man married to two women sells his field, and the first wife writes a waiver to the buyer. The second wife can collect from the buyer, and the first from the second, and so on, until they compromise. The same applies to a creditor and a woman creditor.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a man married to two wives who sells his field, with the first wife writing a waiver to the buyer, leading to a chain of collection and compromise.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Waiver is ineffective
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Waiver is ineffective
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's assumption that a wife's waiver is valid, citing a baraita that such a statement is meaningless. It answers that the case involves a kinyan (formal acquisition). But even with a kinyan, the wife can claim she acted to please her husband, as in a similar case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's assumption that a wife's waiver is effective, citing a baraita that such a statement is meaningless.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a kinyan (formal acquisition) from the wife.
The Gemara objects that even with a kinyan, the wife can claim she acted to please her husband, citing a similar case.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, while the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda. The baraita states that if a wife signed for the second buyer but not the first, she loses her ketubah according to Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Yehuda says she can claim she acted to please her husband.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir and the baraita to Rabbi Yehuda.
The baraita states that according to Rabbi Meir, if a wife signed for the second buyer but not the first, she loses her ketubah entirely.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the wife can claim she acted to please her husband, so she does not lose her ketubah.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi: Reconciling the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi: Reconciling the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi (the editor) sets an anonymous Mishnah here like Rabbi Meir and elsewhere like Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah deals with a divorced woman, where all agree. Rav Ashi says the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, but he only disputes in the case of two buyers; with one buyer, even Rabbi Meir agrees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi (the editor) sets an anonymous Mishnah here according to Rabbi Meir and elsewhere according to Rabbi Yehuda, implying inconsistency.
Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah deals with a divorced woman, where all agree, so there is no inconsistency.
Rav Ashi says the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, but he only disputes in the case of two buyers; with one buyer, even Rabbi Meir agrees, and our Mishnah involves writing to another (a single buyer).

items.text: New inquiry: Collecting from encumbered property when unencumbered is lost
items.text_en: New inquiry: Collecting from encumbered property when unencumbered is lost
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if unencumbered property is lost, can one collect from encumbered property? It attempts to prove from the baraita about the wife who signed for the second buyer: if she could collect from the first, she would, but the baraita says she loses her ketubah. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that she only loses from the second buyer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if unencumbered property is lost, can one collect from encumbered property?
The Gemara attempts to prove from the baraita about the wife who signed for the second buyer: if she could collect from the first, she would, but the baraita says she loses her ketubah.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the baraita means she only loses from the second buyer, not from the first.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the baraita says 'lost' entirely, and cites another baraita where a creditor who waives rights against a second buyer cannot collect from the first, because the first can say 'you left me a place to collect.' The Gemara distinguishes: there the creditor caused his own loss. The daf ends with Rav Yemar addressing Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the baraita's term 'איבְּדָה' (she lost) implies total loss, and cites a supporting baraita where a creditor who waives rights against a second buyer cannot collect from the first, because the first can say 'you left me a place to collect.'
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing that in the cited baraita, the creditor caused his own loss by voluntarily waiving rights against the second buyer.

sub.text: Rav Yemar's address to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar's address to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: The daf ends with Rav Yemar beginning to address Rav Ashi, introducing a new point or question.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the case of the orchard
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the case of the orchard
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that such cases happen daily, citing a story where an orchard was mortgaged for ten years but dried up after five, and the rabbis wrote a טירפא. It resolves that the buyers brought loss upon themselves since they knew the orchard might dry up.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that such cases happen daily, citing a story where an orchard was mortgaged for ten years but dried up after five, and the rabbis wrote a טירפא (writ of seizure).
The Gemara resolves that the buyers brought loss upon themselves since they knew the orchard might dry up.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on flooded orchards
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on flooded orchards
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha: if the orchards of the חרי (a type of field) are flooded, the creditor collects from the unencumbered property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that if the orchards of the חרי (a type of field) are flooded, the creditor collects from the unencumbered property.

items.text: Abaye's statement on 'my property to you and your remainder to so-and-so'
items.text_en: Abaye's statement on 'my property to you and your remainder to so-and-so'
items.desc_en: Abaye says that if a woman was given property with the stipulation 'my property to you and your remainder to so-and-so' and she married, the husband is considered a purchaser, and the remainder has no claim against the husband. This is compared to a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if a woman was given property with the stipulation 'my property to you and your remainder to so-and-so' and she married, the husband is considered a purchaser, and the remainder has no claim against the husband.

The gemara identifies Abaye's position as aligning with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that the second recipient only gets what the first left over, against Rabbi who allows the second to reclaim from purchasers.

items.text: Contradiction in Abaye's statements
items.text_en: Contradiction in Abaye's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abaye's consistency, citing his earlier statement that advising someone to sell property according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view makes one a 'crafty wicked person'. It resolves that the earlier case involved advising to sell, while here the woman already married.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abaye's consistency, citing his earlier statement that advising someone to sell property according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view makes one a 'crafty wicked person'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between advising to sell (which is forbidden) and the case where the woman already married (which is discussed here).

items.text: Abaye's second statement and the distinction from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's second statement and the distinction from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if the woman sold the property and died, the husband takes from the buyers, the remainder takes from the husband, and the buyer takes from the remainder, but all are placed in the buyer's hands. The Gemara distinguishes this from the Mishnah's case of multiple claimants circling back, because here only the buyer suffers loss.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that if a woman sold property given to her with remainder to another, and then died, the husband takes from the buyers, the remainder takes from the husband, and the buyer takes from the remainder, but all are placed in the buyer's hands.
The Gemara asks why this case differs from the Mishnah's rule of multiple claimants circling back until they reach a compromise.
The Gemara answers that there all claimants suffer loss, but here only the buyer suffers loss.

items.text: Rafram's challenge and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rafram's challenge and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rafram presents Abaye's first statement before Rav Ashi, questioning the contradiction. Rav Ashi resolves that the first case was when the gift was given while she was unmarried, so the husband acquires; the second case was when given while she was married, so the husband does not acquire, as the donor intended the remainder to acquire but not the husband.

sub.desc_en: Rafram presents Abaye's first statement before Rav Ashi, questioning the contradiction between Abaye's two rulings.

Rav Ashi resolves that the first case was when the gift was given while she was unmarried, so the husband acquires; the second case was when given while she was married, so the husband does not acquire, as the donor intended the remainder to acquire but not the husband.

items.text: Extension to creditor and two buyers
items.text_en: Extension to creditor and two buyers
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that the same principle applies to a creditor and two buyers, and similarly to a woman who is a creditor and two buyers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the same principle applies to a creditor.
A baraita teaches that the same rule applies to a creditor and two purchasers.
The Gemara adds that the same applies to a woman who is a creditor and two purchasers.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'we return to you, the one who was married'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'we return to you, the one who was married'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow supported by orphans' property keeps her earnings for them, they are not obligated for her burial, and her heirs who inherit her ketubah are obligated for her burial.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a widow supported by orphans' property: her earnings belong to them, they are not obligated for her burial, but her heirs who inherit her ketubah are obligated for her burial.

items.text: Gemara's inquiry about the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's inquiry about the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah reads 'נִיזּוֹנֶת' (as per the Galileans, implying they must support her) or 'הַנִּיזּוֹנֶת' (as per the Judeans, implying they may choose not to).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a doubt whether the Mishnah reads 'נִיזּוֹנֶת' (as per the Galileans, implying they must support her) or 'הַנִּיזּוֹנֶת' (as per the Judeans, implying they may choose not to).
The Gemara considers the alternative possibility that the Mishnah reads 'הַנִּיזּוֹנֶת' (as per the Judeans), meaning they may choose not to support her.

items.text: Gemara's question on the widow's found property
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the widow's found property
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's ruling that a widow supported by the estate keeps her found property. If the Mishnah says 'she is supported' (נִיזּוֹנֶת), her found property should go to the heirs like a wife's goes to her husband. The Gemara answers that the widow's found property is hers because the heirs do not have the same concern for marital harmony (אֵיבָה) as a husband does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah by citing Rabbi Zeira quoting Shmuel that a widow's found property is hers, and argues that if the Mishnah uses the term 'נִיזּוֹנֶת' (she is supported), the found property should go to the heirs like a wife's goes to her husband.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah indeed uses 'נִיזּוֹנֶת', but the widow keeps her found property because the heirs lack the concern for marital harmony (אֵיבָה) that a husband has.

items.text: Chores a widow performs for the heirs
items.text_en: Chores a widow performs for the heirs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yossi bar Chanina states that a widow must perform all the chores for the heirs that a wife does for her husband, except for mixing his cup, making his bed, and washing his face, hands, and feet.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina rules that a widow performs all labors for the heirs that a wife does for her husband, except for pouring his cup, making his bed, and washing his face, hands, and feet.

items.text: Student's service to his teacher
items.text_en: Student's service to his teacher
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says a student must perform all services for his teacher that a slave does for his master, except for removing his shoe. Rava and Rav Ashi qualify this: it applies only where the teacher is not recognized, and if he wears tefillin, it is not required.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a student (תלמיד) performs all services for his teacher (רב) that a slave (עבד) performs for his master, except for removing his shoe (התרת מנעל).
Rava qualifies that the student's obligation to serve applies only where the teacher is not widely recognized (אין מכירין אותו); where the teacher is recognized, the obligation does not apply.
Rav Ashi further qualifies that even in a place where the teacher is not recognized, if he is wearing tefillin (תפילין) and thus recognizable as a scholar, the student is also exempt from service.

items.text: Punishment for preventing a student from serving
items.text_en: Punishment for preventing a student from serving
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan says that one who prevents his student from serving him is considered to withhold kindness from him, as per the verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that he also removes fear of Heaven from him.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one who prevents his student from serving him is as if he withholds kindness, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that he also removes fear of Heaven from him.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that such a person also removes fear of Heaven (יראת שמים) from the student, citing the verse 'ויראת שדי יעזוב'.

items.text: Widow's seizure of movable property for sustenance
items.text_en: Widow's seizure of movable property for sustenance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if a widow seizes movable property for her sustenance, what she seized is hers. A baraita supports this. Rav Dimi recounts a case where Rabbi Shabbat's daughter-in-law seized a sack of money and the sages could not retrieve it. Ravina limits this to sustenance, not her ketubah. Mar bar Rav Ashi objects that both are collected from land, so the same rule should apply. Rav Yitzchak bar Naftali confirms Ravina's ruling in Rava's name.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if a widow seizes movable property for her sustenance, what she seized remains hers.
A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Elazar's ruling verbatim.
Rav Dimi recounts a case where Rabbi Shabbat's daughter-in-law seized a sack of money and the sages could not retrieve it.
Ravina limits the ruling to sustenance, but for her ketubah payment, the property is taken from her.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects that both sustenance and ketubah are collected from land, so the same rule should apply to both.
Rav Yitzchak bar Naftali confirms to Ravina that they say in Rava's name that Ravina's ruling is correct.

items.text: Widow who delays claiming sustenance
items.text_en: Widow who delays claiming sustenance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yossi ben Zimra says that if a widow waits two or three years without claiming sustenance, she loses it. The Gemara questions why both are needed and resolves that the difference is between a poor and rich widow, or between an immodest and modest one. Rava adds that this applies only retroactively, but she may claim future sustenance.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yossi ben Zimra
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yossi ben Zimra
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yossi ben Zimra rules that a widow who waited two or three years without claiming sustenance loses her right to it.
The Gemara questions why the statement mentions both two and three years, since if two years already cause loss, three years is obvious.
The Gemara resolves that the two cases refer to different situations: one is a poor widow and the other a rich widow.
Alternatively, the Gemara explains that the difference is between an immodest widow and a modest one.
Rava qualifies that the loss applies only retroactively (למפרע), but for future sustenance (להבא) she may still claim.

items.text: Burden of proof when heirs claim they paid sustenance
items.text_en: Burden of proof when heirs claim they paid sustenance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan raises a question: if the orphans say they gave sustenance and the widow says she did not receive it, who bears the burden of proof?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks: if the orphans say 'we gave' and the widow says 'I did not receive', who bears the burden of proof?

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara poses a dilemma: when a widow sells property for her maintenance without court authorization, is the property presumed to belong to the orphans (requiring her to bring proof that she sold only for maintenance) or to the widow (requiring the orphans to bring proof that she sold more than her due)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a dilemma: when a widow sells property for her maintenance without court authorization, is the property presumed to belong to the orphans (requiring her to bring proof) or to the widow (requiring the orphans to bring proof)?

items.text: Attempted resolution from Levi's baraita
items.text_en: Attempted resolution from Levi's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Levi that distinguishes between a widow who has not remarried (the orphans must bring proof) and one who has remarried (she must bring proof). This seems to resolve the dilemma in favor of the widow's presumption before remarriage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Levi's baraita, which distinguishes between a widow who has not remarried (the orphans must bring proof) and one who has remarried (she must bring proof), seemingly resolving the dilemma in favor of the widow's presumption before remarriage.

items.text: Analysis of the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Analysis of the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi suggests that the dilemma is actually a dispute between Tannaim: Rabbi Yehuda requires the widow to specify which items were sold for maintenance and which for her ketubah, implying the property is presumed to belong to the orphans; Rabbi Yosei allows her to write a general statement, implying the property is presumed to belong to her.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi introduces the dilemma as a dispute between Tannaim, citing the baraita where Rabbi Yehuda requires the widow to specify which items were sold for maintenance and which for her ketubah, while Rabbi Yosei allows a general statement.

The Gemara infers that the Tannaim dispute the underlying presumption: Rabbi Yehuda holds the property is presumed to belong to the orphans, while Rabbi Yosei holds it is presumed to belong to the widow.

The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that both Tannaim may agree the property is presumed to belong to the widow, and Rabbi Yehuda merely advises the widow to specify to avoid being called a glutton.
The Gemara supports this alternative by noting that Rabbi Yochanan's dilemma cannot be resolved from the Mishnah, which also teaches good advice, so here too the baraita teaches good advice.

The Gemara offers another alternative: both Tannaim agree the property is presumed to belong to the orphans, and Rabbi Yosei's leniency follows Abaye Keshisha's parable of a dying man who gives money to his creditor, which can be taken either as payment or as a gift.

items.text: First alternative interpretation: both agree with widow's presumption
items.text_en: First alternative interpretation: both agree with widow's presumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the forced inference: perhaps both Tannaim agree that the property is presumed to belong to the widow, and Rabbi Yehuda merely offers good advice to avoid being called a glutton. This is supported by a parallel case where Rabbi Yochanan's question cannot be resolved from the Mishnah for the same reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the inference from the Tannaitic dispute is inconclusive: perhaps both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei agree that the property is presumed to belong to the widow (נִכְסֵי בְּחֶזְקַת אַלְמָנָה קָיְימִי), and Rabbi Yehuda's requirement to specify is merely good advice to avoid being called a glutton.

sub.text: Supporting argument from Rabbi Yochanan's question
sub.text_en: Supporting argument from Rabbi Yochanan's question
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports this objection by noting that if not for this reasoning, Rabbi Yochanan's unresolved question could have been answered from the Mishnah; therefore, the Mishnah must be understood as offering good advice, and the same applies here.

items.text: Second alternative interpretation: both agree with orphans' presumption
items.text_en: Second alternative interpretation: both agree with orphans' presumption
items.desc_en: Alternatively, perhaps both Tannaim agree that the property is presumed to belong to the orphans, and Rabbi Yosei's leniency is based on a parable of Abaye the Elder: a dying man who says 'give 200 zuz to my creditor' may be paying a debt or giving a gift, so the widow's general statement is sufficient because she could be selling for either purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation: both Tannaim agree that the property is presumed to belong to the orphans (נִכְסֵי בְּחֶזְקַת יַתְמֵי קָיְימִי), and Rabbi Yosei's leniency is based on a different reasoning.

Abaye the Elder provides a parable: a dying man who says 'give 200 zuz to my creditor' may be paying a debt or giving a gift, so the widow's general statement is sufficient because she could be selling for either purpose.

items.text: Opening statement on the widow's sale
items.text_en: Opening statement on the widow's sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that if the widow takes property as a gift, her power is not as great as when she sells it for sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that if the widow takes property as a gift, her power is not as great as when she sells it for sustenance.

items.text: Dispute over the frequency of sale for sustenance
items.text_en: Dispute over the frequency of sale for sustenance
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute how often the widow may sell property for her sustenance: Rav Huna says once every twelve months, Rav Yehuda says once every six months. Both agree the buyer provides sustenance every thirty days. Baraitot support both opinions, and Ameimar rules in accordance with Rav Yehuda, dismissing Rav Huna's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's and Rav Yehuda's dispute: Rav Huna says the widow sells once every twelve months, Rav Yehuda says once every six months, and both agree the buyer provides sustenance every thirty days.
Two baraitot are cited: one supports Rav Huna's position, the other supports Rav Yehuda's position.
Ameimar rules in accordance with Rav Yehuda, and when Rav Ashi asks about Rav Huna's view, Ameimar dismisses it as not accepted.

items.text: Can the widow reclaim sold property for her ketubah?
items.text_en: Can the widow reclaim sold property for her ketubah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a widow who sold property for sustenance can later reclaim it to collect her ketubah. The question is framed in light of Rav Yosef's principle that a widow's sale imposes responsibility on the orphans. The Gemara attempts to resolve this from a baraita, concluding that if she left a remainder, she cannot reclaim; if not, she can. The Gemara rejects an alternative interpretation that the baraita merely offers good advice.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rav Sheshet whether a widow who sold property for sustenance can later reclaim it to collect her ketubah.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the dilemma's background
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the dilemma's background
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dilemma is based on Rav Yosef's principle that a widow's sale imposes responsibility on the orphans, and asks what the halakha is.

sub.text: Gemara's formulation of the two possibilities
sub.text_en: Gemara's formulation of the two possibilities
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two possibilities: either she can reclaim because the guarantee rests on the orphans, or the buyers can argue that she accepted responsibility for her own actions.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's answer citing a baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's answer citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita that a widow sells until only the value of her ketubah remains, and she relies on the remainder; this implies that if she left a remainder she cannot reclaim, but if not, she can.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might only offer good advice, but then rejects this by noting the precise wording 'she relies,' concluding that the baraita teaches a legal distinction.

items.text: Sale made under duress: does it revert if money is no longer needed?
items.text_en: Sale made under duress: does it revert if money is no longer needed?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a sale made because the seller needed money for a specific purpose (e.g., to buy oxen) reverts if the need passes. It brings two stories: one where Rav Pappa returned land as a matter of piety, and another where Rav Nachman ruled that a sale of fields made due to a grain shortage reverts because it was a mistaken sale. The Gemara concludes that the halakha is that such sales do revert.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if someone sold property because he needed money for a specific purpose, and in the end he did not need the money, does the sale revert or not?

The Gemara brings a story where a man sold land to Rav Pappa to buy oxen, but later did not need the money, and Rav Pappa returned the land; the Gemara notes that Rav Pappa acted beyond the letter of the law.

The Gemara brings another story: during a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat, but when wheat arrived, Rav Nachman ruled that the mansions must be returned to their owners.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of the second proof
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of the second proof
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that in that case the sale was made in error because the ship with wheat was already in the bays, so the sellers would not have sold had they known.
Rami bar Shmuel objects that Rav Nachman's ruling would discourage future buyers, but Rav Nachman responds that drought is not common; Rami bar Shmuel counters that in Neharde'a drought is frequent.
The Gemara concludes that the halakha is: if one sold property and in the end did not need the money, the sale is reversed.

items.text: Mishnah: Widow's sale with or without court
items.text_en: Mishnah: Widow's sale with or without court
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow, whether from betrothal or marriage, may sell property without a court. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: from marriage she may sell without court, but from betrothal she may only sell with a court because she has no sustenance rights. The Gemara begins to explain the reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a widow, whether from betrothal or marriage, may sell property without a court.
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: a widow from marriage may sell without a court, but from betrothal she may only sell with a court because she has no sustenance rights.
The Gemara begins to explain the reasoning behind the Mishnah's distinction.

items.text: Debate on the reason for the widow from betrothal's restriction
items.text_en: Debate on the reason for the widow from betrothal's restriction
items.desc_en: Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan dispute why a widow from betrothal cannot sell her ketubah without a court: Ulla says it is due to charm (חינא), Rabbi Yochanan says it is because a man does not want his wife to be shamed in court. The difference between them is a divorced woman: according to Ulla, she also needs charm, but according to Rabbi Yochanan, he does not care about her shame.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a widow from betrothal cannot sell her ketubah without a court.
Ulla answers that the reason is due to charm (חינא), meaning the widow needs to appear attractive to potential buyers.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the reason is because a man does not want his wife to be shamed in court.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions.
The Gemara explains that the difference is a divorced woman: according to Ulla she also needs charm, but according to Rabbi Yochanan the husband does not care about her shame.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah regarding a divorced woman
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah regarding a divorced woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's view from the Mishnah which states that a divorced woman may only sell in court. According to Rabbi Yochanan, this is fine because he does not care about her shame, but according to Ulla, she also needs charm, so why is she restricted? The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's view from the Mishnah that a divorced woman may only sell in court, arguing that if charm is the reason, she too needs it.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a divorced woman may not sell without court.

items.text: Objection from the first clause of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Objection from the first clause of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if it is Rabbi Shimon, then the first clause of the Mishnah already taught that a widow from betrothal may not sell without a court, so why repeat the case of a divorced woman? The Gemara explains that one might have thought that a divorced woman, whose charm is greater, would require charm, so the Mishnah teaches that she too is restricted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, then the first clause already taught that a widow from betrothal may not sell without a court, so why repeat the case of a divorced woman?
The Gemara answers that one might have thought that a divorced woman, whose charm is greater, would require charm, so the Mishnah teaches that she too is restricted.

items.text: Support from the phrase 'all who have no sustenance'
items.text_en: Support from the phrase 'all who have no sustenance'
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Ulla from the Mishnah's phrase 'all who have no sustenance', suggesting it includes a divorced woman. However, it is rejected: it refers to a 'divorced and not divorced' woman, as per Rabbi Zeira, where the husband is still liable for her sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Ulla by citing the Mishnah's phrase 'all who have no sustenance', asking whether it includes a divorced woman.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that the phrase refers to a 'divorced and not divorced' woman, as per Rabbi Zeira, where the husband is still liable for her sustenance.

items.text: Challenge from the law of heirs selling without court
items.text_en: Challenge from the law of heirs selling without court
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla from a baraita that states heirs may sell the ketubah without a court, just as the widow could. According to Rabbi Yochanan, this is consistent because the husband does not want his heirs to be shamed either. But according to Ulla, what charm is there for heirs? Ulla explains the case is when the heir is a daughter or sister, who also need charm.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla from a baraita that allows heirs to sell the ketubah without court, asking what charm (חֵן) exists for heirs.
Ulla explains that the baraita refers to a case where the heir is a daughter or sister, who also need charm (חֵן) to find a husband.

items.text: Mishnah: Partial sale of ketubah and the divorced woman
items.text_en: Mishnah: Partial sale of ketubah and the divorced woman
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a woman sold, mortgaged, or gave away part of her ketubah, she may not sell the remainder except in court. The Sages say she may sell even four or five times. She may sell for sustenance without a court, writing 'I sold for sustenance'. A divorced woman may only sell in court.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the rule that a woman who sold part of her ketubah may only sell the remainder in court, with the Sages permitting multiple sales, and a divorced woman restricted to court sales.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author as Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Mishnah's author as Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Shimon, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir says that if a woman sold or mortgaged her ketubah, she loses her sustenance, while Rabbi Shimon says even if she sold only half, she loses her sustenance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir says a woman who sold or mortgaged her ketubah loses her sustenance, while Rabbi Shimon says even selling half suffices to lose sustenance.

items.text: Debate on the principle of partial money being like all money
items.text_en: Debate on the principle of partial money being like all money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon holds that partial money is not like all money, while the Rabbis hold it is. But a baraita shows the opposite: regarding a bogeret (matured girl), Rabbi Meir disqualifies her due to partial virginity, while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon validate her. The Gemara resolves that the dispute there is based on scriptural interpretation, not the principle of partiality.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon holds that partial money is not like all money, while the Rabbis hold it is.
The Gemara objects that a baraita shows the opposite: regarding a bogeret (matured girl), Rabbi Meir disqualifies her due to partial virginity, while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon validate her.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute there is based on scriptural interpretation: Rabbi Meir derives from the verses that a 'בתולה' (virgin) includes even partial virginity, but 'בתוליה' (her virginity) requires all virginity.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold that 'בתולה' (virgin) implies completeness, but 'בתוליה' (her virginity) includes even partial virginity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah interpretation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the phrase 'in her virginity' from the Mishnah to mean that all her virginity signs must be intact, whether she had intercourse in the usual way or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the Mishnah's phrase 'בבתוליה' (in her virginity) to require that all signs of virginity be intact, whether intercourse was performed in the usual manner or not.

items.text: Case of a widow seizing a cup for ketubah
items.text_en: Case of a widow seizing a cup for ketubah
items.desc_en: A woman seized a silver cup for her ketubah and demanded sustenance. Rava ruled that the orphans must provide sustenance, disregarding Rabbi Shimon's opinion that partial payment is not like full payment.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case of a woman who seized a silver cup for her ketubah.
The woman demanded sustenance from the orphans.
Rava ruled that the orphans must provide sustenance, disregarding Rabbi Shimon's opinion that partial payment is not like full payment.

items.text: Inquiry about oath and announcement for a widow selling without court
items.text_en: Inquiry about oath and announcement for a widow selling without court
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rava asks Rav Yosef whether a widow who sells without court needs an oath. Rav Yosef clarifies that the question of an announcement (הכרזה) is not needed, citing Rabbi Zeira's ruling that a widow who appraises for herself does nothing. The Gemara analyzes the case and concludes that she needs an oath but not an announcement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rava sends a query to Rav Yosef asking whether a widow who sells property without a court requires an oath.
The Gemara interjects: should you also ask about the need for an announcement (הכרזה)?
Rav Yosef replies that the question of an announcement is unnecessary, citing Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav Nachman that a widow who appraises for herself has done nothing.
The Gemara objects: if the case involved an announcement, why would she have done nothing?
The Gemara resolves: rather, it must be without an announcement, and for herself she has done nothing, but for others her sale is valid.
The Gemara rejects this: actually, it is with an announcement, and they ask her 'who appraised for you?'
The Gemara brings a supporting story of a man who appraised orphans' property for himself and was questioned by Rabbi Ammi.
The Gemara concludes the halacha (הלכה): she requires an oath but does not require an announcement (הכרזה).

items.text: Mishnah: Widow selling for more or less than value
items.text_en: Mishnah: Widow selling for more or less than value
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a widow sells land worth 200 zuz for 100, or 100 for 200, her ketubah is collected. If she sells land worth 101 for 100, the sale is void, even if she offers to return the extra. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the sale stands if she leaves a significant portion. If she sells to multiple buyers, only the last sale is void.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if a widow sells land worth 200 zuz for 100, or 100 for 200, her ketubah is collected.
The Tanna Kamma rules that if she sells land worth 101 zuz for 100, the sale is void, even if she offers to return the extra dinar.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the sale stands if she leaves a significant portion of the field (9 kav for a field, half kav for a garden, or a beit rova according to Rabbi Akiva).
The Mishnah concludes that if she sells to multiple buyers, only the last sale (where the price was short) is void, and all previous sales stand.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's logic
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's logic
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why selling for 200 when it is worth 100 is invalid (since she caused a loss), but selling for 100 when it is worth 200 is also invalid (since she gained). Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha begins to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why selling for 200 when it is worth 100 is invalid (since she caused a loss), but selling for 100 when it is worth 200 is also invalid (since she gained).

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha begins to answer the Gemara's question.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Baraita
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that if the shaliach adds an extra coin, the entire sum goes to the shaliach, while Rabbi Yosei says they divide it. This sets up the dispute about the shaliach's authority.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah by noting that Rabbi [Yehuda] taught that the entire sum goes to the owner, and cites a Baraita to substantiate.
The Baraita specifies the dispute: if the agent adds an extra coin, Rabbi Yehuda says all goes to the agent, Rabbi Yosei says they divide.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Yosei's Position
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Yosei's Position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: another baraita has Rabbi Yosei saying the entire sum goes to the principal. Rami bar Chama resolves this by distinguishing between an item with a fixed price and one without.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita has Rabbi Yosei saying the entire sum goes to the principal, contradicting the earlier baraita where he says they divide.

Rami bar Chama resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an item with a fixed price (קִצְבָה) and one without: when the item has a fixed price, they divide; when it has no fixed price, the entire sum goes to the principal.

items.text: Rav Pappa's Halakhic Ruling
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's Halakhic Ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that for an item with a fixed price, they divide; for an item without a fixed price, the entire sum goes to the principal. The Gemara notes this is merely a restatement of the earlier resolution.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that for an item with a fixed price (דבר שיש לו קצבה), the parties divide; for an item without a fixed price (דבר שאין לו קצבה), the entire sum goes to the principal.
The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa's ruling is merely a restatement of the earlier resolution (שינוייא דשנינן שינוייא הוא), not a novel teaching.

items.text: New Inquiry: Adding Quantity
items.text_en: New Inquiry: Adding Quantity
items.desc_en: A new question is raised: if the principal said 'buy me a litra' and the shaliach bought a kor, does the shaliach acquire the litra as an addition to his instructions, or is he overstepping entirely, acquiring nothing?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new inquiry: if the principal said 'buy me a litra' and the agent bought a kor, does the agent acquire the litra as an addition to his instructions, or is he overstepping entirely, acquiring nothing?

items.text: Proof from a Ma'aseh with Guests
items.text_en: Proof from a Ma'aseh with Guests
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod cites a case: the householder said 'give them one piece,' the shaliach said 'take two,' and the guests took three. The Gemara analyzes whether the shaliach is adding to or overstepping his instructions, concluding that the case is where the shaliach added his own intent.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod citing Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod citing Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod cites a case from Ravina: the householder said 'give them one piece,' the shaliach said 'take two,' and the guests took three; all three parties committed מעילה (misuse of consecrated property).

The Gemara argues: if the shaliach is 'adding to his words,' then the householder's liability is explained; but if he is 'overstepping his words,' the householder should be exempt based on the rule that a shaliach who deviates bears liability.
The Gemara resolves that the shaliach explicitly added 'one from the householder's intent and one from mine,' so he was both adding and staying within his agency, reconciling the case.

items.text: Proof from a Widow's Sale
items.text_en: Proof from a Widow's Sale
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a widow's ketubah was 100 and she sold property worth 100 and a dinar for 100, the sale is void. The Gemara initially interprets this as selling for her 100, but Rav Huna bar Rav Natan explains it is where she sold at a discount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as evidence: if a widow's ketubah was 100 and she sold property worth 100 and a dinar for 100, the sale is void.
The Gemara initially interprets the baraita as selling for her full 100 plus a dinar, yet the sale is void, implying that even a small excess invalidates the sale.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan rejects the interpretation, explaining that the case is where she sold at a discount (אוזיל), not for the full value.

items.text: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that the Mishnah's first clause deals with a case where the woman did not go (to a different place), while the latter clause deals with a case where she did go. It then rejects this, arguing that both clauses deal with a case where she went, and the latter clause teaches that only when she goes with orphans is her sale void, but if she goes on her own, her sale is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that the Mishnah's first clause deals with a case where the woman did not go (to a different place), while the latter clause deals with a case where she did go, citing the Mishnah's example of selling to multiple buyers.

The Gemara rejects the initial assumption, arguing that both clauses deal with a case where she went, and the latter clause teaches that only when she goes with orphans is her sale void, but if she goes on her own, her sale is valid.

items.text: Inference from the first clause
items.text_en: Inference from the first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the first clause that if a woman with a ketubah of 200 sold property worth 100 for 200, or property worth 200 for 100, she has received her ketubah. It then considers a potential concern that we might distinguish between this case and the latter clause, but the Mishnah teaches that there is no such distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the first clause of the Mishnah that if a woman with a ketubah of 200 sold property worth 100 for 200, or property worth 200 for 100, she has received her ketubah.
The Gemara resolves a potential concern that we might distinguish between this case and the latter clause, teaching that there is no such distinction.

items.text: Question about an agent who deviates from instructions
items.text_en: Question about an agent who deviates from instructions
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a different case: if someone told an agent to buy a לִיתְכָּא (a small measure) and he bought a כּוֹרָא (a large measure), it is clearly an addition to his instructions. But if he told him to buy a כּוֹרָא and he bought a לִיתְכָּא, is it considered a deviation? The Gemara presents two possibilities: the agent might say he did what was best for the principal, or the principal might object to having multiple documents.

sub.text: Alternative version of the Gemara's question
sub.text_en: Alternative version of the Gemara's question
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the discussion, stating that the case where an agent is told to buy a לִיתְכָּא (small measure) and buys a כּוֹרָא (large measure) is clearly an addition to his instructions.
The Gemara poses the real question: if the principal told the agent to buy a כּוֹרָא (large measure) and he bought a לִיתְכָּא (small measure), what is the halacha?

The first possibility suggests the agent can claim he acted for the principal's benefit, saying 'I did what was best for you,' since if the principal did not need the money, he could not back out of the deal.
The second possibility counters that the principal may object, saying 'I do not want multiple documents (שטרות) to be recorded against me.'

items.text: Proof from a baraita about a gold dinar
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about a gold dinar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina from Sura brings a proof from a baraita: if someone gave a gold dinar to an agent to bring a חָלוּק (cloak) and the agent brought three cloaks and three טַלִּית (mantles), both the principal and the agent have misused consecrated property. The Gemara explains that this case involves the agent bringing items worth six for three, so the agent added to his instructions, which is why the principal is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina from Sura cites a baraita: if one gave a gold dinar for a cloak and the agent brought three cloaks and three mantles, both principal and agent misused consecrated property.
The Gemara infers: if the agent fulfilled his mission and added to instructions, the principal is liable; if he deviated, why would the principal be liable?
The Gemara resolves: the case is where the agent brought items worth six for three, so he added to the principal's instructions, explaining the principal's liability.

items.text: Objection and resolution from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Objection and resolution from Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the agent brought items worth six for three, why is the agent liable? It then cites Rabbi Yehuda who says that in this case the principal did not misuse, because he can claim he wanted a large cloak and got a small, bad one. The Gemara explains that 'bad' means bad in price, as the principal could say that if the agent had brought a cloak worth six, it would have been worth twelve.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the agent brought items worth six for three, why is the agent liable for misuse (מעילה)?
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the principal did not misuse (מעל), because he can claim he wanted a large cloak and received a small, bad one.
The Gemara explains that 'bad' (רע) means bad in price, as the principal could argue that if the agent had brought a cloak worth six, it would have been worth twelve.

items.text: Supporting inference from the baraita
items.text_en: Supporting inference from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita is precise, as it states that Rabbi Yehuda agrees in the case of קִטְנִית (beans) that both have misused, implying that in the cloak case he disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita's precise wording that Rabbi Yehuda agrees in the case of קִטְנִית (beans) that both have misused, implying that in the cloak case he disagrees.

items.text: Gemara's first question: inferring from the Mishnah's case of legumes
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: inferring from the Mishnah's case of legumes
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to infer a rule from the Mishnah's statement that legumes are sold by the se'ah for a sela and by the kav for a perutah. It questions how this is possible, since if one pays a sela, he should receive more legumes. Rav Pappa explains that the case is where they measure by kav, and the seller says 'a kav for a perutah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to infer a rule from the Mishnah's statement that legumes are sold by the se'ah for a sela and by the kav for a perutah, questioning how this is possible since paying a sela should yield more legumes.
Rav Pappa explains that the case is where they measure by kav, and the seller says 'a kav for a perutah', resolving the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Second attempt: the case of a woman selling her ketubah
items.text_en: Second attempt: the case of a woman selling her ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where a woman with a ketubah of 400 zuz sells portions to different buyers, and the last sale is invalid because the price was too low. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that this applies only to small items (קַטִּינֵי), and the same applies here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as a supporting source: a woman with a 400-zuz ketubah who sells portions to different buyers, where the last sale is invalid because the price was too low.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that the baraita applies only to small items (קַטִּינֵי), and the same principle applies here.

items.text: Dispute: 'to one' – does it exclude two?
items.text_en: Dispute: 'to one' – does it exclude two?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one says 'to one' without specifying, does it mean only one or does it include multiple? Rav Huna says it means only one, while Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna say it includes even a hundred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the dispute: if one explicitly says 'to one and not to two' it is clear, but if one says 'to one' without qualification, what is the law?
Rav Huna rules that 'to one' means only one, excluding two.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna rule that 'to one' includes even two or a hundred.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling: agent's error vs. principal's error
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling: agent's error vs. principal's error
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman is asked about a case where an agent errs. He rules that 'to one' includes even a hundred, but only if the principal himself errs; if the agent errs, the sale is void because the agent was sent to correct, not to damage. The Gemara questions this from the principle that there is no overcharge for land, but Rav Nachman distinguishes between the principal's error and the agent's error.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna ask Rav Nachman about a case where an agent errs.
Rav Nachman rules that 'to one' includes even a hundred, but only if the principal himself errs.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's objection
sub.desc_en: They ask whether the ruling applies even if the agent erred.
Rav Nachman clarifies that his ruling does not apply when the agent errs.
The Gemara objects that there is no overcharge (אונאה) for land, so why should the agent's error void the sale?
Rav Nachman distinguishes: the rule of no overcharge for land applies when the principal errs, but if the agent errs, the sale is void because the agent was sent to correct, not to damage.

items.text: Proof from terumah: agent vs. principal
items.text_en: Proof from terumah: agent vs. principal
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks a proof that there is a difference between an agent and a principal. It cites a Mishnah where an agent who errs in tithing by up to ten percent still produces valid terumah, whereas a principal who errs even by a small amount produces valid terumah. This shows that the agent's error is treated more strictly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source showing that an agent's error is treated differently from the principal's own error.

A mishna is cited: an agent sent to separate תרומה (priestly portion) who errs by up to ten percent still produces valid תרומה, showing the agent's act is measured against the owner's presumed intent.
A baraita contrasts the principal himself: even if he separated as much as one-twentieth, his תרומה is valid, proving the agent is treated more strictly than the principal.

items.text: Return to the baraita: limited to small items
items.text_en: Return to the baraita: limited to small items
items.desc_en: The Gemara again cites the baraita about the woman selling her ketubah, and Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi again explains that it applies only to small items (קַטִּינֵי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita about a woman selling her ketubah to multiple buyers, where the last sale is void, to question whether this proves that a person is particular about having many documents.
Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi answers that the baraita is limited to small tracts of land (קַטִּינֵי) that cannot be sold as a single unit, so it does not prove the general case.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: court's appraisal and the agent's status
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: court's appraisal and the agent's status
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the court's appraisal is off by a sixth, the sale is void; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says it stands, but if they issued a document, even a greater discrepancy is valid. The Gemara asks: in the case of an agent, whose opinion does he follow?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: in the case of an agent, whose opinion does he follow — the Tanna Kamma or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?

items.text: Dispute over the status of the agent
items.text_en: Dispute over the status of the agent
items.desc_en: Rava and Rav Shmuel bar Bisna report conflicting traditions from Rav Nachman: Rava says the agent is like judges (so he cannot buy for himself), while Rav Shmuel bar Bisna says he is like a widow (so he is a single individual, unlike a court). The halakha is decided in favor of the latter view.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports Rav Nachman's ruling that an agent is like judges (דיינין), meaning he cannot buy for himself, excluding a widow who may buy for herself.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna reports a conflicting tradition from Rav Nachman that an agent is like a widow (אלמנה), i.e., a single individual, unlike a court which is many.
The gemara rules that the halakha follows the view that an agent is like a widow.

items.text: Distinction from the case of terumah
items.text_en: Distinction from the case of terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the agent is not like a messenger for terumah, who can deviate within limits. It answers: there, the owner anticipates variation, but here, the agent's error is not anticipated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the agent here is not like a messenger for תרומה (priestly portion), who can deviate within limits and still have his action valid.

The Gemara answers: there, the owner anticipates variation in generosity, so the agent's deviation is within expected bounds; here, the agent's error is not anticipated, so the owner can say 'you should not have erred.'

items.text: The power of the court and the case of orphans dividing property
items.text_en: The power of the court and the case of orphans dividing property
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chanina reports Rav Nachman's ruling that the law follows the Sages. The Gemara questions this, citing Rav Nachman's own statement that a court appoints an appraiser for orphans and they cannot later object, invoking 'the power of the court'. The Gemara resolves: the cases differ—one where the court erred, one where it did not. If no error, the orphans could object only about 'spirits' (unseen defects).

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chanina citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chanina citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chanina reports Rav Nachman's ruling that the law follows the Sages.
The Gemara questions Rav Nachman's ruling, citing his own statement about the power of the court (כֹּחַ בֵּית דִּין) that prevents orphans from objecting to an appraiser's division.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the court erred (טָעוּ) and where it did not; if no error, the orphans could only object about unseen defects (רוּחוֹת).

items.text: Two versions of a story about Rabbi
items.text_en: Two versions of a story about Rabbi
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi and Rav Safra report different versions of a story where Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) attempted to act like the Sages. In one version, he reversed his ruling after Parta's objection; in the other, he never carried it out. The Gemara suggests they dispute whether an error in a Mishnah is reversible, but concludes they only dispute the facts of the story.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) actually ruled like the Sages, but after Parta objected invoking the principle of 'מה כח בית דין יפה' (the power of the court), Rabbi reversed his ruling.
Rav Safra's version differs: Rabbi only sought to act like the Sages but never carried it out after Parta's objection.
The Gemara suggests that the two versions dispute a legal principle: whether an error in a Mishnah (טעה בדבר משנה) is reversible (חוזר) or not.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion and concludes that all agree an error in a Mishnah is reversible; the dispute is merely factual about what happened in the story.

items.text: Liability of a widow or court selling orphan property
items.text_en: Liability of a widow or court selling orphan property
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that both a widow and a court who sell orphan property bear responsibility for defects. The Gemara notes this is obvious for a widow, but the novel point is for a court, lest one think the court is exempt due to 'the power of the court'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that both a widow and a court who sell orphan property bear responsibility for defects.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious, especially regarding the widow.
The Gemara explains that the novel point is about the court, lest one think the court is exempt due to 'the power of the court'.

items.text: Opening statement on court sales
items.text_en: Opening statement on court sales
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one who buys from the court does so with the awareness that a protest may arise, and the Mishnah teaches this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one who buys from the court does so aware that a protest may arise, and the Mishnah teaches this.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's limit
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's limit
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that a court sale is valid even if the price is off by half. Rav Huna bar Yehuda quoting Rav Sheshet sets the limit at half the value.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: up to what amount of deviation is the sale valid?

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheshet answers: up to half (the value).

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheshet answers that the limit is up to half the value.

items.text: Supporting baraita
items.text_en: Supporting baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling that a court sale of an item worth 200 for 100 or vice versa is valid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports this: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that if the court sold 200 worth for 100 or 100 for 200, the sale stands.

items.text: Court sale without announcement
items.text_en: Court sale without announcement
items.desc_en: Amemar quoting Rav Yosef rules that if a court sold without announcement, they are considered to have erred in a Mishnaic matter and must reverse the sale. The Gemara questions this, noting that they certainly erred, and explains that the statement teaches that even the court itself must reverse, not just the agent.

sub.desc_en: Amemar in the name of Rav Yosef rules that a court that sold without announcement is considered to have erred in a Mishnaic matter and must reverse the sale.
The Gemara objects that the court certainly erred, citing the Mishnah that requires a 30-day announcement for orphans' property and a 60-day announcement for consecrated property.
The Gemara explains that without Amemar's statement one might have thought only the agent must reverse, but the court itself need not; Amemar teaches that even the court must reverse.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Amemar from a Mishnah that says if judges undervalue or overvalue by a sixth, the sale is void, implying that if the price is exact, the sale is valid even without announcement. The Gemara deflects by saying the Mishnah refers to a case with announcement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar from a baraita: if judges undervalue by a sixth, the sale is void; if sold at fair value, it stands. Does this imply without announcement? Ameimar deflects: it refers to with announcement.
The Gemara deflects by saying the Mishnah refers to a case with announcement.
