items.text: Refutation of the deflection
items.text_en: Refutation of the deflection
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the deflection by noting that the latter clause of the Mishnah explicitly deals with announcement, so the first clause must be without announcement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this: the latter clause explicitly mentions an announcement, so the first clause must refer to without announcement.

items.text: Resolution: distinction by property type
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction by property type
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between items that require announcement and those that do not. Slaves, movables, and documents do not require announcement due to risk of flight or theft.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between items that require announcement (הכרזה) and those that do not, listing slaves, movables, and documents as exempt due to risk of flight or theft.

items.text: Alternative resolution: time-based distinction
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: time-based distinction
items.desc_en: Another resolution distinguishes between times when announcement is made and times when it is not, such as for taxes, sustenance, and burial, as per the Nehardeans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution distinguishing between times when announcement is made and times when it is not.
The Nehardeans state that for taxes, sustenance, and burial, property is sold without announcement.

items.text: Another alternative: location-based distinction
items.text_en: Another alternative: location-based distinction
items.desc_en: A third resolution distinguishes by location, citing Rav Nachman that Nehardea never used an iggeret bikoret. Rav Yosef bar Minyomei explains this is because they were called 'consumers of announced property.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a third resolution: the dispute depends on location — whether the court is in a place that announces sales or not.
Rav Nachman testifies that Nehardea never used an איגרת ביקורת (announcement document), supporting the location-based distinction.
The Gemara speculates that the reason Nehardea did not announce was because they were experts in valuation.

Rav Yosef bar Minyomei rejects the speculation and explains that the true reason is that Nehardeans were called 'consumers of announced property,' implying they would buy property only after it was announced elsewhere.

items.text: Sale of orphans' movables
items.text_en: Sale of orphans' movables
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel says orphans' movables are appraised and sold immediately. Rav Chisda quoting Avimi says they are sold in markets. The Gemara reconciles: one refers to a nearby market, the other to a distant one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that orphans' movables are appraised and sold immediately.
Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi says they are sold in markets.
The Gemara resolves that the two rulings do not conflict: one refers to a nearby market, the other to a distant one.

items.text: Rav Kahana's delay of orphan's beer
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's delay of orphan's beer
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana delayed selling an orphan's beer until the festival to get a better price, despite potential depreciation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana held wine belonging to an orphan; he delayed selling until the festival to get a better price, despite some depreciation.

items.text: Ravina's question about transporting orphan's wine
items.text_en: Ravina's question about transporting orphan's wine
items.desc_en: Ravina asked Rav Ashi if he could transport an orphan's wine along with his own to a port. Rav Ashi ruled it was permitted, as it is no better than his own.

sub.text: Story about Ravina and Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Story about Ravina and Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Ravina held wine belonging to an orphan relative; he asked Rav Ashi if he could transport it with his own wine, and Rav Ashi permitted it.
Rav Ashi permits it, ruling that the orphan's wine is no better than Ravina's own.

items.text: Mishnah: Ketubah rights of mi'un, secondary, and aylonit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ketubah rights of mi'un, secondary, and aylonit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a mi'un woman, a secondary wife, and an aylonit have no ketubah, no fruit usufruct, no sustenance, and no worn garments. However, if a man married her initially as an aylonit, she has a ketubah. An almanah to a high priest, etc., have a ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a mi'un woman, a secondary wife, and an aylonit have no ketubah, no fruit usufruct, no sustenance, and no worn garments.
The Mishnah adds an exception: if a man married her initially as an aylonit, she does have a ketubah.
The Mishnah lists other women who do have a ketubah: an almanah to a high priest, etc.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on mi'un
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on mi'un
items.desc_en: Rav teaches that a minor who leaves via get has no ketubah, and certainly a mi'un woman. Shmuel teaches that a mi'un woman has no ketubah, but one who leaves via get does. Shmuel's reasoning is that a mi'un woman does not disqualify from the priesthood or from brothers, while a get does. A mi'un woman need not wait three months.

sub.desc_en: Rav teaches that a minor who leaves via a get (bill of divorce) has no ketubah, and certainly a mi'un (refusal) woman has none.
Shmuel teaches that a mi'un woman has no ketubah, but one who leaves via a get does have a ketubah.
The Gemara notes that Shmuel is consistent with his own earlier statement distinguishing mi'un from get regarding ketubah.
Shmuel explains that a mi'un woman does not disqualify from the brothers (yibbum) or from the priesthood, while a get does disqualify, justifying the difference in ketubah.
Shmuel adds that a mi'un woman need not wait three months before remarrying, unlike a woman divorced by get.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that a woman who leaves through a get must wait three months, since this was already taught in the Mishnah about mi'un. It answers that the case of a woman who leaves through a get was not previously taught, so it is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to teach that a woman who leaves through a get must wait three months, since this was already taught in the Mishnah about mi'un.
The Gemara answers that the case of a woman who leaves through a get was not previously taught, so it is necessary to state it here.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about the status of a minor's marriage
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about the status of a minor's marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree about the legal status of a minor's marriage. Rabbi Eliezer holds it is insignificant, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds it is fully valid except that she leaves through mi'un.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute, citing Rabbi Eliezer's position that a minor's marriage is essentially void, with no husband's rights, except that she needs mi'un (formal refusal).
Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the minor's marriage is fully valid, granting the husband all rights, except that she leaves through mi'un.

items.text: Aligning Rav and Shmuel with the Tannaim
items.text_en: Aligning Rav and Shmuel with the Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav follows Rabbi Eliezer and Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehoshua. It clarifies that all agree on Rabbi Eliezer's position; the dispute is only regarding Rabbi Yehoshua's view. Shmuel fully accepts it, while Rav limits it to the minor's property rights over her husband, not the reverse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav follows Rabbi Eliezer and Shmuel follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Gemara clarifies that all agree on Rabbi Eliezer's position; the dispute is only regarding Rabbi Yehoshua's view.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel fully accepts Rabbi Yehoshua's view, while Rav limits it to the minor's property rights over her husband, not the reverse.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction between types of property
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction between types of property
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya reports in Shmuel's name that a woman who leaves through mi'un loses only melog property but not iron-sheep property. Rav Pappa questions this, analyzing whether it applies to a minor who performs mi'un, an aylonit, or a shniya, concluding it applies to a shniya as a rabbinic penalty.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chiyya to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya reports in Shmuel's name that the rule about a woman who leaves through mi'un losing only melog property applies to melog property, but she retains iron-sheep property.

Rav Pappa questions which case Shmuel's distinction applies to, first considering a minor who performs mi'un and showing that the distinction is irrelevant because she takes both types if they exist and loses both if they do not.
Rav Pappa next considers an aylonit, showing that the distinction would be reversed: she should take melog property (which is in her domain) but not iron-sheep property (which is not in her domain).

Rav Pappa concludes that Shmuel's distinction applies to a shniya (a woman forbidden to her husband by a secondary incest prohibition), where the rabbis penalized her by taking her melog property and giving him her iron-sheep property.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's inference about a cloak
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's inference about a cloak
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi infers from Rav Kahana's statement that if a husband brought a cloak as melog property, it becomes principal and he cannot use it until it wears out. Rav Nachman disagrees, holding it is merely produce.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi infers from Rav Kahana's statement that if a husband brought a cloak as melog property, it becomes principal (קרנא) and he cannot use it until it wears out.
The Gemara objects that Rav Nachman holds the cloak is merely produce (פירא), not principal, and resolves that Rav Nachman disagrees with Rav Shimi bar Ashi's inference.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on additional ketubah and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on additional ketubah and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that women who leave without a ketubah still receive the additional amount (tosefet), but not the basic 200 zuz. A baraita supports this, distinguishing between those who leave without a ketubah (who lose both) and those who leave due to a bad reputation (who take what is before them). Rav Huna adds that a woman who committed adultery does not lose her ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that certain women have no ketubah.
Shmuel rules that the Mishnah's denial of ketubah applies only to the basic 200 zuz, but the additional amount (תוספת) is still given.
A baraita supports Shmuel: women who leave without a ketubah (e.g., the מְמָאֶנֶת) lose the basic 200 zuz but keep the תוספת.
The baraita distinguishes: women who leave without a ketubah due to transgression lose both basic and תוספת, while those leaving due to a bad reputation take what is before them.
The baraita supports Rav Huna's ruling that a woman who committed adultery (זִינְּתָה) does not lose her ketubah.

items.text: Dispute about בלאות after adultery
items.text_en: Dispute about בלאות after adultery
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Nachman that if a woman committed adultery, she forfeits her worn-out garments (בלאות). Rav Nachman objects: if she committed adultery, did her garments commit adultery? The Tanna then teaches that she does not forfeit them.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Nachman that if a woman committed adultery, she forfeits her worn-out garments (בלאות).
Rav Nachman objects: if she committed adultery, did her garments commit adultery?
The Tanna then teaches that she does not forfeit them.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's attribution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's attribution
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the first teaching is the opinion of Rabbi Menachem the anonymous, but the Sages say that if she committed adultery, she does not forfeit her בלאות.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the first teaching is the opinion of Rabbi Menachem the anonymous, but the Sages say that if she committed adultery, she does not forfeit her בלאות (property rights).

items.text: Dispute about an אילונית and an אלמנה
items.text_en: Dispute about an אילונית and an אלמנה
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where a man married a woman with a condition. Rav Huna distinguishes between an אילונית (a woman who cannot bear children) and an אלמנה (widow): an אילונית is a partial woman, so if he knew, she has a ketubah; if not, she has none. A widow is a full woman, so she always has a ketubah. Rav Yehuda disagrees, saying both are partial women, and only if he knew does she have a ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, introducing the case of a man who married a woman with a condition.

Rav Huna distinguishes between an אילונית (ailonit) and an אלמנה (widow): an אילונית is a partial woman, so if he knew, she has a ketubah; if not, she has none. A widow is a full woman, so she always has a ketubah.
Rav Yehuda disagrees, saying both are partial women, and only if he knew does she have a ketubah.

items.text: Objection to Rav Huna from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Huna from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought: if he married her assuming she was a certain type and she was found to be that type, she has a ketubah. This implies that in a standard case (סתמא), she has no ketubah. The Gemara reinterprets the baraita to avoid this implication, but another baraita explicitly states that if he married her without specification (סתם), she has no ketubah. This is a refutation of Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if he married her with a presumption and she was found to be that type, she has a ketubah, implying that in a standard case (סתמא) she has no ketubah.

The Gemara rejects the implication, reinterpreting the baraita: do not say that in a standard case she has no ketubah; rather, say that if he married her presuming she was not so and she was found to be so, she has no ketubah.
The Gemara objects: if in a standard case she does have a ketubah, the baraita should have taught that case, and all the more so the case where he married her knowingly.

A second baraita explicitly states: if he married her knowingly and she was found to be so, she has a ketubah; if he married her without specification (סתם), she has no ketubah. This is a conclusive refutation of Rav Huna.

items.text: Defense of Rav Huna
items.text_en: Defense of Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna was misled by the Mishnah's formulation. He thought that since the Mishnah distinguishes regarding an אילונית but not regarding an אלמנה, it implies that an אלמנה always has a ketubah even in a standard case. But in truth, the Mishnah only mentions the widow in the context of the dispute about the אילונית.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge against Rav Huna by explaining that he was misled by the Mishnah's formulation: he thought the Mishnah's distinction regarding an אילונית (a woman with male-like characteristics) but not regarding an אלמנה (widow) implied that a widow always has a ketubah even in a standard case, but in truth the Mishnah only mentions the widow in the context of the dispute about the אילונית.

items.text: Mishnah: Supporting a daughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: Supporting a daughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a man marries a woman and stipulates to support her daughter for five years, he is obligated. If she marries another, the new husband is also obligated. The first husband must send support to where the daughter is. They cannot both support her together; one provides food, the other pays its value. If she marries, the husband provides food, and the others pay its value. If they die, the daughters are supported from unencumbered property, but the woman from encumbered property, as she is a creditor. The prudent would write: on condition that I support your daughter for five years while you are with me.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the heading 'We return to you, the chapter of the widow who is supported'.
The Mishnah states that if a man marries a woman and stipulates to support her daughter for five years, he is obligated.
The Mishnah rules that if she marries another, the new husband is also obligated, and the first husband must send support to where the daughter is.
The Mishnah states that the two husbands cannot both support her together; one provides food, the other pays its value.

The Mishnah rules that if she marries, the husband provides food, and the others pay its value; if they die, the daughters are supported from unencumbered property, but the woman from encumbered property as a creditor.
The Mishnah concludes that the prudent would write: on condition that I support your daughter for five years while you are with me.

items.text: Gemara: The force of a verbal obligation
items.text_en: Gemara: The force of a verbal obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about one who says 'I owe you a maneh.' Rabbi Yochanan says he is obligated, Reish Lakish says he is exempt. The Gemara clarifies the case: it is where he said 'I owe you a maneh by a document.' Rabbi Yochanan holds that the mention of a document is as strong as saying 'you are my witnesses,' while Reish Lakish disagrees. The Gemara then attempts to prove from the Mishnah that a verbal obligation is binding, but the proof is not fully resolved.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens by citing a dispute: one who says 'I owe you a maneh' — Rabbi Yochanan says he is obligated, Reish Lakish says he is exempt.
The gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If he said 'you are my witnesses,' why would Reish Lakish exempt? If he did not say 'you are my witnesses,' why would Rabbi Yochanan obligate?

The gemara answers: it is where he said 'I owe you a maneh by a document'; Rabbi Yochanan holds that the mention of a document is as strong as saying 'you are my witnesses,' while Reish Lakish disagrees.
The gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that a verbal obligation is binding, asking: does the Mishnah not refer to a similar case where no document was written?

items.text: Opening Gemara: Acquisition by speech in שטרי פסיקתא
items.text_en: Opening Gemara: Acquisition by speech in שטרי פסיקתא
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to documents of fixed marriage gifts (שטרי פסיקתא), citing Rav Giddel's statement that when a father specifies amounts for his son and daughter and they stand and betroth, they acquire by mere speech.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to documents of fixed marriage gifts (שטרי פסיקתא), citing Rav Giddel's statement.
Rav Giddel reports in Rav's name that when a father specifies amounts for his son and daughter and they stand and betroth, they acquire by mere speech.

items.text: Challenge from a written promise to a priest
items.text_en: Challenge from a written promise to a priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a challenge: if one writes to a priest 'I owe you five sela,' he must pay, but his son is not redeemed. The Gemara distinguishes because the debt is Torah-mandated, and the writing only clarifies the priest. Ulla explains that Torah law considers the son redeemed upon payment, but the rabbis decreed against redemption by document to prevent confusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that a written promise can effect acquisition, citing a case where one writes to a priest 'I owe you five sela' — the priest collects, but the son is not redeemed.
The Gemara distinguishes the case because the debt is Torah-mandated, and the writing merely clarifies which priest receives payment.
Ulla resolves that by Torah law the son is redeemed upon payment, but the rabbis decreed against redemption by document to prevent confusion with standard debt documents.

items.text: Rava's citation of a Tannaitic dispute about guarantors
items.text_en: Rava's citation of a Tannaitic dispute about guarantors
items.desc_en: Rava cites a Tannaitic dispute: a guarantor who signs after the document's sealing collects from unencumbered property. Rabbi Yishmael rules he collects from unencumbered property, but Ben Nannas argues he collects from neither, comparing to someone who says 'let him go, I'll pay'—the guarantor is exempt because the loan was not made on his reliance.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a Tannaitic dispute: a guarantor who signs after the document's sealing collects from unencumbered property.
Rabbi Yishmael rules that the guarantor collects from unencumbered property.
Ben Nannas objects that the guarantor collects from neither unencumbered nor encumbered property.
Ben Nannas explains his position with a parable: one who says 'let him go, I'll pay' is exempt because the loan was not made on his reliance.

items.text: Attribution of positions to Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Attribution of positions to Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yishmael and Reish Lakish holds like Ben Nannas, but notes that regarding Ben Nannas's position, everyone agrees (no dispute).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yochanan's position aligns with Rabbi Yishmael and Reish Lakish's position aligns with Ben Nannas.
The Gemara clarifies that regarding Ben Nannas's position, there is no dispute among all authorities.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is specifically according to Rabbi Yishmael's opinion. Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yishmael, while Reish Lakish argues that Rabbi Yishmael's leniency only applies where the biblical lien is involved, but not here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is specifically within Rabbi Yishmael's opinion: Rabbi Yochanan holds like Rabbi Yishmael, while Reish Lakish limits Rabbi Yishmael's leniency to cases where the biblical lien (שיעבודא דאורייתא) applies, not here.

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement in the name of Rav
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement in the name of Rav
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel quotes Rav: When a father says 'How much will you give to your son?' and 'How much will you give to your daughter?' and they stand and betroth, these are matters acquired by speech.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel transmits Rav's statement that when a father promises amounts for his son and daughter and they then betroth, these commitments are acquired by speech alone.

items.text: Rava's limitation and the Gemara's objection
items.text_en: Rava's limitation and the Gemara's objection
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that Rav's ruling applies only to a minor daughter, where the father benefits from the betrothal, but not to an adult daughter. The Gemara objects, citing Rav himself who applied the ruling even to an adult daughter, explaining that the benefit is the mutual goodwill between the families.

sub.desc_en: Rava suggests that Rav's ruling applies only to a minor daughter (נערה), where the father receives benefit from the betrothal, but not to an adult daughter (בוגרת), where he receives no benefit.
The Gemara objects, citing Rav himself who applied the ruling even to an adult daughter, explaining that the benefit is the mutual goodwill (הנאה) between the families.

items.text: Whether these matters may be written
items.text_en: Whether these matters may be written
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether these verbal commitments may be written down. Rav Ashi says they may not. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita where wise men would write such conditions, but resolves that 'write' means 'say'. The Gemara then supports this usage from a mishna where 'write' is interpreted as 'say'.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether these verbal commitments may be written down, and Rav Ashi responds that they may not.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where wise men would write such conditions, and resolves that 'write' means 'say'.
The Gemara supports the interpretation that 'write' means 'say' by citing a mishna where 'write' is interpreted as 'say' by Rabbi Chiyya.

items.text: Attempted proof from betrothal documents
items.text_en: Attempted proof from betrothal documents
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that such commitments can be written from the rule that betrothal documents may only be written with both parties' consent. The Gemara deflects, saying this refers to actual betrothal documents, citing a dispute between Rabba and Ravina versus Rav Pappa and Rav Sherevya about betrothal without the woman's knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that betrothal documents may be written with consent, implying that commitments (שטרי פסיקתא) are also written.

The Gemara deflects, explaining that the baraita refers to actual betrothal documents (שטרי אירוסין ממש), not commitments, citing a dispute between Rabba and Ravina versus Rav Pappa and Rav Sherevya about betrothal without the woman's knowledge.

items.text: Proof from the case of a widow's ketubah
items.text_en: Proof from the case of a widow's ketubah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about daughters and a widow supported from different properties, suggesting a written commitment. The Gemara explains it refers to a formal acquisition (kinyan). It then distinguishes between the widow, who was present at the kinyan, and the daughters, who were not. Further analysis considers a divorced and remarried wife, and ultimately explains that daughters already have a lien by rabbinic enactment, so the kinyan does not add anything.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as a proof: when the husband dies, the daughters are supported from unencumbered property, but the widow is supported from encumbered property because she is like a creditor.
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a case where they performed a formal acquisition (קִנְיָן) from the husband.
The Gemara objects: if there was a kinyan, why should the daughters not also benefit from encumbered property?
The Gemara answers that the kinyan was performed for the widow but not for the daughters.
The Gemara explains the rationale: the widow was present at the time of the kinyan, so it benefits her, but the daughters were not present, so it does not benefit them.
The Gemara objects: we are dealing with a case where the widow was present at the kinyan, but how can that be? It must be a case where he divorced her and remarried her.

The Gemara answers differently: the widow, who does not have a rabbinic lien (תְּנַאי בֵּית דִּין), benefits from the kinyan, but the daughters, who already have a rabbinic lien, do not benefit from the kinyan.
The Gemara objects: does the kinyan actually detract from the daughters' position?

The Gemara resolves: the reason the daughters do not benefit from the kinyan is that since they already have a rabbinic lien, the kinyan is merely a bundle of documents (צְרָרֵי) that does not add anything.

items.text: Rav Chisda's inference about a daughter with her mother
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's inference about a daughter with her mother
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda infers from the mishna that a daughter stays with her mother. The Gemara questions whether this refers to an adult daughter or a minor, citing a story where a minor son was left with his mother and was killed. The Gemara then suggests that if it is a minor, the mishna should have specified 'to the place where she is'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda infers from the mishna that a daughter stays with her mother.
The Gemara questions whether Rav Chisda refers to an adult daughter or a minor daughter.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a minor son left with his mother who was killed, suggesting the mishna may refer to a minor due to a similar concern.
The Gemara resolves that if it were a minor, the mishna should have specified 'to the place where she is', implying it refers to an adult daughter.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's phrase 'to the place of her mother'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's phrase 'to the place of her mother'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'to the place of her mother' and concludes that a daughter always goes with her mother, whether she is an adult or a minor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the purpose of the mishna's phrase 'to the place of her mother'.
The Gemara concludes that a daughter always lives with her mother, whether she is an adult or a minor.
The Gemara transitions to the next part of the mishna, citing the rule that two men may not jointly say they will support the girl together.

items.text: Case of the mill rental and analogy to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Case of the mill rental and analogy to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: A story is told of a man who rented a mill and later bought his own. Ravina thought this paralleled the Mishnah's case of two people supporting one woman, but Rav Avira rejected the analogy because a woman has only one stomach, while the mill can be used for multiple customers. The Gemara adds that if the renter has no other grinding work, the owner cannot force him to buy his own mill, but if he does, it is considered 'middat Sedom' and he can be compelled.

sub.desc_en: A story is told of a man who rented a mill for grinding; when the owner became rich and bought his own mill, he demanded cash payment, but the renter insisted on continuing to grind as originally agreed.
Ravina thought to compare this case to the Mishnah where two men support one woman, suggesting the renter should pay cash instead of grinding.
Rav Avira rejected the analogy because a woman has only one stomach, while the mill can be used for multiple customers, so the renter can continue grinding and the owner can sell the ground grain.

The Gemara rules that if the renter has no other grinding work, the owner cannot force cash payment, but if the renter does have other work, it is considered 'middat Sedom' and he can be compelled to pay cash.

items.text: Mishnah: Widow's right to stay in husband's or father's house
items.text_en: Mishnah: Widow's right to stay in husband's or father's house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a widow says she does not want to move from her husband's house, the heirs must support her there and provide lodging according to her honor. If she says she wants to go to her father's house, the heirs can condition support on her living with them, unless she is young and they are young, in which case she is supported in her father's house.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: a widow who refuses to leave her husband's house is supported there by the heirs, who must provide lodging according to her honor.
The Mishnah states the second case: a widow who wishes to return to her father's house may be denied support by the heirs unless she lives with them.
The Mishnah concludes with an exception: if the widow is young and the heirs are young, she is supported in her father's house.

items.text: Baraita: Widow's usage rights and the condition in the ketubah
items.text_en: Baraita: Widow's usage rights and the condition in the ketubah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a widow may use the dwelling, slaves, bedding, and vessels as she did during her husband's lifetime, based on the ketubah clause that she dwell in his house and be supported. Rav Yosef adds that 'in my house' excludes a dilapidated house.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a widow may continue using the dwelling, slaves, bedding, and vessels as she did during her husband's lifetime, based on the ketubah clause that she dwell in his house and be supported.
Rav Yosef adds that the clause 'in my house' excludes a dilapidated house (בִּקְתִּי), meaning the widow is not entitled to a ruined dwelling.

items.text: Rav Nachman: Orphans who sold the widow's dwelling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: Orphans who sold the widow's dwelling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that if orphans sold the widow's dwelling, their sale is void. The Gemara distinguishes this from Rabbi Asi's ruling about orphans selling diminished assets, because here the dwelling was encumbered to her from her husband's lifetime.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that if orphans sold the widow's dwelling, their sale is void.
The Gemara questions why this ruling differs from Rabbi Asi's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that orphans who sold diminished assets have a valid sale.
The Gemara distinguishes: there the assets were not encumbered to her from her husband's lifetime, but here the dwelling was encumbered to her from her husband's lifetime.

items.text: Abaye: Collapsed dwelling and the question of renovation
items.text_en: Abaye: Collapsed dwelling and the question of renovation
items.desc_en: Abaye states that if the widow's dwelling collapsed, the heirs are not obligated to rebuild it, and even if she offers to build it herself, they do not listen to her. Abaye then raises a question about the case where she renovated it, which remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states a received tradition: if the widow's dwelling collapsed, the heirs are not obligated to rebuild it.
A baraita supports Abaye's statement and adds that even if the widow offers to rebuild it herself, the court does not listen to her.
Abaye raises an unresolved question: what is the law if the widow renovated the dwelling herself?

items.text: Discussion of the widow's support and the blessing of a crowded house
items.text_en: Discussion of the widow's support and the blessing of a crowded house
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that if the widow says she cannot move, the heirs give her support where she is, citing Rav Huna that the blessing of a house is in its crowding. It then lists examples of the sages' language for blessing, wealth, and healing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the widow says she cannot move from her husband's house, the heirs must support her there.
The Gemara asks: should the heirs give her support according to the blessing of the house where she lives?
The Gemara cites Rav Huna's principle that the blessing of a house is in its crowding, supporting the idea that the widow's presence adds blessing.
The Gemara asks: should the heirs give her support according to the blessing of the house?
The Gemara answers: indeed, that is the case.
Rav Huna states that the language of the sages for blessing, wealth, and healing is distinct, and the example of blessing is the one just mentioned.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a clever buyer who hires the seller's place to acquire produce, illustrating the sages' language for wealth.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah forbidding chewing wheat and placing it on a wound on Passover because it leavens, illustrating the sages' language for healing.

items.text: Rabbi's deathbed instructions
items.text_en: Rabbi's deathbed instructions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on his deathbed instructs his sons to honor their mother, keep the lamp, table, and bed in their places because he would visit home every Friday evening. He also praises his servants Yosef Chofni and Shimon Efrati. He then tells the Sages not to eulogize him in the cities.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's deathbed instructions to his sons: honor their mother, keep the lamp, table, and bed in their places, and appoint Yosef Chofni and Shimon Efrati as his attendants.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi needed to command honoring his mother, since it is already a Torah commandment, and suggests she was his stepmother (אשת אב).
The Gemara answers that honoring a stepmother is also a Torah obligation, citing a baraita that derives it from the verse, but notes the extra 'vav' includes an older brother.
The Gemara resolves that the Torah obligation applies only during the parent's lifetime, but after death the command is not biblical, so Rabbi's instruction was necessary.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi instructed to keep the lamp, table, and bed in their places.

The Gemara answers that Rabbi would visit home every Friday evening, and tells a story about a neighbor who knocked and was told to be quiet because Rabbi was there, after which Rabbi stopped coming to avoid slander against earlier righteous people.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi's statement about Yosef Chofni and Shimon Efrati serving him after death referred to this world.
The Gemara answers that when they saw their biers preceded his, they understood he meant the World to Come.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi said this to prevent people from thinking the servants had some merit of their own, rather than that Rabbi's merit protected them.
The baraita continues: Rabbi then summoned the Sages and instructed them not to eulogize him in the cities.

items.text: Rabbi's instructions for burial and leadership
items.text_en: Rabbi's instructions for burial and leadership
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi instructs that he should not be eulogized in towns, that his son Shimon is wise, his son Gamliel is the nasi, and Chanina bar Chama should sit at the head. The Gemara begins to analyze these instructions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi instructs that his son Shimon is wise, his son Gamliel is the nasi, and Chanina bar Chama should sit at the head.

items.text: Reason for not eulogizing in towns
items.text_en: Reason for not eulogizing in towns
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi's instruction not to eulogize him in towns was initially thought to be due to the burden, but when people saw that eulogies in cities drew crowds, they understood it was for honor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that Rabbi's instruction not to eulogize him in towns was due to the burden (טִרְחָא) on the townspeople.
Seeing that people eulogized in large cities and everyone came, the Gemara concludes that Rabbi's instruction was actually due to honor (יְקָרָא).

items.text: Reason for thirty-day delay in establishing yeshiva
items.text_en: Reason for thirty-day delay in establishing yeshiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the thirty-day delay in establishing the yeshiva was because Rabbi did not want to be considered greater than Moses, for whom Israel mourned thirty days, and then they alternated between mourning and studying for twelve months.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi's instruction to establish a study session after thirty days was because he did not consider himself greater than Moses, citing the verse about the thirty-day mourning for Moses and the subsequent twelve-month period of mixed mourning and study.

items.text: Story of the laundryman at Rabbi's funeral
items.text_en: Story of the laundryman at Rabbi's funeral
items.desc_en: A bat kol declared that all who attend Rabbi's funeral are destined for the World to Come. A laundryman who did not attend later heard this, climbed a roof, fell, and died, and a bat kol declared him also destined for the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: A story is told that on the day of Rabbi's burial, a heavenly voice declared that all who attended were destined for the World to Come, and a bath attendant who missed it later died and was also declared destined for the World to Come.
A laundryman who regularly attended Rabbi but missed the funeral hears the bat kol, climbs a roof, falls, and dies.
A second bat kol declares that even the laundryman is destined for the World to Come.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi's appointment of Shimon and Gamliel
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi's appointment of Shimon and Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi said 'Shimon my son is wise, Gamliel my son is nasi', implying a preference. Levi questions the need for this statement. Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi defends it, citing the verse about Yehoshafat. The Gemara explains that Gamliel did not fill his father's place in wisdom but did in fear of sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of Rabbi's statement 'Shimon my son is wise, Gamliel my son is nasi', asking what he intended to convey.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi meant: 'Even though Shimon my son is wise, Gamliel my son is the nasi' — emphasizing that Gamliel was appointed despite Shimon's greater wisdom.
Levi objects, questioning whether such a statement was necessary at all.
Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi rejects Levi's objection, telling him that the statement was necessary for him and his entire generation.

The Gemara clarifies Levi's difficulty by citing the verse about Yehoshafat giving the kingdom to Yehoram the firstborn, and explains that Gamliel did not fill his father's place in wisdom, unlike Yehoram who filled his father's place.
The Gemara resolves the issue by explaining that although Gamliel did not fill his father's place in wisdom (חכמה), he did fill his place in fear of sin (יראת חטא), justifying Rabbi's appointment.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chanina bar Chama and Levi's departure
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chanina bar Chama and Levi's departure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Chama did not accept the position at the head because Rabbi Apas was older. Rabbi Apas sat at the head, Rabbi Chanina outside, and Levi sat with him. After Rabbi Apas died, Rabbi Chanina took the head, leaving Levi without a companion, so he went to Babylonia. The Gemara considers alternative explanations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rabbi Chanina bar Chama refused the head position because Rabbi Apas was older, so Rabbi Apas sat at the head, Rabbi Chanina outside, and Levi sat with him.

After Rabbi Apas died, Rabbi Chanina took the head, leaving Levi without a companion, so Levi went to Babylonia, and Rav deduced this from the report that a great man arrived in Nehardea and lectured on the crown.
The Gemara objects: perhaps instead Rabbi Chanina died and Rabbi Apas remained seated, and Levi still had no companion and came to Babylonia.
The Gemara answers: if you wish, say that Levi was subordinate to Rabbi Apas, so he would not have left while Rabbi Apas was alive.

Alternatively, since Rabbi said 'Chanina bar Chama shall sit at the head,' the decree must have been fulfilled, as it is written about the righteous: 'You shall decree a word and it shall be established for you.'

items.text: Discussion about Rabbi Chiyya's presence at Rabbi's death
items.text_en: Discussion about Rabbi Chiyya's presence at Rabbi's death
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Chiyya could have been present at Rabbi's death if he died earlier, citing various baraitot about signs of a good death. Rabbi Chiyya explains he cried over Torah and mitzvot. The Gemara resolves the contradiction, and then recounts the dispute between Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Chiyya about preserving Torah, with Rabbi Chiyya describing his method of teaching children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Chiyya could have been present at Rabbi's death if he died earlier, citing Rabbi Chiyya's own statement that he saw Rabbi's grave and wept.
The Gemara adds another contradiction: Rabbi Chiyya said that on the day Rabbi died, the sanctity of the study hall ceased, implying he was alive then.
A baraita is cited describing Rabbi Chiyya visiting Rabbi during his illness and finding him crying, along with a list of signs of a good or bad death.
Rabbi Chiyya explains to Rabbi that he is crying over Torah and mitzvot, not over his own suffering.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by either reversing the earlier assumption or explaining that Rabbi Chiyya was busy with mitzvot and Rabbi did not want to interrupt him.
The Gemara shifts to recount a dispute between Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Chiyya, where Rabbi Chanina boasts that if Torah were forgotten, he could restore it through his pilpul.

Rabbi Chiyya describes his method of ensuring Torah is never forgotten by planting flax, weaving nets, trapping deer, feeding orphans, writing Torah scrolls, and teaching children in a systematic way.
Rabbi praises Rabbi Chiyya's deeds, and when asked if they surpass even his own or his father's, Rabbi responds that such a comparison should never be made.

items.text: Rabbi's final instructions to his sons and his burial place
items.text_en: Rabbi's final instructions to his sons and his burial place
items.desc_en: Rabbi calls his sons: to Shimon he gives the orders of wisdom, to Gamliel the orders of leadership, advising him to act with authority. The Gemara questions this with the verse about honoring Torah scholars, and resolves it by distinguishing private from public conduct. Finally, it discusses Rabbi's burial place, initially in Beit She'arim but moved to Tzippori due to illness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi calls for his younger son Shimon and transmits to him the orders of wisdom.
Rabbi calls for his older son Rabban Gamliel, transmits the orders of leadership, and instructs him to act with authority and strictness toward students.
The Gemara objects: How could Rabbi advise strictness, when the verse commands honoring those who fear God, exemplified by King Yehoshafat who stood and honored Torah scholars?
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: in private one should honor Torah scholars, but in public the leader may act with authority.
A baraita states that Rabbi was buried in Tzippori, though a place was prepared for him in Beit She'arim, and another baraita cites the verse 'צֶדֶק צֶדֶק תִּרְדֹּף' to follow Rabbi to Beit She'arim.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi was originally in Beit She'arim, but when he became ill they moved him to Tzippori, where he died and was buried.

items.text: The death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.text_en: The death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how the Sages decreed a fast and prayed for Rabbi's recovery, but his maidservant, seeing his suffering, prayed for his death. She threw a jug from the roof, startling the Sages into silence, and Rabbi died.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: on the day of Rabbi's death, the Sages decreed a fast and prayed for his recovery.
The Sages decreed that anyone who announces Rabbi's death will be stabbed with a sword.
Rabbi's maidservant went up to the roof and prayed that the earthly beings (the Sages) would overcome the heavenly beings (the angels) in their request for Rabbi's soul.
Seeing Rabbi's repeated suffering when entering the restroom, the maidservant changed her prayer, asking that the heavenly beings overcome the earthly ones.
The maidservant threw a jug from the roof, startling the Sages into silence, and Rabbi died.

items.text: Bar Kappara's eulogy
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's eulogy
items.desc_en: The Sages send Bar Kappara to investigate Rabbi's condition. He finds Rabbi has died, tears his garment, and delivers a eulogy comparing Rabbi to the Ark of the Covenant. When asked directly, he avoids saying Rabbi died.

sub.desc_en: The Sages send Bar Kappara to investigate Rabbi's condition, and he finds that Rabbi has died.

Bar Kappara tears his garment, reverses the tear, and delivers a eulogy comparing Rabbi to the Ark of the Covenant, saying the angels (אֶרְאֶלִּים) overcame the mortals (מְצוּקִים) and the Ark was captured.
The Sages ask Bar Kappara directly whether Rabbi has died.
Bar Kappara avoids stating directly that Rabbi died, saying 'You say it, but I am not saying it.'

items.text: Rabbi's final prayer and heavenly response
items.text_en: Rabbi's final prayer and heavenly response
items.desc_en: At his death, Rabbi raises ten fingers and declares he toiled in Torah without personal benefit. A bat kol responds with a verse from Isaiah, promising peace in his resting place.

sub.desc_en: At his death, Rabbi raises ten fingers toward heaven and declares that he toiled in Torah with all ten fingers and never derived personal benefit even from his little finger.
Rabbi prays that peace be upon his resting place, and a bat kol (heavenly voice) responds with the verse from Isaiah promising peace for those who rest on their beds.

items.text: The reception of the righteous and the wicked
items.text_en: The reception of the righteous and the wicked
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the plural 'מִשְׁכְּבוֹתָם' in the verse, citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada and Rabbi Elazar. They describe how three groups of ministering angels greet the righteous, while three groups of destructive angels greet the wicked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse uses the plural 'מִשְׁכְּבוֹתָם' instead of the singular 'מִשְׁכָּבְךָ'.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada citing Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada citing Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul, who describes how ministering angels greet the righteous at death with the verse 'יָבֹא בְּשָׁלוֹם יָנוּחוּ עַל מִשְׁכְּבוֹתָם'.
Rabbi Elazar elaborates that three groups of ministering angels greet the righteous with verses of peace, while three groups of destructive angels greet the wicked with verses of doom.

items.text: Mishnah: Statute of limitations for ketubah collection
items.text_en: Mishnah: Statute of limitations for ketubah collection
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a widow collects her ketubah indefinitely while in her father's house, but only for 25 years in her husband's house (Rabbi Meir citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel). The Sages reverse the rule: indefinite in the husband's house, 25 years in the father's house. If she dies, her heirs must mention the ketubah within 25 years.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule of Rabbi Meir in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: a widow collects her ketubah indefinitely in her father's house, but only for 25 years in her husband's house, because she spends the equivalent in favors.
The Sages state the opposite: a widow collects indefinitely in her husband's house, but only for 25 years in her father's house.
The Mishnah adds that if the widow dies, her heirs must mention the ketubah within 25 years.

items.text: Abaye's question about the 25-year limit
items.text_en: Abaye's question about the 25-year limit
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the 25-year limit applies equally to a poor woman and a wealthy one like Marta bat Baitos. Rav Yosef answers that the limit is proportional to the camel's load.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the 25-year limit applies equally to a poor woman and a wealthy one like Marta bat Baitos.
Rav Yosef answers that the limit is proportional to the camel's load, i.e., a wealthy woman spends more per year.

items.text: Unresolved question about tripling the time
items.text_en: Unresolved question about tripling the time
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו) regarding Rabbi Meir's opinion: whether the 25-year period is tripled for some reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו) regarding Rabbi Meir's opinion: whether the 25-year period is tripled for some reason.

items.text: Abaye's question about the exact moment of sunset
items.text_en: Abaye's question about the exact moment of sunset
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the 25-year limit is exact to the moment of sunset. Rav Yosef confirms that even a moment after sunset she forfeits, comparing it to the precise measure of a mikveh.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the widow's collection deadline is exact to the moment of sunset, implying that even a moment after sunset she forfeits by מחילה (waiver).
Rav Yosef confirms that the deadline is exact, comparing it to a mikveh (מקוה) where even a drop less than forty se'ah invalidates immersion.

items.text: Dispute about the effect of possessing the ketubah document
items.text_en: Dispute about the effect of possessing the ketubah document
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav reports that Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei testified before Rabbi that if the widow holds the ketubah document, she can collect indefinitely. Rabbi Elazar disagrees, saying even with the document she is limited to 25 years.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei testified before Rabbi that if the widow holds the ketubah document, she can collect her ketubah indefinitely.
Rabbi Elazar disagrees, asserting that even with the ketubah document in hand, the widow can only collect within twenty-five years.

items.text: Objection from the law of a creditor and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the law of a creditor and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita about a creditor who collects without mentioning his debt, implying a widow who does not mention her ketubah forfeits it. The Gemara resolves that the case is where the debtor admits the debt. A further objection from Rabbi Ila'a is similarly resolved.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita that a creditor collects without mentioning the debt, implying a widow who does not mention her ketubah forfeits it.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita deals with a case where the debtor admits the debt, not where the creditor holds a document.
Rabbi Ila'a objects from a baraita that a divorcée is like a creditor and collects even without mentioning, implying a widow forfeits.
The Gemara resolves that this case too is where the husband admits the debt.

items.text: Introduction of a baraita about claiming the ketubah
items.text_en: Introduction of a baraita about claiming the ketubah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita from the school of Bar Kaza that begins to discuss a widow who demands her ketubah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak introduces a baraita from the school of Bar Kaza that begins to discuss a widow who demands her ketubah.

items.text: Question about the dispute's context and the halakha
items.text_en: Question about the dispute's context and the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Nachman bar Yaakov whether the dispute between the Sages and Rabban Gamliel applies when the ketubah document is in her hand or not, and which opinion is the halakha. Rav Nachman bar Yaakov responds that the dispute is when the document is not in her hand, but when it is, she collects indefinitely, and the halakha follows the Sages.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's question to Rav Nachman bar Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's question to Rav Nachman bar Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda asks Rav Nachman bar Yaakov whether the dispute between the Sages and Rabban Gamliel applies when the ketubah document is in her hand or not, and which opinion is the halakha.
Rav Nachman bar Yaakov responds that the dispute is when the document is not in her hand, but when it is, she collects indefinitely, and the halakha follows the Sages.

items.text: Dispute over whether tosefet is included
items.text_en: Dispute over whether tosefet is included
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Bar Kappara that the ruling only applies to the basic ketubah (maneh matayim), but the additional amount (tosefet) she may collect. Rabbi Avahu says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that even tosefet she does not collect, citing Rabbi Aivu and Rabbi Yannai that the condition of the ketubah is like the ketubah itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Bar Kappara that the ruling applies only to the basic ketubah (מנה מאתיים), but the additional amount (תוספת) she may collect.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that even the additional amount (תוספת) she does not collect, citing Rabbi Aivu and Rabbi Yannai that the condition of the ketubah is like the ketubah itself.

items.text: Supporting tradition and clarification
items.text_en: Supporting tradition and clarification
items.desc_en: It is also stated that Rabbi Abba said in the name of Rav Huna in the name of Rav that the ruling applies only to the basic ketubah, but tosefet she may collect. Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna if Rav indeed said this, and Rav Huna asks whether he is saying it in silence or as a drink, to which Rabbi Abba replies he is saying it in silence.

sub.desc_en: A supporting tradition is cited: Rabbi Abba said in the name of Rav Huna in the name of Rav that the dispute applies only to the basic ketubah (מנה מאתיים), but the tosefet (additional sum) she may collect.
Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna whether Rav indeed said this ruling.
Rav Huna asks Rabbi Abba whether he is saying this tradition in silence (as a reliable tradition) or as a drink (carelessly).
Rabbi Abba replies that he is saying it in silence, indicating the tradition is reliable.

items.text: Story of the widow supported by her brother-in-law
items.text_en: Story of the widow supported by her brother-in-law
items.desc_en: The sister-in-law of Rav Chiyya Aricha was a widow living in her father's house, and he supported her for 25 years. When she asked for sustenance or her ketubah, he refused. She brought him to court before Rabbah bar Sheila, who ruled that since she was in her father's house out of shame, she can collect her ketubah indefinitely, just as when she is in her husband's house.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces the case: the sister-in-law of Rav Chiyya Aricha was a widow living in her father's house, and he supported her for 25 years in his home.
The widow asks for sustenance or her ketubah, and the brother-in-law refuses both.
The widow brings the case to Rabbah bar Sheila, who asks the brother-in-law to explain the facts; the brother-in-law confirms he supported her for 25 years.
Rabbah bar Sheila rules that just as a widow in her husband's house can collect her ketubah indefinitely because shame prevents her from claiming, so too here, and orders the brother-in-law to pay.

items.text: Dispute over the validity of the adrakhta
items.text_en: Dispute over the validity of the adrakhta
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Sheila did not heed the ruling and wrote an adrakhta (court order) against the brother-in-law's property. The brother-in-law came before Rava, who affirmed the ruling. The widow then asked for the produce from the property, but Rava found that the adrakhta lacked the required clause 'and it is known to us that these properties are of the deceased,' so he declared it invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Sheila ignores the ruling, writes an adrakhta (court order) against the brother-in-law's property; the brother-in-law comes before Rava, who affirms the ruling.
The widow asks Rava for the produce from the property from the day of the adrakhta until now.
Rava examines the adrakhta and finds it lacks the required clause 'and it is known to us that these properties are of the deceased,' so he declares it invalid.
The widow asks to collect produce from the completion of the announcement period until now.
Rava explains that the rule about produce applies only when there is no error in the adrakhta; since there is an error, the adrakhta is useless.

items.text: Rava's final ruling on the adrakhta
items.text_en: Rava's final ruling on the adrakhta
items.desc_en: The widow argued that Rava himself said that a scribal error is assumed to be corrected, but Rava responded that here even Rabbah bar Sheila would err, as initially he thought all properties were the husband's, but in reality, the brother-in-law might improve them and cause a scandal. Therefore, the adrakhta is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The widow objects to Rava's rejection of her claim, arguing that Rava himself previously ruled that omission of the guarantee clause is a scribal error and should be treated as if written.

Rava rejects the widow's argument, stating that in this case it cannot be considered a scribal error because even Rabbah bar Sheila erred, thinking that all properties are the same since they all belong to the heir.

Rava explains the true reasoning: the widow might improve the heir's property while the husband's property depreciates, leading the heir to demand an exchange and causing a scandal against the court, so the adrakhta must specify the husband's property.

items.text: Introduction of the next Mishnah
items.text_en: Introduction of the next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The daf concludes with the statement 'We return to you, the one who marries' and begins the next Mishnah about the two judges of decrees in Jerusalem, Admon and Chanan ben Avishalom, listing their rulings, starting with Chanan's two rulings.

sub.desc_en: The daf concludes the previous chapter and transitions to the next Mishnah.
The Mishnah introduces the two judges of decrees in Jerusalem, Admon and Chanan ben Avishalom, and begins detailing Chanan's rulings.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about when the widow swears
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about when the widow swears
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Hanan and the high priests' sons regarding whether a widow swears only at the end or both at the beginning and end of collecting her ketubah. Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas agrees with the high priests' sons, while Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai supports Hanan's position.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Hanan's position that a widow swears only at the end of collecting her ketubah, not at the beginning.
The sons of high priests dispute Hanan, asserting that the widow must swear both at the beginning and at the end.
Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas agrees with the sons of high priests.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai rules that Hanan spoke correctly, so the widow swears only at the end.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and resolution regarding the number of judges
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and resolution regarding the number of judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's mention of three judges of fines and a baraita mentioning three judges of decrees. It resolves that the judges of fines also decreed decrees, citing a baraita about the valuation of saplings. Another contradiction about the names of the judges is resolved by attributing the inclusion of Nachum to Rabbi Nathan, who was not accepted by the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah's three judges of fines and a baraita listing three judges of decrees, noting a double difficulty: the number of judges and the nature of their roles.
The Gemara resolves the first difficulty by noting that the Mishnah only lists prominent judges, but the second difficulty—why judges of fines are called judges of decrees—remains.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by explaining that the judges of fines also decreed decrees regarding fines, citing a baraita about the valuation of saplings by the decree-makers in Jerusalem.
The Gemara raises another contradiction: a baraita lists three judges of decrees including Nachum, whereas the earlier baraita listed only Admon and Chanan.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by attributing the inclusion of Nachum to Rabbi Nathan, whose opinion was not accepted by the Sages.

items.text: Clarification: Many judges, but only a few decree-makers
items.text_en: Clarification: Many judges, but only a few decree-makers
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there were many courts in Jerusalem, but the discussion is specifically about the judges who decreed decrees, not all judges.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous list by citing Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rabbi Oshaya that there were 394 courts in Jerusalem, implying many more judges than the three listed.
The Gemara resolves that the many courts were for general judging, but the discussion is specifically about the decree-makers (גוזרי גזירות), who were only a few.

items.text: Salary of the decree-makers
items.text_en: Salary of the decree-makers
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi states that the decree-makers in Jerusalem received a salary of 99 maneh from the Temple treasury, and if they were not satisfied, they would increase it. The Gemara corrects that it means if they were not sufficient, they would increase it, not if they were unwilling.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Asi states that the decree-makers in Jerusalem received a salary of 99 maneh from the Temple treasury, and if they were not satisfied, they would increase it.
The Gemara objects: 'If they were not satisfied' — are we dealing with wicked people who would refuse a salary?
The Gemara corrects: it means 'if they were not sufficient' (the salary was inadequate), and even if they were unwilling, they would increase it.

items.text: The case of Karna: Taking payment for judging
items.text_en: The case of Karna: Taking payment for judging
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses Karna, who took a fee from both litigants and judged them. It questions whether this is permitted, given the prohibition of bribery. The Gemara distinguishes between a bribe and a fee for lost work time, and further distinguishes between a fee for judging and a fee for idleness. It concludes that Karna took a fee for idleness that was obvious, as he would sit at the ferry and they would give him a zuz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of Karna, who took a fee from both the winner and the loser and judged them.
The Gemara questions how Karna could do this, citing the verse 'וְשׁוֹחַד לֹא תִקָּח' (and you shall not take a bribe).
The Gemara suggests that since Karna took from both sides, he would not be biased, but then rejects this by asking whether lack of bias alone permits taking a bribe.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the verse 'וְשׁוֹחַד לֹא תִקָּח' prohibits even taking a bribe to acquit the innocent or convict the guilty, not just to pervert justice.
The Gemara distinguishes that the prohibition applies only to a bribe (שוחד), but Karna took a fee for lost work time (אגר בטילא), not a bribe.
The Gemara objects that even a fee for idleness is not permitted, citing a baraita that a judge who takes a fee for idleness is 'repulsive' (מכוער), though his judgment is valid.

The Gemara resolves that the prohibition of a 'repulsive' fee applies only to non-obvious idleness, but Karna's idleness was obvious (בטילא דמוכחא) because he would sit at the ferry and they would give him a zuz.

items.text: Rav Huna's practice: Requesting a helper
items.text_en: Rav Huna's practice: Requesting a helper
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a similar practice of Rav Huna, who would ask litigants to provide someone to draw water for him before he judged their case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's practice of requesting a helper to draw water before judging, as a precedent for taking compensation for lost work time.

items.text: The severity of bribery: Blinding the wise
items.text_en: The severity of bribery: Blinding the wise
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu comments on how bribery blinds even the wise, comparing it to a medical treatment with uncertain outcome. The baraita expounds on the verse, stating that bribery blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous, implying that even a great sage who takes a bribe will not leave the world without blindness of heart.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu opens by marveling at how bribery blinds recipients, comparing it to a medical treatment with uncertain outcome, and cites the verse that bribery blinds the clear-sighted.

The baraita expounds the verse, stating that bribery blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous, and clarifies that even a great sage who takes a bribe will not leave the world without blindness of heart.

items.text: Opening statement on bribery
items.text_en: Opening statement on bribery
items.desc_en: Even a completely righteous person who takes a bribe will not leave the world without mental confusion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a general statement that even a completely righteous person who takes a bribe will not leave the world without mental confusion.

items.text: Derasha on the judge as king or priest
items.text_en: Derasha on the judge as king or priest
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rav Nachman bar Kohen's derasha: If a judge is like a king who needs nothing, he establishes the land; if like a priest who goes around the threshing floors, he destroys it.

sub.text: Rav Dimi reporting Rav Nachman bar Kohen
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi reporting Rav Nachman bar Kohen
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rav Nachman bar Kohen's derasha: a judge who is like a king needing nothing establishes the land, but one like a priest seeking gifts destroys it.

items.text: Judge who borrows is disqualified
items.text_en: Judge who borrows is disqualified
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheilah says a judge who borrows is disqualified unless he has something to lend. The Gemara objects from Rava who borrowed, and answers that Rava did so to honor them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheilah rules that a judge who borrows an item is disqualified from judging unless he has something to lend in return.
The Gemara objects from Rava, who borrowed from the house of bar Maryon even though they did not borrow from him.
The Gemara answers that Rava borrowed only to honor them, not for personal benefit, so it does not disqualify him.

items.text: Reason for bribery and disqualification for love or hate
items.text_en: Reason for bribery and disqualification for love or hate
items.desc_en: Rava explains that bribery makes the judge feel close to the litigant, like himself, and one cannot see fault in oneself. Rav Pappa adds that one should not judge someone he loves or hates.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks the reason for the prohibition of bribery and explains that accepting a bribe makes the judge feel close to the litigant as himself, and one cannot see fault in oneself.
The Gemara glosses the word 'שוחד' (bribe) as 'שהוא חד' (that it is sharp), implying it sharpens the judge's bias.
Rav Pappa adds that a person should not judge someone he loves or hates, because love blinds him to faults and hate blinds him to merits.

items.text: Abaye and Rava on local affection for a scholar
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava on local affection for a scholar
items.desc_en: Abaye says townspeople's love for a Torah scholar is not because he is especially good, but because he does not rebuke them. Rava reflects on his own experience as a judge, realizing that litigants' attitudes change.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the townspeople's love for a Torah scholar is not because he is especially virtuous, but because he does not rebuke them in matters of Heaven.
Rava reflects on his own experience as a judge in Mehoza, realizing that litigants' attitudes toward him shift based on whether they win or lose, so he can no longer assume universal affection.

items.text: Verbal bribery and stories of disqualification
items.text_en: Verbal bribery and stories of disqualification
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that even verbal bribery is forbidden. Examples: Shmuel, Amemar, and Mar Ukva disqualified litigants who performed small favors for them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that even verbal bribery is forbidden, and asks for examples.
Shmuel disqualified a litigant who helped him off a ferry, illustrating verbal bribery.

sub.text: Story about Ameimar and Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Story about Ameimar and Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Ameimar and Mar Ukva each disqualified litigants who performed small favors, further illustrating verbal bribery.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha disqualify themselves
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha disqualify themselves
items.desc_en: Two stories: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei disqualified his tenant who brought fruit early due to a case; Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha disqualified a man who brought him first shearing. Both later regretted and cursed bribe-takers.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei's tenant, who regularly brought fruit on Friday, brought it on Thursday because he had a case; Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and disqualified himself.

Rabbi Yishmael appointed other judges to hear the case, but while walking he thought of arguments for the tenant and cursed bribe-takers, reasoning that if he, who did not accept anything, is biased, how much more so those who accept bribes.

A second story: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, was brought first shearing by a man who had a case; Rabbi Yishmael questioned why he didn't give it to a local priest, then disqualified himself and refused the gift.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha appointed other judges, but while walking he thought of arguments for the litigant and cursed bribe-takers, repeating the same reasoning as the previous story.

items.text: Rav Anan and the gift of first fruits
items.text_en: Rav Anan and the gift of first fruits
items.desc_en: Rav Anan disqualified a man who brought him a gift, but accepted it when told it was like bringing first fruits to a Torah scholar. He then sent the case to Rav Nachman, who suspected Rav Anan was close to the litigant.

sub.desc_en: A man brings Rav Anan a basket of small fish; Rav Anan asks his business, learns he has a case, and disqualifies himself from judging.

The man explains he does not need Rav Anan's judgment but wants him to accept the gift so as not to prevent him from fulfilling the mitzva of bringing first fruits, citing a baraita that bringing a gift to a Torah scholar is like offering first fruits.

Rav Anan initially refuses but accepts after hearing the reason; he then sends the man to Rav Nachman with a note that he is disqualified, leading Rav Nachman to infer that Rav Anan is a relative of the litigant.
The narrative shifts to Rav Nachman, who is presiding over an orphans' case when he receives the message.

items.text: Priority of honoring Torah over other positive commandments
items.text_en: Priority of honoring Torah over other positive commandments
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that when a positive commandment conflicts with another positive commandment, the one involving honoring Torah takes precedence. Therefore, a judge should recuse himself from an orphan's case to avoid bias, as the honor shown to him may intimidate the litigant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that when two positive commandments conflict, the one involving honoring Torah takes precedence, and a judge should recuse himself from an orphan's case because the honor shown may intimidate the litigant.

items.text: Story of Rav Anan and Elijah's withdrawal
items.text_en: Story of Rav Anan and Elijah's withdrawal
items.desc_en: Rav Anan was accustomed to Elijah visiting him and teaching him the Seder of Elijah. When Rav Anan acted in a way that showed bias (as per the previous rule), Elijah stopped coming. After fasting and praying, Elijah returned but was agitated, and Rav Anan had to appease him until he taught him the Seder again.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the story of Rav Anan, who was accustomed to Elijah visiting and teaching him the Seder of Elijah.
The gemara relates that after Rav Anan acted with bias, Elijah withdrew; Rav Anan fasted and prayed, and Elijah returned but was agitated.
The gemara concludes that Rav Anan appeased Elijah until he taught him the Seder again, which is why there are two versions: Seder Eliyahu Rabbah and Seder Eliyahu Zuta.

items.text: Rav Yosef's refusal to pray during a plague
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's refusal to pray during a plague
items.desc_en: During a plague in Rav Yosef's time, the rabbis asked him to pray. He declined, citing Elisha's example: even when 2,200 rabbis would take leave of him, Elisha did not pray during a plague. The Gemara explains the proof from the verse about Elisha's servant and the hundred men.

sub.desc_en: The narrator sets the scene: during a plague in Rav Yosef's time, the rabbis ask him to pray for mercy.
Rav Yosef declines, arguing by קל וחומר (a fortiori) from Elisha, who did not pray during a plague even when 2,200 rabbis would take leave of him.
The Gemara asks: from where do we know that so many rabbis remained with Elisha? It cites the verse about Elisha's servant and the hundred men.
The Gemara objects: if the verse meant all the rabbis together before a hundred men, that would be too few during a famine.
The Gemara resolves: rather, each individual rabbi had a hundred men before him, proving the large number of Elisha's disciples.

items.text: Numbers of rabbis remaining after lectures
items.text_en: Numbers of rabbis remaining after lectures
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how many rabbis remained after the lectures of various great sages: 1,200 after Rav's house, 800 after Rav Huna's (who taught with 13 interpreters), 400 after Rabbah and Rav Yosef (who called themselves orphans), and 200 after Abaye or Rav Pappa or Rav Ashi (who called themselves orphans of orphans).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the declining numbers of rabbis remaining after the lectures of successive generations of sages, from 1,200 after Rav to 200 after Abaye, Rav Pappa, or Rav Ashi.

items.text: Payments from Temple chamber for various services
items.text_en: Payments from Temple chamber for various services
items.desc_en: Several amoraim state that various professionals were paid from the Temple chamber (תרומת הלשכה): inspectors of blemishes, teachers of slaughter and kemitzah for priests, correctors of books, and women weaving the curtains. Rav Nachman adds that women weaving the curtains should be paid from Temple funds for building maintenance, not the chamber.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Redifa citing Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Redifa citing Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Redifa citing Rabbi Ami states that the inspectors of blemishes in Jerusalem received their wages from the Temple chamber (תרומת הלשכה).
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states that sages who teach the laws of slaughter (שחיטה) to priests received their wages from the Temple chamber.
Rav Giddel citing Rav states that sages who teach the laws of kemitzah (קמיצה, the priestly scooping of the meal-offering) to priests received their wages from the Temple chamber.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan states that the correctors of books (מגיהי ספרים) in Jerusalem received their wages from the Temple chamber.
Rav Nachman citing Rav states that women who weave the curtains (פָּרֹכוֹת) received their wages from the Temple chamber.
