Rav Nachman objects to Rav's ruling, asserting that the women weavers should be paid from the Temple funds for building maintenance (קדשי בדק הבית), since the curtains are considered part of the building structure.

items.text: Objection to Rav Nachman and resolution
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Nachman and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraisa is cited that women weaving the curtains, the house of Garmu (for showbread), and the house of Avtinas (for incense) all received payment from the chamber, contradicting Rav Nachman. The Gemara resolves that the curtains in question were for the gates (דבבי), not the main curtains, citing Rabbi Zeira's teaching about thirteen curtains in the Second Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa listing women weaving the curtains, the house of Garmu for showbread, and the house of Avtinas for incense, all receiving payment from תרומת הלשכה (the chamber fund), contradicting Rav Nachman's ruling.

The Gemara resolves that the baraisa refers to curtains for the gates (דבבי), not the main sanctuary curtains, citing Rabbi Zeira's teaching that the Second Temple had thirteen curtains: seven for the gates, one for the Heikhal entrance, one for the Ulam entrance, and two in the Holy of Holies with two corresponding in the upper chamber.

items.text: Women raising children for the red heifer
items.text_en: Women raising children for the red heifer
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that women who raise their children for the red heifer ceremony were paid from the chamber. Abba Shaul says that wealthy women of Jerusalem would support them voluntarily.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that women who raise their children for the red heifer ceremony were paid from the chamber (תרומת הלשכה).
Abba Shaul says that wealthy women of Jerusalem would support them voluntarily, not from the chamber.

items.text: Rav Huna's inquiry to Rav
items.text_en: Rav Huna's inquiry to Rav
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav a question, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asks Rav a question, setting up the next discussion.

items.text: Initial question about sacred vessels
items.text_en: Initial question about sacred vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether sacred vessels can be made from Temple building funds or only from the chamber funds. The answer is given: they are made only from the chamber funds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether sacred vessels (כלי שרת) may be made from Temple building funds (קדשי בדק הבית) or only from the chamber funds (תרומת הלשכה).
The answer is given: sacred vessels are made only from the chamber funds (תרומת הלשכה).

items.text: Objection from Chronicles and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Chronicles and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a verse in Chronicles where leftover silver was used for vessels. The answer distinguishes between cases where funds were collected with a surplus and where they were not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a verse in Chronicles where leftover silver was brought before the king and Jehoiada and made into sacred vessels.
The Gemara answers that the objector was taught the Writings but not the Prophets, citing a verse in Chronicles that explicitly states the silver was given to the workers and not made into vessels.

items.text: Reconciliation of verses and Rabbi Avahu's condition
items.text_en: Reconciliation of verses and Rabbi Avahu's condition
items.desc_en: The Gemara reconciles the conflicting verses: one case is where they collected and had a surplus, the other where they did not. Rabbi Avahu explains that the court stipulates that surplus funds go to sacred vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the two verses contradict each other.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one verse refers to a case where they collected and had a surplus, the other where they did not.
The Gemara asks what happens when they collected and had a surplus.
Rabbi Avahu explains that the court stipulates in advance: if the funds are needed for the Temple, they are used; if not, they go to sacred vessels.

items.text: Tanna of Rabbi Yishmael's school and Rava's interpretation
items.text_en: Tanna of Rabbi Yishmael's school and Rava's interpretation
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives that vessels come from chamber funds based on the phrase 'the rest of the silver.' Rava explains that 'the silver' refers to the first silver, not the surplus itself.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives that vessels of service come from the chamber fund (תרומת הלשכה) based on the verse 'the rest of the silver,' interpreting it as silver that has leftovers, which is the chamber fund.
The Gemara questions whether the verse might refer to the surplus itself rather than the original silver.
Rava explains by analogy: just as 'the burnt-offering' (העולה) means the first burnt-offering, so too 'the silver' (הכסף) means the first silver, not the surplus.

items.text: Baraita on sources for various Temple items
items.text_en: Baraita on sources for various Temple items
items.desc_en: A baraita lists that incense and communal offerings come from chamber funds, while the golden altar, frankincense, and vessels come from surplus libations. The altar, chambers, and courtyards come from building funds.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited as an objection, listing that incense and communal offerings come from chamber funds, while the golden altar, frankincense, and vessels come from surplus libations, and the altar, chambers, and courtyards come from building funds.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on surplus use
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on surplus use
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies this as a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says surplus chamber funds go to vessels, Rabbi Akiva says surplus libations go to vessels, and Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim says surplus libations go to the altar and surplus chamber funds to vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute about the use of surplus תרומה (priestly portion) funds, citing the first opinion that they were beaten into gold plating for the Holy of Holies.
Rabbi Yishmael rules that surplus produce (פירות) goes to the altar's maintenance (קיץ המזבח), while surplus תרומה goes to vessels (כלי שרת).
Rabbi Akiva reverses the allocation: surplus תרומה goes to the altar, and surplus libations (נסכים) go to vessels.
Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim agrees with Rabbi Yishmael that surplus libations go to the altar and surplus תרומה to vessels.
The Gemara notes that both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva disagreed about the status of produce (פירות) as a separate category.

items.text: Explanation of 'produce' and the dispute about profit
items.text_en: Explanation of 'produce' and the dispute about profit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'produce' refers to buying cheap and selling dear, with profit used for the altar. The dispute about 'produce' is clarified: Rabbi Yishmael allows profit from surplus chamber funds, while Rabbi Akiva forbids profit from consecrated property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'produce' (פֵּירוֹת) in the Mishnah refers to.
The Gemara cites a baraita explaining that 'produce' refers to buying cheap and selling dear with surplus chamber funds, and the profit is used for the altar (קֵיץ הַמִּזְבֵּחַ).
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'both did not agree regarding produce'.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael permits profit from surplus chamber funds for the Temple.
Rabbi Akiva forbids profit from consecrated property (הקדש) and also from poor funds.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Akiva's reasoning: for consecrated property, there is no poverty in a place of wealth; for poor funds, a poor person might appear and there would be nothing to give.

items.text: Introduction of a new topic: one who went overseas
items.text_en: Introduction of a new topic: one who went overseas
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion about a person who went overseas, with Rav's statement introduced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new topic about one who went overseas and begins to cite Rav's statement.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute sustenance for a wife
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute sustenance for a wife
items.desc_en: Rav holds that a court may allocate sustenance to a wife whose husband is away, while Shmuel disagrees. Shmuel concedes for the first three months because a man does not leave his house empty, and both agree when the husband is known dead. The dispute is when his death is not known.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a dispute: Rav holds that a court may allocate sustenance (מזונות) to a wife whose husband is away, while Shmuel disagrees, though Shmuel concedes for the first three months because a man does not leave his house empty.

The gemara clarifies that both agree when the husband is known dead; the dispute is only when his death is not known, with Rav ruling that the court allocates sustenance because the husband's property is legally encumbered (משועבד) to her, and Shmuel ruling that they do not.

items.text: Reasons for Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Reasons for Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa offer explanations for Shmuel's concern: either the wife might be suspected of adultery (צררי אתפסה) or the husband might have told her to support herself from her earnings. The practical difference between these reasons is whether the wife is an adult whose earnings are insufficient or a minor whose earnings suffice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind Shmuel's position that the court does not allocate sustenance to a married woman.
Rav Zevid explains that Shmuel is concerned the husband might have secretly given her a bundle of documents (צררי) to support herself, so the court should not intervene.
Rav Pappa explains that Shmuel is concerned the husband might have told her to support herself from her own earnings, so the court should not allocate sustenance.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations of Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa.

The Gemara answers that the difference lies in the case of an adult woman whose earnings are insufficient to support herself: according to Rav Zevid, the concern of a secret bundle applies, but according to Rav Pappa, the husband's instruction to use her earnings is irrelevant if they are insufficient.

Alternatively, the difference is in the case of a minor girl whose earnings suffice for her sustenance: according to Rav Zevid, the concern of a secret bundle still applies, but according to Rav Pappa, the husband's instruction is effective since her earnings are sufficient.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of Chanan
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of Chanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Chanan and the high priests' sons dispute only about the oath, but agree that sustenance is given. Shmuel interprets this as referring to a case where the husband's death was heard, thus not contradicting his view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah of Chanan and the sons of high priests, which implies that sustenance is granted to a wife whose husband went overseas, contradicting Shmuel's view.
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by interpreting the Mishnah as referring to a case where the husband's death was heard, which aligns with his own position.

items.text: Second challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Second challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that if the husband later says he allocated sustenance, he is believed. The Gemara initially questions this, then resolves that it refers to after hearing of death, and the husband's statement is after the rumor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that if a husband who went overseas later says he allocated sustenance, he is believed, challenging the earlier position.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the wife heard a rumor of death, and the husband's statement comes after the rumor, so it is believed.

items.text: Third challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Third challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita says that if the husband says 'support yourself from your earnings' he is permitted, but if the court already allocated, it stands. The Gemara again interprets this as referring to a case where his death was heard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if a husband went overseas and his wife claims sustenance, and he says 'support yourself from your earnings' he is permitted; if the court already allocated, it stands.
The Gemara resolves that this baraita also refers to a case where they heard he died.

items.text: Fourth challenge: court provides for wife but not children
items.text_en: Fourth challenge: court provides for wife but not children
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the court provides sustenance for the wife but not for children or other things. Rav Sheshet explains this as a case where the husband appointed a trustee for the wife. Rav Pappa explains it as a case where the wife heard of his death from one witness, allowing her to remarry, but children cannot inherit based on one witness.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita stating that the court provides sustenance for the wife of a traveling husband but not for his children or other needs.
Rav Sheshet explains the baraita as a case where the husband appointed a trustee for the wife but not for the children, resolving the apparent contradiction.

Rav Pappa explains that the wife heard of her husband's death from one witness, allowing her to remarry and receive sustenance, but children cannot inherit based on one witness, so they receive nothing.

items.text: Explanation of 'other thing'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'other thing'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'other thing' in the baraita: Rav Chisda says it refers to jewelry, Rav Yosef says it refers to charity. The discussion continues with a comparison.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'other thing' in the baraita refers to.
Rav Chisda answers that 'other thing' refers to jewelry (תכשיט).
Rav Yosef answers that 'other thing' refers to charity (צדקה).
The Gemara notes that according to the one who says jewelry, all the more so charity is included, implying a logical comparison between the two positions.

items.text: Opening question on charity vs. adornments
items.text_en: Opening question on charity vs. adornments
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by questioning whether a woman receives charity or adornments, concluding that if she receives charity, she does not get adornments, as the husband does not want her to become unattractive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by questioning whether a woman receives charity or adornments, concluding that if she receives charity, she does not get adornments, as the husband does not want her to become unattractive.

items.text: First proof from yevamah's sustenance
items.text_en: First proof from yevamah's sustenance
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a yevamah who receives sustenance from her husband for three months, but not from the yavam unless he stood trial and fled. Shmuel explains that the yavam is not concerned about her because he is not close to her and her earnings are not pledged to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a yevamah who receives sustenance from her husband for three months, but not from the yavam unless he stood trial and fled.
Shmuel explains that the yavam is not concerned about her because he is not close to her and her earnings are not pledged to him.

items.text: Second proof from woman who says her husband died
items.text_en: Second proof from woman who says her husband died
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah about a woman who goes overseas with her husband and returns claiming he died; she may choose sustenance or collect her ketubah. If she claims divorce, she is supported only up to the value of her ketubah. The Gemara explains this is when she heard he died, and the limitation is because she caused her own loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a mishnah as a second proof: a woman who went overseas with her husband and returned claiming he died may choose sustenance or collect her ketubah; if she claims divorce, she is supported only up to the value of her ketubah.
The Gemara resolves the proof: this case too is when they heard he died, and the limitation to the ketubah value is because she caused her own loss by claiming divorce rather than death.

items.text: Third proof from a minor who refuses marriage
items.text_en: Third proof from a minor who refuses marriage
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet) and has no sustenance; but if she did not refuse, she would receive sustenance. Shmuel explains that this is because a minor cannot create jealousy (tzarerei) and her earnings are insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a minor who refuses marriage (mema'enet) and has no sustenance; but if she did not refuse, she would receive sustenance.
Shmuel explains that this is because a minor cannot create jealousy (tzarerei) and her earnings are insufficient.

items.text: Conflicting rulings of Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Conflicting rulings of Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a case where Rabbi ruled to give sustenance, but Rabbi Yishmael did not. Rabbi Yochanan wonders why Rabbi Yishmael did not give sustenance, since the dispute between Chanan and the high priests' sons is only about oaths, not sustenance. Rav Shemen bar Abba explains that Shmuel in Babylonia interpreted the case as one where they heard the husband died. Ravin reports the opposite: Rabbi did not give, Rabbi Yishmael did. Rabbi Yochanan again questions, and Rav Shemen bar Abba gives the same explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the conclusion is, and Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in Beit She'arim apportioned sustenance, but Rabbi Yishmael in Tzippori did not.
Rabbi Yochanan wonders why Rabbi Yishmael did not apportion sustenance, since the dispute between Chanan and the high priests' sons is only about oaths, not sustenance.
Rav Shemen bar Abba explains that Shmuel in Babylonia already interpreted the case as one where they heard the husband died.
Rabbi Yochanan expresses astonishment that they would go that far in interpreting the case.
Ravin reports the opposite: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not apportion sustenance, but Rabbi Yishmael did.
Rabbi Yochanan again questions why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not apportion sustenance, given the same reasoning.

sub.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba's repeated explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba's repeated explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba again explains that Shmuel in Babylonia interpreted the case as one where they heard the husband died.
Rabbi Yochanan again expresses astonishment at the extent of the interpretation.

items.text: Halakhic conclusions and digression on garments
items.text_en: Halakhic conclusions and digression on garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara rules in accordance with Rav that we grant sustenance to a married woman, and in accordance with Rav Huna citing Rav that a woman can say she will not be supported nor work. It also rules in accordance with Rav Zevid regarding garments from Konya: white and black are permitted, green are forbidden unless they have knots.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules in accordance with Rav that the court apportions sustenance for a married woman whose husband went overseas.
The Gemara rules in accordance with Rav Huna citing Rav that a woman can say to her husband: I will not be sustained and I will not work.
The Gemara rules in accordance with Rav Zevid regarding glazed vessels from Konya: white and black ones are permitted.
Rav Zevid adds that green vessels are forbidden, and even white and black ones are forbidden if they have cracks.

items.text: Mishnah: One who supports another's wife and the dispute of Chanan
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who supports another's wife and the dispute of Chanan
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if a man went overseas and someone supported his wife, Chanan says the supporter loses his money. The high priests' sons say he takes an oath and collects. Rabbi Dosa agrees with them. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai supports Chanan. The Gemara begins to discuss a related mishnah about one who is forbidden benefit from his friend.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case: a man went overseas and someone supported his wife; Chanan rules the supporter loses his money.
The sons of high priests dispute Chanan, ruling that the supporter takes an oath and collects his expenses.
Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas agrees with the sons of high priests.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai supports Chanan, saying the supporter placed his money on a deer's horn (i.e., lost it).
The Gemara shifts to cite a related mishnah about one who is forbidden benefit from his friend.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a priest may perform certain services for a non-priest friend, but if a fee is normally charged, the benefit goes to the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a priest may pay a friend's half-shekel, repay his debt, and return his lost item, but where a fee is normally charged, the benefit goes to the Temple.

items.text: Gemara's question on paying a debt
items.text_en: Gemara's question on paying a debt
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that weighing the shekel and returning a lost object are permissible because they are mitzvot, but paying a debt directly benefits the non-priest, which seems problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: weighing the shekel and returning a lost object are mitzvot, but paying a debt directly benefits the non-priest, which seems problematic.

items.text: First answer: Rabbi Oshaya's resolution
items.text_en: First answer: Rabbi Oshaya's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya identifies the Mishnah as following the opinion of Ḥanan, who holds that if a lender loses his money, the borrower is exempt, so paying the debt does not benefit the borrower.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya identifies the Mishnah as following the opinion of Ḥanan, who holds that if a lender loses his money, the borrower is exempt, so paying the debt does not benefit the borrower.

items.text: Second answer: Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Second answer: Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava explains that even according to the Rabbis, the case involves a borrower who stipulated that he would not repay, so the payment is a gift, not a debt repayment.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a borrower who stipulated that he would not repay, so the payment is a gift, not a debt repayment.

items.text: Analysis of the two answers
items.text_en: Analysis of the two answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rava does not accept Rabbi Oshaya's answer (he prefers to align with the Rabbis) and why Rabbi Oshaya does not accept Rava's answer (since the borrower still has no direct benefit from the payment).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Rava does not accept Rabbi Oshaya's answer: Rava prefers to align his interpretation with the Rabbis.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Oshaya does not accept Rava's answer.
Rabbi Oshaya explains that even though the borrower has no direct benefit (הנאה) from the payment, the lender still benefits, so the case does not fit Rava's reasoning.

items.text: Conclusion of previous Gemara
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous Gemara
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a previous question about embarrassment, concluding that the defendant still derives benefit from the embarrassment he causes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the defendant still derives benefit from the embarrassment he causes, concluding the previous discussion.

items.text: Mishnah: Admon on inheritance and support
items.text_en: Mishnah: Admon on inheritance and support
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents Admon's ruling: when a man dies leaving sons and daughters, if the estate is large the sons inherit and the daughters are supported; if small, the daughters are supported and the sons beg. Admon objects: 'Because I am a male, I lose out?' Rabban Gamliel agrees with Admon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Admon's ruling about inheritance division between sons and daughters, with Rabban Gamliel agreeing with Admon.

items.text: Gemara: Explaining Admon's complaint
items.text_en: Gemara: Explaining Admon's complaint
items.desc_en: Abaye explains Admon's complaint: 'Because I am a male and fit to study Torah, I lose out?' Rava objects: does only one who studies Torah inherit? Rather, Rava explains: 'Because I am a male and fit to inherit large estates, I lose out in small ones?'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Admon meant by his statement, and Abaye explains that Admon complained about losing inheritance because he is male and expected to study Torah.

Rava objects to Abaye's explanation, arguing that inheritance is not conditional on Torah study, and instead explains that Admon meant he lost out in the case of limited assets despite being male and eligible to inherit abundant assets.
Rava objects: does only one who studies Torah inherit, and one who does not study does not inherit?
Rava explains instead: Admon complained, 'Because I am a male and fit to inherit large estates, I lose out in small ones?'

items.text: Mishnah: Admon on partial admission of oil jugs
items.text_en: Mishnah: Admon on partial admission of oil jugs
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a case: one claims jugs of oil and the defendant admits to the jugs (but not the oil). Admon says: since he admitted part of the claim, he must swear. The Sages say: this is not a partial admission of the same type. Rabban Gamliel agrees with Admon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Admon and the Sages about a partial admission to a claim of jars of oil, with Rabban Gamliel supporting Admon.

items.text: Gemara: Inference for the Sages and challenge to Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Gemara: Inference for the Sages and challenge to Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Sages' position that if one claims wheat and barley and admits to barley, he is exempt. This challenges Rav Nachman citing Shmuel, who says one who claims wheat and barley and admits to one is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Sages' position in the Mishnah that if one claims wheat and barley and admits to barley, he is exempt from an oath.
The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman citing Shmuel, who holds that one who claims wheat and barley and admits to one is liable, contradicting the inferred exemption.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's resolution and question to Admon
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's resolution and question to Admon
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav says the mishnah deals with a claim of a specific measure. If so, what is Admon's reasoning?

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav answers that the Mishnah deals with a claim by measure, prompting the Gemara to question Admon's reasoning.
The Gemara asks: if the claim is about a specific measure, what is Admon's reasoning for requiring an oath?

items.text: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava explains that all agree: if one says 'ten full jugs of oil', both oil and jugs are claimed; if 'ten jugs of oil in your pit', only oil is claimed. They dispute when one says 'ten jugs of oil I have with you': Admon says this language includes jugs, the Sages say it does not.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that everyone agrees that when one claims 'ten full jars of oil in your pit', the oil is claimed but the jars are not.
Rava resolves that the dispute is when one claims 'ten jars of oil I have with you', where Admon holds the language includes jars and the Sages disagree.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that if the language includes jugs, the defendant is liable, challenging Rabbi Chiya bar Abba who says one who claims wheat and barley and admits to one is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, who ruled that admitting to one of two types exempts from an oath, by noting that if the language included jars, one would be liable.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's analogy and Ravina's objection
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's analogy and Ravina's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi says the case is like one who claims a pomegranate with its peel. Ravina objects: a pomegranate without its peel is not preserved, but oil is preserved without jugs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that the case is like claiming a pomegranate with its peel, but Ravina objects that oil can be preserved without jars unlike a pomegranate without its peel.
Ravina objects: a pomegranate without its peel is not preserved, but oil is preserved without jugs, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Final resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Final resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the case: the plaintiff claims ten jugs of oil, the defendant says 'oil never existed, but you have five jugs and five you do not.' Admon says the language includes jugs, so via gilgul shevuah he swears about the jugs and also about the oil. The Sages say the language does not include jugs, so what he claimed he did not admit, and what he admitted he did not claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case is where the plaintiff claims ten jars of oil and the defendant admits to five jars but denies the oil.
The Gemara resolves that Admon holds the language includes jars, allowing a rolling oath on the oil, while the Sages hold the language excludes jars, so there is no partial admission.
The Sages hold that the language does not include jugs, so what he claimed he did not admit, and what he admitted he did not claim.

items.text: New mishnah: Father-in-law reneging on dowry
items.text_en: New mishnah: Father-in-law reneging on dowry
items.desc_en: The mishnah introduces a case where a father pledges money to his son-in-law and then backs out.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a new case about one who pledges money to his son-in-law and then defaults.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Admon's ruling on a father's failed dowry
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Admon's ruling on a father's failed dowry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a woman whose father promised a dowry but did not give it. Admon rules that she can say, 'My father promised, what can I do? Either marry me or divorce me,' while the Sages say she must wait until her hair turns white. Rabban Gamliel agrees with Admon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the Sages' ruling that a woman whose father failed to pay the promised dowry must wait until her hair turns white, and then presents Admon's dissenting opinion that she can demand either marriage or divorce.
Rabban Gamliel endorses Admon's position, stating that he sees Admon's words as correct.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute via a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute via a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not align with a baraita taught by Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, which states that the dispute between Admon and the Sages is only when the woman herself promised the dowry, not when her father promised. In the latter case, all agree she can claim her father's promise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not align with a baraita taught by Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, who limits the dispute to cases where the woman herself promised the dowry.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The baraita explains that the dispute between Admon and the Sages is specifically when the woman herself promised the dowry, not when her father promised it.
The baraita concludes with Rabban Gamliel again endorsing Admon's position.

items.text: Distinction between adult and minor daughter
items.text_en: Distinction between adult and minor daughter
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the dispute applies only to an adult daughter, but for a minor, the court forces the husband to give a get. Rava clarifies that the coercion is on the husband, not the father.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states that the dispute applies only to an adult woman, but for a minor, the court compels action.
The Gemara questions whom the court compels, noting that if it were the father, the opposite would be expected.
Rava clarifies that the court compels the husband to give a גט (bill of divorce).

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's endorsement as a halakhic rule
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's endorsement as a halakhic rule
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar quotes Chizkiya that wherever Rabban Gamliel says 'I see the words of Admon,' the halakha follows Admon. Rava asks Rav Nachman if this applies even to a baraita, and Rav Nachman limits it to the Mishnah.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar in the name of Chizkiyah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar in the name of Chizkiyah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar reports in the name of Chizkiyah that wherever Rabban Gamliel says 'I see the words of Admon,' the הלכה (binding law) follows Admon.
Rava asks Rav Nachman whether this rule applies even to a baraita (external teaching).
Rav Nachman responds that the statement was made only about the Mishnah, not about baraitot.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's statement on Hanan and Admon's rulings
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's statement on Hanan and Admon's rulings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rabbah bar Yirmeya that for Hanan's two rulings, the halakha follows him and similar cases, but for Admon's seven rulings, the halakha does not follow similar cases. The Gemara refines this, concluding that for Admon, some rulings are followed and some are not, depending on Rabban Gamliel's endorsement.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rabbah bar Yirmiyah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rabbah bar Yirmiyah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Rabbah bar Yirmiyah a general rule about Chanan and Admon, and the Gemara asks what this statement means.

The Gemara considers a possible interpretation that the rule denies both the law and its parallels for Admon, but objects because Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar's statement establishes that the law follows Admon wherever Rabban Gamliel endorsed him.
The Gemara rejects the first interpretation and proposes that the rule means the law follows Admon himself but not his parallels, implying that the law follows Admon in all his cases.
The Gemara objects again, noting that Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar's statement implies the law follows Admon only where Rabban Gamliel explicitly endorsed him, not in all cases.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by interpreting that for Admon, some cases follow him and his parallels, while others follow only his parallels, and the rule about Rabban Gamliel's endorsement applies only where he explicitly said 'I see the words of Admon.'
The Gemara objects again: Chizkiyah's statement implies that halakha follows Admon only where Rabban Gamliel explicitly endorsed him, not in all cases.
The Gemara resolves: for Hanan the halakha follows him and similar cases; for Admon, some rulings are followed (where Rabban Gamliel endorsed) and some are not, but similar cases are never followed.

items.text: Mishnah: A claimant who signed as a witness on the deed
items.text_en: Mishnah: A claimant who signed as a witness on the deed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where someone challenges ownership of a field but had signed as a witness on the deed. Admon says the second (the deed) is easier for him, and the first (his claim) is harder. The Sages say he loses his right. If he made the deed a sign for another, he loses his right.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a new case: one who challenges a field sale but signed as a witness on the deed, and Admon rules that the second purchaser is preferable to him and the first is more difficult.
The Sages rule that the challenger has lost his right to contest the sale.
The Mishnah adds that if he made the deed a sign for another, he also loses his right.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between witness and judge
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between witness and judge
items.desc_en: Abaye limits the Mishnah's ruling to a witness, but a judge who signed does not lose his right, citing a baraita that witnesses only sign after reading the document.

sub.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to a witness, but a judge who signed does not lose his right.
Abaye supports his ruling with a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya that witnesses only sign a document after reading it, implying a judge who signed without reading may not have lost his right.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on marking a field as a sign for another
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on marking a field as a sign for another
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one marks a field as a sign for another, he loses his rights to it. Abaye qualifies this, saying it only applies when marking for another, but if he marks for himself, he does not lose his rights, as he can claim he did so to facilitate the sale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general rule: if one marks a field as a sign for another, he loses his rights to it.
Abaye qualifies the rule: it applies only when marking for another, but if he marks for himself, he does not lose his rights.
The Gemara explains Abaye's reasoning: the seller can claim he made the mark to facilitate the sale, and he could have given a protest (מודעא) but didn't, as he trusted intermediaries.

items.text: Case of a guardian and the claim of a single furrow
items.text_en: Case of a guardian and the claim of a single furrow
items.desc_en: A man marked a field for another, died, and appointed a guardian. The guardian came before Abaye, who initially said the man lost his rights. However, the guardian argued that the father could have claimed he only made a single furrow, and Abaye accepted this based on Rabbi Yochanan's ruling. Abaye then advises appointing a guardian who can argue for the orphans.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a man marked a field for another, died, and appointed a guardian, who then came before Abaye.
Abaye tells the guardian that the father, having marked the field for another, lost his rights.
The guardian objects that if the father were alive, he could have claimed he only made a single furrow.
Abaye accepts the argument, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that such a claim is believed, and orders giving one furrow.
The guardian adds that if the father were alive, he could claim he repurchased the field from the other party.
Abaye again accepts, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on repurchase claims, and advises appointing a guardian skilled in advocating for orphans.

items.text: Mishnah: Admon and the Sages on a lost path
items.text_en: Mishnah: Admon and the Sages on a lost path
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a person went overseas and lost the path to his field. Admon says he may take a short path, while the Sages say he must buy a path for a hundred maneh or fly through the air.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a person went overseas and lost the path to his field; Admon says he may take a short path, while the Sages say he must buy a path for a hundred maneh or fly through the air.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Admon's dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Admon's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Sages' reasoning, as Admon's position seems reasonable. Rav Yehuda explains the case involves four people surrounding the field. Rava clarifies the dispute: all agree about four from four sources, but they disagree about one from four sources. Admon holds the claimant has a path, while the Sages say the claimant must remain silent or the deeds will be returned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Sages' reasoning, as Admon's position seems reasonable.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains the case involves four people surrounding the field from four sides.
The Gemara then questions Admon's reasoning given this scenario.

Rava clarifies the dispute: all agree about four from four sources, but they disagree about one from four sources; Admon holds the claimant has a path, while the Sages say the claimant must remain silent or the deeds will be returned.

items.text: Case of a date palm promised to a daughter
items.text_en: Case of a date palm promised to a daughter
items.desc_en: A man said a date palm should go to his daughter, but the orphans divided the estate without giving her the palm. Rav Yosef thought this matched the Mishnah, but Abaye distinguished it, noting that here the palm is with the orphans. The solution is to give her the palm and then re-divide the estate.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a man promised a date palm to his daughter, but the orphans divided the estate without giving it to her.
Rav Yosef thought this case matches the Mishnah's dispute between Admon and the Sages.
Abaye distinguishes the case: here the palm is in the orphans' possession, unlike the Mishnah where each neighbor can push the claimant off.
Abaye proposes the remedy: give her the palm and then re-divide the entire estate from the beginning.

items.text: Case of two halves of a date palm
items.text_en: Case of two halves of a date palm
items.desc_en: A man left two halves of a date palm for his daughter. Rav Ashi questioned whether people call two halves a date palm. Rav Mordechai cited Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava that they do.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case where a man said 'a date palm for my daughter' and died leaving two halves of a date palm.
Rav Ashi questions whether people call two halves of a date palm a 'date palm'.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai citing Avimi in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that Avimi from Hagronya said in the name of Rava that people do call two halves of a date palm a 'date palm'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Admon vs. Sages on a debtor who sold a field
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Admon vs. Sages on a debtor who sold a field
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one party produces a debt document against another, and the latter produces a document showing he sold a field to the former. Admon argues the creditor should have collected the debt at the time of sale, while the Sages say the seller was clever to sell the land to enable future collection.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a creditor and a debtor who sold a field, with Admon arguing the creditor should have collected at sale and the Sages saying the seller was clever.

items.text: Gemara: Explaining the dispute between Admon and the Sages
items.text_en: Gemara: Explaining the dispute between Admon and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages disagree with Admon. It explains that in a place where money is given first and then the document is written, all agree with Admon. The dispute is only where the document is written first and then money is given: Admon says the creditor should have given notice, while the Sages say the creditor has friends who would inform him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the Sages' reasoning, since Admon's argument seems compelling in a place where money is given first and then the document is written.
The Gemara explains the dispute is in a place where the document is written first and money given later, with Admon requiring a protest and the Sages saying the debtor has friends to inform him.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute is only where the document is written first and then money is given: Admon says the creditor should have given notice, while the Sages say the creditor has friends who would inform him.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Two mutual debt documents
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Two mutual debt documents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where two people each produce a debt document against the other. Admon argues that if one owed the other, how could the other have lent to him? The Sages say each collects his debt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where two people each produce a debt document against the other, with Admon arguing the other would not have borrowed if he owed, and the Sages saying each collects.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet debate the ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet debate the ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet. Rav Nachman says each collects, while Rav Sheshet says it is a waste of time; each keeps his own property. The dispute is when one has intermediate-quality land and the other has poor-quality land: Rav Nachman values by the debtor's own property, Rav Sheshet by the creditor's property. The Gemara questions and refines the case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman says each collects, while Rav Sheshet says this is just exchanging pots and each retains his own property.
The Gemara notes that when both have the same quality land, everyone agrees it is just exchanging pots.
Rav Nachman holds that when one has intermediate land and the other poor land, each collects because property is appraised relative to the debtor's own holdings.
The Gemara illustrates Rav Nachman's view: the poor-land owner collects intermediate land, and the intermediate owner then takes the poor land.
Rav Sheshet holds that property is appraised relative to all people, so ultimately each gets back his own type of land.
The Gemara objects to Rav Nachman: why assume the poor-land owner collects first; let the intermediate owner collect poor land first and then collect from him.
The Gemara initially answers that the poor-land owner claimed first, but objects that ultimately they come to collect simultaneously.
The Gemara resolves: the dispute is when one has excellent and intermediate land and the other only poor land, with the two amoraim disagreeing on the appraisal principle.

items.text: Gemara: Reconciling the Mishnah with Rav Sheshet's view
items.text_en: Gemara: Reconciling the Mishnah with Rav Sheshet's view
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains the Mishnah according to Rav Sheshet: the case is where one loan is for ten years and the other for five. The Gemara analyzes the timing, concluding the dispute is when the five-year loan matures on the same day: one holds a person may borrow for the same day, the other holds not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the Mishnah's ruling that each collects, and Rav Nachman interprets it according to Rav Sheshet as a case where one loan is for ten years and the other for five.

The Gemara clarifies the case: if the first loan is for ten years and the second for five, Admon's argument fails because the second debt is not yet due; so it must be the first for five and the second for ten.
The Gemara further questions: if the five-year loan is due, why do the Sages allow collection; if not due, why does Admon object?
The Gemara resolves: the case is on the very day the five-year loan matures, with the dispute being whether a person would borrow for just one day.
The Gemara resolves: the dispute is when the five-year loan matures on the same day; one holds a person may borrow for the same day, the other holds not.

items.text: Gemara: Rami bar Chama and Rava's discussion about orphans
items.text_en: Gemara: Rami bar Chama and Rava's discussion about orphans
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama suggests the Mishnah deals with orphans, but Rava rejects this with two objections. The Gemara then proposes a case where orphans have poor land and the creditor has better land, but concludes that if the creditor has already seized property, he keeps it.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama explains the Mishnah deals with orphans: they collect but we do not collect from them, so 'this collects' means one collects and the other is entitled but cannot collect.
Rava objects with two points: the Mishnah says each collects, and the orphans could be given land and then collected from, as per Rav Nachman's principle.

The Gemara suggests an alternative: let the case be where orphans have poor land and the creditor has excellent and intermediate land, so they collect intermediate and give poor land, since orphans are only collected from poor land.
The Gemara resolves: the rule about orphans only collecting from poor land applies when the creditor has not seized property, but if he has seized, he keeps it.

items.text: Third Mishnah: Three regions for marriage
items.text_en: Third Mishnah: Three regions for marriage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for marriage, there are three regions: Judea, Transjordan, and Galilee. One may not compel a spouse to move from one region to another, but within the same region, one may compel moving from town to town or city to city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states there are three regions for marriage: Judah, Transjordan, and Galilee, and one cannot be compelled to move between regions, but within a region one can be compelled to move between cities or towns.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Moving between dwellings and cities
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Moving between dwellings and cities
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may compel a spouse to move from a bad neighborhood to a good one, but not vice versa, and from a city to a town but not from a town to a city. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that one may not even compel moving from a bad neighborhood to a good one, because a good neighborhood is 'bodek' (tests the body).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: one may compel moving from a city to a town but not from a town to a city.
The Mishnah adds the parallel rule: one may compel moving from a bad neighborhood to a good one, but not vice versa.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects that one may not even compel moving from a bad neighborhood to a good one, because a good neighborhood 'bodek' (tests the body).

items.text: Gemara: Reason for not moving from city to town
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for not moving from city to town
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that moving from a town to a city is permitted because a city has all amenities, but moving from a city to a town is prohibited. This supports Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina's teaching that living in a city is difficult, as derived from the verse about those who volunteered to dwell in Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why moving from a city to a town is prohibited, given that moving from a town to a city is permitted because a city has all amenities.

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina, who derives from a verse that living in a city (כְּרַךְ) is difficult, explaining why moving there is discouraged.

items.text: Explanation of 'bodek' and Ben Sira's saying
items.text_en: Explanation of 'bodek' and Ben Sira's saying
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'bodek' means a change of residence causes illness, as per Shmuel's statement that a change in routine is the beginning of intestinal illness. It then cites Ben Sira's saying that all days of a poor person are bad, and clarifies that even Sabbaths and festivals are included, as per Shmuel's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'bodek' means in the Mishnah and answers with Shmuel's statement that a change in routine causes intestinal illness.
The Gemara cites Ben Sira's saying that all days of a poor person are bad, raising the question of Sabbaths and festivals.

The Gemara resolves that even Sabbaths and festivals are included, applying Shmuel's principle that a change in routine is harmful, and adds Ben Sira's continuation about the poor man's exposure to rain.

items.text: Mishnah: Ascending to Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ascending to Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that everyone may be compelled to ascend to Eretz Yisrael and to Yerushalayim, but no one may be compelled to leave. It then discusses the currency for ketubah payments based on where the marriage and divorce took place, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissenting.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that everyone may be compelled to ascend to Eretz Yisrael and to Yerushalayim, and no one may be compelled to leave, applying equally to men and women.

The Mishnah details the currency for ketubah payments based on the locations of marriage and divorce, with Tanna Kamma ruling according to the place of marriage and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dissenting.

items.text: Gemara: Elaboration on the Mishnah's rulings
items.text_en: Gemara: Elaboration on the Mishnah's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'everyone may be compelled to ascend' includes slaves, and for those who already include slaves explicitly, it includes moving from a good neighborhood to a bad one. 'No one may be compelled to leave' includes a slave who fled from outside the land to the land. Similarly, ascending to Yerushalayim includes moving from a good neighborhood to a bad one, and not leaving includes even from a bad neighborhood to a good one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional case the Mishnah's phrase 'everyone may be compelled to ascend' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it comes to include slaves, who may be compelled to ascend to the Land of Israel.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase includes for the Tanna who already explicitly mentions slaves in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that it includes moving from a good neighborhood to a bad one.
The Gemara asks what additional case the Mishnah's phrase 'no one may be compelled to leave' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes a slave who fled from outside the Land to the Land, whom we tell to sell himself here and go, due to the value of dwelling in the Land of Israel.
The Gemara asks what additional case the Mishnah's phrase 'everyone may be compelled to ascend to Jerusalem' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes moving from a good neighborhood to a bad one.
The Gemara asks what additional case the Mishnah's phrase 'no one may be compelled to leave Jerusalem' comes to include.

The Gemara answers that it includes even moving from a bad neighborhood to a good one, and notes that since the first clause taught 'no one may be compelled to leave', the latter clause also teaches 'no one may be compelled to leave'.

items.text: Baraita: Coercion regarding aliyah and leaving
items.text_en: Baraita: Coercion regarding aliyah and leaving
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a husband wants to ascend to Eretz Yisrael and the wife refuses, she is compelled to go or loses her ketubah. If she wants to ascend and he refuses, he is compelled to go or divorce and pay the ketubah. Similarly, if one wants to leave Eretz Yisrael, the other can prevent it, with corresponding penalties.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if a husband wants to ascend to Eretz Yisrael and the wife refuses, she is forced to go or loses her ketubah; if she wants to ascend and he refuses, he is forced to go or must divorce and pay the ketubah.

The baraita adds parallel rulings for leaving Eretz Yisrael: if the wife wants to leave and the husband refuses, she is forced to stay or loses her ketubah; if the husband wants to leave and she refuses, he is forced to stay or must divorce and pay the ketubah.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding currency
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah regarding currency
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction: the first case follows the place of the lien (marriage), while the second follows the place of collection (divorce). Rabba resolves this by saying the Mishnah deals with leniencies of ketubah, as he holds ketubah is rabbinic. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds ketubah is biblical, hence his ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the mishna's rulings on currency are internally contradictory.
The Gemara elaborates the contradiction: the first case follows the place of the lien, but the second follows the place of collection.
Rabba resolves the contradiction by stating that the mishna teaches leniencies of ketubah, as he holds ketubah is rabbinic.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that ketubah is biblical, hence his ruling to pay in Cappadocian currency.

items.text: Baraita: Currency in promissory notes vs. ketubah
items.text_en: Baraita: Currency in promissory notes vs. ketubah
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses how to collect a debt based on the currency specified in the document. If it says 'Bavel', collect Babylonian currency; if 'Eretz Yisrael', collect that currency; if unspecified, collect local currency. For a ketubah, the rule differs. Rav Mesharshiya explains this applies to the first clause, excluding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view. The Gemara then clarifies that if 'kesef stam' is written, the lender may collect whatever he wants, but not small coins.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a promissory note specifying 'Bavel' or 'Eretz Yisrael' is collected in that currency; if unspecified, the place of collection determines the currency; if 'kesef stam' is written, the borrower may choose what to pay, unlike a ketubah.
The Gemara asks to which clause of the baraita the phrase 'unlike a ketubah' refers.
Rav Mesharshiya explains that the distinction applies to the first clause, excluding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that a ketubah is דאורייתא (Torah law).
The Gemara asks why the borrower cannot pay with ingots (נסכא) when 'kesef stam' is written.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the document specifies 'מטבע' (coin), excluding ingots.
The Gemara asks why the borrower cannot pay with small coins (פריטי).
Rav Pappa answers that people do not designate small coins (פריטי) as 'כספא' (silver currency).

items.text: Baraita: The importance of dwelling in Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Baraita: The importance of dwelling in Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one should always dwell in Eretz Yisrael even in a city with a majority of gentiles, rather than outside the land even in a city with a majority of Jews. Dwelling outside the land is compared to idolatry, as derived from verses. The Gemara relates that Rabbi Zeira would avoid Rav Yehuda because he wanted to ascend to Eretz Yisrael, as Rav Yehuda held that ascending from Bavel violates a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one should always dwell in Eretz Yisrael even in a gentile-majority city, rather than outside the land even in a Jewish-majority city, citing a verse to support that dwelling outside is like having no God.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's implication is absurd—that one outside the land has no God—and resolves that it means dwelling outside is like worshipping idolatry, citing David's lament.
The Gemara relates that Rabbi Zeira would avoid Rav Yehuda because he wanted to ascend to Eretz Yisrael, as Rav Yehuda held that ascending from Bavel violates a positive commandment.

items.text: Interpretation of the three oaths
items.text_en: Interpretation of the three oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the meaning of verses that mention oaths, with Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Zeira offering different interpretations. Rabbi Zeira explains that one verse refers to the prohibition against Israel ascending as a wall, while another is used for Rabbi Yossi's teaching about three oaths. Rav Yehuda counters with another verse.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of the oath
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's explanation of the oath
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that God told Israel that if they keep the oath, it is good, but if not, He will permit their flesh like gazelles and hinds of the field.

items.text: Dwelling in the Land of Israel removes sin
items.text_en: Dwelling in the Land of Israel removes sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that anyone who dwells in the Land of Israel is free from sin, citing a verse. Rava tells Rav Ashi that they interpret this as referring to those who bear illnesses.

items.text: Burial in the Land of Israel is like under the altar
items.text_en: Burial in the Land of Israel is like under the altar
items.desc_en: Rav Anan says that anyone buried in the Land of Israel is as if buried under the altar, based on a scriptural analogy.

items.text: Ulla's death outside the Land
items.text_en: Ulla's death outside the Land
items.desc_en: Ulla, who regularly ascended to the Land of Israel, died outside the Land. Rabbi Elazar initially says he will die on impure land, but when told his coffin arrived, he says that being absorbed after death is not like being absorbed while alive.

items.text: Prohibition to leave the Land for levirate marriage
items.text_en: Prohibition to leave the Land for levirate marriage
items.desc_en: A man asks Rabbi Chanina if he may go down to Be Hoza’a to perform levirate marriage. Rabbi Chanina rebukes him, saying his brother married a Cuthean woman and died, and he should not go down after him.

items.text: Prohibition to leave Babylonia for other lands
items.text_en: Prohibition to leave Babylonia for other lands
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that just as it is forbidden to leave the Land of Israel for Babylonia, so too it is forbidden to leave Babylonia for other lands. Rabba and Rav Yosef add that even from Pumbedita to Bei Kubei is forbidden, and Rav Yosef excommunicated someone who did so.

items.text: The Land of Israel absorbs the worthy
items.text_en: The Land of Israel absorbs the worthy
items.desc_en: Rabba and Rav Yosef say that the worthy of Babylonia are absorbed by the Land of Israel, and the worthy of other lands are absorbed by Babylonia. The Gemara clarifies this refers to burial, not lineage.

items.text: Dwelling in Babylonia is like dwelling in the Land
items.text_en: Dwelling in Babylonia is like dwelling in the Land
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says that anyone who dwells in Babylonia is as if he dwells in the Land of Israel, citing a verse. Abaye says they have a tradition that Babylonia will not see the birth pangs of the Messiah, referring to a specific place called Karna de-Shizavta.

items.text: Resurrection of the dead outside the Land
items.text_en: Resurrection of the dead outside the Land
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that the dead outside the Land will not live, based on a verse. Rabbi Abba bar Memel challenges this with another verse, and Rabbi Elazar responds that the verse refers to Nebuchadnezzar. Rabbi Abba bar Memel then interprets a different verse to include even a Canaanite maidservant in the Land as having a share in the World to Come, and Rabbi Yochanan says that walking four cubits in the Land guarantees a share in the World to Come.

items.text: Righteous outside the Land live through rolling
items.text_en: Righteous outside the Land live through rolling
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if righteous people outside the Land do not live. Rabbi Ila says they live through rolling (gilgul). Rabbi Abba Sala Rabba objects that rolling is a pain for the righteous. Abaye says that cavities are made for them in the ground.

items.text: Jacob and Joseph's concern for burial
items.text_en: Jacob and Joseph's concern for burial
items.desc_en: Karna says that Jacob knew he was a complete righteous person, yet he troubled his sons to bury him in the Land of Israel, implying that the dead outside the Land do not live, or that he feared he would not merit cavities. Similarly, Rabbi Chanina says that Joseph knew he was righteous, yet he troubled his brothers to carry his bones 400 parasangs.

items.text: Story of one who wanted to leave the Land
items.text_en: Story of one who wanted to leave the Land
items.desc_en: The brothers of Rabba sent him a message about Jacob. Ilfa adds that there was a story of a man who was distressed over a woman and wanted to go down (leave the Land), but when he heard this, he rolled himself until his death.

items.text: Advice for one who does not ascend
items.text_en: Advice for one who does not ascend
items.desc_en: The Gemara advises that even if one is a great scholar, learning from oneself is not like learning from a teacher, and if one has no teacher, Rabbi Yochanan is the teacher. If one does not ascend, he should be careful about three things: sitting, standing, and walking, and their proportions. The Gemara discusses the difficulty of standing and sitting.

items.text: Opening statement and support for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on mules
items.text_en: Opening statement and support for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on mules
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a statement about standing being preferable to sitting where there is no leaning, then notes that three sages—Rabbi Yitzchak, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Oshaya—agree that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding mules. Rabbi Yehuda rules that a female mule in heat may only be bred with its own kind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general statement: standing with support is preferable to standing without support.

The Gemara reports that three sages—Yitzḥak, Shimon, and Oshaya—agree that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding mules, citing Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a female mule in heat may only be bred with its own kind.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak identifies the three sages mentioned: Yitzḥak is Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa, Shimon is Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi (or Reish Lakish), and Oshaya is Rabbi Oshaya the Distinguished.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan debate the fate of ignoramuses
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan debate the fate of ignoramuses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that ignoramuses (עַמֵּי הָאֲרָצוֹת) will not live in the resurrection, citing a verse. Rabbi Yochanan objects, arguing that the verse refers to those who neglect Torah for idolatry. Rabbi Elazar then cites another verse to support his position that those who do not engage in Torah study will not be revived.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that ignoramuses (עַמֵּי הָאֲרָצוֹת) will not live in the resurrection, citing a verse and a baraita that interprets the verse as referring to one who weakens himself from Torah.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that God is not pleased with this statement, arguing that the verse refers to one who weakens himself for idol worship, not ignoramuses.
Rabbi Elazar responds by citing a different verse, explaining that anyone who uses the light of Torah is revived by it, and anyone who does not use it is not revived.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's consolation: a remedy for ignoramuses through supporting Torah scholars
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's consolation: a remedy for ignoramuses through supporting Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Seeing Rabbi Elazar distressed, Rabbi Yochanan offers a remedy from the Torah: those who marry their daughter to a Torah scholar, engage in business with Torah scholars, or benefit them from their property are considered as if they cleave to the Divine Presence. This is derived from the verse 'וְאַתֶּם הַדְּבֵקִים בַּה׳' and is repeated with a similar derivation from another verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, seeing Rabbi Elazar distressed, offers a remedy from the Torah: the verse 'וְאַתֶּם הַדְּבֵקִים בַּה׳' (Deuteronomy 4:4) promises life, but questions how one can cleave to the Divine Presence, given the verse describing God as a devouring fire.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse refers to those who marry their daughter to a Torah scholar, conduct business for Torah scholars, or benefit them from their property, as if they cleave to the Divine Presence.
The Gemara provides a parallel derivation from the verse 'לְאַהֲבָה אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ וּלְדׇבְקָה בוֹ' (Deuteronomy 30:20), repeating the same three categories of support for Torah scholars.

items.text: Three statements of Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef about the future
items.text_en: Three statements of Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef about the future
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef makes three predictions: the righteous will sprout and rise in Jerusalem, they will rise in their garments (learned from wheat), and the Land of Israel will produce fine bread and wool garments.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef predicts that the righteous will burst forth and rise in Jerusalem, citing the verse 'וְיָצִיצוּ מֵעִיר כְּעֵשֶׂב הָאָרֶץ' (and they will blossom out of the city like the grass of the earth) and identifying 'city' as Jerusalem.

Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef predicts that the righteous will rise in their garments, derived by a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) from wheat: just as wheat, buried naked, emerges with many layers, so the righteous, buried clothed, will certainly rise clothed.

Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef predicts that the Land of Israel will produce cakes (גלוסקאות) and fine wool garments (כלי מילת), citing the verse 'יְהִי פִסַּת בַּר בָּאָרֶץ' (let abundant grain be in the land).

items.text: The future abundance of wheat and wine
items.text_en: The future abundance of wheat and wine
items.desc_en: The Sages expound on the future fertility of the Land of Israel: wheat will grow as tall as a palm tree, and God will provide a wind to mill it. A single grape cluster will yield large quantities of wine, and the wood will be used for fuel. A story about a large mustard plant and a cabbage stalk illustrates the potential size of produce.

sub.desc_en: The Sages expound that in the future, wheat will grow as tall as a palm tree on mountaintops, and God will provide a wind to mill it, so one can bring a handful of flour to sustain his household.
The Sages add that wheat will be as large as the kidneys of a large ox, and support this with a story of a fox that nested in a turnip weighing sixty litra.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon ben Tachlifa relate stories about a giant mustard plant and a cabbage stalk, demonstrating the enormous size of produce in the Land of Israel.

The Sages conclude that in the future, a single grape cluster will yield thirty garbs of wine, and the wood will be used for fuel, based on the verse 'ודם ענב תשתה חמר' (and you shall drink the blood of the grape as wine).

items.text: Exposition on the vine and the allegory of Israel and God
items.text_en: Exposition on the vine and the allegory of Israel and God
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi explains verses about the future abundance of grapes and wine in the Land of Israel, addressing potential doubts. He then interprets a verse as an allegory where the congregation of Israel asks God for a smile and a showing of teeth, which is sweeter than wine and milk. Rabbi Yochanan derives from this that whitening teeth for a friend is better than giving them milk.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi interprets verses about the future abundance of grapes and wine in the Land of Israel, addressing potential doubts about quantity, color, and quality.
The Gemara asks about the plain meaning of the verse, shifting from the literal abundance to an allegorical interpretation.
Rav Dimi explains that the verse is an allegory where the congregation of Israel asks God for a smile and a showing of teeth, sweeter than wine and milk.
Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse that whitening teeth for a friend is better than giving them milk, supporting the allegorical reading.

items.text: Stories of abundance in the Land of Israel
items.text_en: Stories of abundance in the Land of Israel
items.desc_en: A series of anecdotes illustrate the extraordinary fertility of the Land of Israel: Rabbi Chiya bar Adda's experience with a vine, the goats of Bnei Brak producing a mixture of milk and honey, and various sages testifying to the abundance of honey and milk in different regions.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces Rabbi Chiya bar Adda, a teacher of children for Reish Lakish, who was absent for three days, prompting Reish Lakish to ask why.

Rabbi Chiya bar Adda explains his absence by describing a vine inherited from his father that produced an extraordinary yield of clusters, and Reish Lakish responds that had he not been delayed, it would have produced even more.

Rami bar Yechezkel testifies that in Bnei Brak he saw goats eating figs under fig trees, with honey dripping from the figs and milk flowing from the goats, mixing together, fulfilling the verse 'a land flowing with milk and honey'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai, Reish Lakish, Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai, Reish Lakish, Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov ben Dostai, Reish Lakish, and Rabbah bar bar Chanah each testify to the abundance of honey and milk in different regions of the Land of Israel.

items.text: Opening description of the land's size
items.text_en: Opening description of the land's size
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the dimensions of a certain region in the Land of Israel, measuring twenty-two parasangs by six parasangs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the dimensions of a region in the Land of Israel, measuring twenty-two parasangs by six parasangs.

items.text: Anecdotes of Sages encountering the land's produce
items.text_en: Anecdotes of Sages encountering the land's produce
items.desc_en: Several Sages visit different locations in the Land of Israel and are astonished by the size of its fruits and vegetables, using hyperbolic comparisons to express the land's extraordinary fertility.

sub.desc_en: Three sages visit a place and are brought a peach the size of a large basket from Kfar Hino, eating a third, declaring a third ownerless, and giving a third to their animal.
The following year Rabbi Elazar visits the same place, is handed a similar fruit, and quotes a verse about the land's fruitfulness despite its wicked inhabitants.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi visits Gavla, sees cauliflowers as large as calves, mistakes them for calves, and laments that the land's produce is given to gentiles due to Israel's sins.
The following year Rabbi Chiyya visits the same place, sees cauliflowers as large as goats, mistakes them for goats, and the locals tell him not to repeat his colleague's mistake.

items.text: Comparative fertility of lands and the superiority of the Land of Israel
items.text_en: Comparative fertility of lands and the superiority of the Land of Israel
items.desc_en: A baraita compares the yield of the Land of Israel to that of Egypt, specifically Zoan, and explains that even the rocky parts of Hebron are superior to Zoan's fertile land. The Gemara further clarifies that these comparisons apply only to rocky or non-blessed areas, but in its blessed state the land is incomparable.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by comparing the yield of the Land of Israel in its blessed state (בִּרְכוֹתֶיהָ) to that of Zoan in Egypt, citing Rabbi Meir's testimony about Beit She'an.
The Gemara explains that Egypt is the most fertile land, Zoan is the best part of Egypt, and Hebron is the rockiest part of the Land of Israel.

The Gemara questions the verse that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan, noting the chronological impossibility since Canaan (father of Hebron's builders) was younger than Egypt (father of Zoan's builders).
The Gemara resolves that 'built' means Hebron was seven times more fertile than Zoan, and clarifies that this applies only to rocky areas, while non-rocky areas yield 500 times more.
The Gemara concludes that all these comparisons apply only to non-blessed areas, but in its blessed state the Land of Israel is incomparable, as shown by Isaac's hundredfold yield.

items.text: Anecdotes of the land's productivity and a dispute with a Sadducee and a Samaritan
items.text_en: Anecdotes of the land's productivity and a dispute with a Sadducee and a Samaritan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei describes the yield of a se'ah in Judah, and a Sadducee boasts to Rabbi Chanina about his father's land. Then a Samaritan questions a Jew about the yield of a tree near the Jordan, leading to a dispute about the land's actual productivity.

sub.desc_en: A baraita reports Rabbi Yosei's description of a se'ah in Judah producing five se'ahs of various grain products.
A Sadducee boasts to Rabbi Chanina that his father's single se'ah produced oil, wine, grain, legumes, and pasture, challenging the praise of the land.

sub.text: Samaritan to a Jew from the Land of Israel
sub.text_en: Samaritan to a Jew from the Land of Israel
sub.desc_en: A Samaritan asks a Jew from the Land of Israel how much produce they harvested from a tree near the Jordan.

sub.text: Jew from the Land of Israel
sub.text_en: Jew from the Land of Israel
sub.desc_en: The Jew answers that they harvested sixty kor from the tree.
The Samaritan objects that the Jew's figure is low, claiming they themselves harvested 120 kor from the same tree.

sub.text: Jew from the Land of Israel
sub.text_en: Jew from the Land of Israel
sub.desc_en: The Jew resolves the dispute by clarifying that he was referring to only one side of the tree's yield.

items.text: The Land of Israel compared to a deer
items.text_en: The Land of Israel compared to a deer
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains why the Land of Israel is compared to a deer: just as a deer's skin cannot contain its flesh, so the land cannot contain its produce; and just as a deer is swift, so the land ripens its fruit quickly. A potential objection that the land's fruit might not be fat is refuted by the verse 'flowing with milk and honey'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks why the Land of Israel is compared to a deer and gives two explanations: its skin cannot hold its flesh, and it is swift to ripen fruit.
The gemara raises a potential objection: if the deer is swift but lean, perhaps the land's fruit is also not fat.
The gemara refutes the objection by citing the verse 'flowing with milk and honey,' showing the fruit is indeed fat and sweet.

items.text: Sages' love and longing for the Land of Israel
items.text_en: Sages' love and longing for the Land of Israel
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Asi each expressed their deep love for the Land of Israel through actions and words, demonstrating that even the most minor aspects of the land are precious to them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar, upon ascending to the Land of Israel, requests to be released from one, then two, then three obligations as he progresses in status.
The Gemara cites a verse and interprets it to refer to the secret of intercalation, ordination, and entry into the Land of Israel.

Rabbi Zeira crosses the Jordan River by holding a rope, and a Sadducee rebukes him for the hasty nature of the Jewish people, to which he responds that the place of Moses and Aaron is not guaranteed to him.

sub.text: Narrative about Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Narrative about Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba kisses the rocks of Akko, Rabbi Chanina repairs the roads, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi are mentioned as expressing love for the Land of Israel.

items.text: Love for the dust of the land of Israel
items.text_en: Love for the dust of the land of Israel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Gamda would roll in the dust of the land of Israel, citing the verse that God will favor its stones and dust.

sub.text: Narrative description of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Gamda's practice
sub.text_en: Narrative description of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Gamda's practice
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Gamda would roll in the dust of the land of Israel, citing the verse that God will favor its stones and dust.

items.text: The generation of the Messiah and persecution of Torah scholars
items.text_en: The generation of the Messiah and persecution of Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba that in the generation when the son of David comes, there will be accusations against Torah scholars. Shmuel adds that there will be one affliction after another, citing a verse. Rav Yosef teaches that there will be 'bazozei' and 'bazozei de-bazozei' (a series of afflictions).

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba that in the generation when the son of David comes, there will be accusations (קָטֵיגוֹרְיָא) against Torah scholars.

When Rabbi Zeira stated this before Shmuel, Shmuel added that there will be affliction after affliction (צֵירוּף אַחַר צֵירוּף), citing the verse 'וְעוֹד בָּהּ עֲשִׂירִיָּה וְשָׁבָה וְהָיְתָה לְבָעֵר' (and if there be yet a tenth, and it shall again be for burning).
Rav Yosef taught that there will be 'bazozei' (afflictions) and 'bazozei de-bazozei' (afflictions of afflictions), intensifying the description of suffering.

items.text: Fruit-bearing trees in the land of Israel
items.text_en: Fruit-bearing trees in the land of Israel
items.desc_en: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav that all barren trees in the land of Israel will eventually bear fruit, citing a verse from the prophet.

sub.text: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav that all barren trees in the land of Israel will eventually bear fruit, citing the verse 'כי עץ נשא פריו תאנה וגפן נתנו חילם' (for the tree bears its fruit, the fig and vine give their strength).
